# Design Review Recommendations: ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Executive Summary

The core challenge is replacing the P0D with a detector that reconstructs kinematically complete CC events (μ + leading proton) in a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, while reducing systematics from ~6% to ~4%. The 0.6 m depth along the beam axis is severely constraining. The large forward angular acceptance requirement (catching 25% of muons and 35% of protons beyond 50°) and the low proton momenta (median 450 MeV/c) drive nearly every technology choice.

---

## 1. Active Target: Plastic Scintillator SuperFGD Cube Geometry

**Recommendation:** Deploy a **SuperFGD-style 3D-granular scintillator cube detector** filling the available volume, using ~1 cm³ polystyrene cubes read out on three orthogonal faces by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and MPPCs.

**Justification:**

- The 0.6 m depth (along z) rules out conventional tracker+absorber configurations. A fully-active segmented target solves this by making the target itself the tracker.
- 1 cm³ cubes provide ~1 cm³ vertex resolution, sufficient for fiducial volume definition and secondary interaction rejection.
- Three-view readout (X, Y, Z fibres through each cube) gives genuine 3D hit reconstruction, eliminating the ghost-hit ambiguity of 2D projective designs — critical at the interaction densities relevant here.
- **Critically for protons:** A 450 MeV/c proton has a range of ~9 cm in polystyrene (~1.05 g/cm³). The 0.6 m depth provides ~63 cm, comfortably containing the median proton and protons up to ~900 MeV/c (~50 cm range). The 6% tail above 900 MeV/c exits into the downstream TPCs, which is acceptable.
- The 25–35% large-angle track fraction is well served by the isotropic 3D sensitivity; there is no preferred projection axis.
- Particle identification via dE/dx cube-counting (Bragg peak) distinguishes protons from pions without magnetic field within the target itself.
- Hydrocarbon target (polystyrene, CH) is explicitly stated as acceptable.
- This technology is already being developed by the T2K collaboration (the SuperFGD for the ND280 upgrade), so technical readiness is high and institutional knowledge exists.
- Estimated fiducial mass ~0.9–1.0 t in the available volume provides adequate statistics.

**Specific hardware:** ~2 million 1×1×1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibre arrays (Y-11 or equivalent), Hamamatsu S13360-series MPPCs (50 µm pixel pitch to handle high channel multiplicity with acceptable dark-current noise at modest cost).

---

## 2. Time-of-Flight Walls: Thin Scintillator Planes at Upstream and Lateral Faces

**Recommendation:** Instrument all six faces of the SuperFGD volume with **2–3 cm thick fast plastic scintillator panels** read out by SiPMs, targeting ~200 ps timing resolution per plane.

**Justification:**

- ToF between the upstream face and downstream face (or lateral faces) over ~60 cm gives a velocity measurement. At 450 MeV/c, a proton (β ≈ 0.43) and a pion (β ≈ 0.95) traversing 30 cm produce a ~700 ps ToF difference — well resolved at 200 ps resolution.
- This provides **independent PID** for tracks that are too short for reliable Bragg peak analysis (marginal-range protons near the target edges, or for forward-going tracks exiting into the TPC before stopping).
- The upstream ToF plane also tags beam-coincident events vs. rock muon backgrounds.
- Large-angle tracks reaching the lateral faces are timed, extending PID to the full 4π acceptance.
- Low-mass panels (~2 cm EJ-200 equivalent, ~2.3 g/cm²) introduce minimal secondary scattering at the faces.
- SiPM readout (e.g., 6×6 mm² tiles, Hamamatsu or KETEK) is compact, operates in the 0.2 T field without degradation, and matches the MPPC infrastructure already in ND280.

---

## 3. Downstream Interface: Thin High-Pressure Gas TPC or Low-Threshold TPC Match

**Recommendation:** Ensure the first downstream TPC (TPC1, already existing) is **re-configured with a lower drift field or a dedicated thin upstream module** to reduce the momentum threshold for contained-track matching, and formally include it in the kinematic reconstruction chain for the new target.

**Justification:**

- The 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c exit the SuperFGD. TPC1, with its Micromegas readout and 95:3:2 Ar:CF4:iC4H10 gas, provides momentum measurement by curvature in the 0.2 T field for these tracks.
- A 900 MeV/c proton in the TPC gas has a long enough track (~several cm at relevant pressure) that curvature is measurable. The critical issue is matching SuperFGD edge hits to TPC entry points.
- **No change to the TPC gas is recommended** (the existing mixture is well-optimised), but the **offline matching algorithm and the mechanical interface** between the new upstream target and TPC1 should be formally redesigned. Specifically, remove any dead-material frames from the P0D–TPC interface region.
- This avoids introducing new systematic uncertainties from an unfamiliar gas system while recovering the high-momentum proton fraction.

---

## 4. Lateral Muon Catcher: Thin Scintillator-Iron Sandwich in the Magnet Gap Spaces

**Recommendation:** Install **4–6 layers of 2 cm iron + 1 cm scintillator** in the lateral gaps between the new upstream target and the barrel ECal, as a dedicated muon range stack for large-angle muons that miss the downstream TPCs.

**Justification:**

- 25% of muons exit beyond 50°. Many of these will not enter TPC1. The existing barrel ECal was designed for photon/electron containment and has ~10–15 radiation lengths of Pb-scintillator but limited muon ranging capability (the Pb is too dense per layer for precise range-momentum).
- Iron (at 1.76 cm/MeV range parameter vs. ~1.47 for Pb) gives better ranging precision for sub-GeV muons. A 6-layer sandwich at ~6 kg/m² adds ~1.2 t but provides range measurement to ~±30 MeV/c for muons stopping within it.
- Scintillator readout by WLS + SiPM (consistent with rest of detector) means no new electronics families.
- This is mechanically feasible in the yoke gap spaces also used by the SMRD, using similar thin-slab geometry.
- Without this, the large-angle muon sample is either discarded (losing statistics and introducing angular-acceptance systematics) or handed to the ECal with poorly-known muon energy scale — both unacceptable for the 4% systematic target.

---

## 5. Readout Electronics: Dedicated High-Rate ASIC with ~10 ns Timing

**Recommendation:** Deploy a **dedicated CITIROC-2A or TARGET-C based front-end ASIC** for the SuperFGD MPPC channels, providing per-channel timing to <10 ns and 12-bit charge integration.

**Justification:**

- A ~2 million channel detector (3 fibres per cube × ~700,000 cubes in 2×1.9×0.6 m) is unrealistic; realistic channel count with 1 cm cubes and shared-fibre readout is ~150,000–200,000 channels. This still far exceeds the existing ND280 TFB/AFTER-based system, which was designed for the sparser FGD/TPC topology.
- 10 ns timing per channel is required to associate hits to the correct beam bunch (8 ns bunch spacing in J-PARC), preventing pile-up from adjacent spills corrupting the kinematic reconstruction.
- CITIROC-2A integrates 32 channels with individual trigger outputs, 12-bit QDC, and TDC on-chip, operates at 3.3 V, and is field-proven in scintillator-SiPM applications. It is compatible with the existing MPPC operating voltage range (~60–70 V).
- Alternatively, the WAGASCI/Baby-MIND readout (already in T2K's near detector complex) uses a similar architecture and would minimise new firmware development.
- Online zero-suppression with programmable thresholds is essential to keep data volume manageable given the high channel count.

---

## 6. Calibration: Dedicated UV LED Pulser System per Face

**Recommendation:** Embed a **fibre-coupled UV LED calibration network** (one LED per 100 channels) flashing between beam spills to track MPPC gain drift.

**Justification:**

- SiPM/MPPC gain drifts ~0.5%/°C. The magnet hall temperature varies seasonally. A 1% gain drift propagates to ~1% dE/dx uncertainty, which at the cube-counting level affects proton PID efficiency.
- LED pulsers between spills (the J-PARC spill period is ~2.5 s) add zero dead time.
- This is standard practice in ND280's existing ECal and FGD systems — no new technology, minimal cost, but essential to hold systematics below 4%.

---

## Summary Table

| Change | Technology | Primary Benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | SuperFGD 1 cm³ cubes + WLS + MPPC | 3D vertexing, proton ranging, 4π acceptance |
| Face ToF | Fast scintillator panels + SiPM | PID for marginal tracks, background rejection |
| TPC1 interface | Mechanical dead-material removal | High-p proton recovery |
| Lateral muon catcher | Fe-scintillator sandwich | Large-angle muon momentum measurement |
| Front-end electronics | CITIROC-2A ASICs | High-channel-count timing, pile-up rejection |
| Calibration | UV LED pulser network | MPPC gain stability, dE/dx systematics |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD 3D-granular 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cube active target read out on three orthogonal faces by WLS fibres and MPPCs, providing simultaneous proton ranging, 3D vertex reconstruction, and near-isotropic angular acceptance in the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume.

Based on the detector description and physics requirements, here are the hardware upgrades the proposal should include:

## 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (SuperFGD-style)**
**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene cubes (~1 cm³) with three perpendicular wavelength-shifting fiber readouts per cube, read out by SiPMs.

**Why:** The 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope requires truly 3D tracking to capture the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons exiting at >50° to beam. The current targets only alternate x/y planes perpendicular to beam, creating blind spots for large-angle tracks. Three-fiber readout per cube provides complete 3D hit reconstruction and angular coverage.

## 2. **Time-of-Flight System**
**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator planes with ~100 ps timing resolution (using fast SiPMs and dedicated timing electronics) at upstream and downstream faces of the new target.

**Why:** Critical for proton identification and momentum measurement, especially for the ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that may punch through. TOF distinguishes protons from pions in the 300-800 MeV/c range where range-based PID becomes ambiguous.

## 3. **Enhanced Readout Electronics**
**Technology:** Multi-channel SiPM readout ASICs with improved dynamic range, faster digitization (>60 MHz), and precision timing (<1 ns).

**Why:** The fine segmentation (~10,000-15,000 channels for 0.6 m³ of 1 cm³ cubes) requires dense, low-power electronics. Timing information enables 4D tracking for background rejection and pile-up separation at higher beam intensities.

## 4. **Thin Entrance Window on Magnet Bore**
**Technology:** Lightweight composite or thin aluminum window (~1-2 mm equivalent radiation lengths) replacing existing upstream face.

**Why:** Minimizes multiple scattering before the new target to preserve angular resolution for transverse kinematic imbalance studies. Current photon-tagger mass (16.1 t) suggests substantial material that degrades low-momentum particle reconstruction.

## 5. **Upgraded DAQ System**
**Technology:** Modern FPGA-based readout with increased bandwidth (>10 GB/s aggregate) and larger buffer memory.

**Why:** The new target's channel count is ~3× the existing first target (5,760 bars), and 3-fiber readout triples this again. Kinematically complete event selection requires full readout of magnet volume and calorimeters, demanding higher throughput.

## 6. **Intermediate Timing/PID Layer**
**Technology:** Thin (1-2 cm) plastic scintillator plane at downstream face of new target, with timing resolution ~200-300 ps.

**Why:** Provides additional timing anchor for tracks entering the TPCs and acts as trigger reference. Helps separate forward-going protons from charged pions when combined with range and dE/dx in TPCs.

## 7. **Calibration and Monitoring System**
**Technology:** LED pulser system with light distribution network; cosmic ray trigger upgrade; laser alignment system.

**Why:** To achieve 4% systematic uncertainty (from current 6%), detector response must be calibrated to ~2% level. Dense 3D geometry requires position-dependent calibration. Automated monitoring catches SiPM degradation and ensures long-term stability.

## 8. **Neutron Tagging Enhancement**
**Technology:** Add boron-loaded or lithium-loaded scintillator panels in gaps around the new target volume.

**Why:** For complete event reconstruction, detecting final-state neutrons (via capture γs or recoil protons) helps close kinematic imbalance measurements and identifies multi-nucleon correlations that affect cross-section modeling.

# Design Review Recommendations for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

The key constraints are:
- **Geometric**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m active volume in 0.15 T field
- **Physics**: ~0.7 GeV neutrino beam requiring:
  - ≥25% muon efficiency at all angles (including backward)
  - Proton tracking down to 60 MeV KE (~11 mm range in hydrocarbon)
  - ≤20% hydrogen content by nucleon count

## Recommended Hardware Implementation

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker with Wavelength-Shifting Fiber Readout**

**Technology**: Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (1.0 × 1.0 cm² cross-section) in three orthogonal orientations (XUV configuration with 0°, +60°, -60° or simpler XYZ), arranged in repeating modules.

**Justification**:
- Polystyrene (CH) has 7.7% hydrogen by nucleon count - well below 20% threshold
- 1 cm granularity provides ~3-5 mm position resolution, adequate for 60 MeV protons (11 mm range)
- 4π angular acceptance inherent to 3D design captures backward and perpendicular tracks
- ~100 planes over 90 cm gives excellent tracking redundancy
- Scintillator light yield enables low threshold for minimum ionizing particles
- Similar to proven ND280 (T2K) and MINERvA technologies

### 2. **Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) Readout**

**Technology**: Arrays of ~6×6 mm² SiPMs coupled to wavelength-shifting fibers embedded in each scintillator bar.

**Justification**:
- Immune to 0.15 T magnetic field (unlike PMTs)
- High photon detection efficiency (>40%)
- Compact: allows dense packing
- Timing resolution ~1 ns enables event separation
- Commercial availability and declining costs

### 3. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Modules for Enhanced dE/dx**

**Alternative/Complementary Technology**: Insert 3-5 small TPC modules (40 cm × 40 cm × 20 cm each) at strategic positions within scintillator array.

**Justification**:
- Continuous 3D tracking without dead material between planes
- Superior dE/dx resolution (5-7%) for particle ID
- Excellent for short proton tracks with Bragg peak measurement
- Gas choice (Ar:CH₄ 95:5) keeps hydrogen content low
- Proven in magnetic fields (e.g., ND-GAr, ALICE)
- Covers ~10-15% of volume, maintaining scintillator's 4π acceptance elsewhere

### 4. **Front-End Electronics with Multi-Hit TDCs**

**Technology**: ASIC-based readout with time-over-threshold and multi-hit capability (e.g., CITIROC or similar).

**Justification**:
- Required for pile-up in accelerator environment
- ToT provides crude calorimetry for stopping particles
- Low power essential for ~50,000 channel system
- Multi-hit resolves delta rays and complex topologies

### 5. **Upstream Veto/Tagger Planes**

**Technology**: Two thin (1 cm) plastic scintillator planes with SiPM readout, positioned 10-20 cm upstream of active target.

**Justification**:
- Tags entering particles vs. neutrino-induced tracks
- Critical for backward-going muon identification
- Low mass minimizes interactions before target
- Timing confirms in-time vs. cosmic background

## Configuration Summary

**Layer structure** (repeating): 
- XYZ triplet of 1×1 cm² scintillator bars (3 cm thick module)
- 30 such modules spanning 90 cm
- TPC modules at depths of 20, 40, 60 cm
- Total channels: ~45,000 scintillator + ~20,000 TPC

**Mass composition**: 
- Scintillator (~2.5 tons CH, ρ~1.05 g/cm³)
- TPC gas (~0.1 tons)
- Total nucleons: ~1.5×10³⁰, with ~1.2×10²⁹ hydrogen (8% - safe margin below 20%)

## Alternative Considered and Rejected

**Liquid Argon TPC**: While excellent for calorimetry and tracking, rejected because:
- Zero hydrogen content removes crucial physics signal
- Slower drift limits rate capability
- Cryogenics challenging in warm magnet bore
- Less mature at this scale with magnetic field

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Implement 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker with 1 cm³ voxel size and SiPM readout as the primary active target technology.

# Recommended Hardware Changes for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## 1. What the requirements rule out

**Hydrogen fraction.** The hydrogen limit is the decisive constraint.

- Polystyrene scintillator (CH) has 1 hydrogen nucleon out of 13, about 7.7%. That is far above the 2% limit.
- Water is about 11% hydrogen nucleons.

So the standard choices of a fine-grained scintillator cube target (SuperFGD-style), scintillator bars, or a water target are all excluded. However well they track, the hydrogen subtraction model would no longer hold.

**Matching the far detector.** A far detector with no hydrogen is almost certainly argon-based. The cleanest way to cancel nuclear effects is to put argon in the near detector target too.

**Proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 g/cm².

- In liquid argon that is about 2.5 cm, or roughly 6–8 hits at 3–4 mm pitch. That is reconstructable.
- In plastic it is about 3 cm. (Plastic is already excluded.)
- In 10-bar gaseous argon it is about 2 m. That is easy to see, but the target mass would be only about 90 kg, which gives a poor event rate.

## 2. Recommendations

### A. Replace the target with a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (ArgonCube / ND-LAr-style)

**Design.**
- Fill the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region with optically isolated LAr modules, for example 2×2 or 3×2 modules with short (~30–50 cm) drifts.
- Use native 3D pixel readout (LArPix-type ASICs, ~4 mm pitch).
- Use a resistive-shell field cage.

**Hydrogen.** Hydrogen nucleons in the active volume are essentially zero. That leaves ample margin under 2% even with field-cage and readout material nearby, provided the fiducial cut keeps vertices away from G10 and PCB surfaces.

**Target mass.** About 7 t gross, roughly 4–5 t fiducial. That is ample statistics at 410 m.

**Isotropic acceptance.** Pixel readout gives unambiguous 3D imaging with no wire-plane projection blind angles. Tracks perpendicular to the beam, and backward tracks, are reconstructed as well as forward ones.

**Low-energy protons.**
- Protons down to 60 MeV (~2.5 cm) are identified using dE/dx and the Bragg peak.
- This satisfies the "all angles" proton requirement, since LAr has no preferred direction.

**Pile-up.**
- 410 m from a high-power target means several interactions per spill in the target and surrounding material.
- Short drifts limit the size of the time window.
- Optical segmentation keeps each module's light separate. Combined with pixel 3D readout, this lets overlapping events be separated.

### B. Add fast, segmented light readout inside each module

**Technology.** ArCLight or Light-Collection-Module (WLS + SiPM) tiles on the field-cage walls.

**Purposes.**
- Nanosecond-scale t₀ for each interaction. This gives the drift coordinate and absolute vertex position.
- Association of tracks with beam bunches.
- Rejection of rock muons and through-going pile-up.

The tiles are thin and contain no hydrogenous bulk in the active volume.

### C. Use a thin-walled, compact cryostat that fits inside the warm magnet

**Construction.**
- Thin stainless or aluminium inner walls.
- Vacuum insulation rather than polyurethane foam.

**Reasons.**
- Foam is hydrogen-rich and would add out-of-fiducial hydrogen interactions.
- Vacuum insulation also maximizes active volume within the fixed envelope.
- It keeps the wall material that exiting muons cross small, preserving the downstream momentum measurement.

**Practical checks.**
- Verify mechanical clearance to the magnet coils.
- Confirm stray-field compatibility of the cryogenics and pumps.

### D. Add high-angle and upstream tracking around the LAr target

**The problem.**
- The existing drift chambers sit only downstream. A muon at 90° or backward leaves the target through the sides or the upstream face and misses them entirely.
- Containment cannot fix this: a 0.5–0.7 GeV/c muon ranges about 2–3 m in LAr, more than the target's dimensions.
- Multiple Coulomb scattering in LAr gives momentum only to about 10–15%.
- Charge from curvature inside LAr at 0.15 T is unusable. The sagitta is about 1 cm per metre, swamped by scattering (X₀ = 14 cm).

**The fix.** Install thin gaseous TPCs on the top, bottom, and lateral faces, using some of the volume margin or reducing LAr depth slightly if needed.
- Gas: T2K-type Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀, which is low in hydrogen and low in mass.
- Readout: resistive Micromegas (ERAM).

**What these give.**
- Momentum and charge for side-exiting muons in the 0.15 T field.
- A good lever arm and little multiple scattering, because the medium is gas.
- With A, this meets the ≥25% muon efficiency at every angle.

### E. Surround the target with a time-of-flight layer

**Technology.**
- Thin plastic-scintillator ToF panels (~150 ps resolution) outside the TPC/cryostat envelope, read out by SiPMs.
- An upstream panel to tag backward-going tracks.

**Purposes.**
- Distinguish forward/upward from backward/downward-going tracks. This resolves the inherent sense ambiguity for tracks at 90° and backward.
- Reject entering particles produced in the magnet and in upstream material.
- Provide muon/proton separation at the target exit.

**Hydrogen.** The panels sit outside the fiducial volume, so their hydrogen does not enter the target nucleon count. Interactions in them are vetoed by timing and vertex position.

### F. Upgrade the DAQ for combined triggering

Use a common timing system and spill-synchronized clock across the pixel TPC, light system, side TPCs, ToF, and existing drift chambers. This allows track matching across subsystems and bunch-level time slicing.

## 3. Why not a gas-argon TPC as the target?

A high-pressure gaseous argon TPC offers excellent proton thresholds and native charge measurement in the field. In this envelope, however, it gives only about 100 kg of target. It also needs a heavy pressure vessel and quencher gas, which consumes part of the hydrogen budget (~1% for Ar/CH₄ 90/10). LAr gives about 70× the mass while still meeting the proton and angle requirements. Gaseous argon is better used, as in D, for the exiting-muon spectrometry.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the active target with a modular pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (ArgonCube/LArPix-style), which eliminates hydrogen, matches the far detector nucleus, and gives isotropic 3D tracking of 60 MeV protons and muons at all angles.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Understanding the Constraints

Before proposing upgrades, let me extract the key requirements:

- **Muon reconstruction**: ≥25% efficiency at **all angles**, including 90° and backward-going tracks
- **Proton tracking**: down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in scintillator) — very short tracks
- **Hydrogen content**: ≤2% of target nucleons → essentially **no free hydrogen**, ruling out water, plastic scintillator (CH₂), or hydrocarbon-rich materials
- **Active volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (depth along beam only 0.9 m — relatively shallow)
- **Field**: 0.15 T dipole already present
- **Location**: 410 m from target, flux peaks at 0.7 GeV

The 2% hydrogen constraint is severe and unusual — it immediately eliminates most standard scintillator-based active targets.

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. Primary Active Target: Low-Z Argon-Based Liquid Argon TPC (LAr-TPC) Modules

**Technology**: Modular liquid argon time projection chambers

**Rationale**:
- Argon is 40Ar — essentially **zero free hydrogen** (hydrogen fraction is negligible)
- LAr-TPCs provide mm-scale 3D tracking with continuous sensitivity — ideal for the 60 MeV proton requirement (a 60 MeV proton has a range of ~12 mm in LAr, which is reconstructable)
- Full 4π angular coverage for both muons and protons, with no geometric acceptance gaps
- Charge and dE/dx measurement enables particle identification (proton vs. pion vs. muon)
- Already a mature technology (MicroBooNE, SBND, ArgonCube experience)

**Specific implementation**:
- Use **ArgonCube-style modular LArTPC** design: segment the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume into an array of ~50 independent modules each roughly 0.67 m × 0.67 m × 0.3 m
- Each module has its own cathode/anode and light detection system (LArPix charge readout tiles + ARAPUCA-style light traps)
- Modular design avoids the high-voltage and electron-lifetime challenges of a monolithic LAr volume at this scale
- Charge readout via **LArPix pixelated charge readout** (3D hit reconstruction without ambiguity from multiple tracks — critical for the interaction multiplicities at 0.7 GeV)
- Operating temperature: 87 K; requires cryogenic infrastructure but this is well-established

**Performance on requirements**:
- 60 MeV proton: ~12 mm range in LAr → reconstructable with 3–5 mm pitch pixels ✓
- Backward muons: reconstructed in the LAr volume itself, then matched to downstream trackers ✓
- Hydrogen fraction: ~0.0% ✓

---

### 2. Upstream and Side Veto / Muon Catcher Panels: High-Granularity Scintillator Planes

**Technology**: Extruded scintillator bars with SiPM readout (similar to MINERvA or NOvA-style)

**Rationale**:
- The 0.9 m depth along the beam is shallow — backward-going muons and large-angle muons may re-enter or exit through the upstream face; side panels tag these
- Also serves as a **cosmic ray veto** (at 410 m, cosmic contamination during beam spills needs rejection)

**Specific implementation**:
- 2 cm × 3 cm extruded scintillator bars with WLS fiber + SiPM readout (Hamamatsu S13360 series or similar)
- Planes on upstream face (2.6 m × 2.3 m), both sides (2.3 m × 0.9 m), top and bottom (2.6 m × 0.9 m)
- Two orientations (X and Y) per face for 2D hit position
- ~5 ns timing resolution for in-spill cosmic rejection
- Note: these panels use plastic scintillator (CH-based), so they must be **outside the active target fiducial volume** and not counted toward the hydrogen budget

---

### 3. Downstream Muon Spectrometer Interface: Resistive Plate Chambers or Thin-Gap MWPCs

**Technology**: Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) or Multi-Wire Proportional Chambers (MWPCs)

**Rationale**:
- The existing warm dipole and downstream gas drift chambers provide momentum measurement, but the interface between the new LAr target and the existing spectrometer needs dedicated tracking planes to match LAr tracks to spectrometer tracks efficiently — especially for large-angle muons that only just exit the downstream face
- The existing gas drift chambers may have insufficient granularity near the target exit

**Specific implementation**:
- 3–4 planes of **double-gap RPCs** with 1 cm strip pitch in both X and Y, placed between the LAr target exit face and the first existing drift chamber station
- Strip RPCs: ~1 mm spatial resolution, ~1 ns timing, robust and low-cost per area
- Each plane covers the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m aperture
- Alternatively, if rate is high, replace with **thin-gap MWPCs** (2 mm gap) which handle higher occupancy

**Performance**:
- Provides high-efficiency matching of exiting tracks (including those at angles up to ~70° to the beam) to the downstream momentum measurement
- Enables the 25% efficiency threshold to be met for forward-going muons even when the LAr reconstruction is ambiguous near module boundaries

---

### 4. Light Detection Upgrade Within LAr: ARAPUCA/X-ARAPUCA Tiles

**Technology**: X-ARAPUCA silicon photon detectors embedded in LAr module walls

**Rationale**:
- Scintillation light in LAr (128 nm VUV, ~40,000 photons/MeV) provides **sub-microsecond timing** that is essential for:
  - Determining the absolute drift time (t₀) for each interaction — without this, the drift coordinate is unknown
  - Separating in-spill cosmics from beam neutrino interactions
  - Triggering

**Specific implementation**:
- X-ARAPUCA tiles (wavelength-shifting plates + dichroic filters + SiPMs) mounted on the anode and cathode faces of each LAr module
- Target: >0.5% photon detection efficiency per module (sufficient for t₀ with ~10 detected photons from a 1 GeV interaction)
- SiPM arrays (3 mm × 3 mm cells) operating at LAr temperature (87 K) — well characterized from SBND/DUNE prototypes
- This is part of the LAr module design but deserves separate emphasis because it is what enables the trigger and t₀ for all 3D reconstruction

---

### 5. Thin Tracking Layer at Module Boundaries: Pixel-Readout Silicon or μ-RWELL

**Technology**: Micro-resistive WELL (μ-RWELL) detectors or thin silicon pixel planes

**Rationale**:
- In the modular ArgonCube design, the gaps between modules (~few mm of dead material) create acceptance losses for very short tracks (the 60 MeV protons). A thin high-resolution detector at module interfaces recovers tracks that stop in or near boundaries.
- Also helps with **charge matching** between modules for tracks that cross boundaries

**Specific implementation**:
- **μ-RWELL** panels (~3 mm total thickness including PCB), one per inter-module gap, with 400 μm pitch strip readout
- These operate at room temperature (they are outside the cryostat walls), reading out tracks as they pass through the thin (1–2 mm) gap material
- Alternatively, 300 μm thick silicon strip detectors (single-sided, 50 μm pitch) if budget allows — they provide better resolution but at higher cost
- Coverage: all inter-module vertical and horizontal boundaries

---

### 6. Cryogenic and DAQ Infrastructure

**Technology**: Continuous readout DAQ with FPGA-based data compression

**Rationale**: The LArPix system generates ~O(10 GB/s) raw data; online zero-suppression and hit-finding must run in real time.

**Specific implementation**:
- LArPix ASICs read out via warm FPGA boards (based on the existing ArgonCube/LArPix DAQ stack, e.g., Xilinx Ultrascale+ FPGAs)
- Continuous (~2.5 MHz) sampling with self-triggered threshold-based readout — no external trigger required for charge
- Light system uses a separate fast-trigger path (ARAPUCA + SiPM + waveform digitizers at 250 MHz) that provides the beam-spill gate and t₀
- Synchronization via White Rabbit timing protocol to correlate with beam spill structure

| Carbon (graphite) | 0% | ~7 mm |
| Aluminum | 0% | ~10 mm |
| Silicon | 0% | ~8 mm |
| CH scintillator + 95% Fe by nucleon | ~2% | poor proton vis. |

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Primary Recommendation: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgTPC)

**Rationale:**
- Argon contains zero hydrogen → trivially satisfies the ≤2% constraint
- A TPC provides true 3D tracking with continuous ionization trail
- Short proton tracks (60 MeV KE, range ~8 mm in LAr equivalent) produce measurable ionization over many readout pads in gas at sufficient pressure
- All-angle reconstruction is intrinsic to a TPC — there is no "dead" angular region
- dE/dx measurement in gas allows proton/pion separation and aids track identification

**Specifications:**
- Operating pressure: ~5–10 bar pure argon (increases density → shorter absolute track lengths but more ionization per pad; at 10 bar, 60 MeV proton range ~a few cm, well-reconstructable)
- Active volume: fits within 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m envelope
- Readout: pixelated or strip-based charge readout (e.g., Multi-Pattern Gas Detector — MicroMegas or GEM — with 2D strip or pixel pads at ~3–5 mm pitch)
- Two drift volumes with central cathode along the 2.6 m dimension; drift distance ~1.15 m each side; drift field ~200–500 V/cm
- Drift time for 1.15 m at typical gas drift velocity (~5 cm/μs at 10 bar): ~23 μs — acceptable given the accelerator beam spill structure
- Cathode HV: ~25–50 kV
- The 0.9 m dimension along the beam is the drift direction alternatively, or the 2.3 m transverse — optimize for drift uniformity

**Addresses all requirements:**
- Muons at all angles including backward: ✓ (continuous ionization, TPC reconstructs full helix)
- Short proton tracks: ✓ (at 10 bar argon, 60 MeV proton range ~3–4 cm, fully reconstructable with 3–5 mm pad pitch)
- Hydrogen fraction: ✓ (0%)
- Momentum measurement: forward/large-angle muons exit into existing drift chambers + dipole; backward muons reconstructed by curvature within the TPC field volume or by range

---

### 2. Complementary Upgrade: Thin Low-Mass Scintillator Trigger/Veto Panels

**Purpose:** The TPC has a drift time of ~20 μs, far longer than the beam crossing. Scintillator panels on all six faces of the target volume provide:
- Fast trigger signal (ns timing) to associate TPC ionization with the correct beam spill bucket
- Veto for tracks entering from outside (cosmic rays, beam halo)
- Crude pre-selection for neutrino interaction candidates before full TPC reconstruction

**Specifications:**
- 6 planes of EJ-200 or BC-404 plastic scintillator tiles, 5–10 mm thick
- SiPM readout (avoid PMT for compactness; also the magnet field requires shielding or SiPMs)
- Tile size: ~10 cm × 10 cm for reasonable channel count (~2600 m² → ~600 tiles total for all faces)
- The mass of these panels adds minimal hydrogen: at 10 mm thickness × area, mass ~few kg vs. target argon mass of hundreds of kg → hydrogen contribution negligible

---

### 3. Upgrade of Upstream/Downstream Interface: Light-Weight Field Cage and Sealed Pressure Vessel

**Purpose:** The TPC must fit mechanically within the existing magnet bore and interface with the existing downstream drift chambers.

**Specifications:**
- Thin-wall (5–10 mm) aluminum or carbon-fiber pressure vessel rated to 10 bar
- Field cage constructed from kapton-copper resistive strips (minimize material in active volume and at boundaries)
- Thin window (aluminized mylar or Kevlar-composite) on downstream face to minimize scattering of outgoing tracks before they enter the existing drift chambers
- The pressure vessel outer diameter must clear the magnet warm bore of approximately 2.6 m × 2.3 m

---

### 4. Front-End Electronics and DAQ Upgrade

**Purpose:** The existing DAQ is designed for the wire drift chambers and cannot handle TPC readout.

**Specifications:**
- ASIC-based front-end: e.g., SAMPA (used in ALICE TPC upgrade) or custom equivalent — 32 channels/chip, shaping + 10-bit ADC at 10 MHz sampling
- Channel count: at 4 mm × 4 mm pad size over the 2.6 m × 2.3 m readout plane = ~374,000 pads; with two readout planes = ~750,000 channels
- Data rate: at 10 MHz × 10 bit × 750k channels × duty cycle → requires zero-suppression at the ASIC level; estimated zero-suppressed output ~few GB/spill
- Optical fiber data links from front-end to counting room DAQ servers
- Trigger distribution: synchronize with accelerator RF to associate TPC drift windows with beam bunches
- Online reconstruction farm: GPUs for fast 3D track finding to enable online data reduction

---

### 5. Magnetic Field Map Survey and Correction Coils (Minor Upgrade)

**Purpose:** The TPC uses E × B drift; any magnetic field component transverse to the drift direction causes track distortion (ExB effect).

- Commission a detailed 3D field map of the existing dipole at the target location
- Install small correction coils on the TPC field cage if needed to compensate transverse B components > ~1 mT
- Include field map in track reconstruction software

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Addresses | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| High-pressure argon TPC | All-angle tracking, short protons, H constraint | **Critical** |
| Scintillator trigger/veto panels | Timing, beam association, cosmic veto | High |
| Thin-window pressure vessel + field cage | Mechanical integration, interface to existing magnets/chambers | High |
| New front-end electronics + DAQ | Readout of TPC, online reconstruction | High |
| B-field survey + correction coils | TPC drift accuracy | Medium |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a high-pressure (∼10 bar) gaseous argon time projection chamber, which simultaneously provides zero hydrogen content, continuous 3D all-angle tracking of both muons and short proton recoils down to 60 MeV kinetic energy, and inherent dE/dx-based particle identification, while fitting within the existing magnet volume and feeding tracks into the downstream drift chambers.

This is a fascinating detector design challenge for a near detector in a neutrino beam experiment. Let me analyze the constraints and propose concrete hardware upgrades.

## Key Constraints Analysis:
- Need 4π acceptance (including backward-going muons)
- Need low-momentum proton tracking (60 MeV KE ≈ 110 MeV/c)
- Must limit hydrogen content to <2% of nucleons
- Need precise 3D reconstruction in a confined volume
- Must operate in 0.15 T magnetic field

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades:

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Plastic Scintillator Cubes)**
**Technology:** Extruded plastic scintillator bars (1 cm × 1 cm cross-section) arranged in alternating X-Y-Z orientations every few cm, with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and SiPM sensors.

**Physics Motivation:** 
- Provides full 3D tracking including backward tracks that never reach downstream chambers
- 1 cm granularity enables reconstruction of short proton tracks (60 MeV protons have ~5-10 mm range in plastic scintillator)
- Plastic scintillator (CH) has acceptable but controllable hydrogen content (~14% by nucleon count, requiring ~85% of target mass in this technology)
- Fast timing discrimination between multiple tracks
- dE/dx measurement for particle identification (crucial for distinguishing low-momentum protons from other particles)

### 2. **Time Projection Chamber with Resistive Micromegas Readout**
**Technology:** Argon-based TPC with fine-pitch (3 mm) resistive Micromegas readout pads.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Argon is hydrogen-free, addressing the <2% constraint directly
- Continuous 3D tracking with excellent spatial resolution (~1 mm)
- Superior dE/dx measurement for particle ID over the full track length
- Can reconstruct very short proton tracks down to a few cm
- Full solid angle coverage including backwards tracks
- Proven technology (used in T2K ND280 upgrade, MicroBooNE)
- The 0.15 T field aids electron drift and track sign determination

### 3. **High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC (HPgTPC)**
**Technology:** Gaseous argon TPC operated at 10 atm pressure with GEM or Micromegas amplification.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Increases target mass by 10× vs atmospheric pressure while maintaining TPC advantages
- Still hydrogen-free
- Lower density than liquid/solid allows longer tracks, improving momentum resolution via magnetic deflection
- Excellent calorimetric resolution for low-energy protons
- 3D imaging with minimal dead regions

### 4. **Super-Fine-Grained Tracker (SuperFGD concept)**
**Technology:** 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts per cube, all SiPM readout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- True 3D hit reconstruction (not projective)
- Demonstrated success in T2K ND280 upgrade
- Excellent position resolution for vertex reconstruction
- Nearly isotropic response crucial for backward-going tracks
- Timing resolution enables reconstruction of multiple tracks with similar trajectories
- ~7% hydrogen by nucleon with careful design

### 5. **Straw Tube Tracker (STT) in Target Region**
**Technology:** Dense array of 1 cm diameter straw tubes filled with Ar/CO₂ mixture, operated in the magnetic field.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Hydrogen-free gas mixture
- Excellent spatial resolution (~150 μm)
- High granularity enables pattern recognition in complex events
- Magnetic field provides momentum measurement for tracks as short as 10 cm
- Low mass minimizes secondary interactions
- Can operate at angles down to very shallow relative to straw axis

### 6. **Scintillating Fiber Tracker**
**Technology:** Dense packing of 0.5-1 mm diameter scintillating fibers in alternating orientations, with SiPM readout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Sub-mm position resolution
- Can achieve near-continuous tracking
- Allows very short track reconstruction
- Moderate hydrogen content (~8% by nucleon with proper design)
- Fast timing for high-rate environments

### 7. **Hybrid: Fine-Grained Scintillator + Argon Gas Tracker**
**Technology:** Upstream section (50% of volume) with SuperFGD-style scintillator; downstream section with atmospheric pressure Ar TPC.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Balances hydrogen budget: scintillator provides target mass for statistics while Ar section provides hydrogen-free comparison
- Forward-going tracks traverse both systems (complementary measurements)
- Backward tracks fully contained in scintillator
- TPC provides superior PID for particles reaching it
- Meets <2% hydrogen constraint with proper mass distribution

## Technology Selection Criteria:

Given the specific requirements, the **SuperFGD-style fine-grained scintillator** or **Argon TPC** are most suitable, with the hybrid approach offering the best compromise.

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker with 1 cm³ cube granularity, three orthogonal WLS fiber readouts per cube, and SiPM readout (SuperFGD technology)**

This provides the essential 4π acceptance, sufficient granularity for 60 MeV proton tracks, manageable hydrogen content, and is a mature technology successfully deployed in similar applications.

# Proposed Upgrade: Fine-Grained 3D Scintillator Target with High-Angle TPCs and Time-of-Flight

## 1. Why the current layout limits the analysis

- **Bar geometry.** The present tracking target uses x/y bars perpendicular to the beam, read from the sides, with TPCs only downstream. Efficiency falls sharply for tracks above about 50–60°, and tracks near 90° run along a single bar layer.
- **Lost muons.** About 25% of muons go above 50°. These are lost or poorly measured. That biases the phase space and forces model-dependent extrapolation.
- **Short proton tracks.** A 450 MeV/c proton has about 100 MeV kinetic energy and travels only about 8 cm in polystyrene. That spans only a few 1-cm layers. It is often lost entirely below about 400–500 MeV/c, especially at high angle.
- **Overall effect.** Transverse kinematic imbalance needs both the muon and the proton at all angles. The present target cannot provide this.

## 2. Proposed hardware

### (a) Main element: a 3D-granular cube scintillator target (SuperFGD-type)

**Granularity and size**
- About 2 million optically isolated polystyrene cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³.
- Example arrangement: about 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, roughly 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.56 m, fitting the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Active mass about 2 t, roughly twice one existing tracking target.

**Cube construction**
- Each cube is extruded or injection-moulded, doped with PTP and POPOP.
- The surface is chemically etched to form a reflector.
- Three orthogonal holes of about 1.5 mm hold 1-mm Kuraray Y-11 wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z.
- This gives three 2D projections and true 3D reconstruction.

**Readout**
- About 56,000 channels.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a 1.3 × 1.3 mm² Hamamatsu MPPC (low cross-talk type); the far end is mirrored.
- Front-end boards use CITIROC ASICs, providing charge and timing in two gain ranges.
- Target performance:
  - about 1 ns timing per channel, and better per cube with multiple hits;
  - light yield of tens of photoelectrons per fibre per MIP.

**Expected physics gain**
- Close to 4π acceptance for muons and protons.
- Proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c, since about 3 cm of track still crosses several cubes.
- Ranged protons are measured with dE/dx and Bragg-peak identification.
- Good electron/γ separation.
- Neutron detection via delayed, displaced recoil hits, timed against the vertex.
  - This enables the full δp_T analysis including antineutrino neutron kinematics.
- Hydrocarbon target, which matches the existing target material.
- The downstream water module keeps the carbon/water comparison possible.

### (b) Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the cube target

**Purpose**
- They measure momentum and charge in the 0.2 T field for muons and energetic protons leaving at large angle.
  - About 6% of protons exceed 900 MeV/c and have ranges of about 1 m or more.
- This is where the gain over the side-going acceptance comes from.

**Field cage**
- Thin composite laminate (aramid honeycomb with Kapton and copper strips).
- Low material budget, about 4% X₀, which limits scattering before the calorimeter.

**Readout and gas**
- Resistive (encapsulated) bulk Micromegas modules.
- The resistive layer spreads the charge, so 1-cm pads still give a few hundred µm spatial resolution, about 0.6 mm.
- About 32 modules in total.
- Readout via AFTER/AGET electronics.
- Same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ gas as the existing TPCs, to simplify operations.

**Expected performance**
- dE/dx resolution below about 10%, giving e/µ/p separation.
- σ_p/p of about 10% at 1 GeV/c.

### (c) Time-of-Flight enclosure

**Layout**
- Six planes enclosing the target and HA-TPC system.
- Each plane uses 2.2-m-long, 1-cm-thick EJ-200 plastic bars.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Uses**
- Determines track direction, rejecting backward-entering out-of-fiducial background such as magnet and sand events.
- Separates e/µ/p at low momentum together with the TPC.
- Provides a T0 for drift reconstruction and for cube-based neutron time-of-flight.

### (d) Supporting changes

- Upgrade the downstream TPC/FGD triggering and DAQ to merge with the new system.
- Integrate the ECal and yoke side-muon range detector into the same timing reference.
- Recalibrate using cosmic triggers.

## 3. Expected impact

The upgrade gives near-uniform angular acceptance for muons and protons, which matches the prior near-detector phase space more closely to the far detector's 4π acceptance. It also enables kinematically complete charged-current events, transverse kinematic imbalance, and neutron measurement to constrain nuclear effects. This is the main route to lowering the residual systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the roughly 4% the next phase needs.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a ~2-tonne, ~2-million-cube 3D-readout plastic scintillator target (1 cm cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibres, SiPM readout), flanked by resistive-Micromegas high-angle TPCs and a ToF enclosure.

# ND280-style Near-Detector Upgrade: Recommended Hardware

The existing tracker cannot deliver the kinematically complete events the programme needs. Its planar bar targets with bars perpendicular to the beam, read out by forward/backward gas TPCs, see forward tracks well. They lose most tracks above about 50°, which here means about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons. Each upgrade below closes part of that gap.

## 1. New active target: a 3D-granular scintillator-cube detector

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes. They fill the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, roughly 192 × 182 × 56 cubes and about 2 t of CH.
- The cube surfaces are chemically etched to make them reflective.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes. Wavelength-shifting fibres run along x, y and z, giving three 2D projections of every hit.
- Each fibre is read by an SiPM (about 56,000 channels). The readout must provide nanosecond-level timing and wide dynamic range.

**Why**
- **Near-4π acceptance.** Three orthogonal views remove the dead angles of planar bar layers. High-angle and even backward tracks become reconstructable.
- **Low proton threshold.** A median 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV. Its range in plastic is only a few cm, so protons stopping after a few cubes are lost in coarse bar detectors.
  - 1 cm granularity reconstructs protons down to about 300 MeV/c.
  - It also gives Bragg-peak dE/dx for particle identification.
- **Neutron tagging.** Fine granularity, good timing and a fully active volume let the detector tag neutrons by time-of-flight. This adds information for transverse-kinematic-imbalance studies, especially for antineutrino running.
- **Hydrocarbon target.** Carbon is acceptable for this programme. The downstream water-layer target remains for the C/H₂O comparison.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Argon-based gas TPCs, one above and one below the cube target, each roughly 2 × 2 × 0.8 m.
- Lightweight composite field cages to minimise dead material and multiple scattering.
- Readout by **resistive Micromegas** (encapsulated resistive anode). The resistive layer spreads the charge, giving roughly 0.5 mm resolution with large pads, and suppresses sparks.

**Why**
- High-angle muons leaving the target need measurement of momentum and charge sign (curvature in the 0.2 T field) and dE/dx particle identification.
- The existing downstream TPCs cannot provide this. Coverage by the side muon-range detector is coarse.
- Protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) exit the target and also need these momentum and PID measurements.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new target and TPCs

**Technology**
- Six panels of plastic scintillator bars, each read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Why**
- **Track direction:** distinguishes forward-going from backward-going tracks.
- **Background rejection:** identifies particles entering from outside, such as from the magnet or sand.
- **Particle identification:** adds e/μ/p separation through β.
- **Timing reference:** gives an event time (t₀) for the TPCs.

## 4. Supporting infrastructure

**Electronics**
- SiPM front-end electronics with sub-ns timing for the new channels, for example a CITIROC-based design.
- TPC front-end electronics for the high-angle TPCs.
- Integration of both into the existing DAQ and trigger.

**Mechanics and services**
- Mechanical integration in the space freed by removing the photon-tagging section.
- Gas, cooling, light-tight enclosures and calibration systems: LED injection and a cosmic trigger.

**Existing detectors**
- Retain and recalibrate the existing tracker, the lead-scintillator calorimeters and the return-yoke muon-range planes.

## Combined effect

Together these changes give:
- Full-angle muon and proton reconstruction.
- A lower proton threshold.
- Neutron information.

These are the ingredients needed to cut the flux and cross-section systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the 4% goal.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a 3D-readout fine-grained scintillator-cube target (about 2 million 1 cm³ cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibres per cube, SiPM readout).

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Target Region

## 1. Why the current layout fails

The existing tracking geometry is essentially forward-looking. The gas drift chambers sit downstream of the target, so only tracks that exit the downstream face are momentum- and charge-analyzed. This causes four problems:

- **High-angle muons are lost.** Muons near 90° and backward-going muons never reach the chambers, so the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles cannot be met.
- **Low-energy protons are lost.** A 60 MeV proton travels only about 3 cm in plastic, so a coarse or passive target misses it entirely.
- **Isotropic proton reconstruction needs 3D granularity.** Detectors that read out in 2D projections, such as planar bar layers, are poor at tracks perpendicular to the bars.

## 2. Recommended configuration

The proposal fits the 2.6 m (transverse) × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (along beam) envelope. It is modeled on the T2K ND280 upgrade concept and uses three new subsystems.

### (a) Fine-grained 3D scintillator active target (core change)

**Design**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, chemically etched with a reflective (TiO₂) coating.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibers read by SiPMs (MPPCs).

**Dimensions**
- About 2.0 m × 0.7 m × 0.85 m (along beam), roughly 200 × 70 × 85 cubes.
- About 1.2 million cubes in total.
- Mass about 1.25 t.

**Channel count**
- About 200×70 + 200×85 + 70×85 ≈ 37,000 channels.

**Physics capability**
- The three views give true isotropic 3D tracking, so tracks at every angle, including perpendicular and backward, are reconstructed with similar efficiency.
- A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes, enough to tag it and measure its range and dE/dx.
- The proton threshold reaches about 50–60 MeV kinetic energy. This is far below what an additional set of planar bar layers could achieve.
- Sub-ns single-channel timing allows:
  - track-direction determination,
  - neutron-candidate tagging as an added benefit.

**Hydrogen constraint**
- Polystyrene (CH)ₙ gives 1/(12+1) ≈ 7.7% of nucleons on hydrogen.
- Fibers, coating and glue add only slightly to this.
- This is comfortably under the 20% limit.
- A water-based or hydrogen-rich organic target with a higher hydrogen fraction should be avoided.

### (b) Two high-angle TPCs, above and below the active target

**Placement**
- Each TPC is about 2.0 m wide, about 0.75 m tall and 0.85 m along the beam.
- This uses the 2.3 m vertical space: 0.75 + 0.7 + 0.75 m, plus TOF and clearances.

**Physics role**
- With the dipole field horizontal and transverse to the beam, high-angle tracks leaving the cube volume upward or downward bend in the measured plane.
- The TPCs therefore provide momentum and charge for muons at roughly 40–140° and beyond. This is what fills the perpendicular and backward acceptance that the downstream chambers miss.

**Technology**
- Resistive-anode Micromegas readout.
- Light composite field cage to keep material between the target and the gas low.
- An Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture.
- Expected momentum resolution is about 10% at 1 GeV/c in 0.15 T.

**Stopping tracks**
- Muons and protons that stop inside the cube target are measured by range and dE/dx instead.

### (c) Time-of-flight envelope

**Design**
- Thin plastic scintillator bars (about 1–2 cm thick) on all six faces of the target and TPC assembly.
- Double-ended SiPM readout giving about 150 ps resolution.

**Purpose**
- Unambiguous forward/backward direction for backward-going muons, so they are not mistaken for incoming tracks.
- Rejection of particles entering from outside the target ("sand" muons and interactions in the magnet).
- Particle identification assistance (μ/p/e) at low momentum.

## 3. Supporting items

| Item | Purpose |
|---|---|
| Common front-end electronics with a shared clock | Gives the ~1 ns cube timing and ~150 ps TOF timing a common time base. |
| Field-tolerant SiPMs | Operate in the 0.15 T field. |
| Low-mass mechanical box for the cube array | Uses a carbon-fiber or plastic frame instead of steel to keep non-CH material and hydrogen bookkeeping clean. |
| LED/laser calibration system | Fiber gain and timing calibration. |
| Cosmic and beam-test runs | Measure the angular efficiency map, verifying ≥25% muon efficiency in every angular bin and the proton threshold. |
| Downstream drift chambers | Unchanged; they remain the forward muon spectrometer. |

## 4. Expected performance

**Muon efficiency**
- Forward: downstream chambers.
- High angle: HA-TPCs.
- Remaining backward tracks: TOF plus range in the cubes.
- Together these give near-4π coverage, with efficiency expected well above 25% in all angular bins.

**Protons**
- 3D tracking down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy at any angle.

**Hydrogen fraction**
- About 8% of target nucleons, so the hydrogen-subtraction model remains valid.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a ~2.0 × 0.7 × 0.85 m³ fine-grained 3D scintillator-cube active target (1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibers with SiPM readout), complemented by high-angle TPCs above and below it.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before proposing upgrades, I'll note the key physics requirements driving them:
- Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at **all angles** (including 90° and backward)
- Proton tracking down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.4 cm in iron)
- Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons (constrains material choice)
- Beam peaks at 0.7 GeV — typical final states: 1 muon + 1–3 hadrons, modest multiplicities

---

## 1. Plastic Scintillator 3D-Granular Active Target (Primary Recommendation)

**Technology:** Finely segmented plastic scintillator cubes (~1.5 cm side) read out by wavelength-shifting fibers through 3 orthogonal faces, each fiber read by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM). This follows the SuperFGD design demonstrated for T2K's near detector upgrade.

**Physics motivation:**

The 0.9 m depth along the beam axis is short — a fully-active, isotropic detector is mandatory for the backward and perpendicular muon requirement. A layered tracker has dead material between planes and poor efficiency for tracks at large angles. A 3D-granular structure has essentially no preferred axis: a track at any angle traverses a comparable number of sensitive cubes. With 1.5 cm cubes, a 60 MeV proton has a range of roughly 3–4 cm and crosses ~2–3 cubes, giving a detectable track stub with dE/dx particle identification. Timing on individual cubes (~1 ns resolution with SiPMs) provides time-of-flight separation of protons from pions, and the light yield is sufficient to detect the Bragg peak, essential for proton momentum-by-range.

The hydrogen content of polystyrene (CH) is naturally high — roughly 57% of nucleons are on hydrogen in pure CH — so the cube density or admixture must be tuned. By mixing in a small fraction of denser material or by using a slightly heavier polymer backbone, the hydrogen fraction can be managed, but this requires careful design (see upgrade 4 below).

---

## 2. Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Panels Surrounding the Active Target

**Technology:** Four thin-wall TPCs, each ~2.6 m × 2.3 m in aperture, based on Micromegas or GEM readout planes with Ar:CF₄:isobutane gas mixture. They would flank the active target volume on the four faces parallel to the beam (top, bottom, left, right), with their drift direction transverse to the beam.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing warm dipole provides a 0.15 T field over 6.5 m, but the active target occupies only the upstream 0.9 m. Very high-angle and backward tracks that exit the active target laterally enter these TPC panels before reaching the downstream drift chambers, giving them a momentum measurement via curvature within the magnetic field region. TPCs provide continuous tracking with no material between measurement points, minimising scattering that degrades momentum resolution for low-momentum (~200–500 MeV/c) muons and pions. The dE/dx measurement in the TPC gas also gives additional PID, helping separate muons from pions for tracks that stop or scatter before reaching downstream systems.

The thin entrance windows (< 1% X₀) preserve the low-threshold proton tracking that the active target begins, and the large active area ensures the ≥25% muon efficiency requirement is met for tracks with polar angles from 0° to nearly 180°.

---

## 3. Downstream High-Resolution Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL)

**Technology:** Sampling calorimeter using lead absorber layers (~2 mm) interleaved with plastic scintillator strips (~1 cm width), read out by SiPMs, with ~15 radiation lengths total depth and projective strip orientation alternating X–Y.

**Physics motivation:**

At 0.7 GeV peak flux, neutral pion production is a major background to quasi-elastic interactions. Each π⁰ → γγ, and the photons must be identified and their energy measured to reconstruct the π⁰ invariant mass and reject NC π⁰ events mimicking νₑ appearance or to correctly classify CC interactions for cross-section analyses. The 2 mm Pb layers give Molière radius ~2 cm, adequate for resolving two-photon showers from π⁰ at these energies. Strip readout gives shower position to ~3 mm, enabling γ/e separation via shower shape and conversion point reconstruction. Placing the ECAL immediately downstream of the active target ensures photons from interactions near the upstream face of the target are still contained.

---

## 4. Liquid Argon or Water Target Auxiliary Module (Hydrogen Subtraction Control)

**Technology:** A thin (10–15 cm depth along beam) liquid-water target module with scintillator-bar tracking on each face, insertable on a rail system upstream of the main active target, with an identical-but-empty (or argon-filled) configuration for data-driven subtraction runs.

**Physics motivation:**

This addresses the ≤20% hydrogen nucleon fraction constraint directly. The neutrino community needs hydrogen cross-sections but the far detector has no free hydrogen. The standard approach is statistical subtraction: measure rates on a target with known H fraction, subtract a scaled measurement on the same material without hydrogen (or on pure oxygen). A dedicated water-in / water-out module on the same beam axis, with the same flux, allows the hydrogen cross-section to be extracted model-independently as a data-driven difference. By keeping the hydrogen module thin (minimising reinteractions), tracking with scintillator bars on all 6 faces (3–5 cm wide bars, two orthogonal layers per face), and cross-matching vertices reconstructed in the water with those in the main SuperFGD-style target, one controls systematic uncertainties on vertex position and fiducial volume at the percent level. The hydrogen fraction in this module is ~89% of nucleons (pure water), well above the 20% limit, so it must be treated as a separate analysis sample rather than part of the main fiducial volume — but it provides the indispensable hydrogen reference sample.

---

## 5. Upgrade of Downstream Drift Chambers to Straw-Tube Trackers with Enhanced Timing

**Technology:** Replace or supplement the existing gas drift chambers with straw-tube tracker (STT) modules — 1 cm diameter aluminised mylar straws with Ar:CO₂ gas, read out with TDC+ADC electronics giving < 2 ns single-hit timing.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing drift chambers provide momentum and charge measurement for forward-going tracks, but their timing resolution and segmentation may be insufficient for the high-rate, multi-track events from a fully-active target upgrade. Straw-tube trackers have single-hit efficiencies >99%, are robust in high-occupancy environments, and their individual-straw readout avoids the ambiguity problems of large-cell drift chambers when two or three tracks pass through simultaneously (common in CC multi-pion events at 0.7 GeV). Improved timing (2 ns) allows out-of-time rejection of Michel electrons from stopped muons and helps associate tracks to the correct beam spill sub-structure. The dE/dx capability (20–30 measurement samples per track) also provides a redundant PID handle for pions vs. muons for tracks that traverse many modules before stopping.

---

# ND280 Upgrade Proposal: Replacing the P0D with a 4π Active Target System

## Why the present detector falls short

Both the FGDs and the TPCs are planar and perpendicular to the beam. This creates three problems:

1. **High-angle tracks are lost.** Tracks at large angles, or running nearly parallel to the FGD planes, are poorly reconstructed. About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leave above 50°, and ND280 effectively misses them. Super-K has 4π acceptance, so the near-to-far extrapolation depends on models in exactly this region.
2. **Low-momentum protons are invisible.** FGD bars are about 1 cm wide and alternate in only one view per layer. A proton below roughly 450 MeV/c crosses only a few bars, so the proton threshold sits near the median of the spectrum.
3. **The 6% systematic is dominated by cross-section modelling.** The key uncertainties are 2p2h, nuclear effects, and neutrino energy reconstruction. Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) separates these effects, but it needs the full final state: the muon, the proton, and ideally the neutron.

## Proposed hardware

### 1. SuperFGD: a 3D-granular scintillator target (fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box)

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56.
- The cubes are etched with a reflector coating.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres (x, y, z).
- Readout is about 56,000 MPPC channels with timing better than 1 ns per channel.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, which roughly doubles the current FGD hydrocarbon mass.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three 2D projections give true 3D reconstruction at any angle, which recovers the high-angle muons and protons.
- **Low proton threshold.** Protons down to about 300 MeV/c (a few cubes of track length) can be reconstructed.
- **Momentum by range.** Most protons in the stated spectrum (median 450 MeV/c, ~6% above 900 MeV/c) stop inside the target, so their momentum follows from range and dE/dx.
- **Neutron detection.** Neutrons are seen through isolated delayed hits from secondary proton recoils. Their kinetic energy follows from time of flight relative to the vertex, which allows full TKI on antineutrino CC events (μ⁺ n).
- **Photon and electron identification.** Fine granularity separates γ from e and improves νₑ and π⁰ selection.

### 2. Two High-Angle TPCs above and below SuperFGD

**Technology**
- Field cages about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, made of thin composite laminate to minimise material.
- The same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture as the existing TPCs.
- Readout by **resistive Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, ERAM)**. Charge spreading lets wider pads (about 1 cm) achieve sub-millimetre resolution with fewer channels, and it also protects against sparks.

**Physics motivation**
- Measures momentum and charge from curvature in the 0.2 T field for high-angle muons leaving SuperFGD.
- Provides dE/dx particle identification (μ/π/p/e) with around 10% resolution.
- Together with the existing downstream TPCs, this gives near-4π lepton reconstruction matching Super-K's phase space.

### 3. Time-of-Flight panels surrounding the new target and HA-TPCs

**Technology**
- Six panels of long plastic scintillator bars.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large SiPMs.
- Timing resolution is about 150 ps.

**Physics motivation**
- **Direction tagging.** Distinguishes particles entering from outside (sand muons, magnet interactions) from forward-going tracks born in SuperFGD.
- **Background rejection.** Removes out-of-fiducial backgrounds that matter at high angle.
- **Particle ID.** Adds time-of-flight PID for μ/e and p/π separation, complementing TPC dE/dx.

### 4. Supporting changes

**Electronics, DAQ and triggering**
- Move to new high-channel-count front ends that can handle the much larger channel count:
  - CITIROC-based boards for the SuperFGD MPPCs.
  - AFTER/DAQ-compatible cards for the ERAM readout.
- Read out the full beam spill with nanosecond time stamps. This is needed for neutron time of flight and for the higher beam power after the J-PARC upgrade (above 1 MW).

**Water target**
- Keep FGD2 in place for C/H₂O comparison. Any oxygen-specific constraint then comes from combining SuperFGD (CH) with the FGD2 water layers.

## Expected impact

| Capability | Benefit |
|---|---|
| Full-solid-angle μ and p reconstruction | Better match to Super-K phase space |
| Proton threshold ~300 MeV/c | Recovers protons near and below the median momentum |
| Neutron kinematics | Full TKI, including antineutrino events |
| Doubled target mass | More statistics for the cross-section programme |

These improvements constrain 2p2h, Fermi motion, and final-state interactions, aiming to reduce the flux and cross-section systematic from about 6% to about 4% for T2K-II and Hyper-K.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD-type 3D-segmented scintillator-cube target (1 cm³ cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibres, MPPC readout), paired with high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs and a TOF system, to deliver 4π, low-threshold muon, proton and neutron reconstruction.

# Hardware Upgrades for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## 1. Primary Active Neutrino Target — Super-FGD (Scintillator Cube Detector)

**Technology:** A 3D array of 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, each cube read out by three wavelength-shifting fibres running along x, y, and z axes, each fibre coupled to an MPPC.

**Why:** The existing FGDs have 2D (x/y) layer readout and cannot reconstruct short, steeply angled tracks — precisely the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons leaving at >50° to the beam. The 1 cm³ granularity gives genuine 3D tracking in all directions, allowing kinematically complete CC event reconstruction including the leading recoil proton at large angles. It fits the available 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m volume, provides hydrocarbon target mass, and directly addresses the 6%→4% systematic uncertainty requirement. The polystyrene provides the hydrocarbon target compatible with the stated physics programme, while the 3D topology separates interaction vertex from secondary activity far more effectively than layered detectors.

---

## 2. High-Angle Time Projection Chambers — HA-TPCs

**Technology:** Two (or more) thin-wall TPCs with resistive Micromegas or resistive MicroPixel readout planes, using the same or similar Ar:CF4:iC4H10 gas mixture as existing TPCs, flanking or surrounding the Super-FGD on the top/bottom and lateral faces within the magnet volume.

**Why:** The existing TPCs downstream only catch forward-going tracks efficiently. Protons at >50° — particularly those in the 450 MeV/c median momentum range (range ~few cm in solid scintillator, so they may exit) — need momentum measurement via curvature in the 0.2 T dipole field for tracks exiting the Super-FGD laterally. HA-TPCs provide dE/dx particle identification (critical for distinguishing protons from pions in the recoil system), momentum measurement by curvature, and coverage of the large-angle acceptance gap. The resistive readout suppresses the ion-feedback and spark risk from heavily ionising proton tracks.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Thin planes (~2 cm) of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., EJ-200 or equivalent) with SiPM readout on both ends, achieving ~200–300 ps timing resolution per plane, placed on the upstream and lateral faces of the new target region.

**Why:** Short low-momentum protons (median 450 MeV/c, range a few cm) that stop inside or just outside the Super-FGD cannot be momentum-analysed by curvature if the track is too short. Time-of-flight between the interaction vertex (timestamped by the Super-FGD) and the ToF plane gives velocity and hence mass-based PID and momentum for these stopping protons. This is essential for the ~35% large-angle proton population and for distinguishing protons from pions (critical for transverse kinematic imbalance, δp_T, measurements). It also provides a fast trigger signal and helps reject out-of-time backgrounds.

---

## 4. Replacement or Augmentation of Upstream ECAL Coverage

**Technology:** Additional lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter panels (matching the existing ECal technology — triangular scintillator bars with WLS fibre and MPPC readout) on the upstream face and re-optimised lateral panels around the new target region.

**Why:** Removing the P0D eliminates the existing upstream electromagnetic calorimeter functionality. π⁰ production accompanies CC interactions and must be identified to correctly classify events and control NC-π⁰ background contamination of the signal sample. Without upstream ECal coverage, photons converting upstream of the Super-FGD would be missed, inflating systematic uncertainties. New panels restore hermetic photon containment and preserve the ability to reconstruct π⁰ → γγ for cross-section constraint.

---

## 5. Upgraded MPPC/SiPM Generation for All New Channels

**Technology:** Current-generation SiPMs with lower dark count rate (~70 kcps at room temperature vs. earlier ~1 Mcps), higher photon detection efficiency (~50% PDE), and reduced after-pulsing probability — e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent — deployed on all new detector channels (Super-FGD cubes, ToF, HA-TPC readout where applicable).

**Why:** The Super-FGD alone has O(50,000–200,000) channels (depending on exact array size). Dark counts in the dense 3D array create fake hits that degrade vertex reconstruction and short-track finding, which are critical for seeing the recoil proton. Modern SiPMs substantially reduce this noise floor, improving reconstruction efficiency for the short, heavily ionising proton tracks that are the key observable for the physics case. Additionally, improved PDE gives better light yield uniformity and reduces channel-to-channel calibration systematics.

---

## 6. Upgraded Data Acquisition and Trigger System

**Technology:** Self-triggered, free-running DAQ architecture using high-speed serialiser links (e.g., GBT/lpGBT protocol as developed for LHC upgrades) with FPGA-based online event building, replacing or supplementing the existing triggered readout.

**Why:** The Super-FGD's ~200,000 3D-readout channels and the ToF planes produce data volumes far exceeding the existing ND280 DAQ bandwidth. A self-triggered free-running system timestamps all hits continuously, enabling offline software triggering — essential for efficiently capturing the large-angle, slow proton topologies that are poorly suited to hardware triggers tuned for forward muons. It also future-proofs the system for increased J-PARC beam power under T2K-II.

---

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Super-FGD active target | 3D scintillator cubes + WLS + MPPC | Large-angle proton/muon reconstruction |
| HA-TPCs | Resistive Micromegas, standard gas | Momentum & PID for exiting large-angle tracks |
| Time-of-Flight planes | Fast plastic scintillator + SiPM | PID/momentum for stopping protons |
| Upstream/lateral ECal | Pb-scint + WLS + MPPC (existing tech) | π⁰ reconstruction, photon hermeticity |
| New-generation SiPMs | Low-noise, high-PDE devices | Noise reduction in dense 3D array |
| Free-running DAQ | lpGBT + FPGA online builder | Bandwidth and software-trigger flexibility |
