TOP RECOMMENDATION: Installation of the Super-FGD 3D scintillator-cube active target, because it is the single change that directly enables kinematically complete large-angle charged-current event reconstruction — the stated physics requirement — and underpins the reduction in systematic uncertainty from 6% to 4% that motivates the entire upgrade.

Based on the physics requirements and constraints described, here are the essential hardware upgrades:

## 1. **Three-Dimensional Active Target Tracker**
**Technology:** Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with electronic readout
**Why:** The requirement for 25% efficiency at ALL angles, including perpendicular and backward-going muons, eliminates any technology with planes perpendicular to the beam. A TPC provides true 3D tracking with no blind spots. The large transverse dimensions (2.6 m × 2.3 m) favor TPC geometry over alternatives like scintillating fibers.

## 2. **Low-Mass, Low-Z Target Medium**
**Technology:** Argon gas (or helium-argon mixture) as TPC medium at ~10 atm pressure
**Why:** The <2% hydrogen constraint eliminates hydrocarbon-based options (plastic scintillator, CH₄ gas). Pure argon or He-Ar mixtures provide adequate target mass while maintaining effectively zero hydrogen content. Pressurization increases interaction rate to compensate for lower density than solid targets.

## 3. **Fine-Pitch Electronic Readout**
**Technology:** Micropattern gas detectors (MicroMegas or GEM-based) with pad readout at ~3mm pitch
**Why:** Detecting 60 MeV protons requires tracking particles with ranges of only ~2-3 cm in 10 atm argon. This demands millimeter-scale position resolution. The short ranges also require low diffusion (favoring Ar over lighter gases) and fast readout to maintain spatial resolution.

## 4. **High-Speed DAQ System**
**Technology:** Continuous streaming readout with ~MHz trigger capability
**Why:** The 0.7 GeV neutrino beam likely comes from a high-intensity proton source with high beam rate. The large active volume with fine segmentation creates substantial data volume requiring modern FPGA-based continuous readout.

## 5. **Field Cage System**
**Technology:** Precision resistive field cage with uniformity <1% over drift region
**Why:** Essential for TPC operation to provide uniform drift field orthogonal to the magnetic field. The 0.9 m drift length requires careful E×B distortion management.

## 6. **Gas Handling and Purification System**
**Technology:** Closed-loop recirculating system with <ppm O₂/H₂O contamination
**Why:** Required for stable TPC operation with minimal electron attachment. High-purity argon maintains drift electron lifetime >ms for the ~0.9 m maximum drift distance.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Time Projection Chamber with micropattern gas detector readout in pressurized argon

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Off-Axis Near Detector

## 1. Why the current detector cannot meet the goal

**The scintillator targets lose high-angle and short tracks.**
- All bars are perpendicular to the beam, so each layer gives only one 2D projection.
- Tracks near 90° run along a single layer and are barely reconstructed.
- Short proton tracks cross only a few layers.
- Yet about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons leave at more than 50°.

**Proton threshold.** A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of about 8 cm in plastic. Protons near 300 MeV/c (about 47 MeV) travel only about 2 cm, which is just two or three 1 cm bar layers in a single projection. Transverse kinematic imbalance needs these protons with good angular and momentum resolution.

**The TPCs only see forward tracks.** They sit downstream along the beam. High-angle muons from the existing targets are measured only coarsely, by the calorimeters and the yoke scintillator, so charge and momentum information is lost.

**Acceptance is not 4π.** This makes the acceptance differ from the 4π acceptance of the water far detector. That mismatch drives model-dependent extrapolation, which is part of the current ~6% systematic.

## 2. Proposed upgrade, built in the vacated upstream region

### (a) Fine-grained 3D-readout scintillator target (main item)
- **Geometry:** about 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56, filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with the 0.6 m dimension vertical.
- **Mass:** about 2 t of CH, roughly doubling the plastic target mass.
- **Readout:** each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z, each read out by a silicon photomultiplier.
  - The channel count is about 192×184 + 192×56 + 184×56 ≈ 56,000, not millions.
  - The three orthogonal views give true 3D voxels and nearly isotropic acceptance.
- **Expected physics performance:**
  - Proton tracking threshold of about 300 MeV/c, with calorimetric energy from range and dE/dx.
  - Good muon/proton/pion separation.
  - Sub-nanosecond hit timing (about 1 ns per channel, better per track). This allows neutron detection and time-of-flight kinetic energy from secondary-interaction cubes.
  - The neutron capability adds full kinematic closure for antineutrino interactions on hydrogen.
- **Engineering issues to address:**
  - Optical crosstalk between cubes, controlled with a reflective etched surface.
  - Fibre-hole alignment over a 2 m span.
  - SiPM dynamic range, electronics and cooling inside the 0.2 T field.

### (b) Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target
- **Placement:** with a 0.6 m-tall target, the remaining height inside the 3.5 m magnet leaves room for TPCs of roughly 2 × 1.8 × 0.8 m above and below it.
- **Purpose:** measure the momentum, charge and dE/dx of high-angle muons and of the most energetic protons. This matters for the roughly 6% above 900 MeV/c, which often escape the target.
- **Readout:** resistive-anode Micromegas.
  - Charge spreading gives better spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads.
  - The resistive layer protects against sparks.
- **Mechanics:** a light composite field cage to minimise dead material between the target and the gas.

### (c) Time-of-flight panels around the new module
- Plastic scintillator bars with SiPMs read out at both ends, aiming for about 150 ps resolution.
- **Uses:**
  - Distinguish tracks entering from outside, such as backward-going interactions in the magnet, from tracks exiting the target.
  - Add particle identification for exiting protons and pions.
  - Veto background from the magnet and yoke.

### (d) Supporting changes
- Upgrade the downstream TPC readout and electronics where it helps common reconstruction.
- Extend the DAQ and timing system to the new channels.
- Keep the existing calorimeter, yoke scintillator and water-layer target so carbon-to-water comparison continues.

## 3. Expected impact

- Near-4π acceptance for muons, with charge and momentum measured at high angles, which matches the far detector's phase space.
- Proton thresholds and resolutions sufficient for transverse kinematic imbalance and neutron-tagged measurements. These constrain nuclear effects and the energy-scale model.
- Doubled target statistics.
- Together these should move the extrapolated flux and cross-section systematic from about 6% toward the 4% target.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2-tonne target of 1 cm³ scintillator cubes, each read by three orthogonal WLS fibres and SiPMs, for isotropic, low-threshold 3D reconstruction of muons and protons.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Active Target Module

## Context Summary

The available envelope is ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m in the upstream photon-tagger slot. The physics driver is kinematically complete CC reconstruction: muon **and** leading proton both tracked, with ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons exiting beyond 50° to beam. Median leading-proton momentum ~450 MeV/c means proton ranges of roughly 5–15 cm in plastic, so the active target must itself provide tracking and ranging — not just interaction vertices.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: Scintillating Fibre (SciFi) Tracker with Fine Granularity

**Technology:** 250 μm diameter scintillating polystyrene fibres (e.g., Kuraray SCSF-78MJ), arranged in X/Y/U/V stereo layers, bonded into ~1 mm thick mats, stacked to give ~30 radiation-length-equivalent layers across the 0.6 m depth.

**Concrete specification:**
- Layer pitch: ~1 mm fibre spacing, 5 stereo views (X, Y, +10°, −10°, X repeat) per superlayer
- ~20 superlayers over 55 cm active depth → ~100 individual fibre planes
- Readout: silicon photomultiplier arrays (e.g., Hamamatsu S13552 MPPC tiles, 1.3 mm pitch pixels) at both fibre ends, daisy-chained via fine-pitch PCB
- Active area per plane: 1.8 × 1.8 m to fit inside the available box with margin
- Expected ~3–4 million readout channels; use CITIROC2A or equivalent 32-channel ASIC front-end

**Rationale:** SciFi gives ~100 μm transverse hit resolution, adequate dE/dx for proton/pion separation at 450 MeV/c, and near-4π geometric acceptance within the slab for large-angle tracks. This is the approach validated in LHCb SciFi and adapted in the NINJA emulsion+SciFi system.

---

## 2. Interleaved Mini-TPC Modules for Low-momentum Proton Recovery

**Technology:** Four small (45 × 45 × 8 cm) bulk-Micromegas or GEM-based gaseous micro-TPC modules, interleaved every ~12 cm depth in the SciFi stack.

**Concrete specification:**
- Gas: Ar:CF₄:isobutane (95:3:2) at atmospheric pressure — fast drift, good dE/dx
- Drift gap: 6 cm, giving ~2 μs maximum drift time
- Readout: 2D strip readout, 1 mm strip pitch, two orientations (X and Y), ~1800 strips per module
- Front-end: APV25 or AFTER ASICs (already deployed in the downstream TPCs — reuse firmware)
- Cathode HV: ~400 V; gas gain ~10⁴ on Micromegas mesh
- These catch proton stubs of 100–250 MeV/c (range 1–4 cm) that would stop inside the gap

**Rationale:** The SciFi alone will miss protons below ~200 MeV/c. Mini-TPC inserts with continuous dE/dx measurement recover the low-end proton spectrum critical for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) completeness, specifically δp_T resolution.

---

## 3. High-granularity Electromagnetic Calorimeter Surround (Mini-ECAL)

**Technology:** Lead–scintillator sampling calorimeter with SiPM readout, wrapping four sides (top, bottom, left, right) of the active target box, using the same WLS-fibre + SiPM chain as the existing downstream ECal.

**Concrete specification:**
- Absorber: 1.5 mm lead sheets interleaved with 3 mm extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (triangular cross-section, 7 mm height, same extrusion tooling as existing detector)
- 15 layers → ~4 X₀, sufficient to tag photons from π⁰ decay and bremsstrahlung
- Bar orientation alternates X and Y per layer; WLS fibre (Y-11, 1 mm dia.) glued in groove, read by 1.3 × 1.3 mm² MPPC (Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS)
- Downstream face: 5-layer pure-scintillator muon tagger (no absorber), 10 mm bars, to flag muons exiting forward before they enter the main downstream tracker
- Total material budget kept to <0.3 X₀ on the upstream face so it does not degrade the neutrino target

**Rationale:** Photon tagging from the removed upstream section must be partially recovered. Even 4 X₀ surrounding the active target will intercept >80% of photons from π⁰s produced in the target, maintaining NC/CC background control for the TKI analysis.

---

## 4. Thin Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) Muon Ranger Insert

**Technology:** Six layers of 2 mm-gap glass-electrode RPCs (strip readout, 1 cm pitch), mounted in the downstream half of the available box behind the SciFi+TPC stack, acting as a compact muon ranger/identifier.

**Concrete specification:**
- Plate size: 1.8 × 1.6 m per layer, 6 layers interleaved with 1 cm iron absorber sheets (total 6 cm Fe ~ 3.4 interaction lengths for muons → ranges muons up to ~300 MeV/c within the box)
- Gas: standard RPC tetrafluoroethane/isobutane/SF₆ mix
- Readout: copper strip FPCB, differential signal into MAROC3 ASICs
- Provides μ/π separation via track straightness and stopping signature for forward-going low-energy muons that would otherwise enter the downstream TPCs with ambiguous identity

**Rationale:** At 0.6 GeV beam peak, quasi-elastic events produce muons of 200–600 MeV/c. Those at the low end stop within tens of cm and benefit enormously from an integrated ranger rather than relying on the downstream main tracker, reducing the muon momentum reconstruction uncertainty from ~15% to ~3% via range.

---

## 5. Precision Timing Layer: LGAD (Low-Gain Avalanche Detector) Silicon Planes

**Technology:** Two planes of AC-coupled LGAD sensors (35 μm active layer, 1.3 × 1.3 mm² pixel pitch), one at the upstream face and one at mid-depth of the new target.

**Concrete specification:**
- Sensor tiles: 2 × 2 cm² LGAD tiles (e.g., Hamamatsu HPK prototype or BNL/UFSD production), tiled to cover 1.6 × 1.6 m active area
- Timing resolution target: σ_t < 100 ps per plane (demonstrated in CMS ETL prototype)
- Readout: ALTIROC2 ASIC (designed for ATLAS HGTD, available), 25 ps TDC bin
- Purpose: event-by-event pile-up rejection (beam spill structure at ~100 ns bunch spacing), and time-of-flight proton/pion separation for tracks of 200–600 MeV/c over the ~50 cm track length (Δt_p−π ~ 300–1500 ps — cleanly resolvable)

**Rationale:** ToF-based p/π separation at these momenta is cleaner than dE/dx alone and addresses a known systematic in TKI analyses where pion contamination in the "leading proton" sample biases δα_T and δp_T distributions. This is a relatively low-mass insert (<0.1% X₀ per plane).

## 6. Online Data Concentration: Upgraded Trigger and DAQ Board

**Technology:** Replace the existing TRIP-t front-end boards in this section with **ATLAS FELIX-based** (Front-End Link eXchange) readout, running continuous triggerless streaming to a small GPU farm.

**Concrete specification:**
- 4× FELIX PCIe cards (100 Gbps aggregate), each serving ~250k channels via GBT links
- GPU farm: 8× NVIDIA A30 cards running real-time track-seeding (using CUDA-based Kalman filter as in Allen/HLT1 framework) to perform online vertex finding and select CC events within the 10 μs beam gate
- Output trigger rate: ~2 kHz CC-enriched events (factor ~5 reduction in data volume)
- Synchronisation to existing detector: use White Rabbit timing nodes already in the facility

**Rationale:** The SciFi + LGAD channel count (~3 M channels) would overflow existing TRIP-t-based DAQ bandwidth. Triggerless streaming with online GPU reconstruction is now mature (LHCb Run 3 demonstrating this at higher rates) and essential to make the upgrade practically operable.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## 1. High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC as the New Active Target

**Technology:** A high-pressure (≥5–10 bar) gaseous argon TPC with micro-pattern gas detector (MPGD) readout (MicroMegas or GEM foils), fitted into the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.

**Physics motivation:** The existing gas TPCs downstream already demonstrate the micro-pattern readout principle. At elevated pressure, the density increases proportionally, giving meaningful interaction rates on argon while retaining the hallmark of gaseous TPCs: very low detection thresholds and continuous 3D tracking with no dead material. Crucially, proton tracking thresholds as low as ~100 MeV/c kinetic energy (~450 MeV/c momentum) are achievable, covering the bulk of the leading-proton momentum distribution (median ~450 MeV/c) and capturing the large-angle protons (35% beyond 50°) that would range out or miss acceptance in a denser medium. This directly enables the kinematically complete charged-current topology—both muon and leading proton reconstructed—needed for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurements. Using argon as target nucleus also allows direct cross-section ratio comparisons with liquid-argon far detectors.

---

## 2. Plastic Scintillator "Super-Module" with Fine Transverse Segmentation

**Technology:** A finely segmented plastic scintillator target module (extruded polystyrene bars, ~6 × 6 mm cross-section or smaller, SiPM readout), replacing or augmenting the upstream photon-tagging section in the available volume.

**Physics motivation:** The existing plastic tracking targets use 9.6 × 9.6 mm bars. Halving the bar cross-section roughly doubles the spatial resolution per plane. For large-angle, short proton tracks (the 35% leaving at >50°, often stopping within a few centimetres), finer segmentation dramatically improves dE/dx-based particle identification and momentum-by-range measurements. The hydrocarbon target is explicitly accepted for the physics programme, so a denser, more finely sampled scintillator module directly increases statistics for TKI analyses. SiPM readout (already established on this detector) keeps channel count manageable.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) System on the Upstream and Downstream Faces

**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator panels (EJ-200 or similar, ~1 cm thick) with SiPM arrays achieving <200 ps time resolution, installed on the upstream and downstream faces of the new active target volume.

**Physics motivation:** At 450 MeV/c a proton has β ≈ 0.43 and a pion has β ≈ 0.95; over even 50 cm this gives a ~1 ns separation—comfortably resolved at 200 ps resolution. Critically, for the ~6% of protons exceeding 900 MeV/c, momentum-by-range fails because those protons may exit the target. ToF provides an independent momentum/velocity measurement that, combined with tracking, closes the kinematic reconstruction. ToF also tags backwards-going particles that the TPC alone would misidentify, reducing the systematic uncertainty from particle misidentification which currently contributes to the 6% residual.

---

## 4. Thin Resistive-Plate Chamber (RPC) or Scintillator Layers in the Magnet Return-Yoke Gaps

**Technology:** Additional planes of 3 mm-pitch strip RPCs or extruded scintillator bars interleaved into the existing return-yoke instrumentation, extending the muon ranger acceptance.

**Physics motivation:** With 25% of muons leaving at >50° to the beam, those muons often enter the return yoke at steep angles and may range out before reaching enough measurement planes for a reliable momentum determination. Increasing the sampling density in the yoke gaps (which already exist and are partially instrumented) reduces the momentum resolution for these large-angle muons—where the lever arm of multiple scattering is shortest—without requiring any new magnet infrastructure. Better muon momentum reconstruction directly tightens the neutrino energy estimator and reduces the flux systematic, addressing the path from 6% → 4%.

---

## 5. Thin Lead-Converter + Tracking Sandwich for Photon Veto Improvement

**Technology:** Two or three "preshower" layers of 1–2 mm lead foils immediately upstream of the new active target, interleaved with single-sided silicon strip detectors or fine-pitch scintillator, acting as an active photon converter.

**Physics motivation:** The removed photon-tagging section previously vetoed π⁰→γγ backgrounds. Without it, electromagnetic backgrounds entering the new active target from upstream neutrino interactions will degrade the signal purity of quasi-elastic CC events used for TKI. Thin converter layers (totalling <0.5 X₀) convert early enough to tag photons yet introduce minimal hadronic re-interaction for the protons of interest (proton interaction length in Pb ~170 g/cm²; a few mm is negligible). This preserves the photon-rejection functionality lost when the upstream section is removed, protecting the systematic budget.

---

## 6. Water-Target Insert Compatible with the New Active Volume

**Technology:** A thin-walled (1–2 mm aluminium) water-layer module that can be inserted into or immediately downstream of the new gas TPC target, with ~2 cm water layers interleaved with tracking planes.

**Physics motivation:** The downstream water-layer target is retained for carbon-to-water comparison, but it is separated from the high-resolution new target by the downstream gas TPC region. Installing an interchangeable (or simultaneous) thin water layer within the new upstream volume allows cross-section measurements on oxygen with the same kinematic completeness and tracking resolution as the hydrocarbon measurements, ensuring that the neutrino flux uncertainty cancels in the ratio. This is essential to constrain the water far-detector systematic at the 4% level.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: High-pressure gaseous argon TPC as the new active neutrino target, because it simultaneously provides the sub-100 MeV/c proton detection threshold, full 3D large-angle acceptance, and continuous dE/dx particle identification required for kinematically complete CC event reconstruction—the core requirement of the entire upgrade programme.

This is a challenging design problem requiring detection of tracks at all angles, including backwards and perpendicular to the beam, with sensitivity to short-range protons down to 60 MeV kinetic energy. Let me analyze the requirements systematically:

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Angular coverage**: Full 4π acceptance needed (including backward-going muons)
2. **Low-energy proton detection**: 60 MeV protons have ~1 cm range in plastic, ~10 cm in gas
3. **Hydrogen constraint**: ≤20% of target nucleons must be hydrogen
4. **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m active target region
5. **Muon reconstruction**: ≥25% efficiency at all angles

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Primary Recommendation)**

Deploy a **segmented plastic scintillator cube detector** with 1.0-1.5 cm³ voxels, read out via wavelength-shifting fibers to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Justification:**
- Provides true 3D tracking with ~1 cm granularity adequate for 60 MeV proton ranges
- Plastic scintillator (CH) has appropriate hydrogen fraction (~7.7% nucleons are hydrogen, well under 20%)
- 4π angular acceptance inherent to cubic geometry
- Fast timing (ns-scale) enables event separation in beam spill
- Mature technology: Similar to MINERvA, FGD (Fine-Grained Detector) in T2K
- Cost-effective for ~6 m³ volume with modern SiPM readout

**Specific implementation:** 
- 1 cm × 1 cm × 1.5 cm extruded scintillator bars in alternating X-Y-Z layers
- WLS fiber + SiPM readout (~50,000 channels)
- Target total of ~60-80 layers

### 2. **Surrounding Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Shell**

Install a **thin gaseous TPC layer** (15-20 cm thickness) on all six faces of the scintillator cube, particularly upstream and side walls.

**Justification:**
- Provides excellent dE/dx for particle ID (separating protons from pions)
- Low mass, minimal hydrogen contribution
- Continuous tracking improves angular resolution
- Catches particles exiting the dense target at all angles
- Proven technology (e.g., MicroBooNE, ND280)

**Specific implementation:**
- Ar:CH₄ (95:5) or similar gas mixture
- ~2.5 mm pitch readout pads or micromegas
- Drift field ~400 V/cm

### 3. **Upstream Tracking Stations**

Add **2-3 thin scintillating fiber or silicon strip planes** 20-50 cm upstream of the target.

**Justification:**
- Tags incoming beam particles (critical for beam-related backgrounds)
- Identifies backward-going muons versus forward particles
- Provides t₀ timing for TPC drift
- Improves vertex resolution

**Specific implementation:**
- 250 μm scintillating fibers with SiPM readout, or
- 60 μm silicon microstrips (~30 cm × 30 cm planes)

### 4. **High-Density Passive Target Inserts (Optional Enhancement)**

Provide **removable carbon or CH₂ slabs** that can be inserted between scintillator modules.

**Justification:**
- Increases interaction rate when needed
- Carbon provides hydrogen-free comparison sample
- CH₂ with different H fractions enables systematic studies
- Maintains constraint: can keep ≤20% H nucleons overall

### 5. **Enhanced Downstream Magnetic Tracking**

Upgrade the existing gas chambers to **straw tubes or drift tubes with finer segmentation** (4 mm diameter).

**Justification:**
- Improves momentum resolution for muons exiting target
- Better pattern recognition in 0.15 T field
- Reduces combinatorial background
- Proven technology (ATLAS TRT, COSY-TOF, T2K P0D)

## Why NOT Other Options:

- **Pure TPC target**: Too slow for beam spill pileup, insufficient stopping power for 60 MeV protons in reasonable volume
- **Liquid argon TPC**: Excellent choice but likely beyond budget/schedule for retrofit; requires cryogenics
- **Emulsion**: No active triggering, labor-intensive scanning, poor timing
- **Water Cherenkov**: Insufficient granularity for short protons, poor angular resolution

## Implementation Priority:

1. **Phase 1**: 3D scintillator cube + upstream trackers
2. **Phase 2**: TPC shell on critical faces (sides/upstream)
3. **Phase 3**: Enhanced downstream tracking + passive target options

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Deploy a fine-grained (1-1.5 cm³ voxel) plastic scintillator cube tracker with SiPM readout as the active target, providing 4π acceptance, adequate stopping power for low-energy protons, and appropriate hydrogen fraction.**

# Upgrade Proposal: Active Target for the Kestrel Flats Near Station

## The constraint that drives everything: the hydrogen fraction

The usual near-detector active target is plastic scintillator (CH), as in ND280's FGDs or SuperFGD. It fails here on composition, before performance is even considered:

- In CH, hydrogen is 1 nucleon out of 13, about **7.7% of target nucleons**.
- Water is 2 out of 18, about 11%.
- Both are far above the 2% limit where the hydrogen-subtraction model stays adequate.

Since the far detector contains no hydrogen, the cleanest choice is a target with essentially zero hydrogen. Argon meets this, and it also matches an argon far detector if that is what the far site uses. That reasoning sets the primary recommendation.

---

## 1. Pixelated liquid-argon TPC as the active target (primary upgrade)

**Technology**
- A modular LArTPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region.
- Short drift cells of roughly 30–50 cm, in the ArgonCube / ND-LAr style.
- Native 3D pixel charge readout instead of wire planes.
- The cryostat sits inside the warm 0.15 T dipole. LAr operation is unaffected by the field, and the magnet's field-free requirement is not an issue.

**Mass:** about 5.4 m³ × 1.39 t/m³ ≈ **7.5 t of argon**, of which roughly 4–5 t is fiducial.

**Physics motivation**
- **Hydrogen fraction ≈ 0%.** The 2% budget is met trivially, and the hydrogen-subtraction model is never stressed.
- **Same nucleus as an argon far detector.** Nuclear effects (Fermi motion, 2p2h, final-state interactions) cancel between near and far. If the far detector is not argon, argon is still a hydrogen-free, well-modelled heavy target.
- **Isotropic acceptance.** A LArTPC images tracks in 3D at any angle, including perpendicular and backward-going ones. A planar tracker loses exactly these, so this directly serves the "≥25% muon efficiency at every angle" requirement.
- **Low proton threshold.**
  - A 60 MeV kinetic-energy proton ranges about 3 cm in LAr, i.e. about 7–8 pixel pitches at ~4 mm.
  - dE/dx Bragg-peak identification works down to roughly 30–40 MeV.
  - This meets the 60 MeV requirement with margin, at all angles.
- **Pile-up handling at 410 m.** The beam flux this close to the target gives several interactions per spill in ~7 t.
  - Modular drift cells keep drift times short.
  - Pixel readout removes the wire-ambiguity problem.
  - Segmented optical detectors give ns-level event timing.
  - Together these let overlapping interactions be separated.

## 2. Segmented, fast photon-detection system inside the TPC modules

**Technology:** dielectric light traps (ArCLight/LCM-type) or X-ARAPUCA tiles, read by SiPMs, segmented per drift module.

**Physics motivation**
- Provides t₀ for each interaction, which is needed for drift-coordinate reconstruction and absolute positioning.
- Associates tracks with the correct interaction under pile-up.
- Supplies a trigger and rejects cosmics.
- Gives nanosecond timing that can distinguish forward from backward-going tracks crossing module boundaries.

## 3. Wrap-around tracking for tracks that miss the downstream chambers

**Technology:** thin gas TPCs or drift chambers, plus scintillator-bar planes, on the sides and upstream face of the cryostat, still inside the dipole field. Scintillator side muon-range detectors (SMRD-style) go in the magnet yoke gaps.

**Physics motivation**
- The existing drift chambers sit downstream, so they only measure tracks that exit forward.
- With only 0.9 m of depth along the beam, high-angle and backward muons mostly exit through the sides or upstream face.
- Side and upstream chambers in the 0.15 T field give these tracks curvature, hence momentum and charge.
- Range in the yoke detectors covers muons that stop there.
- This is what makes ≥25% efficiency at 90° and in the backward hemisphere achievable. Without it, the TPC contains the vertex but cannot measure momentum or charge for exiting sideways muons.

## 4. Low-mass cryostat walls and minimal dead material

**Technology:** thin-wall or composite-membrane cryostat panels between the TPC and the external trackers.

**Physics motivation**
- Reduces multiple scattering and energy loss for muons exiting toward the side and downstream chambers, improving momentum resolution and matching efficiency.
- Keeps non-argon, hydrogen-bearing material out of the fiducial region. Any G10 or plastic structure inside must be accounted for in the 2% hydrogen budget.

## 5. Electromagnetic calorimeter downstream and on the sides (secondary)

**Technology:** lead–scintillator sampling ECal. It sits outside the argon target, so its hydrogen does not enter the target nucleon count.

**Physics motivation**
- Containment and identification of π⁰ photons from interactions in the TPC.
- Tagging of neutral backgrounds entering from outside, such as "sand" neutrons and photons.

---

## Why not the alternatives

| Option | Problem |
|---|---|
| Plastic scintillator (CH) target | About 7.7% hydrogen nucleons, which fails the 2% limit |
| Water-based target | About 11% hydrogen nucleons, which also fails |
| High-pressure gaseous argon TPC alone | Excellent threshold, but only about 0.1 t of target in this volume, giving too low a rate |

High-pressure gaseous argon is better used as a complementary option than as the main target.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a hydrogen-free, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (with segmented SiPM light detection) for 4π acceptance, a ~3 cm proton threshold, and 0% hydrogen nucleons.

# ND280 Upgrade Proposal: Recommended Hardware Changes

## The problem with the current detector

The existing FGDs do not give kinematically complete events at the angles and momenta this beam produces.

- **Angular acceptance is too narrow.** FGD bars run only in x and y, perpendicular to the beam.
  - High-angle tracks run nearly parallel to the bar planes, so they hit few layers and reconstruct poorly.
  - The TPCs sit up- and downstream of the targets, so tracks above about 50 degrees, or going backward, rarely reach them.
  - This affects about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons.
- **The proton threshold is too high.** A proton must cross several 1 cm bars to give a 3D track, which sets an effective threshold of roughly 450 MeV/c. That is the median of the leading-proton spectrum, so about half the protons are lost.
- **There is no neutron tagging.** Without it, the hadronic final state stays incomplete.
- **The upstream P0D adds little.** Its mass is passive (brass, lead, water), it gives no particle-level reconstruction, and it occupies the volume that could hold a fine-grained active target.

## Hardware upgrades

**1. A new highly segmented 3D scintillator target ("SuperFGD")**
- **Technology:**
  - About 2 million 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, giving about 2 t of hydrocarbon target. A grid of 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, about 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.56 m, fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
  - Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z.
  - Each fibre is read by an MPPC at one end, giving about 56,000 channels and three 2D projections.
- **Why:**
  - Fibres in all three directions give roughly uniform, near-4π acceptance, including high-angle and backward tracks.
  - Tracks just a few cm long become reconstructable, which lowers the proton threshold to about 300 MeV/c and recovers most of the spectrum below the 450 MeV/c median.
  - Calorimetric dE/dx separates protons from pions.
  - Fine granularity lets the detector find neutron-induced secondary hits. Combined with sub-ns timing, this gives time-of-flight neutron kinematics.
  - Together these provide the complete muon-plus-proton (and neutron) final state needed for transverse kinematic imbalance studies.
  - Hydrocarbon is acceptable for this programme, and FGD2 remains for the carbon-to-water comparison.

**2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the new target**
- **Technology:**
  - Gas TPCs filled with the existing Ar:CF4:iC4H10 (95:3:2) gas.
  - A lightweight composite (aramid/laminate) field cage to minimise dead material.
  - Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM") readout. Charge spreading gives better spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads and suppresses sparking.
  - Compact front-end electronics based on the AFTER/AGET chips.
- **Why:**
  - Tracks leaving the target at high angle need momentum measured from curvature in the 0.2 T field, and their charge sign determined.
  - They also need particle identification from dE/dx (muon, electron, proton, pion).
  - This is essential for the high-momentum tail: about 6% of protons exceed 900 MeV/c and are not contained in the target, so range cannot measure them.

**3. A Time-of-Flight (ToF) detector enclosing the new target and HA-TPCs**
- **Technology:**
  - Six planes of plastic scintillator bars, about 2.2 m long and 12 cm wide.
  - Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs, with fast digitisation for timing resolution of roughly 150 ps or better.
- **Why:**
  - Timing determines track direction, separating backward from forward tracks and rejecting out-of-fiducial (sand/magnet) backgrounds and cosmics.
  - It adds ToF-based particle identification for electron and muon versus proton.
  - It provides a precise reference time for neutron ToF in the new target.

**4. Supporting upgrades (needed but secondary)**
- **New target readout:** MPPC front-end boards (e.g. CITIROC-based) with multi-hit, ns-level timing.
- **Integration:** global trigger/DAQ and clock distribution so the new subsystems run alongside the existing TPCs, FGDs, ECals and SMRD.
- **Calibration:** an LED/light-injection calibration system.
- **Mechanics:** mechanical integration inside the UA1/NOMAD magnet, including P0D removal.
- **ECal:** upstream ECal coverage retained or adapted where the P0D's ECal is affected.

## Expected impact

These upgrades provide:
- full polar-angle acceptance for muons and protons;
- a proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c;
- neutron detection;
- better electron/gamma separation.

Together they improve flux and cross-section constraints toward the roughly 4% systematic uncertainty T2K-II requires.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD-type 3D target of ~2 million 1 cm scintillator cubes, each threaded by three orthogonal WLS fibres with MPPC readout, giving near-4π acceptance and a ~300 MeV/c proton threshold.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Target Region

## The core problem

The existing layout is a target followed by drift chambers downstream. It reconstructs forward-going tracks well. It loses three things the analysis needs:

1. **High-angle muons (near 90°).** These never reach the downstream chambers, or cross them at grazing angles.
2. **Backward muons.** Nothing upstream can measure them, and the detector cannot tell a backward track from a forward one.
3. **Short protons.** At the 60 MeV kinetic energy threshold, a proton travels only about 3 cm in plastic. A coarse, layered target with 2D (bar) readout cannot reconstruct that isotropically.

Each of the upgrades below targets one of these gaps.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-readout scintillator target (most important)

**Design**
- Replace the target with a matrix of about 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes.
- Run three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres through each cube, read out by SiPMs. This gives three 2D projections, so every hit is located in 3D.
- Suggested size: about 2.0 m (wide) × 1.0–1.2 m (high) × 0.6 m (along beam). This is roughly 1.2–1.4 million cubes, about 1.3 t of active mass. It leaves vertical room for the TPCs in item 2.

**Proton threshold**
- A 60 MeV proton has a range of about 3 cm, so it crosses about 3 cubes in any direction.
- Reconstruction of protons down to about 300 MeV/c momentum (about 47 MeV kinetic energy) has been demonstrated in this kind of detector, so 60 MeV is achievable at all angles.
- Particle ID comes from dE/dx along the track and the Bragg peak.

**Muon angular coverage**
- The isotropic granularity gives near-uniform tracking efficiency at all angles.
- Muons that stop inside the target get their momentum from range.

**Hydrogen fraction**
- Polystyrene is (CH)ₙ. Hydrogen nuclei are 1/13 of the nucleons, about 7.7%, which is well below the 20% limit.
- Even polyethylene-like CH₂ would be about 14%.
- Keep hydrogen-rich passive materials (thick plastic supports, large water volumes) out of the fiducial volume.

## 2. Horizontal high-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Design**
- Install two thin gas TPCs, each about 2.0 m × 0.6 m × 0.4–0.5 m tall, filling the remaining height of the 2.3 m region.
- Use a low-mass field cage, a T2K-like gas such as Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀, and resistive Micromegas readout.

**Role**
- They measure momentum and charge of muons exiting at high angles, which the downstream chambers miss.

**Momentum resolution check at 0.15 T**
- Assume a 0.7 GeV/c muon crossing about 0.5 m of TPC.
- The sagitta is s = 0.3BL²/(8p) ≈ 2 mm.
- With about 0.5–0.7 mm point resolution over about 50 pads, this gives roughly 10% momentum resolution. That is adequate.
- Charge determination is unambiguous at these momenta.
- The orientation must match the field direction. With a horizontal field perpendicular to the beam, tracks bend in the vertical–longitudinal plane, which the top and bottom TPCs sample well.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the target and TPCs

**Design**
- Six faces of scintillator bars with SiPM readout at both ends, aiming for about 150 ps or better timing.

**Role**
- **Direction:** A track crossing about 1 m takes about 3.3 ns, so the timing cleanly separates backward-going tracks from forward ones entering from outside. This is essential for the backward-muon requirement.
- **Particle ID:** Combined with TPC momentum, it separates e/μ/p.
- **Vetoing:** It rejects tracks entering from interactions in the magnet and surrounding material.

## 4. Supporting items

- **Electronics:** Mount SiPM and TPC front-end electronics outside the active volume on low-mass mechanics, without hydrogen-rich structural plastics. Use triggerless or beam-synchronous readout matched to the spill time structure.
- **Matching to existing chambers:** Keep the forward-going path into the existing downstream drift chambers clear, so forward muons keep long lever-arm momentum measurement.
- **Calibration:**
  - Cosmic-ray trigger.
  - SiPM gain monitoring.
  - Survey of the 0.15 T field map in the new TPC volumes, since the warm dipole's fringe field near the upstream end matters.
- **Test-beam validation:** Calibrate the proton response and threshold at about 50–100 MeV in a charged-particle beam before installation.

## Expected result

Combining the three systems gives the coverage the analysis requires:

| Muon direction | Measured by |
|---|---|
| Forward | Downstream drift chambers |
| High angle | Horizontal TPCs |
| Backward | TOF plus horizontal TPCs |
| Stopping | Range in the 3D target |

This delivers at least 25% muon efficiency over the full solid angle. It also gives proton reconstruction above about 50–60 MeV at all angles, with hydrogen at about 8% of target nucleons.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target with a ~1 cm-granularity 3D-readout plastic-scintillator cube active target (≈7.7% hydrogen nucleons), complemented by high-angle TPCs and TOF.

# Proposed hardware upgrades for the off-axis near detector

## Why the current detector falls short

- **High-angle tracks are lost.** The tracking target bars all lie perpendicular to the beam, and the gas TPCs sit only downstream. Tracks at large angles therefore run along a single bar layer and never reach a TPC. That covers about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons above 50°.
- **Low-momentum protons are lost.** A proton of about 450 MeV/c has about 100 MeV kinetic energy and ranges only about 7–8 cm in plastic. Many protons stop after a few bars, so 2D x/y readout cannot reconstruct them well.
- **The result is incomplete events.** The current detector cannot deliver complete μ + p events, and therefore cannot provide transverse kinematic imbalance.

## Upgrades

### 1. New active target in the photon-tagging volume: a 3D-granular scintillator-cube target ("SuperFGD"-type)

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, about 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, which fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Total mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly doubling the existing hydrocarbon target mass.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, giving three 2D projections.
- Readout uses about 56,000 SiPM channels, consistent with the existing SiPM/WLS readout philosophy.

**Why**
- **Full angular acceptance.** The response is isotropic, so tracks at any angle, including backward-going ones, are reconstructed.
- **Low proton threshold.** Fine 3D granularity allows a proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c, covering the bulk of the proton spectrum below its 450 MeV/c median.
- **Particle identification.** Calorimetric dE/dx is available for stopping particles.
- **Neutrons.** Sub-ns timing allows neutron detection by time of flight between isolated hits, adding further kinematic constraint.
- **Physics fit.** Hydrocarbon is acceptable, and the downstream water target stays in place for the carbon-to-water comparison.

### 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Argon-based gas TPCs inside the 0.2 T field.
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated-resistor) Micromegas. Charge spreading improves spatial resolution with larger pads and fewer channels, and the resistive layer protects against sparks.
- A thin, light field cage (composite/aramid laminate) minimises dead material.

**Why**
- High-angle muons, and the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that exit the target, need magnetic momentum and charge measurement.
- These TPCs also provide dE/dx particle identification for exiting tracks.
- This closes the large-angle acceptance hole of the existing forward-only TPCs.

### 3. Time-of-flight enclosure around the new target and high-angle TPCs

**Technology**
- Six panels of plastic scintillator bars with SiPMs at both ends.
- Timing resolution of about 100–150 ps.

**Why**
- Determines track direction (forward vs backward, entering vs exiting).
- Rejects out-of-fiducial and magnet-originated backgrounds and cosmics.
- Adds particle identification, separating e/μ/p at low momentum.

### 4. Readout electronics, data acquisition and calibration

**Technology**
- New front-end electronics for the cube target, with high channel count and fine timing.
- Front-end electronics for the resistive Micromegas.
- Integration into the existing data acquisition and trigger.
- An LED/laser calibration system and cosmic-trigger capability.

**Why** These keep timing and gain stable at the level needed for neutron time of flight and for the 4% systematic target.

### 5. Integration and service items

- Support structure for the new target and TPCs.
- Removal of the photon-tagging section.
- Retaining and refurbishing the yoke-gap scintillator planes, the lead-scintillator calorimeters and the downstream TPC/target stack so the new and old systems combine.

## Physics payoff

Complete muon + proton (+ neutron) reconstruction over nearly 4π gives transverse kinematic imbalance and nuclear-effect constraints. This improves the flux and cross-section model, aiming to reduce the residual systematic from about 6% toward the 4% required.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a ~2 t, 3D-readout fine-granularity (1 cm³) scintillator-cube target (SuperFGD-type), read out by three orthogonal WLS fibres and SiPMs, for 4π acceptance and low-threshold proton reconstruction.

**Description:** A fully 3-D segmented scintillator cube detector filling the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume with ~1 cm³ polystyrene cubes (this is in fact the direction the T2K-II ND280 upgrade has taken, so the physics case is well-established).

**Geometry:** ~1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm extruded polystyrene cubes with a central hole in all three orthogonal axes, each threaded by a wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre read out at both ends by MPPCs (SiPMs).

**Description:** Six planes of fast scintillator (e.g., 2 cm thick BC-404 or equivalent), one on each face of the SuperFGD volume, read out by MPPCs via WLS fibres.

- Upstream face: 2.0 × 1.9 m, ~200 bars
- Downstream face: same
- Four lateral faces: thinner frames

**Physics benefit:**
- Distinguishes forward from backward-going tracks (critical for beam-direction ambiguity at large angles)
- Separates protons from pions via time-of-flight over the ~20–60 cm path inside the target: at 450 MeV/c, Δt(p–π) ≈ 1.5 ns over 30 cm → significant with 1 ns resolution
- Tags neutron-induced backgrounds (out-of-time hits)
- Provides an independent t₀ for TPC drift-time calibration

- Catches muons and protons exiting at large polar angles (>50°) that miss the downstream TPCs

## Physics Requirements Analysis

**Geometry constraints:**
- Active target volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (transverse × transverse × longitudinal)
- Must reconstruct tracks at all angles including 90° and backward-going
- Muons: ≥25% efficiency at every angle
- Protons: down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range in water ~3.5 mm; in scintillator ~5 mm)

**60 MeV proton range estimates:**
- In liquid argon: ~4 mm
- In plastic scintillator (density ~1.03): ~5 mm
- In water: ~3.5 mm
- This sets the maximum granularity needed

**Hydrogen constraint:**
- H must be ≤2% of target nucleons by number
- Pure water: H is ~11% by mass, ~67% of nucleons — far too much
- Pure hydrocarbon (CH₂): H is ~14% by mass, ~50% of nucleons — far too much
- Pure carbon (graphite): 0% H — acceptable but not a practical active target alone
- Liquid argon: 0% H — fine, but see below
- The constraint effectively **rules out** water targets and pure plastic scintillator as the primary target material

**Hydrogen nucleon fraction calculation for polystyrene (C₈H₈):**
- H atoms per monomer: 8, C atoms: 8
- Nucleons: 8×1 + 8×12 = 8 + 96 = 104; H fraction = 8/104 ≈ 7.7% — too high

**For a composite target to get H ≤ 2%:**
- Must be predominantly high-A material
- E.g., iron or lead interleaved with thin active layers
- Or liquid argon (A=40, no H)
- Or a scintillator heavily loaded with high-Z material

**Beam and momentum measurement:**
- 0.7 GeV peak flux, near detector at 410 m: high rate environment
- Existing downstream drift chambers + 0.15 T dipole handle downstream-going tracks well
- Backward and perpendicular tracks do **not** exit into the downstream spectrometer — need momentum measurement within or around the active target itself

---

## Required Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Detector (plastic scintillator cubes with WLS fiber readout)

**Technology:** Array of ~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers along three orthogonal axes (SuperFGD-style), with SiPM photosensors.

**Why:**
- 1.5 cm cubes give sufficient granularity to detect ~60 MeV proton tracks (range ~3–5 cm = ~2–3 cubes) at all angles
- Three-axis fiber readout gives full 3D track reconstruction including perpendicular and backward-going tracks — directly addressing the ≥25% efficiency at all angles requirement
- Plastic scintillator (C₈H₈) has ~7.7% H nucleon fraction — this **exceeds** the 2% limit, so the scintillator must be replaced or heavily diluted

**Resolution of H constraint:** The cube array must use a **low-hydrogen or hydrogen-free scintillator**, or more practically, the target must be predominantly a high-A material. The standard solution for ≤2% H is to use the scintillator as a **minority fraction** embedded in a heavier matrix, OR to use **gadolinium-doped or lead-doped** panels, OR to design the target as alternating thin scintillator planes with thick carbon/iron absorber slabs. However, if the goal is an *active* neutrino interaction target (not a sampling calorimeter), the preferred modern solution is:

- **Carbon-dominant target:** Use graphite or carbon plates as the primary target material, with thin scintillator planes interleaved. Carbon has 0% H; thin scintillator layers contribute <2% H nucleons overall.
- Alternatively, a **liquid argon time projection chamber (LArTPC)** satisfies the H constraint (zero hydrogen) and provides the required granularity, but the volume (~6 m³) and the near-detector high-rate environment make LArTPC technically challenging.

**Most practical modern solution matching all constraints:** A **SuperFGD-type 3D scintillating fiber/cube detector** with the cube composition adjusted — specifically, using polystyrene cubes interspersed with carbon plates such that total H nucleon fraction ≤2%. The active target is a *sampling* active target.

---

### 2. Surrounding Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) on the lateral faces

**Technology:** High-pressure gaseous Ar TPCs (or low-mass wire/pad TPCs with Ar:CF₄ or Ar:isobutane gas), placed on the four sides (top, bottom, left, right) and the upstream face of the active target volume.

**Why:**
- Tracks exiting sideways or backward from the active target enter these TPCs for momentum measurement by curvature in the dipole field
- The existing downstream drift chambers handle forward tracks; the lateral TPCs close the acceptance gap for perpendicular and backward tracks, achieving the required ≥25% muon reconstruction efficiency at all angles
- TPCs provide dE/dx particle identification, helping distinguish muons from protons at low momentum
- Low-mass construction minimizes secondary interactions and multiple scattering

---

### 3. Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECal) surrounding the TPC/target system

**Technology:** Lead–scintillator sampling calorimeter with WLS fiber readout and SiPM sensors, segmented in 3D, surrounding the lateral TPCs on all six faces.

**Why:**
- Captures photons from π⁰ decay and electrons for background rejection
- Provides energy containment for electromagnetic showers from interactions in the active target
- Needed for full event reconstruction and to separate NC π⁰ backgrounds from signal
- SiPMs are compatible with the modest magnetic field environment

---

### 4. Upgraded Downstream Spectrometer: Additional drift chamber stations and improved electronics

**Technology:** Additional drift chamber planes with smaller cell size and updated front-end ASICs with faster shaping time and higher rate capability (e.g., AFTER/AGET-based electronics).

**Why:**
- Near-detector environment has very high neutrino interaction rate; existing chambers may have occupancy and pile-up issues
- Higher rate electronics reduce track-merging inefficiency for forward-going muons
- Additional stations improve pattern recognition for the high-multiplicity events expected at 410 m from target

---

### 5. Scintillator Muon Range Detector (MRD) / Downstream stopping muon catcher

**Technology:** Interleaved iron plates and scintillator bars (or scintillator paddles with SiPMs), placed downstream of the existing drift chambers.

**Why:**
- Many muons from 0.7 GeV neutrino interactions stop before exiting the downstream spectrometer
- A range stack measures momentum of stopping muons from range rather than curvature, extending acceptance to low-momentum muons that do not give a reliable curvature measurement
- Iron–scintillator MRD is a proven, cost-effective technology for this role (used in e.g. SciBooNE, T2K ND280)

---

### 6. Beam timing and trigger system: Fine-grained timing with ~1 ns resolution

**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator trigger planes (upstream and downstream of the active target) with SiPM readout and waveform digitizers (e.g., DRS4-based or CAEN V1742).

**Why:**
- At 410 m from target the beam spill delivers many interactions; sub-nanosecond timing isolates individual interaction vertices and suppresses out-of-spill backgrounds
- Timing also separates neutron-induced backgrounds (time-of-flight from interaction point) from prompt interaction products
- Required to tag and reject beam-unrelated cosmic muons

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | 3D scintillator cubes (SuperFGD-type) with carbon-plate moderator to reduce H fraction ≤2%; WLS fiber + SiPM readout | Full 3D tracking of protons to 60 MeV, all-angle acceptance |
| Lateral TPCs | Gaseous Ar TPCs on 4 sides + upstream face | Momentum/charge of sideways and backward muon tracks |
| Surrounding ECal | Pb–scintillator + WLS fiber + SiPM | Photon/electron reconstruction, background rejection |
| Downstream spectrometer electronics | High-rate ASICs (AGET/AFTER) + extra chamber planes | Handle high near-detector rate, reduce occupancy |
| Muon range detector | Fe–scintillator interleaved stack + SiPM | Momentum of stopping muons from range |
| Timing/trigger system | Fast scintillator planes + waveform digitizers | Vertex isolation, background rejection, ToF |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replacement of the passive target region with a 3D segmented scintillator cube active target (SuperFGD-type) using carbon-plate interleaving to keep the hydrogen nucleon fraction ≤2%, read out by WLS fibers and SiPMs along three orthogonal axes — because this single change simultaneously enables all-angle track reconstruction (including perpendicular and backward protons down to 60 MeV kinetic energy), satisfies the hydrogen-fraction constraint that invalidates the hydrogen-subtraction model if violated, and provides the vertex activity information on which every other analysis requirement depends.

This is a challenging active target design problem for a near detector in a neutrino beam experiment. Let me analyze the key requirements and constraints:

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Geometric coverage**: Must reconstruct muons at ALL angles (0-180°), including perpendicular and backward-going
2. **Low proton threshold**: Down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~2-3 mm in plastic, ~1 cm in gas)
3. **Hydrogen constraint**: ≤2% of target nucleons
4. **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m active target region
5. **Existing downstream tracking**: Gas drift chambers in 0.15 T field

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Primary Recommendation)**

**Technology**: Extruded plastic scintillator bars (1-1.5 cm² cross-section) in XYZ orientations with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and SiPM sensors.

**Justification**:
- Provides true 3D tracking capability essential for perpendicular and backward tracks that never reach downstream chambers
- Low hydrogen content possible: polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ can be formulated or diluted to meet <2% nucleon fraction requirement
- Can detect ~60 MeV protons (range ~1 cm) with multiple bar hits
- Fine segmentation (~1 cm) enables vertex resolution and short track reconstruction
- Robust, proven technology (used in MINERvA, T2K ND280)
- SiPM readout works well in 0.15 T field

**Implementation**: Alternate layers of X, Y, and Z-oriented bars in modules throughout the volume.

### 2. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Modules**

**Technology**: High-pressure (10 atm) argon-based TPC with resistive Micromegas or GridPix readout.

**Justification**:
- Excellent 3D tracking and dE/dx for particle ID (critical for separating low-energy protons from other particles)
- Argon has zero hydrogen
- High pressure increases target mass while maintaining tracking resolution
- Can measure very short proton tracks through ionization density
- Continuous tracking enables reconstruction of complex topologies

**Implementation**: Multiple TPC modules (each ~50 cm) stacked with drift in different orientations to avoid blind spots for perpendicular tracks.

### 3. **Hybrid SuperFGD + TPC Design**

**Technology**: Combine fine-grained scintillator cubes (1 cm³ SuperFGD concept from T2K upgrade) with surrounding TPC volumes.

**Justification**:
- SuperFGD provides high-granularity 3D hits with minimal dead space
- TPC regions provide continuous tracking and excellent dE/dx
- Complementary technologies cover each other's weaknesses
- SuperFGD can use low-hydrogen scintillator formulation
- Proven path: SuperFGD prototype successfully tested

### 4. **High-Angle Tracking Planes**

**Technology**: Silicon strip detectors or scintillating fiber planes oriented perpendicular and at 45° to the beam.

**Justification**:
- Specifically addresses high-angle and backward track requirements
- Provides precise position measurements for momentum reconstruction when tracks curve in magnetic field
- Silicon has no hydrogen; organic fibers can be low-hydrogen
- Essential for matching to downstream drift chambers

### 5. **Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL)**

**Technology**: Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter on all six faces.

**Justification**:
- Catches particles exiting at extreme angles (including backwards)
- Provides π⁰/γ rejection and energy measurement
- Improves muon identification for high-angle tracks
- Reduces systematic uncertainties from events not fully contained

## Configuration Recommendation

**Optimal design**: Hybrid system with:
- Core volume: Fine-grained 3D scintillator tracker (1 cm³ cubes or bars)
- Interspersed: Thin horizontal TPC modules every 20-30 cm for dE/dx measurement
- Vertical tracking planes: Every 10 cm for precise high-angle tracking
- Full surround: ECAL on all six faces

**Alternative if budget constrained**: Pure 3D scintillator tracker with excellent granularity and full surround coverage.

## Critical Design Features

- **No dead regions**: Every orientation must have active detection
- **Low-Z, low-hydrogen materials**: Use polystyrene formulations or pure-carbon/argon options
- **Modular design**: Allow calibration and service access
- **Integrated DAQ**: Handle ~10⁶ channels with SiPM/electronics that tolerate 0.15 T field

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Implement a 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker with 1 cm³ resolution, three-axis fiber readout, and SiPM sensors, providing isotropic acceptance and low-threshold charged particle tracking in a low-hydrogen target.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Active Target Module

## Overview of Constraints

The available volume (2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m) is shallow along the beam axis, which severely limits muon ranging but favours a highly granular, low-threshold active-target approach. The physics goal — kinematically complete CC events with both μ and leading proton reconstructed — drives every hardware choice.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: Scintillator Cube ("SuperCube") Tracker

### Design
Deploy a 3D array of **1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes** filling the bulk of the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume, read out by orthogonal WLS fibres threaded through each cube in three views (X, Y, Z). Each cube is coupled to fibres in all three directions; at each fibre end sits an SiPM (1 mm² MPPC, ~50 µm pixel pitch).

### Why this solves the core problem
- **Proton tracking at low momentum**: The 1.5 cm cube pitch gives a projected range threshold of roughly **40–50 MeV/c** for protons (range ~2 mm in polystyrene), capturing the bulk of the 450 MeV/c median distribution and recovering well below the 6% high-momentum tail.
- **Large solid-angle acceptance**: With no dead material boundaries within the active volume, tracks at >50° to the beam (the 25% of muons and 35% of protons of concern) are tracked until they exit the cube volume, where the downstream TPCs or the return-yoke scintillator can range them out. The 3D topology removes the ambiguity from 2D projective readout.
- **dE/dx particle ID**: Cube-by-cube energy deposition distinguishes protons from pions from muons on a track-segment basis, which is essential for the leading-proton selection without a downstream range stack.
- **Neutrino target material**: Polystyrene (CH) is explicitly stated as acceptable; the hydrogen fraction also enables future H–C subtraction analyses.
- **Fiducial mass**: At bulk scintillator density (~1.05 g/cm³) and ~90% active fill factor, the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume yields roughly **2.3 t** of active hydrocarbon target — a significant gain over the 16 t upstream section that was not kinematically complete.

### Implementation notes
- Cubes are individually extruded with a TiO₂ coating for optical isolation, then assembled into ~10 cm thick "super-layers" for handling.
- WLS fibres (Y-11, 1 mm diameter) are routed to SiPM carrier boards at the volume faces; total channel count is of order 50,000–80,000 depending on fibre multiplexing.
- The fibre-to-SiPM coupling boards mount on the outer faces within the existing magnet bore, keeping the active volume boundary clean.
- Low-noise front-end ASICs (e.g., CITIROC or TARGET-C derivatives) with 12-bit ADC and ~10 ns timing provide both charge and time-over-threshold readout for dE/dx.

---

## 2. Thin Upstream Veto / Gamma-Catcher Plane

### Design
Two planes of **0.5 cm thick plastic scintillator paddles** (the minimum needed for MIP detection) placed immediately upstream of the cube volume, with SiPM readout. Total radiation length contributed: ~0.5% X₀.

### Purpose
- Tags charged particles entering from upstream (beam halo, secondary interactions in the magnet nose).
- Provides an upstream boundary for fiducial vertex definition without the photon-converting material of the old upstream section, preserving the low-threshold photon-detection capability needed for π⁰ reconstruction.
- Since the old photon-tagging section is removed, this thin veto partially restores the ability to flag events with upstream activity without converting photons.

---

## 3. Downstream Interface: Thin High-Pressure Gas TPC Transition Layer

### Design
A **small high-pressure argon TPC** (or alternatively a resistive-plate chamber layer) of ~5 cm depth placed at the downstream face of the cube volume, before the first existing micro-pattern TPC.

### Purpose
- Muons exiting the cube volume at large angles that miss the central TPC aperture are captured here with a momentum measurement.
- Provides a ~3 mm space-point resolution bridge between the cube tracker (where the track exit point is defined to ±1.5 cm) and the existing downstream TPCs.
- For the ~25% of large-angle muons, range in the existing return-yoke scintillator combined with the direction from the cube gives momentum to ~5–8% resolution, adequate for TKI reconstruction.

---

## 4. Time-of-Flight Layer Pair for Proton Momentum Cross-Check

### Design
Two planes of **fast scintillator (EJ-200 or equivalent, 1 cm thick, 10 cm × 10 cm tiles)** with SiPM readout at the upstream and downstream faces of the cube volume, achieving ~300 ps resolution.

### Purpose
- For protons stopping inside the cube volume, range gives momentum. For the 6% of protons exceeding 900 MeV/c that punch through, a ~300 ps TOF measurement over the ~0.6 m baseline gives an independent momentum estimate with ~5% resolution at 900 MeV/c.
- Cross-calibrates the cube dE/dx momentum scale in situ using a clean proton sample selected by TOF PID.

---

## 5. Magnet Return-Yoke Scintillator Upgrade (Incremental)

The existing return-yoke scintillator instrumentation should be extended with **~8 additional double-sided scintillator planes** in the upstream (photon-tagger) region of the yoke, now freed of the old detector. This extends the muon-ranging volume for the new active target's large-angle muons, recovering momentum resolution for tracks exiting the sides of the cube volume before reaching the main downstream calorimeter.

---

## 6. Data Acquisition and Trigger

- Replace the front-end boards serving the removed upstream section with **self-triggered, continuous-readout ATCA blades** using the same MPPC + ASIC chain as the cube tracker, keeping a uniform DAQ architecture.
- A software trigger selecting ≥1 track stub in the cube volume + ≥1 downstream TPC hit runs at ~kHz dead-time-free rates consistent with the beam spill structure.
- The existing DAQ backbone (assumed VME/WR timing) is augmented with a White Rabbit grandmaster clock at the new module to synchronise the cube-tracker timestamps to <5 ns with the downstream TPCs.

---

## Expected Performance Gains

| Observable | Current (~6% syst.) | With upgrade |
|---|---|---|
| Proton reconstruction efficiency (p > 200 MeV/c, θ < 70°) | ~30% (downstream TPCs only) | ~85% |
| Muon + proton coincidence efficiency | ~20% | ~65% |
| TKI δpT resolution | ~80 MeV/c | ~25–35 MeV/c |
| Projected systematic uncertainty | ~6% | ~3.5–4% |

The improvement toward the 4% target comes primarily from the kinematically complete event sample enabling direct constraint of multi-nucleon interaction models that currently dominate the residual systematic.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a fully 3D-granular scintillator-cube active target (~1.5 cm cubes, three-view WLS-fibre/SiPM readout) filling the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume, providing sub-centimetre proton tracking from ~50 MeV/c threshold, dE/dx particle identification, and near-4π acceptance for the leading recoil proton needed for transverse kinematic imbalance reconstruction.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## 1. High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC as the New Active Target

**Technology:** A high-pressure (5–10 bar) gaseous argon TPC with micro-pattern gas detector (MPGD) readout (MicroMEGAS or GEM), filling roughly the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, replacing the removed photon-tagging section.

**Physics motivation:** The core problem is achieving kinematically complete charged-current reconstruction — both the muon and the leading recoil proton — in a compact volume. A gaseous argon TPC at elevated pressure provides:
- **Low tracking threshold:** Proton momentum threshold can be as low as ~100 MeV/c (compared to ~300–400 MeV/c in liquid argon or solid scintillator), critical given the median leading-proton momentum of ~450 MeV/c and the need to reconstruct the full distribution.
- **Angular acceptance:** Full 4π steradian track reconstruction captures the ~35% of leading protons and ~25% of muons that exit beyond 50° to the beam. Unlike downstream-biased solid targets, a TPC reconstructs all directions equally.
- **dE/dx particle ID:** Gaseous argon provides clean p/π/μ separation via Bethe-Bloch energy loss over the drift length, essential to identify the leading proton rather than a pion.
- **Target nucleus:** Argon (Z=18, A=40) is a useful nuclear target on its own, and the hydrocarbon acceptability note means polystyrene structural elements contribute usefully.
- **Compactness vs. radiation length:** At 10 bar the density (~17 kg/m³) is sufficient to contain the bulk of recoil protons up to ~600 MeV/c within the 0.6 m depth, while still being far more transparent to photons than liquid or solid targets — preserving photon-tagging capability from the downstream ECal.

---

## 2. Plastic Scintillator Supermodule Surrounding the New TPC

**Technology:** A thin shell (2–3 cm) of segmented plastic scintillator tiles or bars with SiPM readout, acting as a veto/tagger surrounding all faces of the new gas TPC module.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Muon ranging for wide-angle exits:** The ~25% of muons leaving beyond 50° will exit through the lateral faces of the TPC and immediately enter this scintillator shell. Combined with the existing dipole magnet return-yoke scintillator, this closes the muon momentum measurement by range for tracks that never reach the downstream calorimeters.
- **Proton containment tagging:** For the ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that punch through the gas volume, the surrounding scintillator records the exit point and direction, allowing a momentum-by-range lower bound and flagging events where full reconstruction requires the downstream TPCs.
- **Neutron background rejection:** Cosmic and beam-related neutrons creating fake proton tracks are vetoed by requiring no coincident activity in the shell from an incoming neutral particle.
- **Synchronisation:** Provides a fast trigger signal (ns-scale) to gate the slower TPC drift readout, important at the high-flux near-detector location.

---

## 3. Beam-Left/Beam-Right Instrumentation of Remaining Return-Yoke Gaps with Finer-Segmented Scintillator

**Technology:** Replace or supplement existing yoke-gap scintillator planes with finer-pitch (3–4 cm wide strips vs. current coarser modules) extruded scintillator bars with SiPM readout, particularly on the lateral faces subtending 30°–90° from the beam axis.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Wide-angle muon momentum by range:** Currently, side-going muons (>50°) are ranged out in the yoke, but coarse segmentation limits the momentum resolution. Finer segmentation improves δp/p from ~10–15% to ~5–7% for muons stopping in the yoke, directly reducing the flux systematic that the upgrade is targeting (6% → 4%).
- **Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) sensitivity:** TKI variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T) are formed from the muon and proton transverse momenta. Muon transverse momentum resolution dominates the TKI resolution for wide-angle events; better ranging directly improves δp_T resolution from ~30 MeV/c to ~15 MeV/c.
- **Cost-effective:** Extruded scintillator with WLS fibre and SiPM is the same technology already deployed in the detector; no new infrastructure needed for calibration or DAQ.

---

## 4. Time-of-Flight Layer Between New TPC and First Downstream Gas TPC

**Technology:** A 2.0 × 1.9 m plane of fast plastic scintillator (EJ-200 or equivalent, 1 cm thick, 5 cm strip pitch), read out at both ends by fast SiPMs (Rise time < 1 ns), achieving ~200–300 ps timing resolution.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Proton/pion separation at intermediate momenta:** For leading protons between 500–900 MeV/c that traverse from the new TPC into the downstream region, a 200 ps TOF measurement over a ~0.5–1.0 m baseline gives 3σ p/π separation up to ~1 GeV/c — the momentum range containing the ~6% high-momentum tail of protons and the pion contamination from resonance production.
- **Neutron detection:** Beam-induced neutrons that scatter in the new TPC and fake proton recoils can be identified if the TOF layer shows a downstream signal without a matching upstream charged track.
- **Absolute event timing:** Provides event-by-event t₀ for the gas TPCs (which have ~µs drift times), reducing pile-up ambiguity at the near-detector neutrino interaction rate.

---

## 5. Water-Equivalent Passive Target Thin Slices Interleaved in the New Gas TPC

**Technology:** Thin (5 mm) removable panels of CH₂ (polyethylene) and H₂O-equivalent acrylic, interleaved every ~10 cm within the gas TPC active volume, with total radiation length kept below 0.05 X₀ per panel.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Hydrogen subtraction for free-proton interactions:** A primary goal of the near-detector programme is constraining neutrino-nucleus cross sections on water (for the far detector). By taking data with and without CH₂ panels using the statistical subtraction technique (C₈H₈ minus C target), one extracts interactions on free hydrogen, which have no nuclear effects, providing an absolute flux constraint independent of nuclear models. This directly attacks the residual 6% systematic.
- **Carbon-to-water comparison continuity:** The downstream water-layer target remains for C/H₂O comparison; the new upstream hydrogen-extraction data extends this to a three-point (H, C, O) nuclear dependence measurement.
- **Minimal impact on TPC performance:** At 0.05 X₀/panel, electromagnetic showering and secondary scattering are suppressed, preserving the low-threshold proton tracking that is the primary virtue of the gas TPC.

---

| TOF plane | p/π separation at high momentum |

**Technology:** Fine-grained (~1 cm³) plastic scintillator cubes with three-dimensional readout using wavelength-shifting fibers and MPPCs, arranged in true 3D configuration.

**Physics Motivation:** The current FGDs have only X-Y layers perpendicular to the beam, providing poor angular resolution for the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons emitted at >50° to the beam axis. A 3D segmented target with ~1 cm³ granularity in all three dimensions would:

- Complement the 3D target by measuring particles exiting at high angles

- Reduce background from mis-identified pions in the proton sample
- Enable better neutron detection via ToF for neutral final states
- Help separate beam-induced from cosmic-ray backgrounds

**Technology:** Extended lead-scintillator ECAL with better upstream coverage and finer segmentation, possibly supplemented with sampling layers optimized for low-energy photons (~50-200 MeV).

**Physics Motivation:**

## Physics Requirements Analysis

Before proposing hardware, I'll work through the constraints systematically.

**Tracking volume:** ~2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m (depth along beam)

**Key challenges:**
- 25% of muons exit at >50°: need large-angle muon tracking/ranging
- 35% of leading protons exit at >50°: need large-angle proton reconstruction

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. SuperFGD — The Primary Active Target (Core Recommendation)

**Replace the P0D volume with a fully-3D-segmented scintillator target cube detector.**

**Design:**
- Geometry: ~1.8 m × 1.76 m × 0.56 m active volume (fitting within the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope)
- **Granularity:** 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm polystyrene cubes, each cube read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres (one per axis), each fibre read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM/MPPC)
- **Total cubes:** approximately 180 × 176 × 56 ≈ **1.77 million cubes**
- **Total mass:** ~2 tonnes of active scintillator (density ~1.05 g/cm³)

**Why this geometry solves the physics problems:**

| Problem | Solution |
|---|---|
| 35% protons at >50° | Isotropic 3D readout — no dead angles regardless of exit direction |
| Proton median p ~450 MeV/c (range ~20 cm in plastic) | 1 cm cubes give ~20 hit track segments; excellent dE/dx for PID |
| Michel electron tagging for π⁺ | Full 3D topology reconstruction captures decay-at-rest electrons |
| Neutron interactions (for NC background) | 3D topology distinguishes neutron-induced recoils from primary vertex |
| Large-angle muons | Muons tracked through SuperFGD then into surrounding ECAL/SMRD |

**Fibre/SiPM readout:** Each cube has three fibres (X, Y, Z). Using 1.0 mm diameter Kuraray Y-11 WLS fibre, routed to Hamamatsu MPPC (1.3 mm × 1.3 mm, ~667 pixels). The three-view coincidence requirement suppresses noise and achieves effective 3D hit reconstruction without full 3D wiring. This is geometrically equivalent to what has already been prototyped by T2K/NINJA collaborations and is at TRL ~6–7.

**Performance targets:**
- Proton tracking threshold: ~300 MeV/c (range ~8 cm → ~8 cubes, sufficient for direction and dE/dx)
- Proton–pion separation via dE/dx: achievable at <700 MeV/c where Bragg peak region is sampled
- Position resolution per hit: ~3 mm (sub-cube from charge sharing + fibre position)
- Time resolution per hit: ~1 ns (sufficient for CCQE topology separation from beam bucket)

### 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Install six ToF scintillator panels surrounding the SuperFGD on all faces except downstream.**

**Design:**
- 5 planes: top, bottom, left, right, upstream faces
- Bars: extruded polystyrene, 3 cm × 1 cm cross-section, full-width strips
- SiPM readout both ends of each bar
- Target time resolution: **σ_t < 300 ps** per plane

**Physics motivation:**
- Neutron–gamma separation by flight time (critical for NC background)
- Forward–backward ambiguity resolution for short tracks in SuperFGD
- Pion charge-sign discrimination from ToF + range (π⁺ vs π⁻ for Δ resonance studies)
- Cross-check of vertex timing for pile-up rejection during beam spill
- For p = 450 MeV/c proton (β ≈ 0.43): crossing 30 cm of SuperFGD takes ~2.3 ns; a 300 ps resolution gives ~7σ separation from minimum-ionising particles at same momentum

**Technology:** Directly adapted from the T2K ECal ToF upgrade and NA62 RICH; Hamamatsu SiPMs (S13360 series) with fast transimpedance amplifiers and waveform digitisation at 250 MHz give routinely <200 ps resolution on 3 cm bars.

### 3. High-Angle Time Projection Chambers (HA-TPCs)

**Install two thin TPCs immediately upstream and downstream of the SuperFGD, oriented to extend large-angle track coverage.**

**Design:**

**Physics motivation:**
- Muon momentum measurement by curvature for tracks exiting SuperFGD forward or backward at moderate angles
