# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before listing upgrades, let me identify the key physics drivers:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward tracks — this is very demanding for a downstream spectrometer alone
- **Proton tracks down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range in water ~2 mm, in liquid argon ~3 mm) — requires fine-grained, dense active material
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20%** of target nucleons — constrains material choice severely (pure hydrocarbon scintillator would be ~14% H by nucleon count; liquid argon has essentially 0%; water has ~11%)
- The 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume sits inside an existing dipole magnet — the magnetic field is available for momentum measurement

---

## Upgrade 1: Plastic Scintillator 3D-Granular Active Target ("SuperFGD-style" Cube Array)

**Technology:** An array of small (~1 cm³) extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, each read out in three orthogonal directions by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through holes along each axis, coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) at both ends.

**Physics motivation:**

The 0.9 m depth of the target region along the beam is short enough that conventional planar tracking (e.g., stacked scintillator bars read in 2D) has a severe geometric acceptance problem for tracks at large angles. A 3D-granular structure solves this: a particle travelling perpendicular to the beam crosses cubes in the transverse plane and deposits light in the orthogonal fibre directions, so it is reconstructed with the same efficiency regardless of direction. Backward-going muons re-enter the cube array and are tracked identically to forward-going ones. This directly addresses the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles.

For short proton tracks: a 60 MeV proton has a range of roughly 2–3 cm in plastic scintillator (density ~1.05 g/cm³). With 1 cm³ cubes, such a proton traverses only 2–3 cubes but still produces a measurable, directionless 3D stub. The fine granularity provides the spatial resolution to separate the proton stub from the muon track at the interaction vertex.

The hydrogen content of polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ is approximately 7.7% by nucleon number — well within the ≤20% constraint — while still providing a useful hydrogen sample for neutrino–hydrogen cross-section extraction using the transverse-momentum-imbalance technique. The far detector being hydrogen-free means the signal model for hydrogen is derived entirely here; keeping the fraction modest and well-known is essential.

The existing dipole magnet field acts on muons that exit the cube array and enter the downstream drift chambers, so momentum and sign are still measured; the cube array itself provides the vertex and angular information.

**Practical note:** This technology was validated in the T2K ND280 upgrade (SuperFGD, 2 million ~1 cm³ cubes installed 2023), making it a proven, available choice.

---

## Upgrade 2: Time-of-Flight Panels on the Upstream Face and Lateral Surfaces

**Technology:** Panels of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-404), ~1–2 cm thick, tiled with SiPMs, achieving ~200–300 ps timing resolution per panel. Panels placed on the upstream face and four lateral faces of the target volume.

**Physics motivation:**

Backward-going muons exit through the upstream face of the target — there is no magnetic spectrometer there, so their momentum cannot be measured by bending. A time-of-flight (ToF) measurement between the upstream panel and a downstream panel (or between two lateral panels) provides velocity β, and combined with the range measured inside the cube array, gives momentum independently of bending. For muons that stop inside the cube array, range alone gives momentum; for those that exit upstream, ToF is the only handle.

ToF panels on lateral faces additionally help with particle identification at the boundary: a proton and a pion of similar momentum are distinguished by their β at ~200 ps resolution up to a few hundred MeV/c. This is important because the analysis needs to correctly identify and reject pion tracks that could mimic short proton stubs.

The upstream panel also provides a veto/tag for beam-related backgrounds entering from upstream and for dirt muons, improving vertex identification purity.

---

## Upgrade 3: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC Insert (or Low-Mass GEM-based Tracker) for the Downstream Drift Chamber Region

**Technology:** Replace or augment one or more of the existing downstream gas drift chamber modules with a high-pressure (5–10 bar) gaseous argon time-projection chamber (TPC) using GEM or micromegas readout, or alternatively add lightweight GEM tracking planes between existing chambers.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing warm drift chambers measure momentum by curvature in the 0.15 T dipole field. At 0.15 T, the sagitta for a 1 GeV/c muon over 6.5 m is roughly s = 0.3·B·L²/(8p) ≈ 0.3×0.15×42/8 ≈ 90 mm — already measurable, but resolution degrades for high-p tracks. More critically, for muons exiting the target at large angles, their path length in the downstream spectrometer is reduced (a 60° track covers only half the lever arm), degrading momentum resolution precisely in the kinematic region most relevant for the efficiency requirement.

Adding high-pressure gaseous argon TPC modules increases the sampling density and provides dE/dx measurement for particle identification, helping separate muons from pions and protons that escape the target region. The argon nucleus (Z=18, A=40) has negligible hydrogen content, satisfying the constraint. High pressure (×5–10 relative to atmospheric) increases the density and hence the dE/dx signal, enabling proton–pion separation up to ~1 GeV/c. This is a complementary PID handle to the ToF system.

---

## Upgrade 4: SiPM-on-Tile Electromagnetic Calorimeter Panels on Lateral and Downstream Surfaces of the Target Volume

**Technology:** Scintillator-lead sampling calorimeter panels ("SiPM-on-tile" ECAL), each ~10–15 radiation lengths deep, with ~4 cm² tile granularity read out by SiPMs, surrounding the lateral and downstream faces of the active target.

**Physics motivation:**

Neutral pions (π⁰) produced in neutrino interactions decay to two photons; if these are not detected, they cause missing energy and can bias the neutrino energy reconstruction. For cross-section measurements that require knowledge of the full hadronic final state — particularly multi-nucleon interactions where the initial state nucleon momentum matters — undetected π⁰s are a leading systematic.

An ECAL surrounding the target volume converts and measures photon showers that exit the cube array. The granularity allows two-photon separation and invariant-mass reconstruction of π⁰ → γγ. This also helps veto neutral-current interactions that could otherwise mimic charged-current muon events (a π⁰ with one photon absorbed can produce a single electromagnetic shower that resembles a muon track in coarser detectors, though less so in the 3D cube array).

The 0.15 T field is too weak to significantly curve electrons/positrons from photon conversions at relevant energies, so calorimetric measurement is necessary rather than magnetic momentum measurement for neutrals.

---

## Upgrade 5: Thin-Film Resistive Plate Chambers or Scintillator Muon Range Stack Upstream of the Target

**Technology:** A muon range stack — alternating iron absorber plates (5 cm thick) and scintillator detector planes — installed upstream of the target volume, within the available hall space, read out by SiPMs.

**Physics motivation:**

Backward-going muons from neutrino interactions inside the target must be reconstructed with ≥25% efficiency. A muon going backward at, say, 150° to the beam exits through the upstream face. Without an upstream detector, its momentum can only be estimated by range if it stops inside the cube array (possible for low-energy muons) or by ToF (Upgrade 2). A muon range stack upstream allows backward muons to range out in iron with their momentum determined by the depth of penetration, extending coverage to higher muon momenta. The iron absorber is essentially hydrogen-free and does not contribute to the fiducial target mass.

This also provides muon identification by confirming that the track penetrates the absorber (hadrons interact and stop earlier), which is important for the near-detector environment where the neutrino interaction rate is high and track mis-identification is a concern.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3D scintillator cube array (SuperFGD-style) | 4π tracking efficiency; short proton stubs |
| 2 | Fast plastic scintillator ToF panels | Backward muon momentum; PID at boundaries |
| 3 | High-pressure gaseous Ar TPC / GEM tracker | Downstream PID; improved spectrometer resolution |
| 4 | SiPM-on-tile ECAL surrounding target | Neutral pion detection; hadronic state reconstruction |
| 5 | Muon range stack upstream | Backward muon momentum at higher energies |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: 3D-granular plastic scintillator cube array (SuperFGD-style) active target replacing the existing target region, read out in three orthogonal axes by WLS fibres and SiPMs — this is the single change that most directly addresses the core requirements of 4π muon reconstruction efficiency at all angles and reconstruction of short proton tracks down to 60 MeV kinetic energy, while satisfying the hydrogen-fraction constraint.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Target Region

## 1. What the requirements imply

**Muon acceptance at all angles.** In the present layout, tracks are measured only in drift chambers downstream of the target. A muon at about 90° to the beam, or one going backward, never reaches them. Two things are needed:
- tracking that surrounds the interaction volume, and
- timing good enough to tell a backward track from a forward one.

**Low-energy protons at all angles.** A 60 MeV proton has p ≈ 340 MeV/c. Its range in plastic is only about 3 cm, so the target must be:
- fully active (no passive layers),
- finely and isotropically segmented in 3D, and
- able to measure dE/dx along the track.

Planar bar layers would miss such protons when they travel along a bar or perpendicular to the planes.

**Hydrogen limit (≤ 20% of target nucleons).** Candidate target materials compare as follows:

| Material | Hydrogen fraction of nucleons | Acceptable? |
|---|---|---|
| Polystyrene (CH) | 1/13 ≈ 7.7% | Yes |
| Water | 2/18 ≈ 11% | Yes |
| CH₂ liquid scintillator | 2/14 ≈ 14% | Yes |
| Methane-based high-pressure gas target (CH₄) | 4/16 = 25% | No |
| Hydrogen-loaded material | above 20% | No |

## 2. Proposed configuration (within the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region)

**A. 3D-segmented scintillator target (SuperFGD-type)**
- Construction: about 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, each read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres with SiPMs.
- Size: roughly 2.0 m (x) × 1.3 m (y) × 0.9 m (z), about 2.4 × 10⁶ cubes and about 2.4 t of active mass.
- Hydrogen fraction: about 8% of nucleons, including the reflector coating and fibres, well inside the 20% limit.
- Proton response: a 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes in any direction, which allows a dE/dx-based identification near threshold. Using 1 cm cubes is the minimum; if finer pitch is affordable, it would move the proton threshold lower.
- Timing: about 1 ns per channel, which helps separate multiple interactions within a beam spill and helps determine track direction.
- Muon reconstruction inside the target:
  - Many high-angle muons will stop in the cubes. Their momentum then comes from range.
  - Muon decay (Michel electrons) can be tagged from delayed hits.
  - This keeps efficiency up even for tracks that never exit.

**B. High-angle TPCs above and below the target**
- Thin-profile TPCs, about 0.4–0.45 m thick, filling the remaining vertical space.
- Gas: argon-based, for example a T2K-type Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ mixture. Its mass is negligible as target material.
- Readout: resistive micromegas.
- Momentum resolution in the 0.15 T field:
  - A 0.5 GeV/c track has a radius of curvature R ≈ p/(0.3B) ≈ 11 m.
  - Over 0.5 m of track this gives a sagitta of about 3 mm.
  - With about 0.5 mm hit resolution, that yields a usable momentum and charge measurement of roughly 10–20%.
- Purpose: measure the charge and momentum of high-angle and backward muons that leave the target.

**C. Time-of-flight envelope**
- Scintillator bars with SiPMs at both ends, giving better than about 150 ps resolution.
- Coverage: all six faces of the target-plus-TPC assembly, including the upstream face.
- Purpose:
  - unambiguously determine forward versus backward direction,
  - reject particles entering from interactions in the magnet and surrounding material,
  - add particle identification for protons versus muons at low momentum.

**D. Interfaces**
- Electronics and services must work in the 0.15 T field and fit the limited space; SiPM readout is suitable for this.
- The existing downstream drift chambers stay in place for forward tracks, with a matched downstream TOF plane.

## 3. Coverage check

| Muon direction | How it is reconstructed | Expected efficiency |
|---|---|---|
| Forward | Downstream drift chambers | Well above 25% |
| Perpendicular, toward top or bottom | High-angle TPCs | Well above 25% |
| Perpendicular, sideways | Stops in the cubes (range momentum + Michel tag), or exits through the side TOF | Estimated well above 25%, given the 2 m target width |
| Backward | Cubes plus TOF timing | Estimated above 25% |

- **Charge ID:** charge is measured from curvature wherever a track reaches a TPC. Stopped muons need a different handle, such as decay tagging.
- **Protons:** a threshold of about 60 MeV kinetic energy is achievable in all directions because the cube segmentation is isotropic.

These efficiency figures are design estimates, not simulation results. Confirming them needs a full acceptance study, especially for sideways and backward muons and for charge identification of stopped muons.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fully active, finely segmented (~1 cm cube) polystyrene scintillator target with three-view fibre/SiPM readout, giving isotropic 4π tracking and about 8% hydrogen nucleon fraction.

# Proposed Upgrade for the Kestrel Flats Near Station Target Region

## 1. Why the active-target material must be argon

The hydrogen requirement decides this before anything else.

- **Plastic scintillator is excluded.** CH has 1 hydrogen nucleon out of 13, about 7.7%. Polystyrene-based trackers in the T2K ND280 or MINERvA style would be roughly four times over the 2% limit.
- **Water is excluded.** H₂O is 2 out of 18 nucleons, about 11%.
- **Argon passes.** Pure argon has 0% hydrogen. It also matches the target nucleus, presumably, of a hydrogen-free far detector such as a LArTPC. That keeps nuclear-effect systematics correlated between the near and far detectors.

The hydrogen budget therefore points to an argon time projection chamber (TPC).

## 2. Core hardware: a modular liquid-argon TPC with pixel readout

Fill the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m volume with a LArTPC built in the ArgonCube/ND-LAr style.

**Mass and rate**
- The volume holds about 5.4 m³, or roughly 7.5 t of liquid argon.
- At 410 m in a beam peaking near 0.7 GeV, that gives ample statistics.

**Modular layout to handle pileup**
- Divide the volume into roughly 4–6 optically isolated modules, each with a central cathode.
- Use short drift lengths, about 30–50 cm. This keeps drift time around 200–300 µs, limits space-charge effects, and lets the 0.15 T field be tolerated.

**Charge readout**
- Use native 3D pixel readout, such as LArPix-class ASICs at about 4 mm pitch, rather than wire planes.
- This gives unambiguous reconstruction at every angle. Wire planes have blind spots for tracks parallel to the wires or perpendicular to the beam.
- It also handles multiple interactions per spill.

**Proton threshold**
- A 60 MeV kinetic-energy proton ranges about 3 cm in liquid argon.
- With 4 mm pixels that is 7–8 hits, enough for dE/dx particle identification and a Bragg-peak tag.

**Light readout**
- Fit fast, thin light detectors on the module walls, such as ArCLight or LCM tiles read out by SiPMs.
- They provide:
  - ns-level event time zero (t₀), to place interactions in drift and to separate pileup;
  - track direction from timing, to confirm backward-going muons.

**Cryostat**
- Use a thin-wall, low-mass cryostat (aluminium or composite with foam insulation) that fits inside the warm-dipole aperture.
- Keep the material thin on all six faces so that exiting muons reach the external trackers with little scattering.

**Alternative**
- A high-pressure (about 10 bar) gaseous argon TPC would give even lower proton thresholds and natural 4π acceptance.
- Its mass would be only about 90 kg.
- Any quencher must be hydrogen-poor. For example, Ar/CF₄ with about 2% isobutane stays near 0.5% hydrogen nucleons.
- I would choose liquid argon for statistics and keep the gas TPC as a fallback.

## 3. Muon acceptance at all angles

The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks. Muons at 90° and backward muons leave through the sides or upstream face, so the target must be surrounded with instrumentation.

**Side and upstream trackers inside the magnet aperture**
- Add thin trackers on the four lateral faces and the upstream face. Options are drift chambers matching the existing ones, or scintillating-fibre or straw planes.
- These give charge and momentum from curvature in the 0.15 T field.
- Hydrogen in these trackers does not matter, because interactions are fiducialised to the argon.

**Contained and partially contained muons**
- Inside the liquid argon, use range for stopping muons. A 0.7 GeV/c muon ranges about 2–3 m.
- Use multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum estimates for exiting segments.

**Charge sign**
- Curvature inside the liquid argon is weak at 0.15 T, so charge sign comes mainly from the external trackers.
- For stopping μ⁻, nuclear capture versus decay can be used as a complementary tag.

**Muon identification**
- Instrument the magnet return yoke or flux return with scintillator planes, acting as a side muon range detector in the SMRD style.
- This confirms muon ID for large-angle tracks.
- Together with the trackers, this should push muon efficiency above 25% even at 90° and backward angles.

## 4. Supporting items

- **Veto plane** on the upstream face, to reject entering rock muons and interactions in the magnet.
- **Calibration:** a cosmic trigger, plus a UV-laser or pulser system for drift-field and space-charge calibration in the magnetic field.
- **Cryogenics:** argon recirculation and purification to keep electron lifetime well above 1 ms.
- **Data acquisition:** synchronise the TPC, light system and drift chambers to the beam spill clock.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (thin-wall cryostat, SiPM light readout), giving a 0%-hydrogen target with 4π, low-threshold proton and muon reconstruction, complemented by side/upstream trackers in the magnet.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before listing upgrades, I'll establish the governing physics requirements that drive technology choices:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward tracks → need 4π angular coverage, cannot rely solely on downstream spectrometer
- **Proton tracking down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** → range ~3.5 cm in liquid argon, ~2.5 cm in plastic scintillator; requires fine-grained, low-threshold active material
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons** → constrains material choice severely (pure hydrocarbon scintillator would be ~57% H by nucleon count; must dilute or choose heavier target)
- **Active volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** within existing warm dipole at 0.15 T
- **Beam peaks at 0.7 GeV** → typical muon momenta 200–600 MeV/c, typical proton recoil momenta 200–500 MeV/c

---

## Upgrade 1: Fine-Grained Plastic Scintillator Tracker with Steel Absorber Planes (FGT)

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm cross-section) read out with wavelength-shifting fibers and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), interleaved with thin (~1 cm) steel absorber planes every few scintillator layers, arranged in X-Y and X-Y-45° stereo configurations.

**Physics motivation:**

The 60 MeV kinetic energy proton threshold is the hardest single constraint. A 60 MeV proton has a range of roughly 2.5 cm in plastic scintillator. With 1.5 cm bar width, such a track spans approximately 1–2 bars, so bar cross-section cannot be made larger. The bars must be fine enough to identify these as tracks (not single-bar blips) and to measure their angle, which is essential for neutrino energy reconstruction via the struck-nucleon momentum.

The steel planes serve two purposes. First, they bring the average nuclear mass up substantially. Pure polystyrene (CH) has a hydrogen-to-carbon nucleon ratio of 1:12 per molecule, giving a hydrogen nucleon fraction of ~1/(1+12) ≈ 7.7% by nucleon count in the organic alone—actually already below 20%. However, adding steel planes dilutes this further as a safety margin, since SiPM and fiber mass is also hydrogen-bearing, and to provide hadronic interaction length reference. With steel/scintillator mass ratio tuned to keep hydrogen nucleon fraction at ~15%, there is comfortable headroom below the 20% ceiling. Second, steel provides magnetic rigidity reference for range-momentum cross-checks.

The 4π angular coverage for muons is achieved because the scintillator volume itself is tracking medium: a backward-going muon deposits light in bars upstream of the vertex, and the X-Y layering reconstructs the direction without needing the downstream drift chambers. The SiPM readout is insensitive to the 0.15 T magnetic field (unlike photomultiplier tubes), making this geometry practical inside the existing dipole.

Track-by-track dE/dx from pulse-height on each bar provides particle identification between protons, pions, and muons at low momentum where the downstream spectrometer is not useful, via Bethe-Bloch separation.

---

## Upgrade 2: 3D Projection Scintillator Cubes (SuperFGD-style) for the Core Target Region

**Technology:** A lattice of 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes, each read out in three orthogonal directions by three wavelength-shifting fibers (X, Y, Z), with SiPM readout. This is the technology demonstrated by the SuperFGD module in T2K's near detector upgrade.

**Physics motivation:**

The bar-based FGT described above has an intrinsic geometric ambiguity: a track segment parallel to the bar axis deposits light in only one projection and cannot be reconstructed in 3D from that view alone. For the specifically required 90°-to-beam tracks (tracks along the Z beam axis appear as point-like in the X-Y plane) and backward tracks at oblique angles, 3D cube readout eliminates the ambiguity entirely because each cube is a space-point with no projective degeneracy.

The 1 cm side length gives a spatial resolution sufficient to identify a 60 MeV proton: its ~2.5 cm range traverses approximately 2–3 cubes, which is a track rather than a noise hit, and the cube-by-cube energy deposition pattern distinguishes it from a low-energy pion by Bragg-peak shape.

The hydrogen fraction in pure polystyrene cubes is ~7.7% by nucleon count as noted above, well below 20%. However, the mechanical support structure (which may use aluminum frames) adds negligible hydrogen, keeping the budget safe.

The principal advantage over the bar-based approach is **vertex resolution**: the 1 cm³ granularity gives an interaction vertex localized to roughly 0.5 cm in each dimension, which matters for identifying secondary vertices from pion reinteraction (a background to quasi-elastic signal) and for resolving multi-track vertices at 0.7 GeV where two or three final-state tracks are common.

The 25% minimum muon efficiency requirement at all angles becomes achievable because a cube lattice has no dead material in any orientation—the filling fraction approaches 100% of active material with thin fiber holes being the only inefficiency, estimated at <5% per plane.

---

## Upgrade 3: Thin-Gap or Micropattern Gaseous Detectors (MicroMegas or µRWELL) as Tracking Planes Around the Target

**Technology:** Resistive Micromegas or µRWELL (resistive micro-well) detectors, 50–100 µm spatial resolution, arrayed as thin (3–5 mm total) planar tracking layers on the upstream, downstream, and lateral faces of the active target volume.

**Physics motivation:**

The scintillator-based active target measures energy and approximate track direction in its volume, but connecting tracks exiting the target to the external gas drift chambers requires matching through the magnet bore region. A short-track proton that stops inside the active target needs no such matching, but a muon—especially one exiting sideways—must be handed off to the external tracking system.

Micropattern detectors placed on the target-volume boundaries provide high-resolution space points (σ_x ~ 100 µm) that anchor the extrapolation from internal scintillator hits (σ ~ 3–5 mm) to external drift chamber hits. The resulting momentum resolution from the bend in the 0.15 T field over the 6.5 m drift-chamber arm is dominated by the lever-arm precision; the boundary planes reduce the extrapolation uncertainty by a factor of roughly 30 in position.

Crucially, MicroMegas operate stably in 0.15 T magnetic fields (the field is well below the threshold where drift distortions become unmanageable for typical drift-gap geometries of 3–5 mm). They are thin enough—radiation length X/X₀ per plane of order 0.1%—that they do not appreciably range out or scatter the low-momentum protons that stop just inside the target, and they add negligible hydrogen to the nucleon budget.

For the specific case of tracks at 90° to the beam (traveling along X or Y, perpendicular to Z), these tracks exit through the lateral faces of the target. Without instrumentation there, they are lost. Lateral MicroMegas planes on the ±X and ±Y faces catch these tracks and, together with the internal scintillator hits, reconstruct the full trajectory, satisfying the 25% efficiency requirement at 90°.

---

## Upgrade 4: Timing Layer — LYSO or Fast-Plastic Scintillator with SiPM Readout

**Technology:** A thin (5–10 mm) layer of LYSO (lutetium yttrium oxyorthosilicate) or EJ-230 fast plastic scintillator tiles, 5 cm × 5 cm, with SiPM readout, surrounding the target volume on all six faces. LYSO gives ~200 ps timing resolution per tile; fast plastic gives ~100–150 ps.

**Physics motivation:**

At 0.7 GeV peak flux, the neutrino beam spill structure at a typical facility delivers multiple interactions per spill in the near detector. Event pile-up — two neutrino interactions in the same spill within the same active volume — creates combinatorial ambiguity in track-to-vertex association, particularly for the low-momentum protons that travel only a centimeter or two and whose vertex assignment depends entirely on spatial proximity rather than timing.

A 200 ps timing layer on the target boundary, combined with the ~1 ns timing from the scintillator cubes' SiPM readout, allows in-time association of exiting tracks to their production vertex in time, separating interactions that occur within the same spill but at different times. With a typical spill width of several microseconds and interaction rates of a few per spill, two interactions separated by ≥500 ps can be disambiguated — this is achievable with LYSO at the 200 ps level.

Additionally, time-of-flight across the ~20 cm target depth with 200 ps resolution gives β resolution of Δβ/β ~ 3% for a 60 MeV proton (v ~ 0.33c), which provides a cross-check of range-based particle identification. This is especially valuable for distinguishing low-energy protons from neutron-scattered protons that enter from outside the volume (a background to the recoil proton signal).

The hydrogen contribution from LYSO is zero (it contains no hydrogen), satisfying the nucleon budget constraint trivially.

---

## Upgrade 5: Upgraded Gas Drift Chamber Readout — GEM-based or Straw-Tube Replacement

**Technology:** Replace or supplement aging drift chambers downstream of the magnet with Gas Electron Multiplier (GEM) detectors in a large-area configuration, or high-rate small-diameter straw-tube trackers (4 mm diameter), with updated front-end ASICs capable of 10 ns time binning.

**Physics motivation:**

The momentum measurement of the muon relies on the track bend in the 0.15 T field over the downstream spectrometer. The muon momentum resolution drives the neutrino energy resolution: for quasi-elastic interactions at 0.7 GeV, δE_ν/E_ν ~ δp_µ/p_µ. A 5% muon momentum resolution gives 5% neutrino energy resolution, which controls systematic uncertainties in oscillation parameters.

If the existing drift chambers have aging wires, dead channels, or slow readout (limiting them to low-rate operation), the upgraded active target — which will have higher efficiency and thus higher reconstructed event rate — will create readout bottlenecks downstream. The near detector runs in a high-rate environment close to the production target; GEM detectors tolerate particle fluxes of order 10⁵ Hz/cm² without gain degradation, while traditional drift chambers begin to degrade above ~10⁴ Hz/cm².

The backward-going muon requirement is worth noting here: backward muons do not enter the downstream spectrometer at all. Their momentum must be measured by range (if they stop in the active target) or by curvature within the active target scintillator volume using the internal tracking of Upgrade 2. The GEM upgrade thus does not directly help backward muons but ensures the forward muon momentum measurement remains clean and high-resolution as event rates increase.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fine-grained scintillator + steel planes | Proton tracking to 60 MeV, hydrogen budget control |
| 2 | 3D scintillator cubes (SuperFGD-style) | 4π tracking, 90°/backward muons, vertex resolution |
| 3 | MicroMegas/µRWELL boundary planes | Track handoff at all exit angles, 25% muon efficiency |
| 4 | LYSO/fast-plastic timing layer | Pile-up rejection, TOF PID cross-check |
| 5 | GEM or straw-tube downstream upgrade | Forward muon momentum resolution at high rate |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator cube lattice (SuperFGD-style, 1 cm³ cubes with X-Y-Z fiber readout and SiPM) because it simultaneously addresses the two hardest constraints — omnidirectional muon reconstruction including 90° and backward tracks, and proton tracking down to 60 MeV kinetic energy — in a single technology that has been validated at scale, operates inside the existing 0.15 T dipole without modification, and keeps the hydrogen nucleon fraction well within the 20% ceiling.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context Summary

The detector needs to:
- Reconstruct muons at **all angles** (including 90° and backward) with ≥25% efficiency
- Reconstruct **short proton tracks** down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy
- Maintain **hydrogen fraction ≤2%** of target nucleons
- Operate in a 0.15 T magnetic field over 6.5 m

---

## Upgrade 1: Fine-Grained Plastic Scintillator with Embedded WLS Fibers (Replacing Existing Target Material)

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm cross-section), read out via wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), arranged in alternating X–Y planes.

**Physics motivation:**

A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range in plastic scintillator of roughly 3–4 cm. With 1.5 cm bars you get ~2–3 hits on a proton track, which is marginal but sufficient for reconstruction. The key is that the bar cross-section must be small enough to identify these short tracks above noise while also providing 3D hit information from alternating planes. Plastic scintillator (CH composition) has a hydrogen-to-carbon ratio by nucleon count of approximately 1:6 (each CH monomer: 1 H, 12/12 C nucleons → ~1/13 ≈ 7.7% H by nucleon). This **violates the ≤2% hydrogen constraint** as described below, so a mitigation is required (see Upgrade 2), but the scintillator serves as the primary active element for 3D calorimetric reconstruction of the hadronic system.

For muon reconstruction at all angles, a fully active 3D tracker provides hit information regardless of track direction. A muon traveling perpendicular to the beam axis still crosses multiple scintillator layers and can be tracked. The fine granularity means that even a backward-going muon of a few hundred MeV produces a reconstructible track before exiting the upstream face of the target into upstream instrumentation.

The SiPM readout is insensitive to the magnetic field (unlike PMTs), which is important given the 0.15 T environment. Light yield from modern extruded scintillator with WLS fiber is typically 20–40 photoelectrons per MIP, giving excellent hit efficiency.

---

## Upgrade 2: Water or Liquid-Argon Insert Panels to Dilute Hydrogen Fraction

**Technology:** Thin (5–10 cm thick) sealed aluminum vessels filled with water, interleaved every few scintillator planes, acting as passive nuclear target layers within the active volume.

**Physics motivation:**

As noted above, plastic scintillator alone gives ~7–8% hydrogen by nucleon, far exceeding the 2% cap. The far detector uses a material with no free hydrogen (e.g., iron, rock, or a similar dense medium), so the cross-section model for nuclear targets must be transferable. Hydrogen interactions are removed statistically using a subtraction technique, but the model is reliable only when hydrogen contributes ≤2% of the interaction rate.

Interleaving water panels (H₂O: 2 H + 16 O nucleons → ~11% H by nucleon — also too high alone, but the *combination* is tunable) with scintillator in the right ratio can bring the effective hydrogen fraction down. More precisely, one can use **graphite (carbon) or aluminum insert layers** rather than water, since these contain no hydrogen at all, diluting the overall H fraction. For example, alternating one 2 cm graphite panel per 2 cm of scintillator reduces the H fraction by roughly half. The graphite also provides a pure carbon target useful for nuclear cross-section measurements independent of the hydrogen subtraction.

Alternatively, if liquid argon inserts are used, argon nuclei (Z=18, A=40, no hydrogen) provide a heavy nuclear target that is also of intrinsic physics interest for neutrino-argon cross sections relevant to DUNE-era detectors.

The insert panels must be thin enough not to create dead zones that break short proton track reconstruction.

---

## Upgrade 3: 3D Pixel Scintillator or Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperCube" style)

**Technology:** 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes individually read out in three projections via three orthogonal WLS fibers per cube (similar to the SuperFGD technology developed for T2K), with SiPM readout.

**Physics motivation:**

This addresses the most demanding requirement: **protons with 60 MeV kinetic energy** at **all angles**. A 60 MeV proton has a range of ~3.5 cm in plastic. In a traditional 2D-plane scintillator tracker, a proton traveling at 45° to both the beam and the transverse plane might cross only 1–2 planes before stopping, making 3D reconstruction impossible. In a cubic 3D array, the same proton crosses ~3–5 cubes regardless of its direction, because the topology is fully isotropic.

The three-fiber readout scheme means each cube is identified by coincidence of three fiber channels (one per axis), giving unambiguous 3D point reconstruction even for very short, highly ionizing tracks. The high dE/dx of a stopping proton (~10× MIP) produces saturated signals in the cubes it traverses, enabling particle identification via energy deposition profile in addition to range.

This is the single technology that simultaneously solves:
- Short proton track reconstruction at all angles
- Backward muon tracking
- 90° muon tracking
- Full 4π hadronic reconstruction for neutrino interaction topology classification (QE, RES, DIS)

The hydrogen fraction concern remains (same as bar scintillator above), requiring the dilution strategy of Upgrade 2.

---

## Upgrade 4: Upstream and Downstream Thin Tracking Stations with Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Modules

**Technology:** Small-drift-distance gaseous TPCs (argon-based, ~15 cm drift) placed immediately upstream and downstream of the active target volume, with GEM or Micromegas readout planes.

**Physics motivation:**

Muons that exit the upstream face of the active target (backward-going tracks) or at large angles will not be fully contained. These tracks enter the upstream region of the detector where there is currently no active tracking. A thin TPC module upstream provides:

1. **Charge-sign determination** for backward muons before they escape. Even a 10 cm track segment in the TPC, combined with the known magnetic field, constrains the muon momentum via curvature, completing the ≥25% efficiency requirement for backward tracks.
2. **Vertex matching**: Tracks originating inside the active target that point upstream can be matched to the TPC, confirming they are truly backward-going and not beam-related backgrounds entering from upstream.
3. **Efficiency cross-check**: The TPC provides an independent hit for tracks at large angles that the downstream drift chambers are geometrically insensitive to, enabling efficiency measurements directly from data rather than relying on simulation.

Gas TPCs are compatible with the magnetic field if the drift direction is chosen appropriately (drift parallel to B avoids ExB distortions). Argon-based gas (Ar/CO₂ 90/10) gives good electron attachment properties and known drift velocity for the sub-millimeter spatial resolution needed to match to the fine-grained active target.

---

## Upgrade 5: Improved SiPM Readout with Waveform Digitization

**Technology:** Replace any existing multi-anode PMT or simple threshold readout with SiPM arrays coupled to 125–250 MHz waveform digitizers (FADC) per channel.

**Physics motivation:**

Short proton tracks and Michel electrons from stopped pions create overlapping signals in time near the interaction vertex. Waveform digitization enables:

- **Pulse-shape discrimination**: Protons and pions have different dE/dx profiles; waveform integration windows can separate prompt vs. delayed light.
- **Sub-nanosecond timing**: The beam spill structure (~few μs) combined with 1–2 ns resolution per hit allows time-of-flight measurement over the ~30 cm active target depth, giving ~1 ns separation between a 300 MeV/c proton and a pion of the same momentum — enough for PID on marginal tracks.
- **Multi-hit resolution**: In neutrino interactions with several final-state particles, two protons may hit the same scintillator element within a few nanoseconds. Waveform readout resolves these pile-up hits that threshold-based electronics would merge.

This upgrade is incremental (electronics only, no new detector material) but unlocks physics performance that would otherwise require a full hardware replacement.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key Physics Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Fine-grained scintillator bars + SiPM | 3D tracking, all-angle muons, hadronic reconstruction |
| 2 | Graphite/carbon insert panels | H fraction ≤2%, pure nuclear targets |
| 3 | 3D scintillator cube array (SuperFGD) | Short proton tracks at all angles, 4π coverage |
| 4 | Upstream/downstream thin TPCs | Backward muon charge-sign, large-angle efficiency |
| 5 | Waveform digitization readout | PID, pile-up resolution, TOF |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: 3D plastic scintillator cube array (SuperFGD-style, ~1 cm³ cubes with three-axis WLS fiber readout and SiPM readout), because it is the only single technology that simultaneously provides full 4π reconstruction of both the ≥25%-efficiency all-angle muon requirement and the short (~3 cm) proton tracks down to 60 MeV kinetic energy that are otherwise undetectable in any planar geometry.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## 1. Replace the active target with a liquid-argon TPC (pixel readout, modular design)

**Technology:** A liquid-argon time projection chamber filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m target region (about 5.4 m³, roughly 7.5 t). It should be built from optically isolated modules, ArgonCube/ND-LAr style, with:
- short drift lengths (about 50 cm or less),
- native 3D pixelated charge readout at about 4 mm pitch, rather than projective wires,
- a fast scintillation-light system (ArCLight or LCM-type) for t₀ and interaction tagging.

**Why this target material:**
- **Hydrogen limit.** Argon contains no hydrogen, so the hydrogen-nucleon fraction is essentially 0%, well under the 2% limit.
- **Conventional detectors fail the limit:**
  - Plastic scintillator (CH) has about 7.7% hydrogen nucleons.
  - Water has about 11%.
  - Any hydrocarbon-based active target therefore violates the requirement.
- **Far-detector match.** Argon is plausibly the far-detector nucleus, which reduces nuclear-model extrapolation.

**Why a TPC with pixel readout:**
- **Proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 cm in LAr, i.e. many mm-scale pixels. That gives full dE/dx/Bragg-peak identification and range-based energy measurement.
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Fine 3D imaging works equally well for protons and muons at all angles, including backward tracks. Projective scintillator-bar or wire readouts lose tracks at high angles.
- **Pile-up.** At 410 m the event rate is high. Modular optical segmentation and pixels prevent the event overlaps that wires or projective readouts suffer from.

**Alternative:** A high-pressure (around 10 bar) gaseous argon TPC would give even lower proton thresholds. However, it provides about 50× less mass and therefore far fewer interactions. LAr is preferred for statistics.

## 2. Low-mass cryostat that fits inside the warm magnet

**Technology:** A thin-walled, vacuum-insulated cryostat (composite or thin stainless steel, membrane style) shaped to the target box. It should be thermally isolated from the magnet coils and leave the 0.15 T field undisturbed.

**Why:**
- Exiting muons must reach the outer trackers with minimal multiple scattering and energy loss.
- Cryostat walls must not create a dense dead layer that degrades charge and momentum measurement or confuses vertexing.

## 3. Large-angle and upstream trackers surrounding the target

**Technology:** Gas TPCs or drift chambers (or thin scintillator-fibre trackers) lining the top, bottom, and sides of the target region, plus an upstream plane. These complement the existing downstream chambers to give close to 4π coverage inside the magnet.

**Why:**
- A 0.7 GeV muon has a range of about 3 m in LAr, so most muons exit the target and cannot be measured by containment.
- The existing chambers sit only downstream. Muons near 90° or going backward never reach them, which drives efficiency at those angles far below the 25% requirement.
- Side and upstream trackers in the field measure curvature, giving momentum and charge sign for those tracks.

## 4. Time-of-flight system enclosing the target and new trackers

**Technology:** Plastic-scintillator bar panels with SiPM readout at both ends and timing resolution of about 100–150 ps, covering all faces.

**Why:**
- **Direction.** At high angles, a backward-going muon and an incoming entering track look identical without timing. ToF fixes track direction and sense.
- **Background rejection.** It rejects particles entering from outside, such as sand and magnet-yoke interactions.
- **Particle ID.** It supports muon/proton/pion separation for exiting tracks.
- **No hydrogen penalty.** The scintillator lies outside the argon fiducial volume.

## 5. Supporting upgrades

**Electronics, DAQ and trigger:**
- Pixel electronics that remain continuously live and self-trigger.
- A DAQ sized for the beam-spill pile-up at 410 m.
- Timing synchronized to beam-spill and ToF timing.

**Calibration systems:**
- Laser or UV ionization tracks for drift-field and E-field distortion maps.
- Cryogenic purity monitors to track electron lifetime.
- Cosmic-ray triggering.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the active target with a pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC, which provides a hydrogen-free target and 3D tracking of 60 MeV protons at all angles.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## 1. Super-FGD as the Primary Active Neutrino Target

The central piece should be a **3D-granular scintillator cube detector** — specifically the Super-FGD design already under development by the collaboration. Concretely:

- **~2×10⁶ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each 1×1×1 cm³**, arranged in an approximately 192×184×56 cm³ array fitting the available 2.0×1.9×0.6 m box
- Each cube drilled along all three orthogonal axes and threaded with **1 mm Kuraray Y-11 wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers**
- Fiber ends read out by **Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs, 1.3×1.3 mm², 25 µm pixel pitch)**, one SiPM per fiber end (optionally both ends for light yield and position resolution)
- This gives full 3D track reconstruction with ~1 cm³ voxel resolution and no preferred tracking direction, directly solving the large-angle (>50°) acceptance problem for both muons and protons
- Target mass ~2 tonnes of hydrocarbon (CH₂-dominated), compatible with the existing FGD cross-section program

**Why this matters:** Conventional layered FGD geometry loses tracking efficiency beyond ~30–40° because tracks cross few layers. The 3D cube geometry maintains reconstruction efficiency out to near 90°, covering the stated 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50°.

---

## 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes — Surrounding the Super-FGD

Install **six planar ToF panels** (top, bottom, upstream face, downstream face, left, right) assembled from **fast plastic scintillator slabs (EJ-200 or BC-408, ~1–2 cm thick)** with **SiPM readout at both ends via embedded WLS fiber or direct coupling**.

- Target timing resolution: **≤200 ps** per panel (achievable with SiPM + fast shaping electronics)
- Panel segmentation: ~5×5 cm² granularity to handle multi-hit events
- Purpose: 
  - Distinguish protons from pions and muons via ToF + momentum (from curvature or range)
  - Provide an independent trigger and event t₀ for the Super-FGD
  - Identify backward-going particles unambiguously

**Momentum–ToF matching at 450 MeV/c:** A proton at 450 MeV/c (β ≈ 0.43) crossing 60 cm gives a ToF of ~4.6 ns vs. a pion (β ≈ 0.95) at ~2.1 ns — a 2.5 ns separation, well above 200 ps resolution.

---

## 3. Upgraded TPC Readout — Replacement of Bulk Micromegas with Resistive Micromegas or Resistive-Strip Micromegas

For the three existing downstream TPCs (and any new TPC that may be inserted if volume allows):

- Replace current **bulk Micromegas pads** with **resistive-strip Micromegas** (as demonstrated by ATLAS NSW, resistive anode pitch ~250 µm)
- This eliminates spark damage, allows higher gain operation (×3–5 improvement in S/N), and improves spatial resolution to **~70 µm** in the precision coordinate
- Replace existing **AFTER-based FECs** with **DREAM/AFTER2** ASICs offering 50 MHz sampling rate (vs. current 25 MHz) and lower ENC (~500 e⁻ vs. ~800 e⁻)
- Keep the existing Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 gas mixture (well-characterized, good drift velocity ~7.3 cm/µs)

**Impact:** Improved dE/dx resolution (target <7% σ) sharpens proton/pion separation in the momentum range 200–900 MeV/c where the leading-proton spectrum is concentrated, directly reducing cross-section systematic uncertainty.

---

## 4. Thin High-Pressure Time Projection Chamber (HPTPC) Insert — Optional if Volume Permits

If ~20 cm of additional longitudinal space can be recovered by removing P0D infrastructure:

- A **small HPTPC cell (~10 atm Ar:CO₂, ~40×40×20 cm³ active volume)** upstream of the Super-FGD
- **GEM or MicroMegas readout**, fully enclosed, operating at high pressure to increase target mass without mechanical bulk
- **Purpose:** Provides a very low-density (ρ_effective low per unit volume but high actual mass), low-Z, nearly pure-argon nuclear target for carbon/argon cross-section ratio measurements complementing the hydrocarbon and water targets
- This is technically mature (DUNE ND-GAr prototype exists; PEP4 TPC heritage)

This is lower priority than items 1–3 and contingent on space.

---

## 5. SiPM Replacement on Existing ECal Channels (Incremental Upgrade)

The existing lead-scintillator ECals use **Hamamatsu MPPCs (667 or 400 pixel variants)** that show measurable radiation damage after several years of running.

- Replace with **current-generation Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD SiPMs** (lower dark current after irradiation, higher PDE ~50% vs. ~35%, lower cross-talk <2%)
- No structural changes needed; the WLS fiber–SiPM interface geometry is preserved
- Expected gain in energy resolution: ~10–15% improvement in photon detection efficiency, pushing ECal π⁰ reconstruction threshold down and improving the kinematic completeness for electromagnetic final states

---

## 6. Beam-Synchronous DAQ and Trigger Upgrade

- Deploy a **common White Rabbit timing network** (IEEE 1588 PTP variant, <1 ns synchronization) across Super-FGD, ToF panels, TPCs, and ECals
- Replace current TRIP-t/FEE boards with **WaveDAQ or TOFPET2 ASIC-based readout** (already used by MEG II, FOOT experiments) capable of streaming full waveforms at 1 GSa/s per channel for offline pulse-shape discrimination
- Implement an **FPGA-level online track-seed trigger** using Super-FGD hit-cluster multiplicity to reduce data volume while keeping multi-prong events

# Design Review Recommendations: ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Executive Summary

The core challenge is instrumentation of a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume that must reconstruct kinematically complete CC events — specifically muons up to ~25° large-angle exits and protons with median 450 MeV/c (range in plastic ~18 cm) up to 900 MeV/c (~60 cm range) — while reducing systematic uncertainty from 6% to 4%. The 0.6 m depth constraint is tight but workable if technology choices are made carefully.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. SuperFGD Scintillator Cube Active Target (Primary Target Volume)

**Specific technology:** 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres read out by MPPCs (SiPMs, e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS or equivalent), arranged in a ~180 × 190 × 56 cube array filling roughly 1.8 × 1.9 × 0.56 m.

**Justification:**
- The 4π segmentation is the critical departure from strip-based FGD geometry. The existing FGD bar design (9.6 mm × 9.6 mm × 1864 mm) has a tracking threshold of ~100 MeV/c for protons going transversely, and poorly reconstructs large-angle tracks because the lever arm vanishes in the short (z) dimension. Cubic geometry resolves this: a proton at 50° deposits hits in all three projections simultaneously, and 1 cm cubes provide ~5 mm position resolution via charge-sharing and fibre readout, sufficient to reconstruct 450 MeV/c protons over ~18 cube lengths.
- The 1 cm cube size keeps the threshold for proton tracking at roughly 300 MeV/c kinetic energy (~450 MeV/c momentum), matching the stated median proton momentum. At 900 MeV/c (~350 MeV kinetic energy), the proton range is ~60 cm = 60 cubes, well-contained within the 0.6 m depth and easily reconstructed.
- The three-fibre readout per cube, combined with the existing ND280 MPPC procurement infrastructure, makes this technologically conservative while being geometrically revolutionary. The collaboration already has MPPC experience from FGD and ECal.
- This technology is already developed as the SuperFGD baseline for the ND280 upgrade; the review panel should confirm full-scale production readiness and the fibre routing scheme to avoid dead channels in the central region.
- Polystyrene target composition (CH) is explicitly approved for this programme and allows direct comparison with FGD1.
- Estimated ~570,000 cubes for the full volume; the fibre count (~1.7 million channels) is large but manageable with multiplexed MPPC readout at reduced cost per channel.

**Risk flag:** The main risk is fibre-to-MPPC assembly yield and optical cross-talk between adjacent cubes. The collaboration should require a minimum light yield of 15 p.e./MIP and cross-talk below 3% before acceptance.

---

### 2. Thin-Gap Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes — Upstream and Downstream Faces of Target

**Specific technology:** Two planes of 5 mm-thick fast plastic scintillator (e.g. EJ-228, rise time ~0.5 ns) in 2 cm × full-width strips, with SiPM readout at both ends, placed immediately upstream (~5 mm gap) and immediately downstream of the SuperFGD volume.

**Justification:**
- Proton/pion separation is essential for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies. A proton at 450 MeV/c has β ≈ 0.43; a pion at the same momentum has β ≈ 0.96. Over the ~0.6 m target depth the ToF difference is ~1.1 ns, but the entry/exit ToF planes provide a clean external tag of track directionality.
- The downstream ToF plane simultaneously acts as a veto discriminator for beam-direction throughgoing muons, reducing the event-building rate by flagging cleanly forward-going tracks before full reconstruction is invoked.
- The upstream plane provides event T0 to ~200 ps, anchoring drift-time-independent reconstruction in the SuperFGD (which has no intrinsic fast timing from WLS fibres, whose decay time is ~2.7 ns). This T0 is especially important for in-spill pile-up rejection given J-PARC bunch structure (~100 ns bunch spacing in some running modes).
- EJ-228 strips at this thickness introduce <0.3% X₀ material — negligible for the target mass budget.
- The strip geometry (2 cm width) gives ~6 mm transverse position resolution from charge division, sufficient to match to SuperFGD cube rows.

---

### 3. High-Granularity Resistive Micromegas or sTGC Tracking Planes on the Lateral Faces

**Specific technology:** Two resistive-strip Micromegas panels (or small-cell sTGC panels, 2.8 mm pitch) mounted on the left and right lateral faces (the 2.0 m × 0.6 m faces in the horizontal plane), with strip pitch of 3–5 mm, acting as dedicated large-angle muon catchers.

**Justification:**
- 25% of muons exit at >50° to the beam. For a CC event vertex in the centre of the SuperFGD, a 50° muon travels only ~30 cm before exiting the 0.6 m depth — leaving ~8 cm of lateral path before exiting the side. The existing downstream TPC chain cannot reconstruct these muons; they simply escape.
- Thin planar Micromegas panels (5–8 mm drift gap, resistive DLC coating to suppress spark damage) can be installed flush against the lateral magnet faces with minimal structural modification. The T2K TPCs already use bulk Micromegas; the collaboration has the full technology chain for gas system, front-end electronics (AFTER chip), and calibration.
- An alternative is sTGC (as used in the ATLAS New Small Wheel), which achieves 100 µm resolution with 2.8 mm strip pitch and is mechanically robust. Either provides sufficient dE/dx for muon/pion discrimination at momenta above ~200 MeV/c.
- Two lateral panels covering the ±y faces (the 2.0 × 0.6 m faces) are the highest priority; two additional ±x panels would complete 4π lateral coverage but require negotiation with the magnet yoke geometry.
- The momentum of a large-angle muon can be estimated from range (if it stops in SMRD) or from curvature in the 0.2 T field over the lateral panel length. Even 2 m of lever arm in the magnetic field gives σ(p)/p² ≈ 0.3 (GeV/c)⁻¹, adequate for the ~300–600 MeV/c range where these muons concentrate.

---

### 4. Upgraded MPPC Readout with On-Detector CITIROC/TOFPET2 ASICs

**Specific technology:** Replace the current ND280 MPPC readout (AFTER-based, designed for TPC strip readout) for the new target volume with TOFPET2 or CITIROC-2A ASICs (both commercially available, designed specifically for SiPM arrays), mounted on-detector in a 32-channel or 64-channel configuration.

**Justification:**
- The AFTER chip has an analogue shaping time of ~80 ns and was optimised for TPC charge integration, not fast scintillation timing. For the SuperFGD + ToF system, the combination of timing resolution (~1 ns), low-charge sensitivity (threshold ~0.3 p.e.), and simultaneous charge/time measurement in a single ASIC is essential for in-bunch pile-up rejection.
- TOFPET2 provides 50 ps TDC resolution and 10-bit charge measurement in 64 channels; CITIROC-2A provides 16-bit charge resolution at lower cost. Either satisfies requirements.
- On-detector placement reduces the cable plant from ~1.7 million channels to ~27,000 serial data links (at 64:1 multiplexing), which is cabling-feasible within the magnet volume.
- Thermal dissipation (~50 mW/ASIC × ~26,000 ASICs ≈ 1.3 kW total) is manageable with the existing forced-air cooling infrastructure in the magnet bore; a water-cooling rail along the SuperFGD frame perimeter should nonetheless be baselined.

---

### 5. Passive Water-Copper Conversion Layer on the Upstream Face

**Specific technology:** A 10 mm-thick slab of copper (1.1% X₀) followed immediately by a 25 mm water layer (enclosed in thin-wall aluminium) placed 20 mm upstream of the SuperFGD entry face, covering the full 1.9 × 2.0 m aperture.

**Justification:**
- The stated physics programme explicitly accepts hydrocarbon targets, but maximising systematic uncertainty reduction for T2K-II requires a carbon-to-water cross-section ratio measurement in the same near-detector hall with the same flux. The downstream FGD2 provides this for forward-going tracks; the upstream conversion layer extends water-target exposure to large-angle topologies.
- The copper layer converts a small fraction of events to a copper nuclear target (A=63), giving an additional isospin-symmetric cross-section handle, and also acts as a photon converter for any π⁰ → γγ background estimation.
- The 10 mm Cu + 25 mm H₂O is thin enough (total ~1.5% X₀, ~3% nuclear interaction length) that it does not materially degrade the vertex resolution for interactions originating within the SuperFGD proper (which remains the primary fiducial volume), but provides a statistically useful secondary fiducial volume for cross-section ratio measurements.
- This eliminates the need for a separate dedicated water-target detector and costs essentially nothing in terms of readout channels.

---

### 6. SMRD Trigger Path Upgrade for Large-Angle Muon Timing

**Specific technology:** Add a hardware trigger primitive from the SMRD (existing scintillator in magnet yoke gaps) directly to the new SuperFGD front-end trigger logic via a low-latency optical link (e.g. SFP+ at 1 Gbps, <50 ns latency).

**Justification:**
- Large-angle muons at >50° from a SuperFGD interaction vertex will frequently stop in or transit the SMRD, which is already instrumented. Currently, the SMRD trigger is used for cosmic-muon calibration but is not part of the physics trigger primitive chain for the upstream region.
- A direct SMRD→SuperFGD coincidence trigger with <50 ns latency would provide a dedicated large-angle muon CC trigger with high efficiency and low threshold (a track in SMRD + ≥5 hit cubes in SuperFGD), enabling a data-driven measurement of the large-angle muon acceptance without relying solely on simulation.
- The required firmware modification to the existing ND280 DAQ (based on COPPER/FINESSE or the upgraded system) and fibre routing is a few person-months of effort — low cost for a significant systematic benefit.

---

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

Before proposing upgrades, let me work through the constraints:

**Muon reconstruction:** Need ≥25% efficiency at *all* angles including 90° and backward. The existing dipole (0.15 T × 6.5 m → Bρ gives ~1 GeV/c bend radius ~22 m, so sagitta ~18 mm for 1 GeV/c track over 6.5 m) handles forward muons well, but perpendicular and backward tracks need active target instrumentation itself to provide tracking, since they may not reach the downstream drift chambers.

**Proton reconstruction:** 60 MeV kinetic energy protons have range ~16 mm in water (or ~8 mm in iron). This demands very fine-grained tracking with ~few-mm spatial resolution and low-Z, low-density material to give sufficient track length.

**Hydrogen constraint:** ≤2% hydrogen by nucleon count. Water is ~11% hydrogen by nucleon number. Pure CH₂ is ~67% hydrogen. Argon LAr is 0% hydrogen. Scintillator (CH) is ~7.7% hydrogen. This is a *severe* constraint that strongly limits material choice.

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Replacement of Passive Target Material with Low-Hydrogen Scintillating Fiber / Emulsion Hybrid Stack

**Primary active target: 3D scintillating fiber tracker**

Replace the existing target volume with a stack of **scintillating fiber (SciFi) planes** using **polystyrene-based fibers of 250 μm diameter**, arranged in X-Y-U stereo views, with SiPM readout.

- Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has hydrogen fraction by nucleon: 8/(8×12 + 8) = 8/104 ≈ 7.7% — *this exceeds the 2% limit*
- **Solution:** Interleave scintillating fiber planes with **thin lead or steel absorber sheets** to dilute the hydrogen fraction.
  - If fibers occupy fraction *f* of the volume and steel (0% H) occupies (1-f), then H fraction = 7.7% × f ≤ 2% → f ≤ 26% by nucleon count.
  - Using 3 mm steel plates between fiber plane assemblies (~2 mm thick active fiber layers) achieves this while maintaining reasonable tracking efficiency.
  - Spatial resolution of ~100 μm per view from 250 μm fibers.
  - SiPM readout (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series, 1×1 mm² tiles at fiber ends via clear fiber light guides) handles the ~2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse area.

**Why this addresses requirements:**
- 3D hit reconstruction in the fiber planes reconstructs tracks at all angles including 90° and backward — no reliance on downstream spectrometer for these.
- 250 μm fiber pitch gives ~10 hits on a 16 mm proton track (track length >> 5 fibers → reconstructable).
- SciFi planes provide ~ns timing to separate interaction vertex from secondary interactions.

---

### 2. Upgrade of Upstream Magnet Field or Addition of Mini-Coil Around Target Region

The existing 0.15 T dipole field acts over 6.5 m but the *target* occupies only 0.9 m along beam. Tracks emitted at 90° or backward travel entirely within the target volume and see very little bending from the main dipole.

**Proposal:** Install a **compact normal-conducting racetrack coil** around the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target volume itself, adding ~0.3–0.5 T within it. The coil runs outside the active tracking volume.

- At 0.5 T over 0.9 m, a 300 MeV/c track (typical muon momentum at 0.7 GeV ν) has sagitta ~25 mm in the target alone — well measurable with 100 μm resolution fibers.
- This allows momentum determination for tracks that do *not* exit the target volume into the spectrometer.
- Warm copper coil, ~few kA turns, feasible in existing infrastructure.
- The field must be mapped carefully; the SciFi tracker operates in-field (SiPMs tolerate up to ~1–2 T with modest gain reduction, manageable at 0.5 T with appropriate bias adjustment).

---

### 3. Nuclear Emulsion Cloud Chamber (ECC) Modules for Short Proton Tracks (Supplementary)

For the most demanding proton reconstruction (60 MeV, ~16 mm range), add **thin nuclear emulsion films** interleaved with the fiber planes in a subset (~20%) of the target volume.

- Emulsion provides sub-micron spatial resolution, reconstructing proton tracks of even a few mm.
- Use **Emulsion Cloud Chamber** structure: 50 μm emulsion layers on plastic base, interleaved between scintillating fiber planes.
- Emulsion is essentially pure AgBr + gelatin — gelatin (C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁N₂) has some hydrogen, but emulsion layers are thin (~100 μm total); nucleon budget is dominated by Ag/Br (Z=47/35), making hydrogen contribution negligible (<0.5% of target nucleons in this hybrid).
- The fiber planes provide the trigger/timestamp to allow offline matching of emulsion tracks to beam spills.
- Emulsion modules can be replaced between run periods (standard NINJA/NINJA-style operation).

---

### 4. Downstream Drift Chamber Upgrade: Addition of Time-of-Flight Wall

Install a **scintillator time-of-flight (ToF) wall** immediately downstream of the active target (between target and main dipole volume) and one at the downstream face of the magnet.

- **Upstream ToF wall:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m array of 3 cm × 3 cm cross-section BC-408 scintillator bars read by SiPMs at both ends. Timing resolution ~200 ps.
- Provides: (a) event T₀ for drift chamber hit association; (b) n/γ rejection; (c) proton/pion separation via ToF for tracks exiting the target.
- **Proton at 60 MeV KE** (v/c ≈ 0.35) vs **pion at same momentum** are cleanly separated over even 0.5 m baseline at 200 ps resolution (Δt ~ several ns).
- Also improves backward muon identification: backward tracks arrive at the upstream ToF wall and trigger a dedicated readout stream.

---

### 5. Beam-Left and Beam-Right Tracking Wings

The existing geometry is 2.6 m (horizontal) × 2.3 m (vertical) × 0.9 m (along beam). Perpendicular tracks exit through the 2.6 m × 2.3 m side faces.

**Proposal:** Install two **tracking wing stations** on the beam-left and beam-right faces of the target volume, each consisting of 4 planes of drift tubes (3 cm diameter aluminized mylar drift tubes with Ar:CO₂ 70:30 gas, ~150 μm resolution).

- Each wing: 2.3 m (height) × 0.9 m (depth along beam), 4 planes in X, Y, U, V.
- Tracks exiting perpendicular to the beam enter these wings, providing 4+ additional hits and good momentum measurement via curvature in the main dipole field (which has significant horizontal component on these tracks).
- Drift tubes contribute negligible hydrogen (aluminized mylar walls, Ar:CO₂ fill).
- Existing downstream drift chambers already handle forward tracks; wings close the angular gap.

Similarly, add a **backward-going track catcher**: a 2.6 m × 2.3 m plane of scintillating fibers at the upstream face of the target, plus connection to any existing upstream instrumentation.

---

### 6. Upgraded Gas Drift Chambers: Higher-Granularity Central Tracking

Replace the nearest downstream drift chamber station (immediately behind the target) with **straw tube tracker modules** (4 mm diameter Kapton straws, Ar:CO₂, 50 μm wire):

- Finer granularity reduces left-right ambiguity and improves pattern recognition in high-multiplicity neutrino events.
- Kapton/Ar:CO₂ — hydrogen in Kapton (C₂₂H₁₀N₂O₅) is a small contribution to the *downstream* spectrometer, which is not part of the fiducial target volume, so the 2% constraint does not apply here.
- Straw diameter 4 mm → ~150 μm resolution, improvement over existing chambers.

---

| 3D SciFi tracker with steel dilution | All-angle tracking, proton reconstruction, H constraint | 250 μm fiber, steel interleaving, SiPM RO |
| In-target mini-coil | Momentum measurement of non-exiting tracks | 0.3–0.5 T over 0.9 m |
| Emulsion ECC modules | Short proton tracks ≥60 MeV KE | Sub-μm resolution, ~20% volume |
