TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a 3D scintillating fiber tracker (250 μm polystyrene fibers, SiPM readout) interleaved with thin steel sheets to dilute hydrogen below 2% of target nucleons, providing the sub-millimeter 3D hit resolution needed to reconstruct proton tracks down to 60 MeV kinetic energy and muon tracks at all angles including perpendicular and backward without relying on the downstream spectrometer.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before listing upgrades, let me identify the binding physics constraints:

- Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at **all angles** including 90° and backward — this kills passive absorber designs
- Proton tracks down to **~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range in water ~5 mm, in iron ~3 mm) — demands very fine-grained or low-density active material
- Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons — constrains what materials are acceptable
- Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m — roughly 5.4 m³
- Existing downstream spectrometer handles forward muon momentum measurement; the target region itself must handle the rest

---

## Upgrade 1: 3D Plastic Scintillator with Wavelength-Shifting Fiber Readout (SuperFGD-style)

**Technology:** An array of small plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³ each), each cube penetrated by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). This architecture was developed for the T2K ND280 upgrade (SuperFGD) and is well-matched to this problem.

**Physics motivation:**

The 1 cm cube pitch gives a tracking threshold corresponding to proton kinetic energy of roughly 40–50 MeV (range ~4–5 cm in plastic, so actually the threshold is set by requiring ≥2–3 hit cubes, achievable around 50–60 MeV kinetic energy), satisfying the proton requirement. The fully 3D segmentation means there is **no preferred tracking direction**: a track at 90° to the beam crosses the same number of cubes as a forward track, so muon reconstruction efficiency is uniform in angle. Backward-going tracks are reconstructed identically. The plastic scintillator is predominantly polystyrene (CH), with hydrogen constituting roughly 7–8% of nucleons by number — well within the 20% cap. The ~6 ns scintillation time constant and SiPM readout enable time-of-flight separation of protons from pions at the few-hundred-MeV/c scale. The fine granularity also allows dE/dx particle identification along each track.

A fill of this active volume (~5.4 m³) requires on the order of 5 million 1 cm³ cubes and ~15 million SiPM channels — a large but technically demonstrated scale (T2K SuperFGD is ~2 million cubes).

---

## Upgrade 2: Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Panels Interleaved with the Scintillator

**Technology:** Thin resistive Micromegas or GEM-based TPCs, with active gas (e.g., Ar:CF₄:isobutane or Ar:CO₂), arranged as panels sandwiching scintillator modules within the target volume. Each TPC panel is ~2–4 cm thick (drift gap), giving continuous 3D hit positions with ~200 µm resolution.

**Physics motivation:**

The 3D scintillator is superb for short, high-dE/dx proton tracks but its spatial resolution (1 cm) is marginal for momentum measurement of low-momentum muons that stop within the target volume before reaching the downstream spectrometer. TPC panels provide **continuous ionization measurement** with sub-millimeter precision along the full track, enabling curvature measurement within the magnetic field volume. This is especially important for 90° and backward muons that may never reach the spectrometer. The TPC also provides excellent dE/dx resolution (a few percent), sharpening the proton/pion/muon separation that the scintillator begins. The TPC gas contributes additional nuclear target material (argon serves as a cross-section measurement target in its own right, relevant to oscillation experiments), but the low density keeps the material budget low so short proton tracks are not ranged out before being detected.

---

## Upgrade 3: Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL) Panels on the Lateral and Upstream Faces

**Technology:** Layers of lead absorber (2–3 mm per layer) interleaved with scintillator strips or tiles read out by SiPMs, forming a sampling ECAL with ~10–12 radiation lengths total, surrounding the upstream and side faces of the active target. Strip pitch ~1 cm, with two orthogonal orientations for 2D position reconstruction.

**Physics motivation:**

Neutral pions (π⁰) produced in neutrino interactions decay to two photons within nanoseconds. These photons travel up to ~20 cm in the scintillator before converting (radiation length in plastic ~40 cm), meaning many photons **escape the active target laterally or upstream** without depositing energy. Without the ECAL, π⁰ energy goes unmeasured, preventing neutral-current background rejection and exclusive-channel reconstruction. Surrounding the target with a hermetic ECAL caps photon escape and allows full event energy reconstruction. The thin absorber (electromagnetic, not hadronic, depth) keeps the ECAL from ranging out the backward and sideways muons that are central to the analysis — a full hadronic calorimeter would absorb them and defeat the muon angle-coverage requirement. The lead/scintillator technology is well-understood, inexpensive, and easily integrated with SiPM readout matched to the rest of the detector.

---

## Upgrade 4: Precision Timing Layer (Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors, LGADs)

**Technology:** A plane of LGAD silicon sensors (~2 mm pitch) on the downstream face of the active target, providing hit timestamps with ~30–50 ps resolution per plane. Two or three such planes, separated by ~5 cm, form a time-of-flight (TOF) telescope.

**Physics motivation:**

The magnetic spectrometer downstream measures rigidity (p/q), not mass. Separating protons from pions and kaons at momenta of 300–700 MeV/c (the relevant range for recoil particles escaping the target forward) requires TOF at the ~100 ps level over ~1 m baseline — precisely what LGADs provide. This directly reduces the systematic uncertainty on identifying whether a forward-going low-momentum track is a proton (indicating a quasi-elastic interaction) or a pion (indicating resonance production). For interactions on hydrogen — which must be **subtracted** using a model — correct particle identification is essential: a misidentified proton biases the hydrogen content estimate and undermines the ≤20% hydrogen cap requirement. Additionally, the precision timing tags which beam spill bucket the interaction belongs to (the accelerator bunch structure is typically ~2 ns), suppressing out-of-time cosmic ray and beam halo backgrounds.

---

## Upgrade 5: Upstream Veto and Muon-Range Stack Replacement with Active Plastic Scintillator Bars

**Technology:** Replace any passive upstream material with segmented plastic scintillator bars (3 cm × 3 cm cross-section, full lateral extent), read out at both ends by SiPMs. Stack extends ~30 cm upstream of the main active target.

**Physics motivation:**

Neutrino interactions occurring in the material **upstream** of the active target (beam pipe flanges, support structures, cryogenic plumbing if present) can produce muons that enter the target from behind and mimic backward-going tracks from genuine in-target interactions. This background is particularly insidious because the analysis specifically requires backward-muon reconstruction. An upstream veto with ~1 ns timing resolution and segmented spatial readout vetoes such events at high efficiency. The all-plastic construction (no iron or lead) minimizes radiation length, so the veto does not shadow or range out any particles that actually come from within the target.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3D scintillator cubes + SiPMs | Isotropic tracking; short proton tracks; main target mass |
| 2 | Micromegas/GEM TPC panels | Muon momentum in-target; dE/dx PID; low material budget |
| 3 | Pb-scintillator ECAL on lateral/upstream faces | π⁰ containment; full event energy reconstruction |
| 4 | LGAD precision timing planes | TOF PID; bunch tagging; hydrogen subtraction systematics |
| 5 | Active upstream scintillator veto | Backward-track background rejection |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: 3D plastic scintillator cube array with SiPM readout (SuperFGD architecture), because it simultaneously solves the two hardest physics requirements — isotropic muon tracking efficiency including backward tracks, and proton reconstruction down to 60 MeV kinetic energy — within the hydrogen-fraction constraint, and no other single upgrade addresses both at once.

# Upgrade proposal for the off-axis near detector

## Diagnosis

The current detector was optimised for forward-going tracks. Its scintillator bars and TPCs are perpendicular to the beam, so tracks at high angle or going backward run along a single bar layer or miss the TPCs. Three consequences follow:

- **High-angle muons are lost.** About 25% of muons leave above 50°. The far detector, a water Cherenkov, has essentially 4π acceptance, so this mismatch in phase space feeds directly into the flux and cross-section extrapolation.
- **Low-momentum protons are lost.** A proton must cross several 1 cm bars in two views to be tracked, which sets a threshold of roughly 450–500 MeV/c. That is about the median of the leading-proton spectrum, so roughly half the leading protons are lost. Transverse kinematic imbalance (δpT, δαT, δφT) needs both the muon and the proton, with good angle and momentum resolution, and ideally the neutron as well.
- **No neutron information.** Without neutrons, antineutrino energy reconstruction and nuclear-effect constraints remain model-dependent.

The upgrade below uses the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box and the space around it inside the magnet.

## 1. Fine-granularity 3D scintillator target (core upgrade)

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes. Each cube is wrapped in a reflective, chemically etched TiO₂ layer and has three orthogonal holes.
- Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres thread each cube. Each fibre is read at one end by an SiPM, about 56,000 channels in total.
- Approximate size: 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, about 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.56 m and about 2 t. This fits the box and roughly doubles the hydrocarbon target mass.

**Physics motivation**
- **True 3D readout gives isotropic acceptance.** Three projections in every cube give the same response for forward, high-angle and backward tracks. This recovers the 25% of muons above 50° and the 35% of protons at high angle.
- **Lower proton threshold.** Tracking down to about 300 MeV/c, or roughly 4 cm of range, captures most of the leading-proton spectrum and enables kinematically complete TKI measurements.
- **Momentum by range and calorimetry.** Stopping protons, which cover most of the spectrum below 900 MeV/c, get momentum from range and dE/dx with resolution of a few percent. Proton/pion and muon/pion separation comes from Bragg-peak dE/dx.
- **Neutron tagging.** Neutrons are identified as isolated cube hits displaced from the vertex. Timing (about 1 ns per channel combined across fibres) gives neutron kinetic energy by time of flight. This allows full δpT in antineutrino CC0π, which is unique for constraining nuclear effects and antineutrino energy.
- **Photon and electron identification.** Fine 3D granularity provides γ/e separation for νe and NC π⁰ backgrounds, partly replacing the physics of the removed photon-tagging section.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Gas TPCs (Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ "T2K gas") with a lightweight composite field cage to minimise dead material.
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated-anode) Micromegas. Charge spreading across the resistive layer gives about 600 µm or better resolution with fewer, larger pads, and also protects against sparks.
- Each TPC is roughly 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, with drift along the beam axis or the horizontal direction.

**Physics motivation**
- Provides magnetic-field momentum and charge measurement, plus dE/dx PID (better than 10% resolution, for e/µ separation), for tracks leaving the cube target at high angle. Those tracks currently see no TPC.
- Measures the most energetic protons (the about 6% above 900 MeV/c that exit the target) and high-angle muons that do not stop.
- Charge identification gives the wrong-sign background in antineutrino mode.
- Together with the existing downstream TPCs, this gives nearly 4π momentum-analysed acceptance.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

**Technology**
- Six planes of plastic scintillator bars, about 1 cm thick and 12 cm wide, about 2.2 m long.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs, giving roughly 150 ps time resolution.
- The planes enclose the new target and the high-angle TPCs.

**Physics motivation**
- **Track direction.** ToF resolves forward versus backward and inward versus outward tracks. This rejects out-of-fiducial-volume backgrounds, such as particles entering from magnet or sand interactions, that mimic backward-going muons.
- **Particle ID.** It adds PID (p/µ/e) in the momentum range where TPC dE/dx bands cross.
- **Event timing.** It provides a timing reference for neutron ToF in the cube target.

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Readout electronics.** Use common SiPM front-ends with nanosecond timing (CITIROC-class ASICs, for example) and an upgraded DAQ. These must handle the large channel count, higher beam power with a shorter repetition time, and sub-ns timing for neutron kinetic energy.
- **Light-yield monitoring and test-beam calibration.** Charged-particle and neutron test-beam campaigns are needed to establish cube response, crosstalk (a few percent per face) and neutron detection efficiency. These directly control systematics at the 4% goal.
- **Retain the water-layer target downstream.** Combined with the new 3D CH target, the same TKI and CC0π observables can be compared on carbon and on water.

## Expected impact

| Effect | Change |
|---|---|
| Muon acceptance | Nearly 4π, matching the far detector |
| Proton threshold | About 500 → 300 MeV/c |
| Neutron tagging | Neutrons tagged with energy measured |
| TKI | Kinematically complete measurements enabled |

These directly constrain nucleon removal energy, 2p2h and final-state-interaction models. This is the path from about 6% to about 4% systematic uncertainty on far-detector event-rate predictions.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a 2-tonne fine-granularity 3D scintillator-cube active target (≈2 million 1 cm³ cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibres, SiPM readout), complemented by high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs.

This is an interesting neutrino detector design challenge. Let me analyze the requirements systematically:

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Geometric coverage**: Need 4π acceptance including backward-going tracks
2. **Low-momentum protons**: 60 MeV kinetic energy protons have range ~2 mm in plastic, ~10 cm in gas
3. **Muon efficiency**: ≥25% at all angles (muons from ~0.7 GeV neutrinos typically have p ~ 0.3-0.5 GeV/c)
4. **Hydrogen constraint**: ≤2% of target nucleons
5. **Existing assets**: Warm dipole (0.15 T), downstream drift chambers

## Critical Issues with Current Setup

The downstream-only tracking is incompatible with backward-going particle requirements. The hydrogen constraint essentially prohibits liquid or plastic scintillator targets.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) as Active Target**
- Fill the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume with argon gas at ~1-10 atm
- Provides 3D tracking with dE/dx for particle ID
- Can detect short proton tracks (60 MeV protons have ~10-30 cm range depending on pressure)
- Argon has no hydrogen (satisfies <2% constraint)
- Full 4π angular acceptance within fiducial volume
- Electric field parallel to beam direction for drift

### 2. **Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL)**
- Plastic scintillator or lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter on all six faces
- Catches particles exiting the TPC volume
- Provides timing and energy measurement for escaping tracks
- Helps with muon/pion separation via dE/dx at boundaries

### 3. **Improved Downstream Tracking**
- Add straw tubes or micromegas chambers immediately after the TPC
- Better momentum resolution from combining TPC + downstream tracks in magnetic field
- Redundancy for forward-going muons

### 4. **Upstream Veto/Tracker**
- Thin scintillator planes upstream of target
- Reject cosmic rays and beam-induced backgrounds
- Track incoming particles

### 5. **Readout Electronics**
- High-channel-count DAQ for TPC (possibly ~10,000-100,000 channels)
- Trigger system coordinated with beam spill timing
- Needs ~MHz sampling for good spatial resolution

## Alternative Consideration

**Fine-grained solid tracker** (e.g., scintillating bars or fibers): Would provide better spatial resolution but struggles with the backward-going and low-energy proton requirements. The stopping power makes it hard to see 60 MeV protons without making the detector too thick (creating more interactions outside the active volume).

## Why TPC is Optimal

- **Low Z material**: Argon (Z=18) provides low hydrogen content
- **Stopping power**: Adjustable via pressure to optimize for 60 MeV protons
- **Continuous tracking**: No dead material/gaps for short tracks
- **dE/dx**: Particle identification for p/π/μ separation
- **4π coverage**: Intrinsic to the design
- **Proven technology**: Used successfully in many neutrino experiments (e.g., MicroBooNE, ND280)

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a high-pressure gaseous argon Time Projection Chamber filling the entire target volume with electric field parallel to beam direction and readout on both ends to provide 4π tracking coverage and low-threshold proton detection.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near-Detector Active Target

## Key design constraint: the hydrogen limit

The obvious choice would be a finely segmented plastic-scintillator target, like T2K's SuperFGD. It cannot be used here. In CH, hydrogen makes up about 1/13 ≈ 7.7% of target nucleons, far above the 2% limit. Water and other hydrocarbons fail for the same reason.

The active medium must therefore contain essentially no hydrogen. Because the far detector contains no hydrogen, it is very likely argon, so the near target should match its nucleus.

## 1. Active target: modular liquid-argon TPC with pixel readout

**Technology:** an ArgonCube/ND-LAr-style modular LArTPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region (about 5 m³, about 7 t of argon). It would read out charge on native 3D pixels (LArPix-type) rather than wires.

**Why this choice:**
- **Hydrogen content:** argon has 0% hydrogen, so the 2% limit is met with margin.
- **Same nucleus as the far detector:** this cancels much of the nuclear-model uncertainty.
- **Isotropic acceptance:** a TPC reconstructs tracks at any angle, including perpendicular and backward ones. Pixels avoid the ambiguities wires have for tracks parallel to the wire planes.
- **Low proton threshold:** a 60 MeV proton travels roughly 3 cm in liquid argon, which is many millimetre-scale pixels. That is well within reach.
- **Pile-up handling:** at 410 m, several interactions per spill are possible. Modular, optically isolated drift volumes with short drifts (about 30–50 cm) keep pile-up, space-charge effects and diffusion manageable.

## 2. Light-detection system inside each module

**Technology:** ArCLight / LCM-type light traps or SiPM-read wavelength-shifting tiles with nanosecond timing.

**Why:**
- **Event timing:** the drift time does not give the absolute event time (t₀). The light signal provides it, which is needed to place each interaction in 3D.
- **Beam association:** it ties each interaction to a specific beam bunch.
- **Pile-up separation:** it separates overlapping events in the same spill.

## 3. Thin, low-mass cryostat sized to fit the warm magnet

**Technology:** a vacuum-insulated cryostat with thin aluminium or composite walls, fitted inside the magnet's inner volume. It needs feedthroughs for the pixel and light readout.

**Why:**
- **Muon exit:** muons of about 0.7 GeV do not stop in 0.9 m of argon, so they must leave the target to be measured. Dead material in the walls must be minimal to limit multiple scattering and energy loss.
- **Fiducial volume:** wall thickness directly reduces the usable argon volume.

## 4. Upstream and side tracking around the target

**Technology:** gas TPCs or drift chambers placed above, below and on both sides of the target, plus an upstream plane, all inside the 0.15 T field.

**Why:**
- **Coverage gap:** the existing chambers are downstream only. Muons at about 90° or going backward never reach them.
- **What the new chambers provide:** sign and momentum from curvature for these large-angle and backward tracks. This is what achieves the required ≥25% efficiency at every angle.
- **Fallback for partly contained tracks:** multiple-scattering momentum measured in the LAr can supplement them.
- **Hydrogen:** any hydrogen in these chambers (for example gas quenchers) is outside the fiducial target, so it does not count against the 2% limit.

## 5. Time-of-flight scintillator shell around the target and trackers

**Technology:** fast plastic-scintillator bars read by SiPMs, with timing of about 150 ps or better, enclosing the system.

**Why:**
- **Track direction:** comparing hit times separates truly backward-going muons from forward-going particles entering from outside, and from cosmic rays.
- **Particle ID:** it helps distinguish muons from protons.
- **Hydrogen:** the scintillator is outside the fiducial volume, so it does not affect the hydrogen fraction.

## 6. Muon range detector / ECal behind the side trackers

**Technology:** a thin iron–scintillator sampling layer outside the side trackers, where the magnet structure allows.

**Why:**
- **Muon ID:** it confirms muon identity for tracks that leave at large angles.
- **Pion rejection:** it rejects pions misidentified as muons.

## 7. Supporting infrastructure

- **Cryogenics:** argon recirculation and purification to keep electron lifetime high (several ms).
- **Data acquisition:** DAQ integration with the existing drift chambers, so that tracks can be matched across the target, side and downstream systems.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a hydrogen-free, pixel-readout modular liquid-argon TPC (with light-based timing) instead of a plastic-scintillator target.

# Recommended Hardware Changes for the Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target

## The deciding constraint: the target cannot be plastic or water

The usual way to upgrade a magnetized near detector is a fine-grained plastic-scintillator active target, such as a 3D-segmented cube detector (SuperFGD-style) plus high-angle TPCs. That fails the hydrogen requirement here.

- Polystyrene is (CH)ₙ. Each CH unit has 1 hydrogen nucleon out of 13, so hydrogen is about 7.7% of target nucleons. That is roughly four times the 2% limit.
- Water (11% hydrogen) and other organic targets are worse.

Because the far detector contains no hydrogen, a hydrogen-free active medium is the natural choice. The best is the far detector's own nucleus, most plausibly argon, which also removes nuclear-target extrapolation uncertainties. Hydrogen contamination then comes only from trace impurities and dead structural material, all of which can be kept outside the fiducial volume.

## 1. Replace the target region with a modular, pixelated liquid-argon TPC (most important)

**Technology:** ArgonCube / ND-LAr style. This means several optically isolated TPC modules of about 1 m or less, read out by native-3D pixel charge readout (LArPix-type) and segmented light readout (ArCLight or light-trap tiles).

**Mass and rate:**
- 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m ≈ 5.4 m³, or about 7 t of LAr (roughly 4–5 t fiducial). That gives ample statistics at 410 m.
- At 410 m the event rate per spill is high. Short drift lengths (about 30–50 cm) plus module-level optical segmentation give a prompt t₀. Together they keep pile-up manageable and make 3D pixels unambiguous, which wire planes would not be at this rate.

**Isotropic acceptance:** A homogeneous, fully active 3D medium reconstructs tracks at any angle, including perpendicular (90°) and backward tracks. Segmented scintillator geometries and planar trackers lose these.

**Low proton threshold:**
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 cm in LAr. With roughly 4 mm pixel pitch that is about 8 or more space points.
- Calorimetric dE/dx along the Bragg peak gives proton/pion/muon separation and kinetic energy from range.
- Gas TPCs reach lower thresholds but contain too little mass in 5.4 m³ to be viable. A high-pressure argon TPC at 10 bar holds only about 100 kg.

**Muon momentum:**
- Contained muons are measured by range.
- Exiting muons are measured by multiple Coulomb scattering.
- Forward muons can also be measured by curvature in the existing downstream chambers.

**Integration:**
- Use a thin-walled, vacuum-insulated or low-mass membrane cryostat so dead material between the target and the trackers stays small.
- Place the hydrogen-bearing insulation and structure outside the fiducial volume.
- Maintain argon purity below about 0.1 ppb O₂-equivalent for millisecond electron lifetime.
- Choose cryogenic and HV feedthrough routing compatible with the warm 0.15 T dipole. The field is low enough that a cryostat is not a magnetic problem.

**Hydrogen budget:** Include only argon inside the fiducial cut. The hydrogen fraction of the fiducial nucleons is then effectively about 0%, well under the 2% limit, even after counting field-cage and pixel-board material on the module boundaries.

## 2. Add gas tracking chambers on the sides and upstream face of the target, inside the magnet

The existing drift chambers sit downstream, so high-angle and backward muons never reach them. To meet the 25% efficiency requirement at all angles, enclose the LAr cryostat with thin gas TPCs or drift chambers, as in the ND280 upgrade's high-angle TPCs. Resistive-Micromegas readout is a good option.

- They give curvature-based momentum and charge sign for escaping tracks in the 0.15 T field.
- They provide the momentum lever arm that MCS alone gives poorly at high angles.
- They are outside the target, so their hydrogen content does not matter.

## 3. Add a time-of-flight scintillator layer around the whole assembly

Use fast plastic-scintillator bars with SiPMs and roughly 150 ps resolution.

- Direction (forward versus backward) for tracks crossing two ToF layers. This is essential for distinguishing genuine backward muons from entering background.
- A veto for interactions in the magnet, cryostat, and surroundings.
- Additional particle ID.

Again, these sit outside the fiducial volume.

## 4. Supporting items

- **Upgraded DAQ and timing** to handle the spill-structured rate. Combined with the pixel and light readout, beam-synchronized timing allows per-interaction t₀ for drift correction.
- **Calibration systems:** a UV laser and cosmic-ray triggers for field-distortion and electron-lifetime calibration. Optionally, a source or test-beam campaign to measure proton response near the 60 MeV threshold.

## Why not the alternatives

| Option | Problem |
|---|---|
| Plastic scintillator (CH) | About 7.7% hydrogen; violates the 2% limit |
| Water-based target | About 11% hydrogen; violates the limit |
| Passive graphite or metal plus trackers | Loses the low-threshold proton and isotropic reconstruction |
| High-pressure gas argon TPC | Too little mass; low event rate |

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular, pixel-readout (LArPix/ArgonCube-style) liquid-argon TPC, a hydrogen-free, fully active, isotropic 3D target, surrounded by side and upstream gas trackers.

Based on the requirements for this near detector upgrade, here are the hardware upgrades the proposal should include:

## 1. **3D Active Target with Fine Granularity**
**Technology:** Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with resistive micromegas or pixel readout
**Why:** The requirement to reconstruct tracks at all angles, including perpendicular and backward-going tracks, demands true 3D tracking capability with minimal dead regions. A TPC provides continuous 3D space points with ~mm precision in all three dimensions. The drift direction along the beam axis allows measurement of perpendicular and backward tracks that would be invisible to planar detector layers.

## 2. **Low-Z Gas Target Medium**
**Technology:** Argon or helium-based gas mixture (e.g., Ar:CH₄ 90:10 or similar P10 mixture)
**Why:** The <2% hydrogen constraint essentially requires an all-carbon or noble gas target. Hydrogen content in typical plastic scintillators (~14%) or hydrocarbons would violate this requirement. An argon-based TPC gas naturally satisfies this while providing ionization for tracking.

## 3. **High-Pressure Capability**
**Technology:** Pressure vessel rated for 5-10 atm with appropriate feedthroughs
**Why:** To achieve reasonable interaction rates in a gaseous target of only 0.9 m depth, elevated pressure is essential. This increases target density by 5-10× while maintaining the low-hydrogen requirement and excellent tracking resolution.

## 4. **Low-Threshold Proton Detection System**
**Technology:** High-gain amplification (micromegas or GEM foils) with low-noise electronics
**Why:** Detecting 60 MeV kinetic energy protons requires sensing very short, low-ionization tracks. At this energy, protons have ~10 MeV/c momentum and ranges of only a few cm in gas at atmospheric pressure. High gas gain (10⁴-10⁵) and electronics with <1000 e⁻ noise are needed.

## 5. **Fine Segmentation Readout**
**Technology:** Pixel or strip readout with <3 mm pitch
**Why:** Short proton tracks demand fine spatial sampling to reconstruct angles and distinguish signal from noise. For tracks as short as a few cm, pixel/strip pitches of 2-3 mm provide adequate sampling (~10-20 points minimum).

## 6. **Enhanced Electronics and DAQ**
**Technology:** Self-triggered, continuous readout system with ~100 MHz sampling
**Why:** With tracks at all angles and short proton tracks, the detector needs to capture the full 3D event topology without bias. Trigger-less or minimally-triggered readout prevents losses of tracks at unexpected angles or times.

## 7. **Field Cage and HV System**
**Technology:** Resistive field cage with HV up to 50-100 kV for 65 cm drift
**Why:** For TPC operation with the 6.5 m magnet length, a uniform drift field of ~500-1000 V/cm over the 2.6 m transverse dimension requires sophisticated field shaping to minimize distortions that would degrade position resolution.

## 8. **Calibration Systems**
**Technology:** Laser tracks and radioactive source deployment system
**Why:** To achieve uniform tracking efficiency at all angles, spatial distortions from E×B effects, gas non-uniformities, and electronics variations must be mapped and corrected. Regular laser calibration and radioactive source scans are essential.

## 9. **Light Collection System (Optional Enhancement)**
**Technology:** PMTs or SiPMs viewing the target volume
**Why:** Scintillation light from the gas provides an independent t₀ timing reference (critical for drift measurement) and calorimetric information. This improves event selection and enables better background rejection.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: High-pressure TPC with resistive micromegas readout at 3 mm pitch, as it simultaneously addresses the 3D tracking requirement, low-hydrogen constraint, and fine granularity needed for low-energy protons.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Active Target

## Context Summary

The available volume is ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m in the upstream slot, replacing the photon-tagger. The physics demand is kinematically complete CC events: full reconstruction of the muon **and** the leading recoil proton, with ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons exiting beyond 50°, and a median proton momentum of ~450 MeV/c (range in plastic ~20 cm). The 6% → 4% systematic target drives the choice.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: High-Granularity Scintillator Cube Detector ("SuperFGD-style")

**Technology:** 3D-interlocked plastic scintillator cubes, each 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, read out in three orthogonal directions by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Concrete specification:**
- Cube material: polystyrene-based plastic scintillator (same as T2K FGD cubes, well-characterized)
- Cube size: 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm³
- Array size: ~192 × 182 × 56 cubes ≈ **~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m**, filling the available box
- Three fibre axes (X, Y, Z), each fibre threading through a column of cubes and terminating on a SiPM at one or both ends
- SiPMs: 1.3 mm pitch, e.g. Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent, operating at ~25°C with active gain stabilization
- Number of channels: ~(192+182+56) × relevant cross-sections ≈ order 100k channels total (similar to the SuperFGD built for ND280 upgrade, which is 2×1.8×0.6 m with ~2 million cubes and ~56k channels — confirm scaling)
- Readout ASIC: CITIROC-1A or TARGET-C based front-end cards, multiplexed per fibre bundle

**Why this technology:**
- 4π acceptance for short tracks: a 450 MeV/c proton has a range of ~18 cm in plastic, fully contained in this volume even at large angles
- Three-view simultaneous hit gives unambiguous 3D track seeding without a magnetic field inside the target itself
- The 1 cm³ granularity gives ~1 cm vertex resolution, essential for distinguishing leading proton from secondary pion tracks
- Demonstrated: the SuperFGD for the ND280 upgrade (T2K Phase II) has validated this exact geometry; the technology is at TRL 7-8

---

## 2. Surrounding Thin Time-of-Flight (ToF) Walls

**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator panels with SiPM readout, 5 mm thick.

**Concrete specification:**
- Six faces of the active target volume covered by 5 mm BC-404 (or EJ-204) plastic scintillator slabs
- Segmented into ~5 × 5 cm² tiles or 5 cm wide bars per face to maintain position information
- SiPM: 3 × 3 mm² tiles (e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-3050CS), two per bar end
- Target timing resolution: **σ_t < 300 ps** per plane (achievable with this scintillator + SiPM combination and careful signal shaping)
- Readout: waveform digitizer (e.g. DRS4-based or SAMPIC), 200 ps sampling

**Why this technology:**
- ToF between the entry-point hit in the cube target and the ToF wall directly measures β → momentum for protons below ~700 MeV/c (where dE/dx alone is ambiguous versus pions)
- For a 450 MeV/c proton (β ≈ 0.43) traversing ~30 cm, the ToF difference proton vs. pion is ~2 ns — easily resolved at 300 ps
- Proton/pion separation at the 3σ level up to ~700 MeV/c, covering ~94% of the leading proton momentum distribution
- Thin enough (5 mm) not to significantly perturb outgoing tracks before they reach the downstream TPCs
- The NINJA and WAGASCI experiments have demonstrated similar thin scintillator ToF walls in near-detector configurations

---

## 3. Upgrade of Downstream TPC Entrance: Additional Thin MPGD Tracking Layer

**Technology:** MicroMegas or GEM detector plane, 2.0 × 1.9 m active area, installed as a transition tracker between the new target and the first existing TPC.

**Concrete specification:**
- One double-layer MicroMegas panel (bulk MicroMegas technology, as used in existing TPCs)
- Strip pitch: 400 µm in X, 400 µm in Y (two staggered layers at ±7°)
- Gas: Ar/CF₄/isobutane 95/3/2 at ~1 bar
- Spatial resolution: ~100 µm per layer
- Readout: AFTER ASIC (same as existing TPC front-end, minimizing new electronics)
- Thickness: ~0.5% X₀ per layer

**Why this technology:**
- Provides a precise space point and angular measurement for all tracks exiting the new target before they enter the TPC gas volume
- Resolves the track-matching ambiguity when multiple tracks (µ + p + possible π) exit within a few cm of each other
- The 100 µm resolution significantly improves the angular resolution on the muon direction compared to matching cube-to-TPC alone, directly reducing the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) resolution
- Reuses the same AFTER ASIC already in inventory, lowering integration risk

---

## 4. SiPM Readout Upgrade on Existing Downstream Tracking Targets (FGD1/FGD2 equivalents)

**Technology:** Replace existing multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs, first generation, e.g. Hamamatsu S10362-13-050C, 50 µm pixel, 667 pixels) with modern high-dynamic-range SiPMs.

**Concrete specification:**
- Replacement: Hamamatsu S14160-3010PS (10 µm pixel pitch, 90,000 pixels, 3 × 3 mm²) or equivalent
- Same mechanical footprint as existing connectors to minimize PCB redesign
- Updated front-end ASIC: SPIROC2E with extended dynamic range (up to ~3,000 photoelectrons before saturation vs ~200 p.e. for original MPPCs)
- Install active temperature-compensation circuit (Peltier element + PID feedback per 16-channel group) to stabilize gain to <0.1% over beam-spill thermal cycling

**Why this technology:**
- Original MPPCs saturate for highly ionizing slow protons (Bragg peak at track end gives large light yield), distorting dE/dx-based proton identification
- The 10 µm pixel SiPMs increase dynamic range by ~15×, eliminating saturation for proton Bragg peaks up to ~200 MeV/c (the most problematic range for containment assessment)
- Improved dE/dx resolution → better p/π separation in the existing tracking targets at no cost to acceptance
- The temperature stabilization reduces gain drift systematic to <0.1%, directly contributing to the 2% systematic reduction goal

---

## 5. Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter (pre-shower tagger) Around New Target

**Technology:** Sampling calorimeter using lead foil (1 mm) + scintillator tiles (3 mm), SiPM readout.

**Concrete specification:**
- 4 layers of 1 mm Pb + 3 mm scintillator tile (3 × 3 cm² tiles), covering the four lateral faces and downstream face of the new target
- Total thickness: ~1 X₀ per face (sufficient for photon conversion tagging, not full containment)
- SiPMs: same 3 × 3 mm² devices as ToF walls (commonality)
- Position resolution: ~1.5 cm per photon cluster (adequate for π⁰ tagging)

**Why this technology:**
- Identifies photons from π⁰ → γγ adjacent to the interaction vertex, essential for correctly classifying CC-0π events (the signal) versus CC-1π⁰ background
- A 1 X₀ pre-shower layer converts ~63% of photons, dramatically reducing the π⁰ → CC-0π mis-identification systematic
- The existing downstream ECAL is too far from the vertex for near-vertex gammas from the new target position; this fills the geometric gap
- Thin enough (total ~1.6 cm per face) to fit within the available volume with minimal mass addition

---

## System Integration Considerations

| Subsystem | New channels | Dominant systematic addressed |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD cube target | ~100k SiPM channels | Acceptance for large-angle protons |
| ToF walls | ~2k SiPM channels | Proton/pion ID below 700 MeV/c |
| Transition MicroMegas | ~10k strips | Angular resolution / track matching |
| SiPM upgrade (existing) | 0 new, refurbishment | dE/dx saturation for protons |
| Pre-shower ECAL | ~5k SiPM channels | π⁰ background contamination |

The combined effect: large-angle proton acceptance increases from effectively ~0% (photon tagger had no proton tracking capability) to ~90%+ containment for protons below 900 MeV/c; proton/pion separation covers >94% of the momentum spectrum; the leading systematic on signal selection efficiency drops from the ~6% level toward the 4% target.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagger with a 1 cm³ 3D-scintillator-cube active target (SuperFGD geometry, ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m, WLS-fibre + SiPM readout in three orthogonal axes), as this single change delivers the required 4π acceptance for large-angle recoil protons and provides the 3D vertex reconstruction essential for transverse kinematic imbalance analysis.

# Proposed upgrade: a fine-grained 3D scintillator target with high-angle TPCs and a time-of-flight envelope

Each requirement points to a specific choice:

- **Muons at all angles.** Tracks at about 90° or backward never reach the downstream drift chambers. They need tracking and charge/momentum measurement on the sides of the target region.
- **Protons down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy.** These protons range out in about 3 cm of plastic. The target must therefore be fully active, isotropic and segmented at roughly the 1 cm scale.
- **Hydrogen at most 20% of nucleons.** A hydrocarbon target meets this easily. In polystyrene (CH), hydrogen is 1 of 13 nucleons, about 8%. Fibres and coatings change this only slightly. A dense, mostly carbon target also gives the event rate.

## 1. Active target: 3D-segmented plastic scintillator ("SuperFGD-type")

- **Cubes.** Roughly 2 × 10⁶ polystyrene scintillator cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³. Each is chemically etched to give a reflective coating and drilled with three orthogonal holes.
- **Fibres.** Wavelength-shifting fibres, about 1 mm diameter, run through the holes along x, y and z. That is about 56,000 fibres.
- **Photosensors and electronics.**
  - Each fibre is read out at one end by a silicon photomultiplier (MPPC/SiPM, about 1.3 mm), with a mirrored far end.
  - Front-end boards use CITIROC-class ASICs to record charge and hit time, with about 1 ns resolution per channel.
- **Envelope.** About 1.9 m (width) × 1.8 m (height) × 0.6 m (along the beam) inside a light-tight box. This leaves room above and below for the TPCs in section 2.
- **Why this technology.**
  - It has isotropic acceptance.
  - A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes, enough for dE/dx-based proton/pion separation. About 300 MeV/c protons become reconstructible.
  - Its timing also allows neutron detection through delayed, isolated hits.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

- **Configuration.** Two thin TPCs, about 2.0 m × 0.8 m drift × 1.8 m. They sit in the 0.15 T field, so high-angle muons get a charge sign and a momentum resolution of about 10% at 1 GeV/c.
- **Field cage.** A low-mass composite field cage, using an aramid/honeycomb laminate, keeps multiple scattering low.
- **Readout.** Resistive Micromegas, with an encapsulated resistive anode on bulk Micromegas. Charge spreading gives about 0.5 mm resolution with about 1 cm pads and protects against sparks.
- **Gas.** T2K-style Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ gas, read out by AFTER/DREAM-type electronics.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels surrounding the target and TPCs

- **Panels.** Six panels of plastic scintillator bars, about 12 cm × 1 cm × 2.2 m, read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs. Target timing is about 150 ps.
- **Purpose.**
  - Distinguish backward-going muons from forward-going tracks entering from outside, which are otherwise mis-reconstructed as backward.
  - Reject out-of-volume (sand, magnet) backgrounds.
  - Supplement particle identification.

## 4. Supporting work

- Integrate the existing downstream drift chambers so their tracks match to the new target in a common time and space frame.
- Assay the target chemistry so the hydrogen fraction is known precisely. This lets the hydrogen interactions be modelled and subtracted at about 8%, safely under the 20% limit.
- Design the cooling, slow control and SiPM gain monitoring to cope with the high channel count.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fully active, 1 cm-cube 3D-segmented polystyrene scintillator target (SuperFGD-type, three-view WLS-fibre/SiPM readout) flanked by resistive-Micromegas high-angle TPCs.

# Proposed Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## 1. Core upgrade: a 3D-granular plastic-scintillator active target (SuperFGD-style)

**Technology**
- About 1×1×1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, read out by SiPMs. This gives three 2D projections that combine into 3D hits.
- Suggested envelope: about 2.4 m (x) × 1.1 m (y, vertical) × 0.85 m (z, beam). That is roughly 2 million cubes, about 6.5 million channels on a 2D readout, and about 2.2 t of target mass.
- The remaining vertical space (about 1.2 m) is reserved for the tracking chambers in upgrade 2.

**Hydrogen fraction**
- Polystyrene is (CH)ₙ. Per CH unit there is 1 hydrogen nucleon out of 13 nucleons, about 7.7%.
- Including the TiO₂ reflector coating and fibres, the fraction stays at about 7–8%.
- This is well below the 20% ceiling, so the hydrogen-subtraction model remains valid.
- For comparison, a water-based target would be about 11% and still acceptable. Pure hydrocarbon tracker designs are fine. Any hydrogen-rich alternative such as CH₂ is also fine, at about 14%.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Cube granularity is the same in all directions. Tracks perpendicular to the beam or backward-going are reconstructed as well as forward ones. This removes the main weakness of planar bar trackers, which lose tracks running parallel to the planes.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton has a range of about 3 cm in plastic, which gives 3 or more cubes. That is enough for a vertex-attached track and dE/dx identification. Even shorter stubs register as vertex activity, giving an effective threshold of about 300 MeV/c momentum.
- **Neutron tagging.** Fine segmentation and about 1 ns hit timing also allow neutron detection by time-of-flight between isolated hits. This adds transverse-kinematic-imbalance measurements for nuclear-effect constraints.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two thin gas TPCs (Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ "T2K gas") filling the vertical space above and below the scintillator target, each about 0.5–0.6 m tall.
- Field cage made of lightweight composite to minimise dead material.
- Resistive Micromegas readout, which spreads charge and gives about 0.5 mm resolution with fewer pads.

**Physics motivation**
- Muons at high angles exit sideways and never reach the downstream drift chambers.
- These TPCs measure their momentum and charge in the 0.15 T field.
- They also provide dE/dx for μ/e/p separation, which is needed to reject the νₑ and π backgrounds.
- Together with range-out in the scintillator, they guarantee the ≥25% muon efficiency at around 90°.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the target and TPC volume

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars of about 2 cm thickness, read out at both ends by SiPM arrays.
- Timing resolution about 150 ps.
- Panels cover all six faces of the new region.

**Physics motivation**
- They determine track direction unambiguously, separating backward-going muons from forward particles entering from outside.
- They veto out-of-fiducial-volume and sand-muon backgrounds.
- At low momentum they add particle ID (μ/p/e).

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Readout electronics.** Upgrade to common, triggerless electronics (CITIROC/AFTER-type) with sub-ns timestamps across all three subsystems. This is needed for neutron time-of-flight and Michel-electron tagging, which identifies π⁺ below Cherenkov or tracking thresholds.
- **Calibration.** Add an LED/laser calibration system and use cosmic-ray triggers for the cube light yield. Energy-scale stability is critical for proton calorimetry near threshold.
- **Magnet.** No change needed. 0.15 T is sufficient for sub-GeV momentum resolution in the new TPCs, at about 10% for 0.7 GeV.

## Summary

The granular cube target provides 4π vertexing and low-threshold proton reconstruction while keeping hydrogen at about 8% of target nucleons. The high-angle TPCs and TOF panels close the high-angle and backward muon acceptance gap.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a 3D-granular plastic-scintillator cube active target (SuperFGD-style, ~1 cm³ cubes, three-view WLS-fibre/SiPM readout).

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

Before proposing upgrades, let me map requirements to detector challenges:

| Requirement | Challenge |
|-------------|-----------|
| Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at **all angles** including 90° and backward | Standard tracking fails for large-angle/backward tracks without 4π coverage |
| Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3 cm in water) | Very short tracks require fine-grained, high-density active material |
| Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of target nucleons | Excludes plastic scintillator (CH₂ ~14% H by nucleon count), hydrocarbon oils, water |
| Active target with interaction reconstruction | Need vertex resolution, particle ID, dE/dx |

---

## Constraint on Target Material

The hydrogen constraint is severe. Consider nucleon compositions:

- **Polystyrene (CH):** H nucleons ≈ 1/(1+12) ≈ 7.7% — **excluded**
- **Water (H₂O):** H nucleons = 2/18 × (1/1) nucleon fraction ≈ 2/10 = **~18% — excluded**
- **Liquid argon:** 0% hydrogen — acceptable but infrastructure-intensive
- **Iron:** 0% hydrogen — acceptable but poor for short proton tracks
- **Liquid scintillator (mineral oil based, CH₁.₈):** H ≈ 1.8/13.8 ≈ **13% — excluded**
- **Argon gas (high pressure):** 0% hydrogen
- **Lead:** 0% hydrogen
- **Scintillating glass:** SiO₂-based, ~0% H — acceptable
- **Emulsion (without water processing) or nuclear emulsion:** very low H possible
- **High-pressure gaseous argon TPC:** 0% hydrogen, fine-grained, excellent for short tracks

The ≤2% hydrogen constraint effectively **rules out all hydrocarbon and water-based scintillators** as the dominant target mass. The active target must be built around a low-hydrogen medium.

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgTPC) — Primary Active Target

**Replace the existing target region contents with a high-pressure (~10 bar) gaseous argon TPC** filling the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume.

**Rationale:**
- Pure argon: zero hydrogen → satisfies the ≤2% nucleon constraint with large margin
- At 10 bar, density ≈ 0.018 g/cm³; sufficient interaction rate while keeping excellent 3D tracking
- **Full 4π track reconstruction** — the TPC records ionization continuously in all directions; backward-going and 90° tracks are reconstructed identically to forward tracks, meeting the all-angle muon efficiency requirement
- **Short proton tracks:** A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has range ~3–4 cm in 10-bar Ar; TPC spatial resolution of ~1 mm gives ~30–40 measurable space points — reconstructible with good efficiency
- dE/dx particle identification distinguishes protons from pions and muons
- The existing downstream drift chambers and dipole magnet continue to serve for forward muon momentum measurement; the TPC provides the near-4π complement
- Existing field cage can be integrated with minor modifications to the upstream magnet volume

**Key specifications:**
- Drift field: ~100–200 V/cm (modest HV, proven technology)
- Readout: pad-based or pixel anode planes at downstream face; cathode at upstream face
- Gas: Ar + small CO₂ or Ar + CF₄ (no hydrogen-containing quencher — use CF₄, not isobutane)
- Use **CF₄ as quencher** (not CH₄ or isobutane) to maintain H < 2%: pure Ar/CF₄ 95/5 → zero hydrogen ✓

---

### 2. Thin Scintillator Veto/Trigger Planes Around the TPC Volume

Install planes of **low-hydrogen scintillating tiles or bars** (e.g., inorganic scintillator such as GAGG:Ce or BGO tiles, or thin plastic used only as a veto with negligible mass fraction) on all six faces of the TPC volume.

**Rationale:**
- Provide fast trigger signal (TPC is intrinsically slow, ~ms drift time)
- Tag entering beam muons and cosmic rays for rejection
- If plastic scintillator is used, keep total mass negligible relative to argon mass so that the volume-averaged hydrogen nucleon fraction stays well below 2%

**Hydrogen budget check:** If scintillator planes add ~5 kg of CH and argon mass is ~40 kg (10 bar × 2.6×2.3×0.9 m³ × 0.018 g/cm³ ≈ 97 kg Ar), hydrogen nucleon fraction from scintillator ≈ (5/13 × 1) / (97/40 + 5/13) ≈ small — keep scintillator ≤2 kg to ensure compliance.

---

### 3. Upgrade of Downstream Tracking to Improve Large-Angle Muon Acceptance

The existing gas drift chambers downstream of the magnet will miss muons leaving the TPC sideways or backward. Add **two layers of large-area resistive plate chambers (RPCs) or straw-tube modules on the lateral faces** (top, bottom, and sides) of the magnet bore.

**Rationale:**
- Muons exiting at 90° to beam travel radially outward through the magnet yoke gap; lateral RPC planes catch these tracks
- RPCs are thin, low-cost, and provide a 2D hit for linking TPC track segments to the downstream spectrometer
- Backward muons that re-enter the upstream beam line are tagged by an upstream RPC plane

**Specifications:**
- 4 lateral RPC planes (top, bottom, beam-left, beam-right), each ~2.6 m × 2.3 m or ~2.6 m × 0.9 m as geometry allows
- 1 upstream plane (~2.6 m × 2.3 m) for backward-going track tagging
- Strip pitch ~1 cm for adequate position resolution
- Interleave with thin iron absorbers (~5 cm Fe per layer) only if muon ranging is needed; otherwise bare planes suffice for tracking

---

### 4. Low-Mass Field Cage and HV System for the TPC

The existing target region has mechanical infrastructure (support rails, gas systems for the original drift chambers). Upgrade this to:

- **Field cage:** Lightweight copper-clad Kapton strips on G10 frame; total material << 1% X₀ per strip plane so as not to degrade soft proton tracking
- **High-voltage: cathode at −200 kV** for a 0.9 m drift at 200 V/cm (modest, well within existing HV technology at 10 bar)
- **Pressure vessel:** The 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section requires a custom Al or stainless pressure vessel rated to 15 bar (10 bar operating + margin); this is the main mechanical engineering challenge

---

### 5. Upgraded DAQ and Trigger for Continuous Readout

The TPC produces continuous ionization data; replace the existing triggered readout with:

- **Streaming readout** with FPGA-based data compression
- **Hardware trigger** from the scintillator veto planes and the beam spill gate (beam is pulsed, reducing cosmic background)
- Online track-finding firmware to reduce data rate before storage

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Addresses | Priority |
|---------|-----------|----------|
| HPgTPC active target (Ar/CF₄) | All-angle tracking, short proton tracks, H<2% constraint | **Critical** |
| CF₄ quencher (not CH₄/isobutane) | H<2% constraint in gas mixture | Critical |
| Lateral + upstream RPC planes | 90° and backward muon reconstruction efficiency | High |
| Thin trigger scintillator planes | Fast trigger, beam/cosmic tagging | High |
| Lightweight field cage + pressure vessel | TPC operation, low material budget | High |
| Streaming DAQ upgrade | Handle continuous TPC readout | Medium |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target volume contents with a high-pressure (~10 bar) gaseous argon TPC using an Ar/CF₄ gas mixture, providing full 4π track reconstruction for all-angle muons and backward tracks, dE/dx-based proton identification down to 60 MeV kinetic energy, and zero hydrogen content in the target medium.

# Proposed upgrade for the Kestrel Flats near-detector target region

## 1. What the requirements rule out

**Hydrogen fraction.** Plastic scintillator (CH) has about 1 hydrogen nucleus per 13 nucleons, roughly 7.7%. Water is about 11%. A scintillator-cube target or a water target would therefore exceed the 2% hydrogen limit about four times over, so the active target must be hydrogen-free. Argon has no hydrogen, and if the far detector is argon it also matches the target nucleus, which removes the cross-section extrapolation between near and far.

**Acceptance at all angles.** The volume is only 0.9 m deep along the beam. Stacks of planes perpendicular to the beam, as in the current layout, lose tracks near 90° and backward tracks. Uniform acceptance at all angles needs a 3D-imaging, isotropic target.

**Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV proton travels only about 2.5–3 cm in liquid argon. Reconstructing it needs voxel granularity of a few mm.

**Target mass.** A high-pressure gas argon TPC would have excellent thresholds. However, at 10 bar a 60 MeV proton travels more than a metre, and the fiducial mass would be only about 100 kg, so the event rate is low. Liquid argon gives several tonnes in the same volume.

## 2. Primary change: a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC

Replace the target region with a modular LArTPC of the ArgonCube / ND-LAr type, fitted inside a compact cryostat in the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m space.

**Readout and modules**
- Native 3D pixel charge readout at about 4 mm pitch, rather than wires.
- This avoids reconstruction ambiguities at large angles and gives isotropic tracking, including for backward muons and short protons.

**Segmentation and timing**
- Short drift lengths (about 30–50 cm per module) and per-module optical detectors.
- This keeps drift time short and lets each interaction be assigned to its spill or bunch, which is important at 410 m where pile-up is high.

**Mass and rate**
- Active volume after the cryostat is about 4–5 m³, or roughly 5–6 t of argon.
- A fiducial volume of a few tonnes gives a high event rate at this baseline.

**Operation in the magnet**
- Pixel readout and drift at 0.15 T are compatible; E×B effects are small and correctable.
- Use the field for curvature where lever arm allows.
- For contained or long tracks, determine momentum from range and multiple Coulomb scattering.

**Proton identification**
- dE/dx along the track and Bragg-peak identification.
- Expected proton threshold of about 40–60 MeV kinetic energy, at all angles.

**Hydrogen control**
- Keep hydrogenous materials (foam insulation, G10, PCBs, cables) outside the fiducial volume.
- Use a vacuum-insulated, thin-walled steel or aluminium cryostat rather than foam where space is tight.
- Apply a vertex fiducial cut of about 5–10 cm from the walls.
- This keeps the hydrogen nucleon fraction among selected interactions well below 2%.

## 3. Supporting upgrades for muons that leave sideways or backward

The existing drift chambers sit only downstream, so tracks at high angle or going backward never reach them.

**Side and upstream tracking planes** placed in the gap between the cryostat and the magnet yoke:
- Thin gas TPC or scintillator-bar trackers on the four sides and the upstream face.
- They give an exit point and a direction.
- Combined with the in-argon track, they give a curvature lever arm for charge sign.

**Time-of-flight panels** (about 100–200 ps scintillator) around the volume:
- Resolve forward versus backward direction.
- Reject entering cosmic and rock muons.
- Help separate muons from pions.

**Muon range and identification** in the yoke:
- Instrument the magnet return yoke, or reuse existing side muon-range detectors, to tag escaping muons.
- Combined with argon multiple-scattering momentum, this comfortably achieves at least 25% muon efficiency at every angle.

## 4. Additional items

- **Cryogenics and purification:** argon purification to millisecond electron lifetime, and nitrogen-free operation.
- **Upstream veto:** a veto counter to reject entering particles from interactions in the magnet coils.
- **Calibration:** a laser or cosmic calibration system for dE/dx response and the electric-field map.

**Expected outcome:** an argon target with essentially 4π acceptance, protons reconstructed down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy, a hydrogen fraction far below 2%, and charge and momentum measurement for high-angle muons supplied by the new side trackers and time-of-flight panels.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a hydrogen-free modular pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (with surrounding side/backward trackers and ToF) inside the magnet.

# ND280 Upgrade Recommendation: Replacing the P0D Region

## Diagnosis: why the current detector cannot reach about 4%

**Angular acceptance.**
- FGD1 bars are all perpendicular to the beam. Tracks at large angles (above about 60–70°) run nearly parallel to the bar planes, so they hit few layers and are poorly reconstructed.
- The TPCs sit up- and downstream of the FGDs, so high-angle and backward tracks never reach them.
- At this beam, about 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leave at more than 50°. The present phase space is therefore forward-biased, unlike Super-Kamiokande's full 4π acceptance.

**Proton threshold.**
- Protons must cross several bar layers to be tracked. In practice this gives a threshold of roughly 450 MeV/c, about the median of the leading-proton spectrum.
- Half the protons needed for transverse-kinematic-imbalance (TKI) analysis are lost or badly measured.

**Neutrons and timing.**
- No event-by-event neutron or time-of-flight information is available.
- Direction is ambiguous for backward and out-of-fiducial (OOFV) tracks.

## Recommended hardware changes

### 1. Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD): the new active target

**Design**
- About 2 million 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes, read by about 56,000 wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z.
- Readout uses compact MPPCs (e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1325CS class).
- Overall size is about 192 × 182 × 56 cm, with about 2 t of CH target.
- It fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box and roughly doubles the FGD target mass.

**Justification**
- **Uniform 4π acceptance.** Three orthogonal projections give true 3D reconstruction that is isotropic in angle, so high-angle and backward tracks are as well reconstructed as forward ones.
- **Lower proton threshold.** Granularity of about 1 cm brings the threshold to about 300 MeV/c, recovering most of the protons below the 450 MeV/c median. A 450 MeV/c proton (about 100 MeV kinetic energy) has a range of about 8 cm in plastic, so it is contained. Range and calorimetry then give a precise momentum.
- **Neutron detection.** Fast timing (better than about 1 ns per fibre) lets isolated neutron-induced hits be time-of-flight measured. This adds neutron kinematics to the TKI measurement in antineutrino mode.
- **Electron identification.** Fine granularity helps separate electrons from gammas for the νe cross-section measurement.
- **Hydrocarbon target.** This is acceptable for the programme, and FGD2 is retained for the carbon-to-water comparison.

### 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the SuperFGD

**Design**
- Same gas as the existing TPCs, for continuity of calibration.
- Lightweight composite (laminate) field cage, to minimise dead material and multiple scattering.
- Encapsulated **resistive Micromegas (ERAM)** readout.
  - Charge spreading across a resistive layer allows larger pads, which reduces channel count and cost.
  - It maintains or improves spatial resolution (below about 0.6 mm) and dE/dx resolution (below about 10%).
  - The resistive layer also suppresses sparking.

**Justification**
- High-angle muons and the energetic protons exit the SuperFGD transversely, including the 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that are not contained.
- The HA-TPCs give momentum by curvature in the 0.2 T field, charge sign, and dE/dx particle ID for these tracks.
- Muon momentum resolution matches the forward TPCs, giving full-angle muon kinematics comparable to Super-Kamiokande's phase space.

### 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) system enclosing the new target and HA-TPCs

**Design**
- Six planes of about 2.2 m long, 12 cm wide plastic scintillator bars.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Timing resolution is about 150 ps.

**Justification**
- Determines track direction, separating forward from backward-going tracks.
- Rejects OOFV and cosmic backgrounds.
- Provides a time reference that improves particle ID (e.g. proton/muon/electron separation at low momentum).
- Can provide a trigger.

### 4. Supporting changes

**Electronics and DAQ**
- New front-end electronics: CITIROC-based boards for the about 56,000 MPPC channels, and AFTER/DAQ-upgraded electronics for the HA-TPCs.
- These are needed for sub-ns timing and for the higher beam power (more than 750 kW to about 1.3 MW) and repetition rate.
- Integrate the new systems with the existing global trigger and clock.

**Mechanics and calibration**
- A new support structure in the P0D basket.
- LED and cosmic calibration systems.
- Retain the downstream TPCs, FGDs, ECals and SMRD unchanged.

## Expected impact

- Full angular coverage for both the muon and the leading proton.
- Proton threshold reduced from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c.
- Neutron tagging becomes possible.
- About double the target mass.
- Together these give kinematically complete TKI-quality charged-current events. They directly constrain the nuclear-effect and cross-section model uncertainties that dominate the residual 6%, and bring the systematic uncertainty toward the roughly 4% T2K-II goal.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD — a ~2-million-cube, three-view WLS-fibre/MPPC 3D scintillator target giving isotropic acceptance and a ~300 MeV/c proton threshold.

# Kestrel Flats Near Detector: Active-Target Upgrade Recommendations

## 1. The constraint that decides the technology: hydrogen ≤ 2% of target nucleons

The obvious choice for an active target is fine-grained plastic scintillator (FGD/SuperFGD style). It is ruled out here:

- Polystyrene (CH) contains 1 hydrogen nucleon per 13 nucleons, about **7.7%**.
- That is nearly four times the 2% limit. Hydrogen interactions could not be modelled away reliably.

Since the far detector contains no hydrogen, the cleanest option is to match its nucleus. The far detector's target material is not stated. The recommendations below assume it is argon. If it is a different hydrogen-free material, the active target should be built from that material instead.

**Recommendation A (primary): replace the target region with a modular, pixel-readout liquid argon TPC.** Use an ArgonCube / ND-LAr "2x2"-style design with LArPix-type pixel readout.

- **Hydrogen fraction.** Pure LAr contains essentially zero hydrogen. Hydrogenous structure (G10 field-cage supports, cryostat insulation) is kept away from the fiducial volume and removed by fiducial cuts. Hydrogen in the fiducial target stays well below 2%.
- **Mass and rate.** The 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m volume holds about 5.4 m³, or roughly 7.5 t of LAr.
  - At 410 m from the target this gives a high event rate.
  - It also means many interactions per spill, so the detector needs native 3D readout and segmentation.
- **Readout layout.**
  - Segment the volume into roughly 0.5–0.65 m-wide optically isolated modules with short drift lengths. This keeps drift times, diffusion and space-charge effects small.
  - Use pixel (not wire) readout to give unambiguous 3D hits under pile-up.
  - Add segmented, fast light detection (ArCLight / LCM-type) inside each module. This provides ns-scale timing to attach each interaction to its beam bunch and to its exiting tracks.
- **Proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels about 2.5–3 cm in LAr. With about 4 mm pixels that is roughly 7–8 hits, enough to reconstruct the track and identify it by dE/dx (Bragg peak). Because the readout is isotropic, this works at all angles. That directly meets the proton requirement.
- **Cryostat inside the warm dipole.** Use a thin-walled, non-magnetic cryostat (aluminium or stainless membrane with low-mass foam insulation). This keeps dead material between the argon and the external trackers small, which preserves muon matching and momentum resolution.

**Alternative considered: high-pressure gaseous argon TPC (around 10 bar).**

- *Advantages:* lowest proton threshold, full 4π acceptance, and good curvature measurement in 0.15 T.
- *Disadvantages:*
  - Mass is only about 0.1 t, so statistics are low.
  - The quencher adds hydrogen. In Ar–CH₄ 90/10, hydrogen is about 1% of nucleons, which uses half the allowed budget.
- *Verdict:* worth considering as a supplementary low-threshold sample, not as the main target.

## 2. Muon reconstruction at all angles, including perpendicular and backward

The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks. A muon of a few hundred MeV to 1 GeV ranges out over metres in LAr, far more than the 0.9 m target depth. In 0.15 T, its curvature cannot be measured well inside the LAr because multiple scattering dominates. High-angle and backward muons therefore leave through the sides or upstream face without being measured.

**Recommendation B: surround the target with tracking in the magnetic field.**

- Install thin gas tracking detectors above, below and beside the cryostat, plus an upstream plane, inside the magnet's 6.5 m inner volume. Suitable options are resistive-Micromegas TPCs (as in the ND280 upgrade high-angle TPCs) or additional drift chambers.
- These measure momentum and charge from curvature for side-going and backward tracks.
- Hydrogen in these trackers does not matter, because they are not target material.

**Recommendation C: add a time-of-flight scintillator envelope.**

- Fit fast (sub-ns) plastic scintillator panels with SiPM readout around the target, similar to the ND280 upgrade ToF.
- This determines track direction, separating backward muons from incoming entering tracks such as sand muons.
- It also helps reject externally produced backgrounds.

**Supporting measures for muons:**

- Use range in LAr for muons that stop inside it.
- Use multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum estimates for contained segments.
- Together with B and C, these should exceed 25% efficiency at every angle. Validate this with simulation of the full geometry.

## 3. Ancillary hardware

| Item | Reason |
|---|---|
| Argon purification and recirculation | Keeps electron lifetime long enough for full charge collection |
| Cryogenics compatible with the warm magnet | Prevents heat load or vibration from affecting magnet operation |
| Common clock/trigger linking LAr light, pixels, ToF and drift chambers | Enables bunch-level association of tracks across subsystems |
| Calibration (laser or radioactive sources) | Calibrates the low-energy proton dE/dx scale |

## Summary

- **Pixel-readout modular LArTPC** (assuming an argon far detector): meets the hydrogen limit, matches the far-detector nucleus, and gives a 4π proton threshold of about 60 MeV.
- **High-angle and upstream magnetized gas trackers plus ToF:** meet the all-angle muon efficiency requirement.
- **Thin cryostat walls:** preserve track matching to the external trackers.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (ArgonCube/LArPix style) instead of plastic scintillator, which exceeds the 2% hydrogen limit.

# ND280-Style Off-Axis Near Detector Upgrade: Recommended Hardware

The proposal should replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a high-granularity 3D scintillator target. That target should be flanked by new high-angle TPCs and enclosed in a time-of-flight system. The supporting electronics, calibration and mechanics upgrades follow from those three items. Each item is listed below with its technology and justification.

## 1. New active target: 3D-projection fine-grained scintillator ("Super-FGD" type)

**Technology**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ extruded-polystyrene scintillator cubes, with a reflective chemical etch on each cube.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes. Wavelength-shifting fibres run through them in x, y and z, giving three 2D projections per hit.
- Each fibre is read by a SiPM (MPPC), consistent with the existing scintillator readout.
- Overall size is about 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m, filling the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly doubling the existing tracker target mass.

**Why**
- **Full angular acceptance.** The existing bar targets have all bars perpendicular to the beam. Tracks at large angles (above about 50–60°) or backward run along a single plane, which causes poor tracking and acceptance gaps. About 25% of muons and 35% of protons in this beam are at such angles. Isotropic cubes with three-view readout give near-4π reconstruction.
- **Low proton threshold.** The 1 cm granularity lets protons be reconstructed and identified down to about 300 MeV/c, where they travel only a few centimetres. The current threshold is about 450 MeV/c, which coincides with the median proton momentum. Lowering it is essential for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies.
- **Momentum and particle ID for stopping protons.** Most protons stop in the target, so range and dE/dx (Bragg peak) measure their momentum and identify them.
- **Hydrocarbon is acceptable.** The physics programme allows CH, so a plastic target is suitable.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Argon-based gas TPCs, each about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m, with the drift field perpendicular to the beam.
- Lightweight field cages built from composite or aramid laminate, to minimise dead material.
- **Resistive (encapsulated) Micromegas** readout. Spreading charge over pads gives about 0.5–1 mm resolution with large pads, and the resistive layer adds spark protection.
- Front-end electronics using AFTER/DREAM-family ASICs.

**Why**
- High-angle muons and energetic protons escape the target upward or downward. This includes the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, which have about 1 m of range in plastic.
- The HA-TPCs measure these tracks' momentum from curvature in the 0.2 T field, determine charge sign, and identify particles by dE/dx.
- The existing forward TPCs cover only forward-going tracks.

## 3. Time-of-flight enclosure

**Technology**
- Six planes of plastic scintillator bars, each about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm, surrounding the target and HA-TPC system.
- Double-ended readout with arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Why**
- Determines track direction, so backward-going tracks can be separated from forward ones.
- Rejects out-of-fiducial-volume and through-going backgrounds, such as entering cosmic and sand muons, and aids particle identification.

## 4. Neutron capability (using the target's timing)

- Equip the target with sub-nanosecond timing electronics so neutron kinetic energy can be measured from the time of flight between the vertex and the secondary neutron interaction.
- This closes the kinematics for antineutrino TKI and constrains missing energy, which reduces the energy-scale systematics behind the 6% → 4% goal.

## 5. Supporting upgrades

- **Electronics, data acquisition and trigger:** a new high-channel-count SiPM front end (CITIROC-based boards) for the target and TOF, with temperature-compensated SiPM bias. The trigger and DAQ must be integrated with the existing system.
- **Calibration:**
  - A light-injection system for the target.
  - A laser calibration system for the HA-TPCs.
  - An updated magnetic field map.
- **Mechanics:** a low-mass support structure that preserves the existing downstream fine-grained detectors, including the water-layer module kept for carbon-to-water comparison. Upstream side-calorimeter modules should be re-optimised where the photon-tagging section is removed.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2 t, 1 cm³-cube 3D-readout scintillator target (Super-FGD type: three-view WLS fibres + SiPMs) for full-angle acceptance and a low proton threshold.

# Hardware Upgrades for the ND280 Near Detector Proposal

## 1. New Active Neutrino Target in the P0D Volume

**Technology: Super-FGD — a 3D grid of ~1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes**

The available 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m volume should be filled with a fully-active 3D scintillator target built from small (~1 cm side) extruded polystyrene cubes, each read out in all three orthogonal directions by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through holes, with MPPCs at the fibre ends. This architecture (as developed for the SuperFGD) gives:

- **4π acceptance with no dead zones**, critical because 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons exit at >50° and would miss or clip a conventional 2D-layer detector
- **Low tracking threshold for protons**: the ~1 cm granularity gives a range-based momentum threshold of roughly 300–400 MeV/c, covering the bulk of the leading-proton momentum distribution (median ~450 MeV/c) and capturing the ~6% high-momentum tail when combined with downstream TPCs
- **Kinematically complete CC events**: simultaneous 3D reconstruction of the outgoing muon and the recoil proton, enabling transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurements — δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T — that are the primary physics driver
- **Hydrocarbon (CH) target** is explicitly acceptable per the programme requirements, and the carbon-to-water ratio is handled by the retained FGD2
- The ~0.6 m depth in z limits radiation length but is sufficient for the short proton tracks of interest; the 3D readout recovers the angular acceptance that the z-extent alone cannot provide

---

## 2. New High-Angle Time Projection Chambers (HA-TPCs)

**Technology: TPCs with resistive Micromegas or pixel readout (e.g., MM-based with charge dispersion or GridPix), placed on the top, bottom, and lateral faces surrounding the Super-FGD**

The existing TPCs are downstream and cover only forward tracks. Because 25% of muons leave at >50°, a large fraction of muon tracks currently escape undetected or are only partially measured.

- **Top and bottom TPC panels** (thin-window entry, ~600–800 mm drift) flanking the new target volume intercept high-angle muon tracks, completing the muon momentum vector measurement via curvature in the 0.2 T magnet field
- **Resistive strip Micromegas** suppresses ion feedback and allows larger active areas at acceptable cost, with well-established performance in Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ mixtures already qualified at ND280
- **Momentum resolution**: a ~700 mm drift with ~100 µm spatial resolution gives σ(p)/p² ~ few %/(GeV/c) for tracks crossing the full volume in the 0.2 T field, adequate for the energy scale below 1 GeV
- **Sign determination**: critical for distinguishing µ⁻ (CC νµ) from µ⁺ (CC ν̄µ), necessary for the antineutrino running programme in T2K-II
- These TPCs also provide dE/dx particle identification (π/p separation up to ~1 GeV/c), helping identify whether the second track is truly the leading proton

---

## 3. Upgraded Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECal) Coverage Around the New Target Region

**Technology: Updated lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter with increased granularity and updated SiPM (MPPC) readout, covering the upstream and lateral faces of the new target volume**

The removal of the P0D eliminates its incidental photon-veto function in the upstream region.

- **Photon/π⁰ rejection**: neutral-current π⁰ events that fake CC-0π signatures are a leading background; ECal clusters from photon conversions must be identified to control this
- **Higher-granularity scintillator bars** (narrower than existing ECal, e.g., 4 cm instead of ~4–10 cm) in the upstream ECal improve shower position resolution and two-photon separation for π⁰ → γγ reconstruction
- **Updated MPPCs** with lower dark-count rate and higher photon detection efficiency (current generation ~50% PDE vs. ~25% at ND280 construction time) reduce energy threshold and improve timing for neutron detection
- **Neutron sensitivity**: improved timing resolution (~1 ns) in the ECal and Super-FGD enables time-of-flight estimation of neutron momentum — increasingly important as the community recognises neutrons carry significant missing momentum in CCQE-like events, biasing TKI studies if unaccounted for

---
