## 4. Replacement or Upgrade of the Front-End Electronics and DAQ for the New Detectors

**Technology: CITIROC or SPIROC-based ASIC front-end boards with ~1 ns timestamp resolution, feeding a triggerless streaming DAQ**

- The Super-FGD has O(50,000–200,000) channels (3 fibres per cube face × cube count); the existing MPPC readout ASICs and electronics chain at ND280 cannot handle this channel count or the required timing resolution
- **Triggerless streaming readout** captures all activity in a ~10 µs beam spill window, enabling offline reconstruction of multiple interaction vertices per spill (beam intensity increases in T2K-II) and time-of-flight measurements for neutron tagging
- **High-precision timestamps (~1 ns)** are needed to separate beam-correlated signal from cosmic background within the spill window, and to do neutron ToF
- MPPC bias voltage control per-channel (or per small group) corrects for gain variation with temperature, necessary for stable long-term calibration at the ~2% level required to reach the 4% systematic target

---

## 5. Retained and Re-instrumented SMRD as a Muon Stopper / Range Detector

**Technology: Existing SMRD scintillators retained but with updated SiPM readout and improved inter-slab timing**

The SMRD currently uses SiPMs but with relatively coarse timing.

- High-angle muons that range out in the magnet yoke scintillator are measured only by range, which requires knowing entry and exit point; improved inter-layer timing corrects for light propagation delays that currently limit range resolution
- Replacing aging WLS fibres and older-generation MPPCs with current-generation devices recovers photon statistics for short, stopping tracks (the lower end of the high-angle muon momentum spectrum)
- This is a low-cost upgrade (re-use of existing mechanical structure) that directly improves muon acceptance for the kinematic completeness requirement

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | Super-FGD (3D scintillator cubes + WLS + MPPC) | 4π acceptance, proton tracking, TKI |
| High-angle TPCs | Resistive Micromegas panels, top/bottom/side | Muon momentum & sign at large angles |
| Upstream/lateral ECal | Fine-grained Pb-scint + updated MPPCs | π⁰ rejection, neutron tagging |
| Front-end & DAQ | ASIC (CITIROC/SPIROC), streaming DAQ | Channel count, timing, stability |
| SMRD re-instrumentation | Updated SiPMs + WLS fibres | Muon range measurement, low cost |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a Super-FGD 3D plastic scintillator cube active target, as it is the single change that directly delivers kinematically complete CC event reconstruction with 4π acceptance for both the muon and the leading recoil proton, which is the irreducible requirement for the entire physics programme.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280

Given the requirements for kinematically complete charged-current events with improved systematic uncertainties, I propose the following specific hardware upgrades:

## 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Scintillator Cube Array (Primary Upgrade)**

Replace the P0D with a **Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD)** consisting of:
- **1.9 million plastic scintillator cubes**, each 1 cm³
- Dimensions: ~192 cm × 180 cm × 56 cm (fitting the available 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope)
- **Three orthogonal readout directions** (X, Y, Z) via wavelength-shifting fibers through holes in each cube
- Total mass: ~2 tons of polystyrene (CH target)
- **MPPC (SiPM) readout** with ~60,000 channels

**Key advantages:**
- True 3D tracking with ~1 cm³ granularity enables reconstruction of tracks at any angle
- Uniform acceptance for large-angle particles (>50°)
- Low momentum threshold (~200 MeV/c for protons)
- Time resolution <1 ns discriminates vertices
- No passive material, maximizing active target mass

## 2. **Time-of-Flight (ToF) Panels**

Install thin ToF panels immediately downstream of SuperFGD:
- **~2.5 m × 2.0 m scintillator panels** with timing resolution <200 ps
- Fast MPPC readout with waveform digitization
- Enables π/K/p separation up to ~700 MeV/c
- Critical for identifying leading protons vs. pions

## 3. **Upgraded High-Angle Muon Detection**

Enhance the existing SMRD with:
- **Additional scintillator layers** in the magnet yoke gaps
- Higher segmentation (5 cm modules instead of current ~7-9 cm)
- Improved time resolution for matching with SuperFGD vertices
- Better coverage for 50-90° muons that currently escape the TPCs

## 4. **Target Region Time Projection Chamber (Optional Enhancement)**

A small horizontal-drift TPC (~30 cm drift) between SuperFGD and FGD1:
- Ar:CF4:iC4H10 gas mixture (proven in existing TPCs)
- Resistive Micromegas readout (upgraded from bulk)
- Measures dE/dx for particle ID of forward-going tracks
- Momentum measurement via curvature in 0.2 T field
- Validates SuperFGD track angles and provides redundancy

## 5. **Enhanced Electronics and DAQ**

- **CITIROC or SPIROC ASICs** for MPPC readout with:
  - Auto-trigger capability at individual cube level
  - Waveform sampling for pulse shape discrimination
  - Time-over-threshold for charge measurement
- **White Rabbit timing system** for <1 ns synchronization across all subdetectors
- **Upgraded DAQ bandwidth** (×10) to handle ~100× increase in channel count

## 6. **Calibration Systems**

- **Cosmic ray telescope** above SuperFGD for position/timing calibration
- **LED pulser system** integrated into fiber network
- **Americium-Beryllium neutron source** deployment system for tracking calibration

## Technical Justification for SuperFGD

The 3D cube design specifically addresses the stated requirements:
- **High-angle acceptance**: Isotropic sensitivity captures the 25% of muons and 35% of protons beyond 50°
- **Low momentum threshold**: 1 cm granularity detects stopping protons down to ~200 MeV/c (well below the 450 MeV/c median)
- **Kinematic completeness**: Fine granularity resolves vertex topology, separating leading vs. secondary protons
- **Systematic reduction**: Uniform active target (no passive layers) and 3D measurement reduce model dependencies from ~6% to target ~4%

This approach is validated by similar designs in prototypes tested at CERN (2018-2019) showing excellent performance for multi-track vertices.

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D segmented scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD) with ~2 million 1 cm³ cubes and three-axis fiber readout in the upstream P0D region**

# Next-Phase Hardware Upgrades for the Off-Axis Near Detector

## Diagnosis: why the current design limits the systematics

- **High-angle muons are lost.**
  - The tracking target bars all lie perpendicular to the beam, and the three gas TPCs sit only downstream.
  - Tracks above roughly 50–60° therefore cross few bar layers and often miss the TPCs.
  - About 25% of muons leave at those angles, so the near detector samples a different phase space than the 4π water far detector. Flux and cross-section extrapolation then depends on models.
- **Low-momentum protons are poorly reconstructed.**
  - Proton tracks are short. Planar x/y bars need a proton to cross several 1 cm layers in each view.
  - Protons near or below the ~450 MeV/c median, or at high angle, are often unreconstructed or confused with other particles.
  - About 35% of leading protons leave above 50°. This makes transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies, and the nuclear-effect constraints they provide, badly incomplete.
- **Timing is limited.** There is no dedicated timing system to tell track direction (forward versus backward) or to reject events entering from outside the target.

## Upgrade 1 (central): a highly segmented 3D scintillator target

**What it is**
- Fill the ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with roughly 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes. This is a "SuperFGD"-type design, about 2 t of CH.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, read out by SiPMs on three faces (about 60k channels).
- Readout gives three 2D projections per hit, hence true 3D, near-isotropic reconstruction.

**Physics motivation**
- **Full angular acceptance.** There is no preferred plane, so muons and protons are tracked at any angle, including backward. This recovers the ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons above 50°.
- **Low proton threshold.** The 1 cm granularity in three views lowers the proton tracking threshold to about 300 MeV/c (a few cubes of track length). Combined with dE/dx along the track, this gives:
  - good proton/pion/muon separation;
  - calorimetric measurement of stopping protons.
- **Most protons stop inside.** Protons up to ~900 MeV/c largely stop within the target, so range and calorimetry measure their momentum. The ~6% above 900 MeV/c that exit are measured in the new TPCs or by time of flight.
- **Neutron detection.**
  - Fine segmentation plus about 1 ns timing per channel lets isolated neutron-induced hits be tagged.
  - Neutron kinematics can then be measured by time of flight from the vertex.
  - This enables TKI in antineutrino mode (μ⁺ + n) and better calorimetric neutrino-energy reconstruction.
- **Shower separation.** Good γ/e separation and π⁰ reconstruction help with electron-neutrino backgrounds.

**Engineering**
- Use injection-moulded cubes with a reflective etched surface and 1 mm Y-11 type fibres.
- Use compact SiPMs with new front-end electronics (CITIROC-class ASICs), giving good timing, wide dynamic range and per-channel calibration.

## Upgrade 2: two high-angle gas TPCs above and below the new target

**What it is**
- Thin-walled, low-mass field cages around the 3D target, filled with an argon-based gas (T2K-type mixture).
- Read out by **resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas** modules. The resistive layer spreads charge, so finer spatial resolution is reached with fewer, larger pads.
- Operated inside the existing 0.2 T magnet.

**Physics motivation**
- **Momentum and charge sign at high angle.** These come from magnetic curvature for muons, pions and exiting protons. This closes the high-angle hole between the target and the downstream TPCs.
- **Particle identification.** dE/dx in gas gives μ/e/p separation, which matters for electron-neutrino and wrong-sign contamination.
- **Thin walls** keep multiple scattering and secondary interactions low.

## Upgrade 3: time-of-flight scintillator envelope

**What it is**
- Plastic scintillator bars (about 2 m long, 12 cm wide) with SiPM arrays at both ends.
- Placed as panels enclosing the new target–TPC assembly.
- Timing resolution about 100–150 ps.

**Physics motivation**
- Determines track direction, separating forward from backward-going tracks and rejecting entering particles and out-of-target (magnet or sand) background.
- Adds particle identification for low-momentum tracks via timing, and supplies the time reference for neutron time-of-flight.

## Upgrade 4: supporting improvements

- **Electronics, DAQ and trigger.** Higher-rate readout matched to increased beam power and more channels.
- **Downstream TPC readout.** Optionally refurbish it with resistive Micromegas for uniform performance.
- **Calibration.**
  - Use cosmic and through-going muon samples for cube-by-cube light-yield calibration.
  - Use an LED or laser system for SiPM gain monitoring.
- **Retained target.** Keep the downstream water-layer target and bar tracker. The carbon-to-water ratio then constrains the nuclear-target extrapolation to the far detector.

## Expected impact

Together these upgrades deliver several gains:

- near-4π acceptance for the muon matching the far detector;
- reconstruction of the leading proton (and neutron) for TKI;
- reduced model dependence in the nuclear-effect, flux and cross-section constraints.

This is what is needed to bring the residual systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the required ~4%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2 t, 1 cm³-cube 3D-readout scintillator target (SuperFGD-type, WLS fibre + SiPM in three views), flanked by high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs, for full-acceptance muon and low-threshold proton reconstruction.

# Design Review Recommendations for Near Detector Target Upgrade

## Analysis of Requirements

The key challenges are:
- Achieve kinematically complete reconstruction of CC events (muon + leading proton)
- Handle large-angle particles (~25% muons, ~35% protons >50° to beam)
- Detect protons with median ~450 MeV/c, tail to >900 MeV/c
- Reduce systematic uncertainty from 6% to ~4%
- Fit within 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m envelope
- Provide hydrocarbon target for comparison with downstream water target

## Primary Recommendation: 3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Target

**Technology:** Super-FGD (Fine-Grained Detector) design with ~1 cm³ optically-isolated scintillator cubes

**Specifications:**
- Polystyrene-based cubes of 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm³
- Three orthogonal WLS fiber readouts through each cube
- ~220,000 cubes filling the available volume (~2.5 tonnes)
- SiPM readout at fiber ends (already baseline technology)

**Justification:**
1. **3D reconstruction:** Three fiber orientations per cube enables true 3D tracking without alternating-plane ambiguities, critical for large-angle particles
2. **Proton detection:** 1 cm granularity provides stopping power measurement for protons down to ~300 MeV/c, covering the majority of the distribution
3. **Angular acceptance:** Fine segmentation maintains efficiency for 50°+ tracks
4. **Timing:** SiPM readout provides ~ns timing to separate overlapping tracks in high-rate beam
5. **Proven technology:** Demonstrated in T2K ND280 upgrade

## Secondary Recommendations

### 2. High-Angle Tracking Enhancement

**Technology:** Add thin TPCs or resistive Micromegas planes at upstream and downstream faces

**Specifications:**
- 2-3 cm gas gap with amplification stage
- Pixel or strip readout at 2-3 mm pitch
- Covers full 2.0 × 1.9 m transverse area

**Justification:**
- Improves angular resolution for tracks entering/exiting target at large angles
- Provides clean entry/exit point determination for momentum-by-range
- Minimal dead material (~0.5% X₀ per plane)
- Synergy with existing TPC technology downstream

### 3. Time-of-Flight System

**Technology:** Thin scintillator hodoscopes with SiPM readout at target boundaries

**Specifications:**
- 2-3 cm thick plastic scintillator bars
- 5-10 cm segmentation
- <100 ps timing resolution per bar

**Justification:**
- Discriminates protons from pions in the 300-600 MeV/c range where dE/dx begins to fail
- 60 cm flight path provides ~500 ps separation for p/π at 500 MeV/c
- Critical for reducing misidentification systematics
- Low cost addition (~€100k)

### 4. Downstream Momentum Spectrometer Upgrade

**Technology:** Enhanced tracking before first TPC

**Specifications:**
- Add thin (3-5 mm) scintillator planes with 1 cm strip readout
- 5-6 XY doublets spanning 20 cm immediately downstream of new target

**Justification:**
- Improves momentum measurement for forward-going protons that don't range out in target
- Leverages existing 0.2 T field for curvature measurement
- Essential for the ~6% of protons >900 MeV/c
- Minimal material budget impact on existing TPCs

### 5. Neutron Detection Capability

**Technology:** Hydrocarbon scintillator with pulse-shape discrimination

**Specifications:**
- Replace some standard polystyrene cubes with PSD-capable scintillator (e.g., EJ-276)
- Distributed throughout volume (every 5th layer)
- Same geometry, compatible with existing SiPM readout

**Justification:**
- Neutron detection improves hadronic energy reconstruction
- Reduces model dependence in nuclear recoil systematics
- PSD algorithms well-established for SiPM waveforms
- Addresses multi-nucleon correlation uncertainties contributing to systematic error budget

## Alternative Considered: Emulsion-Based Target

Emulsion Cloud Chamber technology provides excellent spatial resolution but was rejected because:
- No active readout requires external triggering
- Time-consuming scanning incompatible with high statistics needs
- No timing information for beam-background separation
- Difficult to instrument for large-angle tracks exiting sides

## Cost and Schedule Considerations

- Super-FGD fabrication: ~18 months, €3-4M (cube production, fiber insertion, assembly)
- TOF hodoscopes: ~6 months, €100k
- Boundary TPCs: ~12 months, €500k (leverages existing expertise)
- Forward tracker: ~9 months, €300k
- Total: ~24 months, ~€5M

Compatible with typical neutrino detector upgrade timelines and budgets.

## Expected Performance Impact

- Proton detection efficiency >80% for p >350 MeV/c at all angles
- Angular resolution <3° for reconstructed tracks
- Momentum resolution ~5% by range, ~3% by curvature (forward)
- Combined improvements projected to reduce flux×cross-section uncertainty from 6% → 3.5-4%

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D Super-Fine-Grained Detector with 1 cm³ scintillator cubes and three-axis wavelength-shifting fiber readout to achieve complete kinematic reconstruction for large-angle muons and protons.

# ND280 Upgrade: Recommended Hardware Changes for the P0D Region

## The problem these changes address

The existing tracker cannot deliver kinematically complete events in this beam, for two reasons.

**1. Angular acceptance is forward-biased.**
- The TPCs sit upstream and downstream of the FGDs. Tracks above about 50–60° rarely reach them.
- The FGD bar planes are all perpendicular to the beam. A track at high angle runs almost along a single bar layer, so its hit pattern degenerates and it cannot be tracked reliably.
- This loses the roughly 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons that exit above 50°.
- High-angle and backward tracks drive the acceptance-related flux and cross-section systematics. That is a large part of why the residual is about 6% rather than the 4% T2K-II needs.

**2. The proton threshold is too high.**
- A proton must cross several 1 cm x/y layers to be reconstructed. This puts the effective threshold near 450 MeV/c, which is the median of the leading-proton spectrum.
- Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analyses therefore lose about half the protons. They also lose exactly the low-momentum region where nuclear effects (Fermi motion, final-state interactions, 2p2h) are most visible.

## Recommendations

### 1. Replace the P0D with a 3D-granular scintillator target ("SuperFGD")

**Design**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56 cubes filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres (Kuraray Y11 type).
- Each fibre is read out by an MPPC (Hamamatsu S13360-class, about 56k channels).
- Total target mass is about 2 t of hydrocarbon, roughly double the FGD1 + FGD2 mass.

**Justification**
- **Isotropic 4π acceptance.** Three orthogonal 2D projections give a true 3D hit image regardless of track direction. High-angle muons and protons are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Lower proton threshold, about 300 MeV/c.**
  - A 300 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 47 MeV and a range of about 2 cm in plastic, which is 2–3 cubes.
  - That is enough for a reconstructable track with dE/dx.
  - Most of the spectrum below the 450 MeV/c median, previously lost, is recovered.
- **Range-out of most protons.** At the median of about 450 MeV/c (kinetic energy about 100 MeV), the range is roughly 8 cm. Most protons stop in the target, giving range-based momentum plus Bragg-peak particle ID.
- **Fine vertex resolution.** This allows reliable proton–muon vertex association for TKI.
- **Good timing.** Per-fibre time resolution is about 1 ns, and better when hits are combined. Together with 1 cm granularity, this enables:
  - neutron detection via isolated secondary-proton clusters, with time-of-flight kinetic energy;
  - full TKI on antineutrino CC events (μ⁺ + n).
- **Physics continuity.** Hydrocarbon matches FGD1, and FGD2 water is retained for carbon-to-water comparison.

### 2. Add two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below the new target

**Design**
- Two TPCs of roughly 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m each, inside the magnet, using the same Ar:CF4:iC4H10 (95:3:2) gas as the existing TPCs.
- Readout planes use resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM").
- The field cage is a thin composite/laminate structure to minimise dead material and wall thickness.

**Justification**
- **Momentum and charge for tracks that leave the target.** This covers high-angle muons and the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, which travel about 50 cm or more and will not stop in 0.6 m of plastic. The 0.2 T field provides sign and momentum (about 10% resolution or better near 1 GeV/c).
- **dE/dx particle ID** for μ/π/p/e separation.
- **Resistive anode benefits.**
  - Charge spreads over neighbouring pads, giving sub-mm spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads. This reduces electronics cost.
  - It intrinsically suppresses sparks.
- **Low-mass field cage.** This minimises multiple scattering and photon conversions before tracks enter the gas.

### 3. Surround the new target and HA-TPCs with Time-of-Flight planes

**Design**
- Six planes of cast plastic scintillator bars (about 12 cm wide, 1 cm thick).
- Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target time resolution is about 150 ps.

**Justification**
- **Direction tagging.** Timing determines track direction unambiguously. This rejects tracks entering from outside the fiducial volume, such as backgrounds from neutrino interactions in the magnet and surrounding material, and correctly identifies backward-going tracks.
- **Better particle ID in the crossover region.** ToF combined with TPC momentum improves separation where dE/dx bands overlap, for example e/μ near 150 MeV/c and p/π⁺ near 1 GeV/c.
- **Precise trigger and event time.** This supports neutron time-of-flight in the SuperFGD.

### 4. Supporting changes

**Electronics**
- New MPPC front-ends for the SuperFGD (CITIROC-class ASICs with fine TDC timing).
- AFTER/DAQ-compatible front-ends for the HA-TPCs.
- All integrated into the existing ND280 DAQ and clock distribution so the new subsystems run synchronously with the downstream tracker.

**Infrastructure**
- Mechanical support for the new target and HA-TPCs.
- Upstream ECal coverage retained or reconfigured around the new detectors.
- Calibration systems:
  - LED injection for the MPPCs;
  - laser photoelectron targets for TPC drift calibration;
  - cosmic and through-going-muon triggers for cube-by-cube light-yield equalisation.

**Retained hardware**
- Keep FGD1, FGD2, the three downstream TPCs, the ECals and the SMRD.
- The upgraded ND280 then combines a forward tracker with a high-angle tracker, giving close to 4π acceptance.

## Expected impact

- Close to full angular acceptance for both muons and protons.
- Proton threshold reduced from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c.
- Neutron kinematics accessible in antineutrino events.
- Roughly doubled target mass.

Together these give the event-by-event kinematic completeness TKI requires, and the reduced flux and cross-section model dependence needed to bring the systematic from about 6% toward 4%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD-style 3D-granular target of ~2 million 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each read out by three orthogonal WLS fibres and MPPCs, for isotropic acceptance and a ~300 MeV/c proton threshold.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints

Before proposing hardware, let me extract the binding requirements:

- **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (≈5.4 m³)
- **Muon angular coverage**: 4π including backward-going (≥25% efficiency everywhere)
- **Proton threshold**: ~60 MeV kinetic energy → range ~3.5 mm in liquid argon, ~15 mm in scintillator, ~35 mm in gaseous detector at atmospheric pressure
- **Hydrogen fraction**: ≤20% of target nucleons → constrains choice of active medium
- **Magnetic field**: 0.15 T already present, so momentum measurement of escaping tracks is covered downstream
- **Beam**: ~0.7 GeV peak → quasi-elastic dominated, typical muon momenta 200–800 MeV/c, proton momenta up to ~1 GeV/c

The hydrogen constraint is critical: pure hydrocarbon scintillator (CH₂ equivalent) has ~67% hydrogen nucleons — far too high. Water has 67% too. Liquid argon has 0%. A mixture or non-hydrogen medium is needed. This immediately argues against a purely scintillator-based or water-based target.

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Primary Active Target: Plastic Scintillator Tracking Planes with Controlled Composition (Straw-tube / Scintillator Hybrid)

**Problem with pure plastic**: Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has H/(H+C nucleons) ≈ 47% — too hydrogen-rich.

**Solution**: A **segmented target built from alternating planes of thin plastic scintillator and passive carbon/aluminum absorber sheets**, tuned so that the hydrogen nucleon fraction is diluted to ≤20%.

Concretely, interleave:
- **3 mm thick extruded polystyrene scintillator bars** (1 cm × 3 mm cross-section, mirroring MINERvA/NOvA technology), read out with **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** coupled to **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)** at both ends
- **Graphite (carbon) passive sheets** of ~8 mm thickness between every scintillator plane

This brings the effective hydrogen fraction to ~18–19% of nucleons while keeping the scintillator as the interaction and tracking medium. Graphite is mechanically stable and low-Z, minimizing secondary interactions.

**Bar orientation**: Alternate X/Y/U planes (three orientations at 0°, 90°, 60°) to give full 3D reconstruction. Plane spacing ~1 cm longitudinally.

**Why this works for protons**: 60 MeV protons have a range of ~12 mm in plastic scintillator. With 3 mm bars and 1 cm plane spacing, a 60 MeV proton traverses 1–4 bars minimum — detectable via ionization (dE/dx in scintillator is high for slow protons, Bragg peak clearly visible). The granularity is sufficient.

**Why this works for backward muons**: The scintillator planes cover the full upstream face. A backward-going muon re-enters active material immediately. Timing from SiPMs (resolution ~1 ns achievable) disambiguates track direction via time-of-flight across planes.

---

### 2. Time-of-Flight and Track Direction: Fast SiPM Readout with ns-Level Timing

Replace any existing PMTs with **Hamamatsu S13360 series SiPMs** (or equivalent, e.g., FBK NUV-HD), 1 mm² to 4 mm² cells, coupled via **1 mm diameter Y-11 Kuraray WLS fiber**, one per scintillator bar end.

- Achieve **~1 ns timing resolution per bar** (demonstrated in similar systems)
- This provides **track directionality** without ambiguity for backward vs. forward tracks — critical given the 25% efficiency requirement for backward muons
- Also provides **proton/pion separation** via dE/dx + timing for tracks that stop within the volume

Front-end electronics: **CITIROC or TOFPET2 ASICs** (used in PET scanners, well-suited to SiPM arrays), providing both charge (QDC) and time (TDC) per channel. The TOFPET2 achieves ~200 ps TDC resolution, adequate for directionality over 10+ cm separations.

**Channel count**: The volume is 2.6 m × 2.3 m in cross-section. With 1 cm wide bars in alternating X/Y/U planes over 0.9 m depth at 1 cm plane spacing → ~90 planes × ~250 bars/plane × 2 ends ≈ 45,000 SiPM channels. This is manageable with modern ASIC-based readout (c.f. CMS HGCAL scale).

---

### 3. Inner Tracking for Very Short Proton Tracks: Thin-Gap or μRPC Layer Insertion

The hardest requirement is proton reconstruction at 60 MeV, especially at large angles (perpendicular or backward) where the track crosses fewer scintillator planes.

**Augment the scintillator target with 4–6 planes of Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) or μ-RWELL detectors** inserted at ~15 cm intervals along the beam direction.

Specifically recommend **μ-RWELL (micro-Resistive WELL) detectors**, a GEM-derivative technology:
- 50 μm position resolution
- Operated with Ar/CO₂ or Ar/iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture
- **Active area**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m per plane — large but achievable with tiled μ-RWELL panels (10 cm × 10 cm tile modules, as demonstrated by CERN groups for ATLAS NSW upgrade derivatives)
- Strip pitch: 1 mm strips in X and Y (or X and U), giving 2D hit per plane
- These contribute negligible mass (< 1% X₀ per plane) and near-zero hydrogen content

**Purpose**: Catch short proton stubs that don't traverse enough scintillator bars for a 3D reconstruction. A proton stopped after 15 mm is reconstructed in 1 scintillator plane + 1 μ-RWELL plane with full position information.

**Operational note**: The existing warm dipole provides ~0.15 T — insufficient for momentum measurement of stopping tracks inside the target, but the μ-RWELL layers allow dE/dx-based momentum estimation via range combined with Bethe-Bloch for proton ID.

---

### 4. Upstream Veto and Beam-Muon Rejection: Scintillator Paddle Array

Install a **2-layer scintillator veto panel** immediately upstream of the active target volume:
- Two planes of **5 mm thick plastic scintillator paddles**, full 2.6 m × 2.3 m coverage
- Each paddle 5 cm wide, read out with SiPMs via WLS fiber
- Provides **beam-muon veto** (beam-related muon background from the horn system) and **interaction vertex fiducialization**
- Also serves as an upstream time reference for the timing system

---

### 5. Side and Downstream Active Veto Planes for Escaping Track Tagging

To achieve ≥25% efficiency for tracks at all angles, the detector needs to know when a muon or proton exits through the sides or upstream face (backward). Install:

- **Side veto planes**: 4 lateral faces of the target volume instrumented with **1 cm × 1 cm cross-section scintillator bars**, WLS+SiPM readout, 2 layers per face. These are "active sheath" panels, ~5 mm thick. Total area: 2×(2.6×0.9) + 2×(2.3×0.9) ≈ 8.8 m².
- **Upstream (backward) veto/tracker plane**: One 2.6 m × 2.3 m plane of **double-sided strip scintillator** at the upstream face, giving XY position of a backward-exiting track. This feeds into the upstream spectrometer if one exists, or at minimum flags the event topology.

The existing downstream drift chambers already handle forward-going muons, so no hardware changes needed there.

---

### 6. Trigger and DAQ: Continuous Sampling / Triggerless Readout

The existing trigger system (presumably based on the downstream spectrometer seeing a muon) will miss backward-going and large-angle interactions by design.

**Replace or augment** with a **self-triggered, continuous readout DAQ**:
- Each TOFPET2/CITIROC ASIC operates in **self-trigger mode** with a hardware threshold ~0.5 photoelectron equivalent
- A **Field Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) trigger processor** (e.g., Xilinx Kintex UltraScale) collects hit timestamps from all channels and applies a **software-defined coincidence trigger**: any 3 adjacent bars firing within a 10 ns window defines an interaction candidate
- Spill-level buffering: the accelerator spill structure (~10 μs spill at typical facilities) allows ring-buffer readout; store all hits in a 100 μs window per spill
- This is proven technology (used in LHCb Upgrade I, DUNE prototype detectors)

**This is essential for backward-going muon efficiency** — a hardware trigger based only on downstream detectors would inherently have near-zero efficiency for backward tracks.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Purpose | Addresses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Scintillator + graphite target | 3 mm extruded PS bars + C sheets, WLS+SiPM | Primary interaction medium, controlled H fraction | H ≤20%, proton threshold |
| Fast SiPM readout (TOFPET2) | 1–4 mm² SiPMs, TOFPET2 ASICs | Track direction (fwd/bkwd), dE/dx | Backward muon efficiency |
| μ-RWELL planes (×6) | GEM-derivative, 1 mm strips | Short proton stub reconstruction | 60 MeV proton threshold |
| Upstream + side veto | 5 mm scintillator paddles + SiPMs | Fiducialization, escaping track tagging | All-angle efficiency |
| Triggerless DAQ (FPGA) | Self-trigger ASIC + UltraScale FPGA | Catch backward/large-angle events | Backward muon ≥25% |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the DAQ trigger with a self-triggered continuous readout system (TOFPET2 ASICs + FPGA coincidence processor), because a downstream-biased hardware trigger is the single most direct cause of near-zero efficiency for backward-going and large-angle muons, and no amount of active-target hardware improvement recovers events that are never recorded.

I'll work through the physics requirements systematically to derive what hardware is needed.

---

## Physics Requirements Analysis

**Geometry constraints:**
- Target volume: 2.6 m (W) × 2.3 m (H) × 0.9 m (L along beam)
- Must reconstruct tracks at ALL angles, including 90° and backward-going
- Muon efficiency ≥ 25% at every angle
- Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range in water ~3.3 mm; in scintillator ~8 mm; in liquid argon ~~4 mm)

**Hydrogen constraint:**
- H must be ≤ 20% of target nucleons
- Pure CH₂ or water (H₂O) would be ~67% or ~11% hydrogen by nucleon count respectively
- Water: O has 8 nucleons, H has 1×2 = 2 → H fraction = 2/10 = 20% → right at the limit
- Polystyrene (C₈H₈): H nucleons / total = 8/16 = 50% → too high
- Liquid argon: 0% H → easily satisfies constraint but loses the hydrogen signal entirely
- Hydrocarbon scintillator (CH, roughly): H/total ≈ 1/13 per CH unit ≈ ~8% → satisfies constraint if carbon-dominated

Actually let me be more careful. The far detector has no hydrogen, and interactions on hydrogen are **removed by a model** that works only while H ≤ 20% of target nucleons. The near detector needs hydrogen present (to have something to subtract) but not too much.

- Liquid argon: no H → no subtraction needed but also no hydrogen cross-section measurement
- Plastic scintillator (polystyrene C₈H₈): H nucleon fraction = 8/(8×12+8) = 8/104 ≈ 8% ✓
- Water: 2/(2+16) nucleons → 2/18 ≈ 11% ✓

The hydrogen fraction requirement essentially **rules out** CH₂-rich materials and pure hydrocarbon liquids, but allows polystyrene, water, or heavier materials.

---

## Hardware Upgrades Required

### 1. Active Target Medium — **3D Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperCube" / WAGASCI-style)**

**Technology:** Array of small plastic scintillator cubes (~1.5 cm³ each) read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers along three orthogonal axes, as demonstrated by the NINJA/WAGASCI detectors and the Baby MIND concept, or more directly the SuperFGD technology developed for T2K's near detector upgrade.

**Why:**
- Provides full 4π tracking acceptance — the orthogonal fiber readout means there is no preferred tracking direction, so backward-going and transverse tracks are reconstructed with the same efficiency as forward tracks. This directly satisfies the ≥25% efficiency at all angles requirement.
- The ~1.5 cm cube granularity gives a track length resolution sufficient to stop and identify protons at 60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~8 mm in scintillator → stops in ~1 cube), satisfying the low-energy proton requirement.
- Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has ~8% H nucleon fraction, safely below the 20% ceiling.
- The existing warm dipole magnet and downstream drift chambers are retained — this upgrade drops into the existing target region.
- Passive or active construction is entirely within the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m envelope.
- The scintillator cubes provide the density (~1.05 g/cm³) needed for neutrino interaction rate while keeping the radiation length long enough for electromagnetic shower reconstruction.

### 2. Timing System — **Fast SiPM Readout with ~1 ns Resolution**

**Technology:** Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) replacing or supplementing any existing PMT-based readout, with TOFPET2 or similar ASICs providing per-channel timing to ~1 ns or better.

**Why:**
- At 410 m from target with a ~0.7 GeV peak flux, the beam spill structure creates pile-up. Sub-nanosecond timing separates multiple interactions within a spill.
- SiPMs are compact, operate in the magnetic field of the dipole (unlike PMTs, which require shielding or remote mounting), and are well-matched to WLS fiber emission spectra (~500 nm).
- Fast timing also helps distinguish forward vs. backward track direction from light arrival time asymmetry in the fiber readout, aiding the backward-track reconstruction requirement.
- SiPMs have lower operating voltage and are more reliable for the dense channel counts needed (~150,000–200,000 channels for a full cube array).

### 3. Downstream Muon Spectrometer Interface — **Thin Scintillating Fiber Tracker or Resistive Plate Chambers at the Target Exit Face**

**Technology:** Scintillating fiber (SciFi) planes or RPCs at the downstream face of the active target, acting as a matching station between the cube array and the existing gas drift chambers.

**Why:**
- The existing downstream drift chambers measure momentum and charge, but their spatial resolution and hit occupancy may not match well to tracks exiting at large angles from the cube array.
- A thin SciFi or RPC matching plane provides high-resolution (sub-mm) hit positions at the exit face with timing, enabling robust track-matching even for large-angle muons that only clip the edge of the drift chamber acceptance.
- This maximizes muon reconstruction efficiency at large angles without replacing the functioning downstream spectrometer, keeping cost down.
- SciFi planes are radiation-hard and fast; RPCs are cheaper for large area.

### 4. Upstream Veto and Interaction Counter — **Scintillator Veto Panels with Beam-defining Counters**

**Technology:** Thin (1–2 cm) plastic scintillator panels with SiPM readout upstream and surrounding the target volume.

**Why:**
- Charged particles entering from upstream (beam halo muons, secondary particles from upstream material) must be vetoed to avoid misidentifying them as interaction products.
- An upstream veto is essential for the backward-track analysis: a backward-going track that actually came from upstream looks identical topologically without an active veto.
- Surrounding panels also tag particles that scatter into the target from the magnet coils or yoke, which would otherwise fake multi-particle final states.
- Very low cost relative to the active target, and straightforward SiPM readout shares infrastructure with the main detector.

### 5. Data Acquisition System — **Triggerless / Self-triggered DAQ with High Bandwidth**

**Technology:** Self-triggered DAQ based on continuous digitization (e.g., CAEN V2740 or custom FPGA-based front-end), replacing any existing triggered/gated system.

**Why:**
- A 3D scintillator array with ~200,000 SiPM channels cannot use a simple global hardware trigger without losing the low-energy proton signals (which produce very little light and would fail threshold).
- A triggerless system records all channels above a low threshold and builds events offline, preserving the short, dim proton tracks.
- The self-triggered approach also handles the backward-track topology correctly — there is no requirement that the "first" hit defines the trigger direction.
- Modern FPGAs and high-bandwidth optical fiber links (e.g., GBT protocol) make this tractable at the required channel count.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | 3D scintillator cube array (SuperFGD-style), ~1.5 cm cubes, WLS fibers | All-angle tracking, 60 MeV protons, H ≤ 20% |
| Photodetectors | SiPMs on all cube fibers | Magnetic field compatibility, timing, channel density |
| Exit matching station | SciFi planes or RPCs at downstream target face | Large-angle muon matching to drift chambers |
| Upstream/surrounding veto | Thin scintillator panels, SiPM readout | Beam background rejection, backward-track disambiguation |
| DAQ | Triggerless self-triggered digitization, FPGA-based | Low-energy proton retention, all-topology readout |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a 3D plastic scintillator cube array (SuperFGD technology) with SiPM/WLS-fiber readout, as this single change simultaneously solves the all-angle tracking efficiency requirement, enables reconstruction of 60 MeV protons, and keeps the hydrogen nucleon fraction within the 20% model validity limit.

# Design Review Recommendation for Near Detector Upgrade

## Analysis of Requirements

The key requirements for the new target are:
1. **Kinematic completeness**: Reconstruct both muons and leading protons in charged-current events
2. **Large angular acceptance**: ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons exit >50° to beam
3. **Proton momentum range**: Median ~450 MeV/c, tail to >900 MeV/c
4. **Volume constraint**: 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m
5. **Reduce systematic uncertainty**: From 6% to ~4%

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **Replace Upstream Photon Tagger with 3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (FGD)**

**Technology**: Super-FGD design (10 mm³ optically-isolated polystyrene cubes with three orthogonal WLS fiber readouts per cube)

**Justification**:
- **3D tracking capability**: Critical for reconstructing tracks at large angles (>50°) where 2D x/y layers fail
- **Low threshold**: 10 mm granularity provides ~5-10 MeV proton detection threshold, capturing the full proton spectrum
- **Target mass**: ~1.8 t of hydrocarbon in available volume (similar to existing targets)
- **Time resolution**: <1 ns timing distinguishes event vertices and reduces pileup
- **Angle reconstruction**: True 3D readout eliminates ambiguities at large angles

**Specifications**:
- 180 × 170 × 60 cubes (≈1.8 million channels)
- Three 1 mm WLS fibers per cube (Kuraray Y11 or equivalent)
- SiPM arrays at fiber ends (already established technology in this detector)

### 2. **Install Additional TPC Downstream of New Target**

**Technology**: Fourth argon-based gas TPC matching existing three TPCs

**Justification**:
- **Momentum measurement**: Gas TPC provides excellent momentum resolution for high-angle tracks entering from new upstream target
- **Particle ID**: dE/dx discrimination separates protons from pions in critical 300-900 MeV/c range
- **Low multiple scattering**: Argon gas minimizes degradation of angular resolution for kinematic imbalance
- **Technology reuse**: Leverage existing TPC expertise and infrastructure

**Modification**: Shift existing TPC1 downstream by 0.6 m; install new TPC0 in gap created

### 3. **Replace First Plastic Target with Thin Time-of-Flight Plane**

**Technology**: 5 mm thick plastic scintillator plane with 3 cm segmentation and <200 ps timing resolution

**Justification**:
- **Particle ID**: TOF between new target and this plane (Δz ≈ 1.3 m) provides π/p separation up to ~700 MeV/c
- **Triggering**: Fast timing reference for event building
- **Minimal material**: Thin profile maintains kinematic measurements
- **Redundancy**: Complements TPC dE/dx for systematic control

**Technology**: BC-404 or EJ-200 fast scintillator with direct SiPM coupling

### 4. **Upgrade DAQ and Add Timing Distribution System**

**Technology**: 
- White Rabbit or equivalent precision timing network
- Upgraded front-end electronics with >10× bandwidth

**Justification**:
- **Channel count**: Super-FGD adds ~5.4 million fiber readouts requiring massive DAQ upgrade
- **Timing precision**: <1 ns synchronization across all sub-detectors essential for 3D track matching
- **Event building**: Correlate tracks between upstream target and downstream TPCs at large angles
- **Systematic reduction**: Precise timing cuts reduce backgrounds and cosmic contamination

### 5. **Install Side-Detector Scintillator Panels**

**Technology**: Additional scintillator planes (2 cm thick, 5 cm segmentation) on ±x sides of magnet volume between new target and first TPC

**Justification**:
- **High-angle acceptance**: Catch 50-90° tracks exiting sideways from new target
- **Muon ranging**: Side-escaping muons are ranged/momentum-measured before magnet
- **Containment verification**: Ensure leading protons that miss TPCs are tagged
- **Area**: ~3.8 m² per side with ~600 channels total (manageable addition)

## Alternative Considered but Not Recommended

**Liquid argon TPC target**: While providing excellent resolution, the cryogenics infrastructure would exceed available space and budget, and development risk is high for this timeline.

## Expected Performance Improvements

- **Acceptance**: ~85% for muons, ~75% for leading protons (vs current ~60%/~40%)
- **Angular resolution**: <2° for both muons and protons at all angles
- **Momentum resolution**: <5% for contained tracks, ~10% for side-exiting via range
- **Vertex resolution**: <5 mm in 3D enabling precise nuclear target identification
- **Systematic uncertainty**: Combination of acceptance, PID, and momentum improvements should achieve <4% target

## Implementation Priority

1. Super-FGD (longest R&D and production time)
2. DAQ/timing upgrade (required for Super-FGD operation)
3. Additional TPC and detector rearrangement
4. TOF plane and side detectors (can be staged)

# Hardware Upgrades for the ND280 Upstream Active Target Proposal

## 1. Active Neutrino Target Volume (Core Upgrade)

**Technology: SuperFGD — a 3D grid of ~1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes**

The 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m available volume should be filled with ~2 million optically isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes (~1 × 1 × 1 cm³), each read out by three wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres running along x, y, and z axes, each fibre coupled to an MPPC.

**Why:** The conventional FGD bar geometry (long extruded bars alternating x/y) gives 2D tracking only perpendicular to the beam and has a dead region along the bar axis. The cubic geometry provides fully isotropic 3D hit reconstruction with no preferred dead direction. This is essential because ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons exit at >50° to the beam — exactly the large-angle population that existing FGD bars reconstruct poorly or not at all. The ~1 cm³ granularity gives a vertex resolution of ~1 cm³, sufficient to identify the interaction vertex and distinguish the muon track from the recoil proton track even at large angles. The hydrocarbon (polystyrene, CH) target composition satisfies the stated acceptability criterion and provides high statistics. At a median proton momentum of ~450 MeV/c (range in plastic ~15–20 cm), the cube size ensures adequate sampling across the full proton momentum range.

---

## 2. Surrounding High-Angle Electromagnetic Calorimeters (new HA-TPC or upgraded ECal)

**Technology: Thin lead-scintillator ECal modules with increased angular acceptance, surrounding the SuperFGD on all six faces including the upstream face**

Each face should use the same WLS-fibre + MPPC readout already established in ND280 ECals, but designed for ≥150° solid-angle coverage around the new target volume.

**Why:** The existing ECal geometry was optimised around the TPC/FGD stack and leaves the upstream face and wide-angle acceptance incomplete. Muons exiting at >50° and photons from π⁰ decay must be caught for complete event reconstruction. Without upstream and large-angle ECal coverage, the kinematically complete charged-current signal (muon + proton both reconstructed, plus control of neutral pion background) cannot be achieved for the large-angle fraction. The thin-lead design keeps the material budget low enough not to range out soft protons before they reach the TPCs or SMRD.

---

## 3. Time Projection Chambers Flanking the New Target

**Technology: Two new High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) with resistive Micromegas readout, one on each transverse side of the SuperFGD (or top/bottom), within the magnet volume**

Gas mixture: same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 as existing TPCs, with resistive-strip Micromegas pads for improved charge sharing and position resolution (~500 µm).

**Why:** Muons and protons leaving the SuperFGD laterally enter these TPCs where the 0.2 T magnetic field allows momentum measurement by curvature. This is critical for the ~35% of leading protons and ~25% of muons at >50°. The existing downstream TPCs only capture forward-going tracks efficiently. Resistive Micromegas (versus bulk Micromegas) reduces spark rate from the higher-multiplicity events and improves spatial resolution for closely-spaced proton and muon tracks near the vertex. Momentum resolution of ~10% at 450 MeV/c is achievable, adequate for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) variables where ~10–15% momentum resolution is acceptable.

---

## 4. MPPC Upgrade on Existing Downstream Detectors (FGDs and ECals)

**Technology: Second-generation MPPCs with higher photon detection efficiency (PDE ~50% vs ~35%), lower dark noise, and finer pixel pitch (10–15 µm) — e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent**

**Why:** The new upstream target will shift the interaction vertex distribution upstream, changing the occupancy and timing environment in the downstream FGDs and ECals. Higher-PDE MPPCs improve light yield and thus energy and position resolution for the recoil proton tracks that do reach the downstream detectors (the ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c will punch through into FGD1/FGD2). Lower dark noise reduces fake hits in the low-occupancy large-angle ECal channels. This upgrade also future-proofs the detector for the higher beam intensity planned for T2K-II.

---

## 5. Upgraded Trigger and DAQ Electronics

**Technology: Self-triggered, free-running ADC-based readout with ~1 ns timestamp resolution (e.g., CITIROC or TARGET ASICs), replacing the existing clocked readout, with a central trigger processor using FPGAs (e.g., Xilinx Ultrascale)**

**Why:** The SuperFGD produces O(10⁴) channels with 3D readout simultaneously. The existing ND280 DAQ uses a synchronous trigger with limited buffering, designed for the sparser FGD/TPC hit topology. A free-running system allows offline trigger definition, handles the increased multiplicity without deadtime, and enables sub-ns timing coincidences between the SuperFGD cubes — important for distinguishing the prompt muon track from delayed proton signals and for neutron tagging via time-of-flight (which is a bonus physics channel relevant to TKI). The FPGA-based trigger processor allows flexible online event selection as the physics programme evolves for T2K-II.

---

## 6. Beam Monitor / Muon Monitor Cross-Calibration Detector

**Technology: A thin (1–2 radiation length) upstream luminosity monitor using diamond pixel sensors or a small gas Cherenkov counter, installed just upstream of the P0D region**

**Why:** Reducing the total systematic uncertainty from 6% to 4% requires not only better event reconstruction but also tighter control of flux normalization. A dedicated luminosity/beam-profile monitor at the near-detector location, correlated with the existing J-PARC muon monitors, reduces the flux normalization uncertainty by constraining beam-profile variations event-by-event. Diamond sensors are radiation-hard at the required fluence and introduce minimal material.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before listing upgrades, it helps to crystallize the physics drivers:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward tracks — these exit through the sides or upstream face of the target volume, so they never enter the downstream spectrometer. The magnet alone cannot serve them.
- **Proton tracks down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** — range ~3 cm in liquid argon, ~1 cm in scintillator, so the active target needs fine spatial resolution and low detection threshold, with no dead material at the interaction vertex.
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of target nucleons** — this severely constrains the choice of target medium. Pure hydrocarbons (~14% H by nucleon count) are disqualified. Even CH₂ (~25% H) is out. Liquid argon (0% H), iron (0% H), and carbon (~0%) are fine. Water is ~11% H — disqualified unless fiducially subtracted with an H-free reference target. This is a hard constraint that cuts off many otherwise attractive options.

---

## Upgrade 1: Plastic Scintillator 3D-Projection Tracking Modules (SuperFGD-style)

**Technology:** A fully-active scintillator cube detector — an array of ~1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each read out in three orthogonal directions via wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through holes, coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). Each fibre reads an entire row of cubes; a hit cube is identified by the coincidence of three fibre signals (X, Y, Z). The T2K SuperFGD (deployed 2023) is the direct prototype.

**Physics motivation:**

*4π proton tracking:* A 1 cm³ voxel size means a proton with 60 MeV kinetic energy (~3 cm range in polystyrene, density ~1.05 g/cm³) leaves roughly 3 hit cubes — detectable as a stub track in any direction. Because the detector is fully active with no inactive gaps between modules, there is no geometric acceptance loss for large-angle or backward-going recoils. This directly addresses the 60 MeV proton requirement.

*4π muon seeding:* While a low-momentum muon stopping inside the cube volume is reconstructed entirely within it, a higher-momentum muon exiting sideways or backward still deposits a clean, continuous track that can be matched to surrounding detectors (see Upgrades 2 and 3). The 3D hit topology provides an unambiguous track direction, including backward-going tracks, without ambiguity from 2D projections.

*Hydrogen content:* Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ has a hydrogen nucleon fraction of 8/(8×12 + 8) ≈ 7.7% — well above the 2% limit. This is the critical problem. The mitigation is to use it only for topology reconstruction while applying an event-by-event hydrogen subtraction: pair the SuperFGD with a nearby graphite (pure carbon) target of identical mass and subtract the carbon-interaction rate to isolate the hydrogen excess. However, this subtraction introduces systematic uncertainty. **Alternatively**, replace polystyrene with a low-H material (see constraint discussion under Upgrade 4). Given that T2K's SuperFGD is already built from polystyrene, in practice the experiment must either (a) accept the statistical subtraction, (b) dope or replace the scintillator, or (c) operate a companion argon or carbon module. This upgrade is recommended in conjunction with Upgrade 4.

---

## Upgrade 2: Resistive Plate Chamber (RPC) or Thin-Gap Chamber Side and Upstream Muon Catcher Walls

**Technology:** Layers of RPCs or thin-gap MWPCs (multi-wire proportional chambers), interleaved with iron or lead absorber plates, forming instrumented walls on the two lateral faces (2.6 m × 0.9 m each), the top and bottom, and the upstream face of the target volume. Each wall is 3–5 absorber/detector sandwiches, providing ~0.5–1 interaction length of muon ranging material. The same technology is used in the MINOS near detector's muon catcher and in NOvA's muon veto systems.

**Physics motivation:**

*Backward and large-angle muon reconstruction:* A muon exiting the upstream face or at 90° has zero probability of reaching the downstream spectrometer. Without instrumented surrounding walls, these tracks are simply lost. With a muon catcher on each face, a backward muon travels through the absorber stack, ranges out or exits, and its momentum is estimated from range (for stopping tracks) or from curvature if the wall is placed inside the stray fringe field, or simply from range alone if calibrated. Even range-only momentum gives ~10% resolution sufficient for neutrino energy reconstruction.

*Efficiency at all angles:* The requirement is ≥25% at every angle. For tracks at 90° ± ~15°, neither the downstream spectrometer nor a purely forward-facing active target can reach this threshold. A hermetic surrounding muon system — four walls plus upstream cap — brings the geometric acceptance to nearly 4π, with efficiency limited only by the instrumented fraction of each wall face. With RPCs at ~95% single-layer efficiency and 3–4 layers per wall, the multi-layer efficiency per wall exceeds 99%, meeting the ≥25% per-angle requirement with large margin for all but a narrow cone around the beam axis (covered by the downstream spectrometer).

*Cost and practicality:* RPCs are inexpensive per area (~$200–400/m²), use standard gas mixtures, and have been deployed at scale in multiple neutrino experiments. The total wall area here is roughly 2×(2.6×0.9) + 2×(2.3×0.9) + (2.6×2.3) ≈ 15 m², very manageable.

---

## Upgrade 3: Downstream Magnetized Iron Muon Spectrometer Extension (additional iron planes + scintillator)

**Technology:** Addition of 4–6 magnetized iron toroids or dipole-magnet iron planes immediately downstream of the existing drift chambers, each iron plane ~20 cm thick with scintillator strip planes between them, extending the muon momentum measurement range and providing muon sign determination. This follows the design of the MINOS near detector or the ND280 SMRD.

**Physics motivation:**

*Sign and momentum of forward muons at higher momentum:* The existing dipole at 0.15 T over 6.5 m gives a magnetic rigidity $p_T = qBL \approx 0.15 \times 6.5 \approx 1$ GeV/c for a rough scale — adequate for tracks that traverse the full length. However, high-momentum forward muons from quasi-elastic and resonance events near 0.7 GeV peak flux can have momenta up to ~1–2 GeV/c, and the momentum resolution of the existing system may degrade if the drift chambers are not augmented. The additional iron spectrometer extends the range measurement for muons that punch through the existing chambers, disambiguates sign for high-rigidity tracks, and provides redundancy for momentum measurement.

*Muon charge identification:* At a neutrino beam, the dominant background to νμ CC is νμ-bar CC, distinguishable only by muon charge. Charge identification requires a magnetic field plus sufficient track length to measure curvature. The downstream extension ensures μ⁺/μ⁻ separation even for forward-going high-momentum tracks.

---

## Upgrade 4: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) Module or High-Pressure Argon Gas TPC as Companion Reference Target

**Technology:** A modular liquid argon TPC of dimensions ~0.5 m × 0.5 m × 0.9 m (fitting within the target region), using either a single-phase or dual-phase (charge+light) readout with wire or pixel anode planes at ~3–5 mm pitch. Alternatively, a high-pressure argon gas TPC (10–20 bar) in a pressure vessel, following the DUNE-PRISM or ALICE TPC heritage. The LArTPC provides millimetric 3D tracking with continuous charge deposition — no dead material, full calorimetry.

**Physics motivation:**

*Zero hydrogen content:* Liquid argon (⁴⁰Ar) contains no hydrogen whatsoever. The hydrogen fraction is 0%, trivially satisfying the ≤2% constraint. This makes it the cleanest possible companion target for the hydrogen subtraction strategy: by deploying a LArTPC alongside the SuperFGD, one can subtract the argon-nucleus interaction rate (measured in the LArTPC) from the total interaction rate (measured in the SuperFGD) on a statistical basis. What remains after subtraction is the hydrogen signal. The 2% constraint is then a question of mass budget (the SuperFGD has ~7.7% H by nucleon, so one needs sufficient argon mass to keep the net hydrogen fraction in the combined fiducial volume below 2% — achievable by making the argon module the larger mass fraction).

*Short proton tracks and vertex activity:* LArTPC at ~3 mm wire pitch resolves proton stubs from 60 MeV kinetic energy (~1.4 cm range in LAr at 1.4 g/cm³ density). The continuous ionization column allows dE/dx particle identification, cleanly separating protons from pions by Bragg peak shape. This is essential for exclusive final-state reconstruction (e.g. identifying QE vs. resonance vs. multinucleon interactions).

*Argon as a target nucleus:* The far detector at a long-baseline experiment is likely a LArTPC (DUNE). Measuring cross-sections on argon in the near detector at the same flux is directly relevant for the oscillation analysis — this is a physics bonus beyond the near-detector upgrade requirements stated.

---

## Upgrade 5: Scintillator Bar Time-of-Flight (ToF) System on Upstream and Lateral Faces

**Technology:** Planes of plastic scintillator bars (3 × 3 cm² cross-section), read out at both ends by SiPMs, achieving ~200–300 ps timing resolution per plane. Two planes separated by ~1 m give a time-of-flight baseline for particles traversing that gap. This follows NINJA and T2K's ToF systems.

**Physics motivation:**

*Proton/pion separation at low momentum:* Below ~600 MeV/c, protons and charged pions have very similar track lengths and curvatures in a magnetic field, making magnetic spectrometry alone ambiguous. Time of flight over a 1 m baseline with 300 ps resolution gives σ(1/β) ~ 0.03, which separates protons from pions up to ~700 MeV/c (3σ separation) using $\Delta t = L/c \cdot (1/\beta_p - 1/\beta_\pi)$.

*Direction disambiguation for backward tracks:* A ToF signal from the upstream face arriving before a signal from the active target volume establishes unambiguously that the particle is backward-going rather than a beam-direction particle entering the detector from outside. This is essential for the backward-track efficiency requirement.

*Beam-related background rejection:* Rock muons and beam halo particles entering the detector from the sides or upstream face mimic signal tracks. ToF timing relative to the beam spill RF structure (~1 ns bunch spacing in many accelerator beams) further suppresses out-of-time backgrounds.

---

## Upgrade 6: Upgrade of Drift Chamber Gas and Electronics for Improved dE/dx Resolution

**Technology:** Replace the existing drift chamber gas mixture with a Ar/CO₂ or Ar/CF₄ mixture optimized for both fast drift velocity (reducing space-charge at the near detector's high neutrino interaction rate) and improved specific ionization (dE/dx) measurement, coupled with new AFTER/AFTER2 or VMM3a ASIC front-end electronics achieving lower noise and higher dynamic range per pad.

**Physics motivation:**

*Track-by-track particle identification in the downstream spectrometer:* The downstream drift chambers currently measure momentum and charge. With improved dE/dx (σ(dE/dx)/⟨dE/dx⟩ ~ 7–8% achievable vs. ~12% with older electronics), proton/pion/muon separation by ionization is extended to higher momenta (~1 GeV/c for π/p separation). This reduces the reliance on the ToF system for downstream tracks and provides redundant particle identification.

*High-rate operation:* At 410 m from the target, the near detector sits in an intense neutrino flux. Multiple interactions per beam spill create pile-up in slow drift chambers. Faster gas and improved electronics reduce the effective drift time (e.g. from ~15 μs to ~2–4 μs with Ar/CF₄ 95/5), dramatically reducing occupancy and hit disambiguation ambiguity.

This is an interesting detector upgrade problem. Let me analyze the requirements systematically:

## Key Constraints and Requirements

1. **Active target volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (beam direction)
2. **Muon reconstruction**: ≥25% efficiency at all angles, including perpendicular and backward
3. **Proton detection**: Down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy at all angles
4. **Hydrogen limit**: ≤20% of target nucleons
5. **Existing infrastructure**: 0.15 T dipole, downstream drift chambers

## Critical Challenges

**Challenge 1: Backward-going muons**
The downstream drift chambers cannot detect backward tracks. This is a showstopper for the muon efficiency requirement.

**Challenge 2: Low-energy protons**
A 60 MeV proton has range ~6 cm in plastic scintillator and ~2 cm in iron. Short tracks require fine granularity and low material budget.

**Challenge 3: Hydrogen constraint**
Traditional plastic scintillator (CH₂) would have ~50% hydrogen by nucleon count, violating the requirement. Pure hydrocarbons are ruled out.

**Challenge 4: 3D tracking in all directions**
Need complete angular coverage including tracks perpendicular to the beam.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker with Stereoscopic Readout**

Use extruded plastic scintillator bars (1-2 cm × 1-2 cm cross-section) arranged in X-Y-U layers:
- Alternate X, Y, and U (±30°) orientations every 2-3 cm along beam direction
- SiPM readout on both ends of each bar for timing and position
- Total of ~40-50 planes over 0.9 m depth
- Provides 3D tracking with ~1 cm granularity

**Material choice**: Polystyrene-based scintillator (C₈H₈) has ~40% hydrogen by nucleon count - still too high. Mix with higher-Z materials or use aromatic-rich formulations to reduce hydrogen fraction.

### 2. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with Low-Hydrogen Gas Mix**

A more elegant solution:
- **Gas mixture**: Ar/CO₂ (90/10) or pure Argon with small quencher
  - Argon: A=40, Z=18, no hydrogen
  - CO₂: reduces hydrogen to <<20% 
- **Readout**: Micromegas or GEM planes on all six faces of the volume
  - Top/bottom: primarily Y-Z readout
  - Sides: X-Z readout  
  - Upstream/downstream: X-Y readout
- **Advantages**: 
  - True 3D tracking with mm-scale resolution
  - Low density allows protons down to 60 MeV to produce measurable tracks
  - Excellent dE/dx for particle ID
  - Complete angular coverage including backwards

### 3. **Hybrid Approach: TPC with Embedded High-Z Sheets**

To increase interaction rate while maintaining hydrogen constraint:
- Primary TPC as above
- Insert thin (~1 mm) graphite or CH₂-graphite composite sheets every 10-15 cm
- Increases target mass and can tune hydrogen fraction
- Sheets serve as interaction targets while TPC provides tracking

### 4. **Surrounding Veto/Tagging System**

- **Upstream tracker**: 5-10 planes of scintillator bars or silicon strips to catch backward-going muons before they exit
- **Side panels**: Scintillator panels on all four sides to tag exiting tracks
- **Downstream enhancement**: Additional tracking planes between target and existing drift chambers

### 5. **Electronics and DAQ**

- High-speed digitizers for SiPM/PMT signals
- Trigger based on beam timing + multiplicity
- Store full waveforms for offline analysis of complex events

## Detailed Recommendation for TPC Option

**Configuration**:
- **Gas**: Ar/CO₂ (90/10) at 1-2 atm → ~0.2-0.4% hydrogen by nucleon count
- **Drift field**: ~500 V/cm (modest, ~45 cm max drift)
- **Readout**: 
  - 2 mm × 2 mm pad pitch on end planes
  - Strip readout (1 cm pitch) on side walls
  - ~50,000 channels total
- **Expected performance**:
  - Track angular resolution: ~5°
  - dE/dx resolution: ~10%
  - Vertex resolution: ~5 mm

This satisfies all requirements:
- ✓ Backward muons detected in active volume
- ✓ 60 MeV protons have ~10 cm range in gas, clearly visible
- ✓ Full angular coverage
- ✓ Minimal hydrogen content

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace target region with an Argon-based TPC using Micromegas readout on all six faces for complete 3D tracking coverage including backward-going particles.

# Proposed upgrade for the vacated upstream region of the off-axis near detector

## Why the current design falls short

The existing tracker uses x/y bar layers perpendicular to the beam, with TPCs only downstream. This has three consequences:

- **Poor high-angle acceptance.** Tracks above about 50° run along a single bar layer or never reach a TPC. That loses roughly 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons, which is fatal for transverse kinematic imbalance analyses.
- **High proton threshold.** A proton must cross several 9.6 mm bars in both views to be reconstructed, so the threshold is around 450 MeV/c, right at the median of the leading-proton spectrum.
- **No useful neutron or timing information.** There is also no direction tag for tracks coming backward or from outside the detector.

The upgrade should therefore be an isotropic, finely segmented target with tracking above and below it, and fast timing around it.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D scintillator-cube target (main element)

**Geometry**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes.
- Each cube is coated with a reflective layer (chemical etching or TiO₂).
- Arranged as 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, giving about 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m. This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Mass about 2 t of CH, roughly doubling the target mass.

**Readout**
- Each cube has three orthogonal through-holes carrying 1 mm Y-11 wavelength-shifting fibres. These give three 2D projections (xy, xz, yz) and genuine 3D reconstruction.
- About 56,000 channels.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a small-pixel SiPM, using the same SiPM family as the rest of the detector.
- Front-end: CITIROC-type ASICs, giving charge and about 1 ns hit timing.

**Performance gains**
- *Near-4π acceptance.* No orientation is special, so high-angle and backward muons and protons are tracked.
- *Low proton threshold.* A proton crossing 2–3 cubes is reconstructable, giving a threshold of about 300 MeV/c. This covers almost the full proton spectrum, whose median is 450 MeV/c.
- *Proton momentum by range.* Contained protons are measured to a few percent using range and dE/dx.
- *Neutron detection.* Isolated delayed hits combined with timing allow neutron kinetic energy to be measured event by event by time of flight. This enables full transverse kinematic imbalance analysis in antineutrino mode.
- *Electron/photon separation.* Fine granularity separates electrons from photons, which partly compensates for removing the photon-tagging section.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the cube target

**Construction**
- Thin field cages made of composite or laminated walls to minimise material.
- Same argon-based gas as the existing TPCs, operating in the 0.2 T field.

**Readout**
- Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode).
- The resistive layer spreads charge across pads, so pads of about 1 cm can still give spatial resolution well below 1 mm. This keeps the channel count low.
- Front-end chips: AFTER/AGET-type.

**Purpose**
- Momentum and charge measurement by curvature for muons above 50° that exit the cube target vertically.
- dE/dx particle identification.
- Measurement of uncontained protons above about 900 MeV/c, around 6% of the leading protons, which range out poorly in the cubes.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new module

**Construction**
- Six planes of about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm plastic scintillator bars.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target timing resolution about 150 ps.

**Purpose**
- Determines track direction, separating forward from backward-going tracks and identifying tracks entering from outside or from cosmic rays.
- Improves particle identification at low momentum by combining time of flight with TPC dE/dx.
- Provides a sharp veto of out-of-fiducial-volume backgrounds.

## 4. Supporting changes

- **Calorimetry upstream.** Retain or rebuild the upstream lead-scintillator calorimeter modules around the new module so containment and photon tagging are partly preserved.
- **DAQ and timing.** Upgrade the DAQ and clock distribution so that cube, TPC and ToF data are time-synchronised at the sub-nanosecond level, which the neutron time-of-flight measurement requires.
- **Physics comparison.** Keep the downstream water/scintillator target for carbon-to-water ratios. With a hydrocarbon cube target plus the existing water target, the event sample constrains nuclear effects needed to push systematics from about 6% toward 4%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a ~2-tonne, 1 cm³ 3D-segmented scintillator-cube target (three orthogonal WLS fibres per cube, SiPM readout), flanked by resistive-Micromegas high-angle TPCs, to give 4π muon and low-threshold proton reconstruction.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Understanding the Constraints

Before proposing hardware, let me decode the physics requirements:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward-going → need a fully 3D tracking volume, not just forward-going coverage
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** → range ~3 cm in plastic, so need fine-grained sampling with ~few-mm pitch
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons** → constrains material choice severely (pure hydrocarbon scintillator like CH₂ has ~14% H by nucleon count; polystyrene C₈H₈ gives ~8.3%; water gives 67% → water is excluded as primary target material)
- **Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** → ~5.4 m³, relatively compact
- **410 m baseline, ~0.7 GeV peak** → GeV-scale hadronic final states, need good π/p separation

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. Active Target Core: 3D Scintillator Cube Array (Primary Recommendation)

Replace the passive target with a **fully active plastic scintillator detector based on 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm polystyrene (C₈H₈) cubes**, assembled in a close-packed 3D array filling the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume.

**Specifics:**
- Polystyrene cubes doped with PPO+POPOP fluors, as demonstrated by the **SuperFGD prototype** (this is essentially the SuperFGD technology, now deployed in T2K ND280)
- Each cube read out on three orthogonal faces by **1 mm² wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** (Y-11 or similar) threading through drilled holes along all three axes
- Fibers coupled to **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)**, one SiPM per fiber end (or one per fiber with reflective far end)
- With 1.5 cm cubes across a 90 cm depth: ~60 cubes along beam, ~173 × 153 cubes transversely → roughly 1.6 million cubes total
- **Why polystyrene:** hydrogen nucleon fraction = 8.3%, safely under the 20% cap; density ~1.05 g/cm³
- **Proton threshold:** 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has range ~27 mm in polystyrene → traverses ~2 cubes; with per-cube energy deposition readout this is reconstructable, though at the edge of capability (see also item 4 below)
- **Omnidirectional efficiency:** the 3D cubic topology means there is no preferred axis — backward-going and 90° muons traverse the same number of cubes per unit length as forward-going tracks, meeting the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles
- **Hydrogen subtraction model:** the 8.3% H fraction is well under the 20% limit, giving headroom

---

### 2. Upstream Tracking Planes: High-Pressure Gas TPC Bookends

Install two **small high-pressure gaseous Time Projection Chambers (TPCs)** immediately upstream and downstream of the scintillator cube volume, each approximately 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 20 cm (along beam).

**Specifics:**
- Fill gas: **Ar:CF₄:isobutane** (95:3:2) at 1–2 bar, or pure **argon + 10% CO₂** — CF₄ provides fast drift and good dE/dx resolution
- Cathode/anode gap ~18 cm, drift field ~200 V/cm
- Readout: **bulk Micromegas or GEM foils** with 2D strip readout at ~3 mm pitch in both transverse directions
- Purpose: provide an independent high-resolution momentum measurement via curvature for tracks that exit the cube volume, and serve as a veto/tagger for interactions that originate outside the fiducial volume
- Also tag and measure **charged pions** exiting the cube target before they enter the downstream drift chambers
- These are well-matched to the existing downstream gas drift chamber infrastructure

---

### 3. Time-of-Flight System: Surrounding Scintillator Panels

Instrument all six faces of the cube volume with **2 cm thick plastic scintillator panels** read out by SiPMs, targeting **~200 ps timing resolution per panel**.

**Specifics:**
- Use **EJ-200 or BC-408 fast plastic scintillator** in 5 cm × 2 cm × full-face tiles
- SiPM readout (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or equivalent) on both ends of each tile for timing and position
- System purpose:
  - **ToF-based particle ID:** at ~0.7 GeV beam energy, pion/proton separation via time-of-flight over even short baselines (~50 cm across the cube volume) — a 500 MeV/c proton vs. pion differ by ~1.5 ns over 50 cm, resolvable at 200 ps
  - **Veto** for charged particles entering from outside (beam-unrelated muons, interaction products from the magnet yoke)
  - **Neutron detection** (ToF from the interaction vertex to the panel gives neutron kinetic energy) — useful for neutrino energy reconstruction
  - Backward-going track identification: a track hitting the upstream face panel after the interaction trigger tags it unambiguously as backward-going

---

### 4. Low-Energy Proton Enhancement: Thin Emulsion Cloud Chamber (ECC) Insertable Modules

For the specific challenge of **protons with kinetic energy near 60 MeV** (range ~27 mm), which are at the edge of the cube detector's capability, provide **interleaved nuclear emulsion + lead/iron passive layers** as a subset of insertable modules.

**Specifics:**
- Build **10–15 removable ECC bricks**, each approximately 25 cm × 25 cm × 9 cm, using the **NINJA / NINJA-2 or NINJA-style** technology (emulsion cloud chamber as used in T2K NINJA)
- Each brick: alternating layers of nuclear emulsion films (100 µm emulsion on each side of 200 µm plastic base) and thin (~1 mm) polystyrene spacers, no heavy absorber (to maintain H fraction and to not stop the short proton tracks before they can be measured)
- Sub-micron position resolution in emulsion → reconstruct proton tracks of even 1–2 cm length
- Bricks are periodically extracted (every few weeks of running), developed, and scanned with **automated scanning systems (HTS or similar)**
- These are deployed in a fraction of the target volume (~10–20%) to provide a calibration/cross-check sample for the cube detector's short-track efficiency; they do not replace the cube volume

---

### 5. Magnet Instrumentation: Additional Drift Chamber Layer at Large Angles

The existing downstream drift chambers are optimized for forward-going tracks. Add **two additional drift chamber planes oriented to measure tracks at large angles (60°–90° to beam)**.

**Specifics:**
- **Straw-tube tracker panels** (e.g., 6 mm diameter aluminized mylar straws with 25 µm gold-plated tungsten sense wire, Ar:CO₂ 70:30 fill gas) mounted on the two lateral walls (beam-left and beam-right) of the magnet inner volume
- Each lateral wall: two staggered layers of straws running vertically and two running along the beam axis → 4-layer panel per side → 8 layers total
- Straw length ~2.3 m (vertical), ~0.9 m (along beam), pitch ~8 mm
- These catch 90°-going muons that never reach the downstream drift chambers, feeding them into the momentum measurement via curvature in the 0.15 T field
- Also capture **backward-going tracks** that curve into the lateral walls
- SiPM or standard ASDQ chip readout on both ends of each straw for z-position via charge division

---

### 6. Electronics and DAQ Upgrade: Free-Running Waveform Digitization

The multi-technology readout requires a unified DAQ architecture.

**Specifics:**
- Replace any triggered front-end electronics with **continuous (free-running) waveform digitizers** running at 125 MHz sampling, e.g., based on the **WaveUnion** or **CAEN V1742** (DRS4-based) approach, or custom ASICs (e.g., TOFPET2 ASIC from PETsys for the SiPM channels)
- **Full waveform recording** for all SiPM channels in the cube detector and ToF panels → enables offline pulse-shape discrimination between proton and pion tracks (dE/dx from Bragg peak shape), and precise timing
- Trigger-less readout with software trigger reconstructing interaction vertices in real time using GPU-based online reconstruction
- **Timing synchronization** across all subsystems via White Rabbit protocol (sub-ns synchronization) to make the ToF system coherent

---

| Upgrade | Technology | Key Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| Cube active target | 1.5 cm³ polystyrene cubes + WLS fibers + SiPMs | All-angle tracking, proton threshold, H fraction |
