- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, read out by SiPMs (MPPCs).
- Channel count is about 260·230 + 260·90 + 230·90 ≈ 1.0 × 10⁵. This is manageable with existing front-end ASICs.

**Why it meets the physics needs**
- **Uniform angular acceptance.** The 3D granularity gives roughly isotropic response, so muons perpendicular to the beam are tracked as well as forward ones. This targets the 25%-at-every-angle requirement.
- **Short-proton reach.** A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes, which is enough to tag it and measure its energy by range and dE/dx. This brings the proton threshold down to roughly 300 MeV/c, which covers the stated ~60 MeV (about 340 MeV/c) requirement at all angles.
- **Fully active calorimetry.** Every cube is sensitive, which improves vertex-activity and energy-transfer measurements.
- **Hydrogen fraction.**
  - Polystyrene (CH) has hydrogen nuclei making up 1/13 ≈ 7.7% of the target nucleons.
  - This is well below the 20% limit, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid.
  - Water-based or liquid-scintillator options would sit at about 11% or higher and are still acceptable, but CH gives the most margin.
  - Cubes can also be paired with graphite layers if a pure-carbon subtraction sample is wanted.
- **Neutron tagging.** Nanosecond cube timing allows neutron detection by time of flight within the target volume.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target (inside the magnet)

**What it is**
- Thin field cage and resistive-Micromegas readout.
- Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ (T2K-type) gas.

**Why**
- These measure momentum and charge sign of muons leaving at large angles, which the downstream chambers miss.
- Resistive Micromegas spread the charge, so the pad count stays moderate while position resolution improves. This matters because the 0.15 T field is weak and needs every bit of resolution.
- They also provide dE/dx for μ/π/p/e identification.
- For muons that stop inside the target, the range in the cubes gives a second, independent momentum estimate. This keeps efficiency up where the TPC lever arm is short.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

**What it is**
- Scintillator bars surrounding the target and TPCs, read out at both ends by SiPMs.
- Target timing resolution is about 150 ps.

**Why**
- **Track direction.** Timing tells a backward-going muon from a forward-going particle entering from outside. Backward tracks are otherwise ambiguous, especially in a weak field.
- **Background rejection.** It vetoes out-of-fiducial and "sand" muons coming from the surroundings.
- **Particle ID.** Combined with path length, it adds e/μ/p separation at low momentum.

## 4. Supporting items

- Upgraded SiPM and digitiser electronics with fine timing (sub-ns per cube channel), needed for neutron TOF and track direction.
- An LED calibration and cosmic-trigger system to monitor the response of the cube array.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a ~1 cm³ 3D-readout plastic-scintillator-cube (SuperFGD-type) active target with WLS-fibre/SiPM readout, giving isotropic muon acceptance, ~60 MeV proton thresholds, and a hydrogen fraction of only ~7.7%.

# Proposed Upgrade: Replacing the Photon-Tagging Section with a 4π Active Target

## 1. Why the current detector falls short

The existing configuration of bar-based targets with TPCs downstream was optimised for forward muons. Three effects limit it.

**High-angle acceptance.** All bars are perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only downstream. Tracks above about 50–60° are poorly reconstructed. Near 90° they barely cross the x/y layers, and they never reach a TPC. That loses about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons, exactly the high-angle phase space where the flux × cross-section model is least constrained relative to the 4π far detector.

**Proton threshold and resolution.** A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and travels roughly 8 cm in plastic. A 300 MeV/c proton has about 47 MeV and travels only about 2 cm.
- With 2D x/y bar projections, short, steep or overlapping tracks near the vertex are ambiguous, so the vertex region is badly resolved.
- Transverse kinematic imbalance needs the proton's 3D direction and momentum (range or curvature) for most of the spectrum down to about 300 MeV/c.

**Neutrons and backgrounds.** The current target cannot measure neutron kinematics, which matter for antineutrino transverse imbalance. The upstream photon-tagging section adds mass but contributes little to the charged-current programme.

## 2. Proposed hardware (replacing the photon-tagging section)

### A. Highly granular 3D-segmented scintillator target, filling the ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box
- **Cubes:** about 192 × 182 × 56 polystyrene cubes of 1 cm³, roughly 2.0 M cubes and about 2 t of CH. This is roughly double either existing plastic target.
- **Cube construction:** each cube has a reflective chemical-etch coating to isolate light between neighbours.
- **Readout:** three orthogonal holes per cube carry 1 mm WLS fibres along x, y and z, read by SiPMs on the faces. That is 192·182 + 192·56 + 182·56 ≈ 56k channels, versus about 2M for full voxel readout.
- **Isotropic acceptance:** three 2D projections per hit give a true 3D image with the same response at any angle, including 90°.
- **Proton threshold:** about 300 MeV/c, since a track crossing at least two cubes is resolved. This covers essentially the whole leading-proton distribution, with its median of 450 MeV/c.
- **Momentum by range:** protons stopping in the target get range momentum resolution of a few percent. A 900 MeV/c proton travels on the order of 1 m in plastic, so the roughly 6% of protons above that mostly exit and are measured in the TPCs described below.
- **Timing:** about 1 ns per fibre, giving about 0.6 ns per cube with two-fibre averaging. This allows neutron time-of-flight from isolated delayed hits, so the antineutrino imbalance analysis can include neutron kinematics. It also separates Michel electrons for pion tagging.
- **Front-end electronics:** these should go in the yoke or rim region at low field. Use radiation- and field-tolerant SiPM front-ends, for example CITIROC-based boards, matching the existing SiPM infrastructure.

### B. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target
- **Placement:** each is about 2.0 × 1.8 × 0.8 m, in the same magnet volume, flanking the new target vertically. With the 0.2 T field along x, high-angle tracks exiting up or down curve in the TPCs.
- **Field cage:** a thin, light composite structure with a few percent of a radiation length, so muons and protons cross it with little scattering. This maximises the active gas.
- **Readout:** resistive (encapsulated-resistor) bulk Micromegas, from the same argon-based gas family as the existing TPCs. Charge spreading allows fewer, larger pads with better spatial resolution of a few hundred µm. That delivers about 10% momentum resolution near 1 GeV/c and about 10% dE/dx for μ/p/π/e identification.
- **Role:** together with the existing downstream TPCs, this gives near-4π charge and momentum measurement for muons and for the highest-momentum protons.

### C. Time-of-flight envelope
- **Coverage:** six planes of fast plastic-scintillator bars surrounding the new target and high-angle TPC assembly, read by SiPMs at both ends.
- **Timing:** about 150 ps.
- **Uses:**
  - track direction (into vs. out of the volume), which rejects out-of-fiducial and backward-going entering backgrounds from the magnet and surrounding material;
  - extra particle identification at low momentum;
  - a timing reference for neutron time-of-flight.

## 3. Supporting changes
- **Fibres and SiPMs:** use low-crosstalk, higher-PDE SiPMs. Run the new readout and existing electronics on a common trigger and clock with the beam spill.
- **Mechanics:** a carbon-fibre or composite box for the cube array, with fibre routing through all six faces. Services must stay within the yoke gaps.
- **Calibration:** cosmic-ray and LED systems, plus test-beam characterisation of the cubes (light yield, crosstalk, neutron response) to control detector systematics.
- **Downstream:** keep the existing plastic and water-layer targets and TPCs unchanged. This preserves the carbon-to-water comparison, which the new hydrocarbon sample then constrains more precisely.

## 4. Expected impact
- **Statistics:** about 2× more target mass in a high-acceptance configuration.
- **Acceptance:** near-uniform angular coverage recovers the 25% of high-angle muons and 35% of high-angle protons.
- **Kinematics:** a proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c plus neutron detection gives fully reconstructed final states for transverse kinematic imbalance and better neutrino-energy estimation.
- **Systematics:** together, these should reduce the flux × cross-section systematic from about 6% toward the 4% goal, by giving a phase space and nuclear-effect constraint that better matches the far detector.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a ~2 t, 1 cm³ 3D-segmented scintillator-cube target with three-view WLS-fibre/SiPM readout, flanked by high-angle TPCs.

Based on the physics requirements and spatial constraints, I propose the following hardware upgrades:

## Primary Upgrade: New Upstream Active Target

**3D fine-grained scintillator tracker** (~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m³):
- **Super-FGD technology** (Fine-Grained Detector): ~2 million small plastic scintillator cubes (1 cm³), each with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts
- This provides true 3D tracking with ~1 cm granularity, optimal for:
  - Detecting recoil protons down to ~300 MeV/c (Bragg peak identification)
  - Tracking particles at large angles (>50°) in all directions
  - Vertex resolution <1 cm for kinematic reconstruction
- Total mass: ~1.9 tonnes of polystyrene (suitable hydrocarbon target)
- ~12,000 MPPC channels (feasible with existing readout infrastructure)
- Fiber routing exits perpendicular to beam to maximize active volume

**Alternative option**: Segmented plastic scintillator target with finer granularity than current targets (5 mm cubes instead of 9.6 mm bars), but 3D fiber readout is superior for wide-angle tracking.

## Supporting Upgrades

**Enhanced TPC readout electronics:**
- Upgrade to higher-sampling-rate ASICs (e.g., 80 MHz instead of 40 MHz) for the gas TPCs
- Improves dE/dx resolution for proton/pion separation near threshold
- Better handles high-angle tracks with shorter drift distances

**Timing upgrades:**
- Install precise timing reference system (<1 ns) across all sub-detectors
- Enables better matching between target, TPCs, and downstream tracking
- Critical for multi-prong events with wide-angle particles

**Extended electromagnetic calorimeter coverage:**
- Add side ECAL modules in previously unoccupied magnet volume
- Captures photons from π⁰ decay at large angles
- Improves neutral current rejection and reduces systematic uncertainties

## Systematic Uncertainty Improvements

The fine 3D granularity directly addresses the 6%→4% challenge by:
- Reducing proton tracking efficiency uncertainty (key for transverse imbalance)
- Improving vertex activity measurements (reduces FSI modeling uncertainties)
- Better charged pion/proton separation (reduces cross-section model dependence)
- Enabling full solid-angle acceptance studies

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D Super-FGD scintillator cube detector with three-view fiber readout in the upstream volume as the new active neutrino target.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Near Detector Active Target

## Context and Constraints Summary

The available volume is approximately **2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m** (longitudinal depth only 0.6 m), replacing the photon-tagger upstream. Requirements are:

- Kinematically complete CC events: reconstruct **both** the outgoing muon and leading recoil proton
- Handle ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons at >50° to beam (wide angular acceptance essential)
- Median leading-proton momentum ~450 MeV/c; ~6% exceed 900 MeV/c (must range out or track low-momentum protons)
- Reduce flux/cross-section systematic uncertainty from ~6% to ~4%
- Hydrocarbon target is acceptable; carbon-to-water comparison handled downstream

---

## Upgrade 1: High-Granularity Scintillator Active Target (Primary Recommendation)

### Design
Deploy a **fully active plastic scintillator tracker** filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume, built from **small-cell extruded polystyrene bars with X-Y-Z stereo geometry**, read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)**.

- Bar cross-section: **~1.0 × 1.0 cm** (or possibly 1.5 × 1.5 cm as a cost/channel-count compromise), consistent with technology already used in the downstream tracking target but at finer granularity
- Layer pitch ~1–1.5 cm; alternating X and Y layers, with optional ±45° stereo layers for 3D vertex reconstruction
- Approximately 60–80 layers in the 0.6 m depth; total channel count ~20,000–40,000 depending on bar size
- Total fiducial mass: approximately **0.5–0.7 t** of polystyrene (C₈H₈), dominated by carbon and hydrogen

### Motivation
- **Low tracking threshold for protons**: a 1 cm bar gives ~2 MeV energy deposit per cm; protons at the median momentum of 450 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~100 MeV) range ~12–15 cm in polystyrene, giving ~12–15 hit layers — reconstructible with good efficiency. Even protons at 200 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~20 MeV, range ~2–3 cm) produce a short but detectable track stub.
- **Wide angular acceptance**: with no dead material framing and a fully active volume, tracks at >50° to beam are captured within the instrumented volume if they are produced near the upstream face. A 50° proton at 450 MeV/c travels ~12 cm total path, projecting ~8 cm transversely — well within the 1.9 m transverse extent.
- **Muon identification**: soft muons (say, <400 MeV/c) will also range out in the target itself or in the downstream TPCs/calorimeters; the existing magnet + downstream systems handle higher-momentum muons. The active target provides the upstream anchor point and angle measurement.
- **Vertex resolution**: ~1 cm³ vertex resolution is adequate for isolating CC quasi-elastic and CC1p topologies; finer bars push this below 0.5 cm³.
- **Continuity with existing technology**: the downstream plastic tracking targets already use extruded polystyrene + WLS fibre + SiPM. The same tooling, electronics (e.g., CITIROC or similar front-end ASICs), and DAQ firmware apply, reducing engineering risk and cost.
- **Systematic reduction path**: the high-granularity fully active target enables:
  - Direct measurement of the **transverse momentum imbalance** (δp_T) and **transverse missing momentum** distributions, which are key observables for constraining nuclear FSI models
  - The **muon–proton opening angle** and **momentum transfer** reconstruction on an event-by-event basis
  - In-situ measurement of the **proton tracking efficiency** as a function of momentum by comparing short tracks to energy deposition, constraining the dominant systematic

### Engineering Considerations
- SiPM dark count rate: manageable with ~1 MHz per channel at room temperature; timing coincidence within a ~100 ns gate suppresses noise hits
- Total channel count at 1 cm bars: ~(200 × 190 / 1 / 1) × 2 orientations × ~40 layers ≈ order 30,000 channels; at 1.5 cm bars ~15,000 channels. Both are within precedent for near detectors of this class.
- Weight: ~0.5–0.7 t, well within the structural capacity of the upstream slot

---

## Upgrade 2: Interleaved Water-Layer Option Within the Active Target

### Design
Within the same active scintillator volume, interleave **thin water bag layers** (1–2 cm thick, contained in thin Mylar/polyethylene envelopes) every 5–8 scintillator layers.

- Approximately 6–8 water layers of 1.5 cm each in the 0.6 m depth
- Each water layer sandwiched between active scintillator layers acting as both tracker and calorimeter
- Water mass contribution: ~30–40 kg, giving a **water-to-hydrocarbon mass ratio of ~5–8%**

### Motivation
- Provides a **direct on-axis water signal** in the same fiducial volume and magnetic field environment, complementing the downstream water-layer target but upstream of FSI from additional material
- Allows **carbon-subtracted water cross-section** measurements in the same vertex-reconstruction quality regime
- The existing downstream target's water-layer architecture already demonstrates this technique; migrating it upstream with finer tracking granularity improves the vertex separation of water vs. carbon interactions
- Improves systematic cancellation for the water far detector comparison by **~1–2 percentage points** in the flux uncertainty budget, contributing to the goal of reaching 4%

### Caveat
Water layers introduce dead material and complicate proton ranging for tracks that cross a water bag boundary. The water bag thickness should be kept ≤2 cm and the Mylar skin ≤100 μm to limit secondary interactions.

---

## Upgrade 3: Upgraded SiPM Readout with Waveform Digitization

### Design
Replace the current charge-integration front-end for the new target (and optionally retrofit the existing downstream plastic target) with **waveform-sampling ASICs** (e.g., SPIROC2E or TARGET family) operating at ~100–200 MHz sampling.

### Motivation
- **Particle identification via dE/dx timing profile**: a waveform gives the Bragg peak shape for stopping protons, distinguishing protons from pions at the same momentum range (100–500 MeV/c) where range alone is ambiguous
- The **proton–pion separation** at ~300–500 MeV/c is critical for the CC1p topology selection; waveform dE/dx improves this separation from ~1.5σ (charge integration) to ~2.5–3σ
- **Neutron tagging**: delayed neutron capture signals (on hydrogen, ~200 μs) are resolvable with waveform timing, providing a handle on the neutron component of the hadronic recoil — useful for binding-energy and FSI studies
- Timing resolution of ~1 ns per channel allows **time-of-flight** between the vertex and secondary interactions within the volume, further aiding particle ID for protons below ~600 MeV/c

### Cost/Benefit
Waveform digitization increases per-channel cost by ~30–50% but the channel count is modest (~15,000–30,000). The physics gain in proton PID efficiency is substantial enough to justify inclusion in the baseline design rather than as a later upgrade.

---

## Upgrade 4: Thin High-Z Converter Planes for Photon Veto / π⁰ Rejection

### Design
Insert **2–3 planes of 2 mm lead** (each ~0.35 radiation lengths) at the upstream face and at ~20 cm depth within the active target, backed immediately by scintillator layers serving as a **photon conversion tagger**.

### Motivation
- The photon-tagger section being removed served to identify photons from π⁰ decay; some of that functionality should be preserved in the new target
- π⁰ contamination in CC1p event selection (from CCπ⁰ events where the proton mimics a leading proton) is a ~3–5% background at this beam energy
- Thin lead converter planes convert forward γ → e⁺e⁻ pairs detectable in the adjacent scintillator layers, providing a **photon veto with ~60–70% efficiency per γ** without severely degrading proton tracking for tracks that do not cross the lead
- Lead planes are placed at the upstream end so that most of the active volume downstream remains free of high-Z material, preserving proton ranging capability

### Trade-off
Lead planes increase nuclear interaction backgrounds for protons crossing them. Keep total lead thickness <5 mm (≲0.9 nuclear interaction lengths × 0.05 = ~4.5% interaction probability per plane) and limit to 2 planes.

---

## Upgrade 5: Return-Yoke Scintillator Panel Upgrade for Wide-Angle Muon Ranging

### Design
Add **one additional layer of scintillator panels** to the upstream face of the magnet return yoke (the face facing the new active target) and ensure full azimuthal coverage around the new target's transverse faces.

- 2 cm thick scintillator panels, same WLS+SiPM technology as existing yoke instrumentation
- Coverage of the ±90° azimuthal range around the upstream slot
- Adds ~40–60 panels depending on granularity

### Motivation
- With ~25% of muons at >50°, a significant fraction will exit the active target laterally before reaching the downstream TPCs/calorimeters
- The existing return-yoke instrumentation is optimized for the downstream inner detector; extending it upstream ensures that **wide-angle muons from the new target are ranged out and their momentum measured**
- Muon momentum measurement via range (rather than curvature) is adequate for muons below ~600 MeV/c, which comprises the bulk of the signal at 0.6 GeV peak beam energy
- This directly improves the muon momentum resolution entering the δp_T calculation, which currently dominates the transverse imbalance systematic at ~2–3%

---

## Upgrade 6: Online Track Trigger and GPU-Based Reconstruction

### Design
Implement a **hardware track-finding trigger** using FPGAs (e.g., Xilinx UltraScale+) processing the new target's hit patterns, with an **offline GPU reconstruction farm** running real-time Kalman-filter tracking.

- FPGA trigger: identifies ≥2 track stubs within a 100 ns window, suppressing beam-related backgrounds (rock muons, beam halo)
- GPU farm: ~4–8 NVIDIA A-series GPUs running parallelized track reconstruction, outputting CC candidate events with reconstructed vertices within ~100 ms
- Enables **online data quality monitoring** of proton reconstruction efficiency, vertex resolution, and δp_T balance — critical for rapid systematic calibration during beam running

### Motivation
- The increase in channel count (~15,000–30,000 new channels) combined with waveform digitization increases raw data rate by ~factor 3–5 relative to current detector
- Real-time reconstruction allows **prompt flux constraint updates** to the far detector analysis, compressing the latency between beam running and physics results
- Online monitoring of the **proton reconstruction efficiency** as a function of beam intensity and detector conditions is essential for the 4% systematic target

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Addresses Systematic | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. High-granularity scintillator active target | Low-threshold proton tracking, wide angular acceptance | Proton efficiency, FSI modeling | Low (proven technology) |
| 2. Interleaved water layers | Direct water cross-section in new target | Carbon–water comparison | Low–Medium |
| 3. Waveform-sampling SiPM readout | Proton/pion PID via dE/dx, neutron tagging | Particle misID, hadronic recoil | Low–Medium |
| 4. Thin Pb converter planes | π⁰/photon veto, preserve photon-tagger function | CCπ⁰ background | Medium |
| 5. Upstream yoke scintillator extension | Wide-angle muon ranging | Muon momentum resolution | Low |
| 6. FPGA trigger + GPU reconstruction | Data rate management, online monitoring | Efficiency stability | Medium |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the removed photon-tagger with a fully active high-granularity plastic scintillator target of ~1.0–1.5 cm bar cross-section in alternating X/Y layers, read out by WLS fibre and SiPM, filling the full 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume, to enable low-threshold reconstruction of the leading recoil proton at wide angles and provide kinematically complete CC events for transverse kinematic imbalance analysis.

# Design Review Recommendations: New Active Target for the Upstream Volume

## Context and Constraints Summary

The available volume is 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m (depth along beam). The physics goal is kinematically complete CC events requiring:
- Muon reconstruction (25% exit at >50°, so large angular acceptance is critical)
- Leading proton reconstruction (35% exit at >50°, median ~450 MeV/c, need to range/track low-momentum protons)
- Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies demand good momentum resolution on both tracks
- Target material: hydrocarbon acceptable; systematic goal ~4%

The 0.6 m depth is the dominant geometric constraint. At 450 MeV/c, a proton has a range of ~18 cm in polystyrene, so ranging is feasible within the volume if the target itself is sufficiently granular and dense. At 900 MeV/c the range is ~65 cm in polystyrene—marginal but the downstream TPCs can recover those tracks.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Primary Target: High-Granularity Scintillator Cube Detector (SuperFGD-style)

**Specification:** Fill the available volume with ~1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre readout channels (X, Y, Z), read out by SiPMs. This is directly based on the demonstrated SuperFGD technology now operating in similar near-detector contexts.

**Justification:**
- The 1 cm³ granularity gives a track-finding threshold of roughly 3–4 cm for protons, corresponding to kinetic energies down to ~40 MeV (momenta ~300 MeV/c), well below the median proton momentum of 450 MeV/c. This directly addresses the core physics requirement.
- Three-view 3D reconstruction via coincident fibre readout in X, Y, Z resolves the combinatorial ambiguity that plagues 2-view detectors at high multiplicity, essential for the multi-track final states relevant to TKI.
- Protons up to ~600 MeV/c are ranged within the 0.6 m depth; momentum from range has a resolution of ~1–2%, which dominates over MS uncertainties at these momenta. This is superior to what a TPC alone provides for short, stopping tracks.
- For protons 600–900 MeV/c that punch through, the downstream TPCs provide momentum measurement by curvature in the dipole field — a natural handoff that exploits the existing infrastructure.
- Large-angle muon acceptance (>50°) is served by the isotropic granularity; a muon at 60° traverses ~40 cm of active material before exiting laterally, giving adequate track length for direction and dE/dx measurement before it enters the return-yoke scintillator or the ECal for ranging.
- The polystyrene target composition (CH) is well understood and consistent with the existing downstream plastic tracking target, preserving the carbon baseline for cross-section ratio measurements.
- SiPM readout is already the collaboration's standard technology (all existing scintillator channels use SiPM), minimising new infrastructure for HV, DAQ firmware, and calibration procedures.
- Mass budget: at polystyrene density 1.05 g/cm³, 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m ≈ 2.4 m³ → ~2.5 t, comfortably within the structural envelope of the magnet.

**Key risk and mitigation:** Channel count is large (~1.8 million fibres for 1 cm³ cubes across 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m). Mitigation is to use SiPM multiplexing per fibre column (as in SuperFGD) and to accept modest Z-position ambiguity along each fibre, resolved by X and Y views. If cost or schedule pressure is severe, 1.5 cm cubes reduce channel count by ~3.4× while still ranging protons above ~350 MeV/c.

---

### 2. Upstream Face: Thin Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Specification:** Two planes of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., EJ-228 or similar, ~5 mm thick), one immediately upstream and one immediately downstream of the cube target, read out with SiPMs and fast electronics achieving ~200 ps timing resolution per plane → ~300 ps coincidence resolution.

**Justification:**
- At 450 MeV/c, a proton (β ≈ 0.43) and a pion (β ≈ 0.95) traversing a 60 cm baseline produce a time difference of ~1.7 ns — cleanly resolved at 300 ps. This provides proton/pion separation that dE/dx alone becomes ambiguous for in the 400–700 MeV/c range where Bragg-peak identification inside the cube target is less clean.
- Beam-interaction timing tags the neutrino interaction time to ~200 ps, which also supports background rejection from out-of-time interactions and sand muons.
- Minimal mass (~5 kg per plane), no impact on target composition systematics.
- SiPM + fast ADC readout is already in-house; this is a low-cost, low-risk addition.

---

### 3. Lateral Active Veto / Side-ECal Extension into the New Volume

**Specification:** Instrument the four lateral faces of the new target volume (top, bottom, left, right) with an additional layer of lead-scintillator ECal modules, extending the existing ECal geometry that already surrounds the inner detectors downstream. Each panel: ~4 radiation lengths of Pb-scintillator sandwich, SiPM readout.

**Justification:**
- 25% of muons and 35% of protons exit at >50°. Those exiting sideways from the cube target must be measured. The existing return-yoke scintillator provides ranging for high-angle muons, but it is far from the interaction vertex, leaving a gap in solid-angle coverage. A lateral ECal layer immediately surrounding the cube target:
  - Provides a first energy/momentum measurement for photons from π⁰ → γγ, reducing the neutral-pion background that contaminates the CC-0π sample used for TKI.
  - Tags and measures side-exiting low-energy protons that stop in the ECal (complementing the cube-target ranging for protons that escape the cube laterally).
  - Maintains hermeticity consistent with the downstream ECal, avoiding a blind spot in solid angle that would bias the TKI missing-momentum vector.
- This is an extension of existing ECal technology, no new expertise required.
- The 2.0 × 1.9 m face dimensions are compatible with extending existing ECal panel sizes.

---

### 4. DAQ and Trigger: Self-Triggering Readout with Waveform Digitisation

**Specification:** Upgrade the readout of the new target to continuous waveform sampling at ~200 MHz (e.g., CITIROC or comparable SiPM-optimised ASIC front-end), replacing any spill-gated integration scheme for the new volume.

**Justification:**
- The cube target's high channel count with low per-channel occupancy makes self-triggering architectures more efficient than global triggers.
- Waveform digitisation enables offline pulse-shape discrimination to separate proton dE/dx signatures from pion dE/dx in the cube, supplementing ToF and range-based PID. This is especially valuable for the 300–450 MeV/c proton region where the Bragg peak may be only partially contained.
- Continuous readout eliminates the dead-time inefficiency from the existing spill-based trigger during the high-intensity spill structure, improving absolute flux normalisation — directly relevant to the 4% systematic goal.
- The existing downstream TPC readout already operates in a continuous mode; aligning the new target readout to the same scheme simplifies the event-building firmware.

---

## Summary Table

| Change | Technology | Key Physics Benefit | Risk Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3D scintillator cube target | 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes + WLS fibre + SiPM | Proton tracking/ranging, 4π acceptance, low threshold | Medium (channel count) |
| ToF planes | Fast plastic scintillator + SiPM | p/π separation 400–700 MeV/c | Low |
| Lateral ECal extension | Pb-scintillator sandwich + SiPM | Hermeticity, π⁰ rejection, side-exiting track recovery | Low–Medium |
| Self-triggering waveform DAQ | CITIROC-class ASIC, 200 MHz sampling | PSD for PID, dead-time reduction, flux normalisation | Low |

---

## Brief Commentary on Alternatives Considered and Rejected

**Liquid argon TPC insert:** Excellent tracking but 0.6 m depth is insufficient for a cryostat with adequate fiducial volume, and the existing GAr TPCs downstream already provide high-resolution tracking for forward-going tracks. The added cryogenic infrastructure risk is unjustified.

**Water Cherenkov insert:** Insufficient granularity for proton tracking at 450 MeV/c; Cherenkov threshold ~1 GeV/c for protons means the leading-proton requirement cannot be met.

**Straw-tube tracker:** Good for forward tracks but poor efficiency for large-angle, short proton tracks — the most critical failure mode for TKI analyses.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the removed photon-tagging section with a 3D scintillator cube detector (1 cm³ polystyrene cubes with three-view WLS fibre and SiPM readout) filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume, providing the low-threshold (~300 MeV/c), large-angle proton tracking and ranging that is the irreplaceable prerequisite for the kinematically complete CC event reconstruction and TKI programme.

# ND280 Upgrade Proposal: A Fully Active 3D Target with High-Angle Tracking

## 1. Why the current ND280 cannot do this

**Angular acceptance**
- FGD1 bars are all perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only downstream of the FGDs.
- A track above about 50–60° travels along a single bar layer, or exits sideways into the barrel ECal. It misses the TPCs, so it gets no momentum or dE/dx measurement.
- That region holds about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons. For a kinematically complete sample, both particles must be measured, so a large share of events fails.
- Backward-going tracks are also poorly separated from incoming tracks, because the FGD timing is not good enough.

**Proton threshold**
- With 1 cm bars in alternating x/y layers, a proton needs several hits in each view to be reconstructed.
- In practice this means roughly 400–450 MeV/c. With a median of about 450 MeV/c, about half the leading protons are lost.
- Short protons near the vertex are also confused with vertex activity.

**What this costs**
- Transverse-kinematic-imbalance (TKI) variables need both the muon and the proton.
- Their resolution is limited by the proton threshold and by angular acceptance, not by statistics.

## 2. Proposed hardware

### (a) Highly segmented 3D scintillator target ("SuperFGD") in the freed P0D box

**Geometry**
- About 2 million 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, roughly 192 × 182 × 56. That is about 1.92 × 1.82 × 0.56 m, which fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m envelope with margin for the frame and fibres.
- Each cube carries three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres along x, y and z.
- The fibres are read out by MPPCs on three faces: 192·182 + 192·56 + 182·56 ≈ 56,000 channels.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly twice FGD1 and FGD2 together. This is acceptable because hydrocarbon is allowed.

**Why this geometry**
- Three projections of every hit give true 3D, isotropic reconstruction. Acceptance is near-uniform over the full 4π, including tracks at 90° and backward tracks.
- The proton threshold drops to about 300 MeV/c (about 3–4 cubes). This recovers most of the proton spectrum below the median.
- Fine segmentation gives:
  - good dE/dx and range-based proton identification;
  - separation of protons from pions;
  - Michel-electron tagging;
  - γ and π⁰ identification without dead material.
- Sub-ns timing per channel (about 1 ns per fibre, better when combined) gives two further capabilities:
  - track direction;
  - neutron detection through isolated delayed hits, with time-of-flight neutron kinematics. This allows TKI on antineutrino CC0π events.

**Construction and readout notes**
- Cubes are injection-moulded and surface-etched for optical isolation. The ~1.5 mm holes keep fibre threading and alignment tolerances manageable.
- Electronics: new MPPC front-end boards based on the CITIROC ASIC.
  - They must provide charge and time.
  - They must handle a dynamic range from a minimum-ionising particle to stopping protons.
  - They must fit within limited space at the magnet inner faces.

### (b) Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs), above and below the new target

**Geometry and gas**
- Each about 2.0 m × 0.8 m × 1.8 m, with the drift direction horizontal and transverse to the beam.
- Same gas as the existing TPCs (Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2), so the gas system and calibration expertise are reused.

**Readout**
- Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode).
- Charge spreading gives better spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads (under about 600 µm).
- The resistive layer also removes spark damage.

**Field cage**
- Thin composite field cage to minimise material between the target and the gas.

**Role**
- Momentum by curvature in the 0.2 T field, and dE/dx particle ID, for high-angle muons.
- Momentum for protons that exit the target. This matters most for the about 6% above 900 MeV/c, which cannot be ranged out.
- Together with the existing downstream TPCs, this gives near-complete momentum coverage for muons.

### (c) Time-of-Flight (ToF) envelope

- Six planes of plastic scintillator bars enclosing the target plus the HA-TPCs.
- Each bar is read out at both ends with arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Uses**
- Unambiguous track direction (forward versus backward).
- Rejection of particles entering from outside the fiducial volume, from interactions in the magnet and ECal.
- Additional particle ID for low-momentum tracks.

### (d) Supporting changes

- Keep the barrel and downstream ECals and the SMRD. Remove the P0D together with its upstream ECal, or partially retain the P0D ECal if space allows.
- Keep FGD2 (the water layers), so carbon-to-water ratios remain possible with the same flux.
- Upgrade the DAQ, clock distribution and trigger to integrate about 56,000 new channels with common timing for the target, ToF and FGDs.
- Calibration systems:
  - LED or light-injection for MPPC gains;
  - a UV laser for HA-TPC drift and field distortions;
  - cosmic and through-going muons for alignment.

## 3. Expected impact

- Near 4π acceptance for both the muon and the leading proton, with the proton threshold reduced from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c.
  - This roughly doubles the usable kinematically complete CC sample.
  - It improves resolution on the TKI variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T).
  - These variables constrain nuclear effects (Fermi motion, 2p2h, final-state interactions) that dominate the residual model uncertainty.
- Angular coverage similar to Super-Kamiokande's 4π acceptance reduces extrapolation errors.
- Added target mass and neutron tagging give further constraints.
- Together these target the residual systematic uncertainty, aiming at about 4% from the current about 6%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a ~2-tonne, 1 cm³-cube 3D-readout scintillator target (SuperFGD, ~2 million cubes, ~56,000 MPPC channels) giving full-solid-angle, ~300 MeV/c-threshold reconstruction of muons and protons, flanked by high-angle TPCs above and below.

This is an excellent detector upgrade challenge. Let me analyze the requirements and propose a comprehensive solution.

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Kinematic completeness**: Must reconstruct both muons and recoil protons
2. **Large-angle acceptance**: ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons at >50° to beam
3. **Proton momentum range**: Median 450 MeV/c, tail to >900 MeV/c
4. **Available volume**: 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m (upstream P0D region)
5. **Systematic uncertainty**: Reduce from 6% to 4%

## Critical Physics Challenges

The current ND280 design is optimized for forward tracking (TPCs downstream), but the large-angle requirement for both muons and protons demands **3D tracking with near-isotropic acceptance**. The 60 cm depth is severely constraining for stopping and measuring high-angle particles.

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **3D Scintillator Tracker (SuperFGD-style) - PRIMARY RECOMMENDATION**

**Technology**: Optically-isolated plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³) in three orthogonal orientations, each read out by three wavelength-shifting fibers (x, y, z), coupled to MPPCs.

**Justification**:
- True 3D tracking with ~1 cm granularity enables reconstruction of high-angle tracks
- Hydrocarbon target (CH) acceptable per requirements
- Demonstrated technology from T2K upgrade R&D (SuperFGD prototype: 2 million cubes, ~2 tons)
- Neutron sensitivity via proton recoils
- Time resolution ~few ns for event topology discrimination

**Specifications for this application**:
- Fill ~1.8 m × 1.8 m × 0.55 m with cubes (leaving space for mechanical support)
- ~1.6-1.8 ton active mass
- ~200,000 cubes, ~600,000 readout channels

### 2. **High-Angle Muon Catcher/Ranger**

**Technology**: Thin horizontal plastic scintillator planes (10-15 planes, 2-3 cm thick) instrumented with wavelength-shifting fibers, filling the remaining volume around and behind the 3D tracker.

**Justification**:
- 60 cm depth insufficient to range out 450 MeV/c muons at large angles
- These planes catch muons exiting the 3D tracker at high angles
- Provides muon range/momentum measurement
- Can distinguish muons from protons via dE/dx and stopping/exiting behavior
- Extends effective acceptance for large-angle muons into SMRD

### 3. **Time-of-Flight System**

**Technology**: Two layers of thin (1-2 cm) fast plastic scintillator with MPPC readout at the upstream face and one layer at the downstream face of the 3D tracker.

**Justification**:
- σ(TOF) ~150-200 ps achievable with modern MPPCs and fast scintillator
- Provides crucial π/p separation at forward angles where dE/dx is similar
- Helps suppress pion contamination in proton selection
- Independent particle ID reduces systematic uncertainties
- Low material budget (~3% X₀ total)

### 4. **Remove P0D Entirely, Keep Other Detectors**

**Justification**:
- FGD2 already provides water target downstream for C/H₂O comparison
- P0D's 16 ton mass and complex structure added limited value relative to its systematic uncertainties
- Removing it provides installation space and improves access
- Simplifies analysis by focusing on well-understood new detector

### 5. **Enhanced TPC Readout (Electronics Upgrade)**

**Technology**: Replace existing TPC front-end electronics with higher-rate, lower-threshold ASIC (e.g., AFTER-based system).

**Justification**:
- Improves low-energy proton detection (threshold currently ~200 MeV/c)
- Better dE/dx resolution for particle ID
- Higher rate capability for T2K-II intensity
- Directly addresses the 6%→4% systematic uncertainty goal
- Modest cost compared to new detector construction

### 6. **SMRD Upgrade with Better Timing**

**Technology**: Replace SMRD MPPCs and readout electronics with modern devices having better timing resolution and dynamic range.

**Justification**:
- SMRD is 15+ years old; modern MPPCs have 2-3× better performance
- Critical for catching high-angle muons that exit the magnet volume
- Better timing helps match tracks to beam bunches
- Improved dynamic range for better energy measurement

## Integration and Calibration

- **Cosmic ray telescope**: Add two small scintillator hodoscopes above/below the magnet for cosmic muon calibration of the 3D tracker
- **Laser calibration**: Implement fiber-coupled laser system for MPPC gain monitoring
- **Neutron source**: Deployable AmBe or Cf-252 source for neutron response calibration

## Expected Performance

- **Acceptance**: >80% for muons and protons at all angles (vs. current ~40% at large angles)
- **Proton momentum resolution**: ~10% at 450 MeV/c via range in 3D tracker
- **Angular resolution**: ~2-3° for protons, ~1° for muons
- **Particle ID**: π/p separation >3σ up to 800 MeV/c
- **Systematic uncertainty**: Target <4% through improved acceptance, particle ID, and reduced model dependence

## Cost and Schedule Considerations

- 3D scintillator cube detector: Most expensive component (~3-5M USD based on SuperFGD prototype)
- TPC electronics upgrade: ~1-2M USD
- TOF and muon ranger: ~1M USD
- SMRD upgrade: ~500K USD
- 3-4 year timeline for construction and commissioning

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D plastic scintillator cube tracker (SuperFGD technology) as the primary neutrino target to achieve near-isotropic acceptance and complete kinematic reconstruction of both muons and recoil protons.

# Proposed upgrade for the Kestrel Flats near-station active target

## Why the obvious choice fails

The usual active target for this kind of job is a fine-grained plastic scintillator. Examples are T2K's SuperFGD, a 3D grid of 1 cm cubes, or scintillator bar trackers. These are ruled out by the hydrogen limit:

- Polystyrene (CH) has about 7.7% of its nucleons as free protons.
- Water, used in water-scintillator targets, has about 11%.

Both are far above the 2% ceiling, and no reconstruction trick can remove that much hydrogen. The target must be essentially hydrogen-free. Since the far detector has no hydrogen, the natural match is argon, assuming the far detector is argon-based.

## 1. Main change: a pixelated liquid-argon TPC

Replace the target region with a liquid-argon time projection chamber (LArTPC) that has 3D pixel readout, in the style of ArgonCube/ND-LAr.

**Mass and layout**
- Use a cryostat that fits the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope.
- After allowing for walls, this leaves an active volume of roughly 2.2 × 1.9 × 0.6 m. That is about 2.5 m³, or about 3.5 t of argon.
- Divide it into about 4–6 optically isolated modules, each with short drift lengths of about 30–50 cm. This needs no external field cage (no "big HV" drift) and keeps diffusion small.
- Each module has a central cathode and two anode planes.

**Charge readout**
- Use pixel readout, such as LArPix-style ASICs at about 4 mm pitch, rather than wire planes.
- Pixels give unambiguous 3D tracks, which matters for the high beam-related pile-up expected at 410 m.

**Light readout and timing**
- Use dielectric light traps (ArCLight or LCM-type) on the module walls.
- This gives roughly ns-scale timing and lets each module be associated with its own beam spill and bunch.
- It also separates overlapping interactions.

**Hydrogen budget**
- Argon contributes no hydrogen nucleons.
- The remaining hydrogen comes from G10/FR4 (circuit boards and module structures), cables, and any foam insulation.
- To stay well under 2%, use a vacuum-insulated, thin-walled cryostat with low-Z walls (aluminium or carbon composite) instead of membrane-plus-foam.
- Minimize plastic inside the fiducial volume.

**Proton threshold**
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 2.5 cm in liquid argon. At 4 mm pixel pitch that is about 6 or more hits, enough to identify it.
- Protons are identified by dE/dx, using the Bragg peak.
- This works in every direction because the response is isotropic.

**Muon momentum**
- For contained or partially contained muons, use range together with multiple Coulomb scattering.
- The 0.15 T field also gives some curvature measurement inside the argon, which helps with charge sign.

## 2. Coverage for high-angle and backward muons

Muons emitted at about 90° or backward will not reach the downstream drift chambers. To close those gaps:

- **Side and top/bottom trackers:** Line the inner magnet faces beside the cryostat with thin tracking layers. Options are resistive-Micromegas or GEM chambers, or a thin gas TPC layer. These measure curvature in the 0.15 T field and determine charge.
- **Upstream backward tracker:** Add a thin tracker upstream of the cryostat to catch backward-going muons.
- **Outer muon identification:** Instrument the magnet return yoke with scintillator planes (side muon range detectors). These provide muon ID and range for muons that exit the magnet sideways.

## 3. Timing and veto

- Surround the cryostat with a thin scintillator time-of-flight (TOF) envelope, using a few cm of plastic.
- This gives the direction (forward vs. backward) for exiting tracks and vetoes incoming particles from outside the detector.
- Keep it outside the fiducial volume so it does not count against the hydrogen budget.

## 4. Integration

- Check the forces on the cryostat in the magnetic field and the routing of cryogenic lines through the magnet.
- The charge readout electronics work in the 0.15 T field.
- Reprocess the downstream drift chamber reconstruction so that tracks starting in the argon are matched to the chambers.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (ArgonCube/LArPix-style, about 3.5 t, vacuum-insulated low-hydrogen cryostat). It gives a 4π, low-threshold active target with essentially zero hydrogen.

Based on the requirements for this near detector upgrade, I need to address several key challenges: 4π acceptance including backward-going tracks, low-momentum proton detection down to 60 MeV kinetic energy, minimal hydrogen content (<2%), and fine-grained tracking in a compact volume.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **Active Target Technology: 3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker**

I recommend a **Super-FGD (Fine-Grained Detector) type system** using small plastic scintillator cubes (1 cm³) with three-orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readout. This provides:
- True 3D tracking capability with ~1 cm granularity
- Low hydrogen content (plastic scintillator ~10-11% H by mass, diluted by fibers and structure to achieve <2% of total nucleons)
- Excellent angular acceptance including perpendicular and backward tracks
- Timing resolution ~1 ns for event reconstruction

**Specifications:**
- ~350,000 cubes of 1×1×1 cm³ extruded scintillator (polystyrene-based)
- Three orthogonal holes per cube for 1 mm diameter WLS fibers
- MPPCs (Multi-Pixel Photon Counters) for fiber readout (~50,000 channels)

### 2. **Alternative/Hybrid Option: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC**

A **resistive Micromegas TPC** filled with high-pressure argon (10 bar) would provide:
- Zero hydrogen content (pure argon)
- Excellent dE/dx for proton identification down to 60 MeV
- Sub-mm spatial resolution
- Full 3D reconstruction

**Specifications:**
- Pressure vessel rated for 10 bar
- Resistive Micromegas with 500 μm pitch
- Pixelated readout (~100,000 channels)
- Integration with existing magnetic field

### 3. **Enhanced Particle ID: Time-of-Flight System**

Add thin (~2 cm) **scintillator planes** at upstream and downstream faces with SiPM readout:
- Timing resolution <100 ps
- Proton/pion separation for tracks <1 GeV/c
- Start time (T0) determination for TPC drift if using option 2

### 4. **Low-Mass Transition Region**

Between active target and downstream drift chambers:
- **Thin silicon microstrip planes** (300 μm sensors, 50 μm pitch)
- 3-4 stations of X-Y planes
- Match tracks from dense target to downstream spectrometer
- Minimal multiple scattering

### 5. **Electronics and DAQ Upgrades**

- **CITIROC or similar ASICs** for SiPM/MPPC readout
- Waveform digitizers at 250 MS/s for energy and timing
- GPU-based online event filtering
- Expanded DAQ bandwidth to ~10 GB/s

## Addressing Specific Requirements

**25% efficiency at all angles:** The 3D cube geometry or TPC provides true volumetric tracking without blind spots, unlike planes which have inefficiencies for tracks parallel to them.

**60 MeV protons:** Range ~2.5 mm in plastic scintillator, ~2 cm in 10-bar argon—both detectable with proposed granularities. The TPC offers superior dE/dx for identification.

**<2% hydrogen nucleons:** 
- Super-FGD: Achievable by optimizing plastic formulation and fiber/air fraction
- High-pressure Ar TPC: Zero hydrogen, uses pure argon

**Backward tracks:** Both technologies provide hermetic coverage; tracks exiting upstream are fully reconstructed.

## Cost-Performance Considerations

The Super-FGD approach is more mature (demonstrated in T2K upgrade) and offers faster timing. The high-pressure TPC provides superior energy resolution and zero hydrogen but requires more R&D for integration with the dipole field.

**TOP RECOMMENDATION:** Install a Super-FGD 3D scintillator cube detector with three-orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readout and MPPC-based electronics, providing true 4π acceptance, sufficient granularity for low-momentum protons, and controllable hydrogen content.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Kestrel Flats Near-Station Active Target

## 1. What the requirements imply

| Requirement | Consequence for the hardware |
|---|---|
| Muons at **all angles**, including perpendicular and backward, at ≥25% efficiency | The downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks. High-angle tracks need tracking *inside and beside* the target, and the detector must tell forward-going from backward-going tracks. |
| Protons down to **~60 MeV kinetic energy** (p ≈ 340 MeV/c) at all angles | A 60 MeV proton travels only ~3 cm in plastic. That needs isotropic, fine 3D granularity of about 1 cm. Layered bar trackers lose short tracks near 90°. |
| Hydrogen nuclei **≤ 20%** of target nucleons | Plastic scintillator (CH) qualifies: H/(C+H) nucleons = 1/13 ≈ **7.7%**, well inside the limit. Water (11%) would also pass. No need for an exotic hydrogen-free scintillator. |
| Fits in 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m, inside a 0.15 T warm dipole | Compact readout that works in a magnetic field, so SiPMs rather than PMTs. A low field makes curvature measurement in dense material poor, so range and timing must do much of the work. |

## 2. Proposed configuration (a hybrid inside the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope)

Layout, viewed along the beam:
- **Top:** high-angle TPC, about 2.4 × 0.45 × 0.8 m.
- **Middle:** 3D scintillator-cube target (1 cm cubes), about 2.4 × 1.2 × 0.8 m.
- **Bottom:** high-angle TPC, about 2.4 × 0.45 × 0.8 m.
- **All six faces:** surrounded by time-of-flight (TOF) panels.

### A. Fine-grained 3D scintillator-cube target (the core)
- **Cubes:** about 2.3 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes. This gives roughly 2.3 t of CH target.
- **Readout:** each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- **Channels:** ≈ 240×120 + 240×80 + 120×80 ≈ **58k SiPM channels**.
- **Why it meets the angular requirement:** its response is nearly isotropic, so tracks at 90° and backward are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Why it meets the proton requirement:**
  - A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes. That is enough for detection and for dE/dx and range energy measurement.
  - The Bragg peak separates protons from pions.
- **Muon momentum:** muons that stop inside (most high-angle muons at this beam energy have p ≲ 300 MeV/c, range ≲ 1 m CH) get momentum from range.
- **Timing:** about 1 ns per channel, sub-ns per track from many hits.

### B. Two high-angle TPCs (above and below the cube block)
- **Geometry:** thin-wall field cages, each about 0.45 m tall, with resistive Micromegas readout.
- **Purpose:** they capture tracks that exit the target sideways, which the downstream drift chambers cannot see. They give:
  - charge sign and momentum from curvature in the 0.15 T field (gas has negligible multiple scattering);
  - dE/dx particle ID.
- **Field direction:** assuming the dipole field is horizontal and transverse to the beam, high-angle tracks bend in the vertical–beam plane. This sets which way the TPCs face; it should be checked against the actual magnet.

### C. TOF envelope
- **Design:** plastic scintillator bars with double-ended SiPM readout, reaching about 150 ps resolution.
- **Coverage:** all faces of the new volume.
- **Purpose:**
  - It determines track direction (forward vs backward), which is essential for backward-going muons and for rejecting entering backgrounds (sand muons, out-of-fiducial events).
  - It adds e/μ/p separation.

### D. Supporting items
- SiPM front-end electronics placed outside the field, or field-tolerant, with readout deep enough to handle beam spills.
- Common clock and trigger synchronisation with the beam and the existing drift chambers.
- Precise mass and composition assay of the cubes (C, H, plus O/Ti from the reflective coating) to fix the hydrogen fraction, expected at about 8%, for the subtraction model.
- A test-beam calibration of proton and muon response before installation.

## 3. Expected performance against the requirements
- **Muon efficiency ≥ 25% at all angles:**
  - Forward muons reach the existing drift chambers.
  - High-angle muons are measured in the TPCs or by range in the cubes.
  - Backward muons are identified by TOF and cube timing.
  - Efficiency should exceed 25% across the full solid angle, and be much higher in most bins.
- **Protons ≥ 60 MeV KE, 4π:** met by the 1 cm 3D granularity. The threshold is roughly 300 MeV/c, which is comparable to existing T2K-style 3D cube detectors.
- **Hydrogen ≤ 20%:** about 7.7%, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid with a wide margin.

## 4. Priorities and risks
1. **Cube target:** most critical; delivers both the 4π muon and the low-threshold proton requirements.
2. **TOF:** needed for direction and therefore for backward muons.
3. **High-angle TPCs:** improve momentum and charge measurement for exiting high-angle muons.

Main risks:
- Cube assembly tolerances and fibre threading at this scale.
- Optical crosstalk between cubes.
- SiPM channel count and cost.
- Space conflict between the TPCs and the cube height. If this is too tight, reduce the TPC height and rely more on range-based muon momentum in the cubes.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fine-grained 3D-readout plastic-scintillator-cube active target (~1 cm cubes, SiPM readout), supplemented by high-angle TPCs and a TOF envelope.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Physics Requirements Analysis

Before proposing hardware, I'll map requirements to detector specifications:

| Requirement | Implication |
|---|---|
| Reconstruct muons up to ~25% at >50° | Low-threshold tracking, large angular acceptance |
| Reconstruct protons, median 450 MeV/c | Very low threshold (~50 MeV kinetic energy), fine granularity |
| 6% protons >900 MeV/c | Sufficient range/momentum resolution at high end |
| Kinematically complete CC events | 4π-ish hermeticity, vertex containment |
| Box: 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m | Severely constrained depth along beam |
| Reduce systematics from 6% → 4% | Good energy scale calibration, well-understood nuclear target |
| Hydrocarbon target acceptable | Polystyrene/scintillator viable |

The 0.6 m depth along beam is the critical constraint. A 450 MeV/c proton has a range of ~19 cm in plastic scintillator, so containment is achievable, but the detector must be highly granular to reconstruct large-angle tracks without long lever arms.

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. SuperFGD — Primary Recommendation (Core Upgrade)

**Description:** A fully-3D-segmented active target composed of ~2 million plastic scintillator cubes, each 1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm, made from extruded polystyrene doped with PPO/POPOP fluors. Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre axes (X, Y, Z) pass through each cube, each fibre read out at one end by a surface-mount MPPC (Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE or similar, ~1 mm² active area, ~667 pixels).

**Geometry fitting the available volume:**
- Active volume: ~1.8 m (x) × 1.76 m (y) × 0.56 m (z beam direction)
- ~1,800 × 1,760 × 560 cubes ≈ 1.77 × 10⁹ cubes — clearly impractical at full density
- Practical implementation: adopt the design developed by the T2K upgrade collaboration (already R&D'd): ~2 million cubes, ~192 × 184 × 56 planes, active mass ~1.9 t

**Key performance parameters:**
- Proton tracking threshold: ~300 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~45 MeV, range ~2.5 cm = 2–3 cubes), compared to ~500 MeV/c in the planar FGDs
- Angular acceptance: essentially 4π for charged particles — no preferred projection axis means tracks at 90° to the beam are reconstructed with the same efficiency as forward tracks
- Position resolution: σ ~ 1 cm / √12 per cube per view, but with 3-view coincidence gives 3D space points with ~3 mm resolution
- dE/dx sampling: each cube is an independent calorimetric sample; proton/pion separation via Bragg peak identification up to ~1 GeV/c
- The 0.6 m depth provides ~56 radiation lengths' worth of sampling depth, adequate for proton range up to ~700 MeV/c before exiting into the downstream TPC

**Why this solves the core problem:** The planar FGD architecture has ~96% efficiency for forward tracks but drops sharply beyond 40°–50°. The 3D segmentation gives uniform efficiency across all angles, directly addressing the 25%/35% large-angle leakage fractions for muons and protons.

**Readout electronics:** ~560,000 MPPCs (3 fibres × ~186,000 cubes per layer, etc.) → use CITIROC-based or SPIROC2D ASICs in daisy-chain readout; sparsified zero-suppressed readout at ~100 ns shaping time to match beam spill structure (2 µs spill at 30 Hz at J-PARC MR).

---

### 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Description:** Six planes of fast plastic scintillator (EJ-230 or BC-420, τ ~ 1.5 ns) surrounding the SuperFGD on all six faces, each plane consisting of 2 cm-thick bars read out by MPPCs at both ends.

**Placement:**
- Upstream face (1): 2.0 m × 1.9 m, 1 plane
- Downstream face (1): 2.0 m × 1.9 m, 1 plane
- Top, bottom, left, right (4 planes): sized to cover lateral faces of the 0.6 m deep box

**Performance:**
- Timing resolution: σ_t ~ 200–300 ps per plane achievable with MPPC readout and waveform digitization (CAEN V1730 or equivalent flash ADC at 500 MHz)
- For a 450 MeV/c proton (β ~ 0.43): TOF over 20 cm = ~1.5 ns, easily separated from pions (β ~ 0.95, TOF ~ 0.7 ns) → Δt ~ 0.8 ns, >2.5σ separation
- For protons up to ~1 GeV/c: TOF still provides ~3σ p/π separation over the 56 cm baseline
- Provides event t₀ to ~300 ps, enabling rejection of out-of-time beam backgrounds and cosmic muons
- Upstream plane vetoes incoming charged particles from beam interactions upstream (P0D region now empty, reducing background)

**Criticality for the physics programme:** Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies require correct particle identification; misidentifying a pion as a proton biases δp_T and δα_T. The TOF planes provide PID at momenta where the SuperFGD dE/dx Bragg-peak method loses power (above ~700 MeV/c).

---

### 3. High-Granularity Electromagnetic Calorimeter (HA-ECAl) Surrounding the SuperFGD

**Description:** A thin lead–scintillator sandwich calorimeter wrapping the lateral and downstream faces of the SuperFGD, with ~4 X₀ total thickness, 2 mm Pb + 3 mm scintillator sampling structure, bars oriented to give 2D projective readout.

**Integration with existing ECal:** The existing downstream ECal (DsECal) and barrel ECals remain in place. The new HA-ECAl fills the gap between the SuperFGD and the existing ECal barrel, ensuring photon containment from π⁰ decay produced at the new target vertex.

**Key specifications:**
- Radiation length of module: ~10 layers of (2 mm Pb + 3 mm scint) = 50 mm total, ~4 X₀
- Photon energy resolution: σ_E/E ~ 10%/√E for E in GeV (adequate for π⁰ mass reconstruction)
- Granularity: 1 cm × 4 cm bars, WLS fibre + MPPC readout (same technology as SuperFGD for supply chain consistency)
- Provides photon veto for NC π⁰ background rejection, crucial for the νµ CC selection purity

---

### 4. Upgraded TPC Front-End and Magnetic Field Tracking Integration

**Description:** The three existing TPCs immediately downstream provide muon momentum measurement via curvature in the 0.2 T UA1 magnet field. For large-angle muons exiting the SuperFGD laterally (into the SMRD or ECal), momentum from range is the fallback.

**Proposed upgrade:**
- Install thin (5 mm) scintillator tracking planes ("tracker planes") on the lateral faces inside the magnet volume between the SuperFGD and the ECal barrel, using the same 1 cm × 1 cm bar technology
- These 4 planes (top, bottom, left, right) each ~1.8 m × 0.5 m, providing 2–3 space points for large-angle tracks before they enter the ECal
- Combined with the SMRD hits in the magnet yoke, this gives a lever arm of ~80 cm at 90°, sufficient for curvature measurement of muons above ~200 MeV/c

**Momentum resolution improvement:** For muons at 60°–90°, the current ND280 resolution is dominated by multiple scattering in the ECal material before enough tracking points are accumulated. The added tracker planes reduce the material-before-first-measurement by ~0.3 X₀.

---

### 5. MPPC Upgrade for Existing FGD2 and ECal Channels

**Description:** Replace the existing 667-pixel Hamamatsu MPPCs (S10362-13-050C, 50 µm pixel pitch) in FGD2 and the nearest ECal modules with the current-generation S13360-1325PE (25 µm pitch, ~1667 pixels, lower dark count rate ~70 kcps at 25°C vs ~1.35 Mcps for older type, higher dynamic range).

**Motivation:**
- The older MPPCs have ~2× higher dark noise and saturate at lower photon flux, degrading dE/dx resolution for highly-ionizing protons near Bragg peak
- New MPPCs improve light yield linearity for heavily-ionizing tracks (δ-rays, protons), reducing the dE/dx systematic uncertainty
- Directly addresses the 6% → 4% systematic goal by improving the cross-section measurement's proton energy scale

**Scale:** ~15,000 channels in FGD2 + near ECal — a manageable replacement during the same shutdown as SuperFGD installation.

---

### 6. Beam Monitor and Flux Constraint Improvements (Upstream of ND280)

**Description:** While not strictly inside ND280, installing a segmented ionization chamber array (NINJA-style thin target) or upgrading the existing muon monitor (MUMON) with a finer-granularity scintillator array improves the input flux constraint fed into the ND280 analysis.

**Within ND280:** Add a gadolinium-doped water Cherenkov veto panel (2 cm thick) on the upstream face of the SuperFGD. Gd-doped water (0.1% GdCl₃) captures neutrons with ~80% efficiency within ~100 µs, tagging neutral-current background events that produce final-state neutrons re-interacting in the SuperFGD. This is a thin (2 cm) vessel with photomultiplier readout at the edges.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Mass/Channels | Key Benefit | Systematic Impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SuperFGD 3D scintillator target** | ~1.9 t, ~560k MPPCs | 4π proton tracking, low threshold | Dominant: angular acceptance |
| ToF scintillator planes | 6 planes, ~2k channels | p/π separation above Bragg-peak range | PID systematic |
| HA-ECAl lateral | ~0.5 t, ~20k channels | π⁰ veto, photon containment | NC background |
| Lateral tracker planes | ~200 channels | Large-angle muon momentum | Muon acceptance |
| MPPC replacement FGD2/ECal | ~15k channels | dE/dx linearity for protons | Energy scale |
| Gd-doped water veto | Small | Neutron background tagging | NC/CC separation |

---

## Critical Integration Notes

1. **The 0.6 m depth** is comfortably matched by the SuperFGD: a 1.9 t, 56-layer-deep cube array fits with ~2 cm margin for mechanical support and the ToF planes.
2. **The existing downstream TPC–FGD–TPC–FGD–TPC stack is unchanged**, preserving FGD2 water-target comparisons.
3. **Power and cooling**: SuperFGD dissipates ~6 kW (electronics); the existing UA1 magnet cooling infrastructure can handle this with modest upgrades to the chilled-water manifold.
4. **WLS fibre and MPPC technology** is already qualified for ND280 conditions (magnetic field immunity of MPPCs confirmed >1 T, well above the 0.2 T operating field).

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D volume with a fully 3D-segmented plastic scintillator active target (SuperFGD) composed of ~2 million 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes read out on three orthogonal axes by WLS fibres and MPPCs, providing near-4π angular acceptance and a ~300 MeV/c proton tracking threshold that directly enables kinematically complete CC event reconstruction including the large-angle muon and proton populations that are unacceptable losses for transverse kinematic imbalance analyses.

# Design Review Recommendations: New Active Neutrino Target

## Overview of the Problem

The core challenge is instrumenting a 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume to achieve kinematically complete CC reconstruction with:
- Large-angle muon acceptance (>50° for ~25% of events)
- Large-angle proton acceptance (>50° for ~35% of events)
- Proton momentum threshold low enough to catch the bulk of the distribution (median ~450 MeV/c), implying tracking down to ~200–250 MeV/c
- Proton momentum resolution good enough for TKI studies (δp_T/p_T ~ few %)
- 0.6 m depth along beam severely constrains ranging ability and longitudinal containment

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. SuperFGD-style Scintillator Cube Active Target (Primary Technology)

**Recommendation:** Fill the available volume with an array of 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes connected by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres per cube, read out by SiPMs — the "Super Fine-Grained Detector" architecture now adopted by T2K's ND280 upgrade.

**Justification:**

- **4π tracking in a compact volume.** The 0.6 m beam-direction depth is the critical constraint. A conventional planar-scintillator FGD gives only ~6 radiation lengths of material in this dimension and cannot reconstruct tracks going at large angles across the thin dimension without severe hit ambiguity. The 3D-connected cube geometry resolves track ambiguity in all three projections simultaneously using the three-fibre readout, enabling reconstruction of stubs as short as 2–3 cubes (~2–3 cm), which is essential for large-angle, short-range protons.

- **Proton tracking threshold.** A proton at 200 MeV/c has a range of ~4 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³). With 1 cm³ cubes this gives ~4 hit cubes — marginally reconstructible. This matches the momentum regime that dominates the leading-proton spectrum (median 450 MeV/c → ~30 cm range, well contained even in the 0.6 m depth if the proton is forward-going). For the ~35% of protons at >50°, they traverse the 1.9 m transverse dimension, where containment is excellent.

- **Hydrocarbon target is acceptable** per the problem statement. Polystyrene (C₈H₈) gives a C:H ratio well-suited to the programme; the downstream water-layer tracker handles carbon subtraction for the water comparison.

- **Mass budget.** At bulk scintillator density (~1.05 g/cm³) the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume holds ~2.4 tonnes — comparable to or better than the removed photon-tagger's active mass, and substantially more target mass than the existing plastic targets downstream, improving statistical power.

- **Demonstrated technology.** The SuperFGD for ND280 has undergone full engineering; the collaboration can adopt the validated cube geometry, WLS fibre routing, and SiPM bias/readout boards, reducing R&D risk relative to a novel approach.

---

### 2. Time-of-Flight Planes on the Upstream and Downstream Faces

**Recommendation:** Mount two planes of fast plastic scintillator bars (e.g., Eljen EJ-200 or equivalent, 2 cm thick, read out at both ends by fast SiPMs with ~200 ps single-bar time resolution) on the upstream and downstream faces of the cube volume.

**Justification:**

- **Proton/pion separation.** At 450 MeV/c, a proton has β ≈ 0.43 and a pion has β ≈ 0.95. Over a 20 cm flight path within or exiting the target, the ToF difference is ~1 ns — cleanly resolved with 200 ps resolution. This is critical for TKI studies because misidentifying a pion as the leading proton directly biases δp_T.

- **Backward-going particle tagging.** The upstream ToF plane tags particles exiting backward, vetoing or reconstructing them, which is important for multinucleon interaction topologies.

- **Beam-bunch timing.** The upstream plane also provides an event T₀ tied to the beam spill fine-structure, improving vertex timing and pile-up rejection.

- **Cost and complexity are low** relative to the primary target technology; standard 2 cm EJ-200 bars read by the same SiPM family already used in the surrounding calorimeter minimise procurement and QC overhead.

---

### 3. Upgrade of Surrounding ECAL SiPM Readout to Increase Dynamic Range and Lower Threshold

**Recommendation:** Replace the SiPMs on the innermost ECAL layers adjacent to the new target volume with devices of higher pixel count (e.g., move from ~400-pixel to ~3600-pixel devices of the same active area, e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-series 3×3 mm²) and add a secondary low-gain readout channel per strip using a resistive voltage divider or dual-output ASIC.

**Justification:**

- **Proton dE/dx at the ECAL boundary.** A proton stopping near the edge of the cube target will deposit a Bragg peak in the first ECAL scintillator layer. High pixel-count SiPMs extend the linear range from ~50 p.e. to ~500 p.e. per channel without saturation, allowing the Bragg peak to be used as a range-energy cross-check rather than a saturated nuisance signal.

- **Photon detection for π⁰ background.** TKI studies require suppression of events where a π⁰ mimics the struck-nucleus recoil signature. The adjacent ECAL's improved linearity at low energy (10–50 MeV γ from π⁰ → γγ) tightens the photon veto, reducing this background without a hardware redesign of the full ECAL.

- **Same SiPM footprint and bias voltage range** as existing devices; the mechanical integration is a drop-in swap in the innermost layer only, limiting installation time during the upgrade stop.

---

### 4. Thin Resistive Plate Chamber or Scintillator-Strip Layers on the Four Lateral Faces for Large-Angle Muon Matching

**Recommendation:** Instrument the four lateral faces of the new target box (the faces parallel to the beam axis) with one layer each of 1 cm-pitch scintillator strips, read out by SiPMs, oriented to give both x and y coordinates on each face (two sub-layers per face, orthogonal orientation, ~3 mm strip pitch feasible with triangular cross-section bars).

**Justification:**

- **Large-angle muon track matching.** A muon leaving at 60° to the beam in the horizontal plane exits through the lateral face after traversing only ~35 cm of the 0.6 m depth. It must be matched to the downstream TPCs or the return-yoke scintillator for momentum measurement. Without dedicated boundary hits, the matching between the cube-target track stub and the downstream tracker relies on extrapolation, introducing a fiducial uncertainty that contributes directly to the systematic error budget.

- **Thin layers preserve mass budget.** Two sub-layers of 3 × 3 mm² triangular bars per lateral face add <5 kg per face, negligible compared to the ~2.4 t active target.

- **Synergy with existing yoke instrumentation.** The return-yoke scintillator already ranges side-going muons; these lateral face planes provide the intermediate space-point that removes the ambiguity in charge-sign assignment when the track curves in the 0.2 T field before reaching the yoke.

---

### 5. Low-Mass Field-Cage / Copper Ground Plane Integration for EMI Shielding of SiPMs

**Recommendation:** Enclose the cube array in a thin (0.5 mm) copper-clad FR4 Faraday cage segmented into quadrants, with each quadrant independently connected to the detector ground reference via the existing slow-control network.

**Justification:**

- **SiPM dark-count sensitivity to RF noise.** The accelerator environment near the target station has significant RF pickup at the beam RF frequency (~500 MHz range). With ~400,000 SiPMs in the cube target (estimated for a 1 cm³ cube array at 1 fibre per face per cube, 3 fibres per cube, ~130,000 cubes, 3 channels each), even a modest coherent noise hit rate from RF pickup would create fake track stubs that bias the proton reconstruction. A segmented Faraday enclosure, standard in SiPM-based detector practice (e.g., NA62 RICH, Belle II TOP), reduces this by >40 dB at the relevant frequencies.

- **Negligible radiation length contribution.** 0.5 mm copper at the boundary of the volume contributes ~0.004 X₀, invisible to the event reconstruction.
