# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

Before proposing upgrades, let me map requirements to detector challenges:

| Requirement | Challenge |
|-------------|-----------|
| Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at **all angles including 90° and backward** | Standard downstream-only tracking fails; need 4π angular coverage |
| Proton tracks down to **60 MeV kinetic energy** (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.4 cm in iron) | Very short tracks; need fine granularity, low-Z material |
| **≤2% hydrogen fraction** of target nucleons | Cannot use hydrocarbon scintillator or water as primary target; need low-H nuclear target |
| Active target within 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³ | Must fit upstream end of existing magnet |
| Existing warm dipole (0.15 T, 6.5 m) and downstream drift chambers remain | Can use field for forward muon momentum; need supplementary tracking inside target |

---

## Hydrogen Constraint — The Critical Driver

This is the most underappreciated constraint. Common active-target materials fail:

- **Plastic scintillator (CH):** ~57% of nucleons are hydrogen — **completely excluded**
- **Water (H₂O):** ~67% hydrogen — **excluded**
- **Liquid argon:** 0% hydrogen — passes, but reconstruction challenges
- **Argon gas TPC:** 0% hydrogen — passes
- **Iron/steel:** 0% hydrogen — passes
- **Liquid helium-4:** 0% hydrogen — passes (exotic)

Materials near the 2% limit:
- Pure **graphite** (carbon): 0% H — passes
- **Aluminium:** 0% H — passes
- Low-outgassing **gas mixtures** (Ar/CO₂, Ar/CF₄): H fraction from CO₂ ≈ 0% — passes

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgTPC) — Primary Active Target

**Replace the target region contents with a High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC operating at ~10 bar.**

- **Geometry:** Fill the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³ volume with a rectangular HPgTPC; cathode plane at beam-upstream face, anode wire planes (or pixel pads) at downstream face plus two side faces.
- **Why gaseous rather than liquid:** A gas TPC provides continuous 3D track reconstruction with no dead material between readout planes, enabling reconstruction of tracks at **any angle** including 90° and backward. Liquid argon TPCs have excellent resolution but are single-readout-direction devices that struggle with tracks parallel to the drift direction and have no self-triggering.
- **Why high pressure (~10 bar):** Increases target mass proportionally; at 10 bar the density is ~17 kg/m³, giving a fiducial mass of ~90 kg of argon in the full volume — adequate statistics. More importantly, it increases dE/dx stopping power so that **60 MeV protons** (range ~20 cm at 1 bar) stop in ~2 cm at 10 bar, well within the active volume and above single-wire resolution.
- **Hydrogen content:** Pure Ar or Ar/CO₂ (97/3) gas. For Ar/CO₂: hydrogen fraction = 0 (CO₂ has no H). Easily satisfies ≤2% H constraint.
- **Drift field:** Apply ~200 V/cm drift field along the 0.9 m (beam) direction; full drift length 45 cm per half-volume (split cathode). Drift time ~4 μs — compatible with beam spill structure.
- **Readout:** 2D projective wire planes (U/V/X) at both endcaps, plus optionally a pixel-pad anode on the side walls to assist 90° tracks. Wire pitch 3–4 mm gives spatial resolution ~1 mm, sufficient to resolve 2 cm proton tracks.
- **Track angle coverage:** With readout on **all six faces** (or at minimum three orthogonal projections), tracks at any angle reconstruct efficiently. Backward muons simply drift toward the upstream endcap readout.

**Key performance:**
- 60 MeV proton range at 10 bar Ar: ~2–3 cm → resolves as ~6–8 wire hits — reconstructible
- Muon at 90°: projects onto side-wall readout and endcap → full reconstruction
- Backward muon: drifts to upstream anode — reconstructed identically to forward tracks
- dE/dx particle ID separates protons from pions down to ~200 MeV/c

---

### 2. Thin Scintillator Trigger and Veto Planes

**Install 1 cm thick plastic scintillator panels on all six faces of the TPC pressure vessel.**

- Provides fast (ns-level) trigger signal since the TPC drift readout is slow (~μs)
- Acts as **muon tagger**: a track exiting any face is identified by which scintillator panel fires, giving immediate angle classification (forward, side, backward)
- Vetos incoming beam-halo muons from outside
- The hydrogen in 1 cm of scintillator contributes negligibly to target nucleon count (scintillator is a surface layer, not the target mass)
- Panels segmented to ~10 × 10 cm² tiles for multiplicity information

**Hydrogen check:** The scintillator is exterior to the gas target. The active target nucleons are the argon gas nucleons. Surface scintillator contributes ~1–2% of total nucleons if kept thin relative to argon mass — must be carefully budgeted. At 10 bar, 90 kg Ar dominates; 6 panels × ~15 kg scintillator = ~90 kg scintillator → this would be problematic. **Solution:** Use thin (3 mm) panels or switch panel material to pure-carbon (graphite-fiber) scintillator-free trigger using **SiPM-read wavelength-shifting fiber arrays embedded in carbon-fiber composite panels**, minimising hydrogen. Alternatively, trigger from the downstream drift chambers (beam timing is known) and use the scintillator only for veto — reducing required coverage.

---

### 3. Upgrade the Downstream Drift Chamber System for Large-Angle Muon Momentum Measurement

**Add two additional drift chamber stations rotated 90° (vertical wires) immediately downstream of the target, plus a station upstream of the target.**

- The existing drift chambers presumably have horizontal wires optimised for forward tracks; adding vertical-wire stations provides the complementary view needed for tracks emerging at large polar angles in the bend plane
- An **upstream station** (just in front of the TPC entry face) catches backward-going muons that exit the upstream face of the target, providing momentum measurement in the magnetic field for those tracks
- These are conventional drift chambers (Ar/CO₂ or Ar/isobutane gas) — well-understood technology, modest cost
- Position the upstream station between the target and the magnet coil/yoke upstream face; fit within the existing magnet bore

---

### 4. Electromagnetic Calorimeter Panels on Side and Upstream Faces of Target Region

**Add thin lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter (electromagnetic, ~10 X₀) panels on the four non-beam faces (top, bottom, left, right) of the target region, plus the upstream face.**

- Captures photons and electrons from π⁰ decay and charged-current quasi-elastic events at large angles
- Assists muon identification for side-exiting tracks (muon punches through; hadron showers in calorimeter)
- Needed for the analysis neutrino energy reconstruction
- Use **lead–scintillating fiber (SciFi)** construction to minimise hydrogen: fibers are ~polystyrene (CH) but lead dominates mass; keep fiber volume fraction low or substitute carbon-fiber reinforced scintillating bars to reduce H
- **Hydrogen budget:** With ~80% Pb by mass in sampling calorimeter, hydrogen fraction from scintillator component is ~0.3% of total calorimeter nucleons. Since calorimeter is exterior to gas TPC, only the gas TPC nucleons count as "target nucleons" for the H constraint — this is fine.

---

### 5. Replacement of Inner Gas Drift Chambers Inside the Magnet (Downstream of Target) with Straw-Tube Trackers

**Replace any existing wire chambers immediately downstream of the active target (inside the magnet volume, non-target region) with straw-tube tracker (STT) modules.**

- Straw tubes (4 mm diameter, Ar/CO₂ fill, Mylar walls) provide excellent position resolution (~130 μm per straw) and work well in the 0.15 T magnetic field
- Critically, straw tubes function in the high-occupancy environment near the target and have good efficiency for large-angle tracks because stereo layers (±5°) provide 3D reconstruction
- **Low mass per radiation length** compared to drift chambers with thick frames — reduces secondary interactions that would confuse reconstruction
- If aluminum straws are used (no hydrogen in the structural material, only Ar/CO₂ fill gas): hydrogen fraction negligible
- Multiple stereo-angle layers (0°, +5°, −5°, 90°) cover all track angles including near-perpendicular

---

### 6. Dedicated Timing Layer — MRPC or Scintillator for Proton ToF

**Add a Multigap Resistive Plate Chamber (MRPC) layer or fast scintillator bars (SiPM readout) at ~50 cm downstream of the target exit face.**

- 60 MeV kinetic energy proton: momentum ~340 MeV/c, velocity β ≈ 0.34, travels 50 cm in ~5 ns beyond expected from light speed → time-of-flight separation of protons from pions at the same momentum is ~2 ns at 50 cm
- MRPC achieves ~50–70 ps timing resolution → clear proton/pion separation up to ~700 MeV/c at 50 cm
- Assists identification of short proton tracks that **exit** the TPC before stopping, supplementing the dE/dx PID
- Hydrogen content: glass MRPCs contain essentially no hydrogen

## Notes on the Hydrogen Constraint in Practice

The ≤2% H limit means: for every 100 nucleons in the target, at most 2 are protons in hydrogen atoms (not bound in heavier nuclei). At 10 bar in the 2.6×2.3×0.9 m³ volume:

- Argon nucleons: ~90 kg × (6.02×10²³/0.040 kg/mol) × 40 ≈ 1.35×10²⁷ nucleons
- 2% limit: allows 2.7×10²⁵ hydrogen nucleons ≈ 45 g of H atoms in free hydrogen molecules or CH bonds
- This is easily satisfied with pure argon or Ar/CO₂ gas with no plastic components inside the active volume

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Next Phase

---

## 1. SuperFGD — 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target (Primary New Target)

**Technology:** A fully-active target composed of approximately 2×10⁶ plastic scintillator cubes, each 1×1×1 cm³, assembled into a ~192×184×56 cm³ block fitting the available 2.0×1.9×0.6 m box. Each cube is threaded by three wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres along orthogonal x, y, z axes, each fibre read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM/MPPC). This is the SuperFGD concept already developed by the T2K collaboration.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Kinematically complete events:** The conventional FGD bar geometry (9.6 mm × 9.6 mm × 1864 mm) reconstructs tracks well only if they travel along the bar length. The 1 cm³ isotropic granularity gives 4π acceptance with no preferred axis. The 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons exiting beyond 50° to the beam — which are largely lost or poorly reconstructed in bar-based FGDs — are fully tracked.
- **Low proton threshold:** With 1 cm³ cubes and ~0.5 cm effective radiation length in polystyrene, a proton stopping inside leaves a measurable Bragg peak. The tracking threshold drops to roughly 300 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~40 MeV), well below the median leading-proton momentum of 450 MeV/c. This is essential to avoid biasing the proton momentum spectrum.
- **Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI):** TKI variables (δpT, δαT, δφT) require both the muon and the leading recoil proton to be reconstructed with their full 3-momentum vectors. Failure to reconstruct large-angle protons introduces a selection bias that mimics nuclear effects. The isotropic acceptance directly reduces this systematic.
- **Particle identification via dE/dx and topology:** The fine granularity allows proton/pion separation through energy deposition profile and Bragg peak identification, crucial for isolating true QE-like events from resonance production backgrounds.
- **Target mass:** At polystyrene density 1.05 g/cm³ the cube array delivers ~700 kg of active hydrocarbon target, roughly matching one FGD in mass but with dramatically superior angular coverage.

---

## 2. High-Angle Time Projection Chambers (HA-TPCs)

**Technology:** Two additional TPCs with enlarged field cage cross-sections, placed immediately upstream and downstream of the SuperFGD, oriented so their active volumes subtend ±45°–±90° relative to the beam axis. Gas: Ar:CF4:iC4H10 (same as existing TPCs, or optionally Ar:CO₂ for reduced material). Readout: resistive Micromegas or pixel-pad Micromegas for improved two-track separation.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Large-angle muon momentum measurement:** The existing downstream TPCs measure muons that exit within ~30–35° of beam. The 25% of muons beyond 50° either range out in the ECAL or escape unmeasured. HA-TPCs placed laterally around the SuperFGD capture these tracks, providing momentum from curvature in the 0.2 T magnetic field.
- **Charge identification:** The magnet bends μ⁺ and μ⁻ in opposite directions. Correct charge assignment of large-angle muons requires a tracking volume that the particle actually traverses with sufficient path length in the field. HA-TPCs ensure this.
- **Proton momentum measurement for high-momentum tail:** The 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c exit the SuperFGD and need external momentum measurement. HA-TPCs with ~20 cm drift provide this, complementing the range-based measurement inside the cube target.
- **Reduction of the 6% → 4% systematic:** The dominant residual systematics are muon acceptance and nuclear interaction modelling. By recovering large-angle muon tracks, the event selection efficiency becomes more uniform in scattering angle, reducing the efficiency-correction systematic.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Six planes of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-404), ~2×2 cm² bar cross-section, arranged as a box around the SuperFGD on all six faces, each bar read out at both ends by SiPMs. Target timing resolution: σ_t ~ 200–300 ps per plane, giving ~150–200 ps between two planes.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Proton/pion separation:** At 450 MeV/c (median proton momentum), a proton takes ~2.5 ns longer than a pion to travel 50 cm. With 200 ps resolution the separation is >10σ at this momentum and remains useful up to ~800 MeV/c. This directly reduces the dominant background of pion contamination in the leading-proton sample.
- **Neutron detection and directionality:** Neutral current and antineutrino interactions produce leading neutrons. A neutron hitting a ToF plane gives a delayed, charge-neutral hit; βγ reconstruction from timing constrains its momentum. This extends the kinematic completeness concept toward multi-nucleon knockout studies.
- **Event direction: beam vs. cosmic disambiguation:** The 200 ps resolution easily distinguishes forward-going beam particles (travel time ~1 ns across 20 cm) from backward-going cosmics, reducing the need for loose timing cuts that accept backgrounds.
- **Vertex timing for pile-up rejection:** At J-PARC beam intensities planned for T2K-II, multiple interactions per spill bucket will increase. ToF planes provide sub-ns vertex timestamps that the cube-fibre readout alone (limited by WLS decay time ~2–3 ns) cannot supply.

---

## 4. Upgrade of SMRD to Thicker Muon-Range Detector with Embedded Tracking

**Technology:** Replace the existing 7 mm SMRD slabs in the magnet yoke gaps with 1 cm thick scintillator bars with two-ended SiPM readout, and add 2–3 layers of RPCs (Resistive Plate Chambers) or thin scintillator tracking planes in the gaps between yoke plates. Total added material ~20 cm iron-equivalent in each lateral wall.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Range-out of large-angle muons:** A muon leaving the SuperFGD at 70° to beam with 500 MeV/c momentum travels ~1.5 m before stopping. It enters the magnet yoke at ~1 m transverse distance. Additional SMRD layers extending range measurement reduce the fraction of muons that "escape" from ~25% to ~10%, improving the large-angle sample statistics by a factor of ~2.
- **Multiple scattering vs. range cross-check:** Measuring both curvature (from TPCs) and range (from SMRD) for the same muon allows an in-situ constraint on the magnetic field map and detector material budget — both important systematic inputs to the flux/cross-section fit.
- **Reduced fiducial-volume systematic:** Currently, events near the ND280 edge have poorly measured muon kinematics because the muon exits. Better SMRD coverage extends the effective fiducial volume at large angles.

---

## 5. Gadolinium-Doped Water Layers in the Retained FGD2

**Technology:** Dissolve Gd₂(SO₄)₃ in the FGD2 water layers to a concentration of ~0.1% Gd by mass (following Super-Kamiokande's GADZOOKS! programme). The existing scintillator bars surrounding the water layers serve as the neutron-capture gamma detector.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Neutron tagging on water:** Thermal neutrons from neutrino interactions on oxygen are captured by Gd with a cross-section ~49,000 barns (vs. ~0.33 barns on hydrogen), releasing an 8 MeV gamma cascade detectable in the surrounding scintillator. This tags multi-neutron final states that are otherwise invisible.
- **Carbon-to-water comparison with neutron constraint:** FGD2 already enables carbon/water cross-section ratios. Adding neutron tagging allows measurement of the full hadronic final state, testing nuclear models (SRC, 2p2h) that are the primary source of the 6% residual systematic.
- **Antineutrino identification:** In the antineutrino beam, ν̄μ + p → μ⁺ + n is the dominant CC quasi-elastic channel. Gd-tagging the recoil neutron provides event-by-event antineutrino identification without relying on muon charge (which requires good track length in the field).
- **Low incremental cost:** Gd doping of an existing water volume is technically demonstrated and inexpensive compared to building new subdetectors.

---

## 6. SiPM and Front-End Electronics Upgrade for All Existing Scintillator Channels

**Technology:** Replace the first-generation MPPCs (Hamamatsu S10362-13-050C, 400 pixels, ~35% PDE) across the ECAL, P0D replacement, and SMRD with current-generation SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent, ~50% PDE at 450 nm, reduced dark count rate, improved gain uniformity). Pair with updated CITIROC or TARGET-C ASICs providing 12-bit ADC and sub-ns timing.

**Physics motivation:**

- **Improved photon counting → better energy resolution:** The ECAL energy resolution for π⁰ reconstruction scales as σ_E/E ~ a/√E ⊕ b. Improved PDE reduces the stochastic term, improving π⁰ mass peak resolution. This tightens NC-π⁰ background rejection, which contributes ~1% to the ν_e appearance systematic.
- **Reduced cross-talk and after-pulsing:** First-generation MPPCs have ~3% optical cross-talk, producing false multi-photon signals. Modern SiPMs achieve <1%, directly reducing the low-energy hit threshold needed for detecting soft gamma rays from nuclear de-excitation — relevant for tagging excited nuclear final states.
- **Better timing for ToF integration:** Sub-ns timing from updated front-ends is prerequisite for the ToF programme described above.
- **Operational longevity:** After ~15 years of operation and radiation dose, existing MPPCs show increased dark current. Replacement restores the original noise performance for the T2K-II run period.

This is an interesting detector design challenge for a near detector in an accelerator neutrino beam experiment. Let me analyze the requirements and constraints:

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Geometric acceptance**: Need 4π coverage including backward-going and perpendicular tracks
2. **Low momentum threshold**: ~60 MeV kinetic energy protons (momentum ~110 MeV/c)
3. **Hydrogen constraint**: ≤2% of target nucleons
4. **Active target volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m
5. **Existing infrastructure**: 0.15 T dipole magnet, downstream gas drift chambers

## Problems with Current Setup

- Gas drift chambers downstream only measure forward-going tracks
- No coverage for backward or perpendicular tracks
- Insufficient tracking in the target region itself for vertex reconstruction and short proton tracks

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Primary Upgrade)**
Install a 3D array of extruded plastic scintillator bars with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) detection:
- Two or three orthogonal orientations (X, Y, U or X, Y, Z) in alternating planes
- ~1 cm bar pitch for adequate spatial resolution
- Plastic scintillator (CH₂)ₙ has ~50% hydrogen by nucleon count - too high
- **Use polystyrene-based scintillator with deuterated components or add high-Z dopants** to reduce effective hydrogen fraction
- Provides 4π angular coverage, low threshold for protons, and 3D tracking

### 2. **Hybrid Target Composition**
To satisfy the hydrogen constraint while maintaining tracking capability:
- Mix plastic scintillator planes with **carbon or hydrocarbon-depleted targets**
- Intersperse planes of pure carbon or CH₂ with different ratios
- Alternatively, use **scintillating fiber technology with smaller diameter fibers** to increase surface-to-volume ratio and improve position resolution while maintaining low hydrogen

### 3. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Alternative**
A gaseous TPC with low-hydrogen gas mixture:
- Use Ar:CO₂ or CF₄-based gas (negligible hydrogen)
- Excellent 3D tracking and dE/dx for particle ID
- Good coverage for all angles
- Lower density means longer proton ranges (beneficial for low-E protons)
- Challenges: complexity, 0.15 T field is weak for a TPC

### 4. **Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) or Micromegas**
Fine-grained gaseous detectors interspersed with passive targets:
- Glass/Bakelite RPCs or Micromegas planes
- Minimal hydrogen content
- Intersperse with graphite or other low-H target planes
- Good position resolution and timing
- 4π coverage capability

### 5. **Silicon Tracking Layers**
High-precision, zero-hydrogen option:
- Silicon strip or pixel detectors
- Excellent position resolution
- No hydrogen contribution
- Very expensive for the required volume
- Could be used in hybrid configuration

### 6. **Optimal Hybrid Solution: Scintillator + TPC**
- **Inner target**: Fine-grained scintillator tracker with minimized hydrogen (using techniques like partial deuteration or optimized CH ratio)
- **Outer tracking**: Small TPC or MPGD (Micro-Pattern Gas Detector) layers surrounding the scintillator to catch wide-angle tracks
- This provides vertex resolution, short track detection, and 4π coverage

## Detailed Recommendation for Scintillator System

- **Configuration**: 1 cm³ cubes of scintillator in a 3D grid, or 1-2 cm pitch extruded bars in 3 orientations
- **Readout**: Multi-pixel photon counters (MPPCs/SiPMs) - compact, work in magnetic field
- **Material budget**: Optimize for ~1-2% hydrogen by nucleon count total
- **DAQ**: High channel count (~50,000-100,000 channels) - use modern ASIC-based systems
- **Particle ID**: dE/dx from multiple samples helps separate protons from pions/muons

## Additional Considerations

- Add **surrounding veto/catcher layers** outside the main target volume for wide-angle tracks
- Ensure **hermetic coverage** around the target region
- Implement **high-speed DAQ** to handle the neutrino beam spill structure

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker with ~1 cm granularity and SiPM readout throughout the target volume, optimized to keep hydrogen below 2% of nucleons while providing complete angular coverage and low momentum threshold.

# Design Review Recommendation for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

The key constraints are:
1. **Geometric coverage**: ≥25% efficiency for muons at all angles including perpendicular and backward-going
2. **Low momentum threshold**: ~60 MeV kinetic energy protons (p ≈ 340 MeV/c, range ~3 mm in plastic)
3. **Hydrogen constraint**: ≤2% of target nucleons
4. **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m 
5. **Magnetic field**: 0.15 T (modest)
6. **Neutrino energy**: ~0.7 GeV peak

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Primary Choice)**

**Technology**: Extruded plastic scintillator bars with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays

**Specifications**:
- Bar dimensions: 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm cross-section
- Three orientations (X, Y, U at 45°) in repeating XYU modules
- Module thickness: ~3 cm (one bar of each orientation)
- Total modules: ~30 to fill 0.9 m depth
- Polystyrene-based scintillator (CH formula gives ~7.7% H by mass, ~1.1% by nucleon count - well within budget)

**Justification**:
- **Angular acceptance**: 3D reconstruction from three orientations allows tracking at any angle, including perpendicular and backward
- **Low threshold**: 1 cm granularity provides ~3 samples for 60 MeV protons, enabling detection and dE/dx measurement
- **Hydrogen requirement**: Polystyrene is ~1% H nucleons, leaving margin for safety
- **Proven technology**: Used successfully in MINERvA, T2K SuperFGD
- **Timing**: Fast scintillator response (~ns) separates interaction products from beam backgrounds

### 2. **High-Density SiPM Readout Electronics**

**Technology**: Multi-channel ASICs with time-over-threshold and timing measurement

**Specifications**:
- CITIROC or similar front-end ASICs
- ~30,000 channels total (both bar ends for position along bar via timing)
- 1 ns timing resolution
- Charge integration for energy measurement

**Justification**:
- Both-end readout provides z-position along bars via timing difference
- High channel density is essential for fine granularity
- Time resolution separates overlapping tracks
- Modern SiPMs operate reliably in 0.15 T field

### 3. **Thin Downstream Tracking Planes**

**Technology**: Resistive Micromegas or thin drift chambers

**Specifications**:
- 3-4 planes with 2 mm pitch
- Located at scintillator exit before existing drift chambers
- Total material budget <0.01 X₀

**Justification**:
- Provides precise angle measurement for forward-going muons
- Confirms track matching to downstream momentum measurement
- Minimal multiple scattering for low-momentum particles
- Validates 3D reconstruction in scintillator

### 4. **Embedded Optical Cameras for Calibration**

**Technology**: Miniature CMOS cameras with LED illumination system

**Specifications**:
- 4-6 cameras viewing internal structure
- Remote-controlled LED calibration system

**Justification**:
- Monitors mechanical stability critical for 3D tracking
- Enables fiber mapping verification
- Documents assembly quality

## Alternative Considered and Rejected

**High-pressure gaseous TPC** (used in some experiments): Would provide excellent 3D tracking and low hydrogen content, but:
- Requires pressure vessel in magnet bore (complex)
- Lower density reduces event rate
- More challenging at low momenta due to diffusion
- Higher technical risk

**Liquid argon TPC**: Excellent imaging but contains no hydrogen (can't fulfill physics requirement of measuring on hydrogen for subtraction).

**Emulsion**: Too labor-intensive for near detector event rates.

## Implementation Notes

- **Construction**: Modular assembly allows testing and replacement
- **Cost**: ~$3-4M for scintillator and SiPMs (based on similar detectors)
- **Timeline**: 18-24 months for construction after design freeze

## 3. **Enhanced Proton Stopping Power in Target Volume**
**Technology:** Hybrid hydrocarbon-heavy target modules
- **Specific implementation:** Alternate dense polystyrene/polypropylene tracking layers (5-10 mm) with thin brass or copper sheets (2-3 mm) every 5-10 cm
- **Why:** The 6% of protons exceeding 900 MeV/c will not stop in pure hydrocarbon within 60 cm depth. Strategic dense layers contain these while maintaining sufficient hydrocarbon interaction mass. Range measurements in dense material improve momentum resolution.

## 4. **Timing System Upgrade**
**Technology:** Precision timing layer at target upstream face
- **Specific implementation:** Fast plastic scintillator tiles (5 × 5 cm²) with SiPM readout, ~200 ps resolution

**Technology:** Compact ECAL module downstream of new target

- **Why:** Separates π⁰ photons from single-photon backgrounds and measures photon energy for events with overlooked neutral pion production, reducing a major background to quasi-elastic event selection. Reduces NC/CC misidentification.

**Technology:** Thin tracking planes with precise position resolution
- **Specific implementation:** Silicon strip detectors or thin scintillating fiber planes (2-3 stations) at upstream face of magnet volume
- **Why:** Tags and measures very forward muons (<10° to beam) that might pass through the target with minimal energy deposition, ensuring no muon losses in the kinematically complete sample. Critical for flux constraint at peak energy.

**Technology:** dE/dx measurement upgrade in target
- **Specific implementation:** Dual-ended readout on all scintillator bars; pulse-shape discrimination electronics

# Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Funding Proposal

## 1. Active Neutrino Target (Primary Upgrade) — Scintillator Bar Tracking Target

**Technology:** 3D grid of extruded polystyrene scintillator bars with WLS fibre + SiPM readout, arranged in X/Y/Z stereo layers, filling the ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m available volume.

**Why:** The existing tracking targets downstream use 9.6 × 9.6 mm bars successfully; a similar or finer pitch (e.g. ~1 cm) in a fully active 3D configuration provides the neutrino interaction target itself as the tracker. This gives kinematically complete CC event reconstruction — both the muon and leading recoil proton are tracked from the vertex outward without a dead fiducial gap. The hydrocarbon (CH) composition is explicitly acceptable per the physics programme. With ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons leaving at >50° to beam, dense 3D coverage in all transverse directions is essential. The ~0.6 m depth is sufficient to track sub-GeV protons over short paths. This directly replaces the removed photon-tagging section and targets the 4% systematic goal through improved hadronic reconstruction for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis.

---

## 2. Fine-Grained Scintillator Bar Pitch Reduction

**Technology:** Reduce bar cross-section from 9.6 × 9.6 mm to ~5 × 5 mm (or ~7 × 7 mm) with dual-ended SiPM readout.

**Why:** The leading-proton median momentum is ~450 MeV/c, corresponding to a range in plastic scintillator of roughly 10–15 cm, with track lengths that may be only a few bars with 9.6 mm pitch. Finer bars improve: (a) vertex separation between the muon and proton tracks, (b) angular resolution for the proton at large angles (>50°), and (c) dE/dx-based proton–pion separation critical for identifying the "leading proton" unambiguously. Dual-ended readout improves hit position resolution along the bar axis.

---

## 3. Upgraded SiPM Readout with Higher PDE and Lower Dark-Count Rate

**Technology:** Replace first-generation SiPMs (e.g. ~25–35% PDE) with current-generation devices (~50–55% PDE, 15 µm cell pitch), e.g. Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD.

**Why:** Low-energy proton tracks (below ~200 MeV/c, in the tail of the distribution) produce faint signals in thin scintillator bars. Higher photon detection efficiency directly improves the low-momentum proton detection threshold, which matters for completeness of the recoil-proton sample and hence for controlling nuclear modelling systematics. Lower dark count rate reduces accidental noise hits that can mimic short proton stubs. The existing WLS-fibre + SiPM architecture is preserved, so this is a channel-for-channel swap compatible with existing front-end electronics designs.

---

## 4. Front-End Electronics with Charge + Time Measurement (QDC/TDC or Waveform Digitisation)

**Technology:** Replace any existing binary or simple charge readout with a waveform-sampling ASIC or dual-threshold QDC+TDC per channel (e.g. CITIROC-based or MUSIC ASIC), providing ~1 ns timing resolution and charge dynamic range covering 1–200 photoelectrons.

**Why:** Proton–pion–muon separation by dE/dx requires reliable charge measurement per bar. Additionally, time-of-flight discrimination between protons and pions for tracks stopping within the target volume at ~450 MeV/c (proton range ~15 cm) requires sub-nanosecond hit timing. Good timing also suppresses out-of-time pile-up from the beam spill structure. This upgrade is essential to exploit the fine granularity of the new active target.

---

## 5. Reinforced or New Structural Support Frame for the New Target Module

**Technology:** Modular aluminium space-frame with precision rail alignment system fitting the existing dipole magnet upstream volume.

**Why:** The 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m installation space sits inside the magnet bore, which constrains access severely. A modular frame allowing the target to be pre-assembled, tested, and inserted as a single sled reduces installation risk and allows removal for maintenance without disturbing the downstream TPCs and tracking targets. Precise alignment (< 1 mm) is needed to match track segments reconstructed in the active target with those in the downstream gas TPCs.

---

## 6. Downstream Return-Yoke Scintillator Plane Extension / Efficiency Recovery

**Technology:** Add or refurbish scintillator planes (extruded scintillator + WLS + SiPM) in the return-yoke gaps covering wider angular acceptance, particularly in the vertical/side directions.

**Why:** With ~25% of muons exiting at >50° from the beam, a significant fraction range out sideways into the return yoke rather than stopping in the downstream calorimeter. The existing yoke instrumentation was designed for the downstream fiducial volume; the new upstream active target moves the interaction vertex ~2 m further from the yoke detectors, increasing the solid-angle demand. Improved muon ranging in the yoke directly reduces the muon momentum uncertainty for large-angle tracks, which are the ones most sensitive to the transverse kinematic variables.

---

## 7. Calibration and Monitoring System: LED Pulser + Radioactive Source Ports

**Technology:** Pulsed blue/UV LED injection system per SiPM channel and periodic deployment of a neutron/gamma calibration source (e.g. ²⁵²Cf or AmBe) via guide tubes in the new target.

**Why:** Achieving the 4% systematic target requires that channel-by-channel gain stability and light yield be monitored continuously across the run. LED pulsers (already used in similar detectors) track SiPM gain and WLS fibre transmission at the sub-percent level between beam spills. A radioactive source cross-calibrates the absolute energy scale relevant to proton dE/dx measurements, essential when comparing proton reconstruction efficiency between CH target and the downstream water layers.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

The current design sends tracks downstream into drift chambers along the beam. That fails the physics requirements in two ways:

- **Muon acceptance:** muons perpendicular to the beam, or going backward, never reach the downstream chambers, so they cannot be reconstructed at 25% efficiency.
- **Proton threshold:** short proton tracks need a target that is itself a fine-grained 3D tracker.

The proposal should therefore include the following.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D scintillator active target (the core change)

**Technology:** About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibers. Each fiber is read out by a SiPM (MPPC). This is the Super-FGD-style design.

**Why:**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal 2D projections give true 3D tracking with equal response in all directions. Layered bar trackers lose efficiency for tracks running along the layers, near 90°.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 cm in plastic, so it crosses roughly 3 cubes. That is enough to form a track and identify it as a proton by dE/dx.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** In CH, hydrogen is 1 of 13 nucleons (about 7.7%), well under the 20% limit, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid. Carbon targets are also comparable to existing cross-section data.
- **Magnet compatibility.** SiPMs work in the 0.15 T field, unlike PMTs.
- **Timing.** Sub-ns timing per channel is an added benefit and also allows some neutron detection.

## 2. High-angle TPCs bordering the target

**Technology:** Thin gas TPCs placed above and below the cube target, or on its sides, inside the 0.15 T field. Readout would use resistive Micromegas with field cages made of low-mass composite.

**Why:**
- Muons leaving near 90° escape sideways and never reach the downstream chambers. These TPCs give them a momentum and charge-sign measurement and dE/dx particle identification.
- Resistive Micromegas spread charge across pads, giving good spatial resolution with fewer channels.
- Low-mass walls minimize multiple scattering. This matters at 0.15 T, where the curvature lever arm is limited.
- This requires splitting the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope. For example, the cube target would occupy roughly the central 1.2–1.4 m of height, with a TPC above and below. Muons that stop in the target can still be measured by range.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new target region

**Technology:** Panels of plastic scintillator bars read out with SiPMs at both ends, achieving about 150 ps timing.

**Why:**
- The panels give each track a direction (forward vs. backward going) from timing. This is what makes backward muons reconstructable rather than confused with incoming tracks.
- They reject particles entering from outside the target region, such as interactions in the magnet or surrounding material.
- They add particle identification by time of flight, separating muons, electrons, and protons.

## 4. Supporting systems

- **Front-end electronics and DAQ:** high channel density and SiPM-compatible, suitable for the O(10⁵–10⁶) cube readout channels and the TPC pads.
- **SiPM gain stabilization:** temperature and gain monitoring, plus an LED calibration system.
- **Mechanics and integration:** a low-mass, non-magnetic support box and integration into the existing dipole and drift-chamber system. The TPCs need gas and high-voltage services.
- **Upstream veto** (optional but useful): rejects incoming beam muons and other through-going particles.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fine-grained 3D-readout plastic scintillator cube target (about 1 cm cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibers, SiPM readout), complemented by high-angle TPCs and time-of-flight panels.

# Design Review: Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target Upgrade

## Analysis of Requirements

Before recommending hardware, I'll map the physics requirements to detector constraints:

1. **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles** — including 90° and backward tracks. This means the active target cannot rely on downstream spectrometers alone; the target itself must track and identify muons with enough length to match into the magnet/drift chambers or perform standalone momentum measurement.

2. **Proton reconstruction down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** — 60 MeV protons have a range of ~12 mm in water and ~35 mm in scintillator (density ~1.03 g/cm³). This demands fine spatial granularity and low thresholds; the technology must stop and measure very short tracks.

3. **Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of target nucleons** — This strongly constrains material choice. Plastic scintillator (CH) has ~57% of nucleons as hydrogen. Liquid argon has zero hydrogen. Water has ~11% hydrogen by nucleon count. This is the most architecturally decisive constraint.

4. **Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** — relatively compact, so technologies with large unit-cell sizes (e.g., full-scale LArTPC) are geometrically workable but operationally challenging in this space.

5. **Fits inside existing warm dipole** — no superconducting infrastructure; the solution must tolerate stray fields and fit mechanically.

---

## Hydrogen Fraction Constraint: Quantitative Check

For candidate materials, hydrogen fraction by nucleon number (protons+neutrons):

| Material | Formula | H nucleon fraction |
|---|---|---|
| Plastic scintillator | CH₁.₁ (approx) | ~54% |
| Liquid scintillator | CH₁.₈ (mineral oil) | ~63% |
| Water | H₂O | 11.1% |
| Liquid argon | Ar | 0% |
| Carbon (graphite) | C | 0% |
| Iron | Fe | 0% |
| Polystyrene | (C₈H₈)ₙ | ~50% |
| Acrylic (PMMA) | C₅H₈O₂ | ~38% |

**Plastic scintillator is immediately disqualified** as a bulk target material (~54% H >> 2%). This eliminates the most common choice for near detectors (e.g., MINERvA-style scintillator strips).

Liquid argon satisfies the hydrogen constraint trivially. Carbon-based passive absorbers with active readout can work if hydrogen content is managed. A **high-pressure gaseous argon or pure argon target with embedded tracking** would have zero hydrogen.

However, the preferred approach used by modern experiments (e.g., NINJA, WAGASCI, NuPRISM, SAND) for this precise problem is a **low-density, fine-grained tracking volume** — but it must be hydrogen-poor.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. PRIMARY: Replace bulk target with a High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgAr TPC)

**Technology:** High-pressure gaseous argon TPC, operating at ~10 bar, with micropattern gas detector (MPGD) readout — specifically **Micromegas or GEM planes** at the anode faces, with cathode at center and two drift volumes. Segmented into modules fitting the 0.9 m depth.

**Justification:**

- **Hydrogen content = 0%** — argon has no hydrogen, satisfying the ≤2% constraint with large margin and enabling clean subtraction if any small H-containing materials are unavoidable in structural components.

- **60 MeV proton tracking:** At 10 bar argon (density ~16.6 kg/m³), a 60 MeV proton has a range of approximately 170 mm — easily reconstructed with mm-scale spatial resolution from the TPC. Compare to liquid argon where 60 MeV protons range ~8 mm but the resolution is adequate; in gas at 10 bar the track is ~20× longer than in LAr, giving excellent dE/dx particle ID and angular reconstruction.

- **All-angle muon reconstruction:** A TPC provides fully 3D tracking of all charged particles without geometric dead zones. Backward-going and sideward-going muons are reconstructed as naturally as forward ones. The drift field can be oriented along beam (or transverse) to optimize. Muon tracks exiting the TPC gas volume enter the existing drift chambers downstream or through the magnet iron for momentum measurement. For muons stopping inside, the 3D range gives a momentum estimate.

- **No directional bias:** Unlike scintillator-strip or fiber geometries that have preferred orientations, a TPC images tracks in all directions.

- **Compatible with existing magnet:** Gaseous TPCs operate in magnetic fields; the 0.15 T dipole actually improves the momentum measurement of tracks curving within the gas, and is not problematic for MPGD readout (Micromegas are field-tolerant).

- **Charge measurement:** dE/dx vs. range provides proton/pion separation. At these momenta (60 MeV protons, up to several hundred MeV pions), Bethe-Bloch separation in gas is excellent.

**Implementation notes:** Operate at ~10 bar in a pressure vessel fitting the 2.6 × 2.3 m cross-section. Use modular construction with 4–6 Micromegas anode planes reading out 2D strip patterns, giving ~1 mm resolution. Electronic readout via existing or new ALICE-TPC-style FEC boards adapted for high-rate neutrino beam spills. Cathode high voltage ~100 kV across ~45 cm half-drift at 10 bar (E/P ~ 100 V/cm/bar is typical for Ar/CO₂ 90/10 mixtures). Add a small admixture of CO₂ or CF₄ as quencher, verifying the H content of CF₄ is zero (it is) or CO₂ is acceptable (C and O only — H fraction ~0%).

---

### 2. Thin Electromagnetic Calorimeter Panels on All Six Faces of the Active Target Volume

**Technology:** Lead-scintillating fiber (Pb-SciFi) "preshower/ECAL" panels, ~10 radiation lengths total, with SiPM readout, lining all six faces of the TPC pressure vessel. Total thickness ~5 cm per face.

**Justification:**

- **Muon identification and angular efficiency:** A muon track exiting any face of the TPC (including sides and upstream face for backward tracks) must be tagged as a muon, not a pion. Thin calorimeter panels detect the absence of an electromagnetic shower (MIP signal only = muon candidate) and measure the exit point and direction, enabling matching to the external drift-chamber spectrometer even for large-angle tracks.

- **Backward muon recovery:** A backward-going muon exits the upstream face of the target. Without an upstream detector element, it enters dead material and is lost. ECAL panels on the upstream face catch and identify it, and the existing beam infrastructure or an additional small spectrometer upstream can measure its momentum. The 25% efficiency floor at backward angles requires this coverage.

- **Photon/π⁰ detection:** Neutral pion backgrounds (π⁰ → γγ) produce electromagnetic showers that must be distinguished from signal. The ECAL panels provide this.

- **Low hydrogen content:** Pb-SciFi uses polystyrene fibers embedded in lead. The mass is dominated by lead (~70% by mass); hydrogen nucleon fraction in the total active-target system (TPC gas + ECAL panels) remains well below 2% because the ECAL panels surround but are not part of the neutrino interaction target mass. If scrupulous accounting is needed, the ECAL mass can be excluded from the fiducial target definition.

- **SiPM readout:** Operates in the 0.15 T dipole without degradation (SiPMs are insensitive to this field level, unlike PMTs which require magnetic shielding).

---

### 3. Upstream Muon Spectrometer Insert (Mini-Spectrometer)

**Technology:** Three stations of silicon microstrip detectors (or small-gap resistive plate chambers, RPCs) interleaved with thin aluminum absorber (~1–2 cm total), mounted immediately upstream of the TPC pressure vessel, covering the full 2.6 × 2.3 m aperture.

**Justification:**

- **Backward muon momentum measurement:** Backward-going muons from neutrino interactions (antineutrino-like topologies or final-state radiation effects) exit the upstream face and must have their momentum measured to satisfy the ≥25% efficiency at all angles. The existing downstream drift chambers cannot see them. A compact upstream tracker provides range-based or small-deflection-based momentum measurement for backward tracks.

- **Silicon strips or RPCs:** Silicon strips give ~50 μm position resolution but are expensive at this scale. RPCs (small-gap, ~0.3 mm gap glass RPCs) are cost-effective at 2.6 × 2.3 m, have ~1 mm resolution, operate well in modest magnetic fields, and have low mass (thin glass, no hydrogen in glass = SiO₂). Three-station RPC with 2 cm Al absorber allows range measurement of muons stopping within it and deflection measurement of through-going ones.

- **Hydrogen content of RPCs:** Glass (SiO₂) and aluminum — zero hydrogen. The gas mixture (typically C₂H₂F₄/iso-C₄H₁₀/SF₆) contains hydrogen in isobutane, but the gas volume fraction of the total detector mass is negligible; the hydrogen fraction contribution is <<0.1% of target nucleons.

---

### 4. Beam-Synchronized Timing Layer

**Technology:** Thin (3 mm) plastic scintillator paddles with SiPM readout forming a veto/timing plane on the upstream face, **used only for timing, not as target material**, with individual paddle mass <<1 kg total.

**Justification:**

- The HPgAr TPC has a drift time of order ~10–50 μs (at 10 bar, drift velocity ~5 cm/μs at 100 V/cm, so 45 cm drift = ~9 μs). The beam spill structure must be used to associate TPC events with the correct beam bucket. Thin scintillator paddles (total mass ~a few kg, negligible H contribution to target nucleon count) provide t₀ timing to <1 ns, resolving ambiguity in which drift window a track belongs to.

- The small amount of plastic scintillator here is not part of the fiducial target volume and is excluded from the hydrogen accounting, which applies only to the active target region inside the TPC.

---

### 5. Upgraded Downstream Track-Matching Interface

**Technology:** Addition of one station of large-area silicon strip detectors (or scintillating fiber tracker, SciFi, in hydrogen-free configuration using carbon-fiber support structure) between the TPC exit face and the first existing drift chamber station.

**Justification:**

- **Large-angle track matching:** Tracks leaving the TPC at large angles to the beam axis (approaching 90°) have very short lever arms to the existing drift chambers and may miss them entirely given the 2.6 × 2.3 m aperture vs. the drift chamber active area. An interface station with large active area catches these tracks and provides a seed for the downstream spectrometer.

- **Charge sign measurement efficiency:** The 25% efficiency floor applies not just to track finding but to charge-sign determination (μ⁺ vs. μ⁻ for neutrino vs. antineutrino). An additional point measurement immediately downstream improves the efficiency of connecting TPC tracks to the magnetic spectrometer for large-angle tracks.

- **SciFi with carbon-fiber support:** Scintillating fibers are polystyrene (CH) but the total mass of a single tracker plane is small. If necessary, replace with thin-film silicon strips on carbon-fiber to eliminate H entirely. Carbon-fiber support contributes only C.

---

## Summary Table

| Recommendation | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | HPgAr TPC at 10 bar, Micromegas readout | H≤2%, 4π tracking, 60 MeV protons, all-angle efficiency |
| Face calorimetry | Pb-SciFi ECAL with SiPM, all 6 faces | Muon ID at all exit angles, backward muon tagging, π⁰ rejection |
| Upstream spectrometer | 3-station small-gap RPC + Al absorber | Backward muon momentum measurement |
| Timing layer | Thin scintillator paddles (non-target) | TPC drift-window t₀, beam synchronization |
| Downstream interface | Large-area SciFi or Si-strip station | Large-angle track matching to existing drift chambers |

---

## Critical Design Considerations

**Pressure vessel engineering** is the dominant technical risk. A 10-bar vessel of ~2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³ requires careful mechanical design; the walls must be thin enough to minimize tracking gaps but strong enough for safety. Aluminum alloy walls of ~15–20 mm with internal support ribs are feasible; finite-element analysis required. The vessel must be non-magnetic to avoid perturbing the dipole field map.

**Gas purity and recirculation** at 10 bar requires a closed-loop gas system with Ar/CO₂ purification to maintain electron lifetime >1 ms. This is established technology (ALICE TPC, T2K ND280 TPCs) but must be scaled to this pressure.

**High-voltage stability** at 10 bar is well-characterized; Paschen curve minimum is well below operating point, and operation at this pressure with Micromegas is demonstrated by T2K and DUNE prototype work.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the existing target region with a high-pressure gaseous argon TPC (10 bar, Micromegas readout), which simultaneously satisfies the hydrogen-fraction constraint (zero hydrogen in argon), provides fully 4π three-dimensional tracking needed for all-angle muon reconstruction, and gives sufficient track length for 60 MeV recoil protons — none of the other changes are viable without solving this central technology choice first.

# Upgrade proposal: Kestrel Flats near detector, active-target region

## Requirements

- **Target composition.** The far detector has no hydrogen, and the hydrogen-subtraction model holds only while H nuclei are ≤20% of target nucleons. Counting nucleons, the options compare as follows:
  - Polystyrene (CH)n: 1 H nucleon per 13 total, about 7.7%.
  - Water: 2/18, about 11%.
  - Polyethylene (CH₂): 2/14, about 14%.
  - All are compliant, so a hydrocarbon scintillator is acceptable and still gives a near-far carbon/oxygen-like nuclear target.
- **Muon acceptance.** Muons must be reconstructed with at least 25% efficiency at every angle, including 90° and backward. The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks, so the target itself, plus new trackers around it, must cover the transverse and backward directions.
- **Proton threshold.** Protons down to 60 MeV kinetic energy (p ≈ 340 MeV/c) must be seen. Their CSDA range in plastic is only about 3 cm, so the target needs roughly 1 cm granularity in all three dimensions, with no preferred orientation.
- **Track direction.** Backward-going tracks must be distinguished from forward-going tracks that enter from outside, which requires good timing.

## 1. Main upgrade: 3D-granular plastic-scintillator cube target ("SuperFGD"-type)

**Technology**
- Optically isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes of 1 cm³.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Fibres are read out by SiPMs/MPPCs with waveform-digitising electronics.

**Size**
- The volume would be about 2.0 m × 1.7 m × 0.9 m (beam). This is reduced from the full 2.6 × 2.3 m to leave room for the high-angle trackers in section 2.
- That gives about 3 million cubes, about 3 t of target mass.
- The three projections need roughly 200×170 + 200×90 + 170×90 ≈ 67k channels.
- At 0.7 GeV, 3 t gives an ample CC event rate at 410 m.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal 2D projections reconstruct tracks equally well at any angle. This contrasts with planar bar trackers, which lose tracks near 90°.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes, giving vertex-activity and dE/dx (Bragg peak) identification. Pion/proton/muon separation comes from dE/dx.
- **Muons by range.** High-angle, low-momentum muons (typically below 500 MeV/c at these energies) can be measured by range when contained.
- **Timing.** Sub-ns cube timing allows neutron detection by time-of-flight to isolated hits. This aids transverse-kinematic-imbalance and calorimetric energy reconstruction.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** The CH target keeps H at about 8% of nucleons, well inside the 20% model limit. A full gaseous-H or CH₂-heavy design would be worse for both rate and model validity.

## 2. High-angle tracking above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two thin "high-angle" gas TPCs, roughly 2.0 m × 0.9 m × 0.3 m each, fill the remaining transverse space inside the magnet.
- They use resistive-anode Micromegas readout for good spatial resolution with modest channel count.

**Physics motivation**
- Muons exiting sideways never reach the downstream drift chambers. These TPCs supply curvature momentum and charge sign in the 0.15 T field, plus dE/dx particle ID.
- Together with range-out in the cubes, this ensures the ≥25% muon efficiency at 60–120°.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars (about 1 cm thick) enclosing the target-plus-TPC box.
- Read at both ends by SiPM arrays, giving roughly 150 ps resolution.

**Physics motivation**
- Determines track direction, so a genuine backward muon from the target can be separated from an inward-going particle from out-of-fiducial or magnet interactions.
- Also improves e/μ/p separation at low momentum and supplies an external-background veto.

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Electronics and DAQ.**
  - Waveform digitisation per channel gives charge, time and Michel-electron tagging. Michel tags help identify stopped muons and pions.
- **Calibration.**
  - An LED/laser light-injection system for SiPM gain and timing monitoring.
  - Cosmic-ray triggers to map per-cube light yield across about 3M cubes.
- **Magnet-compatible mechanics.**
  - A non-magnetic support box, so that SiPMs and readout work unaffected in the 0.15 T field.
- **Downstream tracker interface.**
  - Retain or refurbish the existing drift chambers for forward muons, sharing timing with the new subsystems.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a ~1 cm³ 3D-readout plastic-scintillator cube active target (SuperFGD-type, CH ≈ 8% hydrogen nucleons) flanked by high-angle TPCs and a TOF envelope.

Based on the requirements for this near detector upgrade, here are the hardware upgrades the proposal should include:

## 1. **3D Active Target Tracker with High-Pressure Gaseous Hydrogen**
**Technology:** High-pressure (10-20 atm) time projection chamber (TPC) with hydrogen-rich gas mixture (e.g., H₂:Ar or CH₄-based)
**Why:** Provides the required hydrogen content (controllable below 20% nucleon fraction when mixed), enables 3D tracking for all track angles including backward-going particles, and allows detection of short-range recoil protons down to 60 MeV kinetic energy through ionization measurement.

## 2. **Fine-Grained Readout Plane with Pad or Pixel Architecture**
**Technology:** Multi-layer micropattern gas detector (Micromegas or GEM-based) with 2-3 mm pitch pixelated readout
**Why:** Required to achieve sufficient spatial resolution for short proton tracks (~few cm range at 60 MeV) and to reconstruct tracks at all angles, especially those perpendicular to the beam direction where conventional wire chambers have poor resolution.

## 3. **High-Rate, Multi-Channel Electronics**
**Technology:** Modern ASIC-based continuous readout system (e.g., AFTER or similar chip) with ~50,000-100,000 channels
**Why:** The 2.6 m × 2.3 m area with mm-scale granularity requires many channels; accelerator neutrino beams have high instantaneous rates requiring fast electronics; continuous/streaming readout captures all activity for complex multi-track events.

## 4. **Field Cage and HV System**
**Technology:** Lightweight field cage with resistive field-shaping strips, capable of 400-600 V/cm drift field
**Why:** Essential for TPC operation to ensure uniform drift over the 0.9 m drift distance along the beam; must be non-intrusive to minimize inactive material that would create detection gaps for perpendicular and backward tracks.

## 5. **Gas Handling and Monitoring System**
**Technology:** Recirculating gas system with purification, pressure control to ±0.1%, and continuous monitoring of composition, temperature, and pressure
**Why:** Maintaining stable, pure gas conditions is critical for consistent electron drift velocity and gain; pressure stability ensures predictable hydrogen nucleon fraction; hydrogen safety systems required.

## 6. **Calibration System**
**Technology:** UV laser tracks and/or radioactive source deployment system
**Why:** Need to map the drift field, measure electron drift velocity variations, calibrate energy response for short proton tracks, and monitor detector stability over time; particularly important for achieving 25% efficiency uniformly at all angles.

## 7. **Enhanced DAQ and Computing Infrastructure**
**Technology:** GPU-based online computing cluster for real-time 3D reconstruction
**Why:** High channel count and event complexity (multiple tracks at various angles) require substantial computing power; online reconstruction helps with trigger decisions and data volume reduction while ensuring backward tracks aren't lost.

## 8. **Improved Target Region Containment/Shielding**
**Technology:** Low-mass entrance window and optimized side walls with minimal inactive material
**Why:** Tracks perpendicular to the beam must exit into the gas chambers with minimal scattering; backward-going particles need sufficient containment to be measured before exiting upstream.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: High-pressure time projection chamber with hydrogen-rich gas and fine-grained pixel readout, as this single integrated system directly addresses all the critical requirements: hydrogen target content control, 4π angular coverage including backward tracks, low-energy proton detection, and 3D reconstruction capability.

# ND280 Upstream Upgrade Proposal

The P0D would be replaced by three new systems:

1. A 3D-granular scintillator target.
2. Two high-angle TPCs, one above and one below the target.
3. A time-of-flight envelope around the whole upstream region.

All of this sits inside the existing UA1 magnet. The downstream FGD/TPC tracker stays as it is.

## 1. Active target: "SuperFGD", a fully 3D-segmented cube scintillator

**Why the present design fails.** FGD-style planes have bars perpendicular to the beam. Tracks at large angle run along a single bar layer and are poorly reconstructed. Short proton stubs are lost, and the acceptance collapses beyond about 60°. That is exactly where about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the protons go.

**Geometry**
- About 2 million optically isolated polystyrene cubes, each 1 × 1 × 1 cm³.
- Arranged as 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, giving about 1.92 × 1.82 × 0.56 m³.
- This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Target mass is about 2 t of CH, roughly twice FGD1 + FGD2.

**Cube construction**
- Extruded polystyrene doped with about 1.5% PTP and 0.01% POPOP.
- Surface chemically etched to form a white diffuse reflector (about 50–80 µm), which keeps cubes optically isolated.
- Three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes drilled through each cube.

**Readout**
- About 56,000 Kuraray Y-11 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres, threaded along x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read at one end by a Hamamatsu S13360-1325-class MPPC. The far end is mirrored.
- Expected light yield is about 40–50 p.e. per fibre per MIP-cube.
- Each cube gives three 2D projections, so the event is reconstructed in 3D with roughly isotropic, close to 4π acceptance.

**Physics gains**
- **Proton threshold.** A 1 cm pitch means about 300 MeV/c protons (≈1–2 cm range) leave a reconstructable track.
  - The median 450 MeV/c proton has kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of about 8 cm, so it is fully contained.
  - Its momentum then comes from range and dE/dx.
- **Neutron tagging.** Fast timing (about 1 ns per channel, sub-ns per cube with three fibres) allows neutron tagging by time of flight to isolated secondary hits. This gives full transverse-kinematic-imbalance reconstruction for antineutrinos.
- **Electrons and gammas.** Better e/γ separation than the P0D.

**Electronics**
- CITIROC-based front-end boards (or equivalent) with high/low-gain charge and timestamps.
- Mounted outside the target in the magnet gaps.
- Supported by a light-tight carbon-fibre/composite box.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below SuperFGD

These capture high-angle muons and the high-momentum protons (the roughly 6% above 900 MeV/c) that exit the cube target.

**Size and gas**
- Each is about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m.
- Same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ (95:3:2) gas as the existing TPCs.
- Drift field about 275 V/cm.

**Readout: resistive bulk Micromegas (ERAM)**
- A DLC/Kapton resistive layer spreads the charge. This allows larger pads (about 10 × 11 mm) and fewer channels.
- Spatial resolution better than about 0.8 mm.
- dE/dx resolution better than about 10%, for μ/p/e particle ID.
- The resistive layer also gives intrinsic spark protection.
- 8 modules per endplate.
- Read out with AFTER/AGET-based front ends.

**Field cage**
- Thin composite construction (aramid/honeycomb laminate with a Kapton strip foil).
- About 3–4% X₀, which minimizes multiple scattering and dead material next to the target.

**Measurement**
- Magnetic momentum and charge sign for particles leaving SuperFGD at large angle.
- Resolution about 10% at 1 GeV/c.

## 3. Time-of-Flight system

**Layout**
- Six planes fully enclosing SuperFGD + HA-TPCs.
- Each plane uses about 2.2 m cast plastic bars (EJ-200 type, about 12 cm × 1 cm), each read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.

**Performance**
- Time resolution about 150 ps.

**Physics roles**
- Determines track direction (inward vs. outward-going), rejecting out-of-fiducial and backward backgrounds.
- Supports particle ID (p/μ/e) together with dE/dx.
- Provides a T0 for the TPCs.

## 4. Supporting changes

- Remove the P0D and reuse its cradle/basket.
- Add new low-voltage, cooling and DAQ integration into the ND280 clock and trigger.
- Keep FGD2 (water layers) unchanged for the C/H₂O comparison.
- Recalibrate the SMRD/ECal timing to the new TOF.

## Net effect

- The high-angle and backward acceptance gap is closed for both muons and protons.
- The proton threshold drops to about 300 MeV/c.
- Neutron kinematics are added.
- The target mass is doubled.

Together these directly target the drop in systematic uncertainty from about 6% to about 4%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD, a ~2 t target of ~2 million 1 cm³ optically isolated scintillator cubes read by three orthogonal WLS fibres with MPPCs, giving 3D, 4π, low-threshold reconstruction of muons and protons.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

Before proposing upgrades, let me map requirements to hardware constraints:

| Requirement | Challenge |
|-------------|-----------|
| Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at **all angles** including perpendicular and backward | A downstream-only spectrometer misses large-angle and backward tracks entirely |
| Proton KE down to ~60 MeV (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.6 cm in iron) | Very short tracks need fine-grained, low-density active material |
| Hydrogen fraction ≤2% of nucleons | Excludes hydrocarbon-rich scintillator as primary target; needs careful material choice |
| 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume | Must instrument fully in 3D |
| 0.7 GeV peak flux | Multi-pion events, moderate multiplicities, contained vertices needed |

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Replace Passive Target with a 3D Scintillator Cube Array (Primary Recommendation)

Replace the existing passive target material with an array of **small plastic scintillator cubes** (e.g., 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm) read out on three orthogonal faces by **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres** threaded through each cube, following the SuperFGD/SND@LHC design heritage.

- **Granularity**: 1.5 cm cubes give ~1.5 cm 3D space points, sufficient to resolve 60 MeV proton tracks (~3–4 cubes long)
- **4π tracking**: Isotropic hit pattern means no geometric acceptance hole for any track angle, satisfying the perpendicular and backward-going muon requirement
- **Low density**: ~1.0 g/cm³, comparable to water; protons range out in a reconstructable number of cubes
- **Scintillation timing** (~1 ns) distinguishes forward from backward-going tracks via time-of-flight across the volume and resolves multiple interaction vertices per spill

**Hydrogen content concern**: Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has ~7.7% hydrogen by nucleon count — far above the 2% limit. This is addressed in item 3 below.

---

### 2. Add Thin Time-Projection Chambers (TPCs) Interleaved with Scintillator Modules

Insert **gaseous TPCs** (e.g., Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ or pure Ar with Micromegas/GEM readout) as thin active layers interleaved every ~15–20 cm through the target volume in the transverse (XY) planes.

- Provide **continuous 3D track reconstruction** with dE/dx particle identification
- Gas medium has negligible hydrogen fraction (~0% for pure Ar, controllable)
- **Charge sign** of short tracks measured from curvature within the magnet volume
- Momentum measurement of stopping tracks from range + curvature combination
- TPC drift along the beam axis (Z); 50–100 µm spatial resolution achievable

Practical format: panels of ~2.6 m × 2.3 m active area, ~5–8 cm drift gap, ~12–18 panels fitting within the 0.9 m depth.

---

### 3. Use a Low-Hydrogen or Hydrogen-Controlled Target Configuration

Since the hydrogen constraint (≤2% nucleon fraction) conflicts with plastic scintillator, implement one of two strategies:

**Option A — Carbon/Argon dominant target**: Replace scintillator cubes with **liquid argon mini-TPC cells** or **graphite/carbon absorber slabs** instrumented with thin-film sensors. Pure ⁴⁰Ar or ¹²C targets have zero hydrogen.

**Option B — Composite target with fiducial bookkeeping**: Use the scintillator cube array but restrict the physics fiducial volume to regions bounded by **water or liquid argon target modules** that dominate the nucleon count. Thin scintillator planes serve only as tracking layers (not as the interaction target). Target modules could be:
- Removable **water-filled acrylic cells** (H₂O: ~11% H by nucleon, but ¹⁶O dominates at ~89%; blending with argon panels achieves the ≤2% average)
- **Liquid argon sandwich layers**: argon has zero hydrogen; alternating Ar and thin scintillator readout layers can dilute hydrogen below 2% by mass

Recommend **Option B with water targets** as water has well-understood cross-sections and the hydrogen subtraction model is most mature for H₂O targets.

---

### 4. Upgrade the Surrounding Muon Identification System

The existing drift chambers downstream reconstruct forward muons well, but the new requirement for backward and perpendicular muons demands instrumentation on **all six faces** of the target volume:

- **Upstream face**: Add a 2.6 m × 2.3 m array of scintillator tracking planes (3–4 layers, X–Y stereo) immediately upstream of the target, backed by ~20 cm of iron as a muon range stack
- **Side faces (4 lateral surfaces)**: Add scintillator paddle arrays or resistive plate chambers (RPCs) on the ±X and ±Y faces of the magnet bore; the warm magnet yoke steel can serve as partial muon absorber/range stack
- **Downstream face**: Existing drift chambers retained; add scintillator trigger hodoscope for timing
- **Goal**: Muon identification and momentum-by-range for tracks exiting any face; combined with the magnet field for curvature measurement of tracks that traverse sufficient path length (~30–50 cm in field)

For backward-going muons that stop inside the target volume, **range-based momentum reconstruction** from the cube array hit count is sufficient provided the cube-to-cube light yield is calibrated to ≲5% uniformity.

---

### 5. Add a High-Resolution Timing Layer

Install **fast scintillator timing planes** (e.g., LYSO bars or fast plastic with SiPM readout, σ_t ~ 100–200 ps) on the upstream and downstream faces:

- Resolves ambiguity between forward and backward-going tracks when curvature is small (low-momentum or nearly perpendicular tracks)
- Enables **time-of-flight proton/pion separation** over the ~50 cm scale of the target for momenta up to ~600 MeV/c
- Provides beam-spill pile-up rejection at the ~1 ns level

---

### 6. Electronics and DAQ Upgrade

- Replace triggered readout with **continuous waveform digitisation** at ≥250 MHz sampling on all SiPM channels (target: ~500k channels for full cube array)
- Implement **online FPGA-based clustering** to reduce data rate before storage
- Synchronise timing across subsystems to <1 ns using a White Rabbit or similar precision timing network
- This is essential because the 4π tracking geometry generates complex multi-hit patterns requiring full waveform information for disambiguation

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Addresses |
|---------|-----------|
| 3D scintillator cube array | 4π proton tracking, short track reconstruction |
| Interleaved TPCs | 3D muon tracking, dE/dx PID, low hydrogen |
| Water/argon target modules | Hydrogen ≤2% constraint |
| 6-face muon identification | Perpendicular and backward muon efficiency |
| Fast timing planes | Track direction, TOF PID, pile-up rejection |
| Continuous waveform DAQ | Full event reconstruction in complex topology |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a fully 3D fine-grained scintillator cube array (≲1.5 cm cubes, WLS fibre readout, SiPM photosensors) interleaved with thin water target modules to keep the hydrogen nucleon fraction below 2%, providing isotropic acceptance for both short proton tracks and backward/perpendicular muons simultaneously.
