# Proposed upgrade of the Kestrel Flats near-detector target region

The main problem is acceptance. A thin target followed by downstream drift chambers sees forward tracks well, but loses tracks near 90° and backward-going tracks, and short protons stop in passive material. The upgrade should fill the region with a fine-grained, isotropic 3D tracking target, surround it with gas tracking for high-angle muons, and add timing so the direction of every track is known.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D scintillator active target (main item)

**Concept.** Build the target from about 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes (polystyrene with PTP and POPOP dopants, etched reflective surface). Each cube has three orthogonal holes, and each hole holds a 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibre (Kuraray Y-11 type). This is the SuperFGD design.

**Size and channel count.**
- To leave room for the side trackers in section 2, I'd make it about 2.0 m wide × 1.8 m high × 0.6–0.7 m deep. That is roughly 2.2–2.5 million cubes and about 2 t of target.
- The fibres are read in three projections, giving about 60–70k channels rather than millions.
- Readout uses 1.3 mm SiPMs (MPPCs) on the fibre ends, with timing front-end electronics. CITIROC-type ASICs on a time-over-threshold or ADC scheme would work.
- A mirror on the far fibre end improves light yield.

**Why it meets the requirements.**
- **Isotropic muon acceptance.** The three-view cube readout reconstructs tracks equally well in any direction, including near 90° and backward. Planar bar detectors cannot do this.
- **Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV proton travels only about 3 cm in plastic (roughly 3 g/cm²). That gives a short track of about 3 cubes. With about 40–60 photoelectrons per cube per MIP, protons from roughly 50–60 MeV kinetic energy are reconstructable, and dE/dx in the last cubes identifies them.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has 1 hydrogen nucleon in every 13, about 7.7%. Fibres, reflector and supports add little hydrogen. This is well below the 20% limit.
- **Optional far-detector matching.** If the far detector's nuclear target differs, passive layers or modules of that material could be interleaved for cross-target comparison. Water or argon cells would also keep the hydrogen fraction under 20%.
- **Neutron reconstruction.** Sub-nanosecond hit timing (about 0.9 ns per channel, better per track) allows time-of-flight neutron detection.

## 2. High-angle gas TPCs above and below the target

- Place two thin TPCs, about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m each, above and below the target inside the 0.15 T field. Use an Ar–CF₄–iC₄H₁₀ gas mixture (T2K-type).
- Read them out with **resistive Micromegas** (encapsulated resistive-anode type) for good charge spreading and point resolution of about 0.3–0.5 mm.
- Build the field cages from light composite (aramid/laminate) to minimise dead material.
- They measure momentum and charge of muons exiting near 90°, which miss the downstream chambers. They also give dE/dx particle ID to separate muons from pions and electrons.

## 3. Time-of-flight enclosure

- Surround the target and TPC assembly with plastic scintillator bars (about 2 m long, 12 cm wide) read at both ends by arrays of large SiPMs.
- The target ~100–150 ps timing resolution distinguishes forward from backward going tracks unambiguously. It also helps reject particles entering from outside and improves electron/muon separation.

## 4. Supporting items

- **Mechanics.** A carbon-fibre or low-Z support box for the cubes, with survey and fibre-routing panels.
- **Calibration.** A cosmic-ray trigger plus an LED/laser light-injection system for SiPM gain and timing calibration.
- **Magnetic field.** Map the field over the new volume. At 0.15 T, the low momentum resolution for short tracks comes mainly from range in the target.
- **Integration.** Common clock and DAQ distribution to all subsystems, and integration with the existing downstream drift chambers so forward tracks keep full momentum measurement.

Together these give at least 25% muon efficiency at all angles, protons down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy, and a hydrogen fraction of about 8%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fine-grained 3D-readout plastic scintillator cube active target (SuperFGD-style, ~1 cm³ cubes, three-view WLS fibres with SiPM readout), with resistive-Micromegas high-angle TPCs around it.

# Design Review Panel Recommendation: ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Executive Summary

The core challenge is instrumented-target design that simultaneously provides sufficient neutrino interaction rate, near-4π acceptance for large-angle tracks (>50°), and momentum resolution adequate for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis — all within 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m and constrained by the existing magnet field geometry.

---

## 1. Primary Active Target: Scintillator-Based SuperFGD

**Technology: Plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³), 3D grid readout**

Replace the P0D volume with a "SuperFGD" — an array of approximately 2 × 10⁷ extruded polystyrene cubes, each ~10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm, drilled along all three axes (x, y, z) for WLS fibre readout, each fibre read by a MPPC.

**Justification:**
- The existing FGD bar geometry (1D segmentation per layer) fails to reconstruct tracks at >50°; a fully 3D granular structure provides isotropic spatial resolution (~1 mm effective vertex resolution) regardless of track angle, directly addressing the stated 25%/35% large-angle loss for muons and protons respectively.
- The 1 cm³ cell size gives a proton tracking threshold of approximately 300–350 MeV/c kinetic energy (range ~3–4 cm, crossing 3–4 cells), compatible with the median proton momentum of 450 MeV/c and capturing the bulk of the distribution.
- Hydrocarbon target (polystyrene, C₈H₈) is explicitly acceptable per the physics programme; this gives high statistics for the hydrogen/carbon comparison when combined with FGD2's water layers downstream.
- The ~0.6 m depth constraint is satisfied: a 56-layer deep structure at 1 cm pitch fits with margin for support frames.
- This technology has been prototyped by the T2K collaboration (the Baby MIND and SuperFGD prototype beam tests at CERN 2017–2021 demonstrate exactly this concept); the collaboration has in-house expertise.
- Target mass in the available volume: ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.56 m active, density ~1.05 g/cm³ → approximately **2.0 tonnes**, roughly doubling the upstream interaction statistics relative to FGD1+FGD2 combined.
- The 3D topology allows dE/dx-based particle identification: proton/pion separation is achievable up to ~1 GeV/c using Bragg peak identification in the cube array, covering the stated 6% tail above 900 MeV/c.

**Specific hardware elements:**
- ~2 × 10⁷ Kuraray Y-11(200) WLS fibres (1 mm diameter) along x, y, z axes
- Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE MPPCs (1.3 mm × 1.3 mm, 25 μm pixel pitch): ~600,000 channels; at ~$5–8 USD/channel this is the dominant cost item and should be reviewed against budget
- Custom injection-moulded cubes with 3 perpendicular holes, interlocked without adhesive (friction fit + compression frame), following the CERN prototype fabrication procedure

---

## 2. Upstream Veto / Gamma Catcher: Thin Scintillator Panels

**Technology: Extruded scintillator hodoscope planes**

Install two layers of 5 mm thick extruded scintillator panels (Fermilab-style, triangular cross-section, staggered) on the upstream face and four lateral faces of the SuperFGD volume, each read by a single MPPC via WLS fibre.

**Justification:**
- Charged-current event selection requires rejection of interactions occurring in material upstream of the active target (remaining P0D support structure, target walls). An upstream veto panel with >99% efficiency for minimum-ionising particles is essential.
- Lateral panels extend soft-track containment: tracks exiting sideways at large angles are tagged before entering the ECal, allowing the ECal to serve as a range stack rather than merely a veto.
- Thin (5 mm) panels introduce negligible additional material (<0.5% X₀) upstream of the target, keeping the neutrino interaction vertex clean.
- Same WLS + MPPC technology as the SuperFGD reduces procurement complexity and allows shared calibration infrastructure.

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight System: Fast Plastic Scintillator Planes

**Technology: Dedicated TOF planes, 200–300 ps resolution**

Install thin (1 cm) fast plastic scintillator planes (EJ-230 or BC-420) at the upstream and downstream faces of the SuperFGD, read by large-area SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE) with fast front-end ASICs (TARGET or MUSIC chips).

**Justification:**
- The leading-proton median momentum is 450 MeV/c (kinetic energy ~100 MeV), giving β ≈ 0.73 for protons versus β ≈ 1 for pions of the same momentum. Over a ~60 cm flight path, Δt ≈ 0.9 ns — comfortably resolved at 200 ps resolution — providing proton/pion separation independent of dE/dx for forward-going tracks that do not stop in the SuperFGD.
- TOF also provides backward/forward track direction disambiguation: a critical degeneracy in a symmetric 3D detector with no drift time reference.
- Beam timing structure at J-PARC (8 bunches/spill, ~580 ns bunch width) means out-of-time interactions from beam halo or cosmics are suppressed at the ~ns level.
- The T2K-II TOF prototype (demonstrated at CERN test beam 2019) achieved 174 ps resolution with EJ-230 and 6 mm SiPMs; this is directly applicable.
- Impact on TKI analysis: incorrect proton identification is a leading systematic in current analyses; independent TOF confirmation reduces this uncertainty by an estimated factor of 2–3 for forward protons.

---

## 4. Thin High-Pressure Gas TPC Option for the Downstream Buffer

**Technology: Small-volume TPC as downstream tracker**

Retain a thin (10–15 cm deep) gas TPC (Ar:CF4:iC4H10 or pure Ar with CF4 admixture) immediately downstream of the SuperFGD within the available 0.6 m envelope, using resistive Micromegas pads.

**Justification:**
- Tracks exiting the downstream face of the SuperFGD — primarily forward-going muons and high-momentum protons — enter the existing TPC1 downstream, but there is a ~5–10 cm dead zone in the current geometry between the P0D region and TPC1. A thin buffer TPC eliminates this acceptance gap.
- The 0.2 T field gives a sagitta of ~1 mm for a 1 GeV/c track over 50 cm, marginal but measurable; the downstream full TPCs provide the primary momentum measurement. The buffer TPC primarily extends pattern recognition for tracks at 20–40° that clip the corner of TPC1.
- Gas TPC adds negligible material (~0.05% X₀/cm for Ar-based gas at 1 atm).
- **Caveat for panel:** This component is optional if the SuperFGD's inherent 3D tracking plus existing TPC1 provide sufficient acceptance. The panel recommends a detailed GEANT4 acceptance study before committing to this hardware, as it competes for the available 0.6 m depth with SuperFGD active volume. If the SuperFGD occupies 56 cm, only ~4 cm remain — insufficient for a useful TPC drift. **Recommendation: drop the buffer TPC and maximise SuperFGD depth to ~58 cm.**

---

## 5. Calibration Infrastructure

**Technology: LED pulser system + cosmic muon trigger**

Install a dedicated UV-LED pulser network (one LED per 100 MPPCs, controlled by a common clock) and a dedicated cosmic trigger scintillator paddle pair (above and below the magnet yoke, read by PMTs) operating between spills.

**Justification:**
- With ~600,000 MPPC channels, gain drift with temperature and radiation is a leading calibration systematic. LED pulsing at the 0.1–1 p.e. level measures gain to <0.3% per channel per hour, meeting the requirements for <4% total systematic.
- Cosmic muons traversing the full 1.9 m lateral dimension provide a continuous geometric alignment sample and dE/dx calibration reference independent of beam. Expected cosmic rate through the SuperFGD volume: ~100 muons/second, giving ~10⁷ tracks/day, sufficient for per-cube efficiency maps.
- Both systems are low-cost additions (<2% of total detector cost) with outsized impact on systematic uncertainty control.

---

## Systematic Uncertainty Impact Summary

| Change | Primary Uncertainty Addressed | Estimated Reduction |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD (3D cubes) | Large-angle track acceptance | ~1.5% on total |
| TOF planes | Proton/pion ID; direction ambiguity | ~0.8% on total |
| Upstream veto | Interaction vertex purity | ~0.4% on total |
| LED+cosmic calibration | MPPC gain stability | ~0.3% on total |

Combined, these changes are designed to bring the upstream detector contribution to the ND280 systematic budget from its current ~6% to the T2K-II target of ≤4%.

---

## Critical Risk Items for the Panel

1. **Channel count / cost**: 600k MPPC channels is a significant procurement and QA challenge. The panel recommends reviewing whether 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm cubes (reducing channel count by ~3×) remain consistent with proton tracking threshold requirements before finalising the cube size.
2. **Structural integrity**: The interlocked cube assembly must survive the magnet's fringe field forces and seismic loads at J-PARC. A mechanical prototype test at full scale is mandatory before production commitment.
3. **Readout bandwidth**: 600k channels at the J-PARC spill rate requires careful front-end ASIC selection (CITIROC or equivalent) and data concentration architecture review to avoid deadtime.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a 3D plastic scintillator cube (SuperFGD) active target of ~1 cm³ granularity with x/y/z WLS-fibre and MPPC readout, as this single change provides the near-4π acceptance for large-angle proton and muon tracks that is the primary kinematic limitation of the current detector and is the prerequisite for all TKI-based systematic reduction goals.

# Design Review Recommendations for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis Requirements Summary
- **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m in 0.15 T magnetic field
- **Critical needs**: 
  - ≥25% muon efficiency at ALL angles (including perpendicular and backward)
  - Proton tracking down to ~60 MeV KE at all angles
  - ≤20% hydrogen content by nucleon count
  - 3D reconstruction capability

## Recommended Hardware Configuration

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Primary Recommendation)**

**Technology**: Extruded plastic scintillator bars (1.0 cm × 1.0 cm cross-section) in X-Y alternating layers, read out by wavelength-shifting fibers and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Justification**:
- **Angular coverage**: Fine segmentation with XY layers provides true 3D tracking essential for perpendicular and backward tracks that would be poorly measured in beam-oriented geometries
- **Low-energy protons**: 60 MeV protons have ~1 cm range in plastic scintillator; 1 cm granularity enables detection and stopping power measurement
- **Timing**: <5 ns timing resolution separates forward/backward ambiguities in magnetic field
- **Low hydrogen**: Plastic scintillator (CH₁.₁) has ~45% hydrogen by nucleon count—TOO HIGH alone
- **Proven technology**: Successfully deployed in MINERvA, T2K ND280

**Specification**: ~90 layers of alternating X-Y orientation, ~2600 bars per layer, ~235,000 channels total

### 2. **Hydrocarbon Target Dilution with High-Z Passive Layers**

**Technology**: Interleave every 3-4 scintillator layers with 2 mm lead or iron sheets.

**Justification**:
- **Hydrogen reduction**: Reduces effective hydrogen fraction from 45% to ~15-18% while maintaining tracking
- **Nuclear target diversity**: Provides heavy nuclear targets matching far detector composition
- **Controlled systematics**: Well-understood nuclear effects on lead/iron
- **Minimal tracking impact**: Thin sheets don't significantly degrade tracking resolution

**Alternative considered**: Pure polystyrene bars would reduce hydrogen slightly but insufficient; C₈H₈ still ~38% hydrogen.

### 3. **Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Insert (Central Region)**

**Technology**: Small gaseous TPC module (1.0 m × 1.0 m × 0.6 m) with resistive Micromegas readout, using Ar:CH₄ (95:5) at 1 atm, positioned in central target volume.

**Justification**:
- **Low hydrogen**: Gas target has ~0.5% hydrogen by nucleon at 1 atm—negligible contribution
- **Superior resolution**: ~1 mm spatial resolution for detailed vertex reconstruction
- **dE/dx particle ID**: Continuous ionization measurement distinguishes protons/pions/muons
- **Complementary acceptance**: Handles complex topologies that challenge scintillator tracking
- **Minimal material**: Doesn't obstruct particles entering surrounding detectors

**Risk mitigation**: MicroBooNE and ND-GAr demonstrate feasibility; keep volume fraction <25% of total

### 4. **Silicon Vertex Detector Upgrade**

**Technology**: 4-5 layers of AC-coupled silicon microstrip sensors (50 μm pitch) within first 10 cm of target volume.

**Justification**:
- **Vertex resolution**: <100 μm resolution critical for separating primary vertex from secondary interactions
- **Short proton tracks**: Silicon captures very short proton stubs that may not reach scintillator layers
- **Minimal hydrogen**: Pure silicon contributes zero hydrogen
- **Angle measurement**: Precise initial angle determination for tracks going perpendicular or backward

**Specification**: ~300 cm² per layer, ~6000 channels total

### 5. **Enhanced Photon Detection System**

**Technology**: Add wavelength-shifting reflector panels on all six inner magnet walls with dedicated SiPM readout.

**Justification**:
- **π⁰ reconstruction**: Critical for neutral current background rejection and energy reconstruction
- **Wide angle coverage**: Captures photons at all angles, especially backward-going
- **Energy measurement**: Calorimetric information for electromagnetic showers
- **Minimal space**: Uses otherwise inactive surfaces

## Implementation Priority

**Phase 1** (Essential for basic requirements):
- 3D scintillator tracker with passive absorber layers
- Enhanced photon detection

**Phase 2** (Performance optimization):
- Central TPC module
- Silicon vertex detector

## Cost-Benefit Analysis

| Component | Channels | Est. Cost | Addresses Critical Need |
|-----------|----------|-----------|------------------------|
| Scintillator | 235k | $3-4M | All-angle tracking, protons |
| Passive layers | N/A | $200k | H₂ fraction requirement |
| TPC | 20k | $1.5M | Vertex resolution, PID |
| Silicon | 6k | $800k | Short protons, vertex |
| Photon system | 2k | $300k | π⁰ rejection |

## Alternative Rejected: LAr TPC
Liquid argon would provide excellent imaging but:
- Zero hydrogen (need some for cross-section model constraints)
- Poor timing resolution creates forward/backward ambiguities
- Slow drift limits rate capability at near detector location

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Implement 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker with interleaved passive absorber layers to achieve all-angle tracking coverage while meeting the hydrogen fraction constraint.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target Upgrade

## Constraints Analysis

Before recommending technologies, let me extract the binding constraints:

1. **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (~5.4 m³)
2. **Muon tracking**: ≥25% efficiency at **all angles**, including 90° and backward — this kills any technology with strong forward bias
3. **Proton tracking**: down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range in water ~3 cm, range in scintillator ~4 cm) — requires fine granularity or low-density medium
4. **Hydrogen fraction**: ≤20% of target nucleons by number — this constrains material choice severely
5. **Existing magnet**: 0.15 T over 6.5 m — momentum measurement handled downstream; the active target must handle **angular and vertex reconstruction**
6. **Beam peak**: 0.7 GeV — typical final states: 1 muon + 1–3 hadrons, modest multiplicities

---

## The Hydrogen Constraint — A Critical Starting Point

This constraint is frequently underappreciated. Consider candidate materials:

| Material | H fraction (by nucleon number) |
|---|---|
| Pure CH₂ (polyethylene) | 2/16 = **12.5%** ✓ |
| Pure CH (polystyrene base) | 1/13 ≈ **7.7%** ✓ |
| Water (H₂O) | 2/18 ≈ **11.1%** ✓ |
| Liquid argon | **0%** ✓ |
| Pure CH₄ gas | 4/16 = **25%** ✗ |
| C₃H₈ (propane) | 8/44 ≈ **18.2%** ✓ barely |
| Pure hydrogen | **100%** ✗ |

Plastic scintillator (polystyrene-based, ~CH) passes comfortably. Liquid argon passes trivially. Gaseous detectors need careful gas choice.

---

## Recommendation 1: Plastic Scintillator with 3D Crossed-Cube Granularity (SuperFGD Architecture)

**Technology**: The Super Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD) concept — a lattice of ~1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes, each read out on three orthogonal axes via wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Justification**:

- **Isotropic tracking**: 3D crossed-fiber readout has no preferred tracking direction by construction. A track at 90° to the beam crosses the same number of cubes as a forward track of the same length. Backward-going muons are reconstructed identically to forward ones. This directly satisfies the hardest geometric requirement.
- **Short proton tracks**: A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range of ~3.5 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³). At 1 cm³ cube size, this gives ~3–4 lit cubes — sufficient for a track stub, angle measurement, and dE/dx-based PID to distinguish protons from pions.
- **Hydrogen fraction**: Polystyrene C₈H₈ gives H/(H+C) ≈ 8/16 = **8 nucleons in 8**, so 8H per 16 total nucleons = **50% by count** — wait, this needs careful handling.

> **Recalculation**: Polystyrene monomer C₈H₈. Nucleon count: 8×12 (carbon) + 8×1 (hydrogen) = 96 + 8 = 104. Hydrogen fraction = 8/104 ≈ **7.7%**. ✓ Well within the 20% limit.

- **No hydrogen-rich additive needed**: The base scintillator already satisfies the constraint without dilution.
- **Self-supporting, fully active**: No passive absorber layers, maximizing fiducial mass and interaction rate.
- **Demonstrated technology**: SuperFGD is being installed in T2K's ND280 upgrade; beam tests confirm ~1 cm³ cube performance, ~50 p.e. per cube, SiPM noise manageable.
- **SiPM operation in magnetic field**: SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields (unlike PMTs), compatible with the 0.15 T dipole environment.

**Implementation for this volume**: 260 × 230 × 90 cubes ≈ **5.4 million cubes**, with fibers running in X, Y, Z. Approximately 260+230+90 = 580 fiber planes × ~600 fibers/plane ≈ 350,000 SiPM channels. This is large but within current production capability (T2K SuperFGD has ~56,000 channels for a smaller volume; scaling is a procurement and cost challenge, not a physics or technical barrier).

---

## Recommendation 2: Retain and Upgrade the Downstream Gas Drift Chamber — Add a Straw Tube Tracker (STT) Interface Layer

**Technology**: A 2–3 radiation length straw tube tracker (aluminized Mylar straws, ~1 cm diameter, Ar/CO₂ or Ar/isobutane gas fill) as a transition layer between the active target and the existing drift chambers.

**Justification**:

- **Track matching**: The existing warm dipole + downstream drift chambers measure momentum by curvature. Tracks leaving the SuperFGD cube target must be matched into the downstream tracker. A straw tube layer provides high-precision hit positions (σ ~150 µm per straw) for clean matching.
- **90° and large-angle muons**: A muon leaving the SuperFGD sideways (along ±X or ±Y, perpendicular to beam Z) will not enter the downstream tracker at all. The straw tube layer, if extended to wrap the sides of the active target volume, intercepts these tracks. **Straw tube layers on the lateral faces** of the 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section capture transverse muons for momentum measurement via the magnet field integral along their path.
- **Gas hydrogen fraction**: Ar/CO₂ (80/20) has zero hydrogen. Ar/isobutane introduces some hydrogen (C₄H₁₀ → 10H per 58 nucleons ≈ 17%), but at 20% isobutane fraction in the gas, and given the small material budget of the straw walls themselves, the **effective hydrogen contribution to the overall target nucleon count is negligible** (gas density ~1.7 kg/m³ vs. ~1050 kg/m³ for the cube target).
- **Muon backward tracking**: Backward muons re-enter the SuperFGD and are tracked there; the STT is not needed for them specifically. But the STT aids in resolving charge-sign ambiguity for tracks that curve in the magnet and re-enter the active target.
- **Existing infrastructure reuse**: The collaboration already has experience with the downstream drift chambers; straw tube technology is closely related and can share gas and HV infrastructure.

---

## Recommendation 3: Timing Layer — Scintillator Trigger Planes with Sub-nanosecond Resolution

**Technology**: Thin (5–10 mm) plastic scintillator planes with SiPM readout on the upstream face and the four lateral faces of the active target, achieving ≤500 ps timing resolution per plane.

**Justification**:

- **Beam spill pile-up rejection**: At 0.7 GeV peak energy, the neutrino interaction rate scales with the beam intensity. Timing allows multiple interactions within the same beam spill (~microsecond duration) to be separated.
- **Backward-going track identification**: A backward muon exits the upstream face of the target. Without a dedicated timing plane there, it could be confused with a beam-related particle entering from upstream (e.g., a beam halo muon). A timing plane on the upstream face with ~500 ps resolution confirms the track's direction of travel from time-of-flight across two planes.
- **Neutron tagging**: At 0.7 GeV, quasi-elastic interactions produce neutrons in neutral-current events. Fast neutron timing (~1 ns resolution) enables crude neutron momentum reconstruction via time-of-flight, useful for systematic studies even if not central to the analysis.
- **Low additional cost**: Thin scintillator planes covering six faces of ~2.6×2.3 m² and 2×0.9 m² add modest material (<<1% X₀) and negligible hydrogen contribution.
- **SiPM compatibility**: As with the cube target, SiPMs operate unaffected in the 0.15 T field.

---

## Recommendation 4: Replace or Supplement Upstream Face Coverage with a Micromegas or µRWELL Thin Tracking Plane

**Technology**: One or two layers of Micromegas (Micro-MEsh Gaseous Structure) or µRWELL detectors, using Ar/CO₂ gas, covering the full upstream face (2.6 m × 2.3 m).

**Justification**:

- **Backward muon momentum seeding**: A backward-going muon exits the upstream face and travels toward the neutrino production target direction (upstream). There are no magnets upstream of the near detector in the beam line described. The existing dipole downstream can still measure the momentum of a backward muon **if** the muon is reflected by the magnetic field back through the detector — but at 0.15 T over 6.5 m, the bending radius for a 500 MeV/c muon is r = p/(qB) ≈ 11 m, far larger than the magnet length. Most backward muons will not curve back. Therefore, momentum of backward muons must be estimated from **range within the SuperFGD** (using dE/dx and total path length in cubes). The Micromegas plane at the upstream face provides a **precise entry/exit point and angle** for range-to-momentum conversion, reducing systematic error on track length from ~1 cm (cube size) to ~300 µm.
- **Thin radiation length**: Micromegas active gaps of ~128 µm with a thin copper mesh contribute <<0.1% X₀ — does not disturb the upstream neutrino beam environment or cause rescattering of outgoing particles before they clear the target.
- **Ar/CO₂ gas**: Zero hydrogen contribution.
- **Perpendicular track efficiency**: Tracks at exactly 90° to the beam that exit via the top or bottom (2.6 m × 0.9 m faces) or sides (2.3 m × 0.9 m faces) benefit from the 3D cube tracking. The upstream Micromegas specifically addresses the backward hemisphere.
- **Demonstrated at scale**: Micromegas planes at this area scale (~6 m²) have been built for ATLAS New Small Wheel (~2500 m² total); the technology is mature.

---

## Recommendation 5: Light-weight Muon Momentum System for Large-Angle Tracks — Do Not Add a Downstream Magnet Range Stack

**What NOT to do (and why)**:

It might be tempting to add a magnetized iron range stack immediately downstream to catch large-angle muons before they miss the existing drift chambers. **Do not do this.**

- Iron has zero hydrogen, which is fine, but its high density (7.87 g/cm³) means a 25 cm iron slab adds more material than the entire active target. Any shower in the iron contaminates the event reconstruction.
- Large-angle muons that miss the existing downstream tracker can have their momentum estimated from range in the SuperFGD cube target, which is sufficient at this beam energy (mean muon momentum ~400–600 MeV/c → range ~100–200 cm in plastic scintillator → measurable to ~3% from range alone if scintillator response is well-calibrated).
- The existing warm dipole already provides momentum measurement for forward tracks. The design should exploit what exists.

---

## Summary Table

| Recommendation | Technology | Addresses |
|---|---|---|
| 1 (Primary) | SuperFGD plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³) + WLS fibers + SiPMs | All-angle tracking, short proton tracks, H fraction |
| 2 | Straw tube tracker interface layer (lateral faces) | Large-angle muon momentum, track matching |
| 3 | Thin scintillator timing planes on all 6 faces, SiPM readout | Pile-up rejection, backward track direction, neutrons |
| 4 | Micromegas/µRWELL on upstream face | Backward muon track seeding and angle precision |
| 5 (Avoid) | ~~Magnetized iron range stack~~ | — |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the existing passive target with a SuperFGD-style lattice of ~1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes read out on three orthogonal axes via WLS fibers and SiPMs, providing intrinsically isotropic 3D tracking that simultaneously satisfies the all-angle muon efficiency requirement, resolves short (~3–4 cube) proton tracks from 60 MeV protons via dE/dx, and keeps the hydrogen nucleon fraction at ~7.7%, well within the 20% model validity limit.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Next Phase

---

## 1. SuperFGD — 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target (Primary New Target)

**Technology:** A monolithic array of approximately 2×10⁶ plastic scintillator cubes, each 1×1×1 cm³, assembled into a ~192×184×56 cm block fitting the available 2.0×1.9×0.6 m upstream volume. Each cube is threaded by three wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres along orthogonal x, y, z axes, each fibre read by an MPPC at one end (the other end mirrored). Total ~57,600 channels.

**Physics motivation:**
- The 1 cm³ granularity gives an effective tracking threshold of roughly 3 mm, corresponding to a proton kinetic energy threshold of ~40 MeV (momentum ~300 MeV/c), well below the median leading-proton momentum of 450 MeV/c. This is essential to reconstruct the leading proton in the majority of CC events.
- The fully 3D readout eliminates the x/y ambiguity of planar FGDs: tracks at any angle — including the 35% of leading protons and 25% of muons that exit beyond 50° — are reconstructed without ghost hits or pattern-recognition failure at large angles. Conventional 2D-layered detectors lose efficiency precisely at these large polar angles.
- Complete 4π angular acceptance is required for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) variables (δp_T, δα_T, δφ_T), which demand simultaneous reconstruction of the muon and leading proton 3-momenta. Missing even one large-angle proton biases the TKI distributions, propagating directly into cross-section and flux systematics.
- The hydrocarbon (CH) scintillator target is explicitly acceptable per the physics programme, and the carbon content is well-matched to that of the downstream FGD1 for consistent systematic comparisons.
- The fine segmentation also provides dE/dx-based particle identification (π±, p, μ separation), reducing backgrounds from charge-exchange and secondary interactions within the target itself.

---

## 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Six planes of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., 7 mm thick EJ-230 or similar), each roughly 2.0×2.0 m², instrumented with large-area MPPCs or SiPMs via WLS bars, surrounding the SuperFGD on all six faces (upstream, downstream, and four transverse faces). Target time resolution: σ_t ≈ 0.3–0.5 ns.

**Physics motivation:**
- At 450 MeV/c a proton has β ≈ 0.43 (γ ≈ 1.11), while a pion at the same momentum has β ≈ 0.95. Over a 50 cm path, Δt ≈ 1.3 ns — comfortably resolved at 0.5 ns resolution. This extends proton PID down to momenta where dE/dx in the SuperFGD is ambiguous and before the proton range is long enough for TPC identification.
- Directional ambiguity (is the particle entering or exiting?) is broken unambiguously by ToF, critical for large-angle tracks that cross only a few cm of SuperFGD before exiting.
- Neutron detection: ToF identifies neutral particles exiting as n vs. γ, relevant for NC background rejection and future neutron-TKI studies.
- The ToF also provides an independent, precise event time stamp, reducing pile-up confusion at J-PARC's 8-bunch beam structure (~580 ns spill).

---

## 3. High-Pressure Gas TPC (HPTPC) or Upgraded TPC Readout with Resistive Micromegas

**Technology:** Upgrade the three existing TPCs — or add a dedicated smaller TPC module between SuperFGD and the downstream ECal — by replacing the existing bulk Micromegas with resistive-strip Micromegas pads (strip pitch ~1–3 mm, resistive layer to suppress ion back-flow and sparks). Alternatively, replace the gas mixture Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 with a higher-drift-velocity mixture (e.g., add a small He fraction) to improve timing.

**Physics motivation:**
- The existing TPCs provide muon momentum measurement by curvature in the 0.2 T magnet field, but their momentum resolution degrades for high-angle tracks. Resistive Micromegas improves the point resolution from ~700 μm to ~200 μm, directly improving δp/p for muons above 1 GeV/c.
- The 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c are too penetrating to stop in the SuperFGD (~30 cm of plastic) and must be measured by curvature in the TPC; improved resolution here directly reduces the high-momentum tail uncertainty in TKI distributions.
- Resistive readout reduces the discharge rate by ~100×, improving detector live-time and reducing systematic uncertainty from inefficiency corrections — directly relevant to the target of reducing overall systematics from 6% to 4%.

---

## 4. Thin Upstream Gamma-Veto / ECal Extension

**Technology:** Two planes of Pb–scintillator sampling calorimeter (2 mm Pb + 10 mm plastic scintillator strips, ~4 X₀ total) placed immediately upstream of the SuperFGD, 2.0×1.9 m², with WLS fibre + MPPC readout. This extends the existing downstream and barrel ECal coverage to close the upstream solid-angle gap.

**Physics motivation:**
- π⁰ production (NC and CC) generates photons that convert and can mimic proton recoil tracks in the SuperFGD if they enter from upstream. Closing the upstream gap vetoes these photons before they reach the active target.
- For TKI studies, a contamination of NC π⁰ events mimicking CC-0π is a leading source of selection uncertainty. The veto reduces this background, directly improving the purity of the CC signal sample.
- It also tags photons from outside the fiducial volume, allowing a data-driven estimation of the external-background rate — an important cross-check for the 4% systematic target.

---

## 5. SMRD Timing Upgrade

**Technology:** Replace the existing WLS-fibre + PMT readout of the SMRD scintillator slabs in the magnet yoke gaps with SiPM (MPPC) readout, adding offline waveform digitization (flash-ADC at 250 MHz). This achieves σ_t ≈ 1 ns per SMRD slab vs. the current ~5 ns.

**Physics motivation:**
- The SMRD is the primary muon-range detector for muons that escape the inner detectors laterally. At 0.6 GeV beam energy, a significant fraction of muons produced at >50° stop in or range out through the magnet yoke. Improved timing allows ToF-assisted momentum measurement, complementing curvature for these large-angle muons that may traverse only a short arc in the TPC.
- Better SMRD timing also improves cosmic-ray rejection during the beam spill (8-bunch structure), reducing the accidental background rate in the new upstream target — particularly important since the SuperFGD occupies a region that was previously largely passive.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key physics driver |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD | 1 cm³ scintillator cubes, 3-axis WLS+MPPC | 4π proton reconstruction, TKI completeness |
| ToF planes | Fast scintillator, σ_t ~0.5 ns | Proton PID at low p, direction disambiguation |
| Resistive Micromegas TPC | Resistive-strip pads, ~200 μm resolution | High-p proton & muon momentum resolution |
| Upstream gamma veto ECal | Thin Pb–scintillator sampling | NC π⁰ background rejection |
| SMRD SiPM upgrade | Flash-ADC waveform, σ_t ~1 ns | Large-angle muon ranging, cosmic rejection |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream P0D volume with a SuperFGD 3D scintillator-cube active target, as it is the singular change that enables kinematically complete CC event reconstruction with full 4π angular acceptance for both the muon and leading recoil proton — the prerequisite for all transverse kinematic imbalance analyses — while its fine granularity and dE/dx PID directly address the dominant sources of the residual 6% systematic uncertainty that T2K-II must reduce to 4%.

# Hardware Upgrades for Near Detector Enhancement

## 1. **New Active Neutrino Target: 3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (FGT)**

**Technology:** Super-fine granularity plastic scintillator with multi-dimensional readout
- **Specific design:** ~10 million 1×1×1 cm³ scintillator cubes or extruded bars in crossed layers (X-Y-Z configuration)
- **Readout:** Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber planes embedded through the volume, each fiber read by multi-pixel silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)
- **Alternative:** Extruded scintillator bars of 5-6 mm cross-section in alternating triplets (0°, +60°, -60°) for 3D reconstruction

**Why:** 
- Large angular acceptance for the 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50° 
- Fine granularity enables reconstruction of short, low-energy proton tracks (450 MeV/c median → ~20-30 cm range in plastic)
- 3D readout essential for separating close tracks and measuring angles precisely for transverse kinematic imbalance
- 2.0×1.9×0.6 m volume provides ~2.3 m³ ≈ 2.4 t fiducial mass

## 2. **Upgraded Gas TPC Systems**

**Technology:** Higher-pressure argon TPCs (replacing existing low-pressure design)
- **Specific upgrade:** Increase operating pressure from ~1 atm to 5-10 atm
- **Enhanced readout:** Finer-pitch micromegas or resistive MM with charge/timing separation for improved dE/dx

**Why:**
- Higher stopping power to contain the 6% of protons >900 MeV/c (current atmospheric pressure inadequate)
- Better momentum resolution through multiple scattering and range measurements
- Improved particle ID for proton/pion separation through high-resolution dE/dx

## 3. **Extended Tracking in Magnet Volume**

**Technology:** Additional low-mass tracker planes inside magnet
- **Specific design:** 10-15 planes of thin (5 mm) scintillator with embedded fibers, positioned at 15-20 cm intervals
- **Alternative:** Straw tube tracker arrays for minimal material

**Why:**
- Momentum measurement via curvature for high-angle tracks entering magnet from new upstream target
- Critical for the 25% of muons exiting at large angles
- Improved charge identification and momentum resolution

## 4. **Enhanced Electromagnetic Calorimeter Upstream Cap**

**Technology:** Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter with fine longitudinal segmentation
- **Specific design:** 30-40 layers of 2 mm lead + 5 mm scintillator, positioned immediately downstream of new target
- **Readout:** Individual layer readout with 10×10 cm² transverse segmentation

**Why:**
- Photon detection/rejection from π⁰ production (critical background to exclusive channels)
- Electron identification for νₑ background rejection
- Shower energy measurement for neutral current background estimation

## 5. **Time-of-Flight (ToF) System**

**Technology:** Fast scintillator planes with precision timing
- **Specific design:** 2-4 planes of 5 mm fast plastic scintillator with SiPM arrays
- **Timing resolution:** <200 ps per plane
- **Positions:** Immediately after new target and at magnet entrance/exit

**Why:**
- Particle ID for proton/pion/kaon separation (essential at 450 MeV/c where dE/dx bands overlap)
- Reject cosmic-ray backgrounds
- Validate track matching between detector subsystems

## 6. **Silicon Photomultiplier Array Upgrade**

**Technology:** Replace first-generation SiPMs with modern, higher-performance devices
- **Specific upgrade:** VUV-sensitive SiPMs with:
  - Lower dark count rate (<100 kHz/mm² at 20°C)
  - Improved photon detection efficiency (>40% at 450 nm)

**Why:**
- Improved signal/noise for low-energy proton dE/dx measurements
- Better timing resolution (benefits ToF if integrated)
- Reduced systematic uncertainties in energy calibration

**Technology:** Free-running, continuous readout DAQ
- **Specific design:** 
  - GPU-based online event building and filtering
  - Trigger-less architecture with software event selection
  - 10-100 GB/s sustained throughput

**Why:**
- Capture low-energy recoil activity (protons near threshold)
- Reduce bias from trigger efficiency uncertainties

- Reduction of systematic uncertainties from 6% to 4% requires <2% detector response calibration

# Design Review Recommendations: ND280 Upstream Upgrade

## The problem the upgrade must solve

The current tracker cannot deliver kinematically complete charged-current events across the full phase space. There are two structural reasons.

**1. Angular acceptance.** The FGD bars and the TPC drift volumes all face the beam.
- A track at more than about 50–60° to the beam runs nearly parallel to the FGD layers. It crosses few planes and is badly reconstructed.
- Such a track also misses the downstream TPCs, so its momentum and dE/dx particle identification are lost.
- At this beam that affects about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons. These are exactly the events that transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies and the 6% → 4% systematic goal depend on.
- Backward-going tracks also have no reliable direction (time-of-flight) tag.

**2. Proton threshold.**
- In 1 cm bars a short proton track must cross several orthogonal layers before it can be reconstructed in 3D.
- That pushes the effective tracking threshold to roughly 450–500 MeV/c, close to the median of the leading-proton spectrum (about 450 MeV/c).
- So roughly half the leading protons are lost or mismeasured.

The hardware below targets both problems. It also covers the about 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, which escape any compact target and need magnetic momentum measurement.

## Recommendations

### 1. Replace the P0D with a 3D-granular scintillator target ("SuperFGD")

**Design**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, arranged roughly 192 × 184 × 56 (≈1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m). This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box, with the 0.56 m dimension vertical.
- Active hydrocarbon mass of about 2 t, which roughly doubles the FGD target mass.
- Each cube has a reflective chemical-etch coating and three orthogonal holes.
- Three orthogonal Kuraray Y-11 wavelength-shifting fibres run through the cubes: about 56,000 channels.
- Each fibre is read by a compact MPPC (e.g. Hamamatsu S13360 type, about 1.3 mm, 25 µm pixels).

**Justification**
- Three projections of every hit give near-isotropic (4π) acceptance. High-angle and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- 1 cm granularity in all three views lowers the proton threshold to about 300 MeV/c. This recovers most of the proton spectrum below the 450 MeV/c median, which TKI needs, and improves calorimetric vertex-activity measurement.
- Fine dE/dx sampling separates protons from muons and pions in the target itself.
- Single-cube timing of about 1 ns, with multi-fibre averaging, enables neutron detection by time-of-flight to secondary scatters. This allows TKI-like analyses with neutrons as well.
- Hydrocarbon is acceptable for this programme, and the water-layer FGD2 stays in place for the carbon-to-water comparison.

### 2. Add two High-Angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Design**
- Placed in the remaining P0D volume, each about 2.0 × 1.8 × 0.8 m.
- Use the same T2K gas, Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2, inside the 0.2 T field.

**Readout: resistive Micromegas (Encapsulated Resistive Anode Micromegas, ERAM)**
- A resistive DLC layer spreads the charge over several pads.
- This allows larger pads (about 1 × 1.1 cm). Fewer channels then give better spatial resolution than the existing bulk Micromegas (sub-mm, target ≲ 0.8 mm).
- The encapsulation also protects against sparks.

**Field cage**
- Thin composite (aramid honeycomb/laminate), about 2–3% X₀.
- Keeping it light minimises proton energy loss and photon conversions between the target and the gas.

**Electronics**
- AFTER/AGET-based front ends, matched to the ND280 DAQ.

**Justification**
- High-angle muons (the 25%) and the protons above 900 MeV/c leave the 0.56 m-thick target through its top and bottom faces.
- The HA-TPCs give them a curvature momentum measurement (target ≲ 10% at 1 GeV/c) and gas dE/dx identification, the same quality as forward tracks in the existing TPCs.
- Magnetic momentum is essential above about 900 MeV/c because range is not available for escaping tracks.

### 3. Surround the new tracker with Time-of-Flight planes

**Design**
- Six planes of plastic-scintillator bars (e.g. EJ-200, about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm).
- Read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Justification**
- Determines track direction unambiguously, separating backward-going particles from tracks entering from outside.
- Rejects interactions in the magnet and surroundings, including cosmics.
- Improves particle identification at intermediate momentum.
- Provides the time reference for SuperFGD neutron time-of-flight.

### 4. Supporting changes

- **ECal:** Retain the barrel and downstream ECals, and refit the upstream ECal modules around the new geometry for photon and π⁰ containment.
- **SMRD:** Keep it. It tags and ranges very high-angle muons that exit the magnet.
- **Integration:**
  - Unified MPPC front-end electronics (e.g. CITIROC-based boards) with a common clock, giving nanosecond timing synchronisation across SuperFGD, ToF and the TPCs.
  - Light-tight, mechanically self-supporting cube box in carbon-fibre/composite.
  - In-situ LED calibration for gain and crosstalk monitoring.

## What the combined system delivers

- About 4π muon acceptance.
- Proton reconstruction from about 300 MeV/c up to the highest momenta.
- Neutron tagging.
- Roughly doubled target mass.

Together these give the TKI-capable, kinematically complete event sample needed to bring flux and cross-section systematics from about 6% toward the 4% T2K-II goal.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a 3D-readout 1 cm³ scintillator-cube target (SuperFGD) read by three orthogonal WLS fibres and MPPCs, giving ~4π acceptance and a ~300 MeV/c proton threshold.

# Upgrade Proposal: Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target

## What the requirements imply

The analysis constraints narrow the technology choice before any design begins.

**Hydrogen limit (≤2% of target nucleons).** This rules out the usual plastic scintillator target.
- Polystyrene or CH is about 7.7% hydrogen by nucleon count, so it fails.
- Water is about 11%, so it fails.
- The target medium must be essentially hydrogen-free. The far detector contains no hydrogen and is most likely argon, so argon is the natural choice. It also removes nuclear-model extrapolation between near and far detectors.

**Protons down to 60 MeV kinetic energy at all angles.**
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 2.5–3 cm in liquid argon.
- Detecting it needs millimetre-scale, fully 3D, isotropic imaging.
- Bar or segmented-scintillator geometries have direction-dependent thresholds, so they are not adequate.

**Muons at ≥25% efficiency at every angle, including perpendicular and backward.**
- The existing drift chambers sit downstream and only see forward tracks.
- A 0.15 T field gives negligible curvature inside a dense target.
- Muon momentum therefore has to come from the target itself, using range or multiple scattering, plus new detectors on the sides and upstream face.

**Statistics.** The volume is 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m ≈ 5.4 m³.
- Filled with liquid argon (LAr), that is about 7.5 t.
- Filled with 10-bar gaseous argon, it is about 0.1 t. At a near site with a 0.7 GeV peak, the liquid gives roughly 75× more interactions, which is ample for cross-section systematics.

## Upgrade 1 (core): Modular liquid-argon TPC with pixel readout

**Technology**
- A 2 × 2 (or 3 × 2) array of optically isolated LArTPC modules with short drifts of about 30–50 cm.
- Native 3D pixel charge readout at roughly 4 mm pitch, in the style of LArPix / ND-LAr.
- Housed in a thin-walled, low-mass cryostat that fits the 0.9 m beam-direction slot in the upstream end of the magnet.
- A non-magnetic stainless or aluminium inner vessel with foam or vacuum insulation, keeping the dead material in front of the drift chambers small.

**Physics motivation**
- **Hydrogen-free argon target.** This meets the 2% limit trivially. It is the same nucleus as the far detector, so flux × cross-section constraints transfer directly.
- **Full-solid-angle 3D imaging.** Tracking efficiency is angle-independent, which covers perpendicular and backward muons and protons.
- **Low proton threshold.** Charge is sampled roughly every 4 mm, so a 2.5 cm proton gives about 6–8 hits with a clear Bragg peak. This allows dE/dx particle identification well below 60 MeV.
- **Unambiguous 3D pixels.** Wire-projection ambiguities are removed, which matters at near-detector event rates with pile-up from rock muons and multiple interactions per spill.
- **Short drift and optical segmentation.** These limit space-charge effects, diffusion and pile-up, and allow interactions within one spill to be separated.

## Upgrade 2: Fast photon detection inside each TPC module

**Technology**
- Wavelength-shifting light traps (ArCLight / LCM style) read by SiPMs, lining the module field-cage walls.
- Timing resolution of a few nanoseconds.

**Physics motivation**
- Provides the event time t₀ for drift-coordinate reconstruction, so tracks crossing the cathode or exiting the module are correctly placed.
- Associates each interaction with its beam bunch.
- Rejects through-going rock muons.
- Enables time-of-flight between the target and downstream chambers.
- The SiPMs and shifter material sit at the module boundaries, contribute negligible target mass, and do not affect the hydrogen fraction because the fiducial vertex cut excludes them.

## Upgrade 3: Side and upstream muon trackers outside the cryostat

**Technology**
- Planes on the four lateral faces and the upstream face of the cryostat, inside the magnet volume where space allows. Two options:
  - gas drift or straw-tube chambers, or
  - thin scintillator-strip planes with SiPM readout.
- These are allowed to contain hydrogen because they lie outside the fiducial volume. Interactions in them are removed by the vertex cut.

**Physics motivation**
- A 0.7 GeV muon ranges about 3 m in liquid argon, but the transverse half-widths are only about 1.15–1.3 m. Many high-angle and backward muons therefore exit through the sides or upstream face and never reach the downstream chambers.
- These trackers tag such tracks as muons by matching them to the TPC track and confirming penetration.
- Where the field region allows, they measure curvature and charge sign. Otherwise they still confirm the exit point and direction.
- Combined with in-argon multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum estimates over the ≥1 m path, this secures the ≥25% efficiency at all angles.

## Upgrade 4: Momentum reconstruction for contained and exiting tracks

This is an analysis-hardware co-design item.

**Hardware**
- Ensure the electron lifetime is above about 3 ms via argon purification, so that charge is well measured over the full drift.
- Calibrate with cosmic muons and a laser system.

**Methods**
- Use range for stopping muons and protons.
- Use multiple Coulomb scattering for exiting muons. At 4 mm pitch, MCS resolution is roughly 10–15% over about 1 m of track.
- Use downstream curvature in the existing drift chambers for forward muons.

**Physics motivation**
- Gives a uniform muon momentum estimate across all angles, so the efficiency and kinematics requirements do not depend solely on the downstream spectrometer.

## Upgrade 5: Downstream interface

**Technology**
- An optional thin electromagnetic or timing layer between the cryostat downstream wall and the existing gas drift chambers, such as an argon-free scintillator strip plane.

**Physics motivation**
- Matches TPC tracks to drift-chamber tracks at the cryostat exit and helps with π⁰ photon containment.
- Keeps the existing 0.15 T spectrometer as the charge and momentum measurement for forward muons, giving wrong-sign (antineutrino) separation.

## Options considered and rejected

| Option | Reason for rejection |
|---|---|
| High-pressure gaseous argon TPC | Excellent proton threshold, but only about 0.1 t of target, giving too few events. |
| Scintillator (CH) or water-based targets | Fail the 2% hydrogen criterion. |
| Wire-readout LArTPC | Projection ambiguities at near-detector pile-up rates. Pixels are preferable. |

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular, optically segmented liquid-argon TPC with 3D pixel charge readout (≈7.5 t, hydrogen-free, isotropic mm-scale tracking) instrumented with fast SiPM light detection.

This is a challenging active target design problem with several competing constraints. Let me analyze the requirements systematically:

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Angular acceptance**: Must detect muons at all angles including perpendicular and backward-going tracks (requiring readout on multiple faces)
2. **Low-momentum protons**: Need sensitivity down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~2-3 mm in typical materials)
3. **Hydrogen constraint**: Must keep H nuclei below 2% of target nucleons (essentially requiring non-hydrogenous material)
4. **Large volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m active region
5. **Vertex resolution**: Need to reconstruct interaction points for neutrino physics

## Recommended Hardware Configuration

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Primary Recommendation)**

Implement a **3D segmented plastic scintillator array** with:
- **1-1.5 cm³ cubic scintillator cubes** arranged in XYZ orthogonal layers
- **Wavelength-shifting fiber readout** embedded in each cube
- **SiPM arrays** for photodetection at the edges

**Justification**:
- Fine 1 cm segmentation captures short 60 MeV proton tracks (range ~4 cm in polystyrene)
- 3D segmentation naturally handles all track angles including backwards-going
- Polystyrene (CH₁.₁) can be kept below 2% hydrogen by mass fraction with selective deuteration or by using alternative formulations
- Relatively fast timing (~ns) helps with event pile-up at beam rates
- Proven technology (scaled from T2K, MINERvA experience)

### 2. **Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) - Alternate Option**

If cost is prohibitive, use **fine-pitch glass RPCs**:
- **1 cm strip pitch** in X-Y orientation
- **Multiple doublet layers** (at least 40 layers to fill 0.9 m depth)
- Rotated stereo angles for improved position resolution

**Justification**:
- Lower cost than scintillator
- No hydrogen in glass/gas mixture
- Good spatial resolution
- Proven in neutrino experiments (OPERA, INO)
- **Concern**: May have dead zones for shallow-angle tracks between layers

### 3. **Hybrid Time Projection Chamber with Optical Readout**

Alternative advanced option: **Optical TPC using LAr or gaseous argon**:
- Argon target (zero hydrogen)
- Camera-based charge readout on multiple faces
- Supplemental charge readout planes

**Justification**:
- Excellent 3D tracking and calorimetry
- Pure argon = 0% hydrogen
- Continuous tracking (no segmentation gaps)
- **Concerns**: Technical complexity, may exceed budget/timeline, 0.9 m drift may be challenging

### 4. **Upgraded Magnet Readout Interface**

Regardless of active target choice:
- **Additional tracking planes at target-to-magnet boundary** (2-3 planes of scintillating fibers or silicon strips)
- Ensures muon track linking from target to spectrometer
- Critical for the 25% efficiency requirement at all angles

### 5. **DAQ and Electronics Upgrades**

- **Flash ADC readout** for all channels (>10,000 channels expected)
- **GPS timestamping** synchronized with beam spill structure
- Sufficient buffer depth for beam spill collection (~10 μs windows)

## Implementation Priority

Given the constraints, I recommend the **fine-grained 3D scintillator approach** because:

1. **Meets hydrogen constraint**: Can formulate scintillator with <2% H by nucleon count
2. **Handles all angles**: True 3D readout on all faces
3. **Proton threshold**: Fine segmentation captures ~60 MeV protons
4. **Mature technology**: Lower risk than TPC options
5. **Reasonable cost**: More affordable than Si, less risky than novel detectors

**Cost mitigation**: Use wavelength-shifting fibers with SiPM arrays at edges rather than individual PMTs to keep channel count manageable (~thousands not millions).

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Implement a 3D segmented plastic scintillator array with 1-1.5 cm cubic cells, wavelength-shifting fiber readout, and SiPM photodetection for true 3D tracking of all particles at all angles while maintaining hydrogen content below 2%.**

# Proposed upgrade: an argon active target for the Kestrel Flats near station

## 1. The constraint that decides the technology: hydrogen ≤ 2% of target nucleons

The obvious choice for a 4π active target is fine-grained plastic scintillator, such as a SuperFGD-style 1 cm cube detector. It fails this requirement.

- In polystyrene (CH) about 1 of every 13 nucleons is a hydrogen nucleus, which is about 7.7%.
- Scintillator-plus-water hybrids are no better.

The far detector contains no hydrogen, and only argon is named here as a likely far-detector match. So the right target is argon, which has 0% hydrogen. The only hydrogen sources would then be:

- field-cage supports,
- PCBs,
- G10 and Kapton.

These lie outside the fiducial volume and can be kept far below 2% of the fiducial nucleons.

## 2. Primary recommendation: a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m target region

### Cryostat
- Use a thin-wall, vacuum-insulated cryostat with low-Z walls (aluminium or thin stainless steel) that fits inside the warm magnet bore.
- Thin walls keep the material in front of the downstream drift chambers small, so muons are matched and their momentum and charge measured with little multiple scattering.

### Readout
- Use an ArgonCube / 2×2-demonstrator style layout: about 4 modules, each about 0.65 m wide, with a central cathode and drift lengths of roughly 30–50 cm.
- Read the charge with pixelated anodes (LArPix-type, about 4 mm pitch) to give true 3D readout.
- 3D readout removes the ambiguities of wire planes for tracks at all angles, including perpendicular and backward ones. It also handles the pile-up of several interactions per spill expected at 410 m.

### Light detection and timing
- Install segmented light detectors (ArCLight or light-collection modules) in each module.
- They should give about 10 ns timing, which serves two purposes:
  - assigning a t₀ to each interaction;
  - tagging track direction, so that backward-going muons are identified.

### Target mass
- The fiducial mass is about 5–6 t of argon, which gives ample statistics.

### Proton reconstruction
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 cm in liquid argon. That is roughly 8 pixels, enough for dE/dx particle identification and kinetic energy from range.
- The proton threshold is set by pixel pitch, not by geometry, so it is isotropic.

### Muon reconstruction, which gives isotropic ≥ 25% efficiency
**Forward muons**
- Exiting muons are matched to the existing downstream drift chambers for curvature and charge.

**Sideways and backward muons**
- These need their own momentum measurement:
  - muons that stop in the argon get momentum from range;
  - muons that exit get momentum from multiple Coulomb scattering, with about 10–15% resolution at these energies.
- The 0.15 T field adds a weak curvature, a sagitta of about 1 cm over 1 m at 0.5 GeV. This helps charge sign on long tracks.

**Side and upstream tracker**
- Add thin trackers on the sides and upstream face, inside the magnet.
- Options are thin gas TPCs or MicroMegas planes, or scintillator bar planes with SiPM readout.
- These sit outside the fiducial volume, so their hydrogen does not matter.
- They give exit-point and curvature measurements for high-angle and backward muons.

**Time-of-flight panels**
- Surround the target with a scintillator time-of-flight shell (about 0.5 ns resolution, SiPM readout).
- This confirms track direction, separating backward muons from incoming entering tracks, and rejects external backgrounds.

## 3. Supporting changes
- **Electromagnetic calorimeter:** add a thin lead-scintillator ECal on the sides to catch π⁰ photons and help identify muons at high angles.
- **Cryogenics and purity:** provide argon recirculation and purification sized for an electron lifetime above 1 ms.
- **Outside material budget:** account for all hydrogenous material, keeping hydrogen-containing parts out of the fiducial volume and documenting its total mass.

## 4. Alternative if a cryostat cannot fit
A high-pressure (about 10 bar) gaseous argon TPC gives an even lower proton threshold (a few MeV) and excellent 4π acceptance. Its drawbacks are:

- only about 90 kg of target mass in this volume;
- a heavy pressure vessel.

It is a fallback rather than the baseline.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular pixel-readout (LArPix/ArgonCube-type) liquid-argon TPC in a thin vacuum-insulated cryostat, giving a hydrogen-free 4π active target with about 60 MeV proton thresholds.

I'll work through the physics requirements systematically to derive the necessary hardware.

---

## Physics Requirements Driving Hardware Choices

**Geometry:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m active target volume (~5.4 m³)
**Beam:** ~0.7 GeV peak, 410 m near detector → high neutrino interaction rate
**Key constraints:**
- Muons at all angles (0°–180°) with ≥25% efficiency, including backward and perpendicular
- Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range in water ~3 mm, in scintillator ~6 mm)
- Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons → constrains target material
- Far detector has no hydrogen → need hydrogen subtraction model

---

## Hydrogen Fraction Constraint

This is the dominant material constraint. Pure hydrocarbon targets (CH₂, polystyrene CH) have hydrogen fractions far too high (~33% or ~7.7% by nucleon number for polystyrene). Water (H₂O) gives 2H/(2H+16O) = ~11% — acceptable. Liquid argon has zero hydrogen. The target must be a material where hydrogen nucleons ≤20%.

For polystyrene scintillator (C₈H₈): nucleon count per monomer = 8×12 + 8×1 → H fraction = 8/104 ≈ 7.7% — this is **under** 20% and acceptable. This is key: scintillator is permissible.

---

## Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperFGD-style")

**Technology:** Array of ~1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes (polystyrene-based), each read out in three orthogonal directions via wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).

**Why:**
- Provides ~1 cm³ voxelization enabling reconstruction of very short proton tracks (60 MeV proton range ~2–3 cm in scintillator → ~2–3 cubes, detectable)
- Fully active: no dead material gaps that would lose low-energy recoils
- 3D readout gives unambiguous track reconstruction at all angles including 90° and backward — no projection ambiguities
- Polystyrene H-fraction ~7.7% satisfies the ≤20% nucleon constraint
- Fast timing (~ns) from SiPMs provides beam-spill event isolation and distinguishes forward vs. backward tracks via time-of-flight
- SiPMs are compact, operate without high voltage, tolerate the magnetic field (unlike PMTs, though field-shielding may still be needed at 0.15 T)
- This geometry is proven in T2K's SuperFGD upgrade and SAND at DUNE

---

### 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator panels (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-408) with ~200 ps timing resolution, read out by SiPMs, surrounding the active target on all six faces (upstream, downstream, and four transverse faces).

**Why:**
- Backward-going muons and protons exit the upstream face; ToF distinguishes direction definitively even when magnetic curvature is ambiguous for near-perpendicular tracks
- Provides a trigger on charged particles exiting the active volume at any angle
- Enables momentum-by-range cross-check for stopping particles
- Separates pion/proton/muon by ToF at low momenta where magnetic momentum resolution is poor
- The ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles demands sensitive coverage on all faces; scintillator panels are robust and well-understood

---

### 3. Upstream Veto / Beam-Halo Rejection Scintillator

**Technology:** High-granularity scintillator veto panels (or additional scintillator planes) immediately upstream of the active target, with SiPM readout and ~1 ns timing.

**Why:**
- At 410 m from the target, the near detector sees a broad neutrino beam but also rock muons and beam-related backgrounds entering from upstream
- Backward-going track reconstruction requires knowing whether a track originated inside the volume or entered from outside; a veto plane with high efficiency tags entering tracks
- Protects the hydrogen-subtraction analysis: an external muon misidentified as a backward-going interaction muon would corrupt the sample
- Also identifies charge-current interactions occurring in the material just upstream of the active target

---

### 4. Upgraded Downstream Tracking / Muon Ranger

**Technology:** Magnetized iron-scintillator range stack (alternating iron absorber plates ~2–5 cm thick with scintillator strip planes, SiPM readout), instrumented to act as both a muon catcher and additional spectrometer.

**Why:**
- High-energy forward muons (~few hundred MeV to >1 GeV at 0.7 GeV beam peak) will exit the active target and the existing warm dipole; a range stack downstream measures momentum by range for stopping muons and provides a second momentum measurement cross-check for through-going muons
- The existing gas drift chambers downstream measure momentum of tracks leaving the magnet, but their acceptance for large-angle tracks is limited; the range stack extends angular coverage for forward-going tracks that miss the drift chambers
- Iron-scintillator is well-matched to muon identification: hadrons range out quickly, muons penetrate
- Magnetized sections can provide sign determination for backward-reconstructed tracks that turn forward in the dipole

---

### 5. Replacement / Upgrade of Gas Drift Chambers with Higher-Rate Straw Tube Trackers

**Technology:** Straw tube tracker (STT) modules using 5–10 mm diameter aluminized mylar drift tubes with Ar/CO₂ or Ar/isobutane gas mixture, operating at ~1500–1800 V, with ASIC-based readout.

**Why:**
- The near detector at 410 m sees a very high neutrino interaction rate (orders of magnitude higher than a far detector); existing wire chambers may have rate-capability and aging problems under the upgraded beam intensity that typically accompanies a funding proposal of this kind
- Straw tubes are individually self-supporting and self-shielding; a broken wire in one straw does not affect neighbors (unlike large-area wire chambers), giving higher uptime
- Fine straw pitch (~5–10 mm) gives spatial resolution ~150–200 μm, adequate for momentum measurement in the 0.15 T dipole for muon momentum reconstruction
- Faster ion collection than large-volume drift chambers reduces occupancy per spill
- Can be arranged in stereo angles to improve 3D track reconstruction for the large-angle tracks that the upstream active target sends into the downstream spectrometer

---

### 6. SiPM Readout Electronics Upgrade (DAQ and Front-End)

**Technology:** Self-triggering ASIC front-end electronics (e.g., CITIROC or custom ASIC comparable to those developed for SuperFGD/ND280) with ~1 ns timestamp binning and zero-suppression, feeding an FPGA-based data concentrator and trigger-less or flexible-trigger DAQ.

**Why:**
- The ~1 cm³ cube array will have O(10⁵–10⁶) readout channels; existing DAQ designed for wire chambers cannot handle this channel count
- Self-triggering readout is essential for backward-going tracks (no prompt downstream signal to form a trigger) — the ≥25% efficiency at all angles requirement fails without trigger-less or activity-triggered readout on the active target itself
- Fine time-stamping enables the ToF-based direction measurement
- Zero-suppression in the ASIC reduces data volume to manageable levels
- Adequate dynamic range (single photoelectron to ~50 p.e. for heavily ionizing proton tracks) must be handled without saturation

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | 3D scintillator cube array + WLS fibers + SiPMs | Short proton tracks, all-angle reconstruction, H-fraction |
| ToF planes (6 faces) | Fast scintillator + SiPMs, ~200 ps | Backward/perpendicular muon direction, trigger |
| Upstream veto | Scintillator panels + SiPMs | Background rejection, backward track origin |
| Muon ranger/range stack | Magnetized Fe-scintillator, SiPM | Forward muon momentum, angular acceptance |
| Downstream tracker | Straw tube tracker | High-rate capability, momentum resolution |
| Front-end electronics + DAQ | Self-triggering ASICs, FPGA DAQ | Channel count, trigger-less readout, timing |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replacement of the passive target region with a 3D scintillator cube array read out via WLS fibers and SiPMs, providing the voxelized fully-active target necessary to reconstruct short proton recoil tracks down to 60 MeV kinetic energy, achieve ≥25% muon efficiency at all angles including backward-going tracks, and satisfy the hydrogen nucleon fraction constraint below 20%.

# Kestrel Flats Near Station: Recommended Hardware Changes

## The problem in one line

Today the detector only measures tracks that leave the target region heading downstream into the drift chambers. The physics now needs:

- muons at every angle, including perpendicular and backward;
- protons at every angle, down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy;
- a target in which hydrogen nuclei are at most 20% of the nucleons.

A conventional planar tracker cannot meet the first two requirements, and some target materials violate the third. Each change below addresses a specific requirement.

---

## 1. Replace the target region with a fine-grained, 3D-segmented plastic scintillator target

**Technology:** a SuperFGD-style target, as built for the T2K ND280 upgrade.

- **Cells:** about 1 cm³ optically isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes.
- **Readout:** each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, read out by SiPMs (MPPCs).

**Why this technology:**

- **Isotropic acceptance.** Tracking planes made of bars only measure tracks well within roughly ±60° of the beam. Tracks near 90° run along a single plane and become ambiguous. Cubes read in three views give the same granularity in every direction. Forward, perpendicular and backward tracks are therefore reconstructed equally well, which directly serves the "all angles" muon and proton requirement.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels roughly 3 g/cm² before stopping, which is about 3 cm (about 3 cubes) in polystyrene. That is enough hits to fire three views and identify the proton by dE/dx, including its Bragg peak. Bar or plate trackers with thicker layers lose these short tracks, especially at high angle.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** In polystyrene (CH) there is 1 hydrogen nucleon per 13 nucleons, about 7.7%. This is comfortably under the 20% limit for the hydrogen-subtraction model.
  - The real constraint is the hydrogen-rich materials: hydrocarbon liquid scintillator or polyethylene absorbers must not dominate the target mass.
  - Water as a passive layer (11% hydrogen nucleons) would also be acceptable, but is not needed.
- **Magnetic field compatibility.** MPPCs work in a magnetic field, whereas PMTs would not tolerate the 0.15 T field.

**Scale:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Cubes | 260 × 230 × 90 ≈ 5.4 million |
| Mass | about 5.5–6 t |
| Readout channels (one fibre per row in each of three views) | 260·230 + 260·90 + 230·90 ≈ 104,000 |

- **Calibration:** include an LED calibration system and timing electronics with resolution of about 1 ns or better.

## 2. Add high-angle gas TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology:** thin-walled time projection chambers with resistive Micromegas readout, inside the dipole field.

**Why:**

- Tracks perpendicular to the beam exit through the top, bottom or sides and never reach the downstream drift chambers.
- These TPCs measure momentum and charge from curvature, plus dE/dx for particle identification, for exactly those tracks.
- Resolution needs a long lever arm. At 0.15 T, a 0.5 GeV/c muon has a bending radius of about 11 m. A track length of about 1 m or more is therefore needed for useful resolution, which argues for TPCs roughly 0.7–1 m deep.
- Muons that stop inside the target are measured by range in the scintillator instead.

## 3. Surround the target and TPCs with a time-of-flight system

**Technology:** fast plastic-scintillator bars read out by SiPMs at both ends, with timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Why:**

- **Backward tracks.** For short tracks, the curvature or pattern alone is ambiguous between a backward-going μ⁻ and a forward-going particle of the opposite charge entering from outside. Timing tells which way the track travelled. This makes the backward-muon requirement achievable without picking up wrong-sign or out-of-target backgrounds.
- **Particle identification.** Time of flight adds e/μ/p separation for tracks the TPCs measure poorly.
- **Veto.** It rejects tracks entering from interactions in the magnet and surrounding material, which matters at a station only 410 m from the target with high rates.

## 4. Supporting changes

- **Fiducial-volume edge veto.** Instrument the upstream face, either with a separate active layer or by reserving an outer layer of cubes. Backward-going muons exit upstream, so their selection needs clean "outgoing" versus "entering" separation there.
- **Triggerless or beam-gated, deadtime-free front end.** Use electronics that record the full spill at high occupancy. Event rates at 410 m will be high, so the system must separate pile-up events in time.
- **Target material control.** Use a non-hydrogenous mechanical structure (aluminium or carbon-fibre box). Keep cube reflector coatings and glue low-mass. Measure the elemental composition of the target and audit it so the hydrogen fraction stays well below 20%; a margin of about 8% or less is expected.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a ~1 cm³ 3D-segmented plastic-scintillator cube target (SuperFGD-style) read out by three-view WLS fibres and SiPMs, giving isotropic muon/proton acceptance, ~3 cm proton thresholds, and only ~8% hydrogen nucleons.

Based on the requirements for kinematically complete charged-current events with good reconstruction of large-angle muons and protons, I propose the following hardware upgrades:

## Primary Upgrade: New Active Target for Photon-Tagging Space

**3D fine-grained scintillator tracker** (~2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m):
- **SuperFGD-style extruded polystyrene cubes**: 1 cm³ voxels with three orthogonal 1.5 mm diameter holes for wavelength-shifting fiber readout in X, Y, and Z
- Total mass: ~1.2-1.4 t of hydrocarbon target
- ~360,000 individual cubes providing true 3D tracking with ~1 cm³ granularity
- Three-view fiber readout with MPPC arrays at edges
- Enables reconstruction of short-range, wide-angle protons (critical for the 35% of protons >50°)
- 3D hit information essential for resolving ambiguities in high-angle tracks that project poorly in 2D x/y geometries

## Secondary Upgrades

**Enhanced TPC readout electronics**:
- Upgrade to resistive Micromegas with improved charge spread for better position resolution
- Implement SRS-based APV25 hybrid readout or newer AGET/AFTER chips for higher rate capability
- Better handles large-angle tracks entering TPCs from upstream target

**Extended electromagnetic calorimeter coverage**:
- Add lead-scintillator ECAL modules to upstream sides (flanking new target)
- Improves photon rejection and π⁰ background characterization
- ~0.5 t additional lead-scintillator with 1 cm scintillator / 1.75 mm lead sampling

**Improved timing system**:
- Upgrade all MPPCs to uniform high-gain models (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series with ~40% PDE)
- Implement sub-nanosecond timing across all scintillator systems
- Better time-of-flight discrimination for proton/pion separation below Cherenkov threshold

**Data acquisition upgrade**:
- Increased buffer depth and bandwidth to handle higher granularity from 3D target
- GPU-based online track reconstruction for trigger-level quality monitoring

## Why This Configuration

The 3D SuperFGD-style target addresses the key challenge: **kinematically complete reconstruction requires detecting and measuring both high-angle muons AND high-angle protons**. The existing 2D x/y bar geometry has severe inefficiencies for tracks at >50° to the beam:
- Tracks parallel to bar orientation give poor position information
- Protons with 450 MeV/c range ~40-80 cm in polystyrene depending on angle
- 3D granularity enables reliable vertex reconstruction and track-following even for complicated topologies

The cube geometry with three-view fiber readout has been proven in ND280 upgrade prototypes and provides the necessary angular acceptance while maintaining good energy resolution through stopping power measurements.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D fine-grained scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD-style, 1 cm³ voxels, three-view fiber readout) in the upstream 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m volume to enable kinematically complete reconstruction of high-angle charged-current events.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target Upgrade

## Constraints Summary

Before recommending hardware, let me establish the binding constraints:

- **Fiducial volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (≈5.4 m³)
- **Muon angular coverage**: 4π including 90° and backward-going tracks → requires full 3D tracking with no dead angular regions
- **Proton threshold**: ~60 MeV kinetic energy → range ~3.5 mm in water, ~1.8 mm in iron → demands fine-grained, low-Z material
- **Hydrogen fraction**: ≤20% of target nucleons → constrains choice of active medium
- **Momentum measurement**: provided by downstream spectrometer; active target needs pattern recognition and vertex reconstruction
- **Magnetic field**: 0.15 T already present, aiding charge-sign determination for tracks that exit

---

## Hydrogen Fraction Constraint Analysis
