# Proposed upgrade: a 3D-granular scintillator active target with high-angle TPCs and time-of-flight

## 1. Active target: a finely segmented 3D scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD-style)

**What it is**
- Fill most of the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region with optically isolated **1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes**.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal **1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres**, giving three 2D projections that combine into 3D hits.
- Each fibre is read out at one end by a **SiPM/MPPC** (about 1.3 mm, roughly 50 µm pixels) on fast electronics. CITIROC-type front ends would give about 1 ns timing.
- A mirror on the far fibre end improves light yield.

**Why this geometry fits the requirements**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** There is no preferred plane orientation, unlike a bar or plane tracker. Muons at 90° and backward-going muons are tracked as well as forward ones, which is what the ≥25% efficiency at every angle requires.
- **Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 cm in plastic, so it crosses about 3 cubes. That is enough to reconstruct it and identify it by dE/dx. A standard 1 cm-bar tracker would miss most such short, high-angle tracks.
- **Timing.** Sub-ns timing per cube helps separate track direction and can tag neutrons by time of flight, which is useful extra information.

**Hydrogen constraint**
- Polystyrene (CH) has a hydrogen nucleon fraction of 1/13, about 7.7%, comfortably below the 20% limit of the hydrogen-subtraction model.
- Avoid adding hydrogenous passive material.
- Keep the support structure carbon-fibre or aluminium.

**Size and channel count**
- Use roughly 2.0 × 1.2 × 0.9 m of cubes, leaving room for item 2.
- That is about 2.2 million cubes and about 60k readout channels.
- The full 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m volume would need about 104k channels.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the cube target

**What it is**
- Two thin gas TPCs, each about 0.5 m drift, in the remaining height above and below the cube volume.
- Field cages are made of lightweight composite.
- Readout uses **resistive-anode (encapsulated resistive) Micromegas**. These spread the charge, so position resolution stays good with fewer, larger pads.
- The gas is a T2K-type Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ mixture.

**Why it is needed**
- In the 0.15 T field, these give charge sign and curvature momentum for high-angle muons that never reach the downstream drift chambers.
- They also provide dE/dx for µ/p/e separation.
- Muons that stop inside the cubes are measured by range instead.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

- Surround the target and TPC assembly with **plastic scintillator bars read out by SiPMs at both ends**, with timing resolution around 150 ps.
- This gives unambiguous **forward vs backward direction** for tracks leaving the target.
- It rejects interactions from outside the target (e.g. in the magnet and surrounding material) that enter it.
- It adds particle ID at low momentum.

## 4. Supporting items

- A downstream timing and tracking link to the existing drift chambers, with clock synchronisation across all subsystems.
- Calibration with cosmic rays and an LED/laser light-injection system for the MPPCs.
- Temperature-compensated SiPM bias, since the magnet is warm.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a 3D-granular scintillator active target of 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes read out on three orthogonal WLS fibres by SiPMs (SuperFGD-style), which gives isotropic muon acceptance, 60 MeV proton reconstruction, and only about 8% hydrogen nucleons.

I'll work through the physics requirements systematically to derive what hardware is needed.

---

## Physics Requirements Analysis

**Geometry constraints:**
- Target volume: 2.6 m (W) × 2.3 m (H) × 0.9 m (depth along beam)
- Must reconstruct tracks at **all angles including 90° and backward** with ≥25% efficiency
- Must reconstruct **short proton tracks** down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range in water ~3 cm, in scintillator ~4 cm)
- Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of nucleons → limits how much pure hydrocarbon or water you can use

---

## Hydrogen Fraction Constraint

This is a key design driver. If hydrogen fraction must stay ≤20% of nucleons:

- Pure CH₂ (polyethylene): H fraction = 2/(2+12/1) → nucleon count: 2H + 12 nucleons ≈ 14 nucleons, so H/total = 2/14 ≈ 14% ✓
- Pure CH (polystyrene-like): H/total = 1/13 ≈ 8% ✓
- Water (H₂O): H/total = 2/18 × (nucleon weights) = 2/18 ≈ 11% ✓
- Liquid argon: 0% H ✓ but no hydrogen signal at all
- Polystyrene scintillator (C₈H₈): H/total = 8/104 nucleons... let me recount by nucleon number: 8H + 8×12C = 8 + 96 = 104 nucleons, H fraction = 8/104 ≈ 8% ✓

So the constraint rules out pure liquid hydrogen or high-H-fraction targets but is satisfied by scintillator or water.

---

## Hardware Upgrades

### 1. 3D Scintillator Active Target ("SuperFGD"-style)

**Technology:** Array of plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³ each), optically read out by wavelength-shifting fibers threaded in all three orthogonal directions, each fiber read by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM).

**Why:**
- 1 cm³ granularity gives ~1 cm³ spatial resolution, sufficient to reconstruct tracks of protons with 60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~4–5 cm in scintillator → ~4–5 hit cubes, reconstructable)
- Three-axis fiber readout gives full 3D tracking with no preferred direction, enabling reconstruction of tracks at **all angles** including 90° transverse and backward-going tracks — this is impossible with planar tracking technologies that have a preferred orientation
- Plastic scintillator (C₈H₈, polystyrene-based) gives H nucleon fraction ~8%, safely within the ≤20% requirement
- Fast timing (~1 ns) distinguishes forward from backward tracks via time-of-flight and aids in vertex reconstruction
- The 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m volume filled with ~1 cm cubes requires roughly 5.4 million cubes — consistent with demonstrated technology (ND280 upgrade at T2K)
- Acts simultaneously as target and tracker: no dead material between neutrino interaction point and first measured hit, maximizing efficiency for short tracks
- Charge integration on SiPMs provides dE/dx for particle identification (separates protons from pions)

### 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator panels (e.g., 2 cm thick EJ-200 or BC-408) with SiPM readout on all faces of the active target volume (upstream, downstream, and all four sides), giving timing resolution ~200–300 ps.

**Why:**
- Backward-going tracks exiting the upstream face must be distinguished from forward-going tracks entering from upstream; ToF provides the sign of the track direction independently of the magnetic field, which is essential since the upstream face is toward the beam
- Resolves ambiguity for 90° tracks where magnetic bending gives little momentum information
- Rejects beam-related backgrounds (sand muons, beam halo) by timing relative to beam spill structure
- Improves muon momentum resolution for tracks that stop inside the active target (range + ToF cross-check)
- Separates protons from pions at low momentum using ToF between cubes or between ToF planes

### 3. Upgraded Gas Drift Chamber Readout / Additional Tracking Stations

**Technology:** High-pressure (or atmospheric) Time Projection Chambers (TPCs) with Micromegas or GEM readout, placed downstream of the active target, with an additional station placed **upstream** of the target.

**Why:**
- The existing gas drift chambers downstream are retained for forward muon momentum measurement, but an upstream TPC station is needed to catch backward-going muon tracks that exit the upstream face — currently there is no upstream tracker
- Micromegas/GEM readout gives 2D hit positions with ~300 µm resolution, enabling precise momentum measurement via curvature in the existing 0.15 T dipole for tracks that traverse the full magnet
- For backward-going tracks, the upstream station combined with the ToF planes establishes the track direction and provides the first momentum measurement point
- TPCs provide dE/dx particle identification complementary to the scintillator cubes
- Low-mass construction minimizes interactions upstream that would contaminate the active target fiducial volume

### 4. SiPM Readout Electronics Upgrade (Full Waveform Digitization)

**Technology:** CITIROC or similar Application-Specific Integrated Circuits (ASICs) with waveform digitization at ~200 MHz sampling, replacing any PMT or simple threshold-based readout currently in the detector.

**Why:**
- Full waveform digitization provides precise charge integration (critical for dE/dx-based proton/pion separation), sub-nanosecond timing (required for the ToF system), and pulse shape discrimination
- SiPMs are compact, operate in the magnetic field (PMTs cannot), and are matched to the WLS fiber emission spectrum (~450–500 nm for Y-11 fibers)
- The ~5 million channel count of the 3D scintillator array requires highly multiplexed, low-power readout — modern SiPM ASICs achieve ~64 channels per chip at <1 mW/channel
- Waveform information allows identification of multiple hits per channel within a spill (pileup rejection) and delayed neutron captures, which help characterize the hadronic system
- Backward-going track efficiency requires hits to be unambiguously assigned to the correct beam crossing; fine timing is essential at the ~410 m near-detector location where event rates are high

### 5. Magnet Field Upgrade or Extended Yoke

**Technology:** Extended or shimmed warm iron yoke (or additional coil windings on the existing dipole) to maintain field uniformity over a larger solid angle within the target volume.

**Why:**
- The existing 0.15 T field is specified over the inner volume, but tracks leaving at 90° or backward at large angles may exit the field region before accumulating enough bending to yield a useful momentum measurement; extending the useful field volume by even 20–30 cm at the upstream end would recover efficiency
- Ensuring the muon from interactions at the upstream end of the 0.9 m target traverses sufficient field length (target is at upstream end of magnet) may require the field to begin effectively at the upstream target face; a shimmed yoke achieves this without replacing the magnet
- Maintaining ≥25% muon reconstruction efficiency at all angles requires that even a 90° track crossing only the 2.6 m transverse dimension sees enough integrated Bdl; at 0.15 T over 2.6 m, Bdl = 0.39 T·m, giving ~150 MeV/c momentum threshold — acceptable, but only if the full width is in-field
- Cost-effective compared to magnet replacement: shim coils or extended yoke laminations can be added in a single shutdown

- **Upgraded DAQ:** Multi-GHz waveform digitizers to capture full SiPM waveforms for pile-up rejection and timing
- **Photon detectors around target:** Ring of fast timing photodetectors to tag and veto backwards-exiting particles
- **Resistive plate chambers (RPCs) or scintillator planes:** At the upstream face to catch backward-going particles before they exit the instrumented volume

## 5. **Specific Technical Specifications for 3D Scintillator System**

- **Bar dimensions:** 15 mm × 15 mm × 2600 mm (for X-Y planes) or × 2300 mm (for Z planes)
- **Plane spacing:** 3 mm (1.5 cm bar + 1.5 mm gap)
- **Total planes:** ~300 planes (100 of each orientation)
- **SiPMs:** 6×6 mm² active area, 50 μm pitch, ~3V overvoltage
- **Readout:** Multiplexed readout with waveform digitization at 500 MHz
- **Total channels:** ~40,000 readout channels
- **Material:** Polystyrene-based scintillator (1.05 g/cm³), providing ~0.9 tonnes total mass
- **Hydrogen fraction:** ~14% by mass, ~7.7% by nucleon count

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D orthogonal scintillator bar array with X-Y-Z oriented 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm bars and dual-ended SiPM readout, providing full angular acceptance, low proton energy threshold, and controlled hydrogen content.

# Recommendation for Re-Equipping the Kestrel Flats Near Station Active Target

## The deciding constraint: hydrogen content

The usual choice for this job would be a finely segmented plastic-scintillator tracker, such as a SuperFGD-style 3D cube detector. It gives good isotropic coverage and a low proton threshold, but it must be ruled out here.

- Polystyrene is (CH)ₙ, so hydrogen makes up about 1 of every 13 nucleons, roughly 7.7%.
- That is nearly four times the 2% limit set by the hydrogen-subtraction model.
- Water-based or other hydrocarbon targets fail the same way.

The active medium therefore has to be essentially hydrogen-free. With 5.4 m³ of available volume, the realistic candidates are argon-based TPCs.

## 1. Replace the target region with modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPCs (main change)

**Technology.** Use an ArgonCube / DUNE ND-LAr-style system:
- Several optically isolated LAr TPC modules filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region, giving roughly 7 t of argon.
- Short drift lengths of about 30–50 cm per module.
- 3D pixel charge readout, for example LArPix-type electronics with ~4 mm pitch.

**Why it meets each requirement:**
- **Hydrogen:** Argon contains no hydrogen, so the 2% limit is satisfied with large margin. The only hydrogen is in structural plastics and wall material, which a fiducial-volume cut excludes.
- **Muons at all angles:** A TPC images in 3D natively. Its efficiency is set by track length in the active volume, not by orientation, so tracks perpendicular to the beam and backward-going tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones. Pixel readout avoids the wire-plane ambiguities that make tracks parallel to the wire planes hard to reconstruct.
- **Low-energy protons:** A 60 MeV proton travels roughly 2.5–3 cm in LAr. That spans several pixel hits plus the dE/dx Bragg peak, so these protons can be identified and their energy measured by range.
- **Event pile-up:** At 410 m, a multi-tonne target sees several interactions per spill. Pixel readout is unambiguous in 3D, and segmenting into modules keeps the readout from suffering the pile-up confusion of a large monolithic projective TPC.
- **Compatibility with the magnet:** At 0.15 T, the Lorentz angle for electron drift in LAr is negligible. Pixel ASICs are unaffected by the field.

**Fallback.** A high-pressure argon gas TPC (Ar with ≤10% CH₄ keeps hydrogen at about 1% of nucleons) gives superb thresholds. However, it holds only about 100 kg of target, and fitting a pressure vessel inside the magnet is hard. Treat it as a complement or fallback, not the primary choice.

## 2. Build a low-mass, non-magnetic cryostat

- Use a thin-walled aluminium or composite cryostat, not stainless steel.
- Keep the wall material between the argon and the downstream drift chambers as thin as possible. This limits multiple scattering and energy loss for forward muons whose charge and momentum the magnet spectrometer measures.

## 3. Use SiPM-based light detection for timing

- Install ArCLight or light-collection-module tiles read out by SiPMs inside each module.
- Prompt scintillation light provides the event start time (t₀) and lets interactions within a spill be matched to the beam bunch structure.
- PMTs should be avoided because they are sensitive to magnetic fields; SiPMs work normally at 0.15 T.

## 4. Surround the target with time-of-flight and tracking panels on all sides

The existing drift chambers sit downstream, so they only catch forward-going tracks. To cover high-angle and backward muons:
- Add thin tracking and time-of-flight layers (for example scintillator bars or MRPCs) on the sides and the upstream face.
- Time-of-flight determines direction, separating backward-going tracks from incoming ones and from entering cosmic or rock muons.
- These layers also tag muons that exit sideways. For tracks that exit rather than stop, momentum comes from multiple-scattering measurements in the argon.
- This hardware is outside the fiducial volume, so its hydrogen content does not matter.

## 5. Check the drift chambers and magnet integration

- Confirm that the downstream drift-chamber acceptance matches the new geometry.
- Verify field uniformity at the cryostat location.
- Make sure the cryogenic services do not intrude into the 6.5 m magnet volume.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (ArgonCube/ND-LAr style), because it is hydrogen-free, images tracks isotropically, and resolves 60 MeV protons, whereas a plastic-scintillator target would exceed the 2% hydrogen limit.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

Before proposing hardware, let me work through the constraints:

**Muon reconstruction:** Need ≥25% efficiency at *all* angles including 90° and backward. The magnet gives 0.15 T over 6.5 m → maximum sagitta for a 1 GeV/c track over 6.5 m is ~40 mm — adequate for forward tracks. But perpendicular and backward muons may exit the active target volume laterally or upstream. The 2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse dimensions help contain lateral tracks but backward tracks exit upstream into unequipped space.

**Proton reconstruction down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy:** 
- 60 MeV kinetic energy proton: range in water ≈ 14 mm, in scintillator ≈ 17 mm, in liquid argon ≈ 11 mm.
- This demands fine-grained active material with radiation length and nuclear interaction length large compared to the track length, but with small enough cell pitch to actually see ~1 cm tracks.
- Need dE/dx capability to distinguish protons from pions.

**Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of nucleons:**
- Pure water: H is 2/18 × 18/10 = 11.1% by nucleon count → water is fine (H nucleons/total nucleons = 2/18 ≈ 11%)
- Polystyrene (CH): H fraction = 1/13 ≈ 7.7% → fine
- Liquid argon: 0% hydrogen → fine but no H signal
- Hydrocarbon scintillator oils: need to check per compound

**Volume:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m ≈ 5.4 m³

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (FGST) as Primary Active Target** *(most critical)*

Replace the passive target with a fully active array of plastic scintillator bars arranged in X-Y planes:

- **Bar cross-section: 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm**, length matching transverse dimensions (~2.3 m or 2.6 m)
- **Plane spacing: 1.0 cm** (alternating X and Y views), giving ~90 X-Y plane pairs across the 0.9 m depth
- **Wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber** readout through each bar core, coupled to **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** at both ends for position-along-bar resolution via charge asymmetry (~1 cm resolution achievable)
- **Scintillator material:** polystyrene-based (e.g., Bicron BC-408 equivalent), with hydrogen nucleon fraction ≈ 8% — safely below 20%
- **Why this works for short proton tracks:** 1 cm × 1 cm cells give ≥1 hit for a 60 MeV proton (range ~14–17 mm in scintillator = ~1–2 bar lengths). Two-end readout gives dE/dx and hence particle ID to separate protons from pions. The cell size is the key parameter.
- **Why this works for angular coverage:** A fully active volume with no dead regions means tracks at any angle deposit energy in crossed X-Y planes. A 90° track traverses bars along its full lateral extent.
- **Timing:** SiPM readout with ~1 ns timing separates interaction products from beam backgrounds and helps with track directionality (critical for backward-going tracks — a backward muon has hits ordered in time upstream-to-downstream, opposite to a forward track).

**Scale:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m cross-section, 0.9 m deep → approximately 2×90 = 180 planes, each with ~260 × 230 = ~6×10⁴ bars per plane → ~10⁷ channels total. This is large; a practical implementation would use longer bars (full 2.6 m) read at both ends, reducing channel count. Comparable to NOvA or T2K ND280 FGD technology.

---

### 2. **Upstream Muon Catcher / Backward-Track Spectrometer**

The existing magnet and drift chambers are *downstream*. Backward-going and large-angle muons that exit the upstream face of the active target have no momentum measurement.

- Install a **compact iron-scintillator range stack** immediately upstream of the active target, ~0.5 m deep, with 5 cm iron plates interleaved with 1 cm scintillator planes (X and Y).
- This provides: (a) a muon range measurement for backward tracks stopping in it, (b) a crude momentum estimate from range for tracks up to ~400 MeV/c, and (c) a veto/tag for particles entering the active target from upstream.
- Scintillator planes use the same SiPM/WLS-fiber technology as the active target for uniformity.
- The iron-to-scintillator ratio keeps the hydrogen fraction negligible here (this is not part of the fiducial volume).

**Why needed:** At 0.7 GeV peak neutrino energy, quasi-elastic scattering produces muons with broad angular distributions. Backward muons are kinematically suppressed but not absent; the requirement explicitly demands ≥25% efficiency for backward tracks.

---

### 3. **Lateral Muon Spectrometer Panels**

Large-angle muons exiting the sides of the active target (the 2.6 m × 0.9 m and 2.3 m × 0.9 m faces) pass through the magnet iron yoke or fringe regions with uncertain field.

- Install **resistive plate chambers (RPCs) or large-area scintillator panels** on the four lateral faces of the active target volume, 2–3 layers deep on each face.
- These provide a track seed for matching to drift chamber reconstruction and confirm the exit point and angle.
- Thin (3–5 cm) iron absorbers between layers provide a crude range measurement and filter soft backgrounds.
- This also closes a potential efficiency hole for tracks at ~90° to the beam that exit sideways before curving back into the downstream drift chamber acceptance in the magnetic field.

---

### 4. **Upgrade of Downstream Drift Chambers: Addition of dE/dx Capability and Time Stamps**

The existing gas drift chambers measure momentum and charge but may not provide adequate dE/dx for particle identification, which is needed to:
- Distinguish muons from pions (critical for the neutrino interaction classification)
- Identify protons that make it out of the active target

- **Upgrade gas mixture** to a heavier noble-gas blend (e.g., Ar/CF₄/isobutane) optimized for dE/dx resolution, targeting σ(dE/dx)/(dE/dx) < 5% with sufficient samples.
- Add **TDC readout on existing anode wires** if not already present, to get cluster timing for drift velocity corrections and 3D reconstruction of large-angle tracks.
- This upgrade is relatively low cost compared to new detector construction.

---

### 5. **SiPM Trigger and DAQ System**

The fine-grained scintillator target generates a large channel count. A modern data acquisition system is needed:

- **Self-triggered front-end ASICs** (e.g., based on CITIROC or similar) on each SiPM channel, with zero-suppression and 10 ns timestamp resolution.
- **Online track-finding trigger** using FPGA-based pattern recognition to select neutrino interaction candidates and reject through-going cosmic muons (rate will be high at 410 m from target).
- Cosmic muons also serve as a continuous calibration source for the scintillator response and drift chamber alignment — the DAQ should record a prescaled sample of these.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Addresses | Technology Readiness |
|---|---|---|
| Fine-grained scintillator target (1 cm bars, SiPM) | Short proton tracks, all-angle coverage, H fraction | High (T2K FGD, NOvA heritage) |
| Upstream iron-scintillator range stack | Backward muon efficiency | High |
| Lateral scintillator/RPC panels | 90° muon efficiency | High |
| Drift chamber dE/dx + timing upgrade | Particle ID downstream | Medium (depends on existing hardware) |
| New SiPM-based DAQ | Trigger, channel count, calibration | High |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a fully active fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker of 1 cm × 1 cm cross-section bars in alternating X-Y planes read out by WLS fibers and SiPMs at both ends, providing the hit-level sensitivity to reconstruct short (~1–2 cm) proton tracks from 60 MeV protons via dE/dx and multi-hit topology, while maintaining the hydrogen nucleon fraction below 20% and giving full angular acceptance for muons through continuous active coverage and nanosecond timing for directionality.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Constraints that drive the design

- **Full angular acceptance.** The muon must be reconstructed with ≥25% efficiency at every angle, including 90° and backward. The existing downstream drift chambers only see tracks that exit forward, so high-angle and backward muons are currently lost.
- **Low-energy protons.** Protons with kinetic energy near 60 MeV travel only about 3 cm in plastic (density ~1 g/cm³). The target must be fine-grained and isotropic, so a 3 cm track at any orientation still leaves several hits with dE/dx.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** Hydrogen nuclei must be ≤20% of target nucleons.
  - Polystyrene (CH): 1/13 ≈ 7.7%.
  - Water: 2/18 ≈ 11%.
  - Ordinary hydrocarbon scintillator is therefore acceptable. Hydrogen-rich materials such as polyethylene (CH₂, 2/14 ≈ 14%) are also acceptable but leave less margin.
- **Space.** The envelope is 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (0.9 m along the beam), and the field is 0.15 T.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-readout scintillator-cube target (SuperFGD-type)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each read out along three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres by SiPMs/MPPCs.
- Roughly 2.0 m (width) × 1.0 m (height) × 0.8 m (along the beam) gives about 1.6 million cubes and about 1.6 t of target.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic response.** Unlike planar bar trackers, there is no "blind" angle, so 90° and backward tracks are tracked as well as forward ones.
- **Proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes, enough for a vertex-attached track and dE/dx identification. This pushes the proton threshold down to the level the analysis needs.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** The CH target sits at 7.7% hydrogen nucleons, comfortably inside the hydrogen-subtraction model's validity.
- **Stopping muons.** Muons that stop inside the target get a momentum estimate from range.
- **Neutron tagging.** Nanosecond-level timing allows neutron detection by time of flight to isolated hits, improving energy reconstruction.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Two gas TPCs, each roughly 2.0 m × 0.6 m × 0.8 m, placed above and below the cube target inside the magnet.
- Resistive Micromegas readout for good spatial resolution at low cost per channel.

**Physics motivation**
- Muons emitted near 90° (and steep backward muons) leave the target transversely and never reach the downstream chambers.
- The HA-TPCs measure their momentum and charge sign from curvature in the 0.15 T field.
- They also provide dE/dx particle identification, separating μ from π, p and e.
- This directly restores the ≥25% efficiency at high angle.

## 3. Time-of-flight scintillator envelope

**Technology**
- Thin, long plastic scintillator bars (about 1 cm thick) read out at both ends by SiPMs, aiming for timing resolution better than about 150 ps.
- The bars surround the target-plus-TPC module on all six faces.

**Physics motivation**
- **Direction.** Timing between the target and the ToF panels distinguishes backward-going tracks from forward-entering ones. It also rejects out-of-volume backgrounds such as entering particles and sand muons.
- **Particle ID.** Timing adds particle identification in the momentum range where dE/dx bands cross.

## 4. Supporting electronics, calibration and integration

**Technology**
- Upgraded front-end electronics with fast-timing SiPM digitisers.
- LED and cosmic calibration systems.
- Field-map remeasurement of the 0.15 T dipole after installation.

**Physics motivation**
- These keep the energy scale and timing systematics below the statistical precision expected at 410 m, where event rates are high.

## Summary

The cube target delivers isotropic acceptance and the 60 MeV proton threshold with an acceptable hydrogen fraction. The HA-TPCs and ToF recover high-angle and backward muons with charge and direction information.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a ~1 cm³ 3D-readout plastic-scintillator-cube active target (SuperFGD-type, ~7.7% hydrogen nucleons), complemented by high-angle TPCs above and below it.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Near-Station Active Target

## The constraint that decides everything: hydrogen content

The obvious modern choice for a 4π active target is the T2K ND280-upgrade approach: a fine-grained 3D scintillator-cube detector (SuperFGD-type) between thin high-angle TPCs. **That option is ruled out here.**

- Polystyrene scintillator is roughly (CH)ₙ, so each carbon (12 nucleons) comes with one hydrogen nucleus.
- Hydrogen nuclei are therefore about 1/13 ≈ 7.7% of target nucleons. That is nearly four times the 2% ceiling.
- Other hydrogen-rich actives fail the same way: water (H₂O gives 2/18 ≈ 11%), liquid scintillator, and organic plastics generally.

The far detector contains no hydrogen, so the natural target is the far-detector nucleus itself. Argon is a likely candidate, though this should be confirmed against the actual far-detector material. Argon also removes the nuclear-model extrapolation problem.

## Recommendation 1 (primary): Pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC as the active target

Use a modular, ArgonCube-style LArTPC with 3D pixel charge readout (LArPix-class ASICs). It should sit in a compact cryostat filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region.

**Fit and mass**
- The region is about 5.4 m³.
- After the cryostat and insulation are subtracted, the instrumented volume is of order 3–4 m³, giving a few tonnes of LAr. This is ample at 410 m from a 0.7 GeV beam.

**Hydrogen budget**
- Argon contributes zero hydrogen.
- Inside the fiducial volume, keep hydrogenous material to a minimum:
  - Use resistive-film or metal field shaping and thin G10/PCB anodes.
  - Do not use plastic structural members.
- Place the inner cryostat wall in stainless steel or titanium.
- Keep any foam insulation outside the active volume, where a fiducial cut rejects vertices in it.
- Require an explicit nucleon-fraction audit of all fiducial-volume materials. The target should be well below 2%, for example under 0.5%, to leave margin.

**Proton threshold**
- A 60 MeV proton travels roughly 3–4 cm in LAr.
- With pixel pitch of about 4 mm and 3D readout, this gives about 10 hits with clear Bragg-peak dE/dx.
- Protons are therefore reconstructed isotropically, at all angles, with no projective ambiguity.

**Isotropic muon reconstruction**
- True 3D pixel readout has no wire-angle blind spots. Perpendicular and backward tracks reconstruct as well as forward ones.
- Momentum options:
  - Range, for contained muons.
  - Multiple-Coulomb-scattering fits, for exiting muons (roughly 10–15% resolution).

**Pile-up**
- Use short drift modules, with drift of about 0.4–0.5 m along one transverse axis.
- Add optically segmented light readout (ArCLight/LCM-style detectors on the module walls). This gives ns-scale timing and isolates interactions within the spill.

## Recommendation 2: Thin high-angle gas TPCs around the cryostat

Install gas TPCs with resistive-Micromegas readout above, below and on the sides of the cryostat, wherever clearance in the magnet allows.

- **Why they are needed:** The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward tracks. High-angle and backward muons exiting the LAr need sign-of-charge and curvature measurement in the 0.15 T field to reach the 25% efficiency requirement across the full angular range.
- **Hydrogen impact:** These sit outside the fiducial target, so any hydrogen they carry does not count. Even so, a low-quencher argon/CF₄-based gas is preferred.

## Recommendation 3: Fast timing layer for track direction

Add an outer time-of-flight layer of thin scintillator bars with SiPM readout, about 100–150 ps resolution, around the target and HA-TPCs. Being outside the fiducial volume, its hydrogen content is irrelevant.

- It unambiguously separates backward-going muons from incoming, entering tracks such as sand muons and out-of-fiducial interactions.
- It supplies the event time (t₀) to the TPCs.

## Recommendation 4: Integration items

**Cryostat**
- Use a low-mass, non-magnetic (stainless or titanium) cryostat that fits inside the warm dipole.
- Keep the walls thin so that tracks exiting toward the downstream drift chambers and side TPCs suffer minimal scattering.
- Verify field uniformity and confirm that cryogenic services do not intrude into the 6.5 m tracking volume.

**Calibration**
- Use LAr purity monitors and a laser or cosmic calibration system, so that proton dE/dx, and hence particle ID, remains reliable down to the 60 MeV threshold.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace any hydrocarbon/scintillator active-target concept with a hydrogen-free modular pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (with segmented light readout) so hydrogen stays well under 2% of target nucleons while giving 4π muon and low-threshold proton reconstruction.

# Proposed hardware for the ND280 upstream upgrade

## Why the current detector falls short

- **FGD geometry limits angular acceptance.** FGD bars are all perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only upstream and downstream of them. Tracks at more than about 50° cross few layers, or run along a single bar, and never reach a TPC. That affects about 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons.
- **The proton threshold is too high.** Short protons, below roughly 400–450 MeV/c, cross only a few 1 cm bars, mostly in one view. With the median at about 450 MeV/c, roughly half the leading protons are lost or poorly measured.
- **Neutrons are not reconstructed at all.** Antineutrino transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies need the neutron.

## 1. Main item: a 3D-granular scintillator target ("SuperFGD")

**Structure**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes: 1% PTP, 0.03% POPOP, with a reflective etched/chemical surface coating.
- Layout of about 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, so roughly 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m. This fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- About 2 t of CH target, nearly double the FGD1 mass.

**Readout**
- Each cube has three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes, threaded with 1 mm Kuraray Y-11 WLS fibres along x, y and z.
- This gives three 2D projections, which combine into true 3D hits. Because z-fibres are included, there is no blind direction for any track angle, giving near-4π acceptance.
- The fibres total about 56,000 channels. Each is read at one end by a 1.3 × 1.3 mm² MPPC (Hamamatsu S13360-1325 type, 25 µm pixels). The far end is mirrored.
- Expected light yield is about 40–50 p.e. per MIP per fibre.
- Electronics: CITIROC-based front-end boards (the Baby MIND type), mounted on the detector faces outside the active volume.

**Expected performance**
- Proton tracking threshold of about 300 MeV/c (2–3 cubes).
- Proton/muon/pion particle ID from dE/dx in each cube.
- Sub-ns hit timing, which allows neutron detection by time of flight from isolated secondary hits, giving the neutron kinetic energy. This enables full TKI for antineutrino charged-current events with a neutron.
- Proton momentum is measured by range up to about 900 MeV/c.
- The roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, and most muons, exit into the TPCs below.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

These sit outside the 0.6 m box, in the remaining former-P0D space, roughly 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m each.

- **Field cage:** lightweight composite (aramid honeycomb with Kapton laminates, about 3% X₀) to minimise material between the target and the calorimeters.
- **Gas:** the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 mixture as the existing TPCs, for commonality.
- **Readout:** resistive-anode ("encapsulated resistive") bulk Micromegas.
  - The resistive layer spreads charge, so wider pads (about 10 × 11 mm) still give about 0.6 mm spatial resolution.
  - This lowers channel count and cost and suppresses sparking.
- **Electronics:** AFTER/DREAM-type chips.
- **Physics role:** measure high-angle muons and energetic protons by curvature in the 0.2 T field, with dE/dx for particle ID, and charge sign for the antineutrino mode. Together with the existing forward TPCs, this gives full polar-angle coverage.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

- Six panels of about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm plastic scintillator bars around the new target and HA-TPC module.
- Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of 6 × 6 mm² SiPMs, giving about 150 ps timing.
- **Purposes:**
  - Determine track direction, distinguishing backward-going tracks from incoming ones.
  - Reject out-of-fiducial-volume and sand-muon backgrounds.
  - Improve particle ID for the exiting tracks.

## 4. Supporting changes

- Refurbish or replace the P0D-region ECal coverage where needed so that the TOF and HA-TPC fit.
- Upgrade the trigger and DAQ for the roughly 60k new channels, synchronised to the J-PARC spill clock at the ns level.
- Calibrate with cosmic rays and an LED/laser system on the fibres.
- Keep FGD2 (with its water layers) for the carbon-to-water ratio. Cross-calibrate FGD1 and the new target on carbon.

## Net effect

- Muon acceptance becomes near-4π.
- The proton threshold falls to about 300 MeV/c, and neutrons become measurable.
- Kinematically complete charged-current events, together with the larger target mass, allow flux and cross-section constraints to approach the roughly 4% T2K-II systematic goal.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a ~2-tonne 3D-readout fine-grained scintillator target (SuperFGD: ~2×10⁶ 1 cm³ cubes read by orthogonal x/y/z WLS fibres and MPPCs) for 4π tracking, a ~300 MeV/c proton threshold and neutron time-of-flight.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrade for the ND280 Upstream Region

## 1. Why the current detector falls short

**Angular acceptance.**
- FGD1 bars lie only in x and y, all perpendicular to the beam. Tracks at high angle (above about 50°) or backward run nearly parallel to a bar plane and are poorly reconstructed.
- The existing TPCs sit only downstream of the targets, so they see mainly forward tracks.
- The SMRD and side ECals give range and calorimetry for side-going tracks, but no charge sign and no good momentum.
- About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons exit above 50°. These events currently drop out or are badly measured, which biases the sample toward forward kinematics and differs from Super-K's 4π acceptance.

**Proton threshold.**
- In bar geometry, a proton must cross several layers in both views to be reconstructed. The effective threshold is about 450–500 MeV/c, roughly at the median of the proton spectrum.
- A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of only about 8 cm in CH.
- Transverse kinematic imbalance analyses need the full proton spectrum, so about half the protons are effectively lost.

**Neutrons.** There is no capability for neutron kinematics, which matters for antineutrino events.

## 2. Proposed configuration

Replace the P0D with an active target and surround it with tracking and timing detectors.

### (a) Fine-segmented 3D scintillator target ("Super-FGD")

**Geometry and mass**
- About 2 million optically isolated polystyrene cubes, 1 × 1 × 1 cm³, each with a reflective (chemically etched) surface.
- Array of 192 (x) × 182 (y) × 56 (z) ≈ 1.96 million cubes, about 1.92 × 1.82 × 0.56 m³. This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with room for the mechanical box and readout.
- Mass about 2.0 t of CH. This is roughly the combined mass of FGD1 and FGD2 and doubles the hydrocarbon target.

**Readout**
- Three orthogonal holes per cube hold WLS fibres (about 1 mm diameter) running in x, y and z.
- Each fibre is read by an MPPC at one end, with a mirror at the far end.
- Channel count: 192·182 + 192·56 + 182·56 ≈ 56,000. This is far fewer than one channel per cube, because three 2D projections give 3D hits.

**Performance gains**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three projections give a 3D image for any track direction, including high-angle and backward tracks.
- **Low proton threshold.** Protons down to about 300 MeV/c (kinetic energy about 45 MeV, range about 2 cm, or 2–3 cubes) can be reconstructed, recovering most of the proton spectrum.
- **Particle identification.** Fine dE/dx sampling near the stopping point separates protons from pions.
- **Neutron tagging.** Light yield of roughly 40–50 p.e. per MIP per fibre and sub-ns hit timing allow neutron detection by isolated delayed hits. Time of flight from the vertex then gives neutron energy, enabling antineutrino transverse kinematic imbalance.

**Containment check.** A 900 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 360 MeV and a range of about 1 m. The roughly 6% of protons above this momentum, and most muons, exit the target. They must be measured outside it, which motivates (b).

### (b) Two High-Angle TPCs, above and below the new target

**Purpose.** Measure momentum, charge sign and dE/dx for muons and energetic protons leaving at large angles, in the existing 0.2 T field.

**Size.** Each about 2.0 m (x) × 0.8 m (y, drift) × 1.8 m (z).

**Construction**
- Light composite field cage (aramid/honeycomb sandwich with laminated Kapton/copper strips). This keeps material low for exiting particles.
- Same 95:3:2 Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ gas as the existing TPCs, for common gas handling.

**Readout**
- Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode).
- Charge spreading lets larger pads (about 1 cm) reach under 0.8 mm spatial resolution. This reduces channel count, and the resistive layer prevents sparks.

**Targets**
- Momentum resolution of about 10% at 1 GeV/c.
- dE/dx resolution under 10% for μ/e and p/π separation.

### (c) Time-of-flight envelope

**Layout.** Six planes of plastic scintillator bars enclosing the new target and HA-TPCs. Bars are about 1 cm thick, read out at both ends by large-area SiPM arrays.

**Timing.** About 150 ps resolution.

**Functions**
- Determines track direction (forward versus backward). This removes out-of-fiducial and "sand-muon" backgrounds that mimic backward tracks.
- Provides an extra PID handle for low-momentum particles.
- Gives a precise event T₀.

### (d) Retain and integrate

## Physics Requirements Analysis

**Geometry of the active target:**
2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (transverse × transverse × longitudinal). This is a wide, shallow target — only 0.9 m along the beam. Tracks at large angles and backward-going tracks will be **short** in the longitudinal direction and may exit transversely.

**Key reconstruction demands:**
1. Muons at **all angles ≥ 25% efficiency**, including 90° and backward — requires 4π-ish angular coverage with no dead zones
2. Protons down to **~60 MeV kinetic energy** (range in water ~3 cm, in scintillator ~4 cm) — requires fine spatial resolution and low detection threshold
3. **Hydrogen content ≤ 2% of target nucleons** — severely constrains the target material (see below)

---

## Hydrogen Constraint — The Dominant Design Driver

This is the most restrictive requirement. Consider common materials:

- **Polystyrene scintillator (CH):** H/nucleon ratio ≈ 1/13 ≈ **7.7%** — far too much hydrogen
- **Liquid argon:** 0% hydrogen — passes, but technology challenges
- **Carbon (graphite):** 0% hydrogen — passes
- **Water (H₂O):** H/nucleon ratio = 2/18 ≈ **11%** — far too much
- **Lead:** 0% hydrogen — passes
- **Iron:** 0% hydrogen — passes
- **Liquid scintillator (CH₂ roughly):** ~14% — fails badly
- **Mineral oil (CH₂):** ~14% — fails
- **Argon gas TPC:** 0% hydrogen — passes
- **High-Z scintillator with no H:** not standard
- **Boron carbide, etc.:** exotic

Practically, the target must be **hydrogen-free or nearly so**. Standard organic scintillator is ruled out. This points to:

- **Liquid argon TPC** (LAr TPC)
- **Gas TPC** (argon-based)
- **Solid argon or noble liquid**
- **Thin passive absorber planes (e.g., carbon/graphite) with active gas detectors between them**

Given the existing warm dipole magnet and downstream gas drift chambers, and the near-detector context (high rate, 410 m from target), a **gaseous argon TPC** or a **fine-grained tracker with low-Z, low-hydrogen absorber** is most practical.

A **straw-tube tracker or gas TPC with argon:CO₂ or similar gas** would have negligible hydrogen. CO₂ has no hydrogen; argon has none. Even Ar:CO₂ 70:30 by volume has essentially zero hydrogen.

Alternatively, a **High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC (HPgTPC)** provides the needed 3D tracking.

For the short proton tracks (~60 MeV KE → range ~3–4 cm in solid, longer in gas), a **gas TPC is actually better** than a solid detector because low-momentum protons that would stop in a few mm of solid will travel several cm in gas, making them reconstructable. This is a strong argument for gas.

---

## Hardware Upgrades Required

### 1. Active Target: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgTPC)

**Technology:** Gaseous argon TPC, operating at ~5–10 atm, with multi-wire or micro-pattern gas detector (MPGD) readout (e.g., Micromegas or GEM planes).

**Why:**
- **Zero hydrogen** — argon:CO₂ or pure argon gas has no hydrogen nuclei, satisfying the ≤2% hydrogen constraint that eliminates standard scintillator
- **Low detection threshold for protons:** At elevated pressure, gas density increases, so short proton tracks (~60 MeV KE) have ranges of several cm and are fully reconstructable with mm-scale space-point resolution; in solid scintillator such tracks would be only a few mm long
- **4π angular coverage inherent:** A TPC reconstructs tracks in full 3D regardless of angle — perpendicular and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward tracks, meeting the ≥25% efficiency at all angles requirement
- **Continuous 3D tracking:** Unlike plane-based detectors, a TPC has no angular dead zones from inter-plane gaps
- **Existing magnet is compatible:** The warm dipole already provides the magnetic field for momentum measurement; the TPC sits inside it
- **The existing geometry fits:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m is achievable as a TPC drift volume (drift along the 0.9 m beam direction, or transversely — transverse drift preferred to keep drift distance short and reduce diffusion)

**Design note:** Drift field should be transverse (along the 2.6 m or 2.3 m dimension) rather than along the 0.9 m beam axis, to maximize drift distance and keep readout planes at the sides. Alternatively a double-drift with central cathode drifting ±1.15 m works well.

---

### 2. Cathode, Field Cage, and High-Voltage System

**Technology:** Precision-machined field cage with resistive divider chain; HV feedthrough rated to ~100 kV; low-mass construction (carbon fiber or thin copper-clad kapton strips on insulating frame)

**Why:**
- A TPC requires a uniform drift field (~100–200 V/cm × drift length) — for a 1.15 m half-drift at 200 V/cm that's ~23 kV; for 2.6 m full drift ~52 kV
- Low-mass field cage minimizes secondary interactions and scattering that would confuse the event reconstruction
- Must be designed to avoid hydrogen-containing materials in structural elements where possible (use carbon fiber over fiberglass)

---

### 3. MPGD Readout Planes (Micromegas or GEM arrays)

**Technology:** Large-area Micromegas tiles or GEM foils, covering the full anode plane(s); segmented into ~1 cm² pads with ~1 mm strip pitch in two coordinates

**Why:**
- Provides the 2D hit position on the anode; combined with drift time gives full 3D hit
- Micromegas and GEMs are well-established for large-area coverage (used in ATLAS, T2K, CERN experiments)
- Low-mass compared to wire chambers; minimal hydrogen in construction materials (use kapton/copper, avoid epoxy where possible or select low-H epoxy)
- ~1 mm spatial resolution is sufficient to reconstruct the short proton tracks and to separate multiple tracks from nuclear interactions
- High rate capability needed at 410 m near-detector location

---

### 4. Front-End Electronics and Trigger/DAQ System

**Technology:** Continuously sampling ADC-based readout (e.g., SAMPA chips as used in ALICE TPC, or similar ASIC), zero-suppressed or lossless readout; trigger derived from downstream muon spectrometer or beam timing

**Why:**
- TPC signals are inherently slow (drift time ~microseconds); need a readout window that captures the full drift
- At a near detector 410 m from target, neutrino interaction rates are high — need pile-up rejection and fast readout
- Continuous digitization at ~10 MHz per channel with zero suppression manages data rates
- Must timestamp hits to associate them with beam spills and reject out-of-time cosmics

---

### 5. Upstream and Downstream Veto / Tagger Scintillator Panels

**Technology:** Thin plastic scintillator panels with SiPM readout, surrounding the upstream face and sides of the TPC

**Why:**
- Muons and other charged particles entering the TPC from outside (beam halo, secondaries) must be tagged and rejected or their tracks identified as not originating from neutrino interactions in the fiducial volume
- Needed for charged-current event selection — to confirm the muon exits into the downstream spectrometer
- SiPM readout chosen over PMTs for compactness and operation in the magnetic field (PMTs are sensitive to the 0.15 T dipole field)
- These panels contain plastic scintillator (CH) but are **outside** the active target volume, so their hydrogen does not enter the nucleon count for the target fiducial mass
- Very thin (1–2 cm) to minimize material before the TPC

---

### 6. Upgrade of Downstream Drift Chamber Tracking / Muon Spectrometer Interface

**Technology:** Addition of scintillator hodoscope planes immediately downstream of the TPC exit window, with time-of-flight capability; possible addition of a thin downstream GEM station

**Why:**
- Muons exiting the rear of the TPC (forward-going) need to be matched into the existing gas drift chambers for momentum measurement using the dipole field
- Currently the downstream drift chambers handle this, but a new interface layer is needed to match the TPC hit to the spectrometer track, especially for tracks at large angles that may exit the side of the TPC and miss the downstream chambers entirely
- A hodoscope with ~1 ns timing provides ToF for momentum cross-check on low-momentum tracks
- Side-exiting muons (large angle) need side scintillator panels (see item 5) to confirm they are muons rather than pions

---

### 7. Gas System: Recirculating Purification and Pressure Control

**Technology:** Closed-loop gas recirculation with molecular sieve / OXISORB purification cartridges; pressure regulation to ±0.1% stability; gas purity monitoring via small dedicated drift cell or purity monitor

**Why:**
- HPgTPC at 5–10 atm requires significant gas inventory; recirculation is essential for cost and to maintain purity
- Oxygen and water impurities at ppb level capture drifting electrons — purification must maintain O₂-equivalent impurity below ~100 ppt for long drift distances
- Pressure stability directly affects drift velocity and therefore z-reconstruction accuracy
- Gas purity monitors (small cells with UV photocathode or ⁵⁵Fe source) provide real-time feedback
- The gas mixture (Ar:CO₂ or Ar:CO₂:CF₄) must be chosen to have zero hydrogen while providing appropriate drift velocity and diffusion

---

### 8. Calibration System: Laser and Radioactive Source

**Technology:** UV laser system (e.g., 266 nm Nd:YAG 4th harmonic) with beam steering through fused silica windows; and/or deployable ⁵⁵Fe or ⁸³Kr gas injection for gain calibration

**Why:**
- Drift velocity calibration using laser tracks at known positions (straight lines) corrects for pressure/temperature variations and space-charge distortions
- ⁵⁵Fe (5.9 keV X-ray) or ⁸³ᵐKr (41.5 keV conversion electron) dissolved in the gas at ppm level provides uniform gain calibration across all pads
- Space-charge buildup from positive ions drifting slowly back to the cathode (significant at high neutrino flux) distorts tracks; laser calibration maps and corrects these distortions
- Essential for maintaining <1 mm spatial resolution across the full volume over the life of the experiment

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target TPC | HPgTPC, Ar:CO₂ | Zero H constraint + 4π tracking + low-KE protons |
| Field cage & HV | Low-mass resistive divider, CF construction | Uniform drift field, low material budget |
| Readout planes | Large-area Micromegas or GEM | 3D hit reconstruction, mm resolution |
| Front-end electronics | Continuously sampling ASICs (SAMPA-type) | High-rate readout, full drift window capture |
| Veto/tagger scintillators | Thin scintillator + SiPM (outside fiducial) | External background rejection, muon ID |
| Downstream interface | Scintillator hodoscope + side panels | Large-angle muon matching to spectrometer |
| Gas recirculation system | Closed-loop purifier + pressure control | Electron lifetime, purity, operational stability |
| Calibration system | UV laser + Kr/Fe source injection | Drift velocity, gain uniformity, space-charge |

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target region with a high-pressure gaseous argon TPC (HPgTPC) with Micromegas or GEM readout, because it simultaneously satisfies all three otherwise-conflicting core requirements: the hydrogen-free gas eliminates the nucleon-composition problem that rules out all standard scintillator-based options, the continuous 3D reconstruction provides the required ≥25% muon efficiency at every angle including backward-going tracks with no geometric dead zones, and the low gas density gives centimeter-scale ranges to short low-momentum protons (60 MeV KE) that would be undetectable millimeter-long stubs in any solid detector.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposal: Near-Detector Inner Region

## 1. Why the current design falls short

**High-angle acceptance.** The existing tracking targets use x/y bar planes perpendicular to the beam. The TPCs sit downstream of them. A track at more than about 50–60° runs nearly parallel to the planes and crosses few of them, so it is poorly reconstructed. It also rarely reaches a downstream TPC.
- About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leave at these angles.
- This loss of phase space drives a large share of the flux and cross-section extrapolation uncertainty.
- Backward-going tracks are also poorly identified, because timing between subdetectors is too coarse.

**Proton threshold.** Each 2D plane sees only one projection. Short proton tracks are hard to separate from the vertex activity, and the 9.6 mm bars give a proton tracking threshold of about 450–500 MeV/c. That threshold sits right at the median of the proton spectrum, which is incompatible with transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) measurements needing both the muon and the leading proton.

**Range of a typical proton.** A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of about 8 cm in plastic. A 300 MeV/c proton has about 47 MeV and a range of about 2 cm. A detector that sees a 2 cm track in 3D from any direction needs roughly 1 cm isotropic granularity.

## 2. Proposed upgrades

### (a) Highly segmented 3D scintillator target ("Super-FGD"), filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box

**Geometry**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56.
- Reflective etched surface on each cube.
- Three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes per cube, each carrying a 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibre.
- Mass of about 2 t of CH target, comparable to the two existing targets combined.

**Readout**
- Three 2D projections, giving about 192×184 + 192×56 + 184×56 ≈ 56,000 channels, each with a silicon photomultiplier.
- Front-end electronics compatible with the existing scintillator readout.
- Light yield of about 40–50 photoelectrons per minimum-ionising particle per fibre, so a hit is well defined in all three views.

**Performance gains**
- Near-4π acceptance for muons, since there is no preferred plane orientation.
- Proton tracking threshold of about 300 MeV/c, and calorimetric dE/dx for particle identification.
- Clean vertex-activity measurement.
- Neutron detection: neutrons scatter off hydrogen and produce isolated cube hits. With about 1 ns hit timing, time-of-flight to these isolated hits gives the neutron kinetic energy. This allows full TKI for antineutrino events.
- Better photon/π⁰ conversion tagging partly compensates for removing the photon-tagging section.

### (b) Two high-angle TPCs, above and below the new target

These fill the remaining height of the old photon-tagging volume, each roughly 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m.

**Design**
- Argon-based gas, matching the existing TPCs.
- Thin, low-mass field cage built from composite laminate, to reduce multiple scattering and dead material.
- Readout by resistive Micromegas, where charge spreading lets fewer pads achieve spatial resolution of about 0.5 mm or better.

**Performance gains**
- Momentum resolution of about 10% or better at 1 GeV/c from curvature in the 0.2 T field, for high-angle muons and for protons that exit the target. Protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) range out poorly in 0.6 m of plastic, so TPC curvature is the right tool for them.
- dE/dx separation of electrons, muons and protons.
- Together, the existing downstream TPCs plus the new ones cover forward, backward and high-angle tracks.

### (c) Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new target and the high-angle TPCs

**Design**
- Six planes of long plastic scintillator bars, read out at both ends by large silicon photomultiplier arrays.
- Time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Performance gains**
- Determines track direction, separating forward-going from backward-going tracks and in-going from out-going ones.
- Rejects interactions in the magnet and walls ("out-of-fiducial" background).
- Adds time-of-flight particle identification to the TPC dE/dx.

### (d) Supporting changes

- Upgrade the existing TPC readout and DAQ and the trigger and clock distribution, so all subsystems share sub-nanosecond timing.
- Retain the water-layer target for the carbon-to-water comparison.
- Recalibrate the return-yoke muon ranging scintillators against the new acceptance.

## 3. Expected impact

**Acceptance and thresholds**
- Muon acceptance becomes nearly uniform in cos θ.
- Proton threshold drops from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c, recovering most of the leading-proton sample.
- Neutrons are tagged.

**Physics reach**
- Kinematically complete charged-current events enable TKI measurements (δp_T, δα_T) and reconstruction of nuclear effects.
- The newly covered phase space matches the far detector's 4π acceptance.

**Systematics**
- This directly targets reducing the flux and cross-section systematic from about 6% toward about 4%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a ~2-tonne, 1 cm³-cube 3D-readout scintillator target (Super-FGD) flanked by high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs and time-of-flight panels.

# Design Review Recommendation for Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Requirements

The key constraints are:
- Large angular acceptance (4π, including backward tracks)
- Low momentum threshold (~350 MeV/c for 60 MeV kinetic energy protons)
- Multiple scattering dominates at these momenta
- Hydrogen content ≤20% of target nucleons
- Target volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m
- Must interface with downstream gas drift chambers

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (Primary Recommendation)**

**Technology:** Extruded plastic scintillator bars (1 cm × 1 cm cross-section) in XYZ orientation with wavelength-shifting fiber readout and silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) detection.

**Justification:**
- **Angular coverage:** 3D readout naturally captures tracks at all angles, including perpendicular and backward-going
- **Low threshold:** Scintillator light yield enables detection of 60 MeV protons (range ~6 mm in plastic, producing sufficient ionization)
- **Hydrogen constraint:** Polystyrene (CH) provides 7.7% hydrogen by nucleon count, well below 20% limit
- **Granularity:** 1 cm sampling provides adequate position resolution for vertex reconstruction and multiple scattering momentum measurement
- **Proven technology:** Similar to MINERvA, T2K INGRID designs

**Configuration:** Alternate XYZ plane orientation every 2-3 cm to minimize dead space while maintaining 3D tracking.

### 2. **Time Projection Chamber Insert (Central Region)**

**Technology:** High-pressure argon or argon-methane TPC (5-10 atm) covering central 1 m × 1 m × 0.5 m region.

**Justification:**
- **Superior angle measurement:** Continuous 3D tracking with ~1 mm spatial resolution
- **dE/dx particle ID:** Separates protons from pions/muons crucial for interaction modeling
- **Low hydrogen:** Pure argon = 0% hydrogen
- **Energy threshold:** Can detect and measure 60 MeV protons (range ~4 cm at 10 atm)

**Configuration:** Vertical drift field parallel to magnetic field to minimize ExB effects; readout at top/bottom with Micromegas or GEM amplification.

### 3. **Electromagnetic Calorimeter Downstream Face**

**Technology:** Lead-scintillator sampling calorimeter or ECal modules (recycled from another experiment if available).

**Justification:**
- **π⁰ detection:** Critical for separating ν_μ CC from NC backgrounds
- **Electron identification:** For ν_e backgrounds and systematic studies
- **Energy containment:** Catches shower energy from forward-going particles exiting active target

**Configuration:** 20 radiation lengths (15 cm), positioned between active target and gas drift chambers.

### 4. **Upgraded DAQ and Timing System**

**Technology:** 
- SiPM readout for all scintillator channels (~50,000 channels)
- Waveform digitization at 250 MS/s
- GPS-synchronized timing to <10 ns

**Justification:**
- **Multi-track resolution:** Waveform capture resolves overlapping hits from multi-particle final states
- **Beam timing:** Rejects cosmic backgrounds (critical for backward tracks which can't use downstream chambers)
- **SiPM benefits:** High gain, compact, magnetic field insensitive, cost-effective at scale

### 5. **Thin Nuclear Targets (Removable)**

**Technology:** Thin (2-5 mm) sheets of C, CH₂, Fe, Pb on precision translation stages.

**Justification:**
- **Hydrogen subtraction:** Compare CH₂ vs C to directly measure hydrogen cross sections, reducing model dependence
- **Nuclear dependence:** Measure A-dependence for far detector extrapolation systematics
- **Removability:** Most running with full active target; periodic dedicated runs with thin targets

## Implementation Priority

**Phase 1 (Critical):** 3D scintillator tracker + DAQ upgrade
**Phase 2 (High priority):** Central TPC insert + downstream ECal  
**Phase 3 (Systematics):** Thin target system

## Budget Considerations

- Scintillator bars: ~$500K (materials, extrusion, fiber)
- SiPMs and electronics: ~$2M (50K channels)
- TPC system: ~$1.5M
- ECal: ~$500K (assuming recycled modules)
- DAQ/timing: ~$1M
- **Total: ~$5.5M**

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D fine-grained plastic scintillator tracker with 1 cm bar spacing, XYZ readout geometry, and SiPM-based photodetection for complete angular acceptance and low-threshold tracking.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before listing upgrades, let me crystallize the physics drivers:

- **Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at all angles**, including 90° and backward tracks — this kills most purely-downstream tracker designs
- **Protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy** — range ~3 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in scintillator; requires very fine-grained or low-density active target
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of nucleons** — constrains material choice severely (pure CH₂ or water are both too hydrogen-rich unless diluted)
- **Volume constraint**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m deep (along beam)
- **Inside a 0.15 T dipole** — technology must tolerate magnetic field; SiPM-based readout is preferable over PMTs in-field

---

## Upgrade 1: 3D Plastic Scintillator "SuperCell" Active Target

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator bars arranged in three orthogonal orientations (X, Y, Z layers), read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers coupled to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs). Bar cross-section ~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, comparable to the MINERvA or NOvA scintillator cell geometry but with three-view stereo.

**Physics motivation:**

The 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range of roughly 3–4 cm in scintillator (density ~1.05 g/cm³). To reconstruct such a track with enough hits to determine direction and energy by range, the cell pitch must be ≤1.5 cm, giving 2–3 hits minimum. Three orthogonal views provide unambiguous 3D reconstruction of short, steep-angle, and backward-going tracks without pattern-recognition ghosts that plague two-view systems at high multiplicity.

The scintillator composition (C₈H₈)ₙ gives a hydrogen-to-nucleon ratio of 8/(8×12 + 8) = 8/104 ≈ 7.7% by nucleon count — comfortably under the 20% ceiling, leaving margin for structural material and WLS fiber (also hydrocarbon).

SiPMs are insensitive to the 0.15 T field (unlike PMTs), enabling in-situ placement inside the magnet bore without light-guide routing that would degrade the short-track light yield.

The fine granularity also provides calorimetric energy measurement of hadronic showers, improving the neutrino energy estimator.

---

## Upgrade 2: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon Time Projection Chamber (HPgTPC) Insert or Interleaved Modules

**Technology:** A set of small-diameter (≈30 cm) high-pressure (≈10 bar) argon gas TPCs with cathode/anode wire planes at ~2 mm pitch, interspersed between scintillator modules or occupying a downstream sub-volume of the target region. Drift field ~100–200 V/cm, operating at room temperature. Readout via charge-sensitive ASICs (e.g., ATLAS/CMS strip ASIC derivatives or LADD-style chips).

**Physics motivation:**

Gaseous argon at 10 bar has an effective density of ~0.18 g/cm³ and an argon nucleus (Z=18, A=40). It contains **zero hydrogen**, so allocating a fraction of the fiducial volume to this technology reduces the overall hydrogen fraction and helps keep the global hydrogen nucleon fraction comfortably below 20% if the scintillator modules push it toward the ceiling.

More importantly, a TPC provides continuous 3D hit information with sub-mm spatial resolution over the full drift volume. This is critical for:
- Reconstructing **backward-going muon tracks** that re-enter the TPC from downstream material — the continuous ionization trail is unambiguous regardless of direction
- **dE/dx-based particle identification**: at low momentum (<500 MeV/c), pions, protons, and muons are separated by Bethe-Bloch dE/dx at the several-σ level, reducing the leading systematic on proton/pion misidentification in the hadronic recoil system
- **Angular coverage**: a TPC reconstructs tracks at any angle with equal efficiency as long as they produce ≥3 hits (~6 mm drift in this geometry), including 90° tracks that drift purely along the electric field axis — these appear as point-like charge clusters in wire-plane projection but are recovered in the orthogonal dimension from timing

The gas medium also gives a long radiation length (~110 m at 10 bar), so electromagnetic shower confusion in the target volume is minimized.

---

## Upgrade 3: Downstream Straw-Tube Tracker for Large-Angle Muon Momentum Measurement

**Technology:** Mylar straw tubes of 5–10 mm diameter, operated with Ar/CO₂ (70/30) at slight overpressure, arranged in modules providing X–Y–U–V stereo views, placed immediately downstream of the target volume and before the existing gas drift chambers. Total depth ~40 cm along beam.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing drift chambers measure momentum and charge of tracks that **leave** the magnet. For the new analysis requirement of muon reconstruction at all angles including 90° and backward, the critical gap is **large-angle muons that exit the target laterally** and may never reach the downstream drift chambers. These tracks traverse the fewest radiation lengths inside the magnet volume, making multiple scattering the dominant momentum resolution limit.

A straw-tube tracker immediately downstream of the target provides:
- **Seed tracks for large-angle muons** before they curl in the dipole field and exit laterally, allowing the momentum to be determined from the sagitta measured within the 6.5 m magnetic volume
- **Matching of target-reconstructed track segments** to the downstream spectrometer for tracks that do continue downstream but at angles up to ~40°, with better pointing resolution than the existing chambers alone
- **Veto of cosmic muons** entering from the sides, which is especially important for backward-track selection where the signal and cosmic topologies overlap

Straws tolerate the 0.15 T field without degradation and are well-established at this scale (COMPASS, T2K ND280 tracker). They are mechanically self-supporting and can be installed modularly without disturbing the magnet.

---

## Upgrade 4: Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL) Panels on Lateral Faces

**Technology:** Lead–scintillator sandwich calorimeter panels, 15–20 radiation lengths deep (≈5 cm Pb total), with 1 cm scintillator strips per layer in alternating orientations, SiPM readout. Mounted on the four lateral faces (top, bottom, left, right) of the target volume, within the magnet bore.

**Physics motivation:**

Muons that exit the target perpendicular to the beam exit through the **lateral faces** of the target volume and immediately leave the instrumented region if nothing is there to catch them. Without lateral containment, the ≥25% efficiency requirement at 90° cannot be met for any muon momentum, since there are simply no detector hits after the target boundary.

The ECAL panels serve dual purposes:
1. **Muon tagging and crude momentum estimation by range**: a minimum-ionizing muon at 90° deposits ~200–300 MeV in 15–20 cm of scintillator; the panel measures the entry angle, track length, and whether the muon stops or exits, giving a range-based momentum estimate good to ~10–15% — sufficient for the ≥25% efficiency requirement since the main need is reconstruction, not high resolution
2. **π⁰ / photon reconstruction**: neutral pions from the hadronic recoil system decay to photon pairs; detecting these in the lateral ECAL closes the neutral-pion background that otherwise enters the muon-candidate sample through photon conversion mimicking electrons or misidentified showers in the target

The lead-scintillator technology is robust in-field (SiPM readout), compact, and cost-effective at this ~10 m² total panel area.

---

## Upgrade 5: Thin Silicon Pixel Vertex Detector at the Upstream Face

**Technology:** Monolithic Active Pixel Sensors (MAPS), 50–100 μm thick, 25–50 μm pixel pitch, arranged in 4–6 planes over a ~20 cm depth at the very upstream end of the target region. Similar technology to ALICE ITS2 (ALPIDE chip) or the planned DUNE ND-LAr pixel plane.

**Physics motivation:**

The most difficult track-reconstruction challenge in the active target is the **interaction vertex**: at the neutrino interaction point, a proton recoil (track length 1–3 cm), one or more pions (some very short before they interact), and the outgoing muon all originate within millimeters of each other. Associating hits to tracks and identifying the primary vertex among secondary interactions (pion charge-exchange, proton elastic scatters) requires spatial resolution well below the scintillator bar pitch.

A thin silicon pixel insert at the upstream face provides:
- **Vertex resolution ~100 μm** in the transverse plane, compared to ~4–5 mm from the scintillator bars — this suppresses the "primary vertex smearing" systematic that enters the cross-section measurement
- **Identification of very short proton stubs** (≤1 cm) that produce only 1 scintillator hit but leave 3–4 silicon pixel hits, reconstructable as a track rather than noise
- **Angular resolution on the muon at large angles** where even a 2-point measurement in silicon at 20 cm baseline gives a direction measurement to <0.5°

The thin silicon minimizes the material budget (<0.1% X₀ per plane), keeping multiple scattering small for the short low-momentum proton tracks.

---

## Upgrade 6: Beam Timing and Trigger Upgrade — Precision Timing Planes

**Technology:** Plastic scintillator planes read by SiPMs with waveform-digitizing electronics (e.g., DRS4-based or CATIROC ASIC), achieving <200 ps time resolution per hit, placed at upstream and downstream faces of the target.

**Physics motivation:**

Backward-going track reconstruction is topologically ambiguous with purely spatial information: a track from the downstream drift chambers pointing upstream looks identical to a backward-going track from a neutrino interaction. Time-of-flight disambiguation at the 200 ps level over a 1 m baseline gives a velocity measurement that separates:
- **Backward-going protons** (β ~ 0.5–0.7 at 60–200 MeV kinetic energy) from forward-going muons (β ≈ 1) — a 200 ps resolution over 50 cm gives Δt ~ 300 ps between proton and muon hypotheses, a ~1.5σ separation useful in a likelihood framework
- **Cosmic muon rejection**: out-of-spill cosmics that fake backward-going beam tracks are removed by correlating hit times with the beam extraction time to <1 μs, and in-spill cosmics are separated by the direction of propagation in the timing planes

The timing upgrade also enables **multi-interaction pile-up rejection**: at the 0.7 GeV peak flux, the near detector at 410 m sees a high neutrino interaction rate per spill, and vertex disambiguation using timing prevents two interactions within the same beam crossing from being merged into one event.

---
