# Design Review Recommendations for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Executive Summary

The core challenge is achieving kinematically complete CC event reconstruction in a compact volume (2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m) where ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons exit at >50° to beam, with proton momenta peaking around 450 MeV/c. This demands fine granularity, low tracking threshold, and near-4π angular acceptance — all within the tight longitudinal budget of 0.6 m.

---

## 1. Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Detector (SuperFGD)

**Technology:** An array of ~2 × 2 × 2 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, each read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres (one per axis) coupled to MPPCs, in a ~192 × 182 × 30 cube arrangement (approximately 1.0 M channels).

**Justification:**

- The existing FGD bar geometry (9.6 mm × 9.6 mm × 1864 mm bars in alternating x/y planes) provides only 2D projective tracking and is essentially blind to tracks at large angles to the beam, precisely the population that is problematic here. A 3D cubic topology provides genuinely isotropic 3D hit reconstruction with no preferred axis.
- A 2 cm cube pitch gives ~1 cm track position resolution and a proton tracking threshold of approximately **450 MeV/c** (range ≈ few cm in polystyrene) for straight tracks. For the median proton momentum of 450 MeV/c, the range is ~15–20 cm, giving ~8–10 cubes — sufficient for momentum-by-range measurement, which is the primary proton momentum method here.
- Critically, protons below ~500 MeV/c are **range-contained** within the 0.6 m depth for most angles, and dE/dx in the dense scintillator array provides particle identification sufficient to separate protons from pions (Bragg peak visibility at end of range).
- The ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c will largely exit into the downstream TPCs, where curvature measurement takes over — this is acceptable as a designed handoff.
- Three-fibre readout per cube with MPPCs (1 mm² pixel size, same technology as existing ECal/FGD) is industrially established and compatible with existing T2K DAQ infrastructure, reducing risk.
- The collaboration has already R&D-validated this exact concept (the SuperFGD prototype was tested at CERN in 2021–2022 with cosmic rays and test beams), so this is not a speculative technology.
- Hydrocarbon target (polystyrene, CH ≈ (C₈H₈)ₙ) satisfies the stated requirement; carbon cross-section comparison with the downstream FGD2 water layers remains intact.
- Estimated mass: ~2 × 1.9 × 0.6 m at ~1.05 g/cm³ gives ~2.3 t, comparable to P0D-without-water, well within the magnet's load history.

---

## 2. Downstream TPC Upgrade: High-Pressure or Enlarged-Acceptance TPC with Resistive Micromegas

**Technology:** Replace or supplement the existing TPC1 (immediately downstream) with resistive-strip Micromegas readout pads at finer pitch (~1 mm strip pitch vs. current ~7 mm pad pitch), and extend the active drift window to improve acceptance for large-angle muon tracks exiting the SuperFGD.

**Justification:**

- 25% of muons exit at >50° to beam. Muons from the downstream face of a 0.6 m-deep target at 50° have a transverse displacement of ~0.71 m at the front face of TPC1, which is already near the TPC acceptance edge. Resistive Micromegas with finer segmentation provides better spatial resolution (~100 μm vs. ~500 μm current) on the pad row direction, improving the momentum measurement of these large-angle, short-lever-arm tracks.
- The resistive layer (DLC-coated or resistive paste) eliminates the ion-feedback and spark-damage problems of standard bulk Micromegas, extending MPPC/electronics lifetime in a higher-occupancy running environment (T2K-II higher beam intensity).
- Gas composition (Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀) can remain unchanged, preserving calibration continuity.
- The improvement in momentum resolution at large angles directly reduces the systematic on the muon kinematics entering the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) calculation, attacking the 6%→4% systematic target from the muon side.

---

## 3. Thin Time-of-Flight Scintillator Planes: Surrounding the SuperFGD

**Technology:** Six planes of fast plastic scintillator (e.g., 7 mm Bicron BC-420 or equivalent), one on each face of the SuperFGD volume, read out by MPPCs via short WLS fibre or direct coupling, targeting ~200 ps time resolution per plane.

**Justification:**

- At 450 MeV/c, a proton (β ≈ 0.43) and a pion (β ≈ 0.95) traversing ~20 cm produce a ToF difference of ~0.9 ns — cleanly resolvable at 200 ps resolution (>4σ separation). This provides **independent particle identification** for tracks exiting the cube array before they reach the TPC, covering precisely the high-angle, short-range population.
- For the ~35% of leading protons at >50°, these protons may exit laterally (through the side faces), never reaching a TPC. Without a ToF system on the lateral faces, these protons are identified only by range/dE/dx in the cubes, which degrades for tracks that exit rather than stop. ToF on lateral faces provides a cross-check and a primary PID method for exiting tracks.
- The upstream ToF face also provides a beam timing reference, enabling rejection of out-of-time backgrounds and sand muons, and can establish the interaction time (t₀) independently of TPC drift time for events where no TPC track is present.
- These planes are thin (7 mm ≈ 0.04 radiation lengths each), so they add negligible material before the downstream detectors.
- Fast plastic scintillator + MPPC is proven in multiple ND280 upgrade contexts and is low-cost and low-risk.

---

## 4. MPPC Upgrade to Higher Dynamic Range / Lower Dark Current Devices

**Technology:** Replace the current Hamamatsu S12571-025C MPPCs (25 μm pixel, ~1600 pixels/mm²) on the SuperFGD fibres with the newer S14160-1315PS series (15 μm pixel, ~4489 pixels/mm²) or equivalent low-noise, high-pixel-density MPPCs.

**Justification:**

- The 2 cm cubes will be read by 1 mm diameter WLS fibres; at T2K-II beam intensity the per-channel occupancy in the SuperFGD increases. The dE/dx Bragg-peak identification of stopping protons requires the last few cubes along the track to be in the linear (non-saturated) regime of the MPPC. High pixel density MPPCs have a significantly higher dynamic range before saturation and lower afterpulsing rates, which are important for the dense ionization near the Bragg peak.
- Lower dark current (achieved by smaller pixel size and lower operating voltage) reduces the accidental coincidence rate that could fake a cube hit and corrupt the 3D track reconstruction.
- These devices are already in production, have been evaluated by the collaboration for the ECal upgrade, and require no new readout ASIC — they are compatible with the existing AFTER/CITIROC-based front-end ASICs with minor threshold adjustment.

---

## 5. Data Acquisition: Streaming Readout with Waveform Digitisation

**Technology:** Replace the current triggered, charge-integrated readout (Trip-t frontend boards with 23 ns shaping) on the SuperFGD channels with a streaming waveform digitiser architecture (e.g., 100 MHz FADCs, as developed for the WAGASCI/Baby-MIND detectors or adapted from the Mu2e DTC concept), zero-suppressed at the FPGA level.

**Justification:**

- T2K-II will increase beam intensity toward 1.3 × 10²¹ POT/year, increasing in-spill pileup. The current triggered architecture cannot separate two interactions within the same ~8 μs spill bucket if they are closer than the shaping time. Full waveform digitisation preserves the pulse shape (necessary for dE/dx PID on the Bragg peak), separates pile-up interactions in time within a spill, and allows offline software triggering — essential for rare processes like single-proton events with no muon in the TPC.
- For the ToF planes (Recommendation 3), sub-ns time resolution requires waveform sampling rather than peak-detect charge integration.
- The data volume increase is manageable: with zero-suppression the SuperFGD hit rate is dominated by the ~5% occupancy during a spill, and modern FPGA-based data concentrators (e.g., ATCA-based) handle this at modest cost.

---

## Summary Table

| Recommendation | Primary Physics Driver | Technology Readiness |
|---|---|---|
| 3D SuperFGD scintillator cube array | 4π tracking, proton PID/range | TRL 7 (prototype beam-tested) |
| Resistive Micromegas TPC upgrade | Large-angle muon momentum | TRL 6–7 (R&D complete) |
| Thin ToF scintillator planes | Proton PID for exiting tracks | TRL 8 (deployed elsewhere) |
| High-density MPPC replacement | Bragg peak, saturation margin | TRL 9 (commercial) |
| Streaming waveform DAQ | Pileup, dE/dx waveform shape | TRL 6–7 (prototype stage) |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D volume with a 3D array of 2 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes (SuperFGD) read out by three orthogonal WLS fibres and MPPCs per cube, providing isotropic 4π tracking acceptance and proton identification by range and Bragg-peak dE/dx across the full relevant momentum range.

# Proposed hardware upgrade for the off-axis near detector

## 1. The problem with the current design

The existing plastic targets cannot deliver kinematically complete events at this beam.

- **Wrong orientation for high-angle tracks.** All bars are perpendicular to the beam and read out in alternating 2D x/y views. Tracks at large angle, especially those near 90°, run along a single bar or layer. They are badly reconstructed and often lost.
- **Most of the high-angle phase space falls in that gap.** About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons leave at more than 50°.
- **The TPCs sit only downstream.** High-angle and backward muons escape into the side calorimeters or yoke without a momentum or charge measurement.
- **Short protons are lost.** A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of a few cm. The 2D layered views confuse tracks that short near the vertex.

TKI analyses need both the muon and the leading proton across full solid angle, so this is the dominant acceptance limit. It also feeds the 6% → 4% systematic gap: limited angular acceptance relative to the 4π water far detector drives model-dependent extrapolation.

## 2. Proposed upgrades

### (a) New active target in the upstream box: a 3D-readout fine-granularity scintillator ("super-FGD")

**Geometry and readout**
- About 2 × 10⁶ optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, roughly 192 × 184 × 56, filling the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- About 2 t of CH target.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal WLS fibres in x, y and z, read by SiPMs at one end. This is about 55–60k channels, in the same fibre-plus-SiPM technology already used.

**Why this design fits the requirements**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal 2D projections give genuine 3D reconstruction, independent of track direction. This recovers the >50° muons and protons.
- **Low proton threshold.** A proton crossing 2–3 cubes, about 300 MeV/c, is reconstructible. Most of the 450 MeV/c-median spectrum is then measured by range.
- **Full calorimetric dE/dx** for p/π/μ separation and vertex-activity measurement.
- **Range limit is acceptable.** Protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) usually exit or reinteract. This can be handled by curvature measurement in the TPCs, or flagged.
- **Neutron detection.** Sub-ns timing per cube (about 1 ns per fibre, better when combined) allows time-of-flight measurement of neutron-induced isolated hits. This adds neutron kinematics to TKI on antineutrino events.

**Options considered and rejected**
- **Finer bars, still 2D:** do not solve the high-angle problem.
- **Liquid-argon TPC:** wrong nucleus and a cryogenics burden.
- **Water-based target:** unnecessary, since hydrocarbon is acceptable and the downstream water-layer target stays for C/H₂O comparison.

### (b) High-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Design**
- Two thin-walled field-cage TPCs, each roughly 2.0 × 0.8 m in the transverse plane and about 2 m long, in the freed upstream region.
- Same argon-based gas as the existing TPCs, for commonality.
- Lightweight composite field cage to minimise material and multiple scattering.
- Resistive (encapsulated-resistor) Micromegas readout. This spreads charge across pads, so larger pads give comparable resolution with fewer channels and protects against sparks.

**Purpose**
- Measure momentum and charge in the 0.2 T field for muons exiting the target at high angle.
- Measure dE/dx for PID, including μ/e separation for the νe sample.
- Measure momentum for protons above range.

**Integration caveat:** This requires that the vacated region allow space beyond the 0.6 m target box. The removed photon-tagging section (about 2.4 m long) should allow it, and placement should be checked against the magnet inner volume.

### (c) Time-of-flight panels enclosing the target and new TPCs

- Six panels of plastic scintillator bars read by SiPM arrays at both ends.
- Timing resolution of about 150 ps.

**Purpose**
- Determine track direction (forward versus backward going).
- Reject out-of-fiducial and sand-muon backgrounds.
- Improve e/μ/p separation at low momentum.

### (d) Supporting changes

- **Common readout electronics** for the new channels, such as a CITIROC-based front end, with synchronisation to the existing DAQ and clock.
- **Calibration** of the new target:
  - LED injection.
  - Cosmic triggers.
  - Cube-by-cube light-yield mapping.
  - Fibre attenuation mapping.
- **Electromagnetic calorimetry.** Replace or extend the upstream electromagnetic calorimetry lost with the photon-tagging section using the existing surrounding lead-scintillator calorimeters, re-arranged where needed. This preserves π⁰ and γ background constraints.
- **Mechanical support.** Use a lightweight, low-mass target box (e.g. carbon fibre/foam) to avoid dead material between the new target and the high-angle TPCs.

## 3. Expected impact on the systematic uncertainty

- **Near-4π acceptance for CC events on CH**, with the muon and leading proton both reconstructed. This enables:
  - Transverse kinematic imbalance variables (δpT, δαT, δφT), constraining nuclear effects such as Fermi motion, 2p2h and FSI.
  - Better energy reconstruction.
- **Neutron tagging** on antineutrino events.
- **Better match** of near-detector phase space to the 4π water far detector, reducing extrapolation dependence on the interaction model.
- **Retained carbon-to-water comparison** through the downstream water-layer target.

Together these are the main route from the ~6% residual to the ~4% target.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2 t, 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m super-fine-grained 3D scintillator target of ~1 cm³ cubes read out on three orthogonal WLS-fibre/SiPM views, flanked by high-angle TPCs, to give full-angle, low-threshold reconstruction of muons and protons.

# Recommendations for the ND280 Upstream Upgrade

## Why the current design falls short

Every recommendation below addresses one of four specific shortfalls.

1. **Angular acceptance is limited.** The FGD bars all lie perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only downstream. Tracks above about 50–60°, and backward tracks, are reconstructed poorly or not at all. That region holds about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons. TKI analyses need both particles, so the combined acceptance loss is large and kinematically biased.
2. **The proton threshold is too high.** A short proton must cross several x/y layers of 1 cm bars to give a 3D track. The resulting threshold is about 450–500 MeV/c, which is roughly the median of the leading-proton momentum distribution. About half the protons are lost, and they are the low-momentum ones that carry the nuclear-effect information.
3. **Some protons cannot be measured by range.** A 900 MeV/c proton (T ≈ 370 MeV) has a range of order 1 m of polystyrene, so it leaves a 0.6 m-thick target. The roughly 6% above 900 MeV/c, and many below, need curvature and dE/dx measurement in a gas TPC at all angles.
4. **Track direction is ambiguous.** Without timing, forward and backward tracks, cosmics and out-of-fiducial (OOFV) entering particles are hard to tell apart. Wrong-sign or entering backgrounds degrade the 6% → 4% goal.

## Recommended hardware changes

### 1. Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD-type 3D-granular scintillator target (most important)

**What to build**
- About 2 × 10⁶ optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes. Each cube has a reflective, chemically etched surface.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes threaded with 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres (e.g. Kuraray Y-11).
- The block is roughly 192 × 182 × 56 cubes, about 2 t of CH, and fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Total channels are about 56k. Each fibre is read at one end by a small MPPC (Hamamatsu S13360-1325-class, 1.3 mm, 25 µm pixels), with a mirrored far end.
- Front-end boards should be CITIROC-based with about 1 ns hit timing, rather than the TripT ASIC.

**Why**
- Three projections give isotropic acceptance: there is no "blind" angle, and high-angle and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- Protons stopping after 2–3 cubes become reconstructable. The proton threshold falls to about 300 MeV/c, recovering most of the region below the 450 MeV/c median.
- Fine-grained dE/dx near the vertex identifies Bragg peaks and separates protons from pions and muons.
- Sub-ns timing per cube allows neutron detection by time-of-flight from isolated neutron-induced hits. This adds the neutron to the TKI picture, especially for antineutrino running.
- The hydrocarbon target is acceptable under the programme brief. FGD2 water layers remain for the carbon-to-water comparison.

### 2. Add two High-Angle TPCs above and below the new target

**What to build**
- Lightweight field cages built from composite or aramid laminate, keeping the material budget at about 1–2% X₀ to limit scattering and conversions.
- The same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ gas as the existing TPCs, for common calibration.
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated resistive-anode) bulk Micromegas. The resistive layer spreads charge so fewer, larger pads still give sub-mm resolution, and it suppresses sparks.
- Upgraded AFTER/AGET-based electronics.

**Why**
- High-angle muons and protons from the target, above about 900 MeV/c or escaping, get curvature momentum in the 0.2 T field. This gives charge sign and a momentum resolution near 10% at 1 GeV/c.
- They also get about 10% dE/dx for e/µ/p identification.
- This closes the 25% / 35% high-angle gap that the downstream TPCs cannot cover.

### 3. Surround the new target-plus-TPC assembly with Time-of-Flight panels

**What to build**
- Six faces of cast plastic scintillator bars, about 2.3 m long and 12 cm wide.
- Each bar read at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Target timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Why**
- ToF between the panels and the target fixes track direction (forward versus backward), rejects entering OOFV and cosmic backgrounds, and gives extra particle identification for e/µ and p/π where dE/dx bands cross.

### 4. Supporting changes

- **Retain the downstream FGD1, FGD2 and TPC tracker, the ECals and the SMRD.** They give continuity with existing T2K data and the water/carbon comparison.
- **Upgrade the downstream TPC readout and DAQ** to match the new electronics, giving a common clock and trigger.
- **Use the same MPPC family and calibration** (LED and cosmic) across the new detectors for efficient long-term operation.
- **Run beam tests (e.g. at CERN) before construction** to verify light yield, optical crosstalk between cubes, and timing.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a SuperFGD-style ~2-tonne target of 1 cm³ scintillator cubes read by three orthogonal WLS fibres and MPPCs, giving 4π acceptance and a ~300 MeV/c proton threshold (complemented by high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs and ToF panels).

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280-II

## 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Segmented Plastic Scintillator Target**

**Technology:** Replace the P0D with a highly-segmented 3D scintillator cube consisting of ~2 million small (1×1×1 cm³) polystyrene cubes with three perpendicular wavelength-shifting fiber readouts per cube.

**Physics Motivation:** 
- The current FGDs only provide 2D x-y segmentation, limiting angular resolution for tracks at large angles (>50°) to the beam
- 3D segmentation enables true 3D tracking from the interaction vertex, crucial since 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons emerge at >50° where 2D tracking degrades
- Fine granularity (~1 cm) provides excellent vertex resolution and low-momentum proton detection threshold (~200 MeV/c), capturing the median 450 MeV/c proton distribution
- Full angular acceptance addresses the systematic uncertainty reduction from 6% to 4% by improving reconstruction of transverse kinematic imbalance

## 2. **Horizontal Time Projection Chambers (TPCs)**

**Technology:** Add two horizontal TPCs above and below the new target volume, with similar Micromegas readout to existing TPCs but oriented to measure tracks perpendicular to the beam axis.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Existing vertical TPCs (optimized for beam-parallel tracks) have degraded momentum resolution for high-angle tracks
- Horizontal TPCs provide excellent momentum measurement via curvature in the 0.2 T field for the 25-35% of particles exiting at large angles
- Critical for measuring the 6% of protons exceeding 900 MeV/c that might escape the target
- Enables charge identification and sign determination for particles at all angles

## 3. **Time-of-Flight System (TOF)**

**Technology:** Install thin (~1 cm) plastic scintillator planes with SiPM readout (~50-100 ps timing resolution) around the new target volume at ~1 m distance.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Provides particle identification (π/K/p separation) in the 300-900 MeV/c momentum range where the proton distribution peaks
- Timing information discriminates forward-going particles from beam-related backgrounds
- Helps distinguish signal protons from secondary pions in hadronic cascades
- The 6 ns beam bunch structure allows out-of-time background rejection

## 4. **High-Angle Electromagnetic Calorimeter (HA-ECAL)**

**Technology:** Optimize the upstream and side ECAL coverage specifically for backwards-going particles, potentially with finer segmentation (~1×1 cm²) plastic scintillator-lead layers in high-angle regions.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Contains electromagnetic showers from π⁰ decay photons produced at large angles
- Distinguishes electrons from muons for νe appearance background studies
- The high large-angle fraction means significant electromagnetic activity occurs where current ECAL coverage may be limited
- Improves energy containment for events with high transverse imbalance

## 5. **Low-Threshold Momentum Analyzer (LTMA)**

**Technology:** Insert a thin resistive plate chamber (RPC) or scintillating fiber tracker immediately downstream of the new target to provide additional low-momentum tracking points.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Enhances tracking of low-momentum protons (200-500 MeV/c) before they range out
- The median proton momentum of 450 MeV/c means many protons stop in or near the target
- Multiple scattering measurements in thin detectors provide momentum estimates even without magnetic deflection
- Improves vertex resolution by providing early tracking points

## 6. **Upgraded DAQ and Trigger System**

**Technology:** Implement a fully-digital, zero-suppressed readout with ~MHz capability and a sophisticated software trigger analyzing 3D hit patterns in real-time.

**Physics Motivation:**
- T2K-II will increase beam power from 500 kW to 1.3 MW, increasing event rates by ~2.6×
- Multiple interactions per beam spill will occur; advanced triggering isolates individual neutrino interactions
- Enables triggering on high-angle tracks that might be missed by beam-direction-biased triggers
- Allows data-driven background estimates through prescaled minimum-bias triggers

## 7. **Neutron Tagging System**

**Technology:** Embed or surround the target with gadolinium-doped scintillator or boron-loaded plastic that captures neutrons with distinctive delayed (~10-100 μs) γ-ray signals.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Neutron kinematics constrain nuclear effects in quasi-elastic scattering
- Distinguishes quasi-elastic (1 proton, 0-1 neutrons) from multi-nucleon emission (multiple nucleons)
- The transverse kinematic imbalance studies require understanding all final-state nucleons
- Neutron detection reduces model-dependence in extracting neutrino energy

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: SuperFGD 3D Segmented Scintillator Target**

The SuperFGD addresses the most critical limitation: inadequate tracking for the ~30% of events with large-angle particles. Its 3D capability directly enables the kinematically-complete reconstruction needed for transverse imbalance studies, while its fine segmentation captures the crucial medium-momentum proton population. This single upgrade provides the largest systematic uncertainty reduction toward the 4% T2K-II goal.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints

Before listing upgrades, the key physics drivers are:

- **Muon reconstruction** at all angles including 90° and backward (≥25% efficiency) — the warm dipole alone will curve forward tracks well but lose perpendicular/backward ones unless there is surrounding instrumentation.
- **Low-energy proton reconstruction** down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3 cm in plastic, ~1.4 cm in iron) — demands fine-grained, low-density active target material.
- **Hydrogen fraction ≤20%** of target nucleons — constrains material choice away from pure hydrocarbon.
- **Neutrino beam peak ~0.7 GeV** — typical hadronic final states are soft; most protons are sub-200 MeV.
- **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m deep along beam.

---

## Upgrade 1: Plastic Scintillator–Steel Sandwich Active Target (Fine-Grained Detector, FGD-style)

**Technology:** Alternating planes of extruded polystyrene scintillator bars (e.g., 1 cm × 1 cm × 2.6 m or 2.3 m) read out with wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres and silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), interleaved with thin steel or brass absorber plates (~1–3 mm thick).

**Physics motivation:**

The 0.9 m depth along beam is shallow, so the active target must itself track and measure hadronic recoils with millimetre-scale granularity. Pure plastic alone (C₈H₈ repeat unit, ~57% hydrogen by nucleon count) violates the ≤20% hydrogen nucleon constraint. Mixing polystyrene planes with steel absorber planes reduces the effective hydrogen fraction: a 1 cm scintillator : 3 mm steel ratio gives roughly 15–17% hydrogen nucleons, satisfying the constraint while keeping most of the fiducial volume active.

The 1 cm × 1 cm bar cross-section gives a minimum detectable track length of about 2 bars (~2 cm), corresponding to a proton kinetic energy threshold of roughly 40–50 MeV in plastic — sufficient for the 60 MeV requirement. Three-dimensional hit reconstruction from X/Y bar planes at each layer provides full 4π track-finding. The low-Z scintillator minimises Coulomb scattering, keeping angular resolution better than ~5° for 100 MeV protons over their full range. The steel absorber also provides enough material to range out and measure proton momentum by range for tracks that stop, without requiring a magnetic rigidity measurement for them.

---

## Upgrade 2: Surrounding Magnetised Muon Catcher (Iron–Scintillator Range Stack with Independent Coil)

**Technology:** A set of iron–scintillator range-detector modules on the four transverse faces (top, bottom, left, right) of the active target volume, each consisting of 3–5 cm iron plates interleaved with scintillator planes, instrumented with SiPMs. A separate toroidal or solenoidal coil (or extension of the existing dipole yoke) magnetises the iron to ~1 T to allow charge-sign determination.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing dipole bends tracks in one plane and the downstream drift chambers catch forward-going muons. Tracks leaving the active target perpendicular to the beam axis never enter the downstream spectrometer and are therefore lost. Tracks going backward never enter it either. Side and upstream muon catchers intercept these tracks.

A 60 cm iron range stack stops a muon of about 500 MeV momentum — appropriate for the 0.7 GeV peak flux, where most muons carry 300–600 MeV. Measurement of range gives momentum resolution of ~10–15% for contained tracks, adequate for neutrino energy reconstruction. Magnetisation at ~1 T over 3–5 interaction lengths gives a bend of several tens of MeV/c, sufficient to determine muon charge sign at the few-σ level for 300–600 MeV tracks — critical for separating neutrino from antineutrino interactions. This directly addresses the ≥25% efficiency at all angles requirement: without it, tracks at 70°–110° to the beam (and backward) have zero magnetic spectrometer efficiency.

---

## Upgrade 3: Time Projection Chamber (TPC) Modules Embedded in the Active Target

**Technology:** Four to six small-volume (roughly 40 cm × 60 cm × 30 cm active) MicroPattern Gaseous Detector (MPGD) TPCs using Micromegas or GEM readout planes, with an Ar:CF₄:isobutane or Ar:CO₂ gas mixture, interspersed as vertical slabs among the scintillator planes. Field cage: copper strip printed on kapton. Pad pitch ~3–5 mm.

**Physics motivation:**

The scintillator bars provide 3D hit information but limited dE/dx resolution (typically σ(dE/dx)/⟨dE/dx⟩ ~ 20–30% per plane). Particle identification of protons vs. pions vs. muons near threshold requires better specific ionisation measurement. A TPC provides continuous dE/dx sampling with ~100 or more samples per track, giving ~5–8% dE/dx resolution — sufficient to separate protons from pions up to ~1 GeV/c and to identify stopping kaons (relevant for strange-particle backgrounds).

For short, steep-angle proton tracks (60–100 MeV kinetic energy, range 2–5 cm), a TPC reconstructs the full 3D helix or straight segment with sub-millimetre spatial resolution, measuring both angle and range simultaneously. The TPC also offers very low effective density in its gas volume, minimising secondary interactions that would confuse the hadronic final state. The drift time gives a precise interaction time stamp (~100 ns resolution), which suppresses out-of-time pile-up at high beam intensity. The Ar-based gas mixture with CF₄ gives a hydrogen nucleon fraction near zero, helping maintain the overall ≤20% hydrogen constraint when averaged across the full hybrid volume.

---

## Upgrade 4: Upstream Veto and Interaction-Vertex Scintillator Plane Array

**Technology:** A 2.6 m × 2.3 m array of 1 cm × 1 cm scintillator bars (or 5 mm–pitch scintillating-fibre ribbon panels), forming three X/Y double-planes immediately upstream of the active target, read out with SiPMs.

**Physics motivation:**

Neutrino interactions on the material immediately upstream of the active target (magnet coil, structural supports, upstream drift chamber frames) produce muons and hadrons that enter the active volume and mimic signal. Without a high-granularity upstream veto, these "dirt" or "rock" interactions contaminate the sample. At 0.7 GeV, rock-muon flux entering the near detector can be 10–100× the neutrino signal rate.

Fine-grained upstream planes distinguish:
- Entering charged tracks (veto signal) from vertex activity consistent with a neutrino interaction (no upstream hits in a cone around the vertex);
- The precise interaction vertex position in Z to within ~1 cm, enabling fiducial volume cuts at the 1–2% systematic level.

The scintillating-fibre option (Sci-Fi, as used in LHCb UT or SciFi tracker) gives ~100 µm spatial resolution if needed, but 1 cm bar pitch is likely sufficient here given the ~1 cm bar pitch of the active target itself. This upgrade directly protects the signal purity for the hydrogen-subtraction model, which is sensitive to background contamination mimicking QE interactions.

---

## Upgrade 5: SiPM-on-Tile Electromagnetic Calorimeter Panels on Top and Bottom Faces

**Technology:** Thin (5–8 radiation-length) lead–scintillator sandwich calorimeter panels using 3 cm × 3 cm plastic scintillator tiles directly coupled to 3 mm × 3 mm SiPMs (the "SiPM-on-tile" technique used in CALICE AHCAL), covering the top and bottom faces of the active target volume.

**Physics motivation:**

The 0.7 GeV beam produces π⁰ final states in roughly 20–30% of NC interactions and in a significant fraction of CC interactions (via resonance production). Neutral pions decay to two photons; if these are not detected, they are misidentified as genuine quasi-elastic events, biasing the neutrino energy reconstruction and the hydrogen subtraction model.

A 5–8 X₀ electromagnetic calorimeter panel on two large faces (top and bottom, 2.6 m × 0.9 m each) intercepts photons that escape the active target laterally, measuring shower energy with ~10%/√E resolution and shower position with ~1 cm resolution. Combined with photon conversion in the active target itself (tracked by TPC and scintillator), this gives π⁰ reconstruction efficiency of ~60–70% — sufficient to apply a π⁰ veto that keeps NC background below the ~5% level needed for the cross-section measurements. The thin profile (~10 cm including lead) fits within the existing magnet bore without blocking the downstream drift chambers.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Scintillator–steel sandwich active target | 60 MeV proton tracking; H fraction control |
| 2 | Magnetised muon catcher on all 4 transverse faces | Muon efficiency at 90° and backward angles |
| 3 | Embedded MPGD/TPC modules | dE/dx PID; short-track reconstruction |
| 4 | Upstream scintillator veto planes | Rock-muon rejection; vertex definition |
| 5 | SiPM-on-tile EM calorimeter panels | π⁰ reconstruction; NC background control |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Magnetised muon catcher modules on all four transverse faces of the active target volume, to achieve the required ≥25% muon reconstruction efficiency at all angles including perpendicular and backward tracks — without which the core analysis requirement cannot be met regardless of any other improvement.

# Proposed hardware upgrade for ND280: replacing the P0D with a high-acceptance tracking target

## 1. What limits the current detector

**Angular acceptance is the main limit.**
- FGD1/FGD2 bars all lie perpendicular to the beam, in x/y layers, and the TPCs sit only downstream.
- Tracks above about 50–60° cross few layers, or run along one layer.
- They also never reach a TPC, so they get no momentum or dE/dx measurement.
- At this beam, about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons are at more than 50°. That is a large, model-dependent hole in phase space.
- Backward-going tracks are also hard to tell from forward ones.

**The proton threshold is high.**
- A proton must cross several 1 cm layers in one or two views to be reconstructed.
- In the FGDs this gives a threshold of roughly 450–500 MeV/c, about the median of the leading-proton spectrum.
- So about half of the leading protons needed for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies are lost.

**The P0D is the wrong tool for this programme.** It was optimised for π⁰ tagging with passive layers, so its tracking and calorimetric resolution are coarse.

## 2. Main upgrade: a 3D-granular scintillator target ("SuperFGD")

**Design**
- Build a target of about 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, for example 192 × 182 × 56 cubes.
- That is about 1.92 m × 1.82 m × 0.56 m, which fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- Mount it horizontally:
  - The 0.56 m dimension is vertical.
  - The 1.82 m dimension is along the beam.
  - This leaves room above and below for new high-angle TPCs (section 3).
- Coat each cube with a reflector, for example by chemical etching.
- Drill three orthogonal holes through each cube, each carrying a 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibre read out by an MPPC. Every hit is then seen in three 2D projections, giving true 3D reconstruction.

**Numbers**
- Channel count: 192×56 + 192×182 + 56×182 ≈ 56,000 MPPCs.
  - This is comparable to the ND280 scintillator channel scale.
  - It reuses the proven fibre and MPPC technology.
- Target mass: about 2 t of CH, roughly double one FGD. That gives about twice the FGD1 event rate from the new region.

**Physics gains**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** The cubic granularity has no preferred direction, so high-angle and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones. This directly recovers the 25% of muons and 35% of protons above 50°.
- **Lower proton threshold, about 300 MeV/c.**
  - A 300 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 47 MeV) has a range of about 2 cm, so it fires 2 or more cubes.
  - A median proton at 450 MeV/c (kinetic energy about 100 MeV) travels about 8 cm, enough for range and dE/dx (Bragg peak) identification.
  - Most of the leading-proton spectrum becomes accessible.
- **Calorimetric vertex activity and fine dE/dx**, useful for π/p/μ separation and for Michel-electron tagging of stopped pions.
- **Neutron detection.** Isolated cube clusters, together with timing (below), let neutron kinetic energy be measured by time of flight. This enables antineutrino TKI and full calorimetric energy reconstruction.

## 3. Two new high-angle TPCs (HA-TPCs) above and below the target

**Role**
- Muons above 50° and energetic protons do not stay in the target.
  - About 6% of protons are above 900 MeV/c. Such a proton has a kinetic energy of about 360 MeV and a range of about 1 m in CH, so it often escapes the target.
- The HA-TPCs measure these tracks' momentum from curvature in the 0.2 T field.
- They also measure dE/dx for μ/e/p separation.

**Design**
- Each chamber is roughly 2.0 m × 0.8 m × 1.8 m, filling the vertical space of the former P0D volume.
- Gas: the same Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 mixture.
- Readout: resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM").
  - The resistive layer spreads the charge, allowing larger pads with fewer channels.
  - It still gives about 0.6 mm spatial resolution and protects against sparks.
- Field cage: a thin, lightweight composite to minimise dead material between the target and the TPC gas.
- Electronics: upgraded front-end and back-end, compatible with the existing TPC DAQ.

**Result:** the target plus the HA-TPCs and existing TPCs give near-4π coverage for muon momentum and charge measurement. They also give electron identification, which improves the ν_e/γ background sample.

## 4. Time-of-flight (ToF) panels enclosing the new module

**Design:** plastic scintillator bars read out at both ends by large-area SiPM arrays, with about 150 ps time resolution, enclosing all faces of the target plus HA-TPC module.

**Uses**
- Determine track direction, rejecting out-of-fiducial, sand-muon and backward-entering backgrounds.
- Separate particles (p/μ/e) near momentum crossovers where dE/dx is ambiguous.
- Provide a precise time reference for neutron time-of-flight in the target.

## 5. Supporting changes

- **Remove the P0D.** Keep the barrel ECal and SMRD, and refurbish ECal coverage around the new module where possible.
- **Upgrade the readout electronics and DAQ** to handle the higher channel count and faster timing needed for neutrons and ToF.
- **Calibrate the cubes in a test beam.** This covers cube-to-cube light yield, optical crosstalk (target below a few percent per face) and proton/neutron response.
- **Keep FGD2 (the water layers)** for the carbon-to-water ratio, as stated. Make the target-to-FGD selection cross-calibratable through common TPC tracks.

## 6. Expected impact

- Near-4π muon acceptance.
- A proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c, compared with about 450–500 MeV/c now.
- Neutron tagging.
- Full charged-current final-state kinematics, enabling TKI-based nuclear-effect constraints. This should cut the residual flux plus cross-section systematic uncertainty from about 6% toward the 4% that T2K-II needs.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a ~2 t, 1 cm³-cube 3D-readout scintillator target (SuperFGD), flanked by high-angle TPCs, to obtain isotropic muon and low-threshold proton acceptance.

# Proposed upgrade of the Kestrel Flats near detector target region

The design below is a fully active, finely segmented 3D scintillator target, with gas TPCs above and below it and a timing shell around it. This follows the approach of the T2K ND280 upgrade, which faced the same angular-acceptance problem. The dimensions are my proposal for fitting this volume and would need confirming against the actual magnet layout.

## 1. Fully active 3D-segmented scintillator target (the core change)

**What it is**
- Polystyrene scintillator cubes, 1 cm³ each, with a reflective chemical-etch coating.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres, such as Y-11.
- Each fibre is read out at one end by a 1.3 mm silicon photomultiplier (SiPM / MPPC).
- The front end uses CITIROC-type ASICs with about 1 ns hit timing.

**Size within the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region**
- About 200 (x) × 80 (y) × 80 (z) cubes, roughly 2.0 × 0.8 × 0.8 m.
- That is about 1.3 million cubes and about 1.3 t of target.
- Readout is about 3 × 16,000 ≈ 50,000 channels.

**Why it meets the muon requirement**
- The cubes give true 3D points with no preferred plane orientation.
- Reconstruction efficiency is therefore nearly flat in angle, including tracks at 90° and backward-going tracks. A plane-based tracker could not do this.

**Why it meets the proton requirement**
- A 60 MeV proton travels about 3 cm in plastic, so it crosses about 3 cubes or more.
- With dE/dx from about 40–60 photoelectrons per MIP per fibre, such tracks can be both reconstructed and identified.
- Vertex activity at these energies stays visible.
- Neutron recoils can also be tagged using cube timing.

**Hydrogen check against the 20% limit**
- In CH, hydrogen makes up 1/13 ≈ 7.7% of nucleons.
- Fibres, coatings and glue raise this only marginally, to below 9%, comfortably within the model limit.
- Do not use water modules or hydrogen-rich gases in the active target.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**What they are**
- Two thin-walled TPCs, each about 2.0 × 0.8 × 0.8 m.
- Field cage: lightweight composite laminate (aramid honeycomb with a Kapton strip foil), so there is little material between the target and the gas.
- Gas: Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀ (95/3/2), which is low in hydrogen and fast.
- Readout: resistive Micromegas (encapsulated resistive-anode type, ERAM), which spreads charge so that 1 cm pads give spatial resolution below 0.6 mm.

**What they do**
- They measure momentum and charge, in the 0.15 T field, for high-angle muons that exit the target vertically. These tracks are poorly covered by the existing downstream drift chambers.
- They provide dE/dx for muon/electron separation.
- Forward tracks continue into the existing downstream chambers.

## 3. Time-of-flight shell

**What it is**
- Plastic scintillator bars, about 12 cm wide and 1 cm thick, surrounding the target–TPC assembly on all six faces where space allows.
- Each bar is read out at both ends by arrays of SiPMs, with waveform digitisation in the SAMPIC class.
- Target timing is about 150 ps per bar.

**What it does**
- It sets track direction (forward versus backward), which removes the main source of mis-reconstructed backward muons.
- It vetoes particles entering from outside, such as the magnet and the sand muons from the rock.
- It provides particle identification for low-momentum particles.

## 4. Supporting items
- Extend the slow-control and DAQ clock across all three subsystems so that cube timing, TPC timing and ToF timing combine in one event.
- Use a non-magnetic carbon-fibre support box for the cube array.
- Install a calibration system: an LED light-injection system for the SiPMs and a laser or ⁵⁵Fe source for the TPCs.
- Check that the cooling, gas and cabling penetrations fit the remaining space at the upstream end of the magnet.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fully active ~1.3 t 3D-segmented scintillator-cube target (1 cm cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibres per cube, SiPM readout), which gives near-isotropic muon acceptance and ~60 MeV proton thresholds at about 8% hydrogen nucleon fraction.

# Design Review Recommendation for ND280 Upgrade

## Analysis of Requirements

The key constraints are:
- **Available space**: 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m (depth along beam)
- **Physics goal**: Kinematically complete CC events with muon + leading proton reconstruction
- **Angular acceptance**: Must handle ~25% of muons and ~35% of protons at >50° to beam
- **Momentum range**: Protons from ~100 MeV/c to >900 MeV/c (median 450 MeV/c)
- **Target systematic**: Reduce from 6% to 4%

The shallow depth (0.6 m) is the critical challenge. This demands:
1. **3D tracking** with excellent angular coverage including large angles
2. **Low material budget** per measurement layer to enable multiple measurements within 60 cm
3. **Fine granularity** for vertex resolution and particle separation
4. **Timing capability** to match beam structure

## Recommended Hardware Configuration

### 1. **SuperFGD: 3D Scintillator Cube Array** (PRIMARY RECOMMENDATION)

Replace the P0D with a **Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD)** consisting of:
- **~2 million plastic scintillator cubes**, 1 cm³ each, arranged in a 192 × 184 × 56 array
- **Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts** through each cube (X, Y, Z)
- **MPPC readout** on all fiber ends (~300,000 channels total)

**Justification**:
- **True 3D tracking**: Measures all three coordinates at each interaction point, essential for large-angle tracks in shallow geometry
- **Optimal granularity**: 1 cm³ provides ~10° angular resolution even for short proton tracks
- **Low threshold**: Detects protons down to ~200 MeV/c with multiple cube hits
- **No dead regions**: Uniform acceptance, unlike layered detectors with inter-plane gaps
- **Hydrocarbon target**: CH composition matches physics requirements
- **Proven technology**: Developed by T2K collaboration, successfully tested in prototypes

### 2. **High-Angle TPC (HA-TPC) Replacement**

Replace the existing horizontal TPCs with **time projection chambers optimized for large-angle acceptance**:
- **Resistive Micromegas readout** with 3 mm pad pitch
- **Field cage redesign** with reduced dead zones at TPC boundaries
- **Increased active volume** in transverse dimensions to capture 50°+ tracks

**Justification**:
- Existing TPCs have poor acceptance at >45° due to geometric constraints
- 35% of leading protons require near-4π coverage from the target
- Resistive MM technology improves spark protection and stability
- Provides momentum measurement for tracks exiting SuperFGD

### 3. **Time-of-Flight (TOF) Walls**

Install **thin scintillator TOF planes** (~2 cm thick):
- **Upstream**: Just before SuperFGD (beam-entry timing)
- **Downstream**: Immediately after SuperFGD, before first HA-TPC
- **Top/Bottom**: Horizontal planes above/below SuperFGD
- **~100 ps timing resolution** using fast scintillator + SiPM readout

**Justification**:
- **Proton/pion separation**: Critical for 300-600 MeV/c momentum range where dE/dx separation fails
- **Event timing**: T0 determination for TPC track matching
- **Background rejection**: Cosmic ray discrimination
- **Minimal material**: ~0.02 X₀, doesn't degrade momentum resolution

### 4. **Extended ECAL Coverage**

Add **lead-scintillator ECAL modules**:
- Close gaps in barrel coverage
- Add **upstream ECAL disk** in front of SuperFGD
- Extend to larger polar angles (up to 60° from beam)

**Justification**:
- Muon range measurement for tracks escaping TPCs at large angles
- π⁰ rejection for charged-current event selection
- Energy containment for electromagnetic component
- Consistent with existing ND280 ECAL technology

## Alternative Considered and Rejected

**Silicon tracking detectors**: While providing excellent resolution, silicon:
- Insufficient mass for target (requires separate target material)
- Limited range measurement (thin active layers)
- More complex and expensive for the required volume
- Not proven at this scale in neutrino experiments

## Expected Performance Improvements

1. **Acceptance**: 90%+ for leading protons vs. ~30% in current configuration
2. **Vertex resolution**: <3 mm in all directions
3. **Angular resolution**: ~5-10° for protons, ~2° for muons
4. **Proton momentum resolution**: ~15% at 450 MeV/c (TPC+range+TOF combination)
5. **Systematic uncertainty**: Path to <4% through improved angular acceptance and particle ID

## Implementation Strategy

- SuperFGD cube production can leverage Japanese and European manufacturing
- MPPC technology is mature (used throughout ND280)
- HA-TPC requires R&D on field cage geometry but uses proven Micromegas technology
- TOF walls use commercial fast scintillator and SiPMs
- Total channel count (~400k) is manageable with modern DAQ systems

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D segmented scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD) with 1 cm³ granularity and three-view WLS fiber readout as the active target

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near-Detector Active Target

## Why the current layout falls short

The existing drift chambers sit downstream of the target region, so they only see forward-going tracks. Muons near 90° and backward-going muons are lost, which breaks the ≥25% efficiency requirement at every angle. Short proton tracks, with kinetic energy around 60 MeV, stop inside any coarse target and are never reconstructed. The upgrade must therefore:

- make the target finely segmented and readable in three dimensions;
- surround it with tracking that covers high angles;
- add timing so the direction of each track (forward or backward) is known.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-readout scintillator active target (SuperFGD-type)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Fibres read out by SiPMs/MPPCs.
- Roughly 2.0 × 1.8 × 0.6 m of cubes inside the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope. This leaves room for the surrounding detectors in items 2 and 3.
- Order of 10⁶ cubes and about 5–6 × 10⁴ channels.

**Why**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal views give the same response for tracks at any angle, including perpendicular and backward tracks. Planar bar detectors lose tracks that run parallel to the bars.
- **Short-proton reconstruction.** A 60 MeV proton travels roughly 3 cm in plastic, so it crosses about 3 cubes. That is enough for a reconstructed track with dE/dx identification. With planar bars it would light only one or two layers.
- **Neutrons.** Timing in the cubes also allows neutron detection, a bonus for the analysis.

**Hydrogen constraint**
- In CH-type plastic, hydrogen nuclei are about 1/13 ≈ 7.7% of the target nucleons. This is well under the 20% limit, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid.
- This rules against a water-heavy or other high-hydrogen-fraction target design that would push toward the limit.
- Fibres, glue and reflector coating are also hydrocarbon, but they do not change the fraction much.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Thin-walled, low-mass composite field cages filled with a T2K-type argon gas mixture.
- Read out with resistive Micromegas (encapsulated-resistive-anode) modules.
- One TPC above and one below the new target, inside the magnet.

**Why**
- These TPCs measure momentum and charge in the 0.15 T field for muons leaving at large angles, which never reach the downstream chambers.
- They also provide dE/dx particle identification to separate muons from pions, protons and electrons.
- Resistive anodes spread the charge, giving good spatial resolution with fewer pads. This matters for momentum resolution in a modest 0.15 T field.
- The low-mass walls keep multiple scattering small, preserving that resolution.

## 3. Time-of-flight scintillator panels enclosing the target and TPCs

**Technology**
- Cast plastic scintillator bars read out at both ends by SiPM arrays.
- Timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Why**
- They determine track direction, so a backward-going muon is not mistaken for an entering forward track.
- They reject particles produced outside the target (for example, from interactions in the magnet) that enter it.
- They improve particle identification at low momentum.
- Panels on the left and right faces also help recover sideways (horizontal, perpendicular) muons that the up/down TPCs do not fully cover. These can be supplemented by any existing side calorimetry for range-based momentum.

## 4. Readout electronics, DAQ and calibration

**Technology**
- Front-end boards with nanosecond-level timing for the SiPM channels of the cube target and the TOF panels (CITIROC-class ASICs).
- AFTER/DREAM-type electronics for the Micromegas pads.
- A common clock and trigger shared with the existing drift chambers, so tracks can be matched between the new and old detectors.
- Calibration systems: an LED system for SiPM gain, and a laser or radioactive source for TPC drift.

**Why**
- Tens of thousands of new channels need sub-nanosecond synchronisation to combine target, TPC, TOF and downstream information.

## 5. Mechanical and services

- A low-mass support structure for the target.
- Stable temperature control, since SiPM gain depends on temperature.
- A gas system for the new TPCs.
- All of it must fit within the 0.9 m beam-direction depth of the target region without degrading acceptance.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a ~1 cm³-cube, three-view WLS-fibre/SiPM plastic-scintillator 3D active target (SuperFGD-type), giving isotropic acceptance and ~60 MeV proton reconstruction at a hydrogen fraction of ~8%, well under 20%.

# Design Review Recommendations: Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target Upgrade

## Analysis of Requirements Before Recommendations

**Key constraints derived from the physics:**
- Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at **all angles**, including 90° and backward-going → need 4π-ish tracking with no dead angular regions
- Proton KE down to ~60 MeV → range ~3 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in scintillator → need mm-scale or better granularity, low threshold
- Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of nucleons → limits pure hydrocarbon targets; must use heavier nuclei dominant composition
- Volume: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (depth along beam only 0.9 m) → relatively shallow along beam
- Existing downstream gas drift chambers provide external momentum measurement → active target primarily needs to seed tracks and measure short recoils

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Replace the existing passive target with a 3D Scintillator Tracker (3DST) as the primary active target

**Technology:** Plastic scintillator cubes (~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm) with wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber readout in three orthogonal directions, based on the SuperFGD/Baby MIND concept (as demonstrated for WAGASCI and T2K ND280 upgrade).

**Justification:**
- The cubic geometry provides **genuinely isotropic tracking** — there is no preferred orientation, so tracks at 90° and backward angles are reconstructed with the same efficiency as forward-going tracks. This directly satisfies the ≥25% at all angles requirement, which a conventional planar scintillator tracker (e.g., fine-grained detector with X/Y planes) fails at for near-perpendicular tracks due to ambiguities and gaps.
- 1.5 cm cubes give a track length threshold of ~1–2 cubes, corresponding to proton KE ≈ 40–50 MeV in plastic scintillator (density ~1.03 g/cm³, dE/dx Bragg peak), covering the required 60 MeV threshold with margin.
- Plastic scintillator (CH composition) has a hydrogen mass fraction ~7.7%. With carbon nucleons counted, hydrogen nuclei make up approximately **H/(H+C) nucleons ≈ 1/(1+12/1×1) ≈** let me compute properly: polystyrene C₈H₈ per monomer, so 8 H and 8×12 C nucleons → H fraction = 8/104 ≈ 7.7%. **This is well within the ≤20% hydrogen nucleon constraint.**
- WLS fiber readout to SiPMs is well-understood, radiation-hard at these fluences, and operates without magnetic field sensitivity (critical inside the dipole at 0.15 T where PMTs cannot be used).
- The technology fits within the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume and can be tiled to fill it essentially completely with no inactive gaps.
- Fast timing (~1 ns) aids pile-up rejection given the accelerator beam structure.

---

### 2. Add upstream and lateral thin-panel veto/tagger scintillator planes

**Technology:** 1 cm thick extruded scintillator bars (as used in MINERvA, NOvA near detector) with SiPM readout, arranged as X/Y double layers on the upstream face and all four lateral faces of the active target.

**Justification:**
- Backward-going muons and large-angle tracks **exit the upstream or lateral faces** of the active target into a region that may have no instrumentation before or beside the magnet bore. Without taggers on those faces, backward tracks that exit laterally lose their charge/momentum measurement and the event cannot be fully reconstructed.
- These panels tag entering cosmics and beam-related backgrounds (charged hadrons, muons from upstream interactions) that would fake neutrino interactions in the active target.
- Thin panels (1 cm) add minimal nuclear material and negligible change to the hydrogen nucleon fraction.
- The lateral panels also allow tracks that are **exactly perpendicular to the beam** to be matched to an exit hit, breaking the left-right ambiguity in the 3DST fiber readout for such tracks.
- SiPM readout is again field-compatible and low-power.

---

### 3. Install a low-mass Time Projection Chamber (TPC) immediately downstream of the active target, within the magnet volume

**Technology:** A rectangular gaseous TPC (~0.5 m along beam, full transverse aperture) with an Ar:CO₂ or Ar:isobutane gas mixture, GEM or Micromegas amplification planes, and pad/strip readout. Field cage at the downstream end of the active-target region, with the existing drift chambers further downstream serving as the external spectrometer.

**Justification:**
- The existing warm dipole plus downstream drift chambers measure muon momentum for forward-going tracks. However, **tracks at large angles to the beam** exit the active target laterally or backward and never enter the downstream spectrometer. A TPC that shares the same magnetic field volume provides **spatial 3D hit information and curvature measurement within the field** for those large-angle muons.
- The TPC gas is very low density (~2 mg/cm³), so it contributes negligibly to the target nucleon count and does not alter the hydrogen fraction constraint.
- GEM/Micromegas TPCs are well established in similar near-detector contexts (T2K, DUNE ND-GAr) and operate reliably in fields of 0.15 T with excellent dE/dx resolution (useful for particle ID, complementing the range-based ID in the 3DST).
- It bridges the momentum resolution gap: very short tracks that curl tightly in the magnet can still be measured inside the TPC rather than needing to reach the distant drift chambers.
- dE/dx in the TPC also allows proton/pion separation for tracks that escape the active target but are too short for the external drift spectrometer.

---

### 4. Upgrade the SiPM readout with waveform digitization (FADC or DRS4-based)

**Technology:** Replace simple time-over-threshold or charge-integrating electronics with 250 MHz+ flash ADC waveform sampling (e.g., using ASICs such as CITIROC 1A or TARGET chips as used in imaging atmospheric Cherenkov telescopes, adapted for this application).

**Justification:**
- The 60 MeV proton requirement means distinguishing **very short, high-dE/dx Bragg-peak signals** in one or two cubes from noise and from overlapping hits. Waveform sampling resolves pulse shape, enabling proton vs. pion vs. Michel electron discrimination via pulse shape analysis — critical for a clean recoil proton sample.
- Neutrino interactions at this flux peak energy (0.7 GeV) produce final states with multiple low-energy hadrons. Waveform digitization enables **hit-time separation at the ~ns level**, resolving secondary hadronic interactions and neutron-induced hits from primary vertex activity within the same ~1 ns beam spill.
- Backward muons that re-enter the active target after scattering off the magnet yoke produce distinctive late-arriving pulses identifiable only with timing.
- This upgrade is fully compatible with the SiPM/WLS fiber infrastructure recommended in point 1 and adds modest cost relative to the physics gain.

---

### 5. Add a thin liquid-argon or water layer sandwich **[Conditional recommendation — flag for further study]**

**Note:** This is flagged as a risk item rather than a firm recommendation. Some analyses may benefit from a small water or hydrocarbon target sub-volume to maximize hydrogen content just at the boundary — but this directly tensions the ≤20% hydrogen nucleon constraint. **The collaboration should explicitly verify** that the 3DST CH composition satisfies the analysis model robustness before introducing any additional hydrogen-rich layer. If the hydrogen model can tolerate it, a thin (few-cm) water plane upstream of the 3DST can provide an almost pure oxygen+hydrogen target for cross-section ratio measurements. If not, this option must be dropped.

---

## Summary Table

| Change | Technology | Key Physics Driver |
|---|---|---|
| 3D scintillator active target | 1.5 cm plastic scintillator cubes + WLS fibers + SiPMs | 4π muon + recoil proton tracking; 60 MeV threshold |
| Face veto/tagger panels | Extruded scintillator bars + SiPMs | Backward/lateral track tagging; background rejection |
| In-field TPC | GEM/Micromegas Ar-gas TPC | Large-angle muon momentum measurement in B field |
| Waveform digitization | 250 MHz FADC per SiPM channel | Proton PID, pile-up resolution, timing |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a fully 3D-segmented plastic scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD-style, ~1.5 cm cubes with orthogonal WLS fiber/SiPM readout), as it simultaneously solves the isotropic muon tracking efficiency requirement, the 60 MeV proton threshold requirement, and the hydrogen nucleon fraction constraint, within the existing magnet volume.

This is an interesting neutrino detector upgrade problem. Let me analyze the requirements:

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Geometry**: Active target volume 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m in a 0.15 T dipole field
2. **Muon tracking**: ≥25% efficiency at ALL angles, including perpendicular and backward-going

The most severe constraint is detecting **backward-going muons** and **very short proton tracks** while maintaining low hydrogen content. Traditional options like liquid scintillator (~14% H by mass) or plastic scintillator (~50% H) violate the hydrogen constraint or have insufficient granularity for short protons.

**Three-dimensional array of extruded plastic scintillator bars with wavelength-shifting fiber and SiPM readout:**

- **Spacing**: Interleave with passive low-hydrogen target planes (see below)
- **Readout**: SiPMs on both ends for timing and position along bar (Δt measurement)
- **Benefits**: 
  - 3D tracking including backward-going particles
  - ~cm-scale tracking for 60 MeV protons
  - Timing for particle ID

### Secondary Components:

**2. Passive Nuclear Target Planes**
- Material: Graphite or CH₂ sheets (if using pure C: 0% H; if using limited CH₂: control the ratio)
- Thickness: 1-2 cm planes interleaved with scintillator planes
- Purpose: Provide nuclear target material while keeping overall H content <10% by mass

**3. High-Granularity Option: Micro-pattern Gas Detector Planes**
- Technology: MicroMegas or GEM-based TPCs in thin layers
- Gas: Ar/CO₂ mixture (zero hydrogen)
- Spacing: Every 5-10 cm through the volume
- Benefits:
  - Excellent spatial resolution (~100 μm)
  - 3D tracking from drift time
  - dE/dx for particle ID
  - Nearly zero hydrogen content

**4. Enhanced Downstream Tracking**
- Extend gas drift chambers closer to target region
- Add timing planes (plastic scintillator hodoscopes) immediately downstream
- Purpose: Improve momentum resolution and charge ID for forward-going muons

**5. Upstream Veto/Tracker**
- Thin scintillator planes upstream of target
- Purpose: Identify and reject entering particles; tag backward-going tracks

**6. DAQ Upgrade**
- High-speed digitizers for SiPM signals
- Trigger system accepting all topologies (no bias against backward tracks)
- Time resolution <1 ns for event reconstruction

## Optimal Configuration

**Hybrid design**: Alternate between:
- Active layers: 1 cm scintillator bars (2-3 orientations per "super-layer")
- Passive layers: 1.5 cm graphite (or controlled C/H ratio target)
- MPGD planes: Every 3-4 super-layers for high-resolution tracking

This gives ~6-8 cm longitudinal segmentation, adequate for ~60 MeV protons (range ~7 cm in scintillator, ~10 cm in carbon).

**Hydrogen budget**: With 50% scintillator / 50% graphite by volume and plastic scintillator at ~10% H by mass, overall target is ~5% H by mass = ~10% H nucleons. ✓

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a fine-grained 3D scintillator bar tracker with ~1 cm bars in three orientations, SiPM readout, and interleaved passive carbon target planes to achieve full angular acceptance while maintaining <10% hydrogen content by mass.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Active Target Module

## Overview of Constraints

The available volume (2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m, ~2.3 m³) in the former photon-tagging bay must deliver:
- Kinematically complete CC events (μ + leading p reconstructed)
- Large angular acceptance (>50° for 25% of muons, 35% of protons)
- Proton tracking down to threshold, up to ~900 MeV/c
- Systematic uncertainty reduction from ~6% to ~4%

The 0.6 m depth along beam is the critical constraint: it limits muon ranging but the downstream TPCs and return-yoke scintillator handle forward muons; the new module must handle the large-angle topology.

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. High-Granularity Scintillator Active Target (Primary Recommendation)

**Technology:** 3D-granular plastic scintillator cube detector based on the SuperFGD concept.

**Implementation:**
- Fill the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume with ~1.5 × 1.8 × 0.55 m active region
- ~1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm optically isolated polystyrene cubes (approximately 1.5 million cubes)
- Each cube read out in three orthogonal directions by wavelength-shifting fibres threaded through 1 mm holes, coupled to SiPMs at the volume edges
- Three-view (X, Y, Z) simultaneous readout provides true 3D hit reconstruction without ambiguity

**Physics rationale:**
- 1 cm³ granularity gives ~3 MeV detection threshold, tracking protons down to ~300 MeV/c kinetic energy (~450 MeV/c momentum), covering the bulk of the leading-proton distribution
- The isotropic readout geometry provides uniform angular acceptance at all azimuthal and polar angles — directly addressing the >50° large-angle requirement
- Short radiation length of polystyrene (~43 cm) means π⁰ photons convert within the volume, aiding neutral particle reconstruction
- Multiple Coulomb scattering in 1 cm steps allows momentum measurement by range (for stopping tracks) and by curvature in the 0.2 T field (for exiting tracks)
- The hydrocarbon (CH~) composition matches the downstream plastic tracking target for systematic cross-checks; carbon-to-water comparison uses the existing downstream water-layer target

**Estimated mass:**
- Polystyrene density ~1.05 g/cm³; active volume ~1.5 t
- Comfortably within structural limits, well under the removed 16.1 t photon-tagging section

**SiPM count and readout:**
- Three faces per axis pair: ~2 × (150 + 180 + 55) × 2 directions ≈ order 20,000–25,000 SiPM channels
- Consistent with existing detector SiPM infrastructure; same WLS fibre + SiPM readout chain already deployed downstream

---

### 2. Thin Upstream Timing Layer

**Technology:** Two planes of 3 mm-thick fast plastic scintillator paddles (EJ-200 or equivalent), segmented to 5 cm × 5 cm pixels, SiPM readout.

**Implementation:**
- One plane at the upstream face, one plane at the downstream face of the new target
- ~400 channels each, ~100 ps timing resolution

**Physics rationale:**
- Provides interaction vertex time-stamp independent of TPC drift-time ambiguity
- Enables beam-spill pile-up rejection at the ~ns level
- Tags through-going muons from upstream interactions (beam halo, secondary interactions in shielding)
- Measures incident flux profile across the face — useful for flux constraint

---

### 3. Thin Electromagnetic Sampling Layer on Downstream Face

**Technology:** 4 layers of 3 mm lead + 5 mm plastic scintillator, segmented to 2 × 2 cm cells, covering the full 2.0 × 1.9 m downstream face.

**Implementation:**
- Total depth ~3.2 cm Pb equivalent (~0.57 X₀), mass ~180 kg
- Fits within residual space between new target and first TPC
- SiPM readout, same chain as main target

**Physics rationale:**
- Tags forward-going photons from π⁰ decay that exit the granular target before converting
- Separates π⁰ background from genuine quasi-elastic events — critical for transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis where π⁰ misidentification mimics missing transverse momentum
- Complements the removed photon-tagging section's function at forward angles
- Improves NC/CC separation for the flux constraint fit

---

### 4. Return-Yoke Scintillator Upgrade for Large-Angle Muon Ranging

**Technology:** Add one additional double-layer of 1 cm × 4 cm scintillator bars (X+Y) to the inner face of the upstream return-yoke gap, specifically on the lateral (non-beam-axis) faces adjacent to the new target location.

**Implementation:**
- Two planes × 2 views × ~40 bars per view ≈ ~320 additional channels
- Uses existing SiPM + WLS readout; slots into existing yoke gap geometry

**Physics rationale:**
- The existing return-yoke scintillator ranges out side-going muons from the downstream region; the new upstream target is physically closer to the lateral yoke faces
- Large-angle muons (>50°) from the new target travel ~0.5–1.0 m before reaching the yoke; adding one instrumented layer increases ranging depth by ~10 cm steel equivalent, extending the momentum reach for stopping muons by ~100 MeV/c
- Improves charge-sign determination for large-angle tracks where TPC lever arm is short
- Low cost (~320 channels) relative to systematic gain

---

### 5. Local Low-Mass Field-Cage Insert (Optional / Longer Term)

**Technology:** Thin-walled aluminium honeycomb field cage with 20 kV/m internal field, surrounding a 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 m central fiducial sub-volume of the granular target.

**Implementation:**
- Requires partial redesign of cube layer arrangement in central region
- Gas-tight enclosure with Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ fill
- Effectively a micro-TPC embedded within the scintillator target

**Physics rationale:**
- Provides dE/dx particle identification (p vs. π separation) independent of range alone
- Resolves proton–pion ambiguity near 450 MeV/c where range difference is small
- However: adds complexity, gas infrastructure, potential HV failure modes; treat as Phase 2 option

## Systematic Uncertainty Path to 4%

The dominant residual ~6% uncertainty comes from flux normalisation and cross-section shape (particularly CCQE vs. multinucleon contributions). The new target reduces it by:

1. **TKI variables** (δpT, δαT, δpL) with kinematically complete events directly constrain 2p2h and final-state interaction models — ~1% gain
2. **Improved π⁰ rejection** via downstream EM layer tightens NC background subtraction — ~0.5% gain
3. **Flux constraint** from precise near-detector event rate with better vertex resolution in the new target — ~0.5% gain

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints

Before proposing hardware, let me extract the key requirements:

- **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (~5.4 m³)
- **Muon reconstruction**: ≥25% efficiency at *all* angles, including 90° and backward-going
- **Proton tracking**: down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3.5 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in plastic scintillator)
- **Hydrogen fraction**: ≤20% of target nucleons → constrains material choice
- **Magnetic field**: 0.15 T already present from warm dipole
- **Beam peak**: 0.7 GeV → typical muon momenta 200–800 MeV/c, protons 100–500 MeV/c

---

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. Active Target Core: 3D Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperCube" style)

**Technology**: Extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes, ~1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm, assembled in a fully-3D interlocked array read out by **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** running through holes along all three axes, with **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** at the fiber ends.

**Rationale**:
- 1.5 cm cubes give a track granularity sufficient to reconstruct proton tracks down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~2.5 cm in scintillator → 1–2 cubes minimum; acceptable with the full 3D hit pattern).
- Three-axis readout gives unambiguous 3D space points, not projected views, enabling reconstruction of **backward-going and transverse tracks** without geometric blind spots — directly addressing the 25% efficiency requirement at all angles.
- Total number of cubes: ~(173 × 153 × 60) ≈ **1.6 million cubes**; this is large but consistent with the Super-FGD design precedent (at T2K/ND280 upgrade) which covers a comparable mass.
- SiPMs are compatible with operation inside or immediately adjacent to the magnetic field (unlike PMTs), since the field is only 0.15 T.

**Hydrogen fraction check**: Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ has hydrogen mass fraction ~7.7%; by nucleon number, H nuclei are ~(8/16) = 50% — **too high**. This must be corrected (see item 3 below).

---

### 2. Hydrogen Fraction Mitigation: Composite Target Layers Interleaved with High-Z Passive Absorber

**Technology**: Replace approximately half the scintillator volume with **thin aluminum or carbon (graphite) passive plates**, 3–5 mm thick, interleaved every ~3 cm along the beam axis between scintillator cube planes.

**Rationale**:
- Pure polystyrene gives ~50% hydrogen nucleons — far above the 20% cap.
- Interleaving carbon/aluminum slabs dilutes the hydrogen fraction. Carbon (graphite) is preferred because it has zero hydrogen, low Z (minimizing multiple scattering for proton tracking), and its nuclear cross-sections are well-measured.
- With ~55% of the total nucleon budget coming from carbon plates (density ~2.2 g/cm³), the hydrogen fraction drops below 20%.
- The plates also serve as **neutrino interaction targets with well-known nuclear composition**, enabling cross-section measurements on carbon separately from hydrogen.
- Plate thickness (~3–5 mm) is thin enough that protons with ≥60 MeV kinetic energy (~1.5 cm range in carbon) can still exit into the scintillator and be tracked.

---

### 3. Upstream Veto and Side-Wall Scintillator Panels

**Technology**: **Plastic scintillator panels**, 1 cm thick, read out by SiPMs via embedded WLS fibers, covering all six faces of the active target volume.

**Rationale**:
- Identifies charged particles entering the active target from outside (beam-related backgrounds, rock muons).
- Critical for tagging backward-going muons that exit through the upstream face — these would otherwise be lost or misidentified.
- Provides a prompt trigger signal (< 5 ns timing resolution with SiPMs) to gate the drift chamber readout downstream.
- The upstream panel also tags interactions occurring in material immediately upstream of the active volume.

---

### 4. Time-of-Flight Layer Between Active Target and Downstream Drift Chambers

**Technology**: **Fast plastic scintillator bars** (EJ-200 or equivalent), 2 cm × 5 cm cross-section, arranged in two orthogonal planes (X and Y), read out at both ends by **fast SiPMs** (rise time < 1 ns, e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series).

**Rationale**:
- Provides **particle ID via time-of-flight** for tracks exiting the active target into the drift chamber region.
- At 0.7 GeV beam, muons and pions are difficult to separate by momentum alone in the drift chambers; a ~1 ns TOF resolution over a ~1 m baseline gives ~3σ π/μ separation up to ~600 MeV/c.
- Pion contamination in the "muon" sample is a leading systematic for the cross-section analysis.
- Two orthogonal planes give 2D position for track matching.

---

### 5. SiPM Readout Electronics Upgrade: Self-Triggering, High-Rate ASIC

**Technology**: Custom or commercial **front-end ASICs** (e.g., TOFPET2 from PETsys Electronics, or CITIROC from Weeroc) with:
- Per-channel threshold discrimination
- Time-over-threshold charge measurement
- ~100 ps timestamp resolution
- Triggerless / self-triggering readout architecture

**Rationale**:
- The 3D cube array will have O(10⁶) channels; charge-integrating ADCs per channel are impractical.
- Time-over-threshold gives adequate charge resolution (energy deposition, hence dE/dx for PID) at high channel count.
- Self-triggering is essential to capture **all-angle, low-energy proton tracks** which may not form a clean trigger pattern.
- Triggerless readout also handles the **backward-going muon** topology where the first hit in time is in the downstream part of the detector, not the upstream part.

---

### 6. Thin Downstream Electromagnetic Calorimeter Sampling Layer

**Technology**: **Lead–scintillator sampling calorimeter**, ~8 radiation lengths total, using 2 mm lead sheets alternating with 3 mm plastic scintillator tiles read out by SiPMs, covering the full 2.6 m × 2.3 m downstream face.

**Rationale**:
- Identifies and measures **π⁰ → γγ** from neutral pion production, a major background to the quasi-elastic signal used to study hydrogen interactions.
- At 0.7 GeV, π⁰ energies are typically 100–400 MeV; 8 X₀ contains ~95% of shower energy.
- Lead–scintillator is compact (~9 cm total thickness) and fits within the magnet bore downstream of the active target without consuming useful tracking volume.
- SiPM readout avoids field sensitivity issues.

---
