| Upgrade | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 3D scintillator cube array | 1.5 cm polystyrene cubes + WLS fibers + SiPMs | Proton tracking to 60 MeV, all-angle muon reconstruction |
| Carbon/Al interleaved plates | Graphite slabs, 3–5 mm | Hydrogen fraction ≤ 20% |
| Six-face veto panels | Plastic scintillator + SiPM | Background rejection, backward muon tagging |
| TOF layer | Fast scintillator bars + fast SiPMs | π/μ separation exiting target |
| Self-triggering ASIC electronics | TOFPET2 / CITIROC | High channel count, all-angle trigger |
| Downstream EM calorimeter | Pb–scintillator sampling + SiPMs | π⁰ rejection for hydrogen subtraction model |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a fully 3D-interlocked array of 1.5 cm polystyrene scintillator cubes read out along all three axes by WLS fibers and SiPMs, interleaved with thin graphite absorber plates to bring the hydrogen nucleon fraction below 20%, providing the granularity needed for short proton tracks and the geometric isotropy needed for all-angle muon reconstruction.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Active Target

## Context and Driving Constraints

The box available (~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m) is shallow along the beam axis, so longitudinal containment of recoil protons is tight. The physics driver is kinematic completeness: both the muon and leading proton reconstructed, with ~35% of protons and ~25% of muons exiting beyond 50°. The median proton momentum is ~450 MeV/c, meaning a range of ~9 cm in plastic (easily contained) but only if the track is found and measured, not just ranged. The 6% tail above 900 MeV/c (~30 cm range in plastic) sets the outer containment scale.

---

## 1. Core Active Target: 3D Scintillator Cube Array ("SuperFGD-style")

**Technology:** A fully-3D array of small plastic scintillator cubes (~1 cm³ each), read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibre axes per cube, each fibre terminated on a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM, e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1350CS or equivalent, 50 µm pitch, 1.3×1.3 mm²).

- Cube dimensions: 1.0 × 1.0 × 1.0 cm³ extruded polystyrene doped with PPO/POPOP fluors, with a TiO₂-loaded white diffuse reflector coating on five faces and a central through-hole on each axis for the fibre.
- Array size to fill the box: ~200 × 190 × 56 layers = approximately 2.1 million cubes, mass ~2.0 t.
- Three fibres per cube (X, Y, Z axes), 1.0 mm diameter Kuraray Y-11 multi-cladding WLS fibre, read at one end, mirrored at the other.
- SiPM count: ~(200+190+56)×appropriate_plane_count; total of order 56,000–70,000 channels depending on fibre bundling strategy.
- **Why:** The 4π granularity means short, large-angle proton tracks (even down to ~3 cm = ~300 MeV/c kinetic energy threshold ~50 MeV) are reconstructed in 3D without ambiguity. No dead material between tracking planes. The isotropic response directly addresses the 35% of protons beyond 50°.

---

## 2. Time-of-Flight Layer: Thin Fast-Scintillator Planes on Upstream and Downstream Faces

**Technology:** Two planes of 5 mm thick EJ-228 (or BC-418) fast plastic scintillator tiles (~10 × 10 cm² tiles), each read by two SiPMs on opposing edges via light guides, one plane on the upstream face and one on the downstream face of the cube array.

- Timing resolution target: σ_t ~ 200–300 ps per plane, achievable with EJ-228 (rise time ~500 ps) and SiPMs with TOFPET2 ASIC readout.
- **Why:** Provides proton/pion discrimination by time-of-flight over the ~0.6 m baseline for momenta below ~600 MeV/c, where dE/dx alone is ambiguous for short tracks. Also flags beam-related backgrounds from upstream.

---

## 3. Surrounding Thin ECAL: Pb-Scintillator Sampling on the Four Lateral Faces

**Technology:** On each of the four side faces (top, bottom, left, right) of the cube array, install a compact electromagnetic calorimeter: 8–10 layers of 2 mm lead + 3 mm scintillator (EJ-200) tiles (~5 × 5 cm²), SiPM readout, total ~6 X₀.

- Total added thickness per face: ~5 cm, fitting within the magnet volume.
- SiPM: Hamamatsu S14160-3010PS, 3×3 mm² cells.
- Readout ASIC: SPIROC2E or equivalent low-power 36-channel chip.
- **Why:** Photons from π⁰ decay produced in the active target must be tagged/vetoed to maintain kinematic completeness. Six radiation lengths suppress punch-through photons into the return-yoke scintillator and allow rough π⁰ energy reconstruction. It also captures electromagnetic energy from muon bremsstrahlung and helps resolve the ~6% high-momentum proton tail that exits the cube array laterally.

---

## 4. Thin Upstream Veto Plane: Multi-Layer Scintillator + Signal Timing Tag

**Technology:** Two layers of 7 mm extruded scintillator bars (the same geometry as existing tracker bars, 9.6 mm pitch), one layer in X and one in Y, each bar read by a single SiPM, placed ~2 cm upstream of the cube array face.

- 2 layers × ~190 bars each ≈ 380 channels.
- **Why:** Rejects charged particles entering from upstream (beam-halo muons, pion charge-exchange products from beam pipe) which would fake interaction vertices. Essential for clean vertex identification in the shallow box geometry.

---

## 5. SiPM Readout Electronics: Waveform-Sampling Front-End

**Technology:** Replace any charge-integrating ASIC scheme with waveform-sampling ASICs, specifically the **DRS4-based** (Paul Scherrer Institut) or **WASA TARGET** ASIC approach, sampling at 2–5 GSa/s over a 200 ns window per channel.

- Group 64 SiPM channels per front-end board; boards mounted on the cube array edge frames.
- Delivers both charge (via integration) and precise timing (via CFD applied offline) simultaneously.
- Power budget: ~5 mW/channel on-chip; total ~350 W for the full cube array — acceptable within the magnet volume ventilation.
- **Why:** The cubes produce ~15–25 photoelectrons per MIP per fibre. Waveform sampling recovers precise hit timing (σ < 1 ns per cube), enabling event time-stamping relative to beam spill at the sub-bunch level, and allows pulse-shape discrimination to separate proton (slower, broader pulse in plastic) from MIP tracks at low momentum.

---

## 6. Mechanical and Cooling Integration

- **Frame:** Carbon-fibre composite frame, ~4 mm wall, to minimize passive material at the edges while supporting the cube array under its ~2 t weight.
- **Cooling:** Copper cooling bars running along fibre-read edges with chilled water (18°C) to stabilize SiPM gain; SiPMs drift ~3%/°C so ΔT < 0.5°C is needed. This is achievable with thin (3 mm diameter) Cu tubes bonded to the SiPM carrier boards.
- **Fibre routing:** WLS fibres exit through grooves in the frame walls; ferrule connectors allow SiPM boards to be removed without disturbing cube array.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Technology | Channels | Key Physics Benefit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3D scintillator cube array | 1 cm³ PS cubes + Y-11 WLS + SiPM | ~65,000 | 4π tracking of large-angle protons |
| ToF planes (×2) | EJ-228 tiles + SiPM + TOFPET2 | ~800 | p/π separation below 600 MeV/c |
| Lateral Pb-scintillator ECAL | 2mm Pb + EJ-200 + SiPM + SPIROC2E | ~4,000 | π⁰ veto, high-p proton containment |
| Upstream veto planes (×2) | Extruded scintillator bars + SiPM | ~380 | Beam background rejection |
| Waveform-sampling readout | DRS4-class ASIC, 2–5 GSa/s | Full system | Timing + pulse-shape discrimination |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a fully 3D plastic scintillator cube array (~1 cm³ cubes, three-axis WLS fibre readout, SiPM per fibre end), because it uniquely provides isotropic sub-centimetre track reconstruction that captures the large-angle short-range recoil protons that are the primary obstacle to achieving kinematically complete events.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Core Design Philosophy

The replacement must fit within ~2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m, track large-angle (>50°) muons and protons down to the Fermi-momentum scale (~200 MeV/c), and reduce systematics from ~6% to ~4%. The depth constraint (0.6 m along beam) is severe and drives every technology choice.

---

## 1. Highly Granular Scintillator Neutrino Target (SuperFGD)

**Technology:** A 3D-grid plastic scintillator cube detector using ~1 cm³ extruded polystyrene cubes, each read out on all three orthogonal faces by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres coupled to MPPCs (SiPMs, e.g. Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE or equivalent).

**Concrete specifications:**
- Cube size: 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm × 1.0 cm polystyrene (same material as FGDs for systematic continuity)
- Array: ~192 × 182 × 56 cubes fitting ~1.92 m × 1.82 m × 0.56 m — well within the box
- Three WLS fibres per cube (X, Y, Z faces), Y-11 or Kuraray SCSF-78
- MPPCs: ~50,000–60,000 channels total (one MPPC per fibre end, with one end mirrored)
- Readout ASIC: CITIROC-1A or equivalent 32-channel SiPM readout chip
- Expected threshold: ~0.5 MeV deposited energy per cube, giving a proton momentum threshold of roughly 200–250 MeV/c (proton range ~1–2 cm)
- 4π solid-angle acceptance for all charged secondaries with no dead zones between modules

**Why critical:** The 3D topology breaks the degeneracy of 2D projective readout. Tracks at >50° are reconstructed as cleanly as forward tracks. Short proton stubs (3–8 cubes) are distinguishable from Michel electrons and nuclear fragments by dE/dx cube-by-cube. This directly addresses the 25%/35% large-angle escape fractions quoted.

**Note:** This is essentially the SuperFGD design already prototyped by the T2K upgrade collaboration; I am being concrete about the technical parameters rather than just naming the concept.

---

## 2. Thin-Gap Time Projection Chambers Surrounding the Target (HA-TPCs)

**Technology:** High-Angle TPCs — six thin rectangular TPCs (three on each of the top/bottom or left/right pairs) flanking the SuperFGD volume, using:

- **Gas:** Ar:CF₄:iC₄H₁₀ 95:3:2 (same as existing ND280 TPCs — reduces systematic difference and simplifies gas infrastructure)
- **Readout:** Resistive Micromegas (bulk-style), 1 cm × 0.7 cm pad size, ~1700 pads per TPC
- **Drift distance:** ~20 cm per TPC (fits within magnet gaps and surrounding ECal space)
- **Dimensions per TPC module:** ~1.8 m × 0.6 m active area, 0.2 m drift
- **Magnetic field:** Existing 0.2 T dipole — momentum resolution for a 450 MeV/c proton from sagitta measurement: σ(p)/p ~ 5–10% over a 1 m lever arm, which is adequate
- **Trigger:** Coincidence with SuperFGD scintillation signal (fast, ~ns timing from SiPMs)

**Concrete performance targets:**
- Muon momentum resolution: σ(p)/p < 5% for forward tracks via range+curvature combination
- Proton/pion separation via dE/dx: >3σ up to ~1 GeV/c (Bethe-Bloch regime)
- These TPCs catch the large-angle muons that would otherwise exit through the magnet yoke gaps

---

## 3. Time-of-Flight (TOF) Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Six planes of plastic scintillator (EJ-200 or BC-408), one on each face of the SuperFGD + HA-TPC assembly.

**Concrete specifications:**
- Scintillator bars: 2 cm thick, 5 cm wide, full-face coverage (~1.9 m × 2.0 m per face)
- Readout: SiPMs (Hamamatsu S13360-3050PE) on both ends of each bar via direct coupling (no WLS fibre — to preserve timing)
- Expected timing resolution: σ_t ~ 200–300 ps per plane, giving a two-plane TOF resolution of ~300–400 ps
- At 400 MeV/c, a proton (β ≈ 0.39) vs. a pion (β ≈ 0.94) separated by >3σ over a 60 cm baseline — directly addresses low-momentum proton identification
- At 900 MeV/c, TOF separation falls to ~1σ over 60 cm, but dE/dx in TPCs takes over there

**Integration:** TOF planes double as a veto for external backgrounds and provide the T0 for TPC drift-time determination (the existing ND280 TPCs use P0D as their T0 — removing P0D creates a T0 problem that the TOF planes solve).

---

## 4. MPPC/SiPM Readout Electronics Upgrade (Front-End)

**Technology:** Replace legacy AFTER-chip based front-end boards with new CITIROC-1A ASICs or the upgraded TOFPET2 ASIC (PETsys Electronics), which offer:

- Simultaneous charge (QDC) + time (TDC, ~50 ps binning) measurement per channel
- Reduced power: ~5 mW/channel vs. ~15 mW/channel for legacy boards
- On-chip zero-suppression to manage the ~50,000-channel readout rate
- PCI-express based data concentrators (FPGA: Xilinx Kintex-7 or equivalent) aggregating to the existing ND280 DAQ framework via standard Ethernet

**Why this matters as a separate line item:** The SuperFGD's 3D cube topology requires genuine 3D hit reconstruction, which demands time-stamped coincidence matching across three fibre axes per cube. Without ~1 ns timing on each MPPC channel, ghost hits from combinatorial ambiguities degrade tracking efficiency for multi-track events — exactly the signal topology needed for transverse kinematic imbalance analysis.

---

## 5. Thin Lead Converter Sheets for π⁰ Tagging (optional inner layers)

**Technology:** Two 1 mm Pb sheets inserted at the upstream and midpoint of the SuperFGD volume.

- Purpose: Convert photons from π⁰ decay into e⁺e⁻ pairs detectable as cube clusters, allowing neutral-pion subtraction in the CC-inclusive sample
- 1 mm Pb = 0.18 X₀ — sufficient for ~15% conversion probability per sheet without severely degrading proton tracking
- This is the lightest intervention that gives any π⁰ sensitivity without a separate ECal module in the tight 0.6 m space

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key parameter addressed |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD cube target | 1 cm³ PS cubes + WLS + MPPC | Large-angle acceptance, short proton stubs |
| HA-TPCs (×6 modules) | Resistive Micromegas, same gas as existing | Momentum measurement + dE/dx PID |
| TOF planes (×6 faces) | EJ-200 + direct SiPM, 200–300 ps | Low-p proton/pion ID, TPC T0 |
| New FE electronics | CITIROC-1A / TOFPET2 ASIC | 3D hit disambiguation, timing |
| Thin Pb converters (×2) | 1 mm Pb sheets in-target | π⁰ background tagging |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D volume with a 3D-granular 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cube (SuperFGD) array read out on all three axes by WLS fibres and MPPCs, since this single change provides 4π acceptance for short proton tracks and large-angle muons simultaneously, directly solving the kinematic completeness requirement that no 2D-projective detector geometry can adequately address within the available 0.6 m depth.

# Upgrade proposal for the Kestrel Flats near station

## The physics problem

The current layout cannot meet the analysis requirements, for three reasons:

- **High-angle and backward muons are lost.** Drift chambers downstream of the target region accept forward tracks well. Muons at 90° or backward travel along the planes of a planar tracker, or never reach the downstream chambers.
- **Short protons are lost.** A proton with 60 MeV kinetic energy has a range of only about 3 cm in plastic, so a coarse-grained target sees it as at most one or two hits.
- **The target material is constrained.** Hydrogen must make up no more than 20% of the target nucleons.

Each upgrade below addresses one of these problems.

---

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-readout scintillator-cube active target (primary upgrade)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with a reflective (chemically etched) coating.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Fibres are read out by SiPMs/MPPCs on three faces, giving three 2D projections that are combined into 3D hits.
- A footprint of roughly 2.0 × 2.0 × 0.6 m (about 2.4 million cubes and about 60,000 channels) fits inside the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region. This leaves room for the detectors in upgrades 2 and 3 above, below and around it.

**Why it meets the requirements**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** The cube granularity is the same in all three directions, so tracking efficiency barely depends on angle. Perpendicular and backward muons are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
  - Muons that stop in the target are measured by range.
  - Muons that exit are measured by curvature in the side TPCs or downstream chambers.
  - This is what brings the efficiency above 25% at every angle.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travelling about 3 cm crosses roughly 3 cubes. Combined with dE/dx from the Bragg peak, this allows proton identification down to about 300 MeV/c momentum, in any direction.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** Polystyrene (CH)ₙ has 1 hydrogen nucleon per 13 nucleons, which is about 7.7%. This is well under the 20% limit.
  - Avoid adding hydrogen-rich passive materials.
  - Optional water-target layers would raise the fraction only to at most about 11%, still within the limit.
- **Neutron tagging.** Hit times at the sub-nanosecond level allow neutron detection by time of flight, which helps reconstruct the event kinematics.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Thin gas TPCs placed in the remaining height of the target region, flanking the cube target.
- Read out with resistive (encapsulated-resistor) Micromegas, which give charge spreading and good spatial resolution with a modest number of pads.
- Field cage built from low-mass composite.

**Motivation**
- Muons at high angle that leave the cube target sideways get a curvature measurement in the 0.15 T field. This gives their momentum and charge sign, which separates μ⁻ from μ⁺ and so separates neutrino from antineutrino interactions.
- Their dE/dx separates muons from electrons.
- Without these TPCs, the muon momentum would be measured by range alone, and only for muons that stop in the target.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the target and TPCs

**Technology**
- Long plastic scintillator bars read out at both ends by arrays of large-area SiPMs.
- Time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**Motivation**
- Timing at the entry and exit points tells which way a track is going. This lets a genuinely backward-going muon from the target be distinguished from an incoming particle from an interaction outside the detector, which removes a major source of background.
- It also improves particle identification in the low-momentum range where TPC dE/dx bands cross.

## 4. Supporting electronics and calibration

- Readout electronics with deep buffering and fine time-to-digital converters (TDCs), to preserve the timing for neutron time of flight and direction tagging.
- A light-injection (LED) calibration system for the SiPMs.
- These keep the 3D hit-matching and proton threshold stable over the run.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fine-grained 3D-readout plastic scintillator-cube active target (≈1 cm cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibres read by SiPMs), which gives isotropic muon acceptance, a proton threshold near 60 MeV kinetic energy, and only about 8% hydrogen nucleons.

Based on the requirements and constraints described, here are my proposed hardware upgrades:

## Primary Target Upgrade: SuperFGD-style 3D Scintillator Detector

**Technology**: Install a three-dimensional optically-segmented plastic scintillator cube in the 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m upstream space.

**Specific implementation**:
- **5 mm × 5 mm × 5 mm scintillator cubes** (smaller than the current 9.6 mm bars) arranged in a true 3D geometry
- ~9.1 million cubes with three orthogonal 1.5 mm wavelength-shifting fiber holes through each cube
- Total of ~27 million readout channels via multiplexed MPPC arrays
- Mass: approximately 3.6 tonnes of polystyrene-based scintillator
- Three-view readout (X, Y, Z) providing true 3D tracking with ~5 mm resolution

**Key advantages**:
- Excellent angular acceptance and reconstruction for tracks >50° to beam
- Low Coulomb scattering for low-momentum protons (450 MeV/c median)
- Proton tracking threshold ~200 MeV/c kinetic energy
- Fine granularity enables vertex reconstruction and particle ID via dE/dx
- Sufficient material to contain most protons <900 MeV/c

## Supporting Upgrades

**1. Enhanced TPC readout electronics**
- Upgrade the three TPCs with resistive Micromegas or pixel readout replacing existing micro-pattern detectors
- Improved charge resolution and timing (~100 ns) for better momentum measurement of exiting particles
- Cost-effective: reuse existing gas volumes and field cages

**2. Timing layers**
- Install thin (1 cm) fast-timing plastic scintillator planes at upstream and downstream faces of new target
- Silicon photomultiplier readout with <500 ps timing resolution
- Enables time-of-flight particle ID for protons vs. pions

**3. Extended electromagnetic calorimetry**
- Add a 10-layer lead-scintillator ECAL module (10 cm total depth) immediately downstream of new target
- Improves π⁰/photon rejection and contains electromagnetic showers from the target
- Uses existing scintillator bar + WLS fiber + MPPC technology

**4. Data acquisition upgrade**
- Replace DAQ with scalable system capable of handling 30× channel increase
- FPGA-based trigger with GPU reconstruction farm for online event selection
- Target: <10% dead time at expected 10⁷ neutrino interactions per year

**5. Magnetic field mapping**
- Precision Hall probe survey and finite-element field modeling
- Critical for momentum reconstruction of large-angle tracks in the 0.2 T field
- Should achieve <1% momentum scale uncertainty

## Alternative Considered

A **high-pressure gaseous argon TPC** (10 bar, similar to DUNE-PRISM concept) would provide excellent resolution but:
- Pressure vessel constraints difficult in available volume
- Lower mass (~0.8 t) means fewer interactions
- More complex and higher risk

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a SuperFGD-style 3D segmented plastic scintillator cube (5mm cube cells, three-view fiber readout) as the new active neutrino target to achieve complete kinematic reconstruction of large-angle muons and low-momentum recoil protons.

# Hardware upgrade plan for the Kestrel Flats near-detector target region

## Why the obvious choice fails

The usual choice for an active target is fine-grained plastic scintillator, as in T2K's SuperFGD. Plastic is CH: about 8 hydrogen nucleons for every 96 carbon nucleons, so roughly **7–8% of the target nucleons are hydrogen nuclei**. That is far above the 2% limit for the hydrogen-subtraction model. Water and other hydrogenous targets fail for the same reason.

The active medium must therefore be essentially hydrogen-free. That points to argon, matching a hydrogen-free far detector.

## Proposed upgrades

### 1. Active target: modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC
Fill the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region with a liquid-argon TPC built as optically isolated modules with 3D pixel readout, in the style of ArgonCube/ND-LAr.

- **Meets the hydrogen limit.** Argon contains no hydrogen in the active volume, so it is far below 2%. Keep all plastic, such as light-detector substrates and field-cage supports, out of the fiducial volume.
- **Reconstructs tracks at every angle.** The LArTPC is fully 3D and nearly isotropic. Perpendicular and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones, unlike planar trackers.
- **Reaches the proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels roughly 3 cm in liquid argon. With about 4 mm pixels that is many hits, enough for dE/dx identification and calorimetry.
- **Handles a high event rate.** At 410 m the rate per spill is high. Pixel readout removes the ambiguities of projected-wire readout, and modules of about 1 m or less limit drift time and pile-up.
- **Purity and support systems.** The detector needs:
  - argon purification and recirculation, to keep electron lifetime well above the drift time;
  - a compact cryostat that fits inside the warm dipole and minimises dead material at the upstream end of the magnet;
  - suitable high voltage.

### 2. Fast light detection inside each module
Add fast light detectors (ArCLight / light-trap style) inside each module.

- They give nanosecond event times, so each interaction can be matched to its beam bunch and kept separate from pile-up.
- They provide the drift-time start (t₀) needed for 3D position.

### 3. Tracking chambers on the sides and upstream face of the target region
Add tracking chambers, such as thin gas TPCs or drift chambers, inside the 0.15 T field around the target region.

- The existing chambers sit downstream and only see forward muons.
- High-angle and backward muons leave the target region through its sides or upstream face. Without these chambers they get no curvature measurement of momentum and charge, so the 25% efficiency requirement at all angles would fail there.
- Hydrogenous materials are acceptable here because these chambers lie outside the fiducial volume.
- For tracks that escape all chambers, multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum estimates in the argon provide a backup.

### 4. Time-of-flight panels surrounding the target region and trackers
Add time-of-flight panels with about 100–150 ps resolution, for example scintillator bars with SiPM readout.

- **Direction.** They establish whether a track is forward- or backward-going, which separates genuine backward muons from entering tracks and from mis-reconstructed forward ones.
- **Rejection of outside background.** They reject particles entering from outside, such as sand muons and interactions in the magnet or cryostat.
- **Particle identification.** They add μ/p/π separation.

### 5. Electronics, DAQ and calibration
- Low-power, cold, self-triggering pixel ASICs, so cryostat heat load stays manageable.
- A DAQ able to handle the spill rate.
- A laser or cosmic-ray calibration system for drift-field and energy-scale calibration.

## Rationale summary

| Requirement | Hardware that satisfies it |
|---|---|
| Hydrogen at most 2% of target nucleons | Argon target |
| Muons at all angles | Isotropic 3D LArTPC, plus side/upstream tracking and time of flight |
| 60 MeV protons | Fine pixel granularity in dense liquid argon |
| High near-detector rate | Modularity, pixels and fast light detection |

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (hydrogen-free, isotropic 3D tracking) instead of a plastic-scintillator active target.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Active Target

## Analysis of Constraints

Before proposing hardware, let me extract the key requirements:

- **Volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (~5.4 m³)
- **Muon reconstruction**: ≥25% efficiency at *all* angles including 90° and backward-going
- **Proton reconstruction**: down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3.5 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in scintillator)
- **Hydrogen fraction**: ≤20% of target nucleons → constrains material choice
- **Beam**: ~0.7 GeV peak → quasi-elastic dominant, moderate multiplicity
- **Existing**: warm dipole at 0.15 T, downstream gas drift chambers

The hydrogen constraint is critical. Pure CH₂ or pure water would give ~67% and ~67% hydrogen by nucleon count, respectively. Carbon gives 0%. A polystyrene scintillator (CH ratio ~1:1 by atom, ~1:12 by nucleon) gives ~8% hydrogen nucleons — safely below 20%. Liquid argon gives 0% hydrogen. This strongly favors plastic scintillator or a carbon-heavy medium.

## Proposed Upgrades

### 1. 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target (Primary Recommendation)

Deploy an array of **1.5 cm × 1.5 cm × 1.5 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes** filling the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m volume, read out by **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** threaded through each cube in all three orthogonal directions.

- **Technology**: SuperFGD-style (as developed for T2K ND280 upgrade) — this is the most directly applicable proven technology
- **Cube count**: ~1.5 cm pitch → roughly 173 × 153 × 60 cubes ≈ **1.6 million cubes**
- **Readout**: Each fiber read by a **silicon photomultiplier (SiPM)**, 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm Hamamatsu S13360 series or equivalent, one per fiber end (or one with mirror on far end)
- **Fiber routing**: Three fiber planes (X, Y, Z) through each cube; ~60,000–100,000 readout channels total depending on fiber multiplexing scheme
- **Why this technology**:
  - 1.5 cm cubes give ~2 cm effective resolution, sufficient to reconstruct 60 MeV protons (range ~3–4 cubes)
  - Fully 4π symmetric response — no preferred direction, directly addresses the 90° and backward-going muon requirement
  - Plastic scintillator (C₈H₈ approximately) gives ~8% hydrogen by nucleon number, satisfying the ≤20% constraint
  - Fast timing (~1 ns) enables track disambiguation in 3D via time-ordered hits
  - Known to work: T2K SuperFGD is ~56 million cubes at 1 cm; this is a smaller, coarser version

**Electronics**: Use **CITIROC-1A** or **MUSIC** ASICs for SiPM readout, with 12-bit ADC for charge and TDC for timing. Trigger on coincidence of ≥3 cubes in any projection.

---

### 2. Thin-Gap Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) as Tracking Planes Between Cube Modules

Interleave **2–3 mm gap RPCs** at ~15 cm longitudinal intervals within or surrounding the cube array.

- **Technology**: Bakelite-electrode RPCs in streamer or avalanche mode, as used in OPERA and INO
- **Strip pitch**: 1 cm in X and Y
- **Purpose**: Provides independent 2D hit confirmation for tracks exiting cube modules; particularly helps with muon angle reconstruction for forward-going tracks that transition from the active target into the downstream drift chambers
- **Why not replace cubes**: RPCs alone cannot reconstruct short proton tracks or provide the 3D calorimetric information needed; they are supplementary

---

### 3. Upgrade of Upstream Face: Thin Scintillator Veto Panels

Install **5 mm thick plastic scintillator panels** with SiPM readout on the upstream, top, bottom, and side faces of the active target volume.

- **Technology**: EJ-200 or BC-408 scintillator, 1D WLS fiber readout at 2 cm pitch, SiPM readout
- **Purpose**: Tag charged particles entering the active volume from outside (rock muons, beam halo); critical for background rejection when analyzing backward-going tracks, which could otherwise be confused with forward-going particles from upstream interactions
- **Veto efficiency target**: >99% for minimum-ionizing particles

---

### 4. Downstream Interface Tracker: Silicon Microstrip Planes

Insert **2 planes of silicon microstrip detectors** at the downstream face of the active target, immediately before the existing gas drift chambers.

- **Technology**: Single-sided AC-coupled silicon strip detectors, 300 μm thick, 100 μm pitch, 10 cm × 10 cm tiles tiled to cover 2.6 m × 2.3 m
- **Why**: The existing gas drift chambers have an unknown (presumably ~cm-scale) spatial resolution and limited efficiency near 90°. The silicon planes provide a high-resolution, high-efficiency interface that precisely matches tracks exiting the cube target to tracks in the drift chambers, enabling momentum measurement of muons that exit the target volume. At 0.7 GeV beam energy, the typical quasi-elastic muon has ~400–600 MeV/c momentum, making momentum measurement in the existing dipole viable if tracking handoff is clean.
- **Channel count**: ~600,000 strips; use **APV25** or **VFAT3** readout ASICs

---

### 5. Magnetic Field Mapping and Compensation Coils

The existing warm dipole gives 0.15 T. For backward-going and 90° tracks that *do not* exit into the downstream drift chambers, momentum can only be measured by range (in the cube target) or by curvature within the active target itself.

- **Upgrade**: Install **3 pairs of small correction coils** around the active target volume to improve field uniformity within it to <2% variation
- **Technology**: Water-cooled copper coils, powered by existing magnet power supply infrastructure
- **Purpose**: Enables use of track curvature within the SuperFGD-style cube array itself for momentum measurement of non-exiting tracks, using the 0.15 T field. At 0.15 T over 90 cm, a 300 MeV/c muon has a sagitta of ~1.7 cm — measurable with 1.5 cm cube granularity if field is well-mapped.
- **Complement with**: A **Hall probe array** of ~50 probes distributed through the volume for precise field mapping, read out quasi-statically.

---

### 6. Slow Control and Calibration System

- **LED pulser system**: One blue LED per 100 fibers, fiber-coupled, for SiPM gain monitoring. Run at 1 Hz between beam spills.
- **Radioactive source calibration**: Deployable ⁶⁰Co or ²⁴¹Am source tubes along fiber channels for absolute energy scale calibration
- **Temperature stabilization**: SiPM gain drifts ~2%/°C; install **PT100 sensors** at 50-point grid with PID-controlled cooling to maintain ±0.5°C across the volume

## Proposed Hardware Upgrade: SuperFGD (Super Fine-Grained Detector)

**Core Design:**
A fully active, fine-grained 3D scintillator cube detector with ~2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ plastic scintillator cubes arranged in a ~192 cm × 180 cm × 60 cm volume. Each cube is read out on three orthogonal faces by wavelength-shifting fibers coupled to MPPCs, providing true 3D tracking.

**Key Features:**

1. **Isotropic acceptance**: Unlike the current FGDs with bars parallel to the beam (blind to one coordinate per layer), the 3D cube geometry provides nearly 4π acceptance for tracks at all angles, crucial for the 25-35% of particles emerging at >50°.

2. **Low threshold and excellent proton tracking**: 1 cm granularity with ~10 MeV energy deposition per cube enables:
   - Proton tracking down to ~200 MeV/c momentum
   - Range-based momentum reconstruction for contained protons up to ~1 GeV/c
   - dE/dx particle identification throughout the entire range

3. **Hydrocarbon target**: CH plastic scintillator mass (~2 tons active target) provides the required hydrocarbon interactions while serving simultaneously as active detector.

4. **Timing resolution**: O(1 ns) timing with MPPC readout enables track directionality determination and rejection of out-of-time backgrounds.

## Complementary Upgrades:

**High-Angle TPC (HA-TPC):**
Insert thin horizontal TPC modules (~10 cm drift) above and below the SuperFGD within the available magnet volume to provide momentum measurement for high-angle tracks escaping the SuperFGD sides. These would use the same gas mixture and Micromegas technology as the existing TPCs.

**Time-of-Flight (ToF) Panels:**
Install timing planes (~100 ps resolution) immediately upstream and downstream of SuperFGD to:
- Provide additional particle ID (proton/pion separation up to ~800 MeV/c)
- Improve vertex timing and background rejection
- Enable better matching with downstream TPCs/FGDs

**Enhanced SMRD:**
Upgrade the existing SMRD modules in the magnet yoke gaps with finer segmentation and timing to better reconstruct high-angle muons that exit through the sides.

**Improved FGD2 Readout:**
Add timing information to FGD2 bars (currently missing) to enable better event matching and vertex determination when tracks enter from SuperFGD.

## Expected Performance Improvements:

- **Acceptance**: >85% for muons and >70% for protons at all angles (vs ~60-70% current)
- **Momentum resolution**: σ(p)/p ~ 10% for contained tracks using range + curvature
- **Angular resolution**: <5° for all reconstructed tracks
- **Proton efficiency**: >80% for p > 300 MeV/c
- **Vertex resolution**: <1 cm in all three dimensions
- **Systematic uncertainty**: Target reduction to <4% through:
  - Better angular acceptance reducing model-dependence
  - Improved proton detection for neutrino energy reconstruction
  - Reduced nuclear effects uncertainty with lighter target
  - Better constraint on multi-nucleon mechanisms via complete kinematics

The 3D cube design has been validated by the WAGASCI-BabyMIND prototype and adopted by the ESSnuSB project, demonstrating technical feasibility.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace P0D with a 3D segmented scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD) providing isotropic 4π tracking acceptance for complete reconstruction of high-angle muons and protons.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near-Station Active Target

The present design has three gaps:

- **Angular coverage.** The only tracking is in the downstream drift chambers, so muons near 90° or going backward are lost.
- **Proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels only about 3 cm in plastic, which is too short for a coarse or planar detector to reconstruct.
- **Target composition.** Hydrogen must stay at or below 20% of target nucleons.

The upgrade package below addresses all three inside the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region and the 0.15 T field.

## 1. Fully active, 3D-granular scintillator target (cube-based "SuperFGD"-style)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with three orthogonal holes for wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Fibres are read out by SiPMs (MPPCs) at one end, giving three 2D projections of every hit.
- The block fills a horizontal slab of roughly 2.6 m (x) × 0.7–0.8 m (y) × 0.9 m (beam), at the vertical centre of the region. That is about 1.6–1.9 t of fully active target.

**Why**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Readout is isotropic, so tracks perpendicular to the beam or going backward are reconstructed as well as forward ones. Planar bar detectors fail here because a 90° track lies within one layer.
- **Short protons.** A 60 MeV proton gives about 3 hits in 1 cm cubes. This makes it reconstructable and identifiable from its Bragg-peak dE/dx, with near-4π coverage.
- **Hydrogen fraction.** In CH, hydrogen is 1/13 ≈ 8% of nucleons, comfortably under the 20% limit. Avoid hydrogen-rich additions such as large water or liquid-scintillator volumes; even H₂O is about 11%.
- **Mass with low passive material.** It provides target mass and vertexing with minimal dead material.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target, inside the magnet

**Technology**
- Two thin TPCs, each about 0.75 m tall, filling the remaining 2.3 m height above and below the target.
- Readout by resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas. Charge spreading allows larger pads and fewer channels while keeping spatial resolution.
- Lightweight composite field cages to minimise dead material between target and gas.
- Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀-type gas.

**Why**
- **Coverage of the inner region.** Muons emitted at large angles or backward exit vertically and never reach the downstream chambers. These TPCs measure their momentum and charge sign in the 0.15 T field.
- **Particle identification.** They also give dE/dx to separate muons, pions, protons and electrons.
- **Efficiency target.** This turns the ≥25% muon efficiency at all polar angles from impossible into achievable.

## 3. Time-of-flight scintillator envelope

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars read out by SiPMs at both ends, with timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.
- They surround the target-plus-TPC assembly on all six faces, including the upstream face.

**Why**
- **Track direction.** Timing separates backward-going tracks from forward tracks entering from outside, which is essential for the backward-muon requirement.
- **Background rejection.** It rejects interactions in the magnet and surrounding material.
- **Low-momentum PID.** It adds particle identification for low-momentum particles.

## 4. Supporting systems

- **Electronics and DAQ:** SiPM electronics with nanosecond timing (enables neutron time-of-flight in the cubes), and TPC front-end electronics.
- **Calibration:** LED and cosmic calibration systems.
- **Mechanics:** a mechanical integration that keeps dead material thin at the target/TPC/TOF boundaries.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fully active, finely segmented (~1 cm) 3D-readout plastic-scintillator cube target (WLS fibres + SiPMs in three views), paired with high-angle TPCs, so muons and ≥60 MeV protons are reconstructed at all angles while hydrogen stays at about 8% of nucleons.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for ND280 Phase-II

## 1. SuperFGD: 3D Scintillator Cube Target

**Technology:** Replace the P0D with a fully-active 3D segmented scintillator detector consisting of ~2 million 1×1×1 cm³ polystyrene cubes with three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readouts per cube.

**Physics Motivation:** 
- The current FGDs only have 2D readout (x-y layers perpendicular to beam), making them blind to tracks at large angles to the beam axis
- With 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons above 50° to beam, the current geometry loses critical angular coverage
- 3D readout with ~1 cm³ granularity enables full 4π tracking of high-angle particles
- True 3D tracking allows reconstruction of transverse kinematic imbalance vectors without projection ambiguities
- The compact 2.0×1.9×0.6 m volume fits the available space while providing sufficient target mass (~2 t)

## 2. Upgraded Time-of-Flight (ToF) System

**Technology:** Add thin plastic scintillator panels with SiPM readout on upstream and downstream faces of the new target, achieving ~150-200 ps timing resolution.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Critical for proton/pion separation at the 450 MeV/c median momentum scale
- The 35% of protons exiting at high angles will traverse much shorter paths, making ToF viable where range-based PID fails
- Separates signal (CC quasi-elastic with protons) from background (CC resonant production with charged pions)
- Reduces systematic uncertainties in modeling pion final-state interactions

## 3. High-Angle TPC Coverage

**Technology:** Install compact resistive-Micromegas TPCs on the top and bottom of the target region, providing tracking coverage at 60-90° to the beam axis.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Existing TPCs have drift perpendicular to beam but limited acceptance for high-angle tracks
- These would catch the most forward-boosted protons that exit vertically
- Provides momentum measurement via curvature in the 0.2 T field for particles that would otherwise only be tracked in scintillator
- Critical for the 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c that have sufficient range to exit the target

## 4. Thin Target Alternative: Hybrid Liquid Argon/Scintillator

**Technology:** Alternate 5 cm liquid argon modules (total ~6-8 modules) with thin (1-2 cm) plastic scintillator tracking planes, all with pixelated charge readout.

**Physics Motivation:**
- LAr provides both target material and continuous tracking medium with excellent dE/dx resolution
- Enables calorimetric energy measurement for low-energy protons that stop in target
- The ~40 cm range of 450 MeV/c protons in LAr means most will be contained
- Scintillator planes provide timing and position anchors for track matching to downstream detectors
- Demonstrates LAr technology directly relevant for DUNE while meeting T2K-II requirements

## 5. Neutron Tagging System

**Technology:** Surround the new target with layers of plastic scintillator doped with boron or gadolinium for neutron capture detection (10-200 μs delayed signals).

**Physics Motivation:**
- Neutron multiplicity discriminates between different reaction mechanisms (QE vs. multi-nucleon knockout)
- Essential for constraining nuclear effects that dominate systematic uncertainties
- At 0.6 GeV, multi-nucleon effects contribute ~30% of the cross-section
- Neutron detection breaks degeneracies in energy reconstruction when the proton is below threshold

## 6. Improved MPPC/SiPM Electronics

**Technology:** Replace existing MPPCs with latest-generation SiPMs having higher photon detection efficiency (>50%) and lower noise, plus multi-hit TDC readout for each channel.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Better timing resolution (<1 ns) improves particle identification and vertex resolution
- Crucial for resolving multiple tracks in the dense 3D detector environment
- Multi-hit capability handles crosstalk between nearby scintillator cubes
- Reduces threshold for detecting minimum-ionizing particles at high angles (longer path, more light)
- Directly improves the 6%→4% systematic uncertainty target through better reconstruction

## 7. Hydrogen-Rich Target Option

**Technology:** Install removable modules filled with polyethylene (CH₂) or liquid scintillator to provide enhanced hydrogen content compared to standard polystyrene (CH).

**Physics Motivation:**
- Hydrogen measurements have minimal nuclear effects, providing crucial "theory-clean" calibration
- By comparing CH₂ to CH measurements, constrain carbon nuclear effects through subtraction
- Complements the existing FGD2 water target for comprehensive nuclear systematics
- Essential for disentangling neutrino-nucleus effects that dominate uncertainties at T2K energies

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: SuperFGD 3D Scintillator Cube Target**

This provides the most critical capability missing from the current detector: full 4π tracking acceptance for the 25-35% of events with high-angle final-state particles. Without this, transverse kinematic imbalance studies cannot be performed, and the 6%→4% systematic uncertainty goal cannot be achieved. The technology is proven (demonstrated in prototypes), fits the available space, and directly addresses the stated physics requirements for kinematically complete event reconstruction.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Near Detector Funding Proposal

## 1. Active Neutrino Target (Primary Upgrade)

**Technology: Scintillating plastic tracker with fine-grained 3D readout — specifically a SuperFGD-style (Super Fine-Grained Detector) cubic scintillator array**

Cubes of ~1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator, each read out by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, filling the available ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m volume.

**Why:** The existing polystyrene bar targets have 9.6 × 9.6 mm bars read in only one transverse direction per layer, giving ambiguities for large-angle tracks. The cubic geometry provides true 3D hit reconstruction with no orientation bias. With ~25% of muons and ~35% of leading protons exiting beyond 50°, isotropic acceptance is critical. The ~1 cm granularity gives a low tracking threshold: protons at 450 MeV/c (median momentum) have a range of roughly 9 cm in plastic, well above threshold, and the 6% tail above 900 MeV/c is also contained or matched to downstream TPCs. Each cube being read in three views eliminates the x/y ambiguity that plagues the existing bar design when multiple tracks are present, which is essential for the transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analysis requiring both the muon and leading proton reconstructed simultaneously.

---

## 2. SiPM Readout Upgrade for the New Target

**Technology: Surface-mount SiPMs with ~1 mm² active area on each fibre end, with updated front-end ASICs (e.g., CITIROC or custom MUSIC-style chips) providing time-over-threshold and coarse timing**

**Why:** The existing detector already uses SiPMs, but the cubic array has ~3× more readout channels per unit volume. Fine-grained timing (~1 ns resolution) helps associate hits from the leading proton (which is slow, ~450 MeV/c → β ~ 0.42) versus the faster muon, reducing combinatorial ambiguity in multi-track events. Modern low-noise SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK) with improved photon detection efficiency (~50% PDE) improve light yield per small cube, keeping detection efficiency high for short proton tracks near threshold.

---

## 3. Downstream TPC Readout Upgrade

**Technology: Upgraded micro-pattern gas detector (MPGD) readout — replace or supplement existing readout with resistive Micromegas or GEM foils with enlarged pad planes and updated electronics (e.g., AFTER/AGET-based front-end)**

**Why:** The new upstream target will push more large-angle, higher-multiplicity events into the TPCs. The ~6% of protons above 900 MeV/c will punch through the new active target entirely and must be momentum-analysed in the TPCs by curvature in the 0.2 T magnet field. Improving pad granularity and dynamic range in the TPCs reduces space-charge distortion effects (relevant for higher-rate running in an upgraded beam) and lowers the momentum resolution uncertainty, directly feeding into the target ~4% systematic budget. Additionally, improved dE/dx resolution helps with proton/pion separation, which is a background concern for TKI analyses.

---

## 4. Instrumented Return-Yoke Scintillator Upgrade

**Technology: Replace or refurbish the yoke scintillator planes with longer, segmented extruded scintillator bars read out by SiPMs at both ends**

**Why:** With 25% of muons leaving at >50° to the beam, a significant fraction range out in the yoke. Two-ended SiPM readout provides hit-position information along the bar via time difference, improving the muon range (and thus momentum) measurement for these side-going tracks. This directly reduces the muon momentum systematic for the large-angle sample that dominates TKI resolution. The existing single-ended readout introduces an asymmetric position uncertainty that biases the reconstructed transverse momentum.

---

## 5. Photon Veto / Electromagnetic Calorimeter Addition Around the New Target

**Technology: Thin lead-scintillator sandwich electromagnetic calorimeter panels (Pb absorber ~2 mm, scintillator strips ~5 mm, SiPM readout) surrounding the new active target on 4 sides**

**Why:** Removing the upstream photon-tagging section (which currently uses brass and lead converters interleaved with scintillator) eliminates the photon detection capability at the upstream end. For CC events with π⁰ production, undetected photons fake missing transverse momentum and bias TKI. Thin ECAL panels (~3–4 X₀) around the new target walls recover photon detection efficiency (photon conversion probability ~95%) without excessive material budget that would re-scatter the leading proton. This is essential for maintaining the π⁰ background rejection that contributes to keeping systematic uncertainties at or below 4%.

---

## 6. Trigger and DAQ Upgrade

**Technology: Triggerless streaming readout with a central FPGA-based event builder (e.g., using the WR (White Rabbit) timing protocol for sub-ns synchronisation across subsystems)**

**Why:** The cubic scintillator array and upgraded TPCs multiply channel counts substantially. A triggerless architecture captures all beam-coincident activity without dead time and enables offline software triggering, which is necessary for efficiently selecting the low-multiplicity CC events (1 muon + 1 proton) against the beam background. It also allows crossing-track rejection and out-of-time cosmic veto in software, reducing the systematic uncertainty from cosmic contamination in side-going muon samples.
