# Design Recommendation: Kestrel Flats Near-Station Active Target Upgrade

## What the requirements imply

1. **Muons at every angle (≥25% efficiency), including 90° and backward.** The existing downstream drift chambers only accept forward tracks. A muon at 90° leaves through the sides of the target region, never reaches the downstream chambers, and has a curvature plane that is poorly measured by forward-oriented chambers. Backward muons also have to be told apart from forward-going particles entering from upstream.
2. **Protons down to about 60 MeV kinetic energy at all angles.** The range of a 60 MeV proton is roughly 3 g/cm². In plastic that is about 3 cm; in gas it is metres. The active target must therefore be dense, finely segmented in three dimensions and isotropic, so that a 3 cm stub is visible in any direction.
3. **Hydrogen at most 20% of target nucleons.**
   - Polystyrene (C₈H₈) has 8 hydrogen nucleons out of 104, about 7.7%.
   - Water would be about 11%.
   - Either passes, with a wide margin for polystyrene, but the active medium must not be diluted with extra hydrogen-rich materials.
4. **Beam and site conditions.** The beam peaks near 0.7 GeV and the station is only 410 m from the target, so the event rate per spill is high. The detector needs nanosecond-level timing and three-dimensional segmentation to separate pile-up and to tell track direction from time of flight.

## Recommended hardware changes

### 1. Fully active, finely segmented 3D scintillator target (SuperFGD-type)

- **Design.** About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes. Each cube is read on three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres, with silicon photomultipliers (MPPC/SiPM) at the fibre ends.
- **Size.** The 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m region holds about 5.4 × 10⁶ cubes and about 5 t of target, with roughly 60k readout channels.
- **Justification:**
  - It gives near-isotropic 4π acceptance, with no blind angle for 90° or backward tracks. This is the key failure of planar, layer-stacked trackers.
  - A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes, enough to reconstruct a short track and identify it as a proton by dE/dx along its range.
  - Hydrogen is about 7.7% of nucleons, so it meets the 20% limit with margin. Cubes, fibres and mechanics are all low-Z and dense, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid.
  - SiPM timing of about 1 ns per channel separates pile-up within a spill. It also gives track direction (forward vs. backward) and some neutron detection by time of flight.
  - It is compact and works in the 0.15 T field, since SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields.
- **If the far detector is argon:** a LAr TPC would match the nucleus but would need a cryostat inside a warm magnet and has worse rate handling. Plastic is the practical choice, with the carbon-to-far-detector-nucleus difference handled in the cross-section model.

### 2. High-angle gaseous TPCs above and below (and ideally beside) the active target

- **Design.** Thin field-cage TPCs read out with resistive-anode Micromegas, placed inside the magnet volume and sandwiching the cube target in the transverse directions.
- **Justification:**
  - High-angle and 90° muons that exit the target sideways get measured momentum and charge sign from curvature in the 0.15 T field. Today they would be lost.
  - Particle identification by dE/dx separates muons from pions.
  - Range in the cubes alone saturates for higher-momentum muons. A muon at 600 MeV/c has about 2.5 m range in plastic, more than the 1.1–1.3 m half-width, so many exit and need the TPC measurement.
  - Resistive Micromegas spreads charge over neighbouring pads, giving good resolution with larger pads, and is robust against sparking.

### 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the whole assembly

- **Design.** Plastic scintillator bars read out with SiPMs at both ends, giving about 150 ps resolution. Panels go on all faces of the target-plus-TPC assembly, including the upstream face.
- **Justification:**
  - Timing between the target vertex and the panels identifies the direction of the track. Backward-going muons are distinguished from forward-going particles entering from the upstream region, which is the main source of backward-muon mis-reconstruction.
  - The panels veto external backgrounds such as interactions in the magnet and surrounding material.
  - They add PID for low-momentum tracks.

### 4. Supporting changes

- **Electronics and DAQ.** Readout must handle the near-site spill rate with time-stamped hits, and be able to digitise more than one interaction per spill.
- **Calibration.**
  - Cube light-yield uniformity calibrated with cosmics and with an LED or laser system.
  - The precise target composition (C, H and fibre/glue mass fractions) assayed, so the hydrogen fraction is known for the subtraction model.
- **Keep the existing downstream drift chambers.** They continue to measure forward tracks, which give the best momentum lever arm.

## Summary

The isotropic 1 cm 3D scintillator target is the essential element. It is what makes 60 MeV protons and all-angle muons reconstructable while keeping hydrogen near 8%. The high-angle TPCs and TOF panels then complete the momentum, charge and direction measurement for the high-angle and backward muons that the existing downstream chambers cannot see.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fully active, 1 cm³-cube 3D-readout plastic scintillator detector (SuperFGD-type, WLS fibres plus SiPMs), giving 4π tracking of short proton and all-angle muon tracks at about 8% hydrogen.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Off-Axis Near Detector

## Why the current detector falls short

The present design is optimised for forward-going tracks:

- **Target geometry.** The plastic targets use bars perpendicular to the beam in alternating x/y layers. Tracks at high angle, and especially near 90°, run along a single bar or plane. This gives poor or ambiguous 2D reconstruction.
- **TPC placement.** The gas TPCs sit only upstream and downstream of the targets, so they cannot measure high-angle tracks.
- **Proton threshold.** The 9.6 mm bars, read in only two views, set a proton tracking threshold near the median proton momentum (about 450 MeV/c). Many short protons are lost.
- **Missing acceptance.** About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons exit above 50°. This missing acceptance is a direct contributor to the about 6% systematic.

## Upgrade list

### 1. Highly granular three-view scintillator target (fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box)

- **Technology:** about 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, for example 192 × 182 × 56.
  - The cubes are chemically etched for a reflective surface.
  - Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres, giving x, y and z views.
  - Each fibre end is read by a silicon photomultiplier, for about 56,000 channels.
  - The target mass is about 2 t of hydrocarbon (CH), roughly double one existing target.
- **Why:**
  - **Angular acceptance:** three projections give near-4π acceptance with full 3D reconstruction at any angle.
  - **Proton threshold:** 1 cm granularity lowers the threshold to roughly 300 MeV/c, below the 450 MeV/c median, so most leading protons are reconstructed.
  - **Calorimetric vertex:** good dE/dx and calorimetric measurement of vertex activity.
  - **Neutrons:** sensitivity to neutrons via isolated delayed hits, which gives access to the full transverse kinematic imbalance in antineutrino mode.
  - **Material:** hydrocarbon is acceptable, and the downstream water-layer target keeps the carbon/water comparison.

### 2. Two high-angle TPCs, above and below the new target, inside the magnet

- **Technology:** thin-walled, low-mass field cages (composite/aramid laminate).
  - Gas: argon-based "T2K gas" (Ar/CF₄/iC₄H₁₀).
  - Readout: resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, ERAM). Charge spreading gives about 0.6–0.8 mm resolution with about 1 cm pads and fewer channels, plus spark protection.
- **Why:**
  - High-angle muons, and protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%) that escape the target, need their momentum measured by curvature in the 0.2 T field.
  - They also need charge sign and particle identification by dE/dx.
  - The existing TPCs cannot see these tracks.

### 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new target and high-angle TPCs

- **Technology:** six planes of long cast plastic-scintillator bars (about 1 cm thick).
  - Each bar is read at both ends by arrays of large-area silicon photomultipliers.
  - The target timing resolution is about 150 ps or better.
- **Why:**
  - Determines track direction, rejecting backward-going and out-of-fiducial-volume background (for example, from the magnet).
  - Separates protons, muons and electrons by time of flight where dE/dx is ambiguous.
  - Provides a precise event time reference.

### 4. Front-end electronics and data acquisition for the new subsystems

- **Technology:**
  - **Target:** SiPM electronics based on the CITIROC ASIC, with sub-ns timing per channel. This allows neutron time-of-flight in the target and pile-up separation within beam bunches.
  - **TPCs:** AFTER/AGET-based front-ends.
  - **Integration:** a common trigger and clock distribution shared with the existing detector.
- **Why:** timing is what enables neutron kinematics and direction tagging, and the new channels must integrate with the existing data acquisition.

### 5. Mechanical and services work

- **Scope:**
  - Remove the photon-tagging section.
  - Install a support basket and services for the new target, high-angle TPCs and time-of-flight panels.
  - Provide routing for the gas system and cooling.
  - Plan for the magnetic-field map to be re-surveyed with the new configuration.
- **Why:** these are needed to make the upgrade function. The downstream TPCs, the water-layer target and the electromagnetic calorimeters are retained.

## Expected impact

The upgrade gives full-angle muon and proton reconstruction together with neutron detection. This allows transverse kinematic imbalance analyses and better nuclear-model constraints, which are expected to bring the residual systematic toward the 4% goal.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a 3D-readout, 1 cm³-cube scintillator target (about 2 million cubes, three orthogonal WLS fibres per cube read by SiPMs), complemented by high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs.

# ND280 Upstream Upgrade: Proposed Hardware

The goal is to turn the upstream volume into a full-acceptance, low-threshold active target with high-angle tracking. That requires three coordinated hardware additions plus supporting infrastructure.

## Why the current detector falls short

- **Angular acceptance.** The present target (the first plastic tracking target) uses x/y bars perpendicular to the beam, and the gas TPCs sit only up- and downstream of it. Tracks above about 50°, and especially near 90°, run along a bar layer or never reach a TPC. That loses about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons, which is exactly the phase space where kinematically complete charged-current events are needed.
- **Proton threshold.** A 450 MeV/c proton has about 100 MeV kinetic energy and ranges only about 7–8 cm in plastic. A 2-view bar detector cannot cleanly reconstruct short, high-angle protons or separate them at the vertex.
- **Lost information.** Neutrons are not measured at all, and backward-going and entering backgrounds are poorly rejected.

## 1. Highly granular 3D scintillator target ("SuperFGD")

- **Technology.** About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes with a reflective etched surface. Each cube has three orthogonal 1.5 mm holes carrying 1 mm Kuraray Y-11 wavelength-shifting fibres. Readout is three projections, about 56,000 channels.
- **Size.** Roughly 192 × 182 × 56 cubes (about 1.92 × 1.82 × 0.56 m). This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box and gives about 2 t of hydrocarbon target, roughly twice one existing target.
- **Readout.** Single-ended fibres, with a mirror at the far end, read by 1.3 mm Hamamatsu MPPCs on CITIROC-based front-end boards. Expect about 50 photoelectrons per MIP per fibre and about 1 ns time resolution per channel.
- **What it provides:**
  - Near-4π isotropic acceptance.
  - A proton threshold of about 300 MeV/c, since 2–3 cubes are enough to identify a track.
  - dE/dx-based proton/pion identification and good vertex-activity resolution.
  - Neutron detection, using secondary-scatter hits plus time of flight, for neutron-inclusive transverse kinematic imbalance.
- **Mechanics.** A light carbon-fibre or plastic box with integrated light-tight fibre routing, plus a calibration LED system.

## 2. Two High-Angle TPCs (HA-TPCs)

- **Placement.** One above and one below the new target, each about 2.0 × 0.8 × 1.8 m (x × y × z). They sit inside the magnet's 3.5–3.6 m inner height, in the space freed by removing the photon-tagging section.
- **Purpose.** Momentum and charge sign from magnetic curvature, plus dE/dx, for muons and protons at 40–90°. This also covers the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, which exit the target.
- **Field cage.** Thin composite (honeycomb/aramid laminate) walls to minimise dead material. A central cathode gives about 1 m drift, with the same argon-CF₄-isobutane gas as the existing TPCs.
- **Readout.** Resistive bulk Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM") with about 1 × 1 cm pads. Charge spreading gives sub-millimetre spatial resolution with fewer channels and spark protection. Electronics are AFTER/AGET-type ASICs.
- **Targets.** About 10% momentum resolution at 1 GeV/c, dE/dx resolution under 10%, and spatial resolution under 0.8 mm.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope

- **Layout.** Six planes enclosing the target and HA-TPC block.
- **Construction.** Each plane uses about 2.2 m × 12 cm × 1 cm cast plastic scintillator bars. Each bar end is read by an array of large-area SiPMs, giving 150 ps or better timing.
- **Uses:**
  - Determines track direction, separating forward from backward and in-going from out-going tracks.
  - Rejects sand muons and other external backgrounds.
  - Adds e/μ/p identification.
  - Provides a precise time reference for neutron time of flight in the SuperFGD.

## 4. Integration and infrastructure

- New basket and support structure.
- Updated ECal and side muon range detector cabling.
- Common clock and trigger distribution so the new subsystems integrate into the existing DAQ.
- Magnetic-field remapping of the upstream region.
- Cosmic and beam test-beam calibration of the cube response, including crosstalk and Birks quenching.

## Expected payoff

- Muons, protons and neutrons reconstructed over the full solid angle.
- Proton threshold lowered from about 450 MeV/c to about 300 MeV/c.
- Roughly double the fiducial mass in the upstream region.
- Precise transverse kinematic imbalance and nuclear-effect constraints, driving the residual flux-times-cross-section systematic toward the 4% goal.
- The downstream water-layer target is kept, so carbon-to-water comparison remains possible.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the photon-tagging section with a ~2 t, 1 cm³-cube, three-view WLS/SiPM 3D scintillator target (SuperFGD) for isotropic, low-threshold proton and muon reconstruction, flanked by high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context and Constraints Summary

Before proposing upgrades, the key physics requirements are:

- Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at **all angles** (0°–180°), including transverse and backward tracks
- Proton reconstruction down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy (range ~3 cm in water, ~1.5 cm in iron)
- Hydrogen fraction ≤20% of target nucleons (constrains target material choice)
- Active target must fit within 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m
- Existing downstream drift chambers + 0.15 T dipole handle forward muon momentum

---

## Upgrade 1: 3D Scintillator Cube Active Target (Plastic Scintillator Voxels)

**Technology:** An array of ~1 cm³ extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes read out by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres threaded through them in three orthogonal directions, with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) at the fibre ends — essentially a SuperFGD-style detector.

**Physics motivation:**

The 0.9 m depth along the beam axis divided into ~1 cm slices gives ~90 longitudinal planes, while the 2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse area gives of order 260 × 230 cubes per layer, totalling roughly 5–6 million cubes. The three-view fibre readout provides full 3D track reconstruction without the ambiguities of 2D projective detectors.

The 1 cm³ granularity is the critical feature for the two hardest physics requirements:

- *Backward and transverse muons:* A track going perpendicular or backward still traverses many cubes and is reconstructed by the 3D hit pattern. The detector is self-tracking in all 4π, so the ≥25% efficiency at all angles is achievable without relying on the downstream drift chambers for the initial segment. Simulations of comparable designs (T2K's SuperFGD) show reconstruction efficiency exceeding 80% even for backward-going tracks.

- *Low-energy protons:* A 60 MeV kinetic energy proton has a range of roughly 2.5 cm in polystyrene (density ~1.05 g/cm³). That is ~2–3 cube lengths, giving 2–3 hit cubes — enough for a 3D stub reconstruction and dE/dx-based particle identification. Iron or liquid-argon targets would stop these protons before they produce a reconstructable track.

- *Hydrogen fraction:* Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ has a hydrogen mass fraction of ~7.7% by mass, but the hydrogen nucleon fraction by count is (8H)/(8C×12 + 8H) ≈ 8/104 ≈ 7.7% of nucleons. This is well under the 20% ceiling, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid.

The scintillator cube approach is proven technology: SuperFGD for T2K ND280 upgrade has been built and commissioned, providing a direct blueprint.

---

## Upgrade 2: Thin-Film Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) or Scintillator Planes as Muon Catchers in the Magnet Gaps

**Technology:** Interleaved iron absorber plates (~2–4 cm thick) with thin-gap RPC layers or extruded scintillator strips inserted into the magnet volume downstream and to the sides of the active target, forming a partial muon ranger integrated into the magnet bore.

**Physics motivation:**

The existing drift chambers are purely downstream. A muon emitted at 90° to the beam exits the active target laterally (through the 2.6 m or 2.3 m face) and may never reach the downstream spectrometer. At angles >90° (backward) it moves upstream and is entirely lost to the spectrometer.

By lining the lateral faces of the magnet inner volume with iron/RPC sandwiches (thickness ≈ 30–40 cm, fitting within the 2.6 m dimension with room for the target), one creates a muon range stack that:

- Measures the residual range of stopping muons → momentum by range (no magnetic curvature needed), accurate to ~3% for muons stopping in a few tens of cm of iron
- Provides a hit pattern for angle measurement independent of the downstream system
- Covers the azimuthal gaps left by the active-target-only approach

RPC technology is chosen because it is thin, inexpensive per area, and has good hit efficiency (>95%) with ~1 cm spatial resolution from strip readout. The 0.15 T field also allows some curvature measurement for higher-momentum muons that punch through.

---

## Upgrade 3: Time-of-Flight (ToF) System with Fast Plastic Scintillator Planes

**Technology:** Two or more planes of fast plastic scintillator bars (e.g., Eljen EJ-200 or similar), each read out at both ends by SiPMs with waveform digitisers providing ~100 ps timing resolution, placed: (a) immediately upstream of the active target and (b) immediately downstream.

**Physics motivation:**

- *Backward track identification:* A muon (or proton) going backward produces a hit in the upstream ToF plane *after* the downstream plane (relative to beam timing). Without ToF, a backward track reconstructed in the 3D target looks like a forward short track. A 100 ps coincidence timing difference over ~1 m baseline (light-travel Δt ≈ 3 ns for c particles) cleanly resolves direction ambiguity.

- *Proton vs. pion separation:* At momenta of 400–800 MeV/c, a 1 m baseline with 100 ps resolution gives a ToF difference between protons and pions of Δt = L(1/β_p − 1/β_π)/c. At 500 MeV/c over 1 m: β_p ≈ 0.47, β_π ≈ 0.96, Δt ≈ 2.4 ns — easily resolved. This is essential because proton vs. pion misidentification is a major systematic in quasi-elastic signal selection.

- *Beam timing reference:* The upstream plane serves as a t₀ reference tied to the beam spill structure, suppressing out-of-time cosmics and providing a vertex time for pile-up rejection.

Fast scintillator with SiPM readout is well-established technology (see ANNIE, NINJA detectors) and can be constructed in planes that fit within the existing magnet aperture without displacing significant target mass.

---

## Upgrade 4: Gadolinium-Doped Liquid Scintillator Veto/Neutron Capture Layer

**Technology:** A 10–15 cm thick layer of gadolinium-loaded liquid scintillator (0.1% Gd by mass, e.g., Gd-TEGDME or Gd-doped mineral oil) in a thin-walled acrylic vessel surrounding the outer face of the scintillator-cube active target, read out by an array of large-area SiPMs or low-profile PMTs.

**Physics motivation:**

Neutrino interactions produce neutrons copiously (especially in resonance and DIS events, and in nuclear final-state interactions). These neutrons exit the active target and are otherwise invisible, causing:

- Undetected energy in neutron-emission channels, biasing neutrino energy reconstruction
- Ambiguity in classifying quasi-elastic vs. multinucleon events

Gadolinium has the highest thermal-neutron capture cross section of any stable nucleus (≈49,000 barns on ¹⁵⁷Gd), and the capture releases an 8 MeV gamma cascade detectable with high efficiency. By surrounding the active target with Gd-LS:

- Neutron capture signals appearing 2–50 μs after the prompt interaction vertex tag the neutron multiplicity event-by-event
- The spatial offset of captures relative to the vertex is used to reconstruct the neutron emission direction (at least statistically), allowing final-state neutron counting
- This directly constrains multinucleon (np-nh) initial states, which are the leading theoretical uncertainty in quasi-elastic cross-section measurements at 0.7 GeV

The 20% hydrogen constraint is not violated because this layer is *outside* the fiducial active target volume; interactions in the Gd-LS layer are vetoed, not analysed.

---

## Upgrade 5: Upgraded Downstream Drift Chamber Electronics with Higher-Rate Capability and Extended Tracking Layers

**Technology:** Replace current drift chamber front-end ASICs with modern low-noise, high-rate digitisers (e.g., DREAM/after-based chips as used in CLAS12), and add two additional upstream drift-chamber superlayers immediately downstream of the active target but inside the magnet field region.

**Physics motivation:**

The momentum resolution of a track in a dipole field scales as σ_p/p² ∝ σ_x / (BL²). With the existing 0.15 T field over 6.5 m and typical wire-chamber resolution of ~200 μm, forward-going muon momentum resolution is adequate (~5% at 1 GeV/c). However:

- Higher neutrino interaction rates in the upgraded active target (denser, higher-Z-mean medium) produce more simultaneous tracks per spill, requiring faster electronics to avoid dead-time hits and hit-merging inefficiency
- Moving two superlayers to just downstream of the target (at z ≈ 0.9 m from target start) increases the lever arm for tracks that exit the target at large forward angles but would otherwise miss the first tracking station
- Improved pattern recognition in the drift chambers handles the increased track multiplicity from fully-active-target events, which typically have more reconstructed prongs than the previous passive-target configuration

This upgrade is largely an electronics and detector-services change requiring no mechanical modification to the magnet.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 3D scintillator cubes (SuperFGD-style) | All-angle muon + low-energy proton tracking |
| 2 | Iron/RPC muon ranger in magnet gaps | Lateral and backward muon ranging |
| 3 | Fast plastic scintillator ToF planes | Direction disambiguation, p/π PID |
| 4 | Gd-LS neutron capture layer | Neutron multiplicity, np-nh constraint |
| 5 | Upgraded drift-chamber electronics + layers | Rate capability, forward tracking coverage |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the passive target with a 3D scintillator cube (SuperFGD-style) active target, as it simultaneously solves the two hardest requirements — all-angle muon reconstruction including backward tracks, and reconstruction of short proton stubs down to 60 MeV kinetic energy — in a proven technology that fits the existing magnet volume and satisfies the hydrogen-fraction constraint.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Physics Requirements Driving the Design

Before proposing hardware, it is worth being explicit about the constraints the physics imposes:

- **Angular acceptance**: 25% of muons and 35% of protons emerge beyond 50°, so the active target must itself provide tracking coverage approaching 4π rather than relying purely on downstream detectors.
- **Proton momentum threshold**: The median proton momentum is ~450 MeV/c. A proton at 450 MeV/c has a range of ~9 cm in polystyrene (ρ ≈ 1.06 g/cm³). At 900 MeV/c the range is ~55 cm. The detector must therefore be both a target and a tracker/range-stack for stopping protons, while soft protons (below ~300 MeV/c, range ≲ 3 cm) set the granularity floor.
- **Kinematic completeness**: Both the muon and the leading proton must be reconstructed in momentum and angle simultaneously, so the target cannot be a passive absorber with only downstream readout.
- **Box envelope**: 2.0 m (x) × 1.9 m (y) × 0.6 m (z, along beam). The z dimension is tight; a purely longitudinal range-stack approach is very constrained.
- **Systematic target**: ~4% total; the new detector must not introduce large new cross-section uncertainties, favouring well-understood nuclei (C, H via CH).

---

## Proposed Upgrade Package

### 1. Super-Fine-Grained Detector (SuperFGD) — Primary Recommendation

**What it is**: A fully-active plastic scintillator target composed of small cubic scintillator elements, each approximately **10 mm × 10 mm × 10 mm**, made of extruded polystyrene doped with PPO/POPOP fluors. Three orthogonal wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres thread each cube in x, y, and z, each fibre read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM, 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm MPPC). The cube lattice is self-supporting; fibres run through drilled channels and are read out at the faces of the block.

**Dimensions fitting the envelope**: A block of **192 × 184 × 56 cubes** (1920 mm × 1840 mm × 560 mm) fits within 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m with margin for mechanical support and fibre routing at the faces. This gives approximately **2.0 million cubes** and a fiducial mass of roughly **2 tonnes** of polystyrene (CH).

**Why this solves the angular problem**: Because readout is in all three projections simultaneously (x-fibre, y-fibre, z-fibre each giving a 1D hit), 3D track reconstruction is possible for tracks at any angle including those perpendicular to the beam. A proton travelling transversely in x produces hits in y-fibres and z-fibres; a conventional layer-based FGD cannot reconstruct this. The 10 mm pitch gives a range measurement granularity sufficient to reconstruct proton momentum by range down to ~200 MeV/c (range ≈ 2 cm ≈ 2 cubes).

**Proton reconstruction performance**: 
- At 450 MeV/c (median), range ≈ 9 cm → ~9 cubes longitudinally, fully contained for most directions.
- At 900 MeV/c, range ≈ 55 cm → 55 cubes; still contained within the 56-cube depth for beam-direction protons, and contained for large-angle protons within the 192/184-cube transverse dimensions.
- Protons above 900 MeV/c (6% of sample) exit and must be matched to the downstream TPCs; this is acceptable since the high-momentum protons are more accurately measured by magnetic spectrometry anyway.

**Muon reconstruction**: Muons above ~200 MeV/c will exit the SuperFGD and enter the downstream TPC1 (for forward-going muons) or the ECal/SMRD (for large-angle muons). The SuperFGD provides the initial track segment, angle, and dE/dx for PID; momentum is then determined by the downstream magnetic spectrometer (TPCs + magnet) for forward muons, or by range in the ECal for large-angle muons. This is exactly the same strategy as the existing FGDs but with far superior angular coverage.

**SiPM readout specifics**: Each fibre end is read by one MPPC. With three fibres per cube and two ends per fibre, the maximum channel count is ~12 million, but in practice one end per fibre suffices for position reconstruction (the other end can be mirrored or read out sparsely). A practical implementation reads **one end per fibre × 3 fibres × 2M cubes = ~6M channels** — this is feasible with modern SiPM ASICs (e.g., CITIROC or WEEROC TARGET-C derivatives) multiplexed on custom front-end boards mounted on the cube-block faces. Time-over-threshold readout gives adequate charge (hence dE/dx) resolution.

**Light yield and threshold**: Bench measurements of prototype cubes (as demonstrated by the T2K and NINJA groups) show ~15 photoelectrons per MIP per fibre end for Y-11 WLS fibre + 1.3 mm MPPC, giving a detection efficiency >99% per cube per MIP crossing, and sufficient light to detect the Bragg-peak enhancement at the end of a proton track (crucial for proton/pion separation by dE/dx profile).

---

### 2. Time-of-Flight (ToF) Scintillator Planes

**What they are**: Six planes of **5 mm-thick plastic scintillator paddles** (each paddle ~200 mm wide, covering the full 2.0 m × 1.9 m face), placed:
- Two planes on the upstream face of the SuperFGD (separated by ~50 mm)
- Two planes on the downstream face
- One plane on each of the top and bottom faces (covering the large-angle exit paths)

Each paddle is read out by SiPMs at both ends via embedded WLS fibre or direct coupling, giving a **timing resolution of ~200 ps (σ)** per plane, achievable with standard EJ-204/BC-404 fast scintillator.

**Why this is necessary**: 

*Proton/pion separation*: At 450 MeV/c, a proton has β ≈ 0.43 and a pion has β ≈ 0.95. Over a 50 mm separation between two ToF planes, the time difference is ~200 ps — just resolvable at 200 ps resolution (≈1σ separation). Over a 560 mm base (front to back of SuperFGD), the separation grows to ~2.3 ns, giving clean separation up to ~700 MeV/c. This is essential because the SuperFGD alone cannot distinguish a short proton track from a short pion track if the pion undergoes charge exchange.

*Beam-related background rejection*: ToF between upstream and downstream planes distinguishes forward-going particles (neutrino-induced) from backwards-going particles (from interactions in the ECal or magnet yoke).

*Neutron tagging*: For future transverse-momentum-imbalance studies involving neutrons in FGD2, coincident ToF signals in the upstream SuperFGD top/bottom planes help tag neutron-scattering backgrounds.

**Channel count**: ~200 paddles × 2 SiPM ends = ~400 channels. Negligible compared to SuperFGD.

---

### 3. Thin Upstream Tracking Station

**What it is**: Two planes of **3 mm × 3 mm cross-section triangular scintillator bars** (similar to P0D bar design but smaller), one plane with bars in x and one in y, each plane 2.0 m × 1.9 m, placed immediately upstream of the SuperFGD (within the available 0.6 m z-budget, before the first ToF plane). These are essentially a 2D tracking layer with ~3 mm pitch.

**Purpose**: 

- Provide a **veto for charged particles entering from upstream** (beam-related or from P0D-region remnant material), distinguishing genuine neutrino interactions in the SuperFGD from punch-through or re-interaction backgrounds.
- Serve as a **flux monitor**: the rate of through-going muons from beam-related backgrounds is proportional to the beam flux, providing a real-time relative flux measurement independent of the neutrino interaction cross section.
- **Improve vertex resolution** for interactions near the upstream face of the SuperFGD by providing an additional space point before the first cube layer.

**Readout**: WLS fibre + SiPM, same technology as FGD bars. ~2 × (2000/3) × (1900/3) ≈ ~800k bars in principle — in practice, bars are ~25 mm wide (matching existing P0D technology) giving ~2 × 80 × 76 ≈ 12,000 channels, manageable with existing Trip-t front-end ASICs.

---

### 4. SiPM Upgrade on Existing ECal Modules Adjacent to the New Target Region

**What it is**: Replace the existing Hamamatsu MPPC S10362-13-050C (50 μm pixel, 667 pixels, 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm) in the **Barrel ECal modules** directly surrounding the new target region with the newer **Hamamatsu S14160-1315PS** (15 μm pixel, ~7500 pixels, 1.3 mm × 1.3 mm).

**Why**: 
- The new target produces significantly more large-angle tracks entering the Barrel ECal than the P0D did. The barrel ECal must reconstruct these muon and proton tracks with good energy and position resolution.
- The older MPPCs have a dynamic range limited by pixel count (~667 pixels); at the high photoelectron yields typical of near-MIP tracks in the ECal scintillator bars, saturation corrections introduce a ~2–3% systematic on energy reconstruction.
- The new 15 μm pixel devices have ~11× more pixels, pushing saturation well above the typical signal range, reducing the saturation correction systematic to <0.5%.
- This directly attacks the existing ~6% systematic at one of its contributors (ECal energy scale uncertainty), contributing toward the 4% T2K-II target.

**Implementation**: The barrel ECal electronics (TRIP-t TFBs) are compatible with the new SiPMs after a bias-voltage adjustment (new devices operate at ~38 V vs ~70 V for old devices, requiring front-end board modification — a minor PCB rework, not a full electronics replacement).

---

### 5. Upgraded Data Acquisition: Continuous Waveform Sampling for the SuperFGD

**What it is**: Replace the beam-spill-triggered, peak-sensing readout paradigm (used in existing FGDs with Trip-t ASICs) with a **continuous waveform digitisation** scheme for the SuperFGD front-end boards, using the **DRS4 chip** (Paul Scherrer Institut) or equivalent (e.g., TARGET-7) operating at 500 MSa/s with 1024 sample depth (~2 μs window).

**Why**:
- The 6M-channel SuperFGD cannot afford dead time within the ~5 μs beam spill (8 bunches × ~100 ns separation). Peak-sensing ADCs can pile-up when two interactions occur in the same spill, which at T2K-II's higher beam power (1.3 MW target) becomes non-negligible.
- Waveform sampling allows **pulse shape discrimination** between proton (slow rise, Bragg peak gives broader pulse when the track stops in a cube) and minimum-ionising pion (fast, narrow pulse) at the single-cube level, providing an additional PID handle independent of range and dE/dx.
- Michel electron tagging (from π → μ → e decay chains) requires timing resolution across the 2.2 μs muon lifetime, which a 2 μs waveform window provides directly.
- Full waveform information improves **SiPM after-pulse and cross-talk rejection**, reducing the fake hit rate that would otherwise generate ghost tracks in the dense 3D hit pattern.

**Data volume**: 6M channels × 1024 samples × 12 bits = ~9 GB per spill before zero-suppression. With a threshold-based zero-suppression retaining only channels with >0.5 photoelectron equivalent signal, occupancy is ~0.1% per spill (estimated from beam simulation), reducing to ~9 MB/spill — manageable with the existing ND280 DAQ bandwidth (~100 MB/s).

---

## Integration Considerations

**Mechanical**: The SuperFGD block (1920 × 1840 × 560 mm, ~2 t) fits within the freed P0D volume. The existing UA1 magnet inner volume allows crane insertion from above with the magnet open; the block sits on a rail system identical to that used for FGD installation. The fibre readout boards on all six faces require ~40 mm clearance on each face — well within the 2.0 m × 1.9 m × 0.6 m envelope if the cube block itself is 1920 × 1840 × 480 mm with 40 mm face boards on each side bringing it to the full 560 mm in z.

**Magnetic field**: The 0.2 T field of the UA1 magnet is horizontal (along y). Tracks in the SuperFGD are too short for magnetic curvature measurement within the block itself (sagitta for a 450 MeV/c proton over 9 cm is ~0.1 mm, unresolvable). The magnet field serves the downstream TPC spectrometer for exiting tracks, unchanged from current operation.

**Calibration**: The SuperFGD is calibrated using through-going cosmic muons (collected between beam spills), which provide a uniform, known dE/dx sample across all 2M cubes. The light yield uniformity across cubes can be mapped using a UV LED pulser injected into each WLS fibre; this procedure is identical to that used for the existing FGDs and ECals.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the freed P0D volume with a SuperFGD — a fully-active ~2-tonne block of ~10 mm polystyrene scintillator cubes read out in three orthogonal projections via WLS fibres and SiPMs — because it simultaneously solves the fundamental angular-acceptance problem for large-angle protons (35% beyond 50°), provides range-based proton momentum reconstruction down to ~200 MeV/c via Bragg-peak tracking in 3D, and directly enables the kinematically complete charged-current event reconstruction required for transverse kinematic imbalance analysis, which no incremental improvement to the existing layered-FGD geometry can achieve.

I'll work through the physics requirements systematically to derive what hardware is needed.

---

## Physics Requirements Analysis

**Muon reconstruction ≥25% efficiency at ALL angles including 90° and backward:**
- Tracks going transverse or backward never reach the downstream drift chambers
- Need tracking coverage that is essentially 4π inside the target volume itself

**Recoiling protons down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy:**
- 60 MeV proton range in liquid scintillator ≈ 3.5 mm; in solid scintillator bars similar scale
- Need very fine-grained, low-threshold tracking within the active target
- Must distinguish proton from pion (particle ID needed)

**Hydrogen ≤2% of target nucleons:**
- Rules out liquid scintillator (CH₂-rich, ~14% hydrogen by nucleon count)
- Rules out plastic scintillator bars as the primary target mass
- Points toward low-hydrogen materials: argon, carbon-dominant targets, or specifically polystyrene with careful accounting — actually polystyrene (CH) has ~8% H by nucleon; liquid argon has zero hydrogen
- The hydrogen-subtraction model works only while H nuclei ≤2% of nucleons, so the target medium must have very low hydrogen content

**Momentum measurement of tracks that don't reach the downstream spectrometer:**
- Need either a magnetic field inside the active target or range-based momentum measurement
- The warm dipole is outside/around the target region; tracks stopping inside need range or additional magnetic measurement

## Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Low-Z, Low-Hydrogen Active Target: Liquid Argon or Gaseous Argon TPC with Embedded Scintillator, OR — most practically — a **Straw-Tube Tracker (STT) with polypropylene/carbon target planes**

**Recommended: Straw-Tube Tracker (STT) with graphite/carbon target panels**

- Carbon target panels (graphite or carbon composite) provide near-zero hydrogen (trace at <1% nucleon fraction), satisfying the ≤2% H constraint
- Interleaved straw tubes (4 mm diameter straws, e.g., Mylar/Kapton with Ar/CO₂ gas) provide hit resolution ~200 µm and can track short proton stubs (tracks as short as a few straws = ~1 cm, adequate for 60 MeV protons with ~3–4 cm range in gas+material)
- Straw-tube trackers are self-supporting, low-mass, 4π-capable within the volume
- **Why not plastic scintillator bars?** Polystyrene has ~8% H/nucleon — violates the 2% constraint
- **Why not LAr TPC?** Argon has zero hydrogen, which is fine, but fitting a cryostat into 2.6×2.3×0.9 m at a near detector is very constrained; also the existing warm dipole is not compatible with cryogenic operation without major infrastructure; and LAr TPC has known challenges with track reconstruction efficiency for very short (<5 cm) stopping protons

### 2. Thin scintillator planes (X-Y) interspersed with STT modules for particle identification and timing

- **Technology: 3 mm thick scintillator tiles or bars with SiPM readout**, arranged in X-Y pairs every ~10 cm along beam
- Provide dE/dx sampling to distinguish protons from pions and muons (Bethe-Bloch)
- Sub-nanosecond timing resolves beam spill structure and vetoes out-of-time backgrounds
- Help with 60 MeV proton ID: a stopping proton in the last few scintillator planes shows characteristic Bragg-peak energy deposition
- SiPMs (not PMTs) chosen because they operate within or adjacent to the magnetic field of the warm dipole without gain degradation
- **Why SiPMs specifically?** The warm dipole's fringe field inside the target region would saturate conventional PMTs; SiPMs are field-immune

### 3. Upgrade the upstream-face and side veto / active wall panels with **high-granularity scintillator + SiPM** to recover backward and large-angle muons

- Tracks going backward (upstream) or sideways exit the active target volume and currently are either lost or hit passive material
- **Technology: Scintillator-strip hodoscope walls (1–2 cm wide strips, SiPM readout) on all six faces of the target volume**
- These provide the ≥25% efficiency at 90° and 180° by detecting the track as it exits, giving at minimum a direction measurement; momentum from range if the track stops in the wall or from curvature in the dipole if it re-enters the drift chamber acceptance at large angles
- The downstream drift chambers already handle forward tracks; the walls complete the 4π coverage

### 4. Add a **compact electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL) layer** surrounding the active target on four sides (excluding upstream beam entrance and downstream drift-chamber exit)

- **Technology: Pb-scintillator sampling calorimeter with SiPM readout**, ~15 radiation lengths, ~10 cm thick
- Needed to measure/veto photons from π⁰ decay that fake the signal in hydrogen-subtraction analysis (a π⁰ misidentified as nothing affects the H model)
- Helps measure electrons from νₑ contamination in the beam
- Also provides additional ranging material for muons and pions exiting sideways, improving momentum resolution for large-angle tracks beyond what the veto planes alone provide

### 5. **Low-mass field-cage / internal mini-TPC insert** (if going gaseous route) OR upgrade of the existing gas drift chambers' upstream modules to finer pitch

- The existing downstream gas drift chambers measure forward tracks well but their most upstream station may be several tens of cm downstream of the target — a gap in coverage
- **Technology: Add two additional drift chamber stations directly at the downstream face of the active target volume**, with 5 mm cell pitch (finer than existing) to handle the higher multiplicity close to the vertex
- This ensures forward-going tracks are picked up before they diverge, improving efficiency and momentum resolution for forward muons

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Active target medium | Carbon/graphite target planes | H ≤ 2% of nucleons |
| 4π tracking | Straw-Tube Tracker (Ar/CO₂, 4 mm straws) | Short proton tracks, all-angle coverage |
| Particle ID + timing | 3 mm scintillator tiles/bars + SiPMs | dE/dx for p/π/µ ID, B-field compatibility |
| Large-angle/backward muon recovery | Scintillator-strip walls on all 6 faces + SiPMs | ≥25% muon efficiency at 90° and 180° |
| Photon veto + side calorimetry | Pb-scintillator ECAL + SiPMs | Protect H-subtraction model from π⁰ fakes |
| Fine-pitch drift stations at target exit | 5 mm cell gas drift chambers | Forward track pickup before divergence |

Based on the experimental requirements described, here are the hardware upgrades the proposal should include:

## 1. **3D Active Target Tracker Technology**
**Technology:** Time Projection Chamber (TPC) with fine-grained readout
**Why:** The requirement for 25% efficiency at all angles, including perpendicular and backward-going muon tracks, demands true 3D reconstruction. A TPC provides continuous tracking in all three dimensions, essential for capturing tracks at any angle relative to the beam axis. The drift time measurement along the beam direction combined with 2D readout provides complete track topology.

## 2. **Low-Z Target Material Selection**
**Technology:** Liquid or gaseous hydrogen (or deuterium) target, potentially as part of the TPC gas mixture
**Why:** The constraint that hydrogen must be ≤20% of target nucleons while still providing a pure hydrogen sample suggests using hydrogen as the active medium itself. A hydrogen-rich TPC gas (e.g., P10: 90% Ar + 10% CH₄, or pure hydrogen/deuterium) allows precise tracking while providing the necessary hydrogen interactions for model-dependent subtraction.

## 3. **Fine-Pitch Readout Electronics**
**Technology:** Micropattern gas detectors (Micromegas or GEMs) with ~3mm pitch
**Why:** Detecting 60 MeV protons (range ~1-2 cm in gas at ~1 atm) requires millimeter-scale position resolution to reconstruct short, stopping tracks and measure dE/dx for particle identification.

## 4. **High-Density Readout Channels**
**Technology:** ~100,000-300,000 channel front-end electronics with continuous digitization
**Why:** For the 2.6m × 2.3m cross-section with ~3mm pitch, approximately 750 × 650 = 487,500 readout pads are needed (likely split between anode planes). This enables the spatial granularity required for low-energy proton reconstruction.

## 5. **Particle Identification System**
**Technology:** Multi-sampling dE/dx measurement capability in the TPC readout
**Why:** Distinguishing ~60 MeV protons from minimum ionizing particles requires detailed ionization measurement along the track. TPC readout with sufficient sampling (~100+ samples per track) provides dE/dx for proton/pion/muon separation.

## 6. **DAQ System Upgrade**
**Technology:** High-bandwidth data acquisition with ~10 μs drift time buffering
**Why:** The TPC drift time across 2.6m requires sustained readout of all channels. At 0.7 GeV neutrino energy and 410m baseline, event rates could be significant, requiring continuous readout without deadtime.

## 7. **Field Cage and HV System**
**Technology:** Uniform electric field cage (~400 V/cm) throughout the 2.6m × 2.3m × 0.9m volume
**Why:** Maintaining uniform electron drift across the full target volume is essential for position reconstruction accuracy. The field cage must be transparent to particles exiting toward the downstream gas chambers.

## 8. **Gas Handling System**
**Technology:** Recirculating gas purification system with O₂ and H₂O removal to <10 ppm
**Why:** Electron attachment in the TPC drift region would destroy tracking performance, particularly for the long drift distances involved.

## 9. **Calibration Systems**
**Technology:** UV laser tracks and/or radioactive source deployment system
**Why:** Regular calibration of drift velocity, electron lifetime, and spatial uniformity is essential for accurate momentum reconstruction of muons matched to downstream chambers and for low-energy proton energy measurement.

## 10. **Integration with Existing Magnetic Field**
**Technology:** Field cage design compatible with 0.15 T transverse magnetic field
**Why:** The dipole field aids charge sign determination but affects electron drift trajectories. The TPC must be designed with E×B corrections, potentially requiring crossed electric and magnetic field operation (E perpendicular to B).

# Proposed hardware upgrades for the Kestrel Flats near-detector target region

## 1. The constraint that decides the design

The 2% hydrogen limit rules out the usual answer, a fine-grained plastic-scintillator active target.

- In CH plastic, hydrogen nuclei are 1 of 13 nucleons, about 7.7%.
- In water, they are 2 of 18 nucleons, about 11%.

Both exceed the 2% cap several times over, before counting fibres, glue and readout. The active target material must contain essentially no hydrogen.

The far detector contains no hydrogen. A noble-liquid target, ideally argon, therefore also gives cross-section results on the same nucleus as the far detector, which is a further benefit.

## 2. Core upgrade: a pixelated liquid-argon TPC as the active target

Replace the target region with a compact, modular liquid-argon TPC with native 3D pixel readout, of the ArgonCube / ND-LAr type.

**Hydrogen fraction.** The argon itself contributes 0% hydrogen. The hydrogen-bearing items are cryostat foam, PCBs and light-detector plastics. Keep these outside the fiducial volume. Millimetre-scale 3D vertex resolution then lets a fiducial cut remove interactions in them. This should keep hydrogen well below 2% of target nucleons.

**Acceptance at all angles.** A homogeneous, fully active volume with 3D readout has no dead planes. It reconstructs perpendicular and backward tracks as well as forward ones. This addresses the main weakness of a planar tracker followed by downstream drift chambers.

**Proton threshold.** A 60 MeV proton travels roughly 3 cm in argon. At about 3–4 mm pixel pitch that gives about 8–10 hits. dE/dx and Bragg-peak identification therefore work down to that energy at any angle.

**Muon momentum without the magnet.** Use range for stopping muons. Backward and high-angle muons are typically low momentum, so many stop. For exiting tracks, use multiple Coulomb scattering.

**Pile-up at 410 m.**
- Divide the volume into optically isolated modules, e.g. 2×2 or 3×2 along x–y, each with short drift (~30–50 cm).
- Add fast, segmented light readout with ns timing, such as ArCLight-type or SiPM-based detectors.
- Together these tie each charge cluster to an individual interaction within the spill.

**Cryostat in a 0.9 m slot.**
- Use a vacuum-insulated, double-walled stainless or aluminium cryostat, not foam membrane, with walls of about 10–15 cm total.
- Make the downstream wall thin so exiting muons still reach the existing drift chambers with little scattering.
- The fiducial argon volume would then be roughly 2.3 × 2.0 × 0.6 m. At about 1.4 t/m³ that is roughly 4 t of argon, which should give ample event statistics near the beam peak (my estimate).
- The magnet is warm, so there is no thermal conflict. The 0.15 T field does not hurt the TPC drift.

## 3. Supporting upgrades for high-angle and backward muons

The downstream drift chambers only see forward-going tracks. Add the following around the cryostat, inside the magnet volume.

**Top and bottom (and if possible side) gas tracking chambers.** These are thin TPCs or drift chambers with an argon-based gas.
- They measure the curvature, and hence charge and momentum, of muons exiting at large angles.
- They have negligible target mass, so they do not affect the hydrogen budget.

**A time-of-flight envelope.** Thin, fast scintillator or MRPC panels surround the cryostat and trackers.
- They resolve forward versus backward direction for exiting tracks.
- They veto entering particles from upstream interactions in the magnet, walls and rock.
- Any hydrogen in them sits outside the fiducial volume.

**An upstream tracking plane or veto.** This catches backward muons that exit the LAr upstream.

**Sign determination for contained muons.** For stopping muons, use μ⁻ capture versus μ⁺ decay. A μ⁺ always gives a Michel electron, while a μ⁻ in argon is mostly captured. This gives a statistical charge separation.

Together these should meet the requirement of at least 25% muon efficiency at every angle:
- Forward muons are measured by the downstream drift chambers.
- High-angle muons are measured by the side and top/bottom trackers plus MCS in the LAr.
- Backward muons are measured by range or MCS in the LAr plus the ToF and upstream plane.

## 4. Fallback option

If cryogenics in this hall are not acceptable, use a high-pressure (~10 bar) gaseous-argon TPC. It also has zero hydrogen and an excellent proton threshold. The drawbacks are:
- Only about 0.1 t of target mass, so far fewer interactions.
- Long proton tracks, so the TPC becomes a precision supplement rather than the main statistics sample.

## 5. Things to avoid

- Any CH or water active target.
- Hydrocarbon-rich drift gas mixtures inside the fiducial region.
- Thick inactive walls on the downstream face, which would degrade the hand-off to the existing drift chambers.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a modular, pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC active target, giving hydrogen-free 4π reconstruction of muons and protons down to 60 MeV.
