# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector

## Context Analysis

The detector needs to:
- Reconstruct muons at **all angles including 90° and backward** (≥25% efficiency)
- Reconstruct **short proton tracks** down to ~60 MeV kinetic energy
- Keep **hydrogen fraction ≤2% of nucleons** (to suppress H interactions for far-detector matching)
- Operate in a **0.15 T dipole field** over a ~6.5 m volume
- Fit within the **2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m** target region

---

## Upgrade 1: Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) Modular Cells — REJECTED on hydrogen grounds

A pure LAr TPC would give excellent tracking but LAr (Ar-40) has essentially zero free hydrogen. However a **hybrid** using LAr is worth considering. Actually, the hydrogen constraint pushes strongly away from hydrocarbon materials. See below.

---

## Upgrade 1: High-Pressure Gaseous Argon TPC (HPgAr TPC)

**Technology:** A time projection chamber filled with argon gas at ~10 bar, with a central cathode and segmented anode readout (e.g., multi-wire proportional chambers or pixel pads on the endcaps and sides).

**Physics motivation:**

The 0.9 m depth along beam is very short. At 10 bar, the density of argon is ~0.018 g/cm³, giving a radiation length of ~1 radiation length per ~10 m — tracks do not spiral excessively. Critically, the **continuous 3D ionization trail** in a TPC records every charged particle from the interaction vertex regardless of direction. A proton with 60 MeV kinetic energy has a range of about 3 cm in 10-bar argon (range ∝ 1/ρ, so from liquid argon range ~1.5 mm × 56 ≈ 8 cm — tracks are resolvable). The TPC records the full 3D helix even for tracks curling back upstream in the magnetic field, satisfying the backward-going muon requirement. Argon-40 has essentially **no free protons** (hydrogen nuclei), so hydrogen contamination is negligible (<0.01%), far below the 2% ceiling. The charge of tracks (sign of curvature in the dipole field) is determined from the drift direction and pad response combined with the external downstream spectrometer for muons that exit.

**Key numbers:** At 10 bar, a 300 MeV/c muon has a sagitta of a few cm over 90 cm, measurable. The 2.6 m × 2.3 m transverse area accommodates an octagonal or rectangular field cage. Drift distance up to ~1.1 m in the transverse plane requires HV of order 100 kV at 1 kV/cm — achievable with standard TPC technology.

---

## Upgrade 2: Scintillating Fiber (SciFi) Tracker Planes

**Technology:** Dense arrays of 250 µm diameter scintillating polystyrene fibers read out by silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), arranged in X-Y-U-V stereo layers, interleaved with thin passive or active material slabs. (Similar to LHCb SciFi Tracker.)

**Physics motivation:**

The SciFi planes provide **sub-millimeter spatial resolution** (σ ~ 100 µm per plane) and fast timing (~1 ns), enabling pattern recognition for the many tracks emerging from a neutrino interaction. Crucially, by using thin planes (< 1 mm fiber diameter per layer) the **material budget per plane is ~0.1% X₀**, so short proton tracks are not prematurely stopped. Polystyrene (C₈H₈)ₙ has hydrogen mass fraction ~7.7%, giving a hydrogen-to-nucleon ratio of about H/(8C+8H) = 8/104 ≈ 7.7% by number — this **violates the ≤2% hydrogen rule**. Therefore SciFi planes must be used only as **thin position-sensing layers interleaved with the HPgAr TPC**, contributing minimally to the total target mass. If SciFi planes constitute ≤25% of total target mass, the effective hydrogen fraction stays below ~2%. Their role is to improve the transverse hit resolution and provide triggering for tracks that may not leave enough ionization in the gas for standalone reconstruction.

---

## Upgrade 3: Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) or Thin-Gap Chambers (TGCs) as Active Veto/Range Stack Walls

**Technology:** 2 mm-gap RPCs with graphite-coated bakelite electrodes and X-Y strip readout, assembled into ~10 layers forming side walls (covering the 2.6 m × 0.9 m and 2.3 m × 0.9 m faces of the target volume), plus a downstream wall.

**Physics motivation:**

Tracks leaving the target volume laterally (90° tracks) or going backward must still be reconstructed. The RPCs form a **hermetic angular acceptance envelope** around the target region. A muon at 90° to the beam exits through the side wall; with ≥10 RPC layers of 2 mm gas (C₂H₂F₄, isobutane — note: isobutane adds hydrogen, so the gas mixture must be chosen carefully, or fluorine-only gases used) each layer provides a hit with ~1 mm resolution. The momentum of side-exiting tracks is measured by the curvature within the target TPC before they reach the wall. Backward muons (cos θ < 0) are caught on the **upstream face**. RPCs have >98% efficiency per layer, so 10 layers give >80% track-finding efficiency per wall. The bakelite mass is small enough to keep net hydrogen contribution below 0.3% of total target nucleon count. Fast RPC timing (< 2 ns) also suppresses out-of-spill backgrounds.

---

## Upgrade 4: Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECal) Panels — Pb/Scintillator Sampling

**Technology:** Lead-scintillator sandwich calorimeter with 1 mm Pb + 3 mm plastic scintillator tiles read by SiPMs, ~15 layers (≈ 5 X₀) surrounding the target on 4 sides and downstream face.

**Physics motivation:**

Neutral pions (π⁰ → γγ) produced in neutrino interactions are a significant background to quasi-elastic events. Without ECal coverage, these photons are invisible. Each ~5 X₀ ECal panel converts >99% of photons from π⁰ decay. The photon energy resolution σ_E/E ~ 15%/√E(GeV) is sufficient to reconstruct the π⁰ mass peak and tag NC π⁰ events. This is essential for the cross-section analysis because misidentified π⁰ events fake quasi-elastic topologies used to study the nucleon. The Pb absorber contains no hydrogen; the scintillator plastic contributes hydrogen but constitutes only ~20% of ECal mass, and the ECal sits **outside** the target fiducial volume, so it does not enter the hydrogen nucleon count. Tile dimensions of ~4 cm × 4 cm match the ~1 cm Molière radius in lead for position resolution sufficient to separate the two γ showers from π⁰ above 200 MeV.

---

## Upgrade 5: Replacement of Warm Dipole with a Superconducting Magnet (Moderate Priority)

**Technology:** A superconducting cos-θ or racetrack-coil dipole magnet providing 0.4–0.5 T over the full 6.5 m length, using NbTi cable at 4.5 K.

**Physics motivation:**

The current 0.15 T field gives a maximum transverse momentum kick of p_T = qBL = 0.3 × 0.15 × 6.5 ≈ 0.29 GeV/c integrated over the full spectrometer. For a 1 GeV/c muon the sagitta over 6.5 m is s = qBL²/(8p) ≈ 0.15 × 6.5²/8 ≈ 0.79 cm — just barely measurable by the drift chambers if their resolution is ~1 mm. Tripling the field to 0.45 T triples the sagitta to ~2.4 cm, reducing the **fractional momentum uncertainty** σ_p/p from ~15% to ~5% at 1 GeV/c. This is crucial because the neutrino energy is reconstructed from the muon momentum and angle: σ_Eν/Eν propagates directly from σ_p/p. With a 0.7 GeV peak flux, most muons are 0.3–1 GeV/c — exactly the range where improved magnetic resolution matters most. The superconducting option avoids the large power consumption (~1 MW) of a warm magnet at higher field.

---

## Upgrade 6: Precision Timing Layer (Low-Gain Avalanche Detectors, LGADs)

**Technology:** 50 µm thick LGAD silicon sensors, 1 cm × 1 cm pads, tiled into planes at the upstream and downstream faces of the target region, achieving σ_t ~ 30 ps per hit.

**Physics motivation:**

The near detector sits only 410 m from the target, so the neutrino beam spill (typically ~10 µs for a slow extraction, or ~1 µs for fast extraction) can produce multiple interactions overlapping spatially. With 30 ps timing, tracks from different interactions (separated by >1 ns) are disambiguated even when their projected vertices overlap in XY. More importantly, **neutrons** produced in the neutrino interaction (which carry away significant energy and bias the energy reconstruction) can be detected via time-of-flight: a 100 MeV kinetic energy neutron travels at β ≈ 0.43, arriving ~1.1 ns later per meter than a prompt photon. With LGAD timing across the 0.9 m depth, neutrons of 50–200 MeV can be tagged with ~20% efficiency via their delayed signal in the downstream ECal or RPC, correcting the neutrino energy estimate.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Physics Goal |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | HPgAr TPC at 10 bar | 3D tracking all angles, no H contamination |
| 2 | SciFi planes (thin) | Sub-mm position resolution, pattern recognition |
| 3 | RPC side/upstream walls | Hermetic acceptance for 90° and backward tracks |
| 4 | Pb/scintillator ECal | π⁰ rejection, photon energy measurement |
| 5 | Superconducting dipole | Improved momentum resolution (σ_p/p factor 3) |
| 6 | LGAD timing planes | Pile-up rejection, neutron TOF tagging |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a 10-bar high-pressure gaseous argon TPC, because it simultaneously provides continuous 3D tracking of all charged particles at any angle (including 90° and backward-going tracks), resolves short proton tracks down to the 60 MeV kinetic energy threshold, and contains essentially zero free hydrogen, keeping the hydrogen nucleon fraction far below the 2% ceiling required for the hydrogen-subtraction model.

Based on the experimental requirements, I need a detector technology that can:
1. Reconstruct tracks at all angles (including perpendicular and backward to beam)
2. Detect short-range protons down to 60 MeV kinetic energy (~3-4 mm range)
3. Keep hydrogen content below 2% of target nucleons
4. Fit within the 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m target region
5. Operate in a 0.15 T magnetic field

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the ND280 Upstream Active Target

## Physics Requirements Analysis

Before proposing hardware, the constraints must be internalized:

- **Volume**: ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m³ (depth along beam severely limited)
- **Kinematic completeness**: muon + leading proton both tracked
- **Large-angle acceptance**: 25% of muons and 35% of protons at >50° to beam
- **Proton momentum range**: median ~450 MeV/c, tail to >900 MeV/c
- **Target material**: hydrocarbon acceptable
- **Systematic goal**: reduce from ~6% to ~4%

The 0.6 m depth along beam is the critical constraint. A 450 MeV/c proton has a range of ~9 cm in polystyrene; a 900 MeV/c proton has ~50 cm range. The detector must therefore be both a **target and a tracker simultaneously**, with sufficient transverse acceptance and angular resolution.

---

## Upgrade Proposals

### 1. SuperFGD: High-Granularity 3D Scintillator Cube Target (Primary Recommendation)

**Description**: Replace the P0D volume with an array of **1 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes**, each penetrated along all three orthogonal axes by wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres read out by MPPCs (SiPMs). The active volume would be approximately **192 × 184 × 56 cubes** (~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m³), giving roughly **~2 million cubes** and a fiducial mass of ~2 tonnes of hydrocarbon.

**Technical implementation**:
- Each cube has three holes drilled along x, y, z; fibres are threaded and read at the face
- Kuraray Y-11 WLS fibre, 1 mm diameter, coupled to Hamamatsu S13360-1325PE MPPCs (50 μm pitch, 667 pixels)
- Cubes manufactured by injection moulding with TiO₂-doped reflective coating on all faces except fibre holes
- Light yield ~15–20 p.e. per MIP per fibre view, adequate for 3D hit reconstruction
- Readout: ~3 × (192 + 184 + 56) ≈ ~1,296 fibre channels per transverse layer; total ~O(50,000) MPPC channels
- Front-end ASICs: CITIROC or equivalent, 64-channel chips with charge and time measurement

**Physics case**:
- **3D point reconstruction** at 1 cm³ granularity gives unambiguous track finding even for heavily ionizing short proton stubs
- A 450 MeV/c proton has ~9 cm range → ~9 cube-lengths, fully contained and reconstructed with good angular resolution (σ_θ ~ few degrees)
- A 50° proton or muon traverses multiple layers in all three views with no dead zones
- The isotropic 4π-like acceptance directly addresses the 35% large-angle proton fraction
- Track-by-track particle identification via dE/dx (Bragg peak visible in cube-by-cube energy deposition) distinguishes protons from pions from muons
- Neutrons can also be detected via recoil proton tagging — bonus for complete final-state reconstruction

**Challenges and mitigations**:
- Large channel count (~50 k MPPCs): mitigated by multiplexing fibres along each axis and using daisy-chain MPPC arrays; proven in prototype studies by T2K/nd280 upgrade collaboration
- Timing resolution ~1 ns per cube sufficient to reject out-of-time backgrounds
- **This detector is already the baseline of the ND280 upgrade (Baby MIND companion); the T2K collaboration has demonstrated prototypes at CERN**

---

### 2. Thin Horizontal Time Projection Chambers (High-Pressure or Atmospheric) for Muon Momentum Measurement

**Description**: Place **two small TPCs** (each ~2.0 × 1.9 × 0.08 m³) immediately downstream of the SuperFGD, inside the available 0.6 m depth. Use Micromegas or resistive-strip GEM readout, Ar:CO₂ (70:30) or similar non-flammable mixture.

**Technical implementation**:
- Drift distance: ~6–8 cm (sufficient for field cage construction within budget)
- Anode segmentation: 1 cm × 1 cm pads, resistive layer to reduce spark damage
- Operating at ~1 atm; E_drift ~200 V/cm, B = 0.2 T (UA1 magnet)
- Momentum resolution from curvature: for a 500 MeV/c track spanning 1.5 m in the magnet, σ_p/p ~ few %; adequate for imbalance studies

**Physics case**:
- Provides **independent momentum measurement** for tracks exiting the SuperFGD forward
- Particle identification via dE/dx in gas complements the solid-scintillator PID
- Acts as a **veto/tagger** for tracks entering from upstream (beam-related backgrounds)
- Improves muon charge identification (critical for ν vs ν̄ separation)

**Key concern**: The 0.6 m longitudinal budget is extremely tight if two TPCs plus SuperFGD are stacked. A realistic split would be **~500 mm for SuperFGD + ~100 mm for one thin TPC plane**. The downstream TPCs (TPC1–3) remain and handle most muon momentum measurement, so this thin TPC is supplementary.

---

### 3. MPPC/SiPM Upgrade for Existing Downstream ECal and SMRD

**Description**: Replace the existing Hamamatsu MPPC S10362-13-050C (667-pixel, 50 μm pitch) used in ECal and SMRD with the newer **S13360 series (50 μm pitch, 667 pixels but improved PDE ~40% vs ~25%)**, or the **Hamamatsu S14160 series** (3 × 3 mm², 50 μm, ~74,000 pixels, PDE >50% at 450 nm).

**Physics case**:
- Higher photon-detection efficiency → lower energy threshold for ECal shower reconstruction
- Better π⁰ → γγ reconstruction efficiency (directly reduces π⁰ background systematic)
- Improved timing resolution → better out-of-time rejection and neutron TOF capability
- Lower dark-noise rate at room temperature in the newer devices reduces accidental coincidences

**Implementation**: The ECal uses ~8,700 MPPC channels; re-instrumentation during LS (long shutdown) is feasible. The improvement in electromagnetic energy resolution from ~10%/√E to ~8%/√E would directly reduce the NC π⁰ background systematic uncertainty.

---

### 4. Thin Scintillator Veto/Tagger Planes Around the SuperFGD

**Description**: Six planes of **1 cm thick plastic scintillator** (extruded, triangular cross-section bars, Fermilab-style) on all faces of the SuperFGD, with MPPC readout and sub-nanosecond timing.

**Physics case**:
- Tags tracks exiting all faces → distinguishes contained from partially-contained events
- Critical for the **~35% large-angle protons**: a proton leaving at 55° in the 0.6 m deep SuperFGD exits a lateral face; the veto plane tags it and its exit momentum can be reconstructed with the downstream detectors plus range
- Cosmic-ray veto during beam spill
- Charge-exchange neutron background rejection by identifying neutral-to-charged conversions at the boundary
- Tight timing (σ_t ~ 0.5 ns) with the MPPC allows time-of-flight mass tagging for slow protons

---

### 5. Thin Lead-Scintillator Gamma Catcher Downstream of SuperFGD

**Description**: A **2 × 1.9 × 0.05 m³** layer of 1 mm Pb + scintillator tiles (similar to ECal but thinner, ~2 X₀ total), placed between the SuperFGD and TPC1.

**Physics case**:
- Converts photons from π⁰ decay that escape the SuperFGD before entering the gas TPC (where they are invisible)
- Reduces the NC π⁰ background contamination in the CC-inclusive sample
- Improves photon energy measurement for the π⁰ invariant mass reconstruction
- Given the box occupies upstream space, this layer fits within the existing ECal envelope without displacing downstream detectors

---

### 6. Beam Monitor Upgrade: Segmented Carbon Target Replica

**Description**: Install a **small segmented ionization monitor** at the upstream face of the new target volume, essentially a thin (1 radiation length) multi-wire proportional counter or microstrip gas counter array, to monitor the neutrino beam transverse profile at ND280 on a spill-by-spill basis.

**Physics case**:
- The 6% → 4% systematic reduction requires improved flux knowledge
- Real-time transverse beam profile monitoring at the near detector location constrains off-axis angle variations (even 0.1° variation in beam pointing shifts the flux peak)
- Cross-checks INGRID and MUMON beam monitoring with an independent in-situ measurement
- Minimal material: ~0.01 X₀, negligible impact on neutrino interaction rate

---

| Upgrade | Primary Benefit | Addresses |
|---|---|---|
| SuperFGD cube target | 3D tracking, large-angle acceptance, PID | Kinematic completeness, proton reconstruction |
| Thin downstream TPC | Muon momentum, charge ID | Systematic on muon kinematics |
| MPPC upgrade (ECal/SMRD) | Lower threshold, better π⁰ rejection | NC background systematic |

## Critical Physics Argument for the Top Recommendation

The bottleneck for kinematic completeness is **proton reconstruction**. The existing FGD bar geometry (1 cm × 1 cm × 186 cm bars, single-axis per layer) gives ambiguities in 3D track reconstruction for tracks at large angles and fails entirely for proton stubs shorter than ~3–4 bar widths. The 1 cm³ cube geometry eliminates the stereo ambiguity by providing **three independent 2D projections from a single 3D hit**, enabling reconstruction of proton tracks as short as 3–4 cm (300–350 MeV/c protons) at any angle. This is the unique enabling technology for the transverse kinematic imbalance programme.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the P0D with a fully-3D granular scintillator cube detector (SuperFGD: ~2×10⁶ injection-moulded 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, each read in x/y/z by WLS fibres and MPPCs), providing isotropic 4π tracking acceptance, dE/dx-based proton/pion/muon separation, and sub-centimetre 3D vertex resolution to achieve kinematically complete CC event reconstruction including large-angle and low-momentum leading protons.

# Kestrel Flats Near Station: Active-Target Hardware Recommendations

## 1. The driving constraint: the target cannot be hydrogenous plastic

The obvious choice for this job is a finely segmented plastic-scintillator cube target in the style of the T2K ND280 SuperFGD. It gives isotropic 3D tracking and good proton thresholds. **The hydrogen limit rules it out.**

- Polystyrene (CH)ₙ has 1 hydrogen nucleon in 13, so **about 7.7% of its nucleons are hydrogen**.
- Water is about 11%.
- Both exceed the 2% budget by a large factor. The hydrogen-subtraction model would not hold for any hydrocarbon or water target, whatever the granularity.

The far detector contains no hydrogen, and argon is the natural match. Argon has 0% hydrogen and gives direct same-nucleus cross sections.

## 2. Recommended changes

### (a) Replace the target region with a modular liquid-argon TPC with pixel readout

Use an ArgonCube / ND-LAr-style design with LArPix-type pixel charge readout.

- **Hydrogen fraction:** zero. Hydrogenous materials (insulation foam, G10, cable jackets) are confined to cryostat walls outside the fiducial volume, where vertex cuts remove them.
- **Isotropic acceptance:** native 3D pixel readout has no wire-projection ambiguity. Tracks perpendicular to the beam, or along the drift direction, reconstruct as well as forward tracks. This directly addresses the at-every-angle muon requirement.
- **Proton threshold:** a 60 MeV proton has a range of about 3 g/cm², or about 2 cm in LAr. With 3–4 mm pixels that is 5 or more hits plus a clear Bragg peak, so protons can be identified by dE/dx and their energy measured by range. Thresholds of about 30–40 MeV are demonstrated in LArTPCs.
- **Pileup:** at 410 m the beam spill will contain several interactions per tonne. Use modules about 0.5–0.7 m wide, each optically isolated with its own light readout (ArCLight/LCM-type). This keeps drift lengths short, limiting diffusion and pileup, and lets scintillation light tag interactions in time.
- **Mass budget:** a cryostat with about 15 cm walls leaves roughly 2.3 × 2.0 × 0.6 m of active argon, about 3.5–4 t. That is ample at a near-detector flux.
- **Cryostat material:** use a thin, low-Z downstream wall so muons reach the existing drift chambers with little scattering.

### (b) Add tracking at high angles: side and top/bottom chambers inside the magnet

Muons above about 60° never reach the downstream drift chambers. A typical 0.3–0.6 GeV muon is not contained in a 2 m transverse depth of LAr.

- Line the four lateral faces of the target region inside the 0.15 T field with thin gas chambers. Resistive-Micromegas TPCs like the ND280-upgrade high-angle TPCs are suitable, or straw tubes.
- These give curvature for charge sign and momentum of side-exiting muons.
- For tracks partly contained in LAr, use multiple-Coulomb-scattering momentum as a cross-check.
- For stopping muons, use range.

### (c) Install a time-of-flight scintillator envelope around the target and side chambers

Use fast plastic bars read out by SiPMs, with about 150 ps resolution.

- Timing gives the track's direction, so a backward-going muon from the target can be told apart from an incoming entering muon or a cosmic. This is essential for the backward-angle efficiency requirement.
- The bars also serve as a trigger and veto for interactions in the upstream wall.
- The plastic lies outside the fiducial volume, so it does not affect the hydrogen budget.

### (d) Upstream veto and instrumented magnet yoke

- Place a veto plane upstream of the cryostat to reject rock and wall muons.
- Instrument the yoke gaps with scintillator, SMRD-style, to measure the range of high-angle muons that escape the side chambers. This protects the 25% floor at 90°.

### (e) Supporting systems

- A cryogenic plant and argon purification sized for electron lifetimes above 3 ms.
- Common DAQ timing across the TPC, TOF and drift chambers.
- A calibration system: laser and/or cosmic tagging to establish the low-energy proton dE/dx scale.

## 3. Alternative considered

A high-pressure gaseous-argon TPC (about 10 bar) would also be hydrogen-free. Its proton thresholds are excellent and all tracks get magnetic momentum measurement. However:

- Its active mass in this volume is only about 0.1 t.
- 60 MeV protons do not stop in it.
- The pressure vessel walls add mass.

It could serve as a later supplementary low-threshold module, but liquid argon is preferred as the main target.

# Recommended Hardware Changes for the Near-Detector Upgrade

## Why the current design falls short

The existing plastic targets use bar layers perpendicular to the beam. This geometry works well for forward tracks but performs poorly at high angle:

- **Muons above about 50°** run along a single bar layer. They rarely reach the downstream TPCs and are often lost into the barrel calorimeter.
- **Low-momentum protons** cross only a few layers before stopping. In 2D x/y layers they are often unreconstructable or confused with other hits.

This matters for transverse kinematic imbalance, which needs both particles. About 25% of muons and 35% of protons exit above 50°, so the current acceptance is strongly forward-biased. That bias is a major contributor to the roughly 6% residual systematic. The upgrade must deliver near-4π acceptance and a low proton threshold.

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-cube scintillator target in the vacated box

**Technology: a SuperFGD-type target.** About 2 million optically independent 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, each threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting fibres. Each fibre is read out at one end by a ~1.3 mm SiPM (Hamamatsu MPPC type).

**Geometry**
- About 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, roughly 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m. This fills the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- I would orient the 0.6 m dimension vertically, so the slab is horizontal and the beam runs along its 1.84 m length. This is my reading of the box, not something the brief states; the integration team should confirm it.
- Mass is about 2 t of CH, a hydrocarbon target, which the programme accepts.

**Readout**
- Three 2D projections give about 56,000 channels (192×184 + 192×56 + 184×56).
- Front-end electronics should be CITIROC-class, with ~1 ns hit timing.

**Justification**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal views remove the dependence on angle inherent in bar layers, so high-angle and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Low proton threshold.** A 450 MeV/c proton (kinetic energy about 100 MeV) ranges roughly 8 cm in plastic, about 8 cubes. This allows full range-based reconstruction of the median proton. The threshold reaches about 300 MeV/c, covering most of the leading-proton spectrum.
- **Contained high-momentum protons.** Protons above 900 MeV/c (the ~6% tail) have kinetic energies above ~360 MeV and ranges of order a metre. They are partly contained, and escapees are measured in the TPCs described below.
- **Calorimetric and timing information.**
  - Fine-grained dE/dx near the vertex separates protons from pions.
  - Michel-electron tagging becomes possible.
  - Neutron detection via isolated delayed hits plus time of flight allows full event kinematics, including on antineutrino samples.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Argon-based gas TPCs with **resistive Micromegas (encapsulated resistive anode, "ERAM") readout**.
- Lightweight composite field cages to minimise material between the target and the gas.

**Justification**
- High-angle muons leaving the slab, and protons too energetic to stop, need magnetic momentum and charge measurement in the 0.2 T field. The existing downstream TPCs cannot see these tracks.
- The resistive anode spreads charge across ~1 cm pads. This gives sub-mm spatial resolution and dE/dx resolution below 10% with a modest channel count.
- The resistive layer also protects the readout against sparking.
- The result is muon and proton momentum and particle identification from 90° down to the forward region, closing the acceptance gap.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new section

**Technology**
- Planes of plastic scintillator bars (around 1 cm thick) around the target-plus-TPC assembly.
- Arrays of SiPMs at both bar ends, giving ~150 ps resolution.

**Justification**
- **Track direction.** Timing resolves forward versus backward-going tracks, rejecting out-of-volume and sand-muon backgrounds that mimic backward tracks.
- **Particle identification.** Time of flight improves e/μ/p separation at low momentum.
- **Neutron kinematics.** Combined with the cube timing, it provides a time-of-flight measurement for neutron candidates.

## 4. Supporting changes

- **Retain the downstream water-layer target unchanged** for the carbon-to-water ratio. Cross-calibrate it to the new cube target using common TPC tracks.
- **Upgrade the electronics and DAQ** to handle the large increase in channel count (~56k cubes plus TPC pads) with synchronised ns-level timing across all subdetectors. Install an LED and cosmic calibration system for per-channel SiPM gain and fibre attenuation.
- **Extend the side muon-range detectors** where geometry allows, to tag muons exiting through the gaps near the new section.

## Expected impact

The new section delivers:
- full-angle muon reconstruction;
- a proton threshold near 300 MeV/c;
- neutron information.

Together these give kinematically complete charged-current samples for transverse kinematic imbalance studies. They also reduce the extrapolation in angle and energy to the far detector, which is the main lever for moving from ~6% toward the ~4% systematic goal.

# Hardware upgrades for the Kestrel Flats near-detector active target

## The governing constraint: hydrogen content

The hydrogen limit of at most 2% of target nucleons rules out the usual active-target choice.

- **Plastic scintillator** (CH, as in fine-grained cube detectors such as SuperFGD) has about 1/13 ≈ 7.7% of its nucleons as hydrogen. It is excluded, however good its angular acceptance.
- **Water-based targets** have about 2/18 ≈ 11% hydrogen nucleons, so they are also excluded.

The active medium therefore has to be hydrogen-free and still dense enough to give a useful event rate. Liquid argon is the natural choice. It fits best if the far detector is argon, and the prompt does not say what the far detector is made of.

## Proposed upgrades

### 1. Active target: modular liquid-argon TPC with pixelated charge readout

This is the central change.

- **Hydrogen fraction:** 0% in the active medium, so the 2% requirement is met with large margin.
- **Mass:** 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m ≈ 5.4 m³, or about 7.5 t of liquid argon. That gives a high event rate at 410 m.
- **Readout:** pixel readout with about 3–4 mm pitch gives native 3D reconstruction and is isotropic. Perpendicular and backward tracks are reconstructed as well as forward ones.
- **Low-energy protons:** a 60 MeV proton has a range of roughly 2 cm in liquid argon, which is about 5–7 pixels. That is enough to detect the track and identify it as a proton from its dE/dx and Bragg peak.
- **Muons:** muons are tagged by range and dE/dx. Momentum comes from range for stopping tracks and from multiple scattering for exiting tracks.
- **Modularity:** an optically and electrically segmented design (ArgonCube-style modules) keeps drift lengths short. A drift of about 0.5 m or less limits diffusion and the effect of argon purity, and segmentation allows pile-up hits within a spill to be separated.

### 2. Light-detection system

- **Technology:** SiPM-coupled wavelength-shifting light collectors inside each module.
- **Purpose:**
  - provide the event start time (t₀) needed to locate hits along the drift direction;
  - associate each interaction with the correct beam bunch;
  - allow a coincidence trigger with the external tracking.

### 3. Low-mass, non-magnetic cryostat inside the existing magnet

- **Inner vessel:** thin aluminium or stainless steel, so that muons and protons exiting the target are not degraded before reaching the trackers.
- **Insulation:** vacuum or minimal foam. Hydrogen-containing insulation and supports must stay outside the fiducial volume, and the fiducial cut should be defined so they contribute negligibly.
- **Fit:** it must sit within the 0.15 T warm-dipole aperture without distorting the field.

### 4. High-angle and backward tracking around the target

The existing downstream drift chambers only see forward-going tracks. A perpendicular or backward muon would be lost, which violates the ≥25% efficiency requirement at all angles.

- **Additional trackers:** gas TPCs or drift chambers above, below and beside the target, plus an upstream plane.
- **Location:** all placed inside the 0.15 T field, so they measure charge and momentum by curvature for muons leaving at any angle.
- **Gas:** hydrogen-free mixtures (for example Ar/CO₂ rather than hydrocarbon quenchers) are preferable. This matters less, since these volumes are not part of the target.

### 5. Time-of-flight layer enclosing the target and trackers

- **Technology:** fast scintillator bars with SiPM readout at both ends, timing resolution of 150 ps or better.
- **Purpose:**
  - determine track direction (forward or backward-going, and entering or exiting) so backward muons are not misidentified as entering background;
  - add particle identification;
  - reject interactions in the magnet and walls.
- **Hydrogen:** the bars are plastic, but they sit outside the fiducial target and are only used for timing.

### 6. Readout, DAQ and trigger

- **Technology:** low-power cryogenic pixel ASICs with continuous self-triggered readout.
- **Purpose:** synchronise with the beam-spill clock to handle multiple interactions per spill and to match target events with tracker and time-of-flight hits.

## Rejected alternatives

| Alternative | Reason for rejection |
|---|---|
| CH scintillator (e.g. SuperFGD) | Fails the hydrogen limit (about 7.7% hydrogen nucleons). |
| Water target | Fails the hydrogen limit (about 11% hydrogen nucleons). |
| High-pressure gaseous argon TPC as the sole target | Hydrogen-free with excellent proton threshold, but far too little mass for the volume. Better suited as a supplementary sample. |
| Wire-plane liquid-argon TPC | Has ambiguities for tracks parallel to the wire planes and handles pile-up worse than pixel readout. |

**Geometry of the target region:** 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m (depth along beam). This is a large, nearly-square transverse cross-section with shallow depth — a squat, wide volume.

**Key reconstruction demands:**
