## Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Liquid Argon Time Projection Chamber (LArTPC) as Active Target
**Technology:** Modular LArTPC filling the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m target volume.
**Why:** Liquid argon is essentially hydrogen-free (⁴⁰Ar nucleus, negligible H), satisfying the ≤2% hydrogen nucleon constraint. LAr provides ~mm-scale 3D tracking with continuous sensitivity, enabling reconstruction of the ~1.5 cm proton tracks from 60 MeV protons. The fine-grained 3D imaging also reconstructs tracks at all angles, including backward-going and 90° muons within the volume.

### 2. Surrounding 4π Scintillator Muon Catcher / Range Stack
**Technology:** Plastic scintillator planes (or extruded scintillator bars with WLS fibers and SiPM readout) enclosing the target volume on all six faces, including upstream and lateral faces, backed by magnetized iron or additional drift chambers on the sides.
**Why:** Muons that exit the LArTPC in any direction — backward, sideways, or at large angles — must be tracked and their momentum measured. The existing downstream spectrometer handles forward muons. New lateral and upstream scintillator/tracking planes with enough material to range out or bend muons ensure ≥25% reconstruction efficiency at every angle. SiPM readout gives good timing for track directionality.

### 3. Upstream Veto and Tracking Planes
**Technology:** Two or three planes of scintillator strips or silicon strip detectors immediately upstream of the target.
**Why:** Backward-going muons exiting the upstream face of the target must be distinguished from beam-related backgrounds entering from upstream. Tracking planes upstream provide the rejection of incoming charged particles and allow backward muon momentum measurement by range combined with the range stack.

### 4. Lateral Magnetized Mini-Spectrometers or Extended Dipole Coverage
**Technology:** Additional smaller dipole magnets or extension of fringe-field instrumentation on the lateral (top/bottom, left/right) exits of the target volume, instrumented with drift tubes or resistive plate chambers (RPCs).
**Why:** The existing downstream dipole only analyzes forward-going tracks. 90° muons leaving the sides or top/bottom have no magnetic analysis. Lateral tracking with even modest field regions allows charge-sign determination and momentum measurement for large-angle muons, completing the 4π requirement.

### 5. High-Voltage and Cryogenic Infrastructure for LArTPC
**Technology:** Cryostat with evacuable insulation vacuum, LAr purification and recirculation system, HV feedthroughs rated to ~100 kV, purity monitors.
**Why:** A LArTPC requires sustained electron lifetime >1 ms (purity <100 ppt O₂-equivalent) for tracks up to ~2.5 m drift. The existing hall at 410 m is surface or near-surface; cosmic shielding and purity systems are infrastructure prerequisites without which the TPC cannot operate.

### 6. Cold Electronics / Warm Feedthrough Signal Chain
**Technology:** CMOS cold ADC/multiplexer ASICs (e.g., LArASIC-heritage chips) mounted on cold motherboards inside the cryostat, with feedthroughs to warm DAQ.
**Why:** The ~1 cm short proton tracks require low-noise charge readout to achieve the signal-to-noise needed for track detection below 1 MIP equivalent. Cold electronics reduce thermal noise by ~√(T) and eliminate long capacitive cables, crucial for hitting the low-energy proton threshold.

### 7. Light Detection System (Photon Detectors)
**Technology:** VUV-sensitive SiPMs or PMTs with tetraphenyl butadiene (TPB) wavelength-shifting coating, deployed as ARAPUCA-style light trap modules or bar-mounted light guides within the LAr volume.
**Why:** Scintillation light in LAr (128 nm) provides t₀ for each interaction, essential for drift-coordinate reconstruction (z-position along drift) and for triggering. Without t₀, the absolute position along the drift direction is unknown and short tracks become unlocatable. Fast light also gives Michel electron and de-excitation topology for particle ID.

### 8. Replacement/Upgrade of Downstream Drift Chambers with Higher-Rate Capability
**Technology:** Straw-tube trackers or micropattern gas detectors (MicroMEGAS or GEM-based) replacing or augmenting the existing gas drift chambers downstream.
**Why:** The near detector sits only 410 m from the target, so neutrino interaction rates are high. Existing drift chambers may have dead-time or space-charge limitations at the beam spill intensity needed for the physics program. High-rate micropattern detectors tolerate higher occupancy and improve forward muon momentum resolution.

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key Requirement Addressed |
|---|---|---|
| Active target | LArTPC | H≤2%, short proton tracks, 3D imaging |
| 4π muon catcher | Scintillator bars + SiPMs | All-angle muon efficiency ≥25% |
| Upstream veto/tracker | Scintillator strips or Si strips | Backward muon ID, beam background rejection |
| Lateral spectrometers | RPCs + small dipoles or fringe-field extension | Charge sign for 90° muons |
| Cryogenic/HV infrastructure | Cryostat, purification, HV | LArTPC operation prerequisite |
| Cold electronics | LArASIC-type cold ADCs | Low-noise readout for 60 MeV protons |
| Photon detection | VUV SiPMs + TPB/ARAPUCA | t₀, triggering, particle ID |
| Downstream tracker upgrade | MicroMEGAS or GEM | High-rate forward muon spectrometry |

# Recommendations for the Upstream Near-Detector Upgrade

**Goal:** cut the residual systematic from about 6% to about 4% by adding full-solid-angle, kinematically complete charged-current (CC) reconstruction on hydrocarbon. The current detector cannot do this for three reasons:

- **Angular acceptance.** The downstream plastic targets use planar bars perpendicular to the beam, and the gas TPCs sit downstream of them. Tracks at large angle or going backward lose efficiency badly. That is where about 25% of muons and about 35% of leading protons go (more than 50° from the beam).
- **Proton threshold.** A 1 cm bar sampled in one view at a time cannot see short protons. Near the 450 MeV/c median, a proton ranges only a few cm in plastic, so reconstruction is poor.
- **Missing hadronic information.** Neutrons are invisible, so transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) studies lose events and resolution.

## 1. Replace the upstream section with a 3D-granular scintillator target (most important)

**Technology:** a "SuperFGD"-type detector of about 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes.

- **Layout:** about 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, roughly 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m and about 2 t. This fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box.
- **Construction:** each cube is etched with a reflector and threaded by three orthogonal 1 mm wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibres.
- **Readout:** about 56,000 channels, using compact Hamamatsu-type MPPC/SiPMs and CITIROC-class front-end electronics.

**Justification:**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three projections of 1 cm granularity reconstruct tracks at any angle, including perpendicular and backward ones. This recovers the high-angle muons and protons the planar bars miss.
- **Low proton threshold.** Protons down to roughly 300 MeV/c (a few cubes) are reconstructed. This covers the bulk of the 450 MeV/c median distribution, which TKI requires.
- **Particle identification and vertexing.** dE/dx per cube gives proton/pion separation. Fine granularity gives clean vertex activity.
- **Neutron detection.** Sub-ns timing per fibre allows neutron tagging by time of flight from the vertex to an isolated secondary hit. This adds neutron kinematics for antineutrino TKI.
- **Mass and target material.** About 2 t of CH roughly doubles the hydrocarbon target mass. The downstream water-layer target keeps the carbon-to-water comparison.

## 2. Add two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology:**
- **Readout:** resistive Micromegas, specifically encapsulated resistive anode (ERAM). Charge spreading gives sub-mm resolution with fewer, larger pads, plus spark protection.
- **Field cage:** lightweight composite (aramid/laminate), to minimise dead material.
- **Gas:** the same argon-based mixture as the existing TPCs, so operation and calibration are shared.

**Justification:**
- **Momentum and charge for high-angle tracks.** Tracks leaving the cube target at large angle get momentum and charge sign from curvature in the existing 0.2 T field, plus dE/dx PID. The existing downstream TPCs cannot see these tracks.
- **Escaping protons.** About 6% of protons exceed 900 MeV/c and will escape the cubes. The high-angle TPCs measure them instead of relying on range, so the TKI sample stays complete.
- **Fit to the magnet.** They fill the vertical space within the 3.5–3.6 m magnet bore.

## 3. Surround the new target and TPCs with a time-of-flight (ToF) system

**Technology:** six panels of plastic scintillator bars with double-ended SiPM readout, giving about 150 ps timing.

**Justification:**
- **Track direction.** Timing separates forward-going from backward-going tracks, and rejects out-of-fiducial-volume backgrounds entering from the magnet and walls. This is critical once acceptance becomes 4π.
- **Particle identification.** ToF adds PID at low momentum, where dE/dx is ambiguous.
- **Neutron timing.** It provides a precise global time reference that sharpens neutron ToF.
- **Calibration.** It gives a cosmic-ray trigger for calibrating the cube and TPC detectors.

## 4. Supporting changes

- **Calorimeter coverage.** Re-instrument or relocate the upstream lead-scintillator ECal modules around the new section to keep photon and π⁰ tagging. This partly compensates for removing the photon-tagging section.
- **Side-muon ranging.** Keep the yoke-gap scintillator planes and check their coverage, so muons exiting through the side are still ranged.
- **Shared electronics and DAQ.** Use a common SiPM electronics and DAQ upgrade across the new and existing scintillator channels, with synchronised timing for ToF and neutron reconstruction.
- **Calibration hardware.** Add LED and cosmic calibration for the new channels.

## Physics payoff

- Near-4π acceptance and a low proton threshold give kinematically complete CC events, with neutrons in the antineutrino case.
- TKI then constrains nuclear effects: Fermi motion, final-state interactions and 2p2h.
- High-angle muon coverage matches the far detector's full acceptance.
- Together these directly attack the flux × cross-section systematic, aiming for about 4%.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a SuperFGD-type 3D-granular target of about 2 million 1 cm³ scintillator cubes with three-view WLS fibre/SiPM readout (about 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m, about 2 t) in the upstream box.

# Hardware upgrade proposal: active target for the Kestrel Flats near station

## 1. The hydrogen constraint rules out the usual choices

The standard near-detector active targets all contain too much hydrogen. Hydrogen nuclei can make up at most 2% of the target nucleons.

| Candidate target | H nuclei / all nucleons | Meets the 2% limit? |
|---|---|---|
| Plastic scintillator (CH), e.g. a SuperFGD-style cube array | ≈1/13 ≈ 7.7% | No |
| Water (H₂O) | 2/18 ≈ 11% | No |
| Liquid scintillator (≈CH₂) | ≈2/14 ≈ 14% | No |
| Argon (liquid, or gas with a small quencher) | 0 (≲0.1% with quencher) | Yes |

A fine-grained scintillator design would otherwise suit the 4π and low-threshold requirements. It fails the 2% limit by a factor of about 4, so subtracting the hydrogen with the model is not allowed. A hydrogen-free noble-element medium is needed. Argon is the natural choice because it is the likely nucleus in a hydrogen-free far detector. You should confirm the actual far-detector target: if it is not argon, the same design logic applies, but the medium should match that nucleus.

## 2. Recommended core change: a modular, pixel-readout LAr TPC filling the target region

**Geometry and mass**
- The 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m³ region holds about 5.4 m³ of LAr, or about 7.5 t.
- It would be built from several optically isolated modules in the ArgonCube / ND-LAr 2×2 style.
- Short drift distances (about 30–50 cm) per module would let it operate in the warm 0.15 T magnet.

**Readout**
- Use native 3D pixel readout (about 4 mm pitch) instead of wire planes.
- Wires are ambiguous for isotropic, high-multiplicity events. Pixels give unambiguous 3D tracks at any angle, including tracks perpendicular to the beam and backward-going tracks.
- Pixels also avoid the "isochronous track" blind spot of wire TPCs.

**Proton threshold**
- A 60 MeV kinetic-energy proton has a range of roughly 2–2.5 cm in LAr. That is about 5–6 pixels, so it can be tracked and identified as a proton by dE/dx.
- This gives the full angular coverage the analysis needs.

**Pile-up**
- At 410 m from the target, a 7.5 t target sees many interactions per spill.
- Segmented light detection (ArCLight / LCM-type tiles on each module) provides about ns timing and the module-level segmentation needed to separate interactions and reject rock muons.

**Hydrogen bookkeeping**
- There is no hydrogenous material in the fiducial volume. G10 field cages and light-detector substrates are thin and kept outside the fiducial cut.
- This keeps hydrogen nuclei far below 2% of the target nucleons.

## 3. Supporting upgrades so muons meet ≥25% efficiency at all angles

The downstream drift chambers see only forward tracks. At about 0.7 GeV, a muon with a range of about 3 m in LAr usually exits a detector that is 0.9–2.6 m across. High-angle and backward muons therefore need separate measurement.

1. **Thin-walled, low-mass cryostat**
   - Use a vacuum-insulated, thin stainless or aluminium membrane.
   - This keeps exiting muons from scattering or ranging out in the cryostat walls before they reach the outer trackers.

2. **Side and upstream muon trackers inside the magnet**
   - Place thin tracking planes on the top, bottom, left, right and upstream faces, between the cryostat and the coils.
   - These could be scintillator bars with SiPMs, or the same drift-chamber technology.
   - They give charge sign from curvature in the 0.15 T field, timing that resolves forward versus backward direction, and matching to the TPC track.
   - The hydrogen in these planes is outside the fiducial target and does not count toward the 2% limit.

3. **Momentum for tracks that do not reach a spectrometer**
   - For contained muons and protons, measure momentum by range.
   - For exiting muons, measure momentum by multiple Coulomb scattering along the long tracks in LAr.

4. **Time-of-flight layer around the cryostat**
   - Sub-ns resolution separates backward-exiting tracks from tracks entering from outside the detector.
   - It also confirms direction for backward muons.

## 4. Fallback or complement (lower priority)

A high-pressure argon gas TPC (about 10 bar, Ar with a few-percent non-hydrogenous or low-H quencher) would give proton thresholds of a few MeV and excellent charge and momentum measurement. However, it would hold only about 0.1 t, roughly 1% of the event rate of the LAr option. It is useful as a thin auxiliary sample for low-energy protons, not as the main target.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a hydrogen-free, modular pixel-readout liquid-argon TPC (≈7.5 t) with segmented light detection, in a thin-walled cryostat surrounded by side and upstream trackers in the magnet.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Kestrel Flats Near Detector Target Region

## Why the current layout falls short

All momentum and charge measurement currently happens in drift chambers downstream of the target. The target region is wide (2.6 m × 2.3 m) but short along the beam (0.9 m). A muon emitted near 90° or backward travels sideways, so it leaves through the side faces and never reaches the downstream chambers. Efficiency at those angles is close to zero, far below the 25% requirement.

Short proton tracks are also lost. A 60 MeV proton stops in about 3 cm of plastic. A conventional bar-type tracker with one 2D view per layer cannot reconstruct a track that short at arbitrary angles.

The three upgrades below fit together inside the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope.

---

## 1. Fine-grained 3D-readout scintillator-cube active target (core of the upgrade)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ polystyrene scintillator cubes, each with a reflective surface coating.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibers, one per axis.
- Fibers are read out by SiPMs/MPPCs with about 1 ns timing.
- Indicative footprint: about 1.9 × 1.8 × 0.6 m. That is roughly 2 million cubes, about 2 t, and roughly 55–60k readout channels.
- This leaves room for the side trackers and timing layers described below.

**Why it meets the proton requirement**
- Every cube is seen in three projections, so the detector gives true 3D points with isotropic granularity.
- Tracking efficiency is therefore nearly independent of angle, including tracks perpendicular to the beam and backward-going tracks.
- A 60 MeV proton crosses about 3 cubes and deposits a large dE/dx. It can be reconstructed and identified, which meets the proton threshold at all angles.

**Other benefits**
- The large, fully active mass gives higher event rates.
- Fine timing allows time-of-flight between separated hits, giving some sensitivity to neutrons.

**Hydrogen constraint**
- In CH, hydrogen nuclei are 1 of every 13 nucleons, about 7.7%.
- This is well under the 20% limit, so the hydrogen-subtraction model stays valid.
- Avoid hydrogen-rich additions such as large water or extra polyethylene volumes. Keep any gas mixtures low-hydrogen.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below (or beside) the cube target

**Technology**
- Thin-walled field cages with a low-mass, low-hydrogen argon-based gas mixture.
- Read out by resistive Micromegas, which spread charge for good spatial resolution with fewer pads and are robust against sparks.
- Placed inside the existing 0.15 T dipole field.

**Why**
- These chambers measure momentum, charge sign and dE/dx for muons and pions that leave the target sideways.
- This covers the high-angle region that the downstream chambers miss, and is what raises muon efficiency at around 90° above 25%.
- Momentum by range in the cube target serves as a complement for tracks that stop.

## 3. Time-of-flight panels surrounding the new target and TPCs

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars read out at both ends by SiPM arrays, with timing resolution of about 100–150 ps.

**Why**
- Timing determines track direction, which separates backward-going muons from forward-going or entering tracks and cosmic rays.
- It also rejects background from interactions outside the fiducial volume, which matters most at backward angles where curvature alone is ambiguous.
- It improves particle identification, separating protons, pions and muons.

## Supporting items

- **Electronics:** SiPM front-end electronics and data acquisition for the cubes and TOF bars, and a pad readout for the TPCs.
- **Calibration:** a calibration system, such as LED injection plus cosmic-ray triggers.
- **Mechanics:** a mechanical frame that fits inside the magnet's inner volume.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target with a ~1 cm³ plastic-scintillator-cube detector read out in three orthogonal views by WLS fibers and SiPMs, giving isotropic 3D tracking for high-angle and backward muons and 60 MeV protons at about 7.7% hydrogen nucleons.

This is an interesting detector design challenge for a near detector in an accelerator neutrino beam experiment. Let me analyze the constraints and propose solutions.

## Key Requirements Analysis

1. **Geometric coverage**: Need 4π acceptance including perpendicular and backward-going tracks
2. **Low momentum threshold**: ~60 MeV kinetic energy protons (corresponds to ~350 MeV/c momentum, range ~1-2 cm in dense material)
3. **Hydrogen constraint**: ≤2% of target nucleons
4. **Active target volume**: 2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m
5. **Muon reconstruction**: ≥25% efficiency at all angles

## Critical Issues with Current Setup

The existing gas drift chambers are **downstream only**, making backward and perpendicular track reconstruction impossible. The warm dipole provides useful momentum analysis but only for forward-going tracks.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **3D Tracking System with Full Angular Coverage**

Install a **fine-grained scintillator tracker** or **Time Projection Chamber (TPC)** as the active target:

- **Option A: Segmented plastic scintillator bars** (e.g., 1×1 cm² cross-section) arranged in XYZ layers with SiPM readout
  - Low hydrogen content materials available (polystyrene-based, <2% H by nucleon count)
  - 3D reconstruction capability
  - Good timing resolution
  
- **Option B: High-pressure argon TPC** (preferred)
  - Essentially hydrogen-free (pure argon)
  - Excellent 3D tracking with ~mm resolution
  - dE/dx for particle ID
  - Continuous tracking volume

### 2. **Surrounding Electromagnetic Calorimeter (ECAL)**

Install **downstream and side ECal modules**:
- Capture particles exiting the active target
- Improve energy reconstruction
- Enhance muon/electron separation

### 3. **Upstream Tracking Stations**

Add **thin tracking planes upstream of the target**:
- Silicon strips or scintillating fibers
- Minimal material to avoid pre-target interactions
- Crucial for reconstructing backward-going tracks by measuring entry angles

### 4. **Side and Rear Drift Chambers**

Extend gas drift chamber coverage:
- Install chambers on lateral sides of the magnet volume
- Add rear tracking station downstream of magnet
- Provides momentum measurement for perpendicular/backward tracks that curl in the field

### 5. **Enhanced Readout Electronics**

- High-speed DAQ to handle increased channel count
- Precision timing (sub-ns) for track matching across subsystems

## Recommended Configuration

Given the constraints, I recommend:

**Active Target**: High-pressure gaseous argon TPC (hydrogen-free, excellent tracking)
**Supplemented by**:
- Thin upstream tracking planes (2-3 stations)
- Side drift chamber panels (left/right)
- Rear tracking station
- Downstream ECal extension

This provides:
- Complete 4π coverage
- Low momentum threshold (TPC shows ~cm-scale tracks)
- Minimal hydrogen content
- Excellent pattern recognition for complex events

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a high-pressure argon Time Projection Chamber with full 3D readout to enable hydrogen-free tracking at all angles with sufficient resolution for low-momentum protons.

# Proposed upgrade for the Kestrel Flats active target (2.6 m × 2.3 m × 0.9 m, in a 0.15 T dipole)

## The main constraint: what the target must be made of

Hydrogen nuclei must make up at most 20% of target nucleons. In polystyrene (CH) the hydrogen fraction is 1/13 ≈ 8%, so plain hydrocarbon scintillator is allowed. That is good news, because it can be both target and tracker. Avoid hydrogen-rich additives or adding large volumes of hydrogenous material.

## 1. Fully active 3D-granular scintillator target (top priority)

**Technology**
- About 1 cm³ optically isolated polystyrene scintillator cubes, in a "SuperFGD"-type layout.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal wavelength-shifting fibres.
- Each fibre is read out by a silicon photomultiplier (SiPM, also called MPPC).
- Suggested size: roughly 1.9 m (width) × 1.4 m (height) × 0.6–0.7 m (along the beam), which is about 1.8 million cubes and 2 t of CH.
- This leaves room inside the 2.6 × 2.3 × 0.9 m envelope for the detectors in sections 2 and 3.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three orthogonal 2D projections give true 3D tracking with no preferred direction. This removes the blind spot that layered bar detectors have for tracks perpendicular to the beam, and it handles backward tracks.
- **Low-energy protons.** A 60 MeV proton travels only about 2.5–3 cm in CH, which is 3 or more cubes. That gives a reconstructable stub plus a dE/dx (Bragg-peak) measurement for particle ID.
- **Fully active.** There is no dead material near the vertex. Calorimetric hadronic recoil and vertex activity can be measured.
- **Material.** Carbon is a light nucleus comparable to the far-detector physics. Hydrogen at about 8% is well under the 20% limit.

## 2. High-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Technology**
- Thin-walled gas TPCs read out with resistive Micromegas.
- Each about 0.4 m deep, sitting in the 0.15 T field.

**Physics motivation**
- Muons near 90° do not reach the downstream drift chambers, so they need their own momentum and charge measurement. The HA-TPCs provide this from curvature, plus dE/dx particle ID.
- Muons that stop in the target are measured by range instead.
- Together these keep muon efficiency at or above 25% at every angle.

## 3. Time-of-flight envelope around the target and TPCs

**Technology**
- Plastic scintillator bars read out at both ends by SiPM arrays.
- Timing resolution of about 150 ps.

**Physics motivation**
- **Backward vs. forward-going tracks.** A track entering from outside looks like a backward-going one leaving the target. Timing distinguishes these, which rejects outside backgrounds and lets genuine backward muons be kept.
- **Particle ID** between electrons, muons and protons, helped by the time measurement.
- **Cosmic-ray tagging.**

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Electronics:** fast, triggerless readout with about 1 ns hit timing in the cube target. This enables neutron detection by time of flight (neutron kinetic energy from a delayed isolated hit) and resolves pile-up within the beam spill.
- **Calibration:** LED/laser gain monitoring for the SiPMs, plus a cosmic-ray trigger.
- **Material budget:** low-mass mechanical support at the target–TPC interfaces.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the target region with a fully active ~1 cm³ 3D-granular plastic-scintillator cube detector (three-view WLS-fibre/SiPM readout), complemented by high-angle TPCs and a ToF envelope.

# Next-phase hardware upgrade proposal: replacing the photon-tagging section with a full-acceptance active target

## Starting point

The present detector has two limitations, and both affect transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) and similar analyses:

1. **Angular acceptance.** The targets are made of planar bars perpendicular to the beam, and the TPCs sit only downstream. Tracks at more than about 50–60° travel along a bar plane or never reach a TPC. That loses roughly 25% of the muons and roughly 35% of the leading protons, and it makes the phase space different from the 4π-like acceptance of the water far detector.
2. **Proton threshold.** With 9.6 mm bars in alternating x/y layers, a short proton fires only a few bars. The tracking threshold is therefore about 450–500 MeV/c, which sits right at the median of the proton spectrum.

Some useful proton ranges in polystyrene, using CSDA estimates:

| Proton momentum | Kinetic energy | Range |
|---|---|---|
| 300 MeV/c | ≈ 46 MeV | ≈ 2 cm |
| 450 MeV/c | ≈ 100 MeV | ≈ 7–8 cm |
| 900 MeV/c | ≈ 360 MeV | ≈ 1 m |

So in a box 0.6–2 m deep, almost all protons stop. Range plus calorimetry is then the natural momentum measurement, provided the granularity is fine and isotropic.

---

## 1. Fine-grained, three-view scintillator-cube target (the new active target)

**Technology**
- About 2 × 10⁶ optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, made by extrusion or injection moulding with a reflective etched surface.
- Array of about 192 × 184 × 56 cubes, i.e. about 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m, which fits the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box. Mass is about 2 t, nearly doubling the plastic target mass.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes for 1 mm WLS fibres. That gives about 56,000 fibres, each read by an SiPM, so the scintillator/WLS/SiPM chain stays the same as the rest of the detector.
- Front-end electronics with about 1 ns per-channel timing and high dynamic range.

**Physics motivation**
- **Isotropic acceptance.** Three projections give a full 3D reconstruction, and no direction is degenerate with a readout plane. High-angle and backward muons and protons are tracked as well as forward ones.
- **Lower proton threshold.** A 300 MeV/c proton crosses about two cubes. The tracking threshold drops from about 450 to about 300 MeV/c, so most of the leading-proton spectrum becomes reconstructable.
- **Proton momentum and particle ID.** Stopping protons get their momentum from range and from the Bragg-peak dE/dx profile, with resolution of a few percent. The fully contained momentum covers up to the ~6% tail above 900 MeV/c, with exiting protons handed over to the TPCs.
- **TKI variables.** The muon and leading proton are both measured near 4π, so δp_T, δα_T and δφ_T become available over most of phase space. These constrain nuclear effects (Fermi motion, 2p2h, final-state interactions) that feed the energy-reconstruction systematic.
- **Neutron detection.** Isolated delayed hits from neutron scatters, combined with ~1 ns timing over metre-scale lever arms, give neutron kinetic energy by time of flight. This enables antineutrino TKI.
- **Electron/photon separation.** Fine granularity separates νe and γ→e⁺e⁻ in the target itself. This partly replaces the photon tagging lost when the upstream section is removed.

## 2. Two high-angle TPCs above and below the new target

**Technology**
- Argon-based gas TPCs with drift along x.
- Light composite (laminated) field cage to minimise dead material.
- Resistive (encapsulated-resistive-anode) Micromegas readout. Charge spreading on the resistive layer gives sub-mm resolution with fewer pads and suppresses sparks.

**Physics motivation**
- They measure momentum (via curvature in the existing 0.2 T field) and dE/dx PID for the large-angle muons and the exiting energetic protons.
- This turns the 50–90° region from a calorimetric-only measurement into a precision momentum measurement.
- The muon charge sign is also measured at high angle, which matters for wrong-sign background in antineutrino mode.

## 3. Time-of-flight panel enclosure around the new target and HA-TPCs

**Technology**
- Six panels of long plastic scintillator bars, read out by SiPM arrays at both ends.
- Target timing resolution of about 150 ps.

**Physics motivation**
- **Direction.** Timing tells forward from backward tracks, so backward-going muons are not confused with forward ones.
- **Background rejection.** It rejects tracks entering from outside the detector (sand and magnet events).
- **Particle ID.** Combined with TPC momentum, it separates e, μ, π and p in the momentum regions where dE/dx bands cross.

## 4. Supporting upgrades

- **Readout electronics.** Upgrade the SMRD and ECal front ends to match the higher-rate, finer-timing DAQ. This aids efficient muon ranging and acceptance consistency.
- **Calibration.** Add a light-injection and cosmic-trigger calibration system for the ~10⁵ new SiPM channels.
- **Kept unchanged.** The downstream water-layer target stays as planned, so carbon-to-water ratios continue to constrain the far-detector target extrapolation.

## Expected impact

- Near-4π muon and proton acceptance.
- Proton threshold around 300 MeV/c.
- Neutron kinematics from time of flight.
- Doubled target mass.

Together these should reduce the flux and cross-section systematic on the far-detector prediction from about 6% toward the 4% goal.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2-tonne, three-view, 1 cm³ scintillator-cube active target (WLS fibres and SiPMs), flanked by high-angle resistive-Micromegas TPCs.

# Proposed hardware upgrade: replacing the upstream photon-tagging section of the off-axis near detector

## 1. What limits the current detector

**Angular acceptance.** The existing tracking targets use bars that all lie perpendicular to the beam, with x/y projections only. The gas TPCs sit downstream of them. As a result:
- Tracks at more than about 50–60° travel along or within a few layers and cannot be reconstructed well.
- Backward-going tracks are almost lost.
- That excludes about 25% of the muons and about 35% of the leading protons, which is a large, model-dependent region of phase space.

**Proton threshold.** With 9.6 mm bars read in two views, a proton needs to cross several layers before it is tracked. In practice the threshold is around 450–500 MeV/c, which is roughly the median of the leading-proton spectrum. Short, isotropic proton tracks are poorly reconstructed or missed.

**Missing hadronic information.** Neutrons and the low-energy hadronic system are not measured. Transverse kinematic imbalance (TKI) analyses need the muon and proton, ideally with the neutron as well.

**Usefulness of the photon-tagging section.** Its photon-tagging and water-subtraction role is now covered more cleanly by the water-layer target downstream, so its volume is better used for a new active target.

## 2. Recommended upgrade

### (a) A finely segmented, 3D-readout scintillator target in the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box

**Design**
- Use about 2 million optically isolated 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes, arranged roughly 192 × 184 × 56. The cubes can be extruded or injection-moulded, with a reflective chemical-etch coating.
- Each cube has three orthogonal holes. Wavelength-shifting fibres run through them in x, y and z, and each fibre is read by a silicon photomultiplier at one end, with a mirror at the other end.
- This needs about 55,000–60,000 channels, read by electronics that supply both charge and timing.
- The target mass is about 2 t of hydrocarbon, roughly doubling the current fiducial target mass. This is acceptable because carbon interactions are allowed for this programme.
- Orientation: put the 0.6 m dimension vertical and the beam along the long axis.

**What it delivers**
- **Full solid angle.** Three readout views per cube give true 3D hits. Tracks at any angle, including high-angle and backward ones, are reconstructed with the same efficiency.
- **Low proton threshold.** Protons are tracked from about 300 MeV/c, where they cross 2–3 cubes. Charge deposition per cube gives dE/dx and range for particle identification and for measuring the momentum of stopping protons. The 450 MeV/c median proton has a range of about 10 cm, so it is contained and measured very well.
- **Neutron detection.** Neutrons are tagged when they produce isolated secondary hits. Their kinetic energy comes from time-of-flight, which needs a time resolution of about 1 ns per channel or better. This allows the full TKI and neutrino-energy reconstruction for antineutrino events.
- **Better π⁰ and γ handling** than coarse bars provide.

### (b) Two high-angle TPCs above and below the target

**Purpose.** High-angle muons, and the roughly 6% of protons above 900 MeV/c, leave the cube target. Their momentum must then be measured by curvature in the 0.2 T field, and they need dE/dx particle identification. The existing TPCs sit downstream and miss these tracks, so new TPCs are needed in the remaining space of the former photon-tagging volume.

**Design**
- Each TPC is about 2.0 m × 0.8 m × 1.8 m.
- Use a thin, lightweight field cage of composite or laminate to minimise dead material and secondary interactions.
- Read out with resistive-anode Micromegas, which spread the charge so the pad count stays low while giving about 0.5 mm spatial resolution.
- Targets: dE/dx resolution under 10%, and momentum resolution under 10% at 1 GeV/c.

### (c) Time-of-flight panels enclosing the new section

**Design.** Cover all faces of the target-plus-TPC assembly with cast-plastic scintillator bars, read out at both ends by arrays of silicon photomultipliers. Aim for a time resolution of about 150 ps or better.

**What they deliver**
- **Track direction.** They separate forward from backward tracks, which removes out-of-fiducial-volume and outside-magnet background, including sand muons.
- **Particle identification near band crossings.** They add identification for protons and positrons where dE/dx bands overlap.
- **Timing reference.** They give a start time for neutron time-of-flight in the cube target.

### (d) Supporting changes

- **Electronics.** Update the front-end and data-acquisition chain to handle the new channels with good timing. The new section must be synchronised with the existing detectors and the beam spill.
- **Calibration.**
  - Cosmic and through-going muon samples.
  - Light-yield uniformity mapping across the cube target.
  - Test-beam characterisation of a prototype, covering proton and neutron response and cube-to-cube optical crosstalk.
- **Optional.** Instrument additional side-calorimeter and yoke regions near the new section to improve muon identification for tracks escaping at very large angles.

## 3. Expected impact

- **Acceptance.** Close to 4π for muons and protons in the new target. This recovers the high-angle and backward populations that are currently missed.
- **Proton reach.** The proton threshold falls from about 450–500 MeV/c to about 300 MeV/c. Proton momentum comes from range for most protons, and from TPC curvature or time-of-flight for the harder tail above 900 MeV/c.
- **New observables.** Kinematically complete CC events allow TKI measurements, which constrain nuclear effects such as Fermi motion, final-state interactions and 2p2h. Neutron kinematics are also accessible.
- **Carbon-to-water comparison.** The downstream water-layer target remains in place for this.
- **Systematics.** Together, these changes give a credible path from about 6% residual systematic uncertainty to about 4%, through much better constraints on cross-section modelling and on the energy-reconstruction bias at the water far detector.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2-tonne, 3D-readout target of 1 cm³ scintillator cubes (three orthogonal WLS fibres per cube, SiPM readout), complemented by high-angle TPCs above and below it.

Based on the physics requirements and constraints described, I propose the following hardware upgrades:

# Proposed Upgrade: A 3D-Granular Active Target with High-Angle Tracking

## 1. Why the current target cannot do the job

- **Angular acceptance.** The existing tracking targets use bars in x/y layers perpendicular to the beam, with TPCs only upstream and downstream. Tracks above about 50–60° run along a single layer, cross few TPC pad rows, or never reach a TPC. About 25% of muons and 35% of leading protons fall in this region, so the acceptance is badly biased. That bias is a major contributor to the residual ~6% systematic.
- **Proton threshold.** A 450 MeV/c proton has a kinetic energy of about 100 MeV and a range of roughly 7–8 cm in polystyrene. A 300 MeV/c proton (about 47 MeV kinetic energy) travels only about 1–2 cm. Two-view bar layers cannot resolve such short stubs near the vertex, and they cannot separate overlapping tracks.
- **Missing transverse momentum.** Transverse kinematic imbalance needs the muon and the leading proton with good momentum and direction resolution over the full solid angle. Ideally it also needs neutron tagging.

## 2. Core change: a 3D-segmented scintillator target

Fill the 2.0 × 1.9 × 0.6 m box with a "super-fine-grained" detector:

**Geometry and channels**
- About 2 million optically isolated 1 × 1 × 1 cm³ polystyrene cubes.
- Arranged roughly 192 × 184 × 56, giving an active volume of about 1.92 × 1.84 × 0.56 m and a mass of about 2 t of CH. That roughly doubles the current target mass.
- Each cube is threaded by three orthogonal WLS fibres. This yields about 56,000 channels, each read out by an SiPM, which is consistent with the existing readout technology.

**What it delivers**
- **Three orthogonal 2D projections.** These give near-4π track reconstruction, with no blind direction relative to the beam.
- **Low proton threshold.** Tracks are seen at about 300 MeV/c, since a few cubes are enough for dE/dx and range identification. Most of the proton spectrum, median 450 MeV/c, is therefore stopped and measured by range and calorimetry.
- **Good vertex activity and π/p/μ separation.** These come from dE/dx and Bragg peaks.
- **Neutron detection.** Isolated delayed hits, read with sub-ns timing (about 1 ns per fibre, better with combined channels), give the neutron momentum by time of flight. This enables full TKI and antineutrino studies.
- **Material consistency.** The target is CH, so the downstream water-layer target remains available for the C/H₂O comparison.

## 3. High-angle TPCs

Add two thin TPCs above and below the new target, inside the magnet. These replace part of the former photon-tagging volume.

- **Purpose.** They measure the sign and momentum of high-angle muons, and of protons above about 900 MeV/c (about 6%), which exit the target. Momentum comes from curvature in the 0.2 T field.
- **Readout.** Use resistive-anode (encapsulated resistive) Micromegas. Charge spreading gives better spatial resolution with fewer, larger pads, at roughly 10% dE/dx resolution.
- **Field cage.** Use a light composite field cage to minimise dead material between the target and the gas volume.

## 4. Time-of-flight envelope

Surround the target and the high-angle TPCs with plastic-scintillator TOF panels, with timing resolution of about 150 ps or better.

- They determine track direction (forward versus backward, entering versus exiting). This rejects out-of-fiducial and magnet-wall backgrounds.
- They add particle identification where curvature and dE/dx are ambiguous.

## 5. Supporting items

- Upgrade readout electronics and DAQ to handle about 56k new channels with good timing.
- Calibrate the cubes in a test beam for light yield, crosstalk and Birks' quenching. Use cosmic and LED monitoring in situ.
- Keep the side muon-range detectors and the electromagnetic calorimeters. Re-optimise the side-ECal coverage around the new modules where geometry allows.

## 6. Expected impact

- Near-uniform acceptance in angle for both muons and protons, with no 50° cliff.
- Proton threshold reduced to about 300 MeV/c, plus neutron kinematics.
- Event-by-event TKI, giving tighter nuclear-model constraints.
- A doubled target mass, with sample statistics enriched in high-angle events.

Together these directly attack the acceptance and nuclear-model systematics that dominate the residual error, making the ~4% goal realistic.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the upstream photon-tagging section with a ~2-tonne 3D-segmented scintillator-cube target (~2 million 1 cm³ cubes read by three orthogonal WLS fibres and SiPMs), complemented by high-angle TPCs and a TOF envelope.

## Design Review Recommendations for the New Active Neutrino Target

Given the constraints and physics requirements, I recommend the following hardware configuration:

### 1. **3D Fine-Grained Scintillator Tracker (SuperFGD-style architecture)**

**Technology:** Extruded polystyrene scintillator cubes (~1 cm³) with orthogonal wavelength-shifting fiber readout in all three dimensions.

**Justification:**
- **Angular acceptance:** The 3D readout provides excellent reconstruction for the 25% of muons and 35% of protons leaving at >50° to beam axis, including tracks perpendicular to beam
- **Kinematic completeness:** Sub-cm granularity enables reconstruction of low-momentum recoil protons (median 450 MeV/c), including stopping protons down to ~300 MeV/c kinetic energy
- **Proven technology:** Successfully demonstrated in ND280 upgrade (T2K); collaboration can leverage existing R&D
- **Mass budget:** ~2 tons of hydrocarbon target material fits within volume constraints
- **Timing:** SiPM readout (already in your system) provides ~ns timing for beam background rejection

**Configuration:** 2.0 m (beam) × 1.9 m × 0.6 m volume with 10 mm cubes → ~2.28 million channels (manageable with existing SiPM arrays and multiplexed readout)

### 2. **Upgrade the Downstream TPC Cathode Plane to Higher Voltage**

**Technology:** Increase electric field from typical 400-500 V/cm to 1 kV/cm in the first TPC immediately downstream.

**Justification:**
- **dE/dx resolution:** Enhanced particle identification for forward-going protons that penetrate the new target
- **Diffusion reduction:** Improved position resolution for linking tracks from target to TPC
- **Muon/pion separation:** Better discrimination at momenta where both are minimum ionizing

**Risk mitigation:** Field cage design modifications needed; prototype first in existing TPC.

### 3. **Add Thin Resistive Plate Chambers (RPCs) at Target Boundaries**

**Technology:** 2-3 planes of thin (~2 cm total) glass RPCs at upstream face and downstream face of new target.

**Justification:**
- **Timing precision:** ~1 ns timing for event T0 determination and pile-up rejection
- **Track multiplicity:** Efficient detection of all charged particles for vertex charge sum
- **Low mass:** ~50 kg per 4 m² plane, minimal material before/after target
- **Directional constraint:** Improves vertex resolution and linking to TPC tracks
- **Cost-effective:** Mature technology, ~$100/channel

**Configuration:** 2 mm gas gap glass RPCs with 1 cm strip readout in orthogonal x-y pairs.

### 4. **Install Time-of-Flight System Between Target and First TPC**

**Technology:** Plastic scintillator paddles (2-3 cm thick) with fast timing SiPMs at both ends.

**Justification:**
- **Proton identification:** TOF over ~1 m distinguishes 450 MeV/c protons from pions at 3σ level
- **High-momentum tail:** Critical for the 6% of protons >900 MeV/c where dE/dx less effective
- **Charge-sign complement:** Magnetic field gives momentum, TOF gives velocity → mass measurement
- **Background rejection:** Cosmic ray and beam background discrimination with <200 ps resolution

**Configuration:** 4 layers of 10 cm × 190 cm paddles, alternating orientation.

### 5. **Replace Downstream Plastic Target Scintillator Bars with Double-Readout**

**Technology:** Add SiPM readout to opposite end of existing 9.6 mm bars in first downstream target.

**Justification:**
- **Timing per bar:** Resolves left-right ambiguities for steep-angle tracks
- **Position resolution:** z-coordinate from timing difference improves from ~30 cm to ~3 cm
- **Energy calibration:** Two measurements per bar improve dynamic range
- **Minimal cost:** Reuse existing bars, add ~6,000 SiPMs and electronics

### 6. **Enhance DAQ with GPU-Based Online Reconstruction**

**Technology:** FPGA pre-processing + GPU farm for real-time 3D tracking and event selection.

**Justification:**
- **Data volume:** 3D target produces ~100× more channels; selective readout essential
- **Online filtering:** Tag kinematically complete events (μ + p identified) for zero-suppression
- **Systematic reduction:** Real-time data quality monitoring → 6% to 4% systematic
- **Calibration:** Online alignment and energy scale tracking
- **Trigger efficiency:** Physics-driven triggers vs. simple threshold

**Implementation:** Leverage existing frameworks (e.g., LArSoft, CUDArt for pattern recognition).

---

## Cost and Schedule Considerations

**Most expensive:** SuperFGD-style 3D target (~$8-10M for scintillator, fibers, SiPMs, electronics)
**Best value:** Double-ended readout upgrade (~$500K)
**Longest lead time:** 3D target production and assembly (24-30 months)

## Risk Mitigation

- **Prototype:** Build and test 20 cm³ module in test beam before full production
- **Fallback:** If 3D scintillator exceeds budget, use 2D fine-grained tracker with RPC planes for third dimension (reduced performance but acceptable)

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Install a 3D fine-grained scintillator tracker with ~1 cm³ cube granularity and orthogonal fiber readout as the new active target**

Based on the requirements for kinematically complete charged-current events with emphasis on large-angle and high-momentum proton reconstruction, I propose the following hardware upgrades:

- Provides true 3D tracking with ~1 cm³ voxels for excellent angular resolution at large angles

- Add thin (5-10 mm) horizontal scintillator planes in the magnet return-yoke gaps
- Current vertical planes may not optimally range out large-angle muons

- Two or three X-Y doublet planes with 2-3 mm pitch
